critical_works.ch1: Plato (c. 428–348 BCE)Original title: Politeiac. 375 BCE · Classical Greek · Classical Athens · Classical Greek Philosophy · Philosophical Dialogue / Early PoeticsThe Philosopher Who Writes Like a Poet and Then Bans the PoetNo document in the history of literary theory opens on a more spectacular contradiction. Plato, whose dialogues represent the most sustained and formally accomplished work of philosophical prose in the ancient world, constructs in the Republic a perfect city (kallipolis) from which the poet must be expelled. The man who gave us the dazzling myth of the cave, the allegory of the sun, the story of Er's descent into the underworld, a writer whose dramatic ear, whose capacity for irony, whose command of register from high abstraction to intimate comedy has never been surpassed in philosophy, this writer declares that Homer, the father of Greek literature, has no place in the city of the good. The scandal is more than historical. It inaugurates Western literary theory as a discipline of anxious self-examination: the permanent question of whether the pleasures of art and the demands of truth can be made to coexist, and what price the community pays if they cannot.The Republic is not a straightforward aesthetic treatise. It is a dialogue about justice (dikaiosyne), about what makes a city and a soul excellent. The discussion of poetry arises twice, strategically placed at critical architectural points in the argument. Book III (370a–403c) addresses the education of the guardians, the warrior class who must be formed into defenders of the ideal state. Book X (595a–608b) returns to poetry after the account of the soul's tripartite nature has been completed, delivering the fullest philosophical statement of the case against the poet. Together, the two books constitute the founding moment of Western poetics, not because they celebrate poetry, but because they force every subsequent thinker to answer them.The Three-Tiered Ontology: Art at Three Removes from TruthTo grasp Plato's argument against the poet, one must first understand the metaphysical scaffolding on which it rests. Plato's universe is organised in a strict hierarchy of being. At the summit stand the Forms (eidē), unchanging, perfect, eternal realities accessible only to philosophical reason. The Form of Bed is not any particular bed; it is the ideal template, what a bed essentially is, the pattern in the mind of the divine craftsman. Below the Forms stands the physical world, the realm of becoming rather than being: the carpenter who makes an actual bed works by approximating the Form, producing a particular object that participates in the Form but falls short of it. Below the physical world, at the third and lowest tier, stands the image, the representation of a representation. When the painter depicts a bed, he does not copy the Form; he copies the carpenter's particular bed, which is itself an imperfect copy of the Form. The painter's image is therefore at three removes from truth. It captures the appearance of an appearance.Plato deploys this ontological argument in Book X with characteristic analytical rigour. Using the example of a bed and a painter, a craftsman (dēmiourgos), a divine maker, and an imitator (mimētēs), Socrates demonstrates that the poet, like the painter, produces eidōla (phantoms, simulacra) rather than realities. The tragedy poet who depicts courage, piety, or justice in his heroes is not representing the Form of Courage; he is depicting the appearance of courageous behaviour in particular men, without any knowledge of what courage actually is (596e–598c). At 602b, Socrates argues that imitative art addresses the lowest part of the soul, the part that judges by appearances rather than by measurement and calculation. Poetry flatters the irrational faculty rather than educating the rational one.Book III: The Education of Guardians and the Critique of Narrative FormThe argument of Book III is more immediately practical than the abstract ontology of Book X. Here Plato's concern is not so much with the metaphysical status of art as with its psychological effects on young souls in formation. The guardians must be courageous, self-controlled, truthful, and pious. Poetry, as currently practised, teaches them none of these things, or rather, teaches them their opposites. The gods in Homer weep and quarrel and deceive and lust; the heroes mourn excessively, cower before death, descend into the underworld and find it a horror. If the young guardian hears that Achilles lies prostrate in grief for Patroclus, or that the gods quarrel like market-day rivals, or that the greatest of heroes pleads for his life in Hades, he will be conditioned to believe that such behaviour is admissible in a great man. This is Plato's first and most visceral objection: poetry corrupts by presenting ignoble models for emulation.What emerges from this is a precise analysis of narrative method. Plato distinguishes between three modes of poetic composition (392c–394c). The first is diegesis (simple narration): the poet speaks in his own voice, telling us what happened. The second is mimesis (imitation): the poet speaks in the voice of a character, becoming, for the duration of the speech, that character, as Homer does when he gives voice to Chryses, or as an actor does when he becomes Oedipus on the stage. The third is a mixture of the two: the alternation between narrative and direct speech that characterises most of the Iliad and Odyssey. Of these three modes, the mixed and fully imitative are dangerous. The simple narrator remains himself; he does not inhabit other souls. But the performer who perfectly imitates a base or irrational character, a grieving woman, a cowardly soldier, risks allowing those states of soul to infiltrate and deform his own character. Habit, as Aristotle would later argue in a different spirit, shapes the self.The extension of this analysis to mousike, the comprehensive Greek term for music, poetry, and rhythm understood as inseparable, is one of the most distinctive features of Plato's approach. Harmony and rhythm, for Plato, are not ornamental additions to content; they are direct agents of psychic formation. Certain musical modes penetrate the soul before the rational faculty can evaluate them. The Mixolydian and Lydian modes, associated with lamentation, erotic longing, and emotional relaxation, are explicitly rejected (398e–399e). The Dorian and Phrygian are endorsed, because they are held to express and thereby cultivate courage in the face of danger and temperance in the face of pleasure. Music in the city of the guardians is not entertainment; it is a programme of psychic engineering. The kallipolis will have music, but it will be carefully selected music, designed to form a specific kind of soul.Book X: The Return of the Poet and the Ontological SentenceWhen Socrates returns to poetry in Book X, the discussion has a different character: it is cooler, more systematic, more decisive. The tripartite psychology of the soul established in Books IV and IX, reason (logistikon), spirit (thumos), appetite (epithumētikon), provides the analytical apparatus for a final judgement. Tragedy and epic, in stimulating the emotional and appetitive parts of the soul, weaken the authority of reason. The pleasure of weeping at a performance is a pleasure that, in daily life, we are ashamed to indulge; tragedy licences and cultivates precisely those emotional responses that the rational soul must learn to govern (605c–606d). Plato's argument here is not simply that tragedy promotes grief, but that it feeds to pathetikon, the suffering, emotional, irrational part, at the expense of logistikon, the reasoning faculty that alone can perceive the Forms and govern the city well.What makes Book X remarkable is the quality of Plato's own ambivalence. At 607b, c, he acknowledges that the quarrel between philosophy and poetry is ancient, he uses the phrase palaia diaphora, and he cites lines of what appear to be popular anti-philosophical verse, evidence that the hostility runs in both directions. He quotes Homer with evident admiration even while rejecting him. At 607c, d, Socrates opens the famous conditional: poetry may return from exile if it can demonstrate, through argument and not merely by producing pleasure, that it is beneficial to human happiness and the political life. The invitation is genuine, if demanding. What Plato wants is a defence of poetry that meets the philosopher's terms, a defence made in prose, with reasons, not one made in beautiful verse that dazzles without illuminating. It is an invitation that Sidney, Shelley, and Arnold will spend two millennia attempting to answer.The Irony of the Dialogue FormAny account of Plato's attack on poetry that does not notice this irony is incomplete. The dialogue form is itself a species of mimesis. When Plato gives voice to Socrates, to Glaucon, to Thrasymachus, he is doing precisely what he condemns: he is giving sustained, vivid, dramatically alive expression to characters who are not himself. He writes the most convincing sophist in the Republic, Thrasymachus, who argues that justice is the advantage of the stronger, and he does so with an energy and rhetorical power that goes well beyond what philosophical neutrality requires. The myths with which Plato punctuates the dialogues, the cave, the ring of Gyges, the fate of Er, are narratives that deploy poetry's tools: concrete imagery, dramatic tension, emotional force. The Republic attacks imitation while practising it. This is not hypocrisy; it is the constitutive problem of the work, and Plato knows it. To use the tools of poetry against poetry is the only strategy available to the philosopher who must operate within the culture poetry has shaped, and it is this self-awareness that lifts the Republic above the merely prohibitive and into the genuinely dialectical.The Long Afterlife: Aristotle, Sidney, Shelley, and the Ongoing QuarrelThe Poetics of Aristotle is impossible to understand without the Republic as its immediate context. Nearly every major move Aristotle makes constitutes a direct or implicit response to Plato's indictment. Where Plato treats mimesis as epistemologically fraudulent, a copy of a copy, Aristotle reconceives it as a natural cognitive instinct: humans learn by imitation from infancy, and the pleasure of imitative art is the pleasure of recognition and understanding. Where Plato censures tragedy for inflaming the emotions, Aristotle defends it on the grounds that katharsis, whatever the precise meaning of that contested term, performs a beneficial function: it does not merely stimulate the emotions but processes and clarifies them. Where Plato excludes the poet for lacking knowledge, Aristotle argues that poetry deals in universals, what kinds of people say and do in certain kinds of situations, and is therefore more philosophically significant than history, which deals only in particulars.Philip Sidney's Apology for Poetry (c. 1579, published 1595) takes up the Platonic challenge with full awareness of its terms. Sidney concedes that "the abuse" of poetry deserves criticism but argues that the right poet, the maker of golden worlds, creates ideal images that nature cannot produce, and thereby moves the reader toward virtue more effectively than the philosopher's abstract precepts or the historian's imperfect examples. Sidney's defence is essentially an attempt to meet Plato on his own ground, to claim that the ideal poet is closer to the Forms than the philosopher supposes. Percy Bysshe Shelley's A Defence of Poetry (1821) performs a more radical inversion. For Shelley, the imagination is itself the organ of moral truth: poets are not imitators of shadows but perceivers of eternal reality, "the unacknowledged legislators of the world." Shelley does not concede Plato's ontology; he reverses it, placing the poet's imaginative apprehension above the philosopher's analytical reason.Matthew Arnold inherits the quarrel in a Victorian register. His insistence that poetry can replace religion as the source of moral authority, that the "criticism of life" offered by great literature constitutes the highest form of human self-understanding, is a renewed claim for poetry's place at the summit of culture, the place Plato had reserved for philosophy. In the twentieth century, the debate recurs in different idioms whenever the question of censorship, propaganda, or politically engaged art arises: in debates about Socialist Realism, about the moral responsibility of the novelist, about the relationship between aesthetic form and political function. Plato's terms, the question of whether art tells the truth, whether it forms or deforms character, whether it serves or corrupts the community, are never simply answered. They are renegotiated by each generation of critics who cannot afford to ignore them.What the Republic establishes, beneath all its particular arguments, is the condition of permanent seriousness. Plato cannot dismiss poetry because he loves it too much. His condemnation is charged with the ambivalence of a man who finds the case for expulsion compelling and who nonetheless writes, in the very act of making that case, some of the most beautiful and powerfully imitative prose in the ancient world. The "old quarrel" is old precisely because it does not resolve: poetry and philosophy require each other as adversaries, and the Republic, in provoking two and a half millennia of response, has done more to sustain serious literary argument than any treatise that simply celebrated the art.
critical_works.ch2: Aristotle (384–322 BCE)Original title: Peri Poetikesc. 335 BCE · Classical Greek · Classical Athens / Macedonia · Classical Greek Philosophy · Philosophical Treatise / PoeticsA Fragment That Became a DisciplineThe Poetics survives as a text of approximately fourteen thousand words, a compressed, elliptical document whose prose is dense to the point of obscurity, whose argumentation leaps where it should walk, and which breaks off before completing its announced agenda, the account of comedy that was to have followed the account of tragedy. Most scholars regard what we have as a set of lecture notes, either Aristotle's own memoranda or a student's summary, a working document, not a finished publication. The treatise contains passages whose syntax is difficult even for expert Hellenists, key terms that Aristotle deploys without adequate definition, and a structural coherence that remains a matter of scholarly dispute. By any ordinary measure of literary survival, it should have joined the majority of Aristotle's work in oblivion. Instead, the Poetics became the most consequential document in the history of literary criticism, governing discussions of tragedy, narrative, and the purpose of art from antiquity through the Renaissance and, in contested but persistent ways, into the present. The paradox of the Poetics is the paradox of its survival: a fragment behaving like a monument.The Empirical Method: Classifying the Poetic SpeciesAristotle approaches poetry as he approaches the study of animals: by observing specimens, distinguishing species, identifying defining characteristics, and asking what function each kind performs. This empirical orientation marks the Poetics as entirely different in spirit from the Republic. Where Plato judges poetry from the summit of a finished metaphysical system, condemning it by reference to Forms and the hierarchy of the soul, Aristotle starts from the particular: which poems have been written, what kinds are there, what are their constituent parts, and which arrangements produce the effects judged to be most successful? The first chapter classifies the objects of poetic imitation (men in action, portrayed as better or worse than the norm), the means (rhythm, language, melody), and the manner (simple narration, dramatic presentation, or a mixture). This taxonomic impulse is not an evasion of philosophy; it is a different kind of philosophical method, one that places weight on evidence rather than deduction.The distinction matters for the history of criticism. Where Plato's approach generates prescriptions from principles (the ideal city requires ideal souls, ideal souls require uncorrupted education, uncorrupted education requires the expulsion of imitative art), Aristotle's approach generates generalisations from practice. He is not primarily interested in whether tragedy should exist; he is interested in how the best extant tragedies achieve their effects, and in what structural features they share. This empirical orientation means that the Poetics is simultaneously descriptive and implicitly normative: when Aristotle argues that Oedipus the King is the ideal tragedy, he is both observing that it exemplifies the tragic form at its most concentrated and implying that future tragedians should aspire to what Sophocles achieved. The prescriptive tendency built into this method becomes a problem in the Renaissance, when Aristotle's observations about Greek practice are converted into rigid laws governing all dramatic composition.Mimesis Redeemed: The Cognitive Pleasure of ImitationThe most philosophically significant move in the Poetics is Aristotle's rehabilitation of mimesis, the very category Plato had deployed to condemn poetry. At 1448b5–17, Aristotle argues that the impulse to imitate is natural in human beings from childhood, and that it distinguishes us from other animals. More than this, the pleasure we take in imitative representations is a cognitive pleasure: we learn from them. When we look at an accurate depiction of a repulsive object, a corpse, a poisonous insect, we take pleasure not in the repulsive object itself but in the recognition of what it depicts. The pleasure is the pleasure of understanding: "this is what that is." By grounding the value of mimesis in the natural human drive towards learning, Aristotle removes the ontological objection at a stroke. The imitator need not have knowledge of the Form to produce a representation from which we learn; what matters is whether the representation correctly identifies the thing imitated and allows us to recognise it.This answer to Plato is elegant but not complete. Aristotle shifts the question from "what is the poet imitating?" to "what do we gain from the imitation?", a shift that relocates value in the transaction between the work and the audience rather than in the correspondence between the work and ultimate reality. It is, in effect, the first move towards a reader-centred aesthetics, and it carries forward into centuries of debate about the moral and cognitive function of literature.The Six Elements and the Priority of PlotChapter VI of the Poetics provides the definition of tragedy and the classification of its six constitutive elements, a passage that has been analysed and contested more than any other in the history of criticism. Aristotle defines tragedy as "an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper katharsis of these emotions" (1449b24–28). The six elements, ordered by importance, are: Plot (mythos), Character (ēthos), Thought (dianoia), Diction (lexis), Song (melos), and Spectacle (opsis). Aristotle is unequivocal about the hierarchy: plot is the soul of tragedy (psychē). Character is secondary. Spectacle is the least artistic element, dependent on the stage machinist rather than the poet.The reasoning behind the primacy of plot is worth dwelling on, because it runs counter to a persistent tendency in modern criticism to treat character as the centre of dramatic value. Aristotle argues that tragedy is not an imitation of persons but of action, of life (bios) as constituted by what people do rather than who they are. The characters in a tragedy matter only insofar as their particular qualities generate or explain the action; a tragedy without character, he suggests, is conceivable, but a tragedy without plot is impossible (1450a24). This distinction is more than academic. It defines the boundary between Aristotelian poetics and later psychologised approaches to drama, approaches that find the tragic meaning of Hamlet in Hamlet's character rather than in the sequence of actions in which his character is expressed and modified.Katharsis, Hamartia, Peripeteia, Anagnorisis: The Technical Vocabulary of TragedyThe four technical terms that the Poetics contributed to the permanent vocabulary of criticism each carry a weight of interpretive controversy that Aristotle himself did not foresee. Katharsis, the term embedded in the definition of tragedy, is the most contested. The Greek word carries meanings ranging from medical purgation to moral purification to ritual cleansing. Jacob Bernays, in his 1857 study, argued for a medical-purgative reading: the audience's emotional responses of pity and fear are discharged, the psyche relieved of excess feeling, in a process analogous to a physical remedy. Gerald Else and Simon Halliwell have argued, in different ways, for a cognitive-clarificatory reading: katharsis denotes not the discharge of emotion but the illumination of the emotions, the audience comes to understand pity and fear as appropriate and morally meaningful responses to serious human experience. The debate is unresolvable from the surviving text alone, partly because the discussion of comedy that may have elaborated the concept is lost.Hamartia, usually translated as "tragic flaw," is an equally problematic term. Aristotle uses it at 1453a10 to describe the kind of error that precipitates the fall of the protagonist: not an act of deliberate wickedness, which would make the fall a punishment we are right to welcome, but an error or miscalculation, a missing of the mark, in a person who is good. The translation as "flaw" misleads because it suggests a defect of character; Aristotle's usage is closer to an error of judgement or a factual mistake. Oedipus's hamartia, his pursuit of the truth about his origins, is not a moral failing but an act of admirable intellectual courage that happens to produce catastrophic results. The irreducibility of hamartia to simple moral defect is what makes Aristotle's account of tragedy philosophically serious: it explains why the best people suffer the worst outcomes without attributing the outcome to vice.Peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) are the structural mechanisms by which the plot achieves its most powerful effects. A reversal is a change of fortune in the opposite direction from that anticipated: the messenger arrives to relieve Oedipus's fear and instead confirms it. A recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hatred between the characters whom the plot has defined as fated for good or ill. When both occur simultaneously, as in Oedipus the King, the effect on pity and fear is maximised. Aristotle also admires the recognition scene of Iphigenia in Tauris, where Orestes and his sister recognise each other before Iphigenia can unknowingly sacrifice her own brother, a recognition that turns potential tragedy into a plot of escape. The two examples reveal the range of Aristotle's formal interest: he is concerned with what structural arrangements produce particular emotional effects, not with a single template of suffering.Poetry and History: The Claim for the UniversalChapter IX of the Poetics contains what is perhaps Aristotle's most memorable and most far-reaching claim: "Poetry is something more philosophic and of graver import than history, since its statements are of the nature of universals, whereas those of history are singulars" (1451b5–7). The historian records what Alcibiades did; the poet represents what a person of a certain kind does or says in accordance with probability or necessity. This is a striking reversal of the ordinary assumption that truth-telling belongs to the historian and fiction to the poet. Aristotle's point is that poetic probability, the kind of thing that must happen or is likely to happen given the characters and circumstances, captures something general and permanent about human behaviour, while the historian's record of actual events captures only what happened on a particular occasion and may therefore be exceptional rather than representative.The implication for narrative form is significant. The tragic poet is not constrained by historical record; what constrains him is internal necessity. The plot must be arranged so that each event follows from the preceding events by probability or necessity, not by the poet's arbitrary will. This is Aristotle's account of the unity of plot, and it is more rigorous and more interesting than the later neoclassical doctrine of the three unities, time, place, and action, which Renaissance commentators, especially Lodovico Castelvetro in his 1570 commentary, derived from the Poetics. Aristotle specifies only the unity of action: a tragedy should have a beginning, middle, and end that form an organic whole, such that removing any part disturbs or destroys the whole (1451a30–35). The unities of time and place are Castelvetro's impositions, not Aristotle's requirements.The Lost Second Book and Its ShadowThe first chapter of the Poetics announces a plan to treat comedy as well as tragedy, epic as well as dramatic poetry. The surviving text fulfils only part of this programme: the account of comedy is largely absent. Whether a second book treating comedy was written and subsequently lost, or whether the project was abandoned, cannot be determined from the surviving evidence alone. The hypothesis that a second book once existed gained support from the so-called Tractatus Coislinianus, a short Greek text that summarises a theory of comedy in terms recognisably parallel to the Poetics' account of tragedy; whether this is a summary of a lost Aristotelian text or an independent compilation remains disputed. The absence of the second book matters for the intellectual history of criticism because it means that Aristotle's framework for literary analysis has always been oriented around the serious and the morally significant, tragedy, epic, rather than around the comic, the parodic, or the satirical. Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose (1980) memorably treated the loss of the second book as an act of deliberate suppression, a fantasy that registers the real anxiety produced by a gap at the centre of the discipline.Reception: Horace, the Renaissance, Richards, FryeThe Poetics reached Latin culture primarily through Horace's Ars Poetica (c. 18 BCE), which is less a translation of Aristotle than a selective and playful reworking in verse of several Aristotelian principles, decorum, the unity of characterisation, the instruction-and-delight formula, for a Roman aristocratic audience. The rediscovery of the Greek text in the fifteenth century and its dissemination after Giorgio Valla's 1498 Latin translation made it the foundational document of Renaissance neoclassicism. Critics such as Julius Caesar Scaliger and Castelvetro converted its empirical generalisations into prescriptive laws governing dramatic composition, producing the rigid doctrine against which Corneille, Dryden, and eventually Dr Johnson argued with varying degrees of impatience.In the twentieth century, the Poetics retained its centrality. I. A. Richards, in Principles of Literary Criticism (1924), drew on Aristotelian categories to develop a psychological account of the value of poetry, a value understood in terms of the organisation and equilibration of emotional responses, a modern reworking of the katharsis concept. Northrop Frye, in Anatomy of Criticism (1957), extended Aristotle's classificatory method into a systematic theory of literary modes and genres, treating the Poetics as the starting point for a comprehensive structural account of all literary production. The trajectory from Aristotle to Richards to Frye describes a continuous tradition of thinking about literature as a structured activity with describable effects on its audience, a tradition that remains, in various forms, central to the academic study of literature.The Limits of the Aristotelian FrameworkAristotle's Poetics is not without limitations that its admirers have sometimes obscured. The exclusive focus on tragedy and epic poetry leaves lyric poetry almost entirely unexamined, an omission that makes the framework poorly suited to the analysis of the poetic mode that, from Sappho to Keats to Plath, has been concerned not with action but with the quality of individual consciousness and feeling. The prescriptive tendency inherent in Aristotle's method, his elevation of certain structural arrangements as objectively superior, has led to criticism that treats his generalisations about Greek tragedy as universal laws, with damaging consequences for the evaluation of non-European dramatic traditions. And the question of what katharsis means, what it is that the best tragedy actually achieves for its audience, remains genuinely open, a sign not that Aristotle was careless but that he was addressing a problem that does not admit of a simple answer.These limitations, however, are also the measure of the work's ambition. A document that covers fourteen thousand words and generates two and a half millennia of commentary has not failed: it has set the terms of an argument that no subsequent account of tragic or narrative art can avoid engaging. The Poetics is not simply the first work of literary criticism; it is the work that made literary criticism possible as a discipline by establishing that poetry is a subject worthy of the same rigorous analytical attention that Aristotle brought to logic, physics, ethics, and biology. That the conversation it initiated remains unfinished is not a defect of the text but evidence of the genuine difficulty of the questions it was the first to pose with precision.
critical_works.ch3: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus, 65–8 BCE)Original title: Epistula ad Pisones / De Arte Poeticac. 19–18 BCE · Latin · Roman Empire (Augustan Rome) · Golden Age of Latin Literature · Epistolary Verse / Prescriptive PoeticsThe Monster at the Door: A Poem About Artistic FailureThe Ars Poetica opens with a monster. Horace asks his addressees to consider a painter who wished to join a human head to the neck of a horse, to drape limbs gathered from every species over the trunk of a beautiful woman, and to finish the figure with the tail of a dark fish:If a painter wished to join a human head to the neck of a horse, and to lay feathers of many a hue on limbs gathered here and there, so that what is a lovely woman on top ends up disgracefully below as a black fish. The image is both ridiculous and precise. Horace is not opening a treatise on aesthetics with a chapter on creativity; he is staging the experience of aesthetic failure. The chimera of the opening lines, part woman, part horse, part fish, is his emblem for the poem that has no unitas, no governing coherence. He asks the Pisones whether they could restrain their laughter at such a sight, and then invites them to recognise that a poem without internal unity is the same thing. The wit is characteristic: Horace is a moralist who works through comedy, and the Ars Poetica is a critical poem before it is a critical treatise.The letter is addressed to a Roman father and his two sons, the Pisones, though their precise identities have occupied scholars since antiquity without producing consensus. The addressees function less as biographical referents than as a useful fiction, a cultivated family circle whose enthusiasm for literature gives Horace his occasion and his occasion its intimacy. The poem runs to 476 hexameter lines. It has no obvious linear argument, no system of numbered propositions. Quintilian later called the poem the Epistula ad Pisones rather than the Ars Poetica, and the title under which it became the foundational text of European prescriptive criticism was supplied by later tradition rather than by Horace himself. The title matters because it creates a false impression of the work's nature. The Ars Poetica is not a treatise. It is a verse epistle that employs the ironic, digressive, and comic registers of Horace's Satires and Epistles to convey critical principles that no straightforward treatise could have rendered with the same rhetorical force.Humano capiti cervicem pictor equinamiungere si velit, et varias inducere plumasundique collatis membris, ut turpiter atrumdesinat in piscem mulier formosa superne.(lines 1–4)Decorum and the Law of Fitting PartsThe critical principle that Horace sets against the chimera is decorum, the principle of appropriateness, the requirement that each element of a literary work fit the whole in which it appears and that the whole fit the subject it treats. The concept does not originate with Horace. Plato considers it in relation to music; Aristotle's concept of to prepon (the fitting) operates throughout the Rhetoric. But Horace makes decorum the organising logic of his entire argument, and he applies it with a range of Augustan examples that made it newly available to later writers. Subject determines style. Style determines metre. Metre determines diction. And diction determines the register of the poem's appeal to its audience. The law of decorum extends from the largest structural choices, which genre to attempt, which legend to refashion, down to the smallest verbal choices, the single word that sits in the wrong position and turns sublimity to bathos. Horace demonstrates as much as he prescribes; the Ars Poetica is itself written with the care for decorum it recommends, deploying a style of elevated familiarity and satiric precision calibrated exactly to a verse epistle addressed to aspiring writers.The doctrine of decorum governs Horace's account of genres. Comic matter must not be told in tragic verse; the tragedy must not descend to the idiom of comedy. Each form has its register, its emotional range, its metrical home. The iambic metre belongs to abuse and invective. The elegy belongs to grief and to the small victories of love. The epic hexameter belongs to deeds of kings and heroes and terrible wars. Horace traces the historical origins of each metre to its appropriate emotional content: not as an arbitrary historical accident, but as evidence that form and feeling have a natural relationship, and that the poet who transgresses this relationship invites ridicule.Aut Prodesse aut Delectare: Pleasure, Profit, and the Renaissance InheritanceThe most quoted formulation in the poem appears near its end: "omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci" (line 343), "he has won every vote who has mixed the useful with the sweet." The surrounding passage states the principle more fully:Aut prodesse aut delectare poetae / aut simul et iucunda et idonea dicere vitae. (lines 333–334)Either to benefit or to delight is the aim of the poet, or to say at one time both what is pleasing and what is apt for life. The alternatives are not in fact equally weighted. Horace goes on to make it clear that the poet who gives both wins the applause of the learned and the love of the crowd. Pure instruction without pleasure loses the reader; pure pleasure without instruction loses the moralist's approval. The mixed aim is the ideal, and the ideal is stated in commercial, democratic terms. "He has won every vote" is the language of the Roman comitia; the poet as orator, the poem as persuasion, and the audience as judges.This formulation became the cornerstone of European poetics for sixteen centuries. Sir Philip Sidney, in An Apology for Poetry (written c. 1579–80, published 1595), restates it as the poet's double purpose of teaching and delighting. He borrows the moral framework from Horace and the neo-Platonic language of the golden world from his own synthesis, but the structural dualism, the poet against the philosopher and the historian, is impossible to imagine without the Ars Poetica. Joachim du Bellay, in the Défense et illustration de la langue française (1549), similarly appeals to the Horatian sanction when arguing for the elevation of the vernacular French poem. John Dryden, in An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668), takes "delight and instruction" as his critical premise and attributes the principle directly to Horace. The phrase aut prodesse aut delectare is the single most cited critical formulation between Aristotle's Poetics and Kant's Critique of Judgment, and it is cited so frequently because it condenses an entire theory of literary value into a grammatically simple opposition.In Medias Res and the Art of the BeginningAmong Horace's prescriptions for the epic poet, the advice on the management of narrative time has had the most persistent practical influence. Addressing the question of how to begin a long poem, he distinguishes the inferior poet, who announces his vast intention in inflated terms only to disappoint with a small result, from the figure of Homer, who begins in medias res, "into the middle of things":Semper ad eventum festinat et in medias res / non secus ac notas auditorem rapit. (lines 148–149)He always hurries to the outcome and snatches his listener into the middle of things as if they were already familiar. The contrast is with the poet who begins from the egg of Leda, ab ovo Ledae, the biological starting point of the whole Trojan myth. Homer begins with the wrath of Achilles in the tenth year of the war. He suppresses nine years of prior events and later manages their recounting through retrospective narration. For Horace, this is the decision of a craftsman rather than a theorist: begin at the point of greatest dramatic pressure, trust the audience's capacity to fill in what precedes.The principle of in medias res became a standard prescription in Renaissance and neoclassical poetics. It governs Aristotle's account of dramatic structure, beginning, middle, end, but Horace makes it a narrative rather than dramatic prescription, and his phrasing is so memorable that the Latin phrase itself entered the critical vocabulary of every European literary tradition. Milton uses the principle consciously in Paradise Lost, as do Virgil in the Aeneid, Tasso in Gerusalemme Liberata, and Pope in The Rape of the Lock. By the nineteenth century, the principle had migrated from epic prescription to the novel and to dramatic theory, becoming what narratologists later called the technique of starting en médias res.The Stages of Life and the Art of CharacterisationOne of the less celebrated but genuinely original contributions of the Ars Poetica is its psychology of the life course as a guide for playwrights and storytellers. Horace divides human life into four stages, boyhood, youth, mature manhood, and old age, and for each stage identifies a distinct set of characteristic passions, desires, and social dispositions. The boy is interested in sports and games, quick to anger, and quick to change. The young man pursues horses, hunting, and love. The man of mature years is acquisitive and cautious. The old man complains of the rising generation, praises the ways of his own youth, and is querulous about the present. For Horace, characterisation is an act of social and psychological decorum: the character's age must determine the character's behaviour, and the playwright who assigns the traits of youth to age or the desires of old age to youth risks the same absurdity as the painter of the chimera.This age-typology had no direct classical antecedent in the form Horace gives it. Aristotle's Rhetoric offers a briefer account of the contrasting dispositions of young and old men, and there are traditions of moralising literature that address the stages of life. But Horace integrates the typology into the practical demands of drama in a way that later writers found directly useful. Shakespeare's description of the seven ages of man in As You Like It, "All the world's a stage", is clearly indebted to the Horatian framework, though it transforms the prescriptive into the melancholic. Neoclassical drama, especially French drama of the seventeenth century in the tradition of Corneille and Racine, treated Horatian age-decorum as one of its organising conventions.Nonumque Prematur in Annum: The File and the Nine-Year RuleThe Ars Poetica closes with two passages that together constitute Horace's account of the poet's moral relationship to his craft. The first is practical and quasi-proverbial: "nonumque prematur in annum" (line 388), "let it be suppressed until the ninth year." The poem, once written, should not be published. It should be held, reviewed, revised, tested against the author's own coldest judgment. What is not published can be emended; what is sent out cannot be recalled. "Nescit vox missa reverti" (line 390), "a word once sent forth cannot come back." The metaphor Horace returns to repeatedly is that of the lima, the file. The craftsman finishes his work with a file. The sculptor files the rough surface of the bronze to its final form. The poet who loves his work enough to file it, to suppress it for nine years and take it up again with a cooler eye, is the craftsman-poet whom Horace admires. The contrast is with the poetaster who rushes into print, infatuated with his own productions.The nine-year rule is partly Horace's own practice, he is known to have revised his Odes with extraordinary care over years of composition, and partly a provocation. No competent poet literally waits nine years to publish. The prescription is a way of insisting on the gap between first composition and final form, on the difference between inspiration and craft. It is Horace's most direct statement of the position he argues throughout: that ars, craft, discipline, and deliberate technique, is not the enemy of natural talent but its necessary companion.Ingenium versus Ars: Nature, Art, and the Refusal of False ChoicesThe debate between natural genius and learned craft runs through the entire poem and reaches its most concentrated expression near its close. Some poets, Horace notes, believe that good poems come from nature, while others maintain that craft alone is sufficient. He refuses the opposition. The talented poet who ignores craft is like a whetstone: it sharpens iron but cannot itself cut. The craftsman without native talent is like a quarryman: he can shape stone but cannot give it life. The Ars Poetica itself embodies this refusal. It is a poem, not a handbook. It teaches through wit and image and the pleasure of exact phrasing. Horace does not separate the didactic from the aesthetic because, in his own practice, they are indistinguishable.The Poem's European AfterlifeAlexander Pope's Essay on Criticism (1711) is, among other things, the most sustained English imitation of the Ars Poetica. Pope takes Horace's epistolary hexameters and renders their principles in heroic couplets, their comic spirit in Augustan wit, and their programme of decorum in the language of taste and reason. Ben Jonson translated portions of the Ars Poetica and drew on its authority in Timber, or Discoveries (published posthumously, 1640) for his account of the poet's duties. The seventeenth-century French critic Boileau modelled his Art poétique (1674) directly on Horace's poem, making the Horatian synthesis of wit, decorum, and moral seriousness the legislative standard for French neoclassicism. The Romantic poets, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats, resisted the Horatian prescriptions without escaping them. Wordsworth's rejection of poetic diction in the Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800) is conducted in the vocabulary of naturalness and sincerity that is only coherent against the background of the rules it refuses.The Ars Poetica is indispensable not because its rules are final, Romanticism showed how provisional they were, but because the argument it frames, between craft and inspiration, between pleasure and instruction, between unity and creative freedom, has remained the argument of literary criticism ever since. Horace opened the poem with a monster. The critics who came after him spent two thousand years deciding what to do with it.
critical_works.ch4: Attributed to Longinus (author unknown; traditionally 'Longinus')Original title: Peri Hypsousc. 1st Century CE (disputed) · Classical Greek · Greco-Roman rhetorical tradition · Greco-Roman Rhetoric / Imperial Period · Rhetorical Treatise / Aesthetic CriticismA Fragment of Fire: The Text That Theorised Its Own SubjectPeri Hypsous, On the Sublime, arrives in the history of criticism with the appropriateness of a proof. A treatise about the experience of aesthetic transport survives in a single damaged manuscript from the tenth century CE. Its author is unknown. Its date is disputed. Its argument is not a system, it is an experience. The manuscript in which the text was preserved attributes it to "Dionysius Longinus" or, in some readings, to "Dionysius or Longinus." The first attribution was long taken to identify the work with Cassius Longinus, the third-century CE Platonist rhetorician and counsellor to Queen Zenobia of Palmyra. Modern scholarship has almost unanimously rejected this identification. The style, the examples, and the critical preoccupations of the text are incompatible with what is independently known of Cassius Longinus. Equally, the identification with the Augustan-era critic Dionysius of Halicarnassus fails to fit the evidence. The author of Peri Hypsous most likely wrote in the first century CE, during the early Imperial period. He cites Cicero, who places a terminus post quem in the late Republic. He does not cite Quintilian, which suggests a terminus ante quem before the end of the first century CE. Beyond these limits, "Longinus" remains a useful convention, the name of a mind whose identity is lost.The condition of the text is itself suggestive. Large sections are missing. Chapters open in mid-argument or close without transition. What remains is perhaps two-thirds of the original, perhaps less. Yet the text exercises a disproportionate influence on its readers, and it exercises this influence precisely because what it describes, the experience of sublimity as a blow that arrests and transports, is something a damaged, incomplete, intensely argued text can demonstrate as well as or better than a polished and complete one. The Peri Hypsous does more than define the sublime; its fragmentary survival performs it.Ekplexis: The Definition and Its StakesLonginus opens by distinguishing his subject from earlier rhetorical treatments. His interlocutor is a named figure, Postumius Terentianus, to whom he addresses the work in the manner of a letter or dedication. He has evidently been reading a treatise on the sublime by a rhetorician named Caecilius of Calacte, and he finds it inadequate, not because it is inaccurate, but because it fails to tell writers how to attain sublimity themselves. This is the practical ambition that drives the whole text: not mere description, but a programme of formation.The definition Longinus offers is not a technical one. Sublimity (hypsos) is "a certain peak and excellence of discourse", not a quality that appears always in the same form, but an effect that strikes the reader with the force of a lightning bolt. The appropriate response to the sublime is not reasoned assent, not measured appreciation, but ekplexis, astonishment, overwhelming. In what is perhaps the most quoted formulation of the entire treatise, Longinus argues that "the effect of elevated language upon an audience is not persuasion but transport": the audience is not reasoned into admiration but ambushed by it. An attentive hearer, he adds, does not consider whether what is said is persuasive or beautiful, he simply finds himself overwhelmed. The test of the sublime is its irresistibility. This shifts the grounds of criticism decisively: where the Aristotelian tradition had centred on the structural properties of the work, its plot, its recognition scenes, its imitation of action, Longinus centres on the audience's experience of the text. The quality being described is not in the poem alone, or in the reader alone, but in the encounter between them.The Five Sources: Nature and Craft in BalanceHaving defined sublimity by its effect, Longinus identifies five sources from which it arises. The first two are gifts of nature; the last three are products of craft. The first is greatness of mind (megalophrosyne), the capacity to conceive elevated and significant thoughts. The second is strong and inspired passion. The third, fourth, and fifth sources, figures of thought and speech, noble diction, and dignified word-arrangement (synthesis), are the domain of the trained writer. This division is important. It situates the Peri Hypsous in the tradition of the ingenium-ars debate that Horace negotiates in the Ars Poetica, but it weights the balance differently. For Longinus, greatness of mind is the irreducible foundation: a writer without the capacity for great thought will produce, at best, technically accomplished mediocrity. The figures and the diction and the arrangement can refine and channel sublime energy, but they cannot generate it.The account of megalophrosyne goes beyond psychology. It is a moral claim. Longinus argues that small-minded people, the envious, the petty, the ambitious for trivial things, simply cannot produce great literature. This is not a claim about class or education. It is a claim about the relationship between a writer's interior life and the literature she or he produces. The remark connects the critical programme of the Peri Hypsous to a tradition of ethical reflection on artistic production that runs from Plato's Ion and Republic through to Schiller and Wordsworth.Sappho and the Grammar of Contradictory FeelingThe most celebrated passage of close reading in the Peri Hypsous is Longinus's analysis of Sappho's phainetai moi fragment, preserved in the treatise itself, and therefore partly surviving because Longinus quoted it. The poem depicts the speaker watching a man seated opposite her beloved, hearing the woman laugh and speak. The speaker then describes the physical symptoms that overwhelm her: her tongue breaks, a subtle fire runs beneath her skin, her eyes see nothing, her ears ring, a cold sweat covers her, she trembles, she turns greener than grass. The poem ends, or, in the surviving text, breaks off, with the speaker acknowledging that she may be near death.Longinus praises the poem not for any single image but for the management of contradictory feeling. He observes that Sappho has selected the most extreme and simultaneous symptoms of passionate experience, the physical convulsions of intense emotion, and gathered them into a controlled unity. The technical term he uses is athroismos, the grouping or concentration of separate elements into a single impression. This is the same faculty he identifies in the grandest passages of Homer and Demosthenes: the ability to overwhelm the reader with a simultaneous rush of multiple intense perceptions. What strikes Longinus most is that Sappho's symptoms are contradictory, she is simultaneously hot and cold, simultaneously sighted and blind, and yet the catalogue does not become incoherent. The contradictions are unified by the emotional experience they describe. This reading of Sappho as a master of controlled intensity is one of the earliest examples in critical history of what would later be called the analysis of paradox and tension.Homer: The Sublime and Its DeclineLonginus treats Homer as the supreme model of the sublime in poetry, and the Iliad as the supreme model within Homer's work. His reading of the Iliad identifies its characteristic sublimity in scenes of divine or heroic violence: the battle of the gods, the wounding of Ares, the rage of Achilles. These passages achieve a transport in the reader that Longinus describes as quasi-divine: reading Homer at his greatest is an experience of being inhabited by something beyond the ordinary human. The Odyssey, by contrast, is treated as the work of an ageing poet. It is still great, still capable of extraordinary passages, but its characteristic mode is narrative rather than elevated; it is concerned with character and incident rather than with the sheer force of bardic power. Longinus makes the comparison carefully: he does not demote the Odyssey from the canon of great literature, but he identifies in it the tendency toward the picturesque and the digressive that is the signature of a mind no longer at the summit of its powers.This literary biography of Homer was controversial in antiquity and remains contested. But the principle it embodies, that sublimity is not an effect a writer can sustain throughout a career or a work, that it occurs in flashes and that even the greatest writers experience its diminution, is central to Longinus's aesthetic. The sublime is by its nature intermittent. To expect it continuously is to misunderstand what it is.Psychrotès and To Ogkeron: The Vices of the Would-Be SublimeLonginus is as attentive to failure as to success. He identifies three principal vices that afflict the writer in pursuit of sublimity. The first is turgidity (to ogkeron): inflated language, the attempt to elevate a small subject by draping it in large words. The second is puerility, a failure of judgement that produces what Longinus calls "the meretricious", the overwrought image that draws attention to itself at the expense of the larger work. The third is frigidity (psychrotès): the opposite of sublimity, the writing that is cold, lifeless, ornate without conviction. These three vices share a common origin: the desire to seem grand without possessing the interior resources that true grandeur requires. They are, in other words, the literary expressions of a small mind wearing large clothes.The attention to failure is more than negative; it is diagnostic. By defining what the sublime is not, Longinus sharpens his definition of what it is. The vices he catalogues recur throughout the history of European literary criticism, Dryden, Pope, and Dr Johnson all engage with the question of false sublimity, and all are in some degree responding to the framework Longinus established.The Political Diagnosis: Sublimity and FreedomIn one of the most arresting chapters of the treatise, chapter XLIV, which comes near the end of the damaged text, Longinus addresses what he calls the problem of the decline of oratory. He poses the question through a fictional dialogue with an unnamed philosopher: why is it, in an age of education, learning, and relative peace, that great oratory and great literature no longer appear? His answer is a political one. Sublimity requires freedom. Not freedom in the political sense alone, though that too is relevant, since great oratory flourishes in contests where something is genuinely at stake, but an interior freedom of mind and spirit. Tyranny produces servility, and servility produces art that flatters rather than aspires, that accommodates rather than demands. The writer who lives under autocracy may produce technically accomplished work, but the vital spark, the megalophrosyne that is the first source of the sublime, is extinguished by the habit of submission.This political diagnosis is remarkable in a rhetorical treatise of the Imperial period. Longinus is writing under the Roman Empire, and the implicit target of his argument is the literary and rhetorical mediocrity that imperialism produces. The observation connects the Peri Hypsous to a tradition of political aesthetics that runs forward to Friedrich Schiller's On the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), to Shelley's Defence of Poetry (1821), and to the Romantic conviction that great art is incompatible with political degradation.Boileau, Burke, Kant, and the Romantic InheritanceThe Peri Hypsous lay dormant through much of the medieval period. The scholar Francesco Robortello published the first printed edition of the Greek text in 1554, and from that point onward the text entered the critical mainstream of European humanism. Nicolas Boileau's French translation of 1674 made Longinus available to an entire generation of French and English critics and explicitly connected the treatise to the neoclassical programme of regulated excellence. For Boileau, the Peri Hypsous was evidence that the ancients understood the difference between mere correctness and true greatness, a distinction he himself was urgently trying to preserve against what he saw as the baroque excess of his contemporaries.Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) reworks the Longinian categories in the language of British empirical psychology, identifying the sublime with terror, darkness, vastness, and obscurity, sensory and psychological conditions rather than literary ones. Burke's treatment is deeply indebted to Longinus even where it differs, and it becomes the most influential single transmission of sublimity theory to the Romantic period. Immanuel Kant's account of the mathematical and dynamical sublime in the Critique of Judgment (1790) takes Burke's psychological account and reformulates it in transcendental terms: the feeling of the sublime is not a response to the object but to the discovery, in the face of natural overwhelm, of the mind's own supersensible dignity. This line of development, from Longinus to Boileau to Burke to Kant, is one of the most productive in the history of aesthetics, and it begins in a damaged tenth-century manuscript whose author cannot be named.For the Romantic poets, Longinus was the ancestor who had understood what they were trying to do. Wordsworth's account of the imagination in the Prelude, the spots of time, the episodes of visionary experience that overwhelm and transform, is a poetic enactment of what Longinus described as the sublime in action. Coleridge's theory of imagination, which distinguishes the mechanical fancy from the organising, elevating power of imagination proper, restates in Romantic terms the Longinian distinction between mere ornament and genuine hypsos. The Peri Hypsous, incomplete and anonymous as it is, proved to be one of the most generative texts in the critical tradition precisely because it refused system, demanded experience, and kept asking its readers whether what they had just read was great or merely correct.
critical_works.ch5: Bharata Muni (traditional attribution; text composed by multiple hands over centuries)Original title: Nāṭyaśāstrac. 200 BCE – 200 CE (scholarly consensus) · Sanskrit · Ancient India · Classical Sanskrit Aesthetics / Drama · Encyclopedic Treatise on the Performing ArtsThe Fifth Veda: Scope, Origin, and the Sacred StageThe Nāṭyaśāstra is the most comprehensive text on the performing arts produced by any ancient civilisation. It encompasses approximately six thousand verses distributed across thirty-six chapters, though the exact number varies between manuscript recensions, and addresses dramaturgy, dance, music, vocal technique, stage architecture, costume, make-up, the management of theatrical companies, casting principles, audience comportment, and, most, the psychology of aesthetic experience. No other ancient critical text attempts anything near this range. Aristotle's Poetics is a concentrated argument of about twelve thousand words. Horace's Ars Poetica is a verse epistle of 476 lines. The Nāṭyaśāstra is an encyclopaedia, a technical manual, a philosophical treatise, and a devotional text simultaneously. The tradition of its composition is complex. Scholarly consensus, drawing on the evidence of its language, metre, content stratification, and relationship to datable traditions in Sanskrit literature and drama, places the core of the text between approximately 200 BCE and 200 CE, with later additions and interpolations extending into the early centuries of the Common Era. The single-author attribution to Bharata Muni is, in the manner of classical Indian textual tradition, a pious fiction that gathers multiple generations of theatrical and scholarly practice under a single legendary name.The text frames its own origin mythologically. In the first chapter, the sage Bharata recounts how the god Brahma, observing that human beings in the Kali Yuga needed a new Veda, one that could be seen and heard by people of all four castes, unlike the Vedas restricted by ritual access, composed the Nāṭya Veda, drawing its recitation (pāṭhya) from the Rig Veda, its song (gīta) from the Sāma Veda, its gesture (abhinaya) from the Yajur Veda, and its emotional content (rasa) from the Atharva Veda. The first performance took place before the assembled gods at the time of a festival celebrating Indra's victory over the demons. The theatre was thus instituted as a sacred event. The stage was built on cosmic principles. The drama was from the beginning not entertainment but a form of devotional and moral practice. This origin narrative is not simply pious ornament. It establishes the ontological status of theatre in the Sanskrit tradition: drama is not a secular mimicry of life but a sacred re-enactment of cosmic order. The audience that watches is participating in something that the gods themselves watched first.The Theory of Rasa: Flavour and Aesthetic ExperienceThe sixth chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra contains the most influential theory of aesthetic experience in the history of Indian criticism, and arguably the most influential theory of spectator response in the ancient world. The chapter opens with the foundational formula:Vibhavānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ."The conjunction of stimulants (vibhāva), resultants (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva) produces the rasa." (Ghosh translation, Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter VI)The word rasa means, in its ordinary usage, juice, sap, taste, or essence, the vital fluid of a thing. In the aesthetic context, it designates something that is not quite translatable by any single English equivalent: the refined emotional flavour that a trained spectator experiences when watching a dramatic performance executed with technical mastery. Rasa is not the raw emotion felt in life, it is not grief, not love, not fear in the ordinary sense. It is the distilled aesthetic experience of these emotions, purified of the self-interested suffering that accompanies them in daily existence. To experience the rasa of grief is not to grieve; it is to savour the aesthetic quality of grief rendered in performance.Bharata identifies eight primary rasas: Śṛṅgāra (the erotic or amorous), Hāsya (the comic), Karuṇa (the pathetic or sorrowful), Raudra (the furious), Vīra (the heroic), Bhayānaka (the terrible), Bībhatsa (the disgusting), and Adbhuta (the marvellous or wondrous). Each rasa has a corresponding permanent emotional state (sthāyibhāva), the deep, enduring emotional disposition that underlies the aesthetic experience. Śṛṅgāra, for instance, corresponds to love (rati) as a permanent state. Karuṇa corresponds to sorrow (śoka). Vīra corresponds to enthusiasm or energy (utsāha). The eighth-century commentator Abhinavagupta, in his immense commentary the Abhinavabharati, added a ninth rasa, Śānta, the serene, which he argued had sama (equanimity) as its permanent state, and which represents the culmination of aesthetic experience in a condition approaching spiritual realisation.Stimulants, Resultants, and Transitory StatesThe mechanism by which rasa is produced from the conjunction of its three components is central to understanding what the Nāṭyaśāstra theory actually claims. The vibhāvas, conventionally translated as stimulants or determinants, are the external causes that set the emotional state in motion: in the case of Śṛṅgāra, these include the beloved person, the season of spring, the moonlit garden, the garland of flowers, the sound of bees. These are the dramatic circumstances, the setting and character that give the emotion its occasion. The anubhāvas, the resultants or consequents, are the external signs through which the inner emotional state reveals itself: the sidelong glance, the trembling lip, the breaking voice, the horripilation. These are what the actor performs, what the spectator reads. The vyabhicāribhāvas, transitory or complementary states, are the subsidiary emotions that accompany the dominant state and give it complexity: joy coloured by impatience, sorrow accompanied by confusion, love complicated by jealousy. These transitory states do not replace the dominant sthāyibhāva; they enrich and modulate it, as spices season a meal without replacing its primary flavour.Bharata adds a fourth category to this analysis: the sāttvikabhāvas, involuntary physical manifestations of deep emotion. These include trembling, sweating, pallor, change of voice, weeping, loss of consciousness, and horripilation, the eight states that occur when an actor of extraordinary skill achieves a total identification with the emotional state being portrayed. The sāttvikabhāvas are involuntary and therefore unfeigned; they are the signs of a genuine inner state rather than a performed one. In this respect, the Nāṭyaśāstra draws a distinction between skilled mimicry and genuine aesthetic inhabitation that anticipates debates about acting theory from Diderot's Paradox of the Actor to Stanislavski's method.Sādharaṇīkaraṇa: The Universalisation of FeelingThe most philosophically sophisticated contribution of the rasa theory, developed most fully by Abhinavagupta in the Abhinavabharati but rooted in Bharata's foundational distinction between everyday emotion and aesthetic emotion, is the concept of sādharaṇīkaraṇa, generalisation or universalisation. The spectator who watches a performance of grief does not identify with the particular grief of a particular character. She or he participates in grief as a general human condition, stripped of the particularity, the self-interest, and the practical urgency that characterise grief in ordinary life. The character's grief is vibhāva, a stimulus. The spectator's response is rasa, an aesthetic experience of grief in its universal form. This process of universalisation, the detachment of the emotional content from its particular occasion, so that it becomes available to any attentive human consciousness, is what distinguishes rasāsvādana (the tasting of rasa) from ordinary emotional response.The comparison with Aristotle's katharsis is inevitable, and has been a subject of comparative aesthetics since the nineteenth century. Both theories centre on the spectator's emotional transformation through watching dramatic performance. But the differences are instructive. Aristotle's katharsis, in the brief formulation of Poetics 1449b, describes a purgation or clarification of pity and fear through their arousal in drama. The mechanism is therapeutic and the effect is relief. Bharata's rasa theory does not describe relief but expansion: the spectator's consciousness is enlarged and purified, brought into contact with a generalised emotional reality that transcends individual suffering. Aristotle's theory is retrospective, catharsis follows arousal; Bharata's theory is participatory, rasa is present throughout the experience, produced by the sustained conjunction of its three components. Where Aristotle addresses two emotions (pity and fear) in the specific context of tragedy, Bharata addresses eight primary flavours across the full range of dramatic performance. The Nāṭyaśāstra is at once less philosophically systematic and more aesthetically comprehensive than the Poetics.Abhinaya: The Four Modes of RepresentationThe Nāṭyaśāstra treats the physical art of performance with a precision that has no equivalent in any other ancient critical text. Abhinaya, representation, expression, or "carrying to the audience", is divided into four types. Āṅgika abhinaya is bodily representation: the use of the body, its limbs, and its gestures to communicate character, emotion, and situation. The text codifies this with extraordinary exactness. There are thirteen movements of the head, seven movements of the eyebrows, six movements of the nose, six movements of the cheek, seven movements of the chin, six movements of the lips, five movements of the neck. The dṛṣṭis, the modes of eye expression, number thirty-six, each corresponding to a particular emotion or situation. The mudrās, hand gestures, are enumerated across multiple chapters, with single-hand gestures (asamyuta) and combined-hand gestures (samyuta) catalogued for hundreds of specific communicative purposes. Vācika abhinaya covers vocal representation: the use of the voice in recitation, song, and speech, including the tonal qualities, tempos, and rhythmic patterns appropriate to different emotional registers. Āhārya abhinaya addresses costume, make-up, props, and scenic elements: the visual codes that communicate character type, social status, age, divine or demonic nature. Sāttvika abhinaya designates the involuntary physical manifestations of genuine emotional states, the same sāttvikabhāvas identified in the rasa theory, elevated here to the status of the highest mode of representation, because they cannot be faked.This fourfold system constitutes the most detailed account of theatrical performance in antiquity. It is a theory of signification as much as a manual of technique: the body of the performer is a system of signs, each gesture, each gaze, each vocal quality, carrying a specific meaning within the convention that the audience has been trained, through exposure to the art form, to read.Stage Architecture and the Theatrical CosmosThe Nāṭyaśāstra devotes early chapters to stage architecture, describing three types of performance space: the vikṛṣṭa (oblong), the caturasra (square), and the tryasra (triangular). Each type is further divided into three sizes, large, medium, and small, and the medium-sized rectangular theatre is recommended as the most generally suitable. The stage is oriented with cosmic significance: its cardinal directions correspond to sacred and mythological associations. The stage space is not neutral. It is a symbolic map of the cosmos, with the deities and directions that govern each zone of the stage determining what kinds of action and speech are appropriate there. The backstage area is guarded by specific deities. The stage posts, the sthambhas, are consecrated before each performance with elaborate ritual. Theatre in the Nāṭyaśāstra is inseparable from sacred geography.This integration of performance, architecture, and cosmology has practical consequences for the tradition of Indian performing arts. Kathakali, Bharatanatyam, Odissi, and Kuchipudi, the classical performing art forms of various Indian regions, all trace their theory and practice to the framework established in the Nāṭyaśāstra, even where centuries of regional development and continuous creative innovation have transformed the specific techniques. The mudrā systems of Bharatanatyam and Kathakali are recognisably descended from the Nāṭyaśāstra hand-gesture classifications, though they have developed their own regional elaborations.Abhinavagupta and the Philosophical DeepeningThe Nāṭyaśāstra was both applied and systematically interpreted. The great Kashmiri philosopher Abhinavagupta, writing around 1000 CE, composed the Abhinavabharati, a commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra that is itself one of the masterworks of Sanskrit philosophical literature. Abhinavagupta interpreted the rasa theory in the light of his non-dual Śaiva philosophy (Trika Śaivism), arguing that the experience of rasa is analogous to, and at its highest moments identical with, the experience of spiritual bliss (ānanda) that the liberated consciousness attains. Rasāsvādana (the tasting of rasa) is more than aesthetic pleasure; it is a temporary liberation from the ego-bound, self-interested consciousness of ordinary life, a momentary experience of the universal, blissful awareness that is the nature of ultimate reality. This philosophical elevation of aesthetic experience to the threshold of the spiritual distinguishes the Indian tradition from both Aristotle's functional account and Longinus's rhetorical one.Anandavardhana's Dhvanyāloka (c. 850 CE), though not a commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra directly, develops the concept of dhvani, suggestion or resonance, as the supreme power of poetic language, arguing that the most elevated poetry communicates its deepest meaning not through explicit statement but through a kind of reverberation beyond the literal sense. Dhvani theory becomes the dominant framework in Sanskrit literary criticism after Anandavardhana, and it feeds back into the understanding of rasa by identifying the power of suggestion as the mechanism through which rasa is most fully transmitted. The relationship between suggestion and emotional response in the Indian tradition anticipates some of the central concerns of modern literary theory, particularly the emphasis on what a text makes present by indirection, what it communicates beyond its propositional content.The Nāṭyaśāstra and ModernityThe text's relationship to modernity is more than a matter of historical influence on classical dance and drama. The American theatre theorist Richard Schechner, one of the founders of performance studies as an academic discipline, engaged seriously with the Nāṭyaśāstra from the 1980s onward, finding in its account of the relationship between performer, performance, and audience a theoretical framework that conventional Western theatrical theory had not developed. His concept of "restored behaviour", the performed re-enactment of pre-coded patterns of action, resonates with the Nāṭyaśāstra's understanding of theatrical performance as the re-presentation of universalised emotional states, not the spontaneous expression of individual feeling. The text has also attracted the attention of cognitive scientists and psychologists working on embodied cognition: the mudrā system, with its precise mapping of gesture onto meaning, provides an unusually rich historical instance of a codified kinaesthetic sign system.What the Nāṭyaśāstra refuses to do is separate the aesthetic from the moral, the technical from the spiritual, or the theoretical from the practical. Its scope is its argument: a performing art conceived at this level of elaboration and mapped onto the cosmos with this degree of seriousness is not entertainment in the modern sense, not culture industry, not a leisure activity. It is a form of knowledge, a mode of ethical formation, and a participation in the order of things. The formula at the heart of the sixth chapter, vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ, is one of the most compressed and consequential sentences in the history of aesthetic theory, and the tradition it inaugurated continues to shape how performers and audiences in India understand what happens when art is done with full technical and emotional mastery.
critical_works.ch6: Anandavardhana (c. 820–890 CE)Original title: Dhvanyālokac. 9th Century CE · Sanskrit · Kashmir, India · Classical Sanskrit Poetics · Poetic TreatiseThe Soul of Poetry: De-centring Ornament and StyleThe Dhvanyāloka opens with one of the most revolutionary declarations in the history of literary theory: "The soul of poetry is suggestion" (kāvyasya ātmā dhvaniḥ). Composed in the ninth century CE by the Kashmiri scholar Anandavardhana, this text reoriented the direction of Sanskrit poetics. Prior to Anandavardhana, Sanskrit literary criticism was dominated by formalist and taxonomic approaches that concentrated on the external features of the poetic text. Theorists such as Bhamaha and Dandin focused on alaṅkāra (poetic ornamentation or figures of speech), mapping the various rhetorical devices that could be applied to language to distinguish poetry from ordinary discourse. Another school, led by Vamana, championed rīti (poetic style or arrangement of words), identifying different regional styles and their corresponding guṇas (poetic qualities or merits). In these early frameworks, poetry was understood primarily as a combination of beautiful sound (śabda) and literal meaning (artha) that had been systematically decorated. The critic’s task was to classify these embellishments.Anandavardhana departs from this formalist consensus by shifting the locus of poetry from the body to the soul. He argues that figures of speech and stylistic arrangements are merely the physical attributes, the limbs and ornaments, of a poem. The true essence of poetry is an interior resonance that transcends these formal components. In the first kārikā (verse statement) of the Dhvanyāloka, Anandavardhana acknowledges that this concept of suggestion (dhvani) was recognized by ancient scholars, but notes that it had been neglected or misunderstood by his immediate predecessors. He identifies three groups of opponents who deny or misunderstand suggestion: those who claim that suggestion does not exist because everything can be explained through existing rhetorical figures; those who argue that suggestion is merely a secondary metaphorical function (bhakti or lakṣaṇā); and those who assert that suggestion is an ineffable, mystical quality that lies entirely beyond the scope of words. The Dhvanyāloka is structured to refute these objections systematically, demonstrating that suggestion is a distinct, definable, and supreme linguistic operation.To establish the existence of this suggested meaning, Anandavardhana introduces the figure of the sahṛdaya, the sensitive, responsive, or "like-hearted" reader. Unlike the logician or the grammarian who parses words for their literal statements, the sahṛdaya possesses a cultivated aesthetic sensibility that can perceive the subtle resonances of poetic language. Anandavardhana writes in the commentary to kārikā 1.2: "That meaning which wins the admiration of refined critics is decided to be the soul of poetry." The validation of dhvani is both logical and experiential; it is confirmed by the response of those readers whose minds have been polished by the constant reading of great literature. By anchoring his theory in the subjective experience of the sahṛdaya, Anandavardhana prepares the way for a cognitive and psychological model of reception, transforming Sanskrit poetics from a taxonomy of devices into a philosophy of aesthetic consciousness.The Threefold Tier of Signification: From Denotation to SuggestionAt the core of Anandavardhana’s theory is a sophisticated model of language that distinguishes three levels of meaning and their corresponding linguistic operations (vṛttis). The first level is the literal or denotative meaning (vācyārtha), which is grasped through the primary power of denotation (abhidhā). This is the direct, dictionary definition of a word, the conventional relation between a signifier and its referent. The second level is the indicative or metaphorical meaning (lakṣyārtha), which is activated through the power of indication (lakṣaṇā). Indication occurs when the literal meaning of a sentence is blocked or incompatible with the context (mukhyārtha-bādha), forcing the reader to reconstruct a secondary meaning based on proximity or association. The classic example in Sanskrit grammar is the phrase "a village on the Ganges" (gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ). Taken literally, this statement is impossible, as a village cannot be built on the flowing water of a river.
