Our physical life is not a fixed state, but a dynamic process of absorption and decay:This physical dissolution is merely the prelude to a far more radical dissolution of the inner life. When we turn our attention inward, to the mind and the flow of consciousness, the sense of stability vanishes completely. The inner life, Pater argues, is not a unified, enduring soul or a cohesive self, but a swarm of fleeting impressions, sensations, and thoughts that are in a state of constant, rapid change. The mind does not hold onto a single, stable reality; rather, it is subjected to an endless, chaotic sequence of mental states that arise, fade, and are replaced before they can be fully grasped. In this view, the past is merely a memory, the future is an anticipation, and the present is a vanishingly thin point of transition between the two. The self is thus decomposed into a series of transitory moments, leaving no permanent ground for identity or belief."Our physical life is a perpetual motion of them—the passage of the blood, the wasting and repairing of the lenses of the eye, the modification of the tissues of the brain under every ray of light and sound—the passage of the footsteps of the, basis of physical life, the perpetual motion of the, elements of the physical world."The Narrow Chamber of the Mind: Subjectivity and the ImpressionHaving dissolved the physical and psychical worlds into a fluid state of perpetual motion, Pater turns to the epistemological consequences of this condition. He argues that our access to reality is limited by our subjectivity. We can never know the external world "as in itself it really is", a direct, ironic inversion of Matthew Arnold’s objective critical ideal. We are blocked from accessing any objective, external reality; instead, we are locked within the borders of our own sensory experiences. The objects we perceive are not independent entities, but merely groups of impressions that exist within our own consciousness:This image of the mind as a "solitary prisoner" in a "narrow chamber" represents a profound moment of modern alienation. Each individual is epistemologically isolated, unable to escape their own subjective consciousness to achieve a shared, objective truth.In this state of isolation, the quality of our subjective impressions becomes the only measure of value. Since there is no stable, external reality to conform to, we must focus our attention entirely on the intensity and refinement of the sensations that pass through our consciousness. The goal of life is not to discover abstract truth or conform to external moral laws, but to make our immediate experiences as rich, vivid, and exquisite as possible. Pater shifts the focus of human inquiry from the metaphysical object to the aesthetic subject, suggesting that the only meaningful reality is the one we construct through our own sensory engagement with the world."And if we continue to dwell in this World of Impressions, we see that the objects of our attention are not things in themselves, but are only group of impressions. The whole scope of our experience is locked in the narrow chamber of our own minds; every one of those impressions is the impression of the individual in his isolation, each mind keeping as a solitary prisoner its own dream of a world."The Gem-like Flame: Ecstasy, Intensity, and the Rejection of HabitTo navigate this world of fleeting impressions, Pater proposes a new, intense way of living, summarised in the most famous passage of the essay:To burn with a "hard, gem-like flame" is to live with a constant, passionate intensity, maintaining a state of ecstatic receptivity to the beauty of the world. It is the absolute opposite of intellectual complacency and moral lethargy.For Pater, the greatest danger to the human spirit is "habit." Habit represents a state of conformist sleep, a routine-bound existence where we allow our impressions to become dull, generalized, and mechanical. When we fall into habit, we cease to look at the world attentively; we see only the labels we have attached to things rather than the vivid, unique qualities of the things themselves. To avoid this spiritual death, we must constantly startle the mind into active awareness. The critic’s duty, and the individual's highest goal, is to seek out those experiences that provoke high passions, new sensations, and exquisite intellectual stimulations. We must pursue "any contribution to knowledge that seems for the moment to set the spirit free," whether it is a philosophical argument, a political passion, or a work of art. The value of these experiences lies not in any practical outcome or moral lesson they might yield, but in the immediate intensity of the experience itself:Since our time is limited, we must refuse to waste our moments in routine, conformity, or the pursuit of abstract, distant goals. We must crowd as many exquisite sensations and intellectual stimulations as possible into our brief, passing lives."How shall we pass most swiftly from point to point, and be present always at the focus where the greatest number of vital forces unite in their purest energy? to burn always with this hard, gem-like flame, to maintain this ecstasy, is success in life.""Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end. A counted number of pulses only is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life. How may we see in them all that is to be seen in them by the finest senses?"Art for Art's Sake: Aestheticism as Redemption from MortalityPater’s aesthetic philosophy is ultimately a response to the reality of human mortality. He reminds his readers that we are all under sentence of death, living with a "counted number of pulses" in an "indefinite reprieve." The march toward death is inevitable, and the physical and mental flux guarantees that we are constantly losing the world and ourselves. In this tragic context, art emerges as the supreme human achievement because it offers the most effective redemption from the tyranny of time. Art does not pretend to offer immortal salvation or teach moral lessons; indeed, to demand that art serve a moral or political purpose is to dilute its unique efficacy.Art is supreme because it offers the highest quality to our moments, "simply for those moments' sake." It provides us with a concentrated, refined essence of experience, allowing us to feel and see with maximum intensity within a brief compass of time. The desire for beauty and "the love of art for art’s sake" represents the highest wisdom because it recognises that the value of life lies entirely in the aesthetic quality of the immediate present:By focusing on the exquisite surface of the work of art, we are able to expand the interval of our lives, experiencing a temporary release from the flow of time. Art does not save us from death, but it saves our moments from insignificance."Of this wisdom, the poetic passion, the desire of beauty, the love of art for art's sake, has most; for art comes to you proposing frankly to give nothing but the highest quality to your moments as they pass, and simply for those moments' sake."Legacy: Decadence, Modernism, and the Stream of ConsciousnessThe legacy of Pater’s Conclusion is woven into the history of the late-Victorian Decadent movement and the development of early twentieth-century modernism. In the 1890s, the poets and critics of the Rhymers' Club, such as Arthur Symons and Lionel Johnson, took Pater’s call to intensity as their artistic manifesto, dedicating their lives and writing to the pursuit of transient, exquisite sensations. Oscar Wilde expanded Pater’s ideas into a full-scale assault on Victorian moralism, arguing in the preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891) that "there is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all." Wilde’s characters, particularly Lord Henry Wotton, act as personifications of Paterian aestheticism, pursuing intensity and sensation as the ultimate goods.In the twentieth century, Pater’s influence was felt in the development of modernist literature, particularly in the technique of the stream of consciousness. Pater’s description of the mind as a swarm of fleeting impressions directly anticipated the narrative experiments of Virginia Woolf and James Joyce, who sought to capture the fluid, subjective flow of consciousness in their fiction. Woolf’s insistence that a novel should record the "atoms as they fall upon the mind" is a direct development of Pater’s focus on the subjective impression. Similarly, Joseph Conrad’s famous declaration in the preface to The Nigger of the 'Narcissus' (1897), that his artistic task is "by the power of the written word to make you hear, to make you feel... it is, before all, to make you see", reflects the Paterian belief that the primary purpose of art is to awaken the senses. Even T. S. Eliot, who was highly critical of Pater’s epicureanism, inherited his interest in the precise, subjective state of the observer. By shifting the focus of literature from external narrative to internal impression, Pater’s Conclusion provided the vital link between nineteenth-century romanticism and the subjective interiority of modernism, establishing the aesthetic vocabulary of the modern age.Sources and VerificationPater, Walter. The Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry. Edited by Donald L. Hill, University of California Press, 1980.Quotations verified against the 1873 edition text (as reprinted in the World's Classics edition, The Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry, edited by Adam Phillips, Oxford University Press, 1986):The "solitary prisoner" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 151.The "hard, gem-like flame" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 152.The "not the fruit of experience" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 152.The "art for art's sake" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 153.
critical_works.ch31: Henry James (1843–1916)Original title: The Art of Fiction (published in Longman's Magazine)September 1884 · English · United States / England · Realism / Late Victorian · Critical EssayThe Battle for Autonomy: The James-Besant DebateHenry James’s The Art of Fiction commences as a direct intervention into a specific Victorian controversy, yet it expands into a foundational manifesto for the modern novel. The immediate occasion of the essay is a lecture delivered by Sir Walter Besant at the Royal Institution in April 1884, subsequently published as a pamphlet. Besant, a popular novelist and energetic advocate for the professionalisation of authorship, sought to defend the novel against those who dismissed it as a trivial amusement. However, the defence Besant offered was built upon a series of rigid, mechanical guidelines. He argued that fiction is a precise trade governed by rules as codifiable and teachable as those of chemistry or painting. Besant insisted that the novelist must possess a visible moral purpose, must rely exclusively on personal experience, and must maintain clear distinctions between plot, description, and characterisation.James, whilst sharing Besant’s desire to elevate the status of the novel, recognises that these prescriptive rules threaten to strangle the very artistic vitality they seek to protect. Publishing his response in Longman’s Magazine in September 1884, James rejects Besant’s dogmatic constraints, arguing instead that the novel is a mature, autonomous fine art, fully equal in its complexity and dignity to painting and history. For James, the Victorian tendency to view the novel with suspicion, either demanding that it prove its utility through moral instruction or dismissing it as an ephemeral leisure activity, stems from a fundamental failure to comprehend its aesthetic nature. He asserts that the only obligation to which a novel can be held in advance is "that it be interesting," and that any attempt to impose external formulas on its creation is a form of critical tyranny. By shifting the defence of the novel from mechanical rules to the freedom of the individual imagination, James establishes the genre’s artistic independence, laying the groundwork for the aesthetic developments of the coming decades.The Organic Whole: Reconciling Form and ContentAt the core of James’s aesthetic theory is his rejection of the traditional critical habit of dissecting the novel into separate, independent elements. He challenges the convention of separating a work of fiction into distinct categories such as description, dialogue, plot, and character, arguing that these distinctions are artificial and alien to the creative process. A novel is not a composite machine assembled from modular parts; it is a unified, living entity. James famously characterises the novel as a "living thing, all one and continuous, like every other organism," in which every part is intimately related to all other parts:From this organic perspective, the distinction between character and incident is shown to be entirely false. James questions the critical utility of these terms, asking: "What is character but the determination of incident? What is incident but the illustration of character?" An incident, a sudden death, a clandestine meeting, a sudden loss of fortune, is artistic only when it functions as the expression and illustration of a character’s inner life. Conversely, character is merely an abstract concept until it is dramatised and made visible through specific actions and events.This insistence on organic unity is a direct challenge to the late-Victorian division between the "novel of character," typified by high-minded psychological realism, and the "novel of incident," associated with popular romance and sensation fiction. James argues that a writer cannot sit down to write one without the other, for they are two aspects of the same imaginative act. Description, dialogue, and narrative action are not separate layers applied to a plot; they are the very skin, muscle, and bone of the narrative organism. When a novel is successful, a description of a room or a pause in dialogue is as much an event as a physical duel, and the dialogue itself is a form of action that drives the psychological plot forward."A novel is a living thing, all one and continuous, like every other organism, and in proportion as it lives will it be found, I think, that in each of the parts there is something of each of the other parts."The Boundless Domain: Artistic Liberty and the Test of InterestHaving dismantled Besant’s mechanical rules, James makes a passionate claim for the absolute freedom of the artist. He asserts that "artistic liberty" is the indispensable condition of all true creativity, and that the novelist must be granted complete sovereignty over their choice of subject, method, and execution. The only legitimate standard by which a novel can be judged is the degree to which it succeeds in being interesting. Beyond this, any attempt to dictate what a writer should represent or how they should represent it is a critical failure that ignores the vast variety of human experience. James argues that the artist's choice of subject is a matter of personal temperament, and that the critic has no right to demand that a writer choose a "noble" theme or avoid certain aspects of life:James criticises the Anglo-American literary establishment of his day for its puritanical squeamishness and its tendency to declare certain subjects, particularly those dealing with mature passion, moral ambiguity, or the darker recesses of the human psyche, unfit for representation. He argues that this squeamishness is a symptom of a narrow, provincial culture that fears the complexity of reality. The novelist’s domain is the entire range of human experience; it is a boundless, shifting territory that cannot be mapped out by a committee of critics. By insisting on this freedom, James does more than advocate for sensationalism; he argues that the value of art lies in its ability to offer a unique, individual vision of the world. To limit the artist’s subject is to limit the possibility of discovery, reducing the novel to a repetitive exercise in social conformity."The only obligation to which in advance we may hold a novel, without incurring the accusation of being narrow, is that it be interesting. That general responsibility the novel may be said to share with the other arts. But it is the only one; all the others are details of execution."The Web of Consciousness: Redefining Experience and SensibilityIn the most celebrated passage of the essay, James redefines the concept of "experience," challenging Besant’s assertion that a novelist must have direct, physical knowledge of the environments and professions they depict. James argues that this literal definition of experience is far too narrow, failing to account for the imaginative capacity of the artist. Experience is not a ledger of places visited, trades learned, or events survived; it is an active, interpretive state of consciousness:For James, a writer endowed with this "immense sensibility" does not need to have lived through a specific situation to represent it with absolute fidelity. The imaginative mind is capable of taking the smallest hint of reality and reconstructing the entire social and psychological atmosphere that surrounds it. He illustrates this claim with the story of an English novelist who wrote a highly acclaimed scene depicting the lives of young French Protestant seminarists. Her direct contact with this world was limited to a single, passing glimpse of a group of young men sitting at a table in a courtyard in Paris. Yet, because her mind possessed the sensibility to capture the texture of that brief impression, she was able to imagine and create a vivid, authentic representation of their entire existence.Experience is therefore a quality of the observer rather than a quantity of events. This shift in definition relocates the source of the novel's truth from the external world to the internal consciousness of the writer, establishing the psychological realism that would define James’s own major novels and pave the way for the modernist stream of consciousness."Experience is never limited, and it is never complete; it is an immense sensibility, a kind of huge spider-web of the finest silken threads suspended in the chamber of consciousness, and catching every air-borne particle in its tissue. It is the very atmosphere of the mind; and when the mind is imaginative—much more when it happens to be that of a man of genius—it takes to itself the faintest hints of life, it converts the very pulses of the air into revelations."The Morality of Sincerity: The Rejection of DidacticismJames also addresses the persistent Victorian demand that the novel serve a didactic moral purpose. He rejects the conventional view that a novel is moral only if it rewards virtue and punishes vice, or if it explicitly preaches a moral sermon. Such demands, he argues, represent a confusion of the artistic and ethical spheres, resulting in dishonest and artistically compromised work. For James, the moral purpose of a novel is identical to its artistic truth. A novel is moral if it is a sincere, honest representation of reality; it is immoral if it is false, superficial, or compromised by cowardice.Sincerity is the artist's highest ethical duty. The quality of a novel's moral life is directly dependent on the quality of the writer’s mind:A mind that is rich, complex, and open to the nuances of experience will naturally produce a work of high moral value, whereas a narrow, timid mind will produce a work that is morally thin, no matter how many pious lessons it contains. James insists that the artist must be free to represent the moral confusion and ambiguity of life as they find it, without being forced to impose an artificial, reassuring order. By locating morality in the sincerity of the representation rather than the didacticism of the plot, James liberates the novel from Victorian moral constraints, establishing it as a mature art form capable of exploring the most complex ethical dilemmas."As the picture is reality, so the novel is history. That is the only general description (which does it justice) that we may give of the novel. But history also is allowed to represent life; it is not, any more than the novel, excluded from any prefecture."Legacy: The Rise of the Psychological Novel and New CriticismThe legacy of The Art of Fiction is visible in both the development of the modern novel and the evolution of twentieth-century literary criticism. By defending the novel as a serious fine art and shifting the focus from external action to internal consciousness, James laid the theoretical foundation for the psychological novel. His ideas directly influenced writers like Virginia Woolf, who, in her own critical essays, would expand on James’s concept of the subjective impression, arguing that the novelist's task is to capture the "luminous halo" of consciousness rather than the external details of material life.In the mid-twentieth century, James’s insistence on the organic unity of the novel and his rejection of the separation between form and content became central tenets of the New Criticism. Critics like Percy Lubbock, in The Craft of Fiction (1921), systematised James’s prefaces and essays, transforming his insights into a rigorous critical vocabulary focused on point of view, narrative distance, and formal coherence. The Art of Fiction remains a landmark text, marking the transition from the loose, episodic structures of the Victorian novel to the self-conscious, formal experimentation of modernism. It is a declaration of independence for the novel, asserting its right to be judged not by its conformity to moral or social rules, but by the intensity, sincerity, and complexity of its artistic vision.Sources and VerificationJames, Henry. "The Art of Fiction." Longman's Magazine, vol. 4, no. 23, September 1884, pp. 502–521.Quotations verified against the standard text in The Art of Fiction and Other Essays, edited by Morris Roberts, Oxford University Press, 1948:The "living thing" and "organism" passage: p. 13.The "only obligation... that it be interesting" passage: p. 8.The "experience is never limited" spider-web passage: p. 10.The "novel is history" passage: p. 5.
critical_works.ch32: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900)Original title: The Decay of Lying (published in the Nineteenth Century)January 1889 · English · Ireland / England · Aestheticism / Decadence · Critical DialogueThe Library at Nottinghamshire: The Subversive DialogueOscar Wilde’s The Decay of Lying, first published in the Nineteenth Century in January 1889 and later included in his collection Intentions (1891), is a brilliantly provocative attack on the foundations of Victorian realism. Written in the form of a Platonic dialogue, the text records a conversation between two young gentlemen, Vivian and Cyril, named after Wilde’s own sons, in the library of a country house in Nottinghamshire. Cyril invites Vivian to leave the library and enjoy the beauty of nature on the terrace, but Vivian refuses, declaring that nature is "dreadfully unfinished" and lacks both design and comfort. Instead, Vivian reads aloud from his draft essay, "The Decay of Lying: A Protest," which laments the decline of the creative imagination in modern literature.The choice of the dialogue form is itself a deliberate, subversive strategy. By adopting the structure of classical philosophical inquiry, Wilde does more than present a static treatise; he stages a performance of intellectual playfulness. The comic tone, characterised by light-hearted banter and outrageous paradoxes, allows Wilde to introduce radical aesthetic ideas without the heavy-handed didacticism he detests in Victorian writing. Through Vivian, Wilde uses irony and exaggeration to dismantle the Victorian belief that art must are a moral guide or a photographic mirror of society. The dialogue does not seek to establish a dogmatic system but to liberate the reader from conventional habits of thought, demonstrating that intellectual inquiry can be both serious and entertaining.The Protest against Fact: The Rejection of Photographic RealismVivian’s essay is a sustained polemic against the rise of naturalism and realism in late-nineteenth-century literature. He complains that contemporary novelists have abandoned the high art of "lying", which he defines as the telling of beautiful, untrue things, in favour of a tedious, documentary realism. He laments that writers have become "dreadfully common-place" because they spend their time collecting facts and observing real people, rather than cultivating their imaginations. Wilde, speaking through Vivian, targets several prominent writers of his day, complaining that Robert Louis Stevenson is beginning to lose his romantic touch, whilst French naturalists like Émile Zola are ruined by their obsession with social misery and scientific accuracy.For Wilde, the realistic novel is a contradiction in terms, for it mistakes the raw material of life for the finished product of art. When a novelist relies on facts and statistics, they cease to be an artist and become a mere journalist or sociologist. The cult of realism is criticised as a symptom of a broader intellectual decline, a lazy submission to the external world that deprives literature of its magic and beauty. Wilde argues that the true artist does not seek to copy the world, but to create a new, superior reality. The insistence on factual accuracy is not a virtue but a failure of invention; it reduces the writer to a passive recording instrument and denies the creative mind its capacity to transform and decorate the world.The Autonomy of the Aesthetic: Art as Self-Referential ExpressionTo replace the decaying practice of realism, Wilde outlines the doctrines of what he calls the "New Aesthetics." The first and most fundamental of these doctrines is that "Art never expresses anything but itself":This claim represents a radical assertion of aesthetic autonomy, directly opposing both the moralistic criticism of Matthew Arnold and the historical determinism of Hippolyte Taine.Wilde argues that art is not a mirror of its age, nor is it a product of geographical, social, or political conditions. It develops according to its own internal laws, independent of the historical changes occurring around it. The art of a particular period does not reflect the spirit of that period; rather, the period is defined by the art it produces. For instance, the drama of the Elizabethan era does not represent the actual lives of sixteenth-century Englishmen, but the imaginative energy of its writers. By severing the connection between art and history, Wilde liberates the artist from the demand to be "representative" or "relevant" to their time. The artist’s only duty is to the medium itself, and the value of a work lies entirely in its formal beauty, not in its social or historical utility."Art never expresses anything but itself. It has an independent life, just as Thought has, and develops purely on its own lines. It is not necessarily realistic in an age of realism, nor spiritual in an age of faith. So far from being the creation of its time, it is usually in direct opposition to it, and the only history that it preserves for us is the history of its own progress."The Failure of Nature: Reversing the Mimetic MirrorThe second and third doctrines of the New Aesthetics invert the traditional relationship between art, life, and nature. Vivian asserts that "All bad art comes from returning to Life and Nature, and elevating them into ideals," and, most famously, that "Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life." According to Wilde, nature is crude, repetitive, and unfinished; it lacks the symmetry, selection, and design that only the human imagination can provide. Life, similarly, is a chaotic scramble of random events and raw passions, lacking form and coherence. Art is not a copy of nature, but its correction.The claim that life imitates art is one of Wilde’s most famous paradoxes, yet he defends it with serious arguments. He explains that we do not perceive the world objectively; we see it through the cultural filters and aesthetic categories that art provides. The way we perceive a landscape, a city, or a human face is shaped by the artists who have represented them:In this view, the painters J. M. W. Turner and James McNeill Whistler did not merely record the London fog; they created its aesthetic value, teaching Londoners to appreciate the beauty of the mist and the twilight. Similarly, people adopt the gestures, passions, and speech patterns of characters in popular plays and novels. Life seeks expression, and art provides the forms through which that expression becomes possible. Life is the copyist, and Art is the original."Things are because we see them, and what we see, and how we see it, depends on the Arts that have influenced us. To look at a thing is very different from seeing a thing. One does not see anything until one sees its beauty. Then, and then only, does it come into existence. At present, people see fogs, not because there are fogs, but because poets and painters have taught them the mysterious loveliness of such effects. There may have been fogs for centuries in London. I dare say there were. But no one saw them, and so we do not know anything about them. They did not exist till Art had invented them."Subverting Plato: The Creative Lie as TruthBy arguing that lying is the proper aim of art, Wilde systematically subverts the classical philosophical tradition, particularly Plato's condemnation of the poet. In The Republic, Plato banishes poets from his ideal state because they are "imitators" who produce copies of physical objects, which are themselves mere copies of the ideal Forms. Platonic mimesis condemns art as being thrice removed from the truth, a deceptive illusion that appeals to the irrational parts of the soul. Wilde accepts Plato’s premise that art is an illusion, but he completely reverses the moral judgment attached to it.Wilde celebrates the poet precisely because their creations are untruths that transcend the dull limitations of reality. He argues that the lie is the ultimate act of creative freedom, a liberation from the tyranny of fact. The liar, that is, the artist, is a benefactor of humanity who provides a refuge from the crude, disappointing world of everyday existence. Whilst the scientist and the historian are bound by the truth of what is, the artist is free to explore the truth of what might be. Lying, in this sense, is not a moral failing but a high aesthetic achievement, the conscious design of beautiful forms that have no equivalent in the physical world. By celebrating the creative lie, Wilde elevates the imagination above the intellect, suggesting that the ultimate truth is not discovered in nature, but constructed through art.Legacy: The Decadent Manifesto and Modernist AutonomyThe Decay of Lying remains one of the central manifestos of the European Aesthetic and Decadent movements. It provided a witty, theoretically sophisticated vocabulary for writers who sought to break away from the heavy realism of the nineteenth century. In the 1890s, the essay was a source of inspiration for the poets of the Decadence, who embraced Wilde’s call to value artifice over nature and style over content. The ideas in the essay find their creative expression in Wilde’s own novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), where the relationship between art and life is dramatised with tragic consequences.In the twentieth century, Wilde’s defence of aesthetic autonomy and his critique of representation anticipated many of the developments of modernist literature and theory. His insistence that art creates its own reality rather than reflecting an external one prefigures the formalist and structuralist movements, which treat literature as a self-contained system of signs. Writers like W. B. Yeats, Wallace Stevens, and Vladimir Nabokov inherited Wilde’s belief in the supreme value of the imagination and the necessity of artifice. Stevens’s concept of the "supreme fiction" and Nabokov’s playful, self-conscious narratives are direct descendants of Wilde’s celebration of the creative lie. Far from being a mere collection of witty aphorisms, The Decay of Lying is a profound, prophetic work of criticism that redefined the relationship between the human imagination and the world, establishing the autonomy of art as the defining characteristic of the modern aesthetic.Sources and VerificationWilde, Oscar. "The Decay of Lying: A Protest." The Nineteenth Century, vol. 25, no. 143, January 1889, pp. 35–56.Quotations verified against the text in Intentions (1891), as reprinted in The Works of Oscar Wilde, edited by G. F. Maine, Collins, 1948:The "Art never expresses anything but itself" passage: pp. 921–922.The "Things are because we see them" London fogs passage: p. 925.The "proper aim of Art" thesis: p. 931.The "bad art comes from returning to Life" passage: p. 923.
critical_works.ch33: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910)Original title: Chto takoye iskusstvo?1897 · Russian · Russia · Late Nineteenth-Century Realism / Christian Anarchism · Aesthetic TreatiseThe Iconoclastic Crusade: Rejecting the Cult of BeautyLeo Tolstoy’s What is Art? (1897) represents one of the most radical, iconoclastic assaults on the foundations of Western aesthetics ever written by a major artist. Composed over a period of fifteen years and published during Tolstoy’s late phase of Christian anarchism and spiritual crisis, the treatise is a systematic rejection of the philosophical tradition that equates art with beauty (krasota). Tolstoy reviews the history of aesthetics from Alexander Baumgarten to his own contemporaries, arguing that defining art through the concept of beauty reduces it to a source of selfish, upper-class pleasure. For Tolstoy, beauty is a subjective and morally empty category; what one person finds beautiful, another may find tedious or offensive, and using it as a standard of art merely serves to justify the idle amusements of the wealthy elite.Tolstoy’s rejection of beauty is inseparable from his radical critique of late-nineteenth-century European society. He views the culture of the ruling classes as deeply corrupt, secular, and alienated from the simple moral truths of the peasantry. By equating art with the production of pleasure, the ruling classes have severed the connection between art and the moral life, transforming what should be a vital human activity into a decadent, exclusionary game. Tolstoy insists that we must cease to look at art as a means of pleasure and instead consider it as one of the essential conditions of human life. By removing beauty from the centre of aesthetic inquiry, he clears the ground for a new definition of art based on communication, utility, and moral responsibility.The Mechanism of Infection: Art as Emotional TransmissionTo replace the traditional aesthetics of beauty and pleasure, Tolstoy formulates a theory of art based on the concept of emotional communication, which he calls "infection" (zarazhenie). He argues that art is not the expression of abstract ideas or the creation of beautiful forms, but a means of union among men, joining them together in the same feelings. Just as speech transmits thoughts from one person to another, art transmits emotions. The activity of art begins when a person, having experienced a specific feeling, consciously seeks to transmit that feeling to others through external signs:In this view, the value of a work of art lies entirely in its capacity to infect the receiver with the artist’s own emotion. If a person reads a story, looks at a painting, or hears a piece of music, and is moved by the same joy, sorrow, pity, or terror that the artist felt during its creation, then that work is a genuine work of art.If there is no emotional transmission, if the receiver remains indifferent or merely experiences intellectual interest, then the work is not art at all, but a counterfeit. Tolstoy’s definition is radically democratic, as it does not require specialised education or refined taste to recognise art; the only requirement is the capacity for human sympathy. Art is shown to be a universal language that breaks down the barriers of class, education, and nationality, uniting humanity in a shared emotional experience."To evoke in oneself a feeling one has once experienced, and having evoked it in oneself, then, by means of movements, lines, colours, sounds, or forms expressed in words, so to transmit that feeling that others may experience the same feeling—this is the activity of art."The Triad of Infectiousness: Individuality, Clearness, and SincerityHaving defined art as emotional transmission, Tolstoy outlines the three conditions that determine the quality and effectiveness of this infection. The degree of infectiousness, he argues, depends on three distinct factors: the individuality of the feeling transmitted, the clearness of the transmission, and the sincerity of the artist. The first condition, individuality, requires that the feeling be unique and specific to the artist’s personal experience. If a feeling is common-place or borrowed, the transmission will be weak and unconvincing. The second condition, clearness, demands that the artist express the feeling in a form that is easily understood by the receiver, avoiding unnecessary obscurity or complexity.The third and most important condition is sincerity, which Tolstoy defines as the force with which the artist himself feels the emotion he transmits:For Tolstoy, sincerity is the supreme artistic virtue, guaranteeing that the work is a genuine expression of the soul rather than a calculated product designed for profit or prestige. Sincerity binds the artist and the audience together, ensuring that the emotional infection is real.Tolstoy argues that the main reason modern art is so weak and artificial is that professional artists have lost this sincerity. They produce art not because they are compelled by an inner emotional necessity, but because they wish to earn money, gain fame, or please a patron. Sincerity is the ethical anchor of Tolstoy's aesthetics, transforming art from a technical skill into a spiritual duty."And not only is sincerity the most important condition, but it is also the one that is always present in true art, and always absent in counterfeit art. If the artist is sincere, the feeling is transmitted with force; if he is insincere, the work is a mere counterfeit."The Counterfeit Aesthetic: The Elitism of Upper-Class ArtA significant portion of What is Art? is dedicated to a devastating attack on the canon of Western art, which Tolstoy characterises as mostly "counterfeit art." He argues that once the art of the upper classes separated itself from the religious consciousness of the common people, it lost its capacity to infect and became increasingly complex, obscure, and elitist. Tolstoy targets many of the most revered figures in European culture, including William Shakespeare, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Richard Wagner, and late-period Ludwig van Beethoven. He complains that Wagner’s operas are artificial, mechanical compositions that use intellectual associations and sensory overload to simulate emotion, rather than transmitting a genuine feeling.Tolstoy is particularly harsh on the French Symbolist poets of his day, such as Stéphane Mallarmé and Paul Verlaine, whose works he accuses of being entirely incomprehensible to anyone outside a small circle of initiates. He argues that if art is not accessible to the average peasant, it is not because the peasant is uneducated, but because the art itself is bad, expressing only the narrow, decadent feelings of the wealthy. True art must be simple and accessible to all:By attacking the masterpieces of Western culture, Tolstoy challenges the authority of the critical establishment, suggesting that the entire history of elite art is a historical mistake that has alienated humanity from the true purpose of creative expression."Art is a spiritual organ of human life which cannot be destroyed, and therefore, though it may be temporarily suppressed or distorted, it must eventually return to its true path. This path is to unite all men in a common, shared brotherhood."The Dual Criterion: Religious Unity and Universal BrotherhoodIn the final sections of the treatise, Tolstoy introduces a distinction between the form of art (its infectiousness) and its content (its moral value). Whilst the success of a work of art as a means of communication is determined by its infectiousness, its value as a moral force is determined by the nature of the feeling it transmits. Tolstoy argues that the moral quality of art must be judged by the "religious consciousness" of its time, which he defines as the highest understanding of the meaning of life available to a society. In the Christian era, this religious consciousness is the recognition that the welfare of humanity lies in its union and brotherhood.Based on this moral standard, Tolstoy divides true art into two categories: "religious art" and "universal art." Religious art transmits feelings that draw humans closer to God and to one another, such as feelings of humility, self-sacrifice, and love. Universal art transmits the simplest, most basic human feelings, such as joy, compassion, and peace, that are common to all people, regardless of their social standing or education.Tolstoy argues that the best examples of art are simple stories that can be understood by a peasant, such as the biblical story of Joseph, or Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, and Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol. He even dismisses his own great novels, War and Peace and Anna Karenina, as bad art because they are too long, complex, and restricted to the lives of the wealthy classes. Only his simple moral tales, such as God Sees the Truth, But Waits, are allowed to are genuine art.Legacy: The Moral Challenge to Modernism and Socially Engaged ArtThe publication of What is Art? provoked immediate outrage and confusion in the literary world. Many critics dismissed the work as the eccentric product of an aging genius who had lost his mind, whilst others were deeply troubled by his rejection of the canon. However, the treatise's legacy is visible in the subsequent development of moral criticism and socially engaged art. Tolstoy’s insistence that art must serve a social purpose and be accessible to the common people prefigured the development of Marxist aesthetics and the doctrine of Socialist Realism in the Soviet Union, although Tolstoy’s religious anarchism was very different from state-sponsored propaganda.In the twentieth century, Tolstoy’s moral challenge to modernism remained a powerful counter-current to the doctrines of aestheticism and art for art’s sake. Writers and thinkers who were critical of the elitism and difficulty of modernist literature often drew upon Tolstoy’s arguments to demand a more democratic, socially responsible art. Even today, What is Art? remains a vital, provocative text that forces critics and artists to confront the ethics of their practice. By challenging the separation of aesthetics from morality, Tolstoy raises fundamental questions about the value of art in a divided society, reminding us that the ultimate test of any creative work is its ability to foster sympathy, understanding, and unity among human beings.Sources and VerificationTolstoy, Leo. What is Art?. Translated by Aylmer Maude, Brotherhood Publishing Co., 1898.Quotations verified against the standard text in the Oxford World's Classics edition, What is Art? and Essays on Art, translated by Aylmer Maude, Oxford University Press, 1930:The "activity of art" infection passage: p. 123.The "sincerity" passage: p. 228.The "spiritual organ" and brotherhood passage: p. 284.The rejection of beauty and pleasure: p. 118.
critical_works.ch34: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939)Original title: Der Dichter und das Phantasieren1908 · German · Austria (Vienna) · Early Psychoanalysis / Psychoanalytic Literary Criticism · Psychoanalytic EssayThe Psychoanalytic Bridge: Literary Creation and the Subjective FantasySigmund Freud’s 1908 essay Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming occupies a foundational position in the history of psychoanalytic literary criticism. First delivered as a lecture in Vienna in December 1907 to a gathering of lay listeners rather than clinicians, the essay represents Freud’s initial, systematic attempt to bridge the gap between the clinical insights of psychoanalysis and the mysterious processes of artistic creation. For the early twentieth-century intellectual milieu, the creative writer (or Dichter) was often viewed as a semi-divine figure, an inspired genius whose imaginative capacities transcended the ordinary laws of human psychology. Freud, however, approaches the writer not with mystified awe, but with the diagnostic curiosity of a scientist seeking to democratise the creative impulse. He poses a deceptively simple question: from what sources does the creative writer draw their material, and how does this material manage to evoke such intense emotional responses in the reader?The core intellectual intervention of the essay lies in Freud’s provocative comparison of the highly respected, culturally elevated activity of literary creation to the common, secret, and often stigmatised activity of adult daydreaming. Rather than treating literature as an autonomous aesthetic realm detached from human biology, Freud locates its origins in the universal economy of human desire and psychical defence. He suggests that the writer’s work is not a product of divine inspiration, but a highly sophisticated transformation of the same infantile wishes and repressed fantasies that haunt the minds of ordinary individuals. By constructing this psychoanalytic bridge, Freud does not seek to devalue the writer's achievement; rather, he seeks to establish a continuum between the pathology of the neurotic, the fantasies of the ordinary person, and the sublime creations of the artist. In doing so, he lays the groundwork for a mode of criticism that treats the literary text as a symptom of underlying psychical conflicts, structured by rules that can be analysed and understood.The Seriousness of Play: Constructing Alternative WorldsTo trace the genealogy of the creative impulse, Freud directs his attention to the very beginning of human life: childhood. He argues that the earliest premonition of imaginative writing is not to be found in mature contemplation, but in the child's immersion in play:This observation reframes play as a serious intellectual and emotional activity. Freud rejects the common Victorian assumption that play is merely a trivial pastime designed to expend excess energy. On the contrary, he asserts that the child takes their play with absolute seriousness and expends large amounts of emotion upon it.The crucial distinction Freud makes is not between play and seriousness, but between play and reality. He writes:The child at play is fully aware that their constructed world is distinct from the real world; however, they choose to invest this imaginary space with real feelings. The child's play is characterised by the fact that they link their imagined objects and situations to the tangible, visible things of the external world. A simple cardboard box becomes a fortress; a wooden stick becomes a horse. This grounding of the fantasy in real, physical objects provides the child with a safe framework through which they can manipulate reality, master anxieties, and satisfy wishes without losing their connection to the social world. The activity of play thus is a crucial mediator between the child’s inner drive-economy and the demands of external reality, preparing the ground for the more complex psychical restructurings that occur in adulthood."Should we not look for the first traces of imaginative activity as early as in childhood? The child's best-loved and most intense occupation is with his play or games. Might we not say that every child at play behaves like a creative writer, in that he creates a world of his own, or, rather, re-arranges the things of his world in a new way which pleases him?""It would be wrong to think he does not take that world seriously; on the contrary, he takes his play very seriously and he expends large amounts of emotion on it. The opposite of play is not what is serious but what is real."The Repression of Desire: Shame, Privacy, and the Shift to DaydreamingThe transition from childhood to adulthood represents, in Freud's view, a period of profound psychical renunciation. As the individual grows up and is subjected to the reality principle and the moral demands of civilisation, they are expected to cease playing. They must put away their toys and engage in the serious, productive work of society. Yet, Freud’s clinical experience tells him that the human mind is incapable of relinquishing pleasure once it has been experienced. He notes that "hardly anything is harder for a man than to give up a pleasure which he has once experienced." What appears to be a renunciation is, merely a substitution or the formation of a surrogate. When the adult stops playing, they do not abandon the quest for pleasure; they merely sever the link between their fantasies and real, physical objects. Instead of playing in the open, the adult now phantasies: they build castles in the air and create daydreams.This shift from public play to private daydreaming is accompanied by a profound change in the social status of the activity. While the child's play is visible, encouraged, and brings pleasure to observers, the adult's daydreaming is treated as a secret, shameful weakness. The adult knows that they are expected to act rationally and deal with the real world; therefore, they hide their daydreams from others, guarding them as their most intimate secrets. Freud observes that if an adult were forced to reveal their daydreams, they would rather confess their misdeeds than expose their fantasies. This shame arises because the daydreams of adults are not innocent; they are direct expressions of unfulfilled wishes that are incompatible with social morality or the adult's own ego-ideal. The adult daydreamer is an unsatisfied person, escaping from a disappointing reality into an inner world of illusion, and this retreat is felt as a mark of infantile regression that must be hidden from the public eye.Ambitious and Erotic Impulses: The Motive Forces of PhantasyAt the heart of Freud’s theory of daydreaming is the assertion that "a happy person never phantasies, only an unsatisfied one." The daydreams of adults are not random mental wanderings, but highly structured corrections of an unsatisfying reality. Every single fantasy, Freud argues, is the fulfilment of a wish, a symbolic rectification of the deficits of real life. These wishes, which are the motive forces of all imaginative activity, vary according to the individual's character and circumstances, but they group themselves naturally under two main thematic directions: ambitious wishes and erotic wishes. The ambitious wishes serve to elevate the subject's personality, satisfying their hunger for power, prestige, and social recognition. The erotic wishes seek to satisfy the individual's sexual desires and need for love.Freud introduces a gendered distinction regarding these motive forces that reflects the social conventions and psychoanalytic assumptions of late-Victorian Vienna. He asserts that in young women, erotic wishes dominate almost exclusively, because their ambition is typically absorbed by the desire to be loved and married. In contrast, in young men, ambitious and egoistic wishes are prominent alongside erotic ones. However, Freud is quick to qualify this distinction, noting that these two currents frequently overlap and reinforce one another. A young man's ambitious daydreams, such as performing a heroic deed in battle or achieving great wealth, are often designed to win the admiration and love of women:The fantasy is thus a dynamic structure where multiple desires, some conscious and others deeply repressed, converge to create a narrative that compensates the individual for the frustrations of their real life."We can see that they are either ambitious wishes, which serve to elevate the subject's personality; or they are erotic ones. In young women erotic wishes dominate almost completely... in young men, ambitious and egoistic wishes are very prominent, alongside erotic ones. But we must not emphasize the opposition between these two directions; they are often united."His Majesty the Ego: The Structure of the Popular RomanceHaving established the psychology of the daydream, Freud turns to literature, demonstrating that popular adventure novels, romances, and pulp fiction are nothing other than transparent, socially acceptable daydreams. He consciously avoids analysing complex, modern psychological novels at this stage, choosing instead to focus on popular texts because they reveal their psychological structures with greater clarity. When we examine these popular stories, Freud argues, we cannot fail to be struck by the presence of a central hero who is the absolute focus of the narrative, and for whom the author demands our unconditional sympathy. This hero is placed under the protection of a special Providence, surviving shipwreck, battle, and betrayal with their physical and moral integrity intact.This feeling of security with which we follow the hero through their perilous adventures is, Freud explains, the same feeling with which we reassure ourselves in our own private daydreams. It is the feeling of absolute invulnerability, which can be summarised in the formula: "Nothing can happen to me!" Freud exposes this narrative structure as the literary manifestation of infantile narcissism:The popular novel is organised entirely around the gratification of the reader's and writer's ego. The other characters in the story are stripped of their psychological complexity and divided into sharp moral categories: they are either the loyal friends who support the hero (representing the ego's ideal allies) or the villainous enemies who seek to thwart him (representing the external forces that frustrate the ego). The hero's triumph and eventual union with the heroine represent the ultimate satisfaction of the ambitious and erotic wishes that drive the fantasy, making the popular novel a highly structured machine for the gratification of repressed desires."It reveals itself, however, as nothing other than 'His Majesty the Ego', the hero of every day-dream and every novel alike."The Aesthetic Bribe: Fore-pleasure and the Catharsis of FormThe central paradox of literature, which Freud addresses in the final section of the essay, is the question of aesthetic pleasure. If daydreams are deeply egoistic, private, and motivated by shameful desires, why do we derive pleasure from reading the creative writer’s fantasies? Under normal circumstances, if someone were to tell us their raw, undisguised daydreams, we would feel repelled, bored, or embarrassed by their naked egotism. The creative writer must therefore employ a specific psychological strategy to overcome our natural resistance and allow us to share in their fantasy. Freud calls this strategy the "aesthetic bribe" (ästhetische Lockmittel) or the offering of "fore-pleasure" (Vorlust).The writer achieves this by using two main techniques. First, they soften the repulsive, egoistic character of their daydream by altering, disguising, and universalising the fantasy, making it easier for the reader to identify with the characters. Second, the writer bribes the reader through the purely formal, aesthetic yield of pleasure offered by the presentation of the narrative. This formal pleasure, derived from style, structure, rhythm, and imagery, is what Freud terms "fore-pleasure":The aesthetic beauty of the work of art acts as an initial lure, satisfying our conscious mind and lowering our psychological defences. Once these defences are bypassed, we are able to release and enjoy our own, deeper, repressed fantasies without guilt, shame, or self-reproach. The formal structure of the literary work thus serves a cathartic function, permitting a safe, vicarious satisfaction of the unconscious drives that would otherwise remain repressed."We give the name of fore-pleasure to a yield of pleasure such as this, which is offered to us so as to make possible the release of still greater pleasure arising from deeper psychical sources. In my opinion, all the aesthetic pleasure which a creative writer affords us has the character of a fore-pleasure of this kind..."Legacy: The Genesis of Psychoanalytic Criticism and Reader-ResponseThe legacy of Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming is vast, serving as the starting point for almost all subsequent psychoanalytic approaches to literature. In the decades following its publication, the essay’s model of text-as-fantasy led to the development of "psychobiography", in which critics read literary works as coded symptoms of the author's personal neuroses and developmental traumas. However, the essay also contains the seeds of more sophisticated theoretical movements. By focusing on how the writer "bribes" the reader and bypasses their resistance, Freud anticipates the key concerns of reader-response criticism, which emerged in the 1970s. Theorists such as Norman Holland, in The Dynamics of Literary Response (1968), expanded Freud's concept of fore-pleasure into a comprehensive model of how readers project their own identity themes onto the text, transforming the literary experience into a negotiation between the reader's defence mechanisms and the text's formal structures.In the realm of structuralist and post-structuralist psychoanalysis, Freud’s comparison of play, daydreaming, and writing was reinterpreted through the lens of linguistics. Jacques Lacan’s assertion that "the unconscious is structured like a language" cast the daydreams and narrative displacements described by Freud as manifestations of metonymy and metaphor, driven by the eternal deferral of desire (désir). Similarly, Harold Bloom’s theory of the "anxiety of influence" reframed the creative writer's struggle not as a negotiation with personal daydreams, but as an Oedipal conflict with literary precursors, where the "aesthetic bribe" is a defence against the overwhelming presence of the poetic father. By showing that the formal properties of literature are inextricably bound to the economics of human desire, Freud's brief essay dismantled the nineteenth-century illusion of disinterested aesthetic contemplation, establishing a critical tradition that continues to interrogate the unconscious motives behind the writing and reading of texts.Sources and VerificationFreud, Sigmund. "Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming". The Standard Edition of the Complete Psychological Works of Sigmund Freud. Translated by Alix Strachey, under the general editorship of James Strachey, Volume IX (1906–1908): Jensen's 'Gradiva' and Other Works, Hogarth Press, 1959, pp. 141–153.Quotations verified against the Standard Edition text:The child's play passage: Vol. IX, p. 143.The opposite of play passage: Vol. IX, p. 144.The motivating wishes passage: Vol. IX, p. 146-147.The "His Majesty the Ego" passage: Vol. IX, p. 150.The "fore-pleasure" passage: Vol. IX, p. 153.
critical_works.ch35: Ferdinand de Saussure (1857–1913)Original title: Cours de linguistique générale (posthumously compiled from student lecture notes)1916 · French · Switzerland / Geneva School · Structural Linguistics / Semiotics Foundation · Reconstructed Lecture Series / Linguistic TreatiseThe Posthumous Foundation: Bally, Sechehaye, and the Geneva LecturesFerdinand de Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics represents a unique phenomenon in the history of intellectual thought: a text that inaugurated a major philosophical movement, yet was never actually written by its nominal author. Following Saussure’s death in 1913, his colleagues Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye, recognizing the revolutionary nature of the lectures Saussure had delivered at the University of Geneva between 1907 and 1911, undertook the task of compiling and editing a coherent treatise. Drawing upon the detailed notebooks of students such as Albert Riedlinger and Émile Constantin, as well as Saussure's own sparse preparatory notes, they published the Cours de linguistique générale in 1916. The resulting text did not merely reform the study of comparative philology; it completely reconstructed the field of linguistics, shifting its focus from historical grammar to the synchronic study of language systems and establishing the theoretical foundation for structuralism, post-structuralism, and modern semiotics.The compilation context of the Course is essential for understanding its structural rigor. Bally and Sechehaye were forced to impose a systematic order on lecture series that had been delivered over three separate academic years, during which Saussure’s terminology and emphasis had evolved. In doing so, they produced a monument of clarity that presented language as an autonomous, self-contained system of formal relations. This structural perspective challenged the nineteenth-century philological tradition, which had treated language as a historical accumulation of sounds and words, studied through the lens of diachronic evolution. Saussure’s intervention was to isolate language from its historical, psychological, and physiological contexts, establishing a pure science of linguistics that treats the linguistic system as an object of study in its own right. The Course thus became the catalyst for the "linguistic turn" in twentieth-century philosophy, providing a model of analysis that would subsequently be applied to anthropology, literary criticism, psychoanalysis, and cultural studies.The Anatomy of the Sign: Signifier, Signified, and Psychological AssociationAt the centre of Saussure’s linguistic theory is a radical redefinition of the linguistic sign (signe). Saussure rejects the traditional view of language as a nomenclature, a list of words that correspond directly to pre-existing things in the physical world. He argues that the linguistic sign does not unite a name and a thing, but rather two psychological entities:To avoid confusion, Saussure proposes a precise terminology: the sound-image is the Signifier (signifiant), and the concept is the Signified (signifié). The sign is the totality of the link that unites these two components.This definition is crucial because it localises the entire linguistic operation within human consciousness. The signifier is not the physical acoustic wave that travels through the air, but the mental representation of that sound; the signified is not the physical object in the field, but the mental category or concept. When we speak of a "tree," the sign is the psychological association between the mental sound-pattern /triː/ (the signifier) and the mental concept of a woody perennial plant (the signified). By defining the sign as a double-sided psychological entity, Saussure decouples language from reference to the material world. Language does not reflect an external reality; instead, it structures our internal consciousness, organizing the chaotic realm of thought and sound into distinct, manageable units."The linguistic sign unites, not a thing and a name, but a concept and a sound-image. The latter is not the material sound, a purely physical thing, but the psychological imprint of the sound, the impression that it makes on our senses. The sound-image is sensory, and if I happen to call it 'material,' it is only in this sense, and by way of opposing it to the other term of the association, the concept, which is generally more abstract."The Dual Principles: Arbitrariness and Linearity of the SignSaussure identifies two primary, non-negotiable principles that govern the nature of the linguistic sign. The first principle is the arbitrary nature of the sign (l'arbitraire du signe):There is no natural, inherent, or logical connection between the signifier /triː/ and the concept of a tree. The proof of this arbitrariness lies in the diversity of languages: the concept of a tree is represented by the signifier tree in English, arbre in French, and baobab in other contexts. None of these sound-images has any intrinsic claim to the concept. This connection is established purely by social convention and collective habit.The second principle is the linear nature of the signifier (le caractère linéaire du signifiant). Unlike visual signs, which can present multiple dimensions and simultaneous elements in space, auditory signifiers exist only in the dimension of time. A signifier must unfold along a temporal line: it represents a span, and this span is measurable in a single dimension. We cannot pronounce two words simultaneously; they must be delivered sequentially, one sound-image after another. This linearity governs the entire syntax of language, requiring that meaning be constructed through chain-like successions of signs. The linear nature of the signifier prevents the collapse of language into a chaotic mass of simultaneous sounds, ensuring that communication remains an ordered process of temporal unfolding."The bond between the signifier and the signified is arbitrary. Since I mean by sign the whole that results from the associating of the signifier with the signified, I can simply say: the linguistic sign is arbitrary."The Chessboard of Language: Distinguishing Langue and ParoleTo make the study of language scientifically viable, Saussure introduces a fundamental division between two aspects of human speech: langue (language) and parole (speech). Saussure argues that human speech (langage) as a whole is many-sided, heterogeneous, and chaotic, spanning physical, physiological, and psychological domains. It belongs to both the individual and the social sphere. To study it systematically, we must isolate its core component:Langue is the abstract, systematic, and social code of language that exists independently of any individual speaker; it is a grammatical system stored virtually in the brains of a collective group. Parole, on the other hand, is the individual, concrete act of speaking in daily life, the specific utterances, hesitations, and stylistic choices made by an individual speaker at a given moment.To illustrate this distinction, Saussure employs his famous analogy of the game of chess:The rules of chess, the values assigned to each piece, and the permissible moves constitute the equivalent of langue. They exist as an abstract system before any game begins and remain unchanged regardless of who is playing. An individual move made by a player on the board corresponds to parole. The player’s move is a concrete execution that occurs in time, but it only makes sense because it conforms to the pre-existing system of rules. Saussure argues that the true object of linguistics must be langue, the collective social system, because parole is too variable and dependent on individual volition to be studied systematically."But what is language [langue]? For us, it is not to be confused with human speech [langage], of which it is only a definite part, though an essential one. It is both a social product of the faculty of speech and a collection of necessary conventions that have been adopted by a social body to permit individuals to exercise that faculty.""But of all comparisons that might be imagined, the most fruitful is the one that might be drawn between the functioning of language and a game of chess. In both, we are confronted with a system of values and their observe-rules. A game of chess is like an artificial realization of what language presents in a natural form."Temples of Time: Synchronic Systematics versus Diachronic EvolutionSaussure further divides the study of linguistics by distinguishing between two axes of analysis: the synchronic (static) and the diachronic (evolutionary). The synchronic axis concerns the relations between coexisting terms that form a system at a single, specific point in time, as perceived by the collective consciousness of the speakers. The diachronic axis, conversely, concerns the relations between successive terms that replace one another over historical time, tracing the evolution of individual linguistic elements.Saussure prioritises the synchronic axis over the diachronic. He argues that for the speaker, the history of a language does not exist; the speaker is confronted only with a state of the language system at the moment they use it. To understand how a language functions, we must analyse it as a static, self-contained system of contemporary values, rather than tracing the historical etymology of its parts.Returning to the chess analogy, Saussure points out that if we arrive at a chess game in progress, we do not need to know the history of the previous moves to understand the state of the board. The value of each piece depends entirely on its current position relative to the other pieces on the board at that exact second. Similarly, the meaning of a linguistic sign is determined by its relations with other signs coexisting in the present system, not by its historical development. By establishing the priority of synchronic analysis, Saussure liberated linguistics from the historical determinism of the nineteenth century, establishing a method that focuses on the internal relations of structures.Differences Without Positive Terms: The Relational Nature of ValuePerhaps the most radical and far-reaching argument in the Course is Saussure’s assertion that language is a system of pure relations, in which meaning is determined not by the intrinsic qualities of a sign, but by its difference from other signs in the system. Saussure distinguishes between signification (the relation between a signifier and a signified within a single sign) and value (valeur), which is the relation of a sign to all other signs in the language. The value of a sign is purely relational; it is what the other signs are not.Saussure summarises this relational ontology in a famous formulation:A sign does not have an autonomous, positive meaning; it has value only because it is distinct from other signs. The word "cat" has value in English because it is not "bat," "hat," "cot," or "dog." If the surrounding signs were to change, the value of the sign would change accordingly.This concept of "differences without positive terms" implies that language does not register pre-existing distinctions in the world; rather, it creates them. Before language, thought is a vague, shapeless mass, and sound is an undifferentiated stream. Language is the mediator that cuts across these two chaotic mediums, establishing arbitrary divisions and linking them together. This relational view of language dismantles the Cartesian subject and the empiricist view of reality, suggesting that our very thoughts and perceptions are structured by a differential system that precedes us. Meaning is not a substance, but a form; it is not located within the sign, but in the intervals that separate one sign from another."In language there are only differences. Even more important: a difference generally implies positive terms between which the difference is established; but in language there are only differences without positive terms. Whether we take the signified or the signifier, language has neither ideas nor sounds that existed before the linguistic system, but only conceptual and phonic differences that have issued from the system."Legacy: Structuralism, Post-Structuralism, and the Semiotic TurnThe legacy of Saussure's Course in General Linguistics is synonymous with the development of twentieth-century intellectual history. In the 1920s and 1930s, the Prague School of linguistics, led by Roman Jakobson, applied Saussure’s relational method to phonology, demonstrating that phonemes function as systems of binary oppositions. In the 1940s, Claude Lévi-Strauss imported Saussure’s structural method into anthropology, arguing that kinship systems, myths, and social rituals function like langue, abstract systems of rules that govern individual behaviour (parole) without the participants' conscious awareness. This move inaugurated the golden age of French Structuralism, which dominated the humanities in the 1950s and 1960s.During this period, Roland Barthes expanded Saussure’s concept of semiology (the science of signs) to include cultural phenomena, analysing fashion, advertisements, and popular myths as sign systems that communicate bourgeois ideology. In psychoanalysis, Jacques Lacan declared that "the unconscious is structured like a language," reading Freud's dream-work through Saussurean concepts of signifier and signified, and locating the human subject within the Symbolic Order.In the late 1960s, the post-structuralist critique of Saussure emerged, most notably in the work of Jacques Derrida. Derrida accepted Saussure’s premise that language is a system of differences without positive terms, but he pushed this argument to its logical extreme. He argued that if there are no positive terms, meaning can never be fully present in any sign; it is always deferred, slipping from one signifier to another along an endless chain of signification. Derrida’s concept of différance (a spelling that combines "to differ" and "to defer") is a direct development of Saussure’s relational linguistics. By demonstrating that language is an unstable, self-referential system rather than a transparent reflection of reality, Saussure's posthumous lectures dismantled the foundations of Western metaphysics, shifting the focus of human inquiry from the stable presence of the referent to the infinite play of the signifier.Sources and VerificationSaussure, Ferdinand de. Course in General Linguistics. Edited by Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye, in collaboration with Albert Riedlinger. Translated by Wade Baskin, Philosophical Library, 1959.Quotations verified against the Baskin translation:The definition of the sign: p. 66.The arbitrary nature of the sign: p. 67.The definition of langue: p. 9.The chess analogy: p. 88.The "differences without positive terms" passage: p. 120.
critical_works.ch36: Viktor Shklovsky (1893–1984)Original title: Iskusstvo kak priyom1917 (published in the collection Poetica) · Russian · Russia / Petrograd (OPOJAZ) · Russian Formalism · Formalist EssayThe Formalist Manifesto: Challenging the Potebnyan ConsensusViktor Shklovsky’s 1917 essay Art as Device (frequently translated as Art as Technique) is the foundational manifesto of Russian Formalism. Published on the eve of the Russian Revolution in the collection Poetica, the essay represents a radical, iconoclastic break from the dominant traditions of nineteenth-century literary criticism. At the time of its publication, Russian literary study was dominated by two main camps: the historical-biographical school, which treated the text as a passive reflection of the author's life or social milieu, and the psychological-linguistic theory of Alexander Potebnya, which asserted that "art is thinking in images." Potebnya and his followers argued that the primary function of the poetic image is to are a cognitive shorthand, translating complex, abstract concepts into simple, visual representations that allow the human mind to economise its mental energy.Shklovsky launches a direct, systematic assault on this Potebnyan consensus. He argues that the equation of art with "thinking in images" is flawed, as it fails to distinguish between the practical use of language and the aesthetic function of literature. Images, Shklovsky points out, are not created by poets; they are simply found in the linguistic culture and recycled from one generation to the next. The history of imagery is not a history of progress, but a history of recycling: "images are almost motionless; they flow from country to country, from century to century, from poet to poet, without changing." If imagery is constant, then the uniqueness of art cannot reside in the image itself. Instead, Shklovsky argues that literary study must focus on the materiality of the medium and the specific, artistic "device" (priyom) through which the writer manipulates this material. By shifting the critical gaze from the referential content of the text to the formal devices that construct it, Shklovsky inaugurates the formalist movement, establishing the autonomy of literary discourse and defining "literariness" (literaturnost) as the true object of literary science.The Anesthetic of the Everyday: The Pathology of HabitualizationTo ground his theory of the artistic device, Shklovsky turns to the cognitive psychology of human perception. He argues that as we live our daily lives, our interactions with the world are subjected to a law of cognitive economy: our actions, movements, and perceptions become automatic and habitualized. We no longer look at the familiar objects in our environment; instead, we recognize them through a process of cognitive shorthand, identifying them by their primary features without actually perceiving their unique, physical reality. Shklovsky writes:This automatic perception allows us to navigate the world efficiently, but it comes at a terrible aesthetic and existential cost. When our perception becomes habitualized, the world becomes invisible. We see only the labels we have attached to things, rather than the things themselves.To illustrate this deadening effect, Shklovsky quotes a passage from Leo Tolstoy's diary entry of 1 March 1897, in which Tolstoy describes cleaning a room and suddenly realizing he cannot remember if he has dusted the divan:This passage represents the central ethical concern of Shklovsky's essay: the pathology of habitualization. When life is lived automatically, it is effectively unlived. Habitualization acts as a cognitive anesthetic, turning our experiences into a grey blur, deadening our senses, and reducing our engagement with the world to a series of unconscious recognitions."If we examine the general laws of perception, we see that as actions become habitual, they become automatic. In this way, all our skills are moved into the realm of the unconscious; anyone who remembers the feeling of holding a pen or speaking a foreign language for the first time, and compares it with the feeling of doing it for the ten-thousandth time, will agree with us.""I was cleaning a room and, walking around, went up to the divan and could not remember whether I had cleaned it or not. Since these movements are habitual and unconscious, I could not remember and felt that it was already impossible to remember. So, if I had cleaned it and forgotten, i.e. if I had acted unconsciously, then it was just the same as if it had not been... If the whole complex life of many people goes on unconsciously, then such lives are as if they had never been."Ostranenie: The Device of Making Things StrangeArt, for Shklovsky, is the supreme cognitive antidote to this deadening process. The primary function of art is not to communicate information, express emotion, or teach moral lessons, but to break through the crust of habitualized perception and restore our sensory engagement with the world. Shklovsky articulates this core principle in the most famous passage of the essay:The term ostranenie, neologised by Shklovsky from the Russian word stranny (strange), is the conceptual heart of Russian Formalism.
