It is often translated into English as "defamiliarization" or "estrangement."The device of ostranenie works by presenting the familiar, everyday objects of our world in an unfamiliar, strange way, forcing the reader to abandon automatic recognition and instead experience the object through active, sensory perception. Rather than allowing us to recognize the stone instantly by its label, art slows down our reading process, forcing us to feel the stone's roughness, its weight, its temperature, to "make the stone stone-like." The aesthetic experience is characterised by this difficulty and duration of perception. By defamiliarizing the world, art does not change the objects themselves; it changes our relation to them, de-automating our minds and returning us to the immediate, vivid reality of our lives."And so, in order to return sensation to our limbs, in order to make us feel things, to make the stone stone-like, there exists that which we call art. The purpose of art is to lead us to a knowledge of a thing through the organ of sight instead of recognition. Art uses the device of 'making things strange' (ostranenie) and the device of slowed-down form, which increases the difficulty and duration of perception. The process of perception in art is an end in itself and must be prolonged; art is a way of experiencing the artfulness of an object; the object is not important."The Equine Observer and the Painted Board: Tolstoy's Defamiliarizing LensTo demonstrate the practical application of ostranenie, Shklovsky provides an extended analysis of the narrative techniques of Leo Tolstoy, whom he regards as the supreme master of defamiliarization. Tolstoy, Shklovsky shows, defamiliarises things by refusing to call them by their common names. Instead, he describes familiar objects and social institutions as if he were seeing them for the first time, and complex social customs as if they were bizarre, illogical rituals.Shklovsky focuses on Tolstoy's short story Kholstomer, which is narrated from the perspective of a piebald horse. By using an equine narrator, Tolstoy is able to present the human concept of private property as a bizarre, unnatural absurdity. The horse observes:By filtering the concept of property through the mind of a horse, Tolstoy strips it of its naturalised, legalistic status, exposing it as a bizarre form of linguistic and social delusion.Similarly, Shklovsky points to Tolstoy's description of the opera in War and Peace. Instead of using the conventional, elevated vocabulary of theatre criticism, Tolstoy describes the performance in terms of its raw, physical components:By reducing the operatic performance to a series of painted boards, green cardboard, and singing people in tight trousers, Tolstoy defamiliarises the entire theatrical convention, exposing the gap between the physical reality of the stage and the suspension of disbelief required by the audience. This device forces the reader to see the artificiality of the performance, stripping it of its romantic prestige and restoring a direct, critical perception of the medium."Many of those who called me their property did not ride me; others rode me. It is not those who do good to me who call me their property, but the coachmen, the veterinarians, and all kinds of strangers. Later, having broadened my field of observation, I became convinced that the concept of 'mine,' which has no other basis than a connection with the human urge to dominate, is applied to a wide range of things... Men say 'my house' and never live in it... People strive in life not to do what they think is good, but to call as many things as possible 'mine.'""In the middle of the stage there were flat boards, at the sides stood painted cardboard representing trees... in the middle sat girls in red bodices and white skirts. One, very fat, in a white silk dress, sat on a low bench, with green cardboard glued behind her. She sang something. When she finished, the man in the tight trousers went up to her, took her hand, and began to sing..."Deforming the Sequence: Fabula, Syuzhet, and the Impediment of FormA crucial theoretical development that emerges from Shklovsky's concept of defamiliarization is the formalist distinction between fabula (story) and syuzhet (plot). While Shklovsky develops this distinction more fully in his later work Theory of Prose (1925), its structural logic is already present in Art as Device. The fabula represents the chronological, causal sequence of events as they would have occurred in real life, the raw material of the narrative. The syuzhet, conversely, represents the actual, artistic arrangement of these events within the literary text, designed to distort, slow down, and complicate the reader's progression through the story.The relationship between fabula and syuzhet is a direct application of the principle of defamiliarization to narrative structure. If a writer were to present a story in a simple, chronological order, the reader's progression would be automatic and rapid; they would read for the "ending," recognizing the plot-pattern without experiencing the artistic structure of the text. To prevent this automatic reading, the writer deforms the chronological sequence through various devices: they introduce flashbacks, flashforwards, parallel subplots, digressions, and stylistic impediments. These narrative delays transform the story into a syuzhet, prolonging the duration of our perception and forcing us to pay attention to the artistic organization of the work. The value of the literary work lies not in the fabula (the raw content of the story), but in the syuzhet (the artistic deformation of that content), making form not a container for meaning, but the very site of aesthetic experience.Materiality and Autonomy: The Literary Work as a System of DevicesThe ultimate consequence of Shklovsky’s formalist theory is a radical revision of the relationship between form and content. In traditional nineteenth-century criticism, form was treated as a passive container designed to hold and communicate a pre-existing content (ideas, morals, historical facts). Shklovsky inverts this hierarchy, asserting that content is merely the material justification or "excuse" for the realization of formal devices. A work of literature is not a message wrapped in a decorative form; rather, it is a unified, autonomous system of devices that exist in a state of dynamic tension with one another.This relational model of the artwork rejects the idea of aesthetic purity. Shklovsky does not suggest that literature is free from historical or social materials; rather, he argues that once these materials enter the literary work, they are subjected to the laws of artistic deformation and lose their non-literary function. A historical fact or a moral argument in a novel is not studied for its historical or moral truth, but for the way it functions as a device within the narrative system, how it creates delay, contrast, or defamiliarization. The literary work is thus an autonomous structure, governed by its own internal laws, and the critic's task is to describe the morphology of this structure, mapping the way its devices interact to create the experience of "literariness."Legacy: From OPOJAZ to Structuralism and the Avant-GardeThe legacy of Art as Device is woven into the fabric of twentieth-century avant-garde art and literary theory. In the immediate post-revolutionary period, Shklovsky’s theories were closely aligned with the experiments of the Russian Futurist poets (such as Vladimir Mayakovsky) and Constructivist artists, who sought to expose the materiality of their mediums, making the paint, the stone, and the word visible to the observer. In the theatre, Bertolt Brecht’s concept of the Verfremdungseffekt (the estrangement or alienation effect) represents a direct theatrical application of Shklovsky’s ostranenie. Brecht sought to expose the artificiality of the theatrical apparatus, preventing the audience from identifying passively with the characters and instead forcing them to adopt a critical, active attitude toward the social contradictions presented on stage.In the realm of literary theory, Shklovsky’s distinction between fabula and syuzhet was adopted by the structuralist narratologists of the 1960s, such as Tzvetan Todorov and Gérard Genette, who transformed it into a rigorous science of narrative analysis. The concept of defamiliarization also anticipated the aesthetic theories of the Frankfurt School, particularly Theodor Adorno’s argument that modern art must use dissonant, difficult forms to resist the automatic, homogenizing pressures of the culture industry. Even in the post-structuralist era, Shklovsky's focus on the material friction of language remained influential, providing a theoretical precursor for the deconstructive analysis of textual self-reflexivity. By demonstrating that the primary task of art is to awaken the human senses from the slumber of habit, Shklovsky's essay established a critical vocabulary that remains vital for any analysis of the relationship between aesthetics, cognition, and everyday life.Sources and VerificationShklovsky, Viktor. "Art as Device". Viktor Shklovsky: A Reader. Edited and translated by Alexandra Berlina, Bloomsbury Academic, 2017, pp. 73–96.Quotations verified against the Berlina translation:The law of habitualization passage: p. 79.The quote from Tolstoy's diary: p. 80.The "return sensation to our limbs" passage: p. 80.The Tolstoy Kholstomer passage: p. 81.The Tolstoy opera passage: p. 83-84.
critical_works.ch37: T. S. Eliot (1888–1965)Original title: Tradition and the Individual Talent (published in The Egoist)September–December 1919 · English · United States / England · Modernism / New Criticism Precursor · Critical EssayThe Anti-Romantic Manifesto of Modernist PoeticsT. S. Eliot’s "Tradition and the Individual Talent," first published in two parts in The Egoist in 1919 and subsequently collected in The Sacred Wood (1920), functions as the foundational document of Anglo-American modernist literary theory. The essay operates as a double-edged sword, simultaneously defining the relationship of the modern artist to the literary past and launching a systematic assault on the legacy of Romanticism. By challenging the nineteenth-century cult of the individual genius, the primacy of self-expression, and the Wordsworthian doctrine of "emotion recollected in tranquillity," Eliot redefines both the nature of poetic composition and the function of critical enquiry. His arguments establish the conceptual framework that would later animate the New Criticism, shifting the focus of literary study away from the biography and psychology of the author and towards the formal autonomy of the text itself.The immediate context of the essay is one of profound cultural dislocation following the First World War. For the modernist generation, the nineteenth-century faith in progress and subjective expression had foundered in the trenches of Europe. Eliot seeks to construct a new classicism characterized by order, restraint, and an objective methodology. He opposes the Romantic view of the poet as an inspired visionary whose work is an effusion of private feeling. Instead, he conceptualizes the poet as a craftsman operating within a vast, pre-existing structure of cultural memory. This redefinition is more than a technical adjustment; it is a radical reorientation of the value assigned to the individual. In Eliot’s formulation, the significance of the artist lies not in their uniqueness or their departure from their predecessors, but in their capacity to assimilate and continue a collective literary inheritance.The Acquisition of Tradition and the Historical SenseEliot’s redefinition of "tradition" represents a departure from the colloquial understanding of the term as a passive, uncritical adherence to the practices of the immediate past. He argues that tradition is not a matter of mere inheritance or blind imitation, noting that "if it were only that, if it were only transmitted to us in the immediate past, it should be positively discouraged." For Eliot, tradition cannot be inherited; it is an active, demanding intellectual achievement that "must be obtained by great labour." This labour requires the development of what Eliot calls the "historical sense," a cognitive faculty that is indispensable for any writer who wishes to produce literature of lasting value.The historical sense involves a complex perception of temporal relations. It demands that the writer remain aware of both the chronological distance of the past and its persistent, active influence on the present:This simultaneous order is not a static repository of dead monuments, but a living, integrated system. The historical sense is therefore a sense of the timeless and of the temporal together. It forces the writer to recognise that their work does not exist in a vacuum, but is continuously compared, contrasted, and aligned with the works that have preceded it. To write with the historical sense is to participate in a dialogue that spans millennia, maintaining an awareness of the contemporary moment while remaining anchored in the foundational texts of Western civilisation.The historical sense involves a perception, not only of the pastness of the past, but of its presence; the historical sense compels a man to write not merely with his own generation in his bones, but with a feeling that the whole of the literature of Europe from Homer and within it the whole of the literature of his own country has a simultaneous existence and composes a simultaneous order.The Organic and Dynamic CanonOne of Eliot’s most influential contributions to literary theory is his description of the literary canon as a dynamic, self-adjusting organism. In his view, the relationship between the past and the present is reciprocal: the past guides the creation of the present, but the creation of a truly new work of art simultaneously alters our understanding of the past. When a new work is introduced into the existing order, a systemic readjustment occurs throughout the entire network of literature:This formulation challenges the linear, progressive view of literary history that treats the past as merely a series of stepping-stones leading to the present. Eliot proposes instead a spatial and synchronic model of literature, in which Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, and the modern poet are contemporaries occupying the same intellectual space.By suggesting that the past is modified by the present as much as the present is directed by the past, Eliot introduces a sophisticated theory of reception. The meaning of an ancient text is not fixed at the moment of its composition; it is constantly rewritten and recontextualised by subsequent additions to the canon. A reader who has encountered Baudelaire or Joyce cannot read Virgil or Shakespeare in the same way as a reader who lived before them. The new work reveals latent qualities, formal possibilities, and thematic connections in the older texts that were previously invisible. The canon remains a living monument because it is subject to this perpetual, structural revision.The existing monuments form an ideal order among themselves, which is modified by the introduction of the new (the really new) work of art among them. The existing order is complete before the new work arrives; for order to persist after the supervention of novelty, the whole existing order must be, if ever so slightly, altered; and so the relations, proportions, values of each work of art toward the whole are readjusted; and this is conformity between the old and the new.The Impersonal Theory of PoetryAt the centre of "Tradition and the Individual Talent" stands the "Impersonal theory of poetry," a polemical challenge to the subjective aesthetics of the Romantic era. Eliot argues that the progress of an artist is "a continual self-sacrifice, a continual extinction of personality." He rejects the idea that poetry is an expression of the poet's unique biographical self, asserting instead that the poet's mind is merely a medium in which experiences, emotions, and phrases can combine in unexpected ways. The value of poetry does not reside in the intensity of the poet's personal feelings, but in the artistic intensity of the process of synthesis.Eliot summarises this position in one of the most famous passages of twentieth-century criticism:This assertion is frequently misunderstood as an advocacy for cold, unemotional literature. However, Eliot does not argue that poetry should lack emotion; rather, he argues that the emotion of art is distinct from the emotion of life. The poet’s job is not to find new emotions, but to use ordinary emotions to create a new aesthetic feeling that may not resemble the personal experiences of the writer at all.By separating the biographical individual from the artistic voice, Eliot shifts the focus of critical inquiry. He declares that "honest criticism and sensitive appreciation are directed not upon the poet but upon the poetry." This statement represents a methodological revolution. It suggests that biographical research, psychological speculation about the author’s intentions, and historical gossip are irrelevant to the evaluation of literary art. The critic’s task is to examine the formal properties of the text, analysing how its various elements are organized to produce a unified aesthetic effect.Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion; it is not the expression of personality, but an escape from personality. But, of course, only those who have personality and emotions know what it means to want to escape from these things.The Catalyst Metaphor and the Chemistry of CreationTo illustrate his impersonal theory of composition, Eliot introduces a celebrated scientific analogy drawn from chemistry. He compares the mind of the poet to a shred of platinum introduced into a chamber containing oxygen and sulphur dioxide:This metaphor serves several functions in Eliot's argument. First, it emphasizes the passivity and neutrality of the creative mind. The poet’s mind is not an active agent of self-assertion, but a receptacle, "a medium, which is only a medium and not a personality, in which impressions and experiences combine in peculiar and unexpected ways."Second, the catalyst metaphor reinforces the distinction between life and art. The "man who suffers" is the biographical individual who experiences grief, joy, anger, or love in their daily existence. The "mind which creates" is the artistic intellect that takes these raw, chaotic feelings and transmutes them into the ordered structure of a poem. The resulting work of art, like the sulphurous acid, contains no trace of the catalyst that brought it into being. The personal sufferings of the poet are merely the raw materials for a process of transformation that renders them universal.Finally, the metaphor implies that the creative process is objective and rule-bound, analogous to a chemical reaction. It rejects the Romantic idea of inspiration as a mystical, unpredictable visitation of genius. Instead, composition is presented as a precise, almost clinical operation in which the medium of the mind facilitates the combination of disparate elements. The quality of the poem depends not on the greatness of the starting materials, but on the efficiency of the catalyst, the refinement and maturity of the poet's mind.When the two gases previously mentioned are mixed in the presence of a filament of platinum, they form sulphurous acid. This combination takes place only if the platinum is present; nevertheless the newly formed acid contains no trace of platinum, and the platinum itself is apparently unaffected; has remained inert, neutral, and unchanged. The mind of the poet is the shred of platinum. It may partly or exclusively operate upon the experience of the man himself; but, the more perfect the artist, the more completely separate in him will be the man who suffers and the mind which creates; the more perfectly will the mind digest and transmute the passions which are its material.The Critical Legacy: From Modernist Manifesto to New CriticismThe influence of "Tradition and the Individual Talent" on subsequent literary theory is immense. By insisting on the autonomy of the poem and the irrelevance of the author’s biography, Eliot laid the groundwork for the New Criticism, which dominated Anglo-American literary studies from the 1930s to the 1950s. Critics such as I. A. Richards, Cleanth Brooks, and W. K. Wimsatt took Eliot’s impersonal theory to its logical conclusion, developing formalist methodologies that prioritised close reading and rejected the "intentional fallacy", the belief that a text's meaning is determined by the author's intended purpose.However, Eliot’s model of tradition has also provoked significant criticism, particularly from post-structuralist, feminist, and postcolonial theorists. Critics have pointed out that Eliot’s "simultaneous order" of European literature is highly exclusive, reflecting a Eurocentric, patriarchal, and class-bound conception of culture. His insistence on a single, continuous line of tradition from Homer to the modern era ignores the marginalized voices, alternative traditions, and historical ruptures that have shaped global literature. Furthermore, his demand for the "extinction of personality" has been interpreted by some critics as a conservative defence of authority, an attempt to insulate the literary canon from the personal, political, and social realities of class, race, and gender.Despite these critiques, the conceptual core of Eliot's essay remains a vital point of reference in debates about the nature of creativity, the structure of the canon, and the limits of historical understanding. By framing the act of writing as a negotiation between the weight of the past and the demands of the present, Eliot ensured that the relationship between tradition and innovation would remain the central problem of twentieth-century aesthetics. His essay continues to challenge readers and writers to consider how new voices can emerge within an established order, and how the monuments of the past continue to speak to the contemporary world.
critical_works.ch38: Georg Lukács (1885–1971)Original title: Die Theorie des Romans1916 (published as a book in 1920) · German · Hungary · Pre-Marxist Hegelian Aesthetics / Western Marxist Precursor · Theoretical TreatiseThe Melancholy Architecture of a World in RuinsWritten in the shadow of the First World War and published first in Max Dessoir’s Zeitschrift für Ästhetik und allgemeine Kunstwissenschaft in 1916, Georg Lukács’s The Theory of the Novel is one of the most remarkable documents of early twentieth-century aesthetic theory. Conceived during a period of intense personal and historical crisis, the work is saturated with a profound intellectual melancholy. Lukács, looking out at a Europe self-destructing in industrialised warfare, experiences what he would later describe in a 1962 preface as a mood of "permanent despair." The treatise employs a historicist, Hegelian framework to chart the evolution of narrative forms, tracing the transition from the integrated, meaningful cosmos of ancient Greece to the fragmented, alienated reality of modern Europe. In doing so, Lukács provides a diagnosis of the modern condition that is as much metaphysical and sociological as it is literary.The intellectual coordinates of the work are defined by the German idealist tradition, particularly the philosophy of G. W. F. Hegel and the concept of historical development. Lukács seeks to understand how the changes in human consciousness and social structures dictate the forms available to the storyteller. He argues that art forms are not arbitrary stylistic choices, but the necessary expressions of a historical epoch's relationship to meaning. The transition from the epic to the novel is therefore not a story of technical progress, but the record of a tragic historical fall. For the young Lukács, writing before his conversion to Marxism, the crisis of the modern world is a crisis of meaning: a state in which the individual is severed from the community, the soul is alienated from the cosmos, and the immanence of value has vanished from daily life.The Integrated Cosmos of the Epic: The Starry Sky as MapLukács begins his analysis with a nostalgic reconstruction of the ancient Greek world, a civilization he characterises as a closed, integrated totality where the division between the self and the world did not yet exist. In this lost golden age, meaning was not something to be sought after or constructed; it was immanent, directly given in the very fabric of existence. Lukács evokes this organic harmony in the celebrated opening line of the treatise:In this epic world, the individual is not an isolated subject confronting an indifferent or hostile objective reality. There is no distinction between interior psychology and external action, between the private citizen and the public sphere. The epic hero is not a seeker of identity; he is the representative of a collective destiny whose actions are immediately meaningful.The literary form that corresponds to this integrated world is the epic. The epic, exemplified by Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, presents a totality of life that is complete and self-contained. It is a world where every object and every gesture participates in a shared, cosmic significance. There are no questions of ultimate purpose in Homer because the characters do not experience doubt; the gods are active participants in human affairs, and the boundary of the horizon is not a limit but a boundary that contains all possible human experience. The epic world is a sphere, a finished and harmonious whole in which the soul is always at home.Happy are those ages when the starry sky is the map of all possible paths—ages whose paths are illuminated by the light of the stars. Everything in such ages is new and yet familiar, full of adventure and yet possession. The world is wide and yet it is like a home, for the fire that burns in the soul is of the same essential nature as the stars.The Birth of the Novel: The Epic of an Abandoned WorldThe historical movement away from ancient Greece is characterised by the collapse of this organic totality. The rise of philosophy, the disintegration of the city-state, and the eventual development of modern capitalism lead to the fragmentation of the world. The individual becomes conscious of themselves as a separate, isolated subject, and the external world is transformed into a cold, indifferent system of laws, what Lukács calls "second nature." In this new historical epoch, the epic becomes impossible. The form that emerges to take its place is the novel.Lukács famously defines the novel in terms that emphasize its relationship to this lost unity:Unlike the epic, which celebrates a present and accepted meaning, the novel is born from the absence of meaning. It is the narrative form of a world that has been "abandoned by God," where the path of human life is no longer illuminated by the stars, and the individual must seek their own way in darkness.The novel is therefore defined by a structural tension. It seeks to reconstruct a totality of life, to build a coherent world within the covers of a book, while remaining conscious that such a totality no longer exists. The form of the novel is inherently problematic, marked by irony and self-consciousness. It cannot simply depict a harmonious universe; it must dramatise the struggle to find meaning in a world where meaning is absent or hidden. The novel is not a monument of certainty, but a process of search, a quest for a lost home that can never be fully recovered.The novel is the epic of an age in which the extensive totality of life is no longer directly given, in which the immanence of meaning in life has become a problem, yet which still retains the longing for totality.Transcendental Homelessness and the Problematic SeekerThe central psychological and philosophical concept of The Theory of the Novel is "transcendental homelessness" (transzendentale Obdachlosigkeit). This term describes the condition of the modern subject, who feels like a stranger in a universe that no longer reflects their inner desires or values. Cut off from the cosmic order and the organic community, the modern individual is characterized by an agonizing division between their interior ideals and the exterior, social reality:The protagonist of the novel is always a "problematic individual," a character whose interiority is highly developed precisely because they are out of joint with their environment.This problematic hero is often "demonically obsessed," driven by a subjective ideal that they seek to impose upon a resistant reality. Lukács identifies two main types of this obsession. The first is the "novel of abstract idealism," exemplified by Cervantes’s Don Quixote, where the hero’s soul is too narrow for the world, clinging to obsolete ideals (like chivalry) and mistaking windmills for giants. The second is the "novel of disillusionment," exemplified by Flaubert’s L’Éducation sentimentale, where the hero’s soul is too wide, possessing a vast, romantic interiority that is gradually crushed and dissipated by the triviality and inertia of bourgeois society. In both cases, the quest of the protagonist is a manifestation of transcendental homelessness: a search for a place where the soul's aspirations can reconcile with the external world.The division of the soul into a subject and an object, the separation of the self from the world, the alienation of man from his fellows and from nature—this is the fundamental condition of the novel. The protagonist of the novel is the seeker; the novel is the biography of the seeker.The Temporal Flow: Time, Memory, and the Experience of DurationIn the epic, time is not a destructive or transformative force; it is static, cyclical, or timeless. The epic world does not experience history or decay; its values are eternal, and its heroes remain essentially unchanged by the passage of years. In the novel, however, time is a constituent element of the form itself. Because the extensive totality of life is no longer given, and because the meaning of the hero's journey is not guaranteed, time must enter the structure of the narrative to show the development of consciousness:Time in the novel is the medium of duration (durée), a force that slowly erodes human illusions, dissolves social structures, and forces the protagonist to confront the discrepancy between expectation and reality.This temporal experience is closely linked to the function of memory and self-consciousness. In the novel of disillusionment, time is experienced as a process of loss and decay, but it is also through memory (recherche) that the hero can achieve a fragile, retrospective understanding of their life. By looking back over the fragmented course of their existence, the protagonist, and the reader, can discern a pattern of meaning that was invisible in the moment of action. Memory becomes the creative power that, if only temporarily, synthesises the fragments of experience into a semblance of totality. The novel’s form is therefore elegiac, structured by the awareness of time passing and the constant effort to rescue meaning from the flow of duration.Time, in the novel, is the resistance of organic life to the abstract form. Only in the novel, where the representation of the extensive totality of life is a problem, does time become a constituent element of the form.The Dialectical Legacy: From Idealism to MarxismThe trajectory of Georg Lukács’s career after the publication of The Theory of the Novel is one of the most famous intellectual conversions of the twentieth century. Within a few years of writing this Hegelian, idealist treatise, Lukács joined the Hungarian Communist Party and turned his attention to historical materialism. In his later works, such as History and Class Consciousness (1923) and The Historical Novel (1937), he sought to ground his aesthetic theories in the material realities of class struggle and the economic structures of capitalism. He came to view his early work with considerable scepticism, criticising its "metaphysical" abstractions and its romantic longing for a pre-modern past.Despite Lukács's own self-critique, The Theory of the Novel remains a seminal text for Western Marxism and sociological aesthetics. His analysis of the novel as the product of historical alienation laid the foundation for the work of Walter Benjamin, Theodor Adorno, and Lucien Goldmann. In the late twentieth century, critics like Fredric Jameson revived Lukács's concepts, arguing that the formal problems of the novel continue to reflect the ideological contradictions of late capitalism. By demonstrating that literary forms are intimately bound up with the historical transformations of human consciousness, Lukács established a critical tradition that refuses to treat the novel as a mere commodity or a neutral technique, insisting instead on its status as a profound and troubled reflection on human homelessness in the modern age.
critical_works.ch39: I. A. Richards (1893–1979)Original title: Principles of Literary Criticism1924 · English · England · New Criticism Foundation / Early Psychological Criticism · Theoretical TreatiseThe Scientific and Materialist Reorientation of CriticismI. A. Richards’s Principles of Literary Criticism, published in 1924, represents a watershed moment in the history of English studies. Writing in the wake of the First World War, Richards set out to rescue literary criticism from what he perceived as a state of terminal vagueness, impressionistic chatter, and late-Victorian aestheticism. He sought to place the study of literature on a rigorous, empirical foundation, drawing on the newly emerging fields of neurological psychology, evolutionary theory, and linguistics. Richards’s project was materialist and secular: he aimed to demystify the experience of art, stripping it of its mystical and transcendental associations, and to explain both the value of literature and the mechanics of reading in terms of human physiology and cognitive organization.The book functions as an assertive critique of the critical status quo. In his introductory chapters, Richards laments that the contemporary critic lacks a coherent vocabulary, operating with terms that are poorly defined and concepts that are psychologically naive. He rejects the traditional separation of the arts from the sciences, arguing that the valuation of literature must be aligned with our understanding of how the human brain functions as an information-processing system. The famous opening sentence of his preface establishes this functionalist perspective: "A book is a machine to think with, but it is a machine that needs an operator." By treating the literary text as a complex stimulus designed to trigger specific psychological states in the reader, Richards shifts the focus of criticism from the abstract beauty of the work to the dynamic interaction between the text and the reader's mind.The Bifurcation of Language: Referential versus Emotive SignificationA cornerstone of Richards’s theory is his rigorous distinction between the two primary functions of language: the scientific (or referential) and the emotive. He argues that the failure to distinguish between these two modes of signification is the source of endless confusion in both philosophy and literary criticism. According to Richards, language is used referentially when it points to objects or states of affairs in the external world; its primary concern is the accuracy of the reference, and its statements are subject to logical verification as either true or false:The scientific use of language is the instrument of objective truth, essential for the accumulation of knowledge and the description of physical reality.In contrast, the emotive use of language, which is the proper domain of poetry, is not concerned with scientific truth or factual accuracy. Poetic statements do not describe the world; they use words to evoke emotional attitudes, balance impulses, and organize the reader's psychological state. Richards calls the assertions made in literature "pseudo-statements." A pseudo-statement may look like a scientific statement, but its value does not depend on its truth-value:To read a poem as if it were a scientific treatise, demanding that its theological, historical, or mythological assertions be factually true, is to commit a category mistake that destroys the work’s aesthetic function. Poetic language is an instrument of psychological adjustment, not of cognitive description.We must distinguish two main uses of language. First, the statement, which is the use of language for the sake of the reference, true or false, which it points to. Second, the expression, which is the use of language for the sake of the effects in emotion and attitude which it produces.A pseudo-statement is a form of words which is justified entirely by its effect in releasing or organising our impulses and attitudes... The truth of a scientific statement is a matter of verification, but the truth of a work of art is a matter of the internal coherence and emotional utility of the attitudes it evokes.The Economy of the Mind: Impulses, Interests, and the Theory of ValueTo explain how literature functions as a psychological organizer, Richards constructs a model of the human mind as a complex, dynamic system of competing forces. He defines the fundamental unit of mental activity as the "impulse," which he describes as "a process in which a tension is created, which is discharged by a response." These impulses are divided into appetencies (desires, seekings) and aversions (fears, avoidances). In Richards’s view, the mind is constantly engaged in a process of negotiation, attempting to satisfy as many of these impulses as possible while minimizing conflict and mutual frustration.This physiological model forms the basis of Richards’s materialist theory of value. He rejects any transcendental, moralistic, or metaphysical definition of the good, arguing instead that value is a function of psychological efficiency:The human mind is a fragile ecosystem; some experiences satisfy a single impulse at the cost of disrupting the entire system, while others coordinate a vast range of impulses, bringing them into a harmonious and productive relationship.For Richards, the arts are the supreme instrument for achieving this psychological organization. The poet is an individual who possesses an unusually stable, flexible, and finely integrated nervous system. Through the medium of the text, the poet communicates this state of high organization to the reader. Reading a great poem is not a passive reception of information, but an active exercise for the nervous system, in which the reader's own impulses are stimulated, balanced, and brought into a state of optimal efficiency. The value of literature is therefore directly tied to its capacity to promote psychological health and resilience.The value of an experience is the degree to which it satisfies impulses without thwarting other impulses of equal or greater importance. The good life is the life in which the greatest possible number of impulses are active and satisfied, with the minimum of friction and self-defeat.Synaesthesis: The Harmonisation of Conflicting ImpulsesThe culmination of the aesthetic experience, in Richards’s system, is a psychological state he terms "synaesthesis." Drawing on the vocabulary of Greek aesthetics and contemporary psychology, Richards defines synaesthesis as a state of equilibrium, a poise of active forces in which opposing impulses are balanced against one another:In synaesthesis, the mind experiences a release from the anxieties, desires, and conflicts of daily life. This is not a state of passive sedation, but of intense, equilibrated alertness.Richards uses the example of tragedy to illustrate this process. Tragedy, he argues, is the most sophisticated of all literary forms because it deliberately evokes the most violent and opposing impulses: pity (the impulse to approach) and terror (the impulse to retreat). In a successful tragic performance, these two incompatible forces do not cancel each other out; instead, they are held in a suspension of perfect equilibrium. The reader or spectator does not feel the urge to run away or to intervene; they experience a state of calm, poised contemplation.This state of synaesthesis has a profound ethical value for Richards, though it is an ethics divorced from moralistic dogma. By balancing conflicting impulses, synaesthesis prepares the individual for action in the real world. It reduces prejudice, eliminates obsessive single-mindedness, and fosters a capacity for complex, nuanced judgment. The equilibrated mind is less vulnerable to fanaticism, panic, or propaganda because it is accustomed to holding multiple, conflicting perspectives in a state of harmonious tension.Synaesthesis is the state in which the mind is in equilibrium, a poise of active forces, where impulses are balanced against one another. In this state, we feel a sense of completeness, of poised readiness, where the mind is free from the necessity of choosing between competing actions because the competing forces have been harmonised.The Demystification of Art: Rejecting the Autonomous Aesthetic FacultyA key polemical target of Principles of Literary Criticism is the Kantian tradition of aesthetics, which treats the experience of art as something unique, disinterested, and separate from the rest of human life. Richards rejects the idea of a distinct "aesthetic emotion" or a separate "aesthetic faculty" that operates independently of our ordinary cognitive and physical processes. He argues that such concepts are metaphysical illusions that isolate art from the world, rendering it a luxury for the elite rather than a necessity for human survival.For Richards, the experience of art is not a mystical retreat from reality, but simply a highly efficient, concentrated version of ordinary human experience:The same neural pathways, the same impulses, and the same cognitive structures that we use to navigate a busy street, make a moral decision, or converse with a friend are deployed in the reading of a poem.By integrating aesthetics into the general science of psychology, Richards seeks to democratise the value of literature. If art is not a mystical realm accessible only to those with a special, innate aesthetic sensibility, then the capacity to read and appreciate literature can be taught, analysed, and improved. Criticism becomes a pedagogical project aimed at helping readers overcome the psychological barriers, such as sentimentality, inhibition, or doctrinal prejudice, that prevent them from experiencing the full, organizing power of the text.Art is not a luxury, nor is it a separate aesthetic faculty. It is the most complex and delicate organisation of ordinary human experience that we possess. The activities of the poet do not differ in kind from the activities of the ordinary man; they differ only in their degree of organization, and in the efficiency with which they coordinate the complex resources of the nervous system.The Pedagogical and Theoretical Legacy: Towards Practical CriticismThe impact of Principles of Literary Criticism on the development of twentieth-century literary studies can hardly be overstated. Together with Richards’s subsequent volume, Practical Criticism (1929), the book laid the foundations for the pedagogical revolution that established English as a central academic discipline at Cambridge and beyond. By showing that the close, analytical reading of text could be separated from biographical and historical scholarship, Richards provided a methodology that could be taught in the classroom to students of all backgrounds.In the United States, Richards’s work was eagerly adopted and modified by the founders of the New Criticism, including Cleanth Brooks, John Crowe Ransom, and Allen Tate. However, the New Critics quickly abandoned Richards’s emphasis on psychology and neurology, viewing his focus on the reader's nervous system as a form of "affective fallacy" that distracted from the objective structure of the text itself. They kept Richards’s technique of close, formalist analysis, focusing on irony, paradox, and the balancing of tensions, while discarding his materialist framework.In the late twentieth century, Richards’s reputation suffered from the general reaction against formalism and the rise of structuralist and post-structuralist theories. Critics pointed out that his model of the "ideal reader" was culturally specific, assuming a universal human psychology that ignored the differences of gender, class, and historical context. Nevertheless, in the twenty-first century, Richards’s work has seen a quiet revival. The emergence of cognitive poetics, empirical aesthetics, and neuroaesthetics has validated many of his early insights, confirming that the experience of literature can indeed be studied as a dynamic, physiological reorganization of the human mind. His insistence that literature is not a decorative luxury but a vital instrument of human survival remains one of the most powerful defences of the humanities ever written.
critical_works.ch40: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941)Original title: A Room of One's Own (based on lectures delivered at Newnham and Girton Colleges)October 1929 · English · England · Modernism / Feminist Literary Criticism · Extended Essay / Feminist ManifestoThe Materialist Preconditions of Aesthetic ProductionVirginia Woolf’s A Room of One's Own, published in October 1929, is the foundational text of modern feminist literary criticism. Developed from a series of lectures delivered at Newnham and Girton, the women’s colleges at the University of Cambridge, in October 1928, the essay operates as a radical demystification of the creative process. Woolf famously announces her central, deceptively simple thesis in the opening pages: "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." By grounding the production of art in the concrete realities of economic security and physical space, Woolf rejects the Romantic myth of the artist as an unmediated genius whose inspiration operates independently of material circumstances. Writing, she insists, is a labor-intensive, social practice that requires leisure, privacy, and financial independence, privileges historically denied to women.The essay’s force lies in its refusal to treat literature as a purely intellectual or spiritual phenomenon. Woolf argues that the history of literature is inseparable from the history of wealth, class, and gender relations. To understand why women have written so few masterpieces, one must look not to their biological capacity or their psychological nature, but to their bank accounts and their domestic arrangements. Throughout history, women’s labour has been unpaid, their property has belonged to their husbands, and their time has been consumed by the endless demands of child-rearing and domestic maintenance. By insisting that "intellectual freedom depends upon material things," Woolf shifts the debate about women's writing away from essentialist assertions of inferiority and towards the structural inequalities of patriarchal society.The Fictionalised Persona: Narrative Strategy and Institutional ExclusionRather than delivering a conventional academic lecture or a structured polemic, Woolf adopts a fictionalised narrator to guide her readers through the process of her investigation. She invites the audience to discard the illusion of objective, authoritative truth, writing, "call me Mary Beton, Mary Seton, Mary Carmichael or by any name you please, it is not a matter of any importance." This narrative strategy allows Woolf to dramatise the experience of exclusion, transforming abstract political complaints into immediate, sensory realities. The reader travels with the narrator as she navigates the physical and institutional spaces of a fictionalised university she calls "Oxbridge," encountering the subtle and overt barriers that define women’s second-class status.The contrast between the male and female colleges is established through two vividly described dinners. At Oxbridge, the narrator attends a luxurious luncheon characterized by intellectual ease, culinary refinement, and financial abundance: the wine flows, the conversation is brilliant, and the dessert is served with a sense of historical continuity. This luxury is contrasted with the dreary dinner served at the women's college, "Fernham," where the food is cheap, the water is served in plain jugs, and the atmosphere is one of institutional poverty. Woolf uses these physical details to illustrate the material disparity between the sexes:This spatial exclusion is further dramatised when the narrator is chased off the university grass by a Beadle because she is a woman, and when she is barred from entering the university library unless accompanied by a male scholar. Through these narrative encounters, Woolf demonstrates that the university, and by extension, the entire tradition of Western culture, is a guarded fortress designed to preserve male privilege and exclude the female mind.One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well. The lamp in the spine does not light on beef and prunes. We cannot write well if we are constantly reminded of our poverty and our lack of status.Judith Shakespeare: The Genealogy of SilenceTo answer the historical question of why there was no female equivalent to William Shakespeare in the Elizabethan era, Woolf constructs a brilliant, tragic thought experiment. She imagines that Shakespeare had a wonderfully gifted sister, whom she names Judith:Judith possesses the same poetic genius, the same quickness of mind, and the same passion for the theatre as her brother. Yet, because she is a woman in a patriarchal society, her destiny is entirely different.While William is educated at the local grammar school, learns Latin, and eventually runs away to London to seek his fortune in the theatre, Judith is kept at home. Her parents deny her education, beating her when she attempts to read her brother’s books, and forcing her into an early, arranged marriage. When Judith rebels and flees to London, she finds every door closed to her. The theatre managers laugh in her face, refusing to train a woman for the stage. Desperate, exploitation follows: she is taken in by an actor-manager, Nick Greene, becomes pregnant by him, and, realizing the impossibility of ever fulfilling her artistic potential in a world that treats her as a commodity, kills herself in despair, buried at some crossroads where the omnibuses now stop.Through the figure of Judith Shakespeare, Woolf represents the vast, silent history of suppressed female talent. Judith is not an isolated casualty; she stands for the millions of women whose creative energy was crushed by the domestic sphere, the lack of education, and the threat of social disgrace. Woolf argues that the "mute inglorious Shakespeares" of history did not fail because they lacked genius, but because the material conditions of their lives rendered the expression of that genius fatal.It is thinkable that she may have been born, or have lived, in the sixteenth century... let me imagine, since facts are so hard to come by, what would have happened if Shakespeare had had a wonderfully gifted sister, called Judith, let us say.Thinking Back Through Our Mothers: The Female Literary LineageWoolf’s materialist history of literature leads to a theory of collective creation. She rejects the idea that great books are the solitary births of isolated geniuses, arguing instead that masterpieces are the accumulation of a communal history:For a woman writer, this collective history is particularly important because she has had no established tradition to support her. Woolf famously declares: "We think back through our mothers if we are women."To write fiction, a woman must have a sense of her own literary ancestry. Woolf traces this lineage, starting with the early pioneers who earned the right for women to write at all. She pays tribute to Aphra Behn, a middle-class woman who made her living by her pen in the seventeenth century, demonstrating that writing could be a respectable profession. This breakthrough allowed subsequent writers like Jane Austen and Charlotte Brontë to inherit a space in which they could work.However, Woolf also identifies the scars that this history of exclusion has left on female writing. She compares the style of Jane Austen, who wrote in the shared family sitting room, with that of Charlotte Brontë. Austen, she argues, managed to preserve a natural, balanced style, writing "as a woman writes, not as a man writes," without anger or defensiveness. In contrast, Woolf argues that Brontë’s style in Jane Eyre is deformed by a justifiable but aesthetically disruptive anger. The protagonist’s sudden outbursts against her domestic confinement are, for Woolf, moments where the writer’s personal resentment overrides the integrity of the fictional world. To write great literature, the artist must transcend their personal grievances, achieving a state of incandescent clarity that anger prevents.For masterpieces are not single and solitary births; they are the outcome of many years of thinking in common, of thinking by the body of the people, so that the experience of the mass is behind the single voice.The Androgynous Mind: Incandescence and the Reconciliation of SexThe final movement of A Room of One's Own introduces Woolf’s theory of the "androgynous mind," a concept she borrows from Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Woolf argues that the greatest creative minds are those that transcend the boundaries of sex-consciousness, fusing both masculine and feminine qualities to achieve a state of incandescence:The purely masculine mind is characterized by a hard, aggressive, linear logic, while the purely feminine mind is characterized by a soft, receptive, associative thinking. When either quality dominates, the work of art becomes sterile.Woolf criticises the modern literature of the 1920s for its obsessive, defensive sex-consciousness. She notes that the rise of the feminist movement has made men writers anxious about their masculinity, leading to a style that is aggressively, defensively patriarchal. Similarly, she warns women writers against writing out of a purely female consciousness, as this leads to a literature of protest rather than creation. The ideal creative state is one of balance and integration, represented by writers like Shakespeare, Keats, and Sterne, whose minds are "man-womanly" or "woman-manly." The androgynous mind does not ignore gender; rather, it allows both elements to collaborate, creating a work that is whole, resonant, and free from the distorting pressures of sexual politics.The androgynous mind is resonant and porous; it transmits emotion without impediment; it is naturally creative, incandescent and undivided. A mind that is purely masculine or purely feminine cannot create lasting art because it is too self-conscious.The Legacy: Woolf and the Foundations of Feminist PoeticsThe legacy of A Room of One's Own is central to the development of feminist theory throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. In the 1970s, during the second wave of feminism, critics like Elaine Showalter drew on Woolf’s work to construct "gynocriticism," a critical methodology dedicated to recovering forgotten women writers and mapping the distinct characteristics of the female literary tradition. Similarly, Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar’s monumental study, The Madwoman in the Attic (1979), expanded Woolf's analysis of Charlotte Brontë and Jane Austen, exploring the psychological conflicts and strategies of subversion deployed by nineteenth-century women writers struggling against patriarchal constraints.In French feminism, writers like Hélène Cixous and Luce Irigaray responded to Woolf’s call for a female style, developing the concept of écriture féminine (female writing), a practice that seeks to dismantle the linear, phallogocentric structures of language and replace them with a fluid, somatic, and associative writing. While some contemporary critics have questioned Woolf's class privileges, pointing out that her demand for "five hundred a year" was a considerable sum that excluded working-class women, her materialist emphasis remains a vital tool for analysing cultural production. In the contemporary era of academic precarity, the gig economy, and the erosion of public funding for the arts, Woolf's reminder that creative work requires physical space, economic security, and structural support remains as urgent and revolutionary as it was in 1929.
critical_works.ch41: William Empson (1906–1984)Original title: Seven Types of Ambiguity1930 · English · England · New Criticism / Close Reading · Practical Criticism / Close ReadingThe Cambridge Genesis and the Audacity of Close ReadingWilliam Empson’s Seven Types of Ambiguity, published in 1930, is one of the most audacious and influential works of literary criticism in the twentieth century. Written largely when Empson was a twenty-three-year-old undergraduate mathematics student at Magdalene College, Cambridge, under the supervision of I. A. Richards, the book represents a brilliant application of analytical rigor to the seeming vagueness of poetic language. Richards had already begun his revolution in English studies with his lectures on practical criticism, demanding that students confront texts directly, stripped of biographical context, historical introductions, or authorial reputations. Empson took this embryonic method of close reading and supercharged it with a hyper-observant, almost microscopic style of analysis. The result was a text that challenged the traditional parameters of literary interpretation and showed that poetic language thrives not on neoclassical clarity or singular referential correctness, but on complexity, density, and the fertile coexistence of multiple meanings.The genesis of the book reflects a unique intersection of scientific training and literary curiosity. Empson's mathematical background provided him with a structural perspective on language; he viewed a poem not as a passive vehicle for emotional expression, but as a complex machine whose linguistic components could be disassembled and analysed. Working under Richards, Empson applied this analytical machinery to the canon of English poetry, producing readings that were dizzying in their detail and speculative energy. Where older critics sought to resolve syntactic difficulties or textual cruxes in favour of a single, harmonious interpretation, Empson revelled in the difficulties themselves, arguing that the true power of poetry resides in its capacity to sustain multiple, often conflicting, lines of thought simultaneously. The audacity of Seven Types of Ambiguity lay in its systematic dismantling of the nineteenth-century view of poetry as a simple cry of the heart, replacing it with an image of the poet as a master engineer of semantic complexity.Redefining Ambiguity as Poetic ResonanceTo execute this project, Empson had to perform a radical redefinition of "ambiguity" itself. In the traditions of classical rhetoric, formal logic, and neoclassical aesthetics, ambiguity was universally regarded as a structural defect. It was seen as a failure of clarity, a symptom of sloppy grammar or imprecise thinking that obstructed the transmission of the author's message. Neoclassical critics like Alexander Pope and Samuel Johnson valued perspicuity and correctness, viewing any linguistic double-dealing as an obstacle to the reader's understanding. Empson turned this long-standing hierarchy on its head, arguing that what is a vice in prose logic is the supreme virtue of poetic discourse. In the opening chapter of the book, Empson establishes his famously broad definition of the term:By defining ambiguity not as a logical error but as "any verbal nuance" that "gives room for alternative reactions," Empson shifts the focus of criticism in two profound ways. First, he locates the meaning of a poem not in a single, static intention hidden in the author's mind, but in the dynamic interaction between the verbal structures on the page and the interpretive capacity of the reader. Second, he argues that the value of poetry is directly proportional to its semantic density. A scientific statement must be unambiguous to be useful, but a poetic statement must be ambiguous to be beautiful. The "machinations of ambiguity," Empson asserts, "are among the very roots of poetry." Poetic language is inherently multi-layered, utilizing the historical associations, syntactic ambiguities, and phonetic echoes of words to create a rich, multidimensional experience that cannot be reduced to a single, paraphrasable message.I propose to use the word "ambiguity" in an extended sense, and shall think any verbal nuance, however slight, which gives room for alternative reactions to the same piece of language, worth writing down, as containing it.The Taxonomy of Complexity: The Seven TypesThe core of Empson’s treatise is his classification of ambiguity into seven distinct types, arranged in a ascending scale of complexity, tension, and psychological conflict. This taxonomy is not a rigid scientific system, but rather a flexible pedagogical tool that allows Empson to demonstrate how different kinds of verbal complexity function in practice.The first type of ambiguity represents the most common and fundamental form of poetic language:In this category, Empson places the standard operations of metaphor and simile. When a poet compares one object to another, the comparison is effective because the reader is invited to hold multiple points of similarity in mind at the same time. The meanings do not conflict; rather, they cooperate to enrich the primary image.The second type of ambiguity occurs when two or more alternative meanings resolve into a single, unified meaning. This type is particularly common in Elizabethan and Jacobean drama, where syntactic flexibility allows a word or phrase to point in two different directions at once. For example, a single adjective might modify both the noun that precedes it and the noun that follows it, forcing the reader to integrate both grammatical possibilities into their understanding of the passage. The alternative readings do not cancel each other out; they collapse into a single, complex apprehension of the text.The third type of ambiguity occurs when two apparently unconnected meanings are given at once, as in puns, wordplay, and allegories. Here, a single word acts as a bridge between two completely different semantic fields. The poet uses this double meaning to suggest a hidden relationship between two disparate ideas, forcing the reader to contemplate both fields of reference simultaneously. In this type, the alternative meanings do not merge into a single sense, but remain distinct, hanging in a state of productive tension.The fourth type of ambiguity occurs when alternative meanings combine to show a complicated state of mind in the author. In this category, the linguistic complexity of the text is no longer just a formal device, but a symptom of the writer's psychological state. The ambiguity reveals that the author is holding two or more different feelings or attitudes towards their subject at the same time, and is using the text to negotiate or express this internal complexity.The fifth type of ambiguity represents what Empson calls a "fortunate confusion." This occurs when a writer is feeling their way towards a thought, or when two metaphors overlap, creating a fertile conceptual blur. In these instances, the writer does not have a clear, pre-conceived message to convey; instead, the process of writing is itself a search for meaning. The ambiguity is not a deliberate choice, but a necessary consequence of the mind operating at the limits of its conceptual and linguistic capacities.The sixth type of ambiguity occurs when a statement says nothing, forcing the reader to invent a meaning. This type includes tautologies, contradictions, and irrelevant details. When a text presents a statement that is logically empty or structurally redundant, the reader's mind, refusing to accept the lack of meaning, is forced to supply its own interpretation. The ambiguity lies in the space between the literal emptiness of the words and the semantic richness that the reader projects onto them.The seventh type of ambiguity represents the most extreme and psychologically intense category. It occurs when two meanings are opposite, showing a fundamental division or unresolved conflict in the author's mind. In these cases, the ambiguity is a symptom of deep psychological contradiction:Here, the poem becomes a battlefield where competing desires, beliefs, or loyalties clash, and the language itself splits under the pressure of this internal division.First-type ambiguities arise when a detail is effective in several ways at once, e.g. by comparisons with several points of likeness, or by a metaphor where several elements of the meaning are relevant.The seventh type of ambiguity occurs when the two meanings of the word, the two values of the ambiguity, are the two opposite meanings defined by the context, so that the total effect is to show a fundamental division in the writer’s mind.Close Reading in Action: The Empsonian MethodThe true power of Seven Types of Ambiguity lies not in its abstract classifications, but in the dazzling, concrete close readings that fill its pages. Empson’s method is characterised by an extraordinary sensitivity to the micro-tensions of syntax and a relentless curiosity about the historical and etymological associations of words.A prime example of this method is Empson's famous analysis of a line from Shakespeare’s Sonnet 73: "Bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang." Empson dissects the comparison between the boughs of trees in winter and the ruined belfries of monastery churches, showing how the line gathers its emotional power through a cluster of overlapping associations:Furthermore, Empson notes that the image evokes the historical trauma of the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII, as well as the contemporary fear of Puritanism, which viewed these ruinous structures with a mixture of hostility and nostalgia. By tracing these diverse threads of meaning, Empson demonstrates that the beauty of the line is not a simple, unified effect, but a complex chord of historical, visual, and architectural suggestions that the reader holds in tension.Empson applies the same microscopic attention to the metaphysical poetry of John Donne and George Herbert. In analysing Donne’s complex syntactic structures, Empson shows how the poet uses double negatives, parenthetical insertions, and shifting pronouns to enact the speaker's intellectual and emotional struggles. Meaning is not presented as a finished product; it is dramatised as a process of active thinking, in which each syntactic choice represents a fork in the road of thought. Through these readings, Empson teaches the reader to slow down, to suspend the desire for quick resolutions, and to appreciate the complex, multi-layered texture of the poetic word.Ruined monastery choirs are places in which to sing, because they were made in a renaissance of social order, and because they are now abandoned, cold, and ruined, and because they have the same shape... and because they are coloured with stained glass and painting like flowers and leaves, and because they are now abandoned by all but the grey walls, coloured like the skies of winter.The Rejection of Neoclassical Clarity and the Legacy of Close ReadingEmpson’s work represents a decisive rejection of the neoclassical demand for clarity and the belief that literature is a machine for conveying pre-formulated truths. Against this view, Empson argues that poetry is a unique mode of discourse that uses language to explore the limits of human consciousness. By showing that even the simplest lyric is shot through with ambiguity and internal contradiction, Empson freed criticism from the duty of policing linguistic correctness, transforming it instead into an act of creative collaboration with the text.The legacy of Seven Types of Ambiguity was immense, though it did not always align with Empson’s own critical commitments. The book became a founding text of the New Criticism, the formalist movement that dominated academic literary studies in the mid-twentieth century. Critics like Cleanth Brooks, John Crowe Ransom, and Allen Tate adopted Empson’s technique of close analysis, making the study of irony, paradox, and tension the core of their methodology. However, the American New Critics quickly grew uncomfortable with Empson’s psychological and authorial interests. In their attempt to establish criticism as an objective discipline, they formulated the "intentional fallacy" and the "affective fallacy," arguing that the critic must focus exclusively on the internal structure of the text, ignoring both the author's biography and the reader's subjective reactions.Empson, by contrast, never abandoned his interest in the human element of literature. For him, ambiguity was not a self-contained linguistic game, but a reflection of the complexity of human life and the difficulty of moral decision-making. He viewed poetry as a means of communicating across differences, and close reading as an ethical training in empathy and nuance. In the late twentieth century, as literary theory shifted towards post-structuralism and deconstruction, Empson's work was reread in a new light. Jacques Derrida and Paul de Man praised his recognition of the instability of language, though they argued that Empson had stopped short of acknowledging the ultimate, unresolvable self-contradiction of all texts. Yet, where deconstruction saw only the failure of language to mean anything stable, Empson saw the triumphs of language in meaning so many things at once. His insistence that literature is a vital, complex, and humanly significant form of communication remains a powerful defence of close reading as an indispensable critical practice.
critical_works.ch42: Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937)Original title: Quaderni del carcere (written in prison, published posthumously)c. 1929–1935 (published in volumes 1948–1951) · Italian · Italy (Fascist Prison) · Western Marxism / Cultural Studies Precursor · Notebook Fragments / Cultural TheoryThe Fascist Prison and the Function of the Imprisoned BrainThe Prison Notebooks of Antonio Gramsci represent one of the most remarkable intellectual achievements of the twentieth century, produced under conditions of extreme physical deprivation and political persecution. Gramsci, a founding member and leader of the Italian Communist Party (PCI), was arrested by Benito Mussolini’s Fascist regime in November 1926, despite his parliamentary immunity. During his trial in 1928, the Fascist prosecutor famously declared: "We must stop this brain from functioning for twenty years." Sentenced to more than two decades of imprisonment, Gramsci was sent to the penal clinic at Turi and later to clinics in Formia and Rome, where his health deteriorated catastrophically. Suffering from tuberculosis, Pott’s disease, and severe gastrointestinal illnesses, he was kept in a state of slow physical decay. Yet, between 1929 and 1935, Gramsci managed to fill thirty-three school exercise books with almost three thousand pages of dense, fragmentary essays, historical analyses, and theoretical notes.Writing under the watchful eye of Fascist prison censors, Gramsci was forced to adopt a highly coded, Aesopian language. He avoided explicit Marxist terminology, replacing sensitive terms with neutral academic equivalents. Marx became "the founder of the philosophy of praxis," Lenin was referred to as "Ilyich" or "the greatest modern theorist of praxis," class struggle was described as the relation of "social groups," and the communist party became "the Modern Prince," a reference to Niccolò Machiavelli’s political treatise. Far from merely hiding his revolutionary commitments, this enforced obliqueness paradoxically liberated Gramsci’s thought from the rigid, dogmatic formulas of Soviet Marxism, which had hardened under Joseph Stalin into an economistic determinism. The fragmentary and open-ended nature of the Prison Notebooks allowed Gramsci to construct a highly sophisticated, flexible, and culturally sensitive Marxist theory that placed human agency, historical specificity, and cultural institutions at the centre of political analysis.The Mechanics of Hegemony: Rule by Consent and CoercionGramsci’s most significant contribution to modern political and cultural theory is his elaboration of the concept of "cultural hegemony" (egemonia culturale). Traditional Marxist theory in the early twentieth century tended to view the state as a simple, unified instrument of class oppression, operating exclusively through the coercive apparatus of the police, the military, and the judiciary. In this view, culture and ideology were dismissed as mere reflections of the economic base, with no autonomous power of their own. Gramsci challenges this reductionist model by dividing the capitalist superstructure into two major spheres: political society and civil society. Political society is the realm of coercion, force, and direct domination, exercised through public institutions such as the state bureaucracy, the police, and the armed forces. Civil society, by contrast, is the realm of consent, persuasion, and moral leadership, operating through private and non-governmental institutions such as schools, churches, media, trade unions, families, and literary organisations.For Gramsci, capitalist rule is maintained both through the raw force of political society and through the intellectual and moral leadership exercised within civil society. Hegemony is the process by which a ruling class wins the "spontaneous consent" of subordinate classes, persuading them to accept its own worldview, values, and economic interests as natural, universal, and beneficial to all. This consent is built by shaping the "common sense" (senso comune) of the masses, the uncritical, fragmented, and traditional way in which ordinary people perceive the world. By aligning civil society institutions with its own interests, the ruling class ensures that its dominance appears not as an act of violence, but as a matter of common-sense reality. In a famous passage from Notebook 19, Gramsci explains this dual nature of class power:Hegemony is never a static, permanent state of affairs; it is a dynamic, continuously contested process. The ruling class must constantly work to maintain, repair, and renegotiate its moral and intellectual leadership, adapting to changing historical circumstances and absorbing the resistance of subordinate groups.The supremacy of a social group manifests itself in two ways, as "domination" and as "intellectual and moral leadership." A social group dominates antagonistic groups, which it tends to "liquidate," or to subjugate perhaps even by armed force; it leads kindred and allied groups. A social group can, and indeed must, already exercise "leadership" before winning governmental power (this indeed is one of the principal conditions for the winning of such power); it subsequently becomes dominant when it exercises power, but even if it holds it firmly in its grasp, it must continue to "lead" as well.The Social Function of IntellectualsCentral to the creation and maintenance of cultural hegemony is the role of intellectuals. Gramsci rejects the traditional, romantic view of the intellectual as a detached, autonomous thinker standing above the conflicts of class society. He argues that intellectuals are defined not by the intrinsic nature of their mental activities, but by the social function they perform within civil society. Gramsci famously asserts that "all men are intellectuals, one could therefore say: but not all men have in society the function of intellectuals." to clarify this, he uses the analogy of physical labour: while everyone might fry an egg or sew a tear in their clothing, we do not classify everyone as a professional cook or tailor. Similarly, while every human being uses their intellect and possesses a specific worldview, only certain individuals occupy the social role of professional intellectuals, whose task is to organise, articulate, and disseminate ideas.Gramsci identifies two distinct categories of intellectuals: traditional intellectuals and organic intellectuals. Traditional intellectuals are those who view themselves as independent of class struggles, representing a historical continuity that transcends political regimes (such as priests, academic scholars, traditional artists, and philosophers). Gramsci argues that this sense of independence is a historical illusion; while traditional intellectuals may feel detached, they historically serve to maintain the ideological stability of the existing order. Organic intellectuals, by contrast, are those who emerge directly from a newly rising social class, created by that class to give it homogeneity, self-consciousness, and political organisation. A rising capitalist class, for instance, produces organic intellectuals in the form of industrial managers, economic experts, engineers, and political publicists. For the working class to challenge capitalist hegemony, it must develop its own organic intellectuals, activists, journalists, union organisers, and educators, who can articulate the experiences of the subaltern classes and build a counter-hegemonic culture.The Disconnect of the National-Popular in Italian CultureGramsci applies this theoretical framework to a detailed critique of Italian history and literature, focusing on the historical concept of the "national-popular" (nazionale-popolare). He observes that Italian literature has historically failed to achieve a national-popular character, in sharp contrast to the literary traditions of France, England, or Russia. Gramsci attributes this failure to the historical separation of Italian intellectuals from the common people. Since the Renaissance, Italian writers and scholars have functioned as a closed, cosmopolitan "caste," writing in a highly refined, classical language (such as literary Tuscan) that was completely alien to the dialect-speaking masses. They were more interested in academic prestige and stylistic purity than in addressing the actual worries, struggles, and needs of the common people.Because Italian literature remained the preserve of an elite caste, the Italian masses felt culturally alienated from their own national writers. Gramsci notes that when the common people read for pleasure, they consistently preferred translated French serial novels (such as the works of Alexandre Dumas or Eugène Sue) because these works, despite their sensationalist plots, captured the popular imagination and dealt with themes of social justice and historical drama. The lack of a national-popular literature in Italy was not merely an aesthetic problem; it was a profound political weakness.
