It is used whenever the speaker and listener need to discuss the language itself, checking whether they are using the same sign system (e.g., "What do you mean by 'poetics'?", or "This word is a noun").The Poetic Function: Oriented toward the Message. It is the focus on the message "for its own sake," showing the formal, tangible qualities of the signs themselves.Jakobson stresses that the poetic function is not restricted to poetry, just as poetry is not exclusively poetic in function. A political slogan like "I like Ike" utilises the poetic function through its rhythmic, rhyming structure to make the message memorable and self-reflective, but its dominant goal is conative. However, in verbal art, the poetic function is the dominant, defining function, subordinating the referential, emotive, and conative aspects to the structural pattern of the message itself.The Projection of Equivalence: The Axis of Selection and the Axis of CombinationThe theoretical climax of Jakobson’s address is his famous definition of the poetic function’s formal mechanism. To explain how poetry achieves its unique density and self-reflexivity, he introduces the two basic axes of linguistic arrangement: the axis of selection and the axis of combination.The Axis of Selection (associated with the paradigmatic dimension of language) involves choosing words from the internal dictionary or lexicon based on relationships of similarity, synonymy, antonymy, or equivalence. For example, if a speaker wants to describe a child, they select a word from a pool of equivalent terms: "child," "kid," "tot," or "youngster." The speaker chooses one based on tone, register, or context. The relationship between these words is one of similarity.The Axis of Combination (associated with the syntagmatic dimension) involves arranging the selected words into a linear, grammatical sequence to form a sentence. If the speaker selects the noun "child" and the verb "sleeps," they combine them into the sequence "The child sleeps." The relationship between these combined words is one of contiguity or syntax.In ordinary, non-poetic communication, the principle of equivalence is used only to select words, whilst the combination is governed by grammatical rules. Jakobson (1960, p. 358) argues that the poetic function alters this relationship:In poetry, equivalence is no longer confined to the internal phase of word choice; it is projected onto the physical sequence of speech. Words are combined both because they fit grammatically and because they share formal similarities in sound, rhythm, syllable count, stress, or meaning. The linear sequence is forced to mirror the associative relationships of similarity, making the structure of the message itself dense, symmetrical, and self-reflective.The poetic function projects the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection into the axis of combination.Phonology, Metaphor, and the Structural Autonomy of the MessageBy projecting the principle of equivalence onto the axis of combination, the poet creates a complex network of formal symmetries. Jakobson demonstrates how this mechanism manifests in various poetic structures, particularly through the use of rhythm, metre, rhyme, and syntactic parallelism.In a metred poem, syllables are arranged into regular patterns of stressed and unstressed units. This means that consecutive units in the sequence are treated as equivalent in duration or accent, forcing the reader to experience the physical, phonological texture of the language. Similarly, rhyme is the repetition of equivalent sounds at regular intervals in the combination, creating a structural link between different words and reinforcing their semantic relationships. Jakobson argues that in poetry, any similarity in sound implies a similarity in meaning; the formal pattern of the text generates new, complex semantic resonances that would not exist in ordinary prose.This projection also explains the structural role of metaphor and metonymy. Jakobson famously associates the axis of selection with metaphor (which relies on similarity) and the axis of combination with metonymy (which relies on contiguity). In poetic discourse, because the combination is structured by similarity, the text becomes highly metaphorical. The message is no longer a transparent window looking out at an external context; instead, it becomes a self-contained, autonomous structure where the signs interact with one another to produce a dense web of internal references. The referential function is suspended or made ambiguous, allowing the aesthetic and formal qualities of the language to take centre stage.The Legacy of Prague Structuralism and the Science of LiteratureRoman Jakobson’s Linguistics and Poetics exercised a massive influence on the development of twentieth-century literary theory, serving as a primary catalyst for the structuralist movement of the 1960s and 1970s. By offering a rigorous, objective model of verbal communication, Jakobson provided a blueprint for critics who wished to move beyond subjective, impressionistic appreciation and establish a true "science of literature." His work was eagerly adopted and expanded by French structuralists such as Roland Barthes, Tzvetan Todorov, and Gérard Genette, who sought to analyse narrative and poetic structures with the same systematic precision that Jakobson applied to phonology and syntax.However, Jakobson’s linguistic imperialism did not escape critique. Post-structuralist critics argued that his model, whilst elegant, was overly rigid and closed, assuming a stable, shared code between addresser and addressee that ignores the inherent instability, ambiguity, and play of language. Deconstructive readers pointed out that the "message" cannot be isolated as a self-contained object, because the context and the code are always contaminated by trace and difference.Furthermore, some literary critics complained that Jakobson’s close linguistic analyses, whilst technically impressive, often failed to explain the historical, political, or emotional significance of a poem, reducing the experience of art to a sterile exercise in grammatical pattern-hunting. Nevertheless, Linguistics and Poetics remains a monumental text. It changed how we read literature, proving that the aesthetic power of poetry is not an elusive, mystical quality, but the direct result of the structural organization of language, where the sound, the syntax, and the sense are woven into a single, indivisible fabric.
critical_works.ch56: Jacques Lacan (1901–1981)Original title: Le Séminaire sur 'La Lettre volée' (published in Écrits)1955; published 1956, collected in Écrits (1966) · French · France · Structuralist Psychoanalysis / Lacanian Theory · Psychoanalytic Seminar / Textual AnalysisThe Primacy of the Signifier: Psychoanalysis through PoeJacques Lacan’s The Seminar on 'The Purloined Letter', first delivered in 1955 as the opening address of his seminar series and later placed at the very beginning of his collected Écrits in 1966, represents one of the most celebrated and complex intersections of psychoanalysis and literary criticism. Rather than using Edgar Allan Poe’s famous detective story as a clinical case study of the author’s psyche, Lacan uses it to illustrate a fundamental, structuralist thesis: that the human subject is constituted and directed by the symbolic order. For Lacan, the path of the subject is determined not by biology, individual agency, or psychological depth, but by the movement and displacement of the signifier, symbolised in Poe's narrative by the purloined letter itself.Lacan’s reading shifts the focus of literary analysis away from the psychological motivations of Poe's characters or the referential meaning of the text. He notes that the contents of the letter are never revealed; we never learn who wrote it, what it says, or why its disclosure would threaten the royal household. The letter is a "pure signifier", an empty vessel that derives its power entirely from its position within a relational network. By tracing how the letter circulates from the Queen to the Minister, and finally to the detective Dupin, Lacan demonstrates that the characters do not control the signifier; rather, the signifier controls them, dictating their actions, their desire, and their subjective identities as it passes through their hands.The Triad of Glances: The Spatial Mapping of IntersubjectivityThe structural core of Lacan’s seminar is his spatial and visual mapping of Poe's narrative into two parallel, symmetrical scenes: the initial theft of the letter in the royal boudoir, and its subsequent recovery by Dupin in the Minister’s office. Lacan argues that both scenes are structured by a triad of glances, borne by three subjects who occupy distinct positions within the symbolic circuit. In each scene, these three positions remain constant, even though they are occupied by different characters.The first position is defined by the First Glance: a gaze that sees nothing, leaving the subject in a state of absolute blindness. In the first scene, this position is occupied by the King, who is completely oblivious to the letter’s presence and the domestic drama unfolding before him. In the second scene, this position is occupied by the Prefect of Police and his officers, whose empirical, hyper-rational search of the Minister's apartments fails to locate the letter because they can only look for it in hidden, expected places.The second position is defined by the Second Glance: a gaze that sees that the first glance sees nothing, and consequently deludes itself into believing that its own possession or concealment of the letter is secure. In the first scene, this is the position of the Queen, who, seeing the King's blindness, leaves the letter exposed on the table, only to watch helplessly as the Minister steals it. In the second scene, this is the position of the Minister, who, seeing the blindness of the police, leaves the letter hanging in plain sight in a card rack, believing that this simple trick makes it invisible.The third position is defined by the Third Glance: a gaze that sees that the first two glances leave the letter exposed, allowing this subject to exploit the situation and seize the signifier. In the first scene, this is the Minister, who recognises the King’s blindness and the Queen’s vulnerability, and substitutes a worthless piece of paper for the compromising letter. In the second scene, this is the detective Dupin, who recognises the blindness of the police and the deluded security of the Minister, and executes an identical substitution to retrieve the letter.Lacan analyses how these positions are structurally determined. The characters do not act out of free will; they are caught in a repetitive machine where the holder of the second glance is always outmanoeuvred by the holder of the third. By entering the circuit of the letter, each character is forced to repeat the behaviour of their predecessor, demonstrating the compulsive power of the symbolic order.The Autonomy of the Signifier: The Letter as an Empty VesselA crucial element of Lacan’s reading is the assertion that the signifier is completely autonomous, existing independently of any fixed signified or referent. The letter in Poe's story has no intrinsic meaning; it is defined solely by its displacement. Lacan uses this to critique the traditional humanist view of language, which treats words as transparent signs pointing to stable concepts or objects in the real world. In the Symbolic Order, the signifier precedes the signified, structuring the subject's reality and desire.To illustrate this autonomy, Lacan points to the psychological transformation that occurs in whoever holds the letter. He argues that the possession of the signifier has a "feminising" effect, trapping the holder in a passive, vulnerable position. The Queen, whilst holding the letter, is reduced to anxious passivity, unable to hide it from the King. When the Minister steals the letter, he does not gain absolute power; instead, he inherits the Queen’s vulnerability. The Minister, previously a man of decisive action, becomes passive, indolent, and blind to his own exposure, repeating the Queen’s mistake of leaving the letter in plain sight. In the Bruce Fink translation of the Écrits, Lacan (2006, p. 21) describes this structural curse:Even Dupin, upon retrieving the letter, is drawn into this same passive circuit. He delays delivering the letter to the Prefect, indulges in a lengthy, self-satisfied monologue, and reveals a personal, retaliatory motive against the Minister, showing that he too has been captured by the signifier's magnetic field. The letter acts as a symbolic master, restructuring the desire of anyone who attempts to possess it.The signifier is not sign, but signifier of the subject... its displacement determines subjects in their acts, in their destiny, in their refusals, in their blindnesses, in their end and in their fate.The Symbolic Post: Why the Letter Always Arrives at Its DestinationThe most controversial and widely debated claim in the seminar is Lacan’s concluding aphorism. To explain why the story must end with the letter returning to the Queen and restoring the initial balance, Lacan asserts that the signifier cannot be lost or diverted permanently. In the translation by Bruce Fink (2006, p. 30), Lacan writes:Lacan does not mean this as a literal claim about postal efficiency or teleological destiny. Rather, it is a structural necessity of the symbolic order.In Lacanian theory, the "destination" of the signifier is not a physical person or a geographical address, but the symbolic slot or position it must occupy within the intersubjective circuit. Even when the letter is stolen or hidden, it is never truly "lost" because its absence actively structures the relationships, desires, and anxieties of the characters. The Queen’s anxiety, the Minister’s delusion, and Dupin’s calculations are all coordinated by the missing letter. A letter always arrives at its destination because, within the Symbolic, the signifier always finds its place, returning to the subject their own message in an inverted form. The subject's path is determined by the trajectory of the signifier; we do not speak language, but are spoken by it, structured by the linguistic codes and symbolic networks that precede our birth.Thus, what the 'purloined letter'—nay, the 'letter en souffrance'—means is that a letter always arrives at its destination.The Derridean Critique: The Purveyor of Truth and the Writerly PlayLacan’s reading of Poe became a major flashpoint in continental philosophy, sparking a famous deconstructive response from Jacques Derrida in his essay Le Facteur de la vérité ("The Purveyor of Truth"), published in The Post Card (1980). Derrida launches a multi-pronged critique of Lacan’s seminar, accusing him of reducing Poe’s complex, polysemic literary text to a simple illustration of psychoanalytic dogma.First, Derrida argues that Lacan ignores the frame narrative and the complex literary structure of Poe's story. By focus exclusively on the two internal scenes, Lacan treats the text as a transparent document containing a structural truth, ignoring the role of the narrator and the writerly play of the prose. Second, Derrida disputes Lacan’s claim that the letter is an empty signifier. He notes that by defining the letter as a signifier that has a single, inevitable destination, Lacan is actually reinstating a form of "transcendental signified", a hidden truth or destination that anchors the text. For Derrida, a letter does not always arrive at its destination; it is in the very nature of writing (what he calls écriture) that it can always be lost, intercepted, fragmented, or fail to arrive. Derrida writes that Lacan's structuralism is a "phallogocentric" attempt to domesticate the radical instability of writing, imposing a clean, triadic structure onto a text that is characterized by infinite dissemination.Lacanian defenders, such as Barbara Johnson, have responded by pointing out that Derrida’s critique itself misreads Lacan. Johnson shows that Lacan’s triadic structure is not a closed system, but an open loop where the positions are constantly shifting, and that the "destination" is the very locus of displacement. This debate remains a classic text in literary studies, illustrating the fundamental tension between structuralism and post-structuralism, and showing the different ways in which psychoanalysis and deconstruction approach the problem of meaning, truth, and the text.The Legacy of Lacanian Literary Criticism: The Intersubjective CircuitDespite the Derridean challenge, The Seminar on 'The Purloined Letter' remains a foundational document for psychoanalytic literary theory and structuralist narrative analysis. It completely transformed how critics approach literature, showing how structural linguistics (derived from Ferdinand de Saussure and Roman Jakobson) can be combined with Freudian psychoanalysis to analyse the formal mechanics of a text.Lacan's seminar shifted literary criticism away from authorial biography and thematic paraphrase toward the study of narrative economy and the circulation of signs. The intersubjective circuit of the letter became a model for analysing how desire, power, and identity are negotiated in narrative fiction. Critics have applied Lacan’s model of the signifier’s displacement to a wide variety of works, from Shakespearean drama to modern detective fiction, demonstrating that the meaning of a text is not a hidden treasure to be excavated, but a dynamic effect generated by the circulation of language. By proving that the subject is always structured by the Symbolic, Lacan's seminar remains a vital reminder that when we read literature, we are more than decoding messages; we are tracing the paths of our own desire through the labyrinth of the signifier.
critical_works.ch57: Jacques Derrida (1930–2004)Original title: La structure, le signe et le jeu dans le discours des sciences humainesOctober 1966 (delivered at the Johns Hopkins University conference) · French · France / Algeria · Post-structuralism / Deconstruction · Conference Paper / Deconstructive CritiqueThe Rupture in the Johns Hopkins SymposiumIn October 1966, Johns Hopkins University hosted an international symposium titled "The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man." Designed to introduce French structuralism, then dominated by the scientific aspirations of anthropology, linguistics, and literary analysis, to the American academic community, the conference was intended to celebrate a unified methodology. Instead, it became the site of a profound philosophical rupture. Jacques Derrida, a relatively young philosopher, delivered a paper that did both critique structuralist methodology from within and dismantled its foundational assumptions. Rather than consolidating structuralism as the new master paradigm of the human sciences, Derrida's presentation announced its limit and initiated the intellectual shift that would come to be known as post-structuralism and deconstruction.Derrida’s intervention targets the very concept of structure that had sustained Western thought. In his opening remarks, he notes that "something has occurred in the history of the concept of structure that could be called an 'event,' if this loaded word did not entail a meaning which it is precisely the function of structural, or structuralist, thought to reduce or to suspect." This event is described as a "rupture," a moment of self-reflexivity where language and structure began to look at themselves, exposing the instability that lies at the core of all systems of meaning. The promise of structuralism had been to locate stable, underlying laws of culture and literature, analogous to the grammar of a language. Derrida demonstrates that this search for stability is itself caught within the classical metaphysical tradition it claims to supersede.The rupture is not a sudden accident but a necessary crisis within the history of philosophy. It occurs when the structurality of structure begins to be thought. Up to this point, structure had been understood as an arrangement of parts around a stable core, but the core itself had been left unexamined. By bringing the structurality of structure into view, Derrida shows that what had previously been taken as a secure foundation is actually a product of linguistic differentiation. The shift from structuralism to post-structuralism is therefore not a rejection of structural analysis, but an expansion of it to the point where the analyst must acknowledge that there is no position outside of language from which a structure can be objectively mapped.The Illusion of the Stable Centre and the Transcendental SignifiedAt the heart of Derrida's critique is the concept of the "centre." Derrida argues that the history of Western metaphysics is a history of structures that have always been anchored by a centre, origin, or ground. The function of this centre is both to orient and balance the system and to limit what Derrida calls the "play" (jeu) of its elements. By providing a fixed point of reference, the centre ensures that the elements of the structure remain coherent and predictable. However, Derrida points out a fundamental paradox in this arrangement: the centre is that which governs the structure, but because it is the organising principle, it must remain immune to the structural laws that govern the rest of the system. It sits both inside and outside the structure. Derrida writes:The centre is therefore not a physical location or an objective reality, but a theological and metaphysical projection designed to ward off the anxiety of infinite instability. Throughout the history of Western philosophy, this centre has received various names: eidos, arche, telos, energia, ousia (essence, existence, substance), aletheia, transcendentality, consciousness, God, or Man. Each of these terms functions as a "transcendental signified", a signified that refers directly to an absolute presence, standing outside the chain of signification and requiring no further translation or interpretation. It is the final authority that stops the play of language.Derrida’s deconstructive move is to show that this transcendental signified is an illusion. Meaning is never fully present in a single sign; it is always deferred, produced through a network of differences. When the centre is recognized as a projection, the structure is "decentred." Without a organising core that stands outside the system, every signified is revealed to be already in the position of a signifier. The absence of a transcendental signified does not mean that meaning is impossible, but rather that it is infinite and unstable. Language becomes a space of play where there are no absolute reference points, and every attempt to establish a final meaning is exposed as a temporary, historical gesture of exclusion.The concept of centered structure is in fact the concept of a play based on a fundamental ground, a play constituted on the basis of a fundamental immobility and a reassuring certitude, which itself is beyond the reach of play. On the basis of this certitude anxiety can be mastered, for anxiety is invariably the result of a certain mode of being implicated in the game, of being caught in the game, of being as it were at stake in the game from the outset.Bricolage and the Demolition of the EngineerTo demonstrate how the centre operates within the human sciences, Derrida focuses on the anthropological work of Claude Lévi-Strauss. Lévi-Strauss’s structuralist project sought to identify the universal structures of human culture by analysing myths and social practices. In The Elementary Structures of Kinship, Lévi-Strauss encounters a conceptual obstacle that Derrida seizes upon: the "incest taboo." In classical anthropology, nature and culture are treated as mutually exclusive categories. Nature is defined as universal, spontaneous, and biological, while culture is characterized as historical, variable, and subject to social law.The incest taboo, however, refuses to fit into this binary opposition. It is universal, occurring in all human societies, which suggests it belongs to nature. At the same time, it is a prohibition, a social rule that regulates behaviour through law, which identifies it as cultural. For Lévi-Strauss, this is a scandal, a breakdown in his analytical categories. Derrida argues that the incest taboo is not a minor exception to the rule, but the point at which the nature-culture binary itself collapses. The opposition between nature and culture is shown to be a historical construction rather than an objective truth. By attempting to force human experience into this artificial division, structuralism exposes its own conceptual limits.Derrida uses this example to re-evaluate Lévi-Strauss’s discussion of "bricolage." In The Savage Mind, Lévi-Strauss contrasts two figures: the "engineer" and the "bricoleur." The engineer is a mythic figure who constructs coherent, totalised systems from scratch, designing tools specifically for the task at hand. The engineer represents the ideal of scientific, rationalist discourse, operating from a position of objective neutrality. The bricoleur, by contrast, is an odd-job man who uses whatever tools and materials are currently available, adapting them to new purposes without pretending to have a master plan.Derrida deconstructs this opposition by asserting that the "engineer" is a fiction. No one can speak or write from a position of absolute neutrality, completely free from the history of the language they inherit. We must always borrow our tools from the very language we seek to critique. Derrida writes:By demonstrating that the engineer is a myth, Derrida reframes the critic’s task. The deconstructive critic does not attempt to construct a perfect, objective theory from a position of exteriority. Instead, like the bricoleur, the critic works within the ruins of the existing system, using its own terms and contradictions to dismantle it from the inside.If one calls bricolage the necessity of borrowing one’s concepts from the text of a heritage which is more or less coherent or ruined, it must be said that every discourse is bricolage. The engineer, whom Lévi-Strauss opposes to the bricoleur, should be the one who constructs the totality of his language, syntax, and lexicon in all their parts. In this sense, the engineer is a myth, a invent-phrase of the bricoleur. As soon as we admit that every finite discourse is bound by a system of differences, the engineer is out of a job and the critic is revealed as a bricoleur.Logocentrism and the Decentring of Western MetaphysicsDerrida’s critique of structuralism is part of a broader critique of what he calls "logocentrism." Logocentrism is the structural bias of Western philosophy that privileges the logos, speech, reason, presence, and truth, over writing. In this tradition, speech is assumed to be directly connected to the speaker’s mind, offering an unmediated expression of thought. Writing, by contrast, has historically been dismissed as a secondary, fallen copy of speech, a technology that introduces distance, absence, and the potential for misunderstanding.This logocentric bias is closely linked to "phonocentrism," which privileges the voice as the medium of presence. When we speak, our voice seems immediately present to us, creating the illusion that thought and expression are unified in the same moment. Derrida argues that this ideal of self-presence is the foundation of Western metaphysics. Structuralism, despite its scientific claims, remains phonocentric and logocentric because it searches for an underlying grammar or system that is present behind cultural phenomena, treating signs as transparent vessels for pre-existing meanings.By decentring the system, Derrida exposes how this hierarchy between speech and writing is constructed to maintain the illusion of presence. Writing is not a secondary addition to speech; rather, what we call "writing", a system of differences, intervals, and deferral, is the condition of possibility for all language, including speech. Derrida terms this primary condition archi-écriture (original writing). By showing that speech is already characterised by the same absence and difference that has traditionally been blamed on writing, Derrida disrupts the logocentric hierarchy, demonstrating that presence is always already mediated by absence.The Two Interpretations of Interpretation: Nostalgia versus AffirmationDerrida concludes Structure, Sign, and Play by identifying two distinct ways of responding to the decentring of structure and the loss of the centre. These two modes represent the fundamental division in modern literary and cultural theory, split between a conservative desire for order and a radical acceptance of linguistic drift.The first mode is characterized by nostalgia. It is an interpretation that seeks to decipher a truth or an origin that is free from play. This mode suffers from the "loss" of the centre, viewing the necessity of interpretation as a form of exile. It dreams of a point where the sign can be transcended, allowing the reader to grasp a full, unmediated presence. This is the path of classic humanism, which continues to search for the stable authorial intention, the historical context, or the organic unity that will resolve all textual ambiguities.The second mode, which Derrida associates with Friedrich Nietzsche, does not look back toward a lost origin. Instead, it affirms play. This mode:To affirm play is to accept that meaning is never finished, that there is no final interpretation that can close the text. It is a posture of active, joyful acceptance of a world of signs without truth, origin, or end.Derrida does not present these two interpretations as a simple choice, nor does he suggest that we can easily discard the first in favour of the second. We are structurally caught between them. Even as we attempt to affirm play, we must use the language of metaphysics to do so. The tension between the nostalgic desire for the centre and the active affirmation of play is the very engine of deconstruction, ensuring that critical reading remains an ongoing, unfinished process of interrogation.In the decades following the Johns Hopkins symposium, Derrida's lecture was recognized as a turning point in literary studies. It challenged the scientific aspirations of structuralism, showing that the structures critics mapped were not objective realities but linguistic constructs. By opening the text to play and denying the possibility of a final, authoritative reading, Derrida did not destroy literary analysis; rather, he liberated it from the tyranny of the centre, transforming the act of reading into an active, creative engagement with the infinite possibilities of language....is no longer turned toward the origin, affirms play and tries to pass beyond man and humanism, the name of man being the name of that being who, throughout the history of metaphysics or of ontotheology—in other words, throughout his entire history—has dreamed of full presence, the reassuring foundation, the origin and the end of play.
critical_works.ch58: Roland Barthes (1915–1980)Original title: La mort de l'auteur (originally published in English in the American journal Aspen)1967 (published in French in 1968) · French · France · Structuralism / Transition to Post-structuralism · Theoretical EssayThe Overthrow of the Author-GodFirst published in 1967 in the experimental American journal Aspen and subsequently in the French journal Manteia in 1968, Roland Barthes’s "The Death of the Author" is one of the most iconoclastic manifestos of modern literary theory. The essay seeks to liberate the literary text from the tyranny of the biographical author, initiating a radical shift in literary analysis from the origin of the text to its destination. For centuries, the dominant tradition of Western criticism had treated the writer as the primary source of meaning, assuming that the critic’s task is to uncover the author's intentions, personal life, and psychological motives. Barthes rejects this genealogical model, asserting that "writing is that neutral, composite, oblique space where our subjects slip away, the negative where all identity is lost, starting with the very identity of the body writing."By declaring the author "dead," Barthes does not deny the physical existence of the person who writes, but rather challenges the functional category of the "Author" as an ideological construction that limits the interpretative possibilities of the text. When an author is assumed to be the ultimate authority over their work, the text becomes a passive container of a pre-determined message. Barthes argues that this focus on the writer’s intentions reduces reading to a search for a secret key, turning the critic into a detective who seeks to solve the mystery of what the author "meant." to overthrow this model is to open the text to a multiplicity of meanings, transforming reading from a passive consumption of authorial wisdom into an active, creative engagement with the play of language.This theoretical rebellion marks a crucial transition from structuralism to post-structuralism. Whilst structuralism had sought to analyse literature through universal, objective systems of language, Barthes’s essay exposes the limits of this scientific ambition. By shifting the focus of literary study from the writer to the reader, Barthes suggests that meaning is not an inherent property of the text that can be scientifically mapped, but a dynamic relation that is produced in the act of reading. The death of the author is therefore the condition of possibility for the birth of a new kind of critical practice, one that treats the text not as a finished monument, but as an ongoing process of signification.The Genesis of the Modern ScriptorTo understand the persistence of the authorial myth, Barthes traces its historical origins, arguing that the figure of the Author is a modern construction. He locates the rise of the Author in the transition from medieval society to modern capitalist culture, showing how it is intimately tied to the development of individualism, empiricism, and the legal structures of property. The capitalist system requires a identifiable subject who can own the text as private property, whilst the empirical tradition of science and philosophy prioritises the individual consciousness as the source of truth. As a result, the history of literature has been written as a history of authors, where the text is treated as a biographical document:Traditional literary history is built upon this positivism, classifying works by their creators and explaining their meaning through the author's biography.Against this historical figure of the Author, Barthes posits the modern "scriptor" (scripteur). Unlike the Author, who is assumed to precede the book in time, think before writing, and stand in a relation of fatherhood to the text, the scriptor is born simultaneously with the writing. The scriptor does not possess a deep, psychological interiority that they express through language; rather, they are a functional hand that traces the movement of the pen. The scriptor has no past or future outside the moment of enunciation. In this view, writing is not a vehicle for a pre-existing thought, but the site of enunciation itself. There is no other time than that of the writing, and the book is not a record of a past event, but an event that takes place "here and now."This shift from Author to scriptor redefines the nature of creative labor. The writer is no longer a solitary genius who pulls original ideas from the depths of their soul. Instead, the scriptor is a figure who enters into a language that has always already been spoken and written. The scriptor’s only power is to mix and combine different writings, to play with the inherited codes of culture without ever being able to claim absolute originality. The scriptor does not express himself; he registers the voices of language itself, acting as a medium through which the text’s constituent codes are brought into contact.The author is a modern character, a product of our society insofar as, emerging from the Middle Ages with English empiricism, French rationalism and the personal faith of the Reformation, it discovered the prestige of the individual, of, as it is more nobly put, the 'human person'. It is thus logical that in matter of literature, it should be the positivism, the epitome and culmination of capitalist ideology, which has attached the greatest importance to the 'person' of the author.The Text as a Multi-Dimensional SpaceHaving displaced the author, Barthes re-conceptualises the nature of the literary work. He rejects the traditional view of the text as a linear sequence of words that releases a single, stable, "theological" meaning, the "message" of the Author-God. Instead, he describes the text as a dynamic, heterogenous space of citation and intertextuality:In this formulation, the text is not an original creation but a collage of cultural fragments. Every word, phrase, and syntax is borrowed from a pre-existing lexicon, meaning that the text is always already a citation.This concept of the text as a "tissue of quotations" destroys the distinction between the creative writer and the critic. If the writer is merely a scriptor who re-arranges existing codes, then writing is already an act of reading and interpretation. Similarly, the critic’s task is no longer to decipher a hidden meaning, but to trace the paths of these various codes as they weave through the text. Barthes uses Balzac’s novella Sarrasine to illustrate this point. He quotes a line describing a castrato singer disguised as a woman and asks who is speaking: Is it Balzac the man, Balzac the author, the narrator, or a general social prejudice about women? The answer, Barthes argues, is that we can never know. In writing, all origins are lost, and the voice becomes a composite of multiple cultural discourses.By treating the text as an open, multi-dimensional space, Barthes refuses the possibility of what he calls "deciphering." to decipher a text is to assume that there is a final, correct reading waiting to be discovered under the surface of the words. Instead, Barthes advocates for a practice of "disentangling." to disentangle a text is to trace its structure, to follow the threads of its different codes, and to observe how they intersect and diverge. This process is endless because the text has no bottom, no final signified that can bring the play of signifiers to a halt.We know now that a text is not a line of words releasing a single 'theological' meaning (the 'message' of the Author-God) but a multi-dimensional space in which a variety of writings, none of them original, blend and clash. The text is a tissue of quotations drawn from the innumerable centres of culture.The Tyranny of the Biographical MethodA substantial portion of Barthes's essay is dedicated to a critique of the biographical method that has dominated academic and journalistic criticism. Traditional criticism, Barthes argues, is obsessed with the writer's personal documents, their letters, diaries, intimate relationships, and psychological neuroses, treating them as the ultimate key to their literary works. If a novel is dark, it must be because the author was depressed; if a poem is complex, it must reflect the author’s intellectual anxieties. This biographical focus creates a hierarchy where the author’s life is treated as the truth of the text, whilst the reader’s response is marginalised as subjective and irrelevant.Barthes argues that this critical obsession is not a neutral intellectual choice, but an ideological strategy that serves to control and limit the text. "To give a text an Author," Barthes writes, "is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing." By attributing the text to a specific historical individual, traditional criticism reassures the reader, providing a comfortable, stable interpretation that prevents the text from challenging the reader's assumptions. It domesticates the transgressive potential of writing, ensuring that it remains within the boundaries of bourgeois common sense.This critique is particularly relevant to the study of modern literature. Barthes notes that several vanguard writers had already attempted to subvert the biographical method from within their own practice. He cites Stéphane Mallarmé, who insisted that "it is language which speaks, not the author," and who sought to eliminate the poet’s personal voice in favour of the play of words. He also points to Marcel Proust, whose À la recherche du temps perdu is a deliberate attempt to complicate the relationship between the writer and the narrator, showing that the self who writes is not the same as the self who lives. These literary examples demonstrate that the disappearance of the author is not a theoretical invention of critics, but a historical development within literature itself.The Liberation of the ReaderThe essay culminates in its famous, revolutionary conclusion, which re-allocates the responsibility of meaning from the writer to the reader. Since the text is composed of a variety of writings drawn from different cultures, its unity cannot be found in its origin, the author, but must be located in its destination, the reader. The reader is the only space where all these diverse cultural codes can come together and form a coherent pattern:This passage redefines the reader not as a consumer of meaning, but as the active site of its production.By asserting that the reader is "without history, biography, psychology," Barthes is not describing a real, empirical reader, but a functional category. Just as the Author is a construct that limits the text, the Reader is a construct that opens it. The Reader is the neutral point of intersection where the multiple voices of the text are gathered. In this sense, the reader’s task is not to discover what Balzac or Shakespeare "meant," but to trace the play of language and construct a meaning that is relevant to the moment of reading.The legacy of "The Death of the Author" is immense. It provided the theoretical justification for the rise of reader-response criticism, reception theory, and the post-structuralist critiques of identity and subjecthood. By challenging the authority of the author, Barthes did not diminish the value of literature; rather, he liberated the text from the constraints of biographical reductionism. The death of the author is not a cause for mourning, but an affirmation of the infinite possibilities of reading, reminding us that literature is an ongoing dialogue that is completed only in the mind of the reader.A text’s unity lies not in its origin but in its destination. Yet this destination cannot any longer be personal: the reader is without history, biography, psychology; he is simply that someone who holds together in a single field all the traces by which the written text is constituted... Classic criticism has never paid any attention to the reader; for it, the writer is the only person in literature... [W]e know that to give writing its future, it is necessary to overthrow the myth: the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.
critical_works.ch59: Michel Foucault (1926–1984)Original title: Qu'est-ce qu'un auteur? (originally delivered as a lecture before the Société française de philosophie)February 1969 · French · France · Post-structuralism / Discourse Theory · Theoretical Essay / CritiqueThe Insufficiency of the Author’s DisappearanceDelivered as a lecture before the Société française de philosophie in February 1969, Michel Foucault’s "What is an Author?" is a direct, critical response to Roland Barthes’s "The Death of the Author." Whilst Foucault shares Barthes’s desire to challenge the traditional humanist obsession with the biographical writer, he finds the simple celebration of the author's disappearance to be theoretically insufficient. For Foucault, declaring the author dead is too easy; it risks repeating the same metaphysical gestures of presence by merely substituting the text or the language in the author's place. Rather than celebrating the writer's absence, Foucault insists on examining the historical, legal, and political mechanisms that have constructed and sustained the authorial figure within Western culture.Foucault begins by asking what it means for a writer to disappear. He notes that modern literature has indeed made a theme of its own self-effacement, where "writing is now linked to sacrifice and to the sacrifice of life itself; it is a voluntary obliteration of the self." However, Foucault argues that this literary theme has not been matched by a rigorous critical analysis of how the authorial subject actually operates in society. Traditional criticism has merely replaced the author’s name with abstract concepts like "writing" (écriture) or "the work" (œuvre), without examining how these concepts continue to perform the same classifying and limiting functions as the author's name.The central task of Foucault's essay is to shift the terms of the debate. The question is not whether the author is physically dead, but rather: How does the author's name function in our society? What are the consequences of its disappearance? Who is allowed to speak, and under what conditions? By raising these questions, Foucault moves the discussion from the realm of aesthetics to the realm of power and discourse theory. The author is not a romantic genius who transcends history, but a historically specific subject-position that is constructed, regulated, and maintained by institutional power.The Genealogy of the Author-FunctionTo analyse the specific role of the writer, Foucault introduces his famous concept of the "author-function" (fonction-auteur). The author-function is not a physical human being, nor is it a simple synonym for the writer. Rather, it is a functional category, a regulatory principle that is used to classify, group, and authenticate discourses. A person's name does not function in the same way when it refers to an individual in everyday life as it does when it refers to an author. If we say "Michel Foucault," we are referring to a historical individual who lived, taught, and wrote; but when we refer to "Foucault" as an author, we are invoking a set of expectations, a coherent body of work, and a system of relations that determines how his texts are read and valued.The author-function is therefore a tool of discourse control. Foucault writes:In our society, not all texts are equal. Some texts require an author’s name to be taken seriously, whilst others do not. An advertisement, a recipe, or a private letter do not require an author-function to be valid; they operate through their immediate utility. A literary text, a philosophical treatise, or a scientific paper, however, historically require the attribution of an author to be considered legitimate.By analysing the author as a function rather than a person, Foucault exposes the historical contingency of our literary categories. The author-function has not always existed, nor has it always functioned in the same way. It is a product of specific historical developments, and its form varies across different periods and cultures. By tracing the genealogy of the author-function, Foucault demonstrates that our modern concept of authorship is not a natural fact of literature, but a historical construction that could, under different social conditions, disappear or be replaced by other modes of organizing discourse.The author is a certain functional principle by which, in our culture, one limits, excludes, and chooses; in short, by which one impedes the free circulation, the free manipulation, the free composition, decomposition, and recomposition of fiction.The Four Structural Pillars of the Author-FunctionTo demonstrate how the author-function operates within Western culture, Foucault identifies four distinct characteristics that define its structure. These characteristics show that the author is not a spontaneous projection of a writer's personality, but a complex institutional operation that constructs a coherent subject out of scattered texts.First, the author-function is linked to the legal system of property and punishment. Foucault argues that the author was not constructed because society wanted to celebrate creative genius, but because the state needed someone to hold responsible for transgressive writing. The author-function emerged when texts became subject to censorship, prosecution, and legal ownership. A writer was identified so that they could be punished if their work challenged the religious or political authorities of the state. Only later, in the late eighteenth century, was this system of liability transformed into a system of property, where the author was granted legal copyright over their work.Second, the author-function does not affect all discourses in the same way. Foucault contrasts the history of science with the history of literature. In the Middle Ages, scientific texts, such as works on medicine, astronomy, or physics, required the name of an author (like Hippocrates or Aristotle) to be accepted as true. In contrast, literary texts, such as epics, plays, and tales, were often circulated anonymously, as their value lay in their entertainment or moral utility rather than their origin. In the modern era, this relationship has been completely reversed. Scientific texts are now accepted as true based on their experimental verification, and the name of the scientist is merely a historical index; the scientific truth of a law does not depend on who discovered it. Literary texts, however, can no longer be read without an author’s name. If a poem or novel is published anonymously, the critic immediately seeks to uncover the "real" writer, as if the text’s validity depends upon this biographical anchor.Third, the author-function is not a natural projection of a writer's personality, but a complex institutional operation. Foucault points out that when we construct an author, we do not simply record the facts of their life. Instead, we project a set of values, such as coherence, development, and sincerity, onto the text. The critic constructs a biographical subject who is assumed to be the source of all the text’s contradictions. Foucault describes this operation:If a text contains a contradiction, the critic explains it as a developmental phase or a deliberate irony on the part of the author, thereby preserving the illusion of a coherent, unified subject.Fourth, the author-function does not refer simply to a real individual, but can give rise to multiple egos or voices within the text. Foucault notes that even in a simple autobiographical narrative, there is a gap between the author who writes, the narrator who speaks, and the character who acts. These different "egos" are all products of the author-function, which allows the text to speak in multiple voices whilst maintaining the illusion of a single, organizing consciousness.These aspects of an individual which we designate as an author (or which comprise an individual as an author) are only the projection, in more or less psychologizing terms, of the operations that we force texts to undergo, the connections that we make, the traits that we establish as pertinent, the continuities that we recognize, or the exclusions that we practice.The Founders of DiscursivityIn the latter part of the essay, Foucault identifies a special class of authors who exceed the boundaries of typical literary or scientific authorship. He calls these figures the "founders of discursivity" (fondateurs de discursivité). Unlike an ordinary novelist, who writes a book and establishes a genre that others can copy, a founder of discursivity does not just write books; they create the conditions for the production of infinite subsequent texts.Foucault cites Karl Marx and Sigmund Freud as the primary examples of these founders. Marx did not merely write Das Kapital; he created a discursive space within which others could write Marxist analyses, debate political economy, and develop new theories of history. Freud did not merely found psychoanalysis; he established a set of rules, concepts, and terminologies that made psychoanalytic discourse possible. The key characteristic of these founders is that subsequent writers do not simply imitate them; rather, they must return to the founder's texts to validate their own work.This "return to the origin" is a unique feature of discursive founders. If a scientist wants to make a new discovery in physics, they do not need to return to the original texts of Galileo or Newton to justify their equations; the science has moved past its origin. In contrast, a Marxist or a psychoanalyst must constantly return to Marx or Freud, as the very truth of their discourse is tied to the interpretation of the founder's words. Foucault writes:By identifying this category, Foucault shows that the author-function can operate at different levels of generality, shaping both individual books and entire fields of knowledge.to say that Marx or Freud founded a discursivity is to say that they made possible not only a certain number of analogies, but also a certain number of differences. They have cleared the space for the introduction of elements other than their own, which, nevertheless, remain within the field of discourse they defined.The Tactical Control of DiscourseFoucault’s analysis of the author-function ultimately is a critique of how our society manages and limits the production of meaning. Traditional humanism has celebrated the author as a source of infinite creativity, a heroic figure who pours original meaning into the world. Foucault reverses this view, showing that the author is actually a ideological tool used to restrict the proliferation of meaning. In a world where language is constantly circulating, the author-function acts as a tactical break, a way of policing what can be said and who can say it.By showing that the author is a historical construction, Foucault invites us to imagine a future where the author-function no longer operates. This would not mean the end of writing, but rather the creation of a new relationship with language. If we stop asking who is speaking, we can begin to focus on the discourse itself: its rules, its exclusions, and its institutional dependencies. Foucault concludes his essay by anticipating this discursive liberation:The legacy of Foucault’s essay lies in this shift from the subject to the system. By exposing the author-function as a mechanism of control, Foucault challenged the foundational assumptions of literary criticism, showing that the author is not the natural origin of the text, but an institutional effect. His work laid the groundwork for subsequent critiques of the subject in post-colonial, feminist, and Marxist theory, reminding us that the study of literature is always also an inquiry into the structures of power that govern our language.We can easily imagine a culture where discourse would circulate without any need for an author. Discourses, whatever their status, form, or value, and regardless of our treatment of them, would unfold in a pervasive anonymity. We would no longer hear the questions that have been rehashed for so long: 'Who really spoke? Is it indeed he and not another? With what authenticity or originality?'... Instead, there would be other questions, like these: 'What are the modes of existence of this discourse? Where has it been used, how can it circulate, and who can appropriate it for himself?'
critical_works.ch60: Louis Althusser (1918–1990)Original title: Idéologie et appareils idéologiques d'État (Notes pour une recherche) (published in the journal La Pensée)1970 (written in 1969) · French · France · Structuralist Marxism / Marxist Literary Theory Precursor · Theoretical EssayThe Problem of Reproduction in Capitalist StructuresFirst published in the journal La Pensée in 1970, Louis Althusser’s "Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses" represents a major development in twentieth-century Marxist theory, with profound implications for literary and cultural criticism. The central problem Althusser addresses is one that classical Marxist theory had left partially unresolved: How does a capitalist social formation ensure its own survival over time? According to traditional Marxist economics, a society must reproduce its forces of production (such as machinery, raw materials, and labor power) and its relations of production (such as the wage-labor relation between capitalist and worker) to continue functioning. Althusser points out that whilst the reproduction of machinery is relatively straightforward, the reproduction of labor power and the relations of production is a far more complex, political process.To reproduce labor power, a capitalist society cannot rely solely on providing workers with a subsistence wage that allows them to return to work each day. It must also ensure that workers are trained in the specific skills required by the modern industrial economy. More importantly, however, Althusser argues that the reproduction of labor power requires the reproduction of the workers' "subjection to the ruling ideology." The state must train workers to accept their place in the capitalist hierarchy, ensuring that they will submit to the authority of the employer without constantly threatening to rebel or overthrow the system.This focus on subjection shifts the Marxist analysis of the state. Classical Marxism had viewed the state primarily as a repressive instrument, a "state apparatus" consisting of the police, the army, and the courts, that is used by the ruling class to enforce its will through direct physical coercion. Althusser does not deny the existence of this coercive power, but he argues that no ruling class can maintain its position through violence alone. To prevent revolution, the capitalist state must secure the consent of the working class, transforming direct coercion into ideological consent. It is this insight that leads Althusser to formulate his theory of Ideological State Apparatuses, showing how cultural institutions, including education and literature, are central to the maintenance of the capitalist order.Repression versus Consent: RSAs and ISAsTo explain how the state secures both coercion and consent, Althusser draws a distinction between two types of state apparatuses: the Repressive State Apparatus (RSA) and the Ideological State Apparatuses (ISAs). This distinction is based on the primary mechanism each apparatus uses to enforce social order.The Repressive State Apparatus consists of institutions that operate primarily through physical violence, coercion, or the threat of force. These include the police, the army, the courts, the prisons, and the state administration. The RSA is a singular, unified entity that is controlled directly by the ruling class through the government. It functions "massively and predominantly by repression," stepping in when the stability of the state is directly threatened by strikes, riots, or revolutionary movements.In contrast, Althusser identifies a plurality of Ideological State Apparatuses. These are distinct, specialized institutions that present themselves to the observer in a decentralized form. Althusser provides a list of these apparatuses:Unlike the RSA, which belongs entirely to the public sphere, many ISAs, such as the family, the church, and private publishing houses, operate within the private sphere. However, Althusser argues that this public/private distinction is an ideological illusion. What matters is not their legal status, but their function: all ISAs, whether public or private, serve to reproduce the relations of production by instilling the ruling ideology in the minds of individuals.Althusser notes that whilst both types of apparatuses use both coercion and ideology, they do so in different proportions. The RSA functions primarily by violence and secondarily by ideology, whilst the ISAs function primarily by ideology and secondarily by silent, symbolic exclusion or punishment.Althusser also offers a historical analysis of these apparatuses, arguing that under pre-capitalist feudalism, the dominant ISA was the Church, which combined religious, educational, and cultural functions to maintain the feudal order. Under modern industrial capitalism, however, the educational system has replaced the Church as the dominant ISA. The school takes children at a young age and subjects them to years of training, teaching them both technical skills and the "rules of good behaviour", which are actually the rules of subjection to the ruling class.I shall call Ideological State Apparatuses a certain number of realities which present themselves to the immediate observer in the form of distinct and specialized institutions. I propose an empirical list of these... the religious ISA, the educational ISA, the family ISA, the legal ISA, the political ISA, the trade-union ISA, the communications ISA, the cultural ISA (Literature, the Arts, sports, etc.).The Materiality of Ideology and Imaginary RelationsTo explain how the ISAs achieve this subjection, Althusser redefines the classical Marxist concept of ideology. In classical Marxism, ideology was often understood as a form of "false consciousness", a system of lies or illusions created by the ruling class to deceive the workers about their exploitation. In this view, ideology is an illusion that can be dissolved by exposing the scientific truth of economic relations.Althusser rejects this definition, asserting that "ideology represents the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real conditions of existence." The illusion of ideology is not that it misrepresents the world, but that it represents the individual’s subjective relationship to the world. A worker does not experience their exploitation as an abstract economic formula; rather, they experience it through a set of imaginary representations, such as "freedom of contract," "national duty," or "personal success", that help them make sense of their daily life whilst masking the structural contradictions of the system.Crucially, Althusser argues that ideology is not a set of abstract ideas floating in the minds of individuals. Instead, "ideology has a material existence." It is always embedded in material institutions, practices, and rituals:A religious believer’s faith, for example, does not exist in the abstract; it exists in the material acts of going to church, kneeling, praying, and participating in sacraments. These rituals are defined by the church as an institution, and it is through these material actions that the believer's subjectivity is constructed.This materiality of ideology has major implications for cultural criticism. It means that literature and art are more than passive reflections of an author’s thoughts or a society's values. They are material practices that take place within specific institutions (such as publishing houses, schools, and theatres) and are governed by specific rituals (such as reading, reviewing, and lecturing). To analyse a literary text is not to discover its abstract "theme," but to examine how it operates as a material practice that participates in the reproduction of the ruling ideology....an ideology always exists in an apparatus, and its practice, or practices. This existence is material... the 'ideas' of a human subject exist in his material actions inserted into material practices governed by material rituals which are themselves defined by the material ideological apparatus from which derive the ideas of that subject.Interpellation and the Hailing of the SubjectThe most famous concept introduced in the essay is Althusser's theory of "interpellation" or "hailing." Interpellation is the mechanism by which ideology recruits individuals and transforms them into "subjects."For Althusser, we are not born as natural subjects; we are constructed as subjects by ideology. The category of the "subject" is itself an ideological product, designed to make us believe that we are free, autonomous individuals when we are actually subjugated to the state. Althusser uses the term "subject" in its double sense: we are subjects who have agency, but we are also subjects who are subjected to a sovereign authority.Althusser illustrates this process with his famous analogy of a police officer calling out to an individual on a street:The moment the individual turns around, they recognize themselves as the target of the call. In doing so, they accept their place in the legal and social structure represented by the police officer. They acknowledge their own subjection, believing that they are acting freely when they are actually responding to the structural demand of the state.Althusser argues that this interpellation is not a single event that happens once in a person's life. Rather, we are always already interpellated by ideology. Even before we are born, our parents, our culture, and our laws have already prepared a place for us within the ideological structure, assigning us a name, a gender, and a class position. We are born into a language that has already defined our relationships, and our entire life is a series of rituals through which we repeatedly recognize ourselves as subjects of the ruling ideology....the most commonplace everyday police (or other) hailing: 'Hey, you there!' Assuming that the theoretical scene I have imagined takes place in the street, the hailed individual will turn round. By this simple one-hundred-and-eighty-degree physical conversion, he becomes a subject. Why? Because he has recognized that the hailing was 'really' addressed to him, and that 'it was really him who was hailed' (and not someone else).The Literary Text as an Ideological ApparatusAlthough Althusser’s essay is a work of general social theory, it has been widely adopted by literary critics to analyse how literature operates within the capitalist state. In Althusser’s framework, literature is not a neutral artistic expression, but a "cultural ISA" that participates in the work of interpellation.A literary text operates by interpellating the reader as a specific kind of subject. When we read a novel, we are not simply observing a story; we are being invited to identify with certain characters, to adopt a specific narrative perspective, and to accept the values and assumptions that govern the fictional world. The text hails us, calling out to us as readers and shaping our moral, political, and aesthetic sensibilities. By encouraging us to empathise with the bourgeois individualist protagonist or to accept the naturalness of the social hierarchy represented in the plot, the text reinforces our subjection to the ruling ideology.However, Althusser’s theory also allows for a more complex view of the relationship between literature and ideology. In subsequent essays, and through the work of his student Pierre Macherey, Althusser argues that art occupies a unique position within the ideological apparatus. Whilst literature is produced within ideology, a great work of art does not simply repeat the dominant myths of its time. Instead, by giving ideology a concrete, aesthetic form, the text can expose the contradictions that ideology seeks to conceal.By representing characters caught in the conflicts of class, gender, and family, the novel makes the gaps and silences of the ideological structure visible to the reader. The text does not escape ideology, but it "makes us see" the limits of that ideology from the inside. The critic’s task is therefore to analyse the structure of the text to uncover these contradictions, showing how the formal innovations of the work are tied to its struggle with the ideological materials of its history.Althusser’s work laid the foundation for structuralist Marxist criticism, exercising a massive influence on theorists such as Terry Eagleton, Fredric Jameson, and Étienne Balibar. By showing that ideology is a material practice that operates through institutions like schools and literature, Althusser challenged the humanist view of the critic as a free interpreter of text, reframing literary analysis as a political intervention in the struggles over subjecthood and power.
critical_works.ch61: Paul de Man (1919–1983)Original title: Blindness and Insight: Essays in the Rhetoric of Contemporary Criticism1971 · English · Belgium / United States (Yale School) · Deconstruction / Yale School · Deconstructive EssaysThe Paradox of Critical Self-DeceptionFirst published in 1971, Paul de Man’s Blindness and Insight: Essays in the Rhetoric of Contemporary Criticism is a foundational statement of American deconstruction, challenging the epistemological foundations of literary analysis. The central thesis of the work resides in a startling paradox: literary critics achieve their most profound insights not despite their blindness, but because of it. De Man argues that the very conceptual framework that enables a critic to penetrate a text is simultaneously the blind spot that prevents them from understanding the rhetorical behaviour of their own language. Critical discourse, by its very nature as a linguistic medium, is structurally divided against itself. It asserts a logic of objective disclosure whilst operating through a network of figures and tropes that undermine that very objectivity.This formulation displaces the traditional hermeneutic assumption that criticism is a secondary, transparent translation of a primary literary truth. For de Man, the critic is not a privileged observer standing outside the labyrinth of language, but a participant caught in its duplicate turns. The history of literary criticism is not a progressive accumulation of objective knowledge, but rather a sequence of creative misreadings. De Man asserts that "criticism is a metaphor for the act of reading," a rhetorical performance that must inevitably misrepresent its own operations. The insights generated by the major critics of the twentieth century, from the American New Critics to European structuralists like Claude Lévi-Strauss and Georg Lukács, are shown to be dependent upon a structural blindness to the figural implications of their own terminology.This blindness is not an individual failing or a remediable error in methodology, but an inescapable condition of linguistic representation. In de Man's view, language is figurative rather than referential; it cannot state a truth without simultaneously staging the impossibility of that truth’s unmediated presence. When a critic attempts to stabilise a text’s meaning by reference to an organic structure, an authorial consciousness, or a historical context, their own language produces a surplus of meaning that disrupts the intended closure. The act of interpretation is therefore always an act of blindness: to see one aspect of a text, the critic must remain blind to the way their own analytical tools are rhetorically implicated in the text's instability.The Rhetoric of Blindness: Derrida, Rousseau, and the Myth of NaïvetyThe conceptual centre of de Man's collection is the essay "The Rhetoric of Blindness: Jacques Derrida's Reading of Rousseau." In this essay, de Man performs a deconstructive reading of Derrida’s reading of Jean-Jacques Rousseau in Of Grammatology. Derrida had argued that Rousseau, whilst serving as a precursor to deconstruction by exposing the instability of presence, remained trapped within a logocentric "metaphysics of presence." According to Derrida, Rousseau’s texts exhibit a classic phonocentric bias, privileging speech (parole) as the medium of authentic presence and dismissing writing (écriture) as a corrupting, artificial supplement that introduces absence and difference. Derrida's reading assumes a diagnostic authority over Rousseau, mapping a structural blindness in Rousseau’s philosophy that only the modern deconstructive critic can expose.De Man dismantles this hierarchy by arguing that Derrida is blind to the fact that Rousseau was already fully aware of the figurality and structural instability of his own language. Rousseau, de Man argues, is not a naïve writer who inadvertently falls into logocentric traps; rather, his texts are highly self-conscious literary performances that systematically deconstruct the very oppositions they seem to assert. When Rousseau appears to celebrate speech over writing, or nature over culture, he does so with a rhetorical irony that exposes the artificiality of these very categories. De Man shows that Rousseau's Confessions and Émile do not require a latecomer critic to deconstruct them because they are already self-deconstructing:Derrida’s reading of Rousseau is thus revealed to be a classic instance of critical blindness producing insight. Derrida arrives at his profound insights into the nature of writing and difference only by creating a fictional, mystified version of Rousseau as a naïve logocentric thinker. Derrida must blind himself to Rousseau's rhetorical self-awareness to construct his own deconstructive paradigm. De Man writes:The confrontation between Derrida and Rousseau becomes a template for de Man's understanding of all literary and critical exchanges. The critic’s blindness to the rhetorical complexity of the source text is the very engine that drives critical innovation. By showing that Rousseau's text "has no blind spots" because it is already aware of its own figural status, de Man challenges the authority of the post-structuralist critic, reframing deconstruction not as a modern invention applied to the past, but as an inherent property of all strong literature."...our reading has shown that these critics' moments of greatest blindness with regard to their own critical assumptions are also the moments at which they achieve their greatest insight.""It seems that this blindness is not a chance error but a necessary movement that is at once a constitutive part of the critic's own discourse and an inherent feature of the literary text itself."Dismantling Organicism: Tropes, Grammar, and the New Critical FallacyA major target of Blindness and Insight is the organicist ideology of American New Criticism. While de Man respects the New Critics’ commitment to close reading, he rejects their central aesthetic goal: the recovery of the text as a unified, coherent object characterised by "organic unity." The New Critics, including Cleanth Brooks and W.K. Wimsatt, sought to resolve the tensions and ambiguities of literary texts by integrating them into a harmonious whole, where form and content, signifier and signified, are fused into an aesthetic synthesis. This approach relies on a clear separation of form and content, treating form as a container that brings order to the chaotic material of experience.De Man argues that this organic model is an ideological illusion designed to mask the structural instability of figurative language. The New Critics achieve their vision of harmony only by ignoring the disruptive behaviour of the tropes they identify. For de Man, there is a fundamental tension in all literary language between grammar and trope, between the logical, rule-governed structures of syntax and the figurative deviations of rhetoric. While grammar seeks to establish stable, literal relationships of meaning, tropes introduce an inescapable indeterminacy that disrupts grammatical logic.The New Critical attempt to reconcile these forces under the banner of irony or paradox is shown to be a defensive strategy to ward off the threat of linguistic disintegration. In his readings of the New Critics, de Man shows that their close readings routinely uncover contradictions that cannot be resolved within an organic framework. The tropes in a poem do not cooperate to build a unified aesthetic object; instead, they function as rhetorical blockages that prevent the text from achieving referential or formal closure. By insisting on the priority of the trope over grammar, de Man shifts the focus of close reading from the detection of unity to the exposure of the text’s internal divisions, showing that the separation of form and content is a rhetorical construct that must be repeatedly deconstructed.The Epistemology of the Trope: Figurality and the Self-Deconstructing TextDe Man’s focus on the trope leads to a radical redefinition of the relationship between literal and figural meaning. In classical rhetoric, figurative language is viewed as an ornamentation of a pre-existing literal meaning, a decorative deviation that can be translated back into literal statements without loss of cognitive content. De Man rejects this instrumental view of rhetoric, asserting that all language is figural, and that what we call "literal meaning" is merely a figure of speech whose rhetorical origin has been forgotten or repressed.This epistemological claim has profound implications for the status of the literary text. If language is inherently figural, then a text cannot refer to an objective reality outside of itself. It can only refer to other signs, caught in an infinite regress of signification. The literary text is not a representation of a human consciousness or a historical event; it is a rhetorical structure that is "self-deconstructing" because it contains within itself the linguistic mechanisms that dismantle its own claims to truth. De Man writes:This self-deconstructive character means that a text’s figurative language constantly undermines its own literal assertions. A poem may state a moral theme or a philosophical proposition, but the imagery and metaphors used to express that theme will inevitably introduce contradictions that mock the literal statement. The text does not need to be dismantled by an external critic; it is already in a state of self-dismantling, exposing the artificiality of its own constructions. The critic’s task is not to solve the text's mysteries or to uncover a hidden, stable meaning, but to track the precise ways in which the text's rhetorical behaviour prevents it from ever saying what it means or meaning what it says.This view of language as a self-deconstructing system challenges the humanist concept of the author as an autonomous creator. The author does not use language as a tool to express pre-existing thoughts; rather, the author is subject to the structural demands of a medium that they cannot control. The text is not a product of the author's intention, but a site where the warring forces of signification play out their conflicts. The "subject" who writes is itself a rhetorical effect, created by the grammar of the text. By displacing the author and the referent, de Man reduces the literary text to a purely linguistic event, whose value lies in its refusal to offer the false comfort of a stable referent or a unified consciousness."The language of criticism is a language of metaphor, and the history of criticism is the history of this metaphor."The Yale School and the Rhetoric of CrisisBlindness and Insight must be understood in its historical context as the theoretical manifesto of the Yale School of criticism. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, de Man, along with colleagues such as J. Hillis Miller, Geoffrey Hartman, and Harold Bloom, transformed the study of literature in the United States by introducing post-structuralist thought to the curriculum.
