This transformation was often experienced by the academic establishment as a profound crisis, a dismantling of the humanist values of historical truth, moral education, and aesthetic appreciation that had sustained literary study for generations.De Man does not shy away from this crisis; indeed, he argues that the rhetoric of crisis is itself a necessary feature of literary history. In the essay "The Rhetoric of Crisis," de Man observes that literature and criticism are always in a state of crisis because they are always confronting the limits of their own language. The sense of crisis that accompanied the rise of deconstruction was not a temporary historical accident, but a manifestation of the structural instability that lies at the heart of all systems of representation. By exposing this instability, de Man did not seek to destroy literary studies, but to liberate it from the mystifications of humanist ideology.The critical resolution of Blindness and Insight is therefore not a promise of new stability, but an invitation to accept the rigour of a reading that refuses to stop at the illusions of presence. De Man’s legacy is a model of reading that is alert to the rhetorical self-deceptions of both literature and criticism. By showing that our most profound insights are always purchased at the price of a necessary blindness, de Man challenges us to examine the limitations of our own analytical tools, ensuring that the act of reading remains a rigorous, open-ended interrogation of the language through which we construct our world.
critical_works.ch62: Harold Bloom (1930–2019)Original title: The Anxiety of Influence: A Theory of Poetry1973 · English · United States (Yale School) · Yale School / Psychoanalytic Poetics · Theoretical Treatise / PoeticsThe Agon of Poetic BelatednessPublished in 1973, Harold Bloom’s The Anxiety of Influence: A Theory of Poetry introduces a dark, combative model of literary history, drawing on Freudian psychoanalysis to explain how poets achieve originality. Bloom rejects the humanist view of literary tradition as a harmonious, orderly treasury of shared values, a model famously articulated by T. S. Eliot in "Tradition and the Individual Talent," where new works seamlessly adjust the relations of the existing order. For Bloom, the history of poetry is not a peaceful succession, but a battleground. It is a psychological arena where latecoming poets (the ephebes) must wage a desperate, patricidal war against their precursors (the literary ancestors) to clear creative space for their own voices. To be a poet is to suffer from a profound sense of belatedness, a fear that all the great poems have already been written and that the latecomer is doomed to be a mere copyist.This struggle is characterised by what Bloom calls "creative misprision" or creative misreading. Bloom asserts that "strong poets" do not read their predecessors objectively or passive-mindedly. Rather, they must deliberately and defensively misinterpret the parent text, swerving away from its authority to convince themselves of their own necessity. Poetic influence is therefore not a gift or a source of inspiration; it is an anxiety, a threat to the poet’s creative survival. Bloom writes:Only "weak poets" imitate their precursors, producing derivative verse that leaves the tradition unchanged. The "strong poet," by contrast, possesses the psychic energy to wrestle with the precursor, engaging in a process of creative deformation that allows them to survive the crushing weight of the past. By reframing tradition as an agonistic struggle, Bloom challenges the formalist focus on textuality, shifting the critic's attention to the unconscious psychological dramas that shape the creation of literature."Poetic history is indistinguishable from poetic influence, since strong poets make that history by misreading one another, so as to clear imaginative space for themselves."Miltonic Precursorship and the Romantic RebellionTo ground his theory of poetic struggle, Bloom focuses on the relationship between John Milton and the English Romantic poets. Milton is the ultimate precursor in the English tradition, a figure of such imaginative power that his shadow threatened to choke the creativity of all who followed. The Romantic poets, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Shelley, and Keats, were obsessed with Milton, and their careers can be read as a collective attempt to overcome his influence. Bloom argues that the central drama of Romanticism is the struggle to write a visionary poetry that could match the sublimity of Paradise Lost without merely reproducing Milton’s theology and style.In Bloom’s psychoanalytic framework, Milton’s Satan becomes the archetype of the strong poet. Satan’s rebellion against God is a mythological representation of the ephebe’s rebellion against the precursor. Satan refuses to accept his created status, asserting that he is self-begotten and free from the authority of the creator. This is precisely the claim that the strong poet must make: they must deny their debt to the precursor, asserting their own imaginative independence. The Romantics identified with Satan because they, too, were engaged in a rebellion against a father figure, attempting to build a new heaven and earth out of their own subjective imaginations.Bloom traces this Miltonic struggle through specific Romantic texts. Wordsworth’s The Prelude, for example, is read as a swerve from Milton’s epic vision, shifting the site of the sublime from the outer cosmos of heaven and hell to the inner recesses of the human mind. Shelley’s Adonais and Keats’s Hyperion fragments are interpreted as direct confrontations with Miltonic style, where the young poets struggle to find a voice that is not immediately drowned out by Miltonic syntax and vocabulary. By showing that the Romantics’ most famous poems are defensive reactions to Milton, Bloom demonstrates that poetic originality is never a simple, spontaneous expression of the self, but is always forged in the crucible of intertextual conflict.The Six Revisionary Ratios: Clinamen, Tessera, and KenosisThe core of Bloom’s treatise is his detailed taxonomy of the six "revisionary ratios", the specific psychological and rhetorical strategies that strong poets employ to defend themselves against the precursor’s influence. These ratios represent a progression, a path of psychological transformation through which the ephebe moves from initial subjection to final, precarious victory.The first ratio is clinamen, which Bloom defines as a "poetic misprision" or a "swerve" from the precursor. The poet reads the precursor’s work up to a certain point, but then swerves away, implying that the precursor’s poem went astray at a crucial moment. The ephebe’s own poem is presented as a correction of this error, an attempt to redirect the tradition along its true path. The clinamen is the initial act of self-assertion, the moment the young poet declares their difference from the father.The second ratio is tessera, which Bloom describes as "completion and antithesis." Drawing on the ancient practice of matching fragments of a broken token to prove identity, the ephebe reads the precursor’s poem and decides that it is incomplete. The later poet does not reject the precursor, but seeks to "complete" their work by retaining its terms whilst reinterpreting them in a new, antithetical direction. The ephebe claims that the precursor did not go far enough, and that only the later poem reveals the full implications of the precursor's vision.The third ratio is kenosis, a "breaking-device" through which the poet attempts to achieve discontinuity with the precursor. Borrowing the theological term for the self-emptying of Christ, Bloom argues that the ephebe performs an act of self-purgation, emptying themselves of their own poetic power to ensure that they are no longer dominated by the precursor. However, this self-emptying is also an emptying of the precursor: by reducing their own scope, the ephebe simultaneously reduces the stature of the ancestor, bringing both down to a more human level where a new beginning is possible.Ascending to the Counter-Sublime: Daemonization, Askesis, and ApophradesThe final three ratios represent the ephebe’s ascent toward the "counter-sublime," where the struggle for originality becomes increasingly intense and solipsistic.The fourth ratio is daemonization, or the "counter-sublime." Here, the ephebe seeks to align themselves with a daemonic power that is older and deeper than the precursor's own inspiration. The poet bypasses the precursor, linking their own voice to a primary, chaotic force that makes the precursor’s sublimity appear secondary and derivative. By invoking this personalized daemonic force, the ephebe achieves a new kind of grandeur that challenges the precursor’s authority on its own terms.The fifth ratio is askesis, a state of "purgation" and "solipsism." The ephebe undergoes a rigorous process of self-limitation, isolating their own creative voice from all external influences. This purgation is designed to achieve a state of absolute autonomy, where only the poet's own voice exists. However, this solipsistic retreat also limits the precursor: by shutting out the world, the ephebe also shuts out the ancestor, refusing to acknowledge the precursor's presence in their work. The poem becomes a site of austere, defensive isolation.The final, most dramatic ratio is apophrades, or the "return of the dead." In this stage, the mature poet is no longer afraid of the precursor’s influence. They throw open the doors of their poem and allow the precursor’s voice to return in its full power. However, this return is characterised by a strange, uncanny reversal: the ephebe’s own work has become so strong, and has so thoroughly reinterpreted the precursor, that the precursor’s poems now sound as if they are imitating the latecomer. The dead return, but they return as the children of the living. Bloom writes:In apophrades, this misinterpretation is so complete that it reverses the order of time. When we read the precursor after reading the ephebe, we cannot help but hear the ephebe’s voice in the precursor’s work. The latecomer has achieved the ultimate victory, conquering both the precursor and history itself."Every poem is a misinterpretation of a parent poem."The Afterlife of the Poetic AgonThe Anxiety of Influence provoked immediate controversy upon its publication. Formalist critics accused Bloom of neglecting the textual reality of poems in favour of a speculative, psychobiographical drama. Marxist and feminist critics pointed out that Bloom’s model of poetry was exclusively masculine and patricidal, relying on an elite canon of "strong men" wrestling with their fathers, whilst ignoring the collaborative, communal, and gendered dimensions of literary creation.Despite these criticisms, Bloom’s work exercised a massive influence on the development of literary theory. Along with Paul de Man and Jacques Derrida, Bloom helped to establish the Yale School as the epicentre of American theory in the 1970s. His ratios provided critics with a powerful set of tools for analysing intertextuality, showing that the relationships between texts are never neutral, but are always charged with conflict and desire.The critical resolution of The Anxiety of Influence lies in its refusal to offer a consoling vision of artistic creation. Bloom strips poetry of its romantic myths of inspiration and self-expression, revealing it to be a site of exhausting psychic labour and defensive warfare. To write a great poem is to engage in a tragic struggle against the past, a struggle that can never be fully won, but must be repeatedly fought. By exposing the anxiety that lies at the heart of the creative process, Bloom challenges us to read literature not as a collection of static monuments, but as an ongoing, dramatic record of the human will wrestling with the limits of time and tradition.
critical_works.ch63: Stuart Hall (1932–2014)Original title: Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse1973 · English · Jamaica / United Kingdom (Birmingham School) · Cultural Studies / Birmingham School · Theoretical Essay / Media TheoryBeyond the Sender-Receiver FallacyOriginally delivered as a paper at the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) in Birmingham in 1973, Stuart Hall’s "Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse" represents a foundational moment in cultural studies and media theory. Hall mounts a systematic critique of the linear communication models that had dominated American social science research since the mid-twentieth century. These traditional models, derived from information theory and behaviourist psychology, conceptualised communication as a linear circuit: Sender -> Message -> Receiver. Meaning was treated as a stable, transparent substance packaged by the sender, transmitted through a neutral medium, and absorbed by a passive recipient. Any breakdown in this transmission was dismissed as mere "noise" or a failure of clarity in the message itself, assuming that a perfect communication of intentions is the default state of human interaction.Hall rejects this mechanical framework, replacing it with a semiotic, cyclical model that views communication as a complex structure of production, circulation, and reception. Drawing on Marxist theories of capital accumulation and structuralist linguistics, Hall argues that a media message is not a transparent window on reality, but a highly coded sign system. The process of communication is divided into two distinct, relatively autonomous moments: encoding and decoding. The production of the message (encoding) and its reception (decoding) are separate practices, carried out by different social actors operating within different institutional networks.Encoding is the moment of production, where cultural institutions, operating within specific ideological and economic contexts, translate raw historical events into coded discourses. Decoding, by contrast, is the moment of reception, where the audience translates the coded discourse back into meaningful practices. Crucially, Hall asserts that these two moments do not necessarily align. The codes of encoding do not govern the codes of decoding; the receiver is not forced to accept the message in the terms proposed by the producer. By separating production from reception, Hall establishes the active role of the audience in the construction of meaning, transforming media analysis from a study of passive effects into an investigation of ideological struggle.The Hegemonic Alignment: The Dominant-Hegemonic PositionTo map the ways in which audiences decode media messages, Hall proposes three hypothetical positions from which decoding can occur. These positions are determined by the viewer’s relationship to the dominant ideology of the society in which the message is produced.The first position is the dominant-hegemonic code. In this position, the viewer accepts the media message "full and straight," decoding it in terms of the preferred code in which it was encoded. The viewer operates fully within the ideological assumptions of the producers, accepting their definitions of events, their moral judgements, and their political priorities as natural, objective, and commonsensical. Hall writes:Within this position, the viewer is aligned with what Hall calls the "preferred reading" of the text. Media producers, as part of the dominant cultural apparatus, encode messages with a "preferred" meaning that supports the interests of the ruling class. This preferred meaning is not forced upon the viewer; rather, it is presented as the only logical, common-sense way to read the message. The dominant-hegemonic decoder accepts this presentation, identifying their own interests with those of the state or the corporation. In doing so, the viewer participates in the reproduction of the hegemonic order, validating the authority of the institutions that control the means of communication. This alignment is not a product of simple brainwashing, but of a shared cultural code that makes the dominant view appear to be the only rational perspective on the world."When the viewer takes the connoted meaning from, say, a television newscast or current affairs programme full and straight, and decodes the message in terms of the reference code in which it has been encoded, we might say that the viewer is operating inside the dominant code."Situational Logics: The Negotiated PositionThe second position is the negotiated code, which Hall identifies as the most common mode of decoding in everyday life. In this position, the viewer does not simply accept or reject the dominant ideology. Instead, they acknowledge the legitimacy of the hegemonic definitions in an abstract, general sense, whilst reserving the right to make exceptions and adaptations at a local, situational level. The negotiated reading is a compromise, a mixture of acceptance and resistance that reflects the contradictory position of the working class within capitalist society. Hall writes:A negotiated decoder might, for example, accept the dominant national discourse on the necessity of economic austerity or wage restraint in the abstract, viewing it as a common-sense solution to a national crisis. However, when it comes to their own union’s strike for better wages, they will argue that their specific case is an exception to the rule, defending their local interests against the very hegemonic logic they have just accepted.Negotiated codes operate through what Hall calls "situational logics," which are sustained by the unequal relations of power in everyday life. The negotiated reading is not a coherent philosophical critique, but a pragmatic negotiation with the demands of survival in a class-divided society. It allows the viewer to navigate the contradictions of their daily experience without directly challenging the legitimacy of the ruling order, showing how hegemony is maintained not through absolute agreement, but through a series of local compromises."Decoding within the negotiated version contains a mixture of adaptive and oppositional elements: it acknowledges the legitimacy of the hegemonic definitions to make the grand significations (abstract), while, at a more restricted, situational (situated) level, it makes its own ground rules – it operates with exceptions to the rule."Reading Against the Grain: The Oppositional PositionThe third and most politically significant position is the oppositional code. In this position, the viewer perfectly understands both the literal and the connotative inflections given to the message by the producers, but rejects them entirely. The viewer deconstructs the preferred reading, identifying its "common-sense" claims as ideological mystifications designed to maintain the power of the ruling class. The oppositional decoder translates the message into an entirely different frame of reference, reading "against the grain" to expose the contradictions of the text. Hall writes:An oppositional reading occurs when, for example, a viewer watches a television programme about national security or industrial dispute and decodes every reference to "national interest" as "class interest." The preferred reading is detotalised, its claims to represent the whole society are broken down, and retotalised within a counter-hegemonic framework, such as socialist politics or anti-colonial struggle.For Hall, the transition from negotiated to oppositional decoding is a crucial political moment. It is the moment when local, situational frustrations are linked to a systemic critique of power, transforming passive discontent into active resistance. By showing that the oppositional reading is a structural possibility in every communicative act, Hall provides cultural critics with a powerful model for analysing how texts can become sites of political struggle."Finally, it is possible for a viewer perfectly to understand both the literal and the connotative inflection given by a discourse but to decode the message in a globally contrary way. He/she detotalizes the message in the preferred code in order to retotalize the message within some alternative framework of reference... He/she is operating with what we must call an oppositional code."Gramscian Hegemony, Semiotics, and the Birmingham SchoolHall’s encoding/decoding model must be understood in the context of the intellectual project of the Birmingham School. Under Hall's directorship, the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) sought to break away from both the economic determinism of orthodox Marxism and the apolitical formalism of traditional literary criticism. To do this, Hall synthesised the semiotics of Roland Barthes and Ferdinand de Saussure with the political philosophy of Antonio Gramsci.From Barthes and Saussure, Hall took the insight that language is a system of signs whose meanings are not fixed by nature but are socially constructed. Meaning is produced through the play of difference, and the relationship between a signifier and its signified is arbitrary and historical. This means that no text has a single, natural meaning; rather, it is open to multiple interpretations, depending on the codes used to decipher it. Hall applies this semiotic insight to media discourse, showing that television programmes are systems of signs that must be interpreted rather than transparent facts.From Gramsci, Hall adopted the concept of "hegemony", the process by which a ruling class maintains power not through physical force (coercion), but by winning the intellectual and moral consent of the subordinate classes. Hegemony is not a static state of domination; it is an ongoing struggle, a constant negotiation that must be repeatedly won and defended in the cultural sphere. The media, in this view, is a key site of hegemonic struggle. The encoding/decoding model shows how hegemony works at the level of language: the dominant-hegemonic position represents the successful achievement of consent, whilst the negotiated and oppositional positions represent the limits of that consent and the potential for resistance.The Model Applied: Literary Texts as Sites of Ideological StruggleAlthough Hall designed his model to analyse the television discourse of the late twentieth century, its principles apply directly to the study of literature. Literature, no less than television, is a coded discourse produced within specific institutional networks (such as publishing houses, academic departments, and literary reviews) and received by readers operating within diverse social and historical contexts.A literary text, when read from a dominant-hegemonic position, appears to be a unified, natural expression of universal human truths. The reader accepts the narrator's authority, identifies with the protagonist's struggles, and validates the moral and social order that structures the fictional world. In reading a Victorian novel like Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre from this position, the reader might view Jane's ultimate marriage to Rochester as a natural, satisfying resolution of her quest for independence, accepting the novel's bourgeois individualist values as universal.However, a reader operating from a negotiated position might accept the novel's general critique of Victorian class and gender hierarchies whilst feeling uneasy about the treatment of Bertha Mason, the "madwoman in the attic." This reader might negotiate their reading by enjoying Jane's personal triumph whilst acknowledging the situational injustice of Bertha's imprisonment, adapting the text to their own modern, progressive sensibilities.Finally, an oppositional reading of Jane Eyre, exemplified by Jean Rhys’s post-colonial novel Wide Sargasso Sea, deconstructs the text entirely. The oppositional reader detotalises the preferred reading by identifying Bertha Mason not as a gothic monster, but as a victim of imperialist and patriarchal exploitation. The novel's happy ending is retotalised as a sinister consolidation of colonial power and domestic confinement. By showing that literature can be decoded in ways that directly contradict its encoding, Hall’s model reframes the act of reading as a political intervention, exposing the library not as a silent sanctuary of universal values, but as a noisy archive of ideological conflict.By denying the possibility of a final, authoritative reading, Hall did not reduce culture to a chaos of subjective interpretations; rather, he mapped the structured, unequal relations that govern how we make sense of our world, showing that the act of decoding is always an act of political choice.
critical_works.ch64: Hélène Cixous (1937–)Original title: Le Rire de la Méduse1975 · French · France · French Feminist Theory / Post-structuralism · Feminist Manifesto / EssayThe Somatic Current: Seizing the Means of InscriptionHélène Cixous’s "The Laugh of the Medusa," first published in French in 1975 as Le Rire de la Méduse and translated into English by Keith Cohen and Paula Cohen in 1976, represents a radical intervention in the fields of literary criticism, feminist theory, and post-structuralist philosophy. At the centre of Cixous’s project is the concept of écriture féminine (feminine writing), a somatic, fluid, and subversive mode of expression designed to shatter the phallogocentric structures of Western thought. Phallogocentrism, a term coined by Jacques Derrida to describe the collusion of phallocentrism (the prioritisation of the male phallus as the primary symbol of power and authority) and logocentrism (the belief in a stable, self-present origin of truth and meaning), is diagnosed by Cixous as a system that has systematically silenced women. For centuries, Cixous argues, the masculine monopoly on language has constructed femininity as a passive void, a dark continent, or a site of lack. To counter this structural erasure, Cixous calls on women to seize the tools of language and write themselves into history, using their bodies, their desires, and their unconscious processes as the very material of their textuality.The act of writing, in Cixous’s formulation, is not a detached, intellectual exercise, but a somatic necessity. The exclusion of women from writing is directly linked to the confiscation of their bodies; by reclaiming the pen, women reclaim their physical autonomy. Cixous frames this reclamation not as a polite request for inclusion within existing literary canons, but as an insurgent act of self-assertion. The feminine voice must erupt into the text, bringing with it the repressed physical reality of female pleasure and experience. This somatic writing is inherently fluid and decentralised, resisting the linear, hierarchical, and rigid syntax of traditional male discourse. By linking textual production directly to the libidinal economy of the female body, Cixous seeks to neutralise the binary oppositions, such as culture/nature, mind/body, and active/passive, that have historically served to justify the subordination of women. Writing becomes the primary arena for the subversion of patriarchal authority, allowing women to dismantle the conceptual frameworks that have defined them only in relation to masculine desires.Beyond Castration: Reclaiming the Medusa’s LaughterA central critical move in Cixous’s essay is her radical re-reading of the classical myth of the Medusa, a myth that Sigmund Freud had famously mobilised in his psychoanalytic theory to explain the masculine fear of castration. In his 1922 essay "Medusa’s Head," Freud argued that the terrifying gaze of the Medusa, with her hair of writhing snakes, represents the boy’s shock at discovering the female lack of a penis, a sight that induces the fear of castration and paralyses the male spectator with terror, turning him to stone. Within this psychoanalytic framework, the feminine is inevitably coded as a threat, a monstrous emblem of mutilation and death that must be conquered, blinded, or decapitated by the heroic male subject (symbolised by Perseus). Cixous rejects this psychoanalytic narrative of terror and lack, identifying it as a phallocentric projection designed to domesticate female power and rationalise male anxiety. She urges women to look at the Medusa directly, bypassing the mediated horror constructed by male mythmakers:The laughter of the Medusa is a powerful emblem of Counter-Hegemonic resistance. It is a laughter that mocks the solemnity of patriarchal systems, the dogmatic claims of psychoanalysis, and the rigid logic of castration. By asserting that the Medusa is beautiful and laughing, Cixous subverts the definition of the feminine as a site of horror, lack, and castration. She transforms the Medusa from a warning sign of male vulnerability into a celebration of female desire, voice, and multiplicity. The snakes, rather than representing castrated substitutes or symbols of lack, become icons of dynamic, pluralistic energy. The Medusa’s gaze no longer paralyses or silences; instead, her laughter invites women to embrace their own complexity and speak from a position of abundance rather than lack. Cixous’s re-reading demonstrates how classical mythology can be deconstructed and repurposed to serve emancipatory ends, showing that the monstrous categories of patriarchal culture are often nothing more than the repressed projections of male anxiety."You only have to look at the Medusa straight on to see her. And she's not deadly. She's beautiful and she's laughing."The Economy of Abundance: Milk, White Ink, and Bodily ExcessTo describe the specific texture and movement of écriture féminine, Cixous employs powerful metaphors of bodily fluids, specifically mother’s milk and what she terms "white ink." These metaphors are contrasted with the dry, transactional, and restrictive economies of masculine writing, which she associates with the law, the father, and the ledger. Masculine writing operates within an economy of scarcity, where meaning is hoarded, boundaries are policed, and exchange is strictly regulated to preserve authority. Feminine writing, by contrast, operates within a libidinal economy of abundance, generosity, and excess. Cixous links this abundance to the maternal body, which she conceptualises not as a site of passive reproduction or domestic confinement, but as a source of limitless, creative power that flows directly into language:This metaphor of writing in white ink suggests that the feminine text is nourished by a maternal current that precedes the acquisition of patriarchal language (the symbolic order). It is a form of writing that remains connected to the pre-Oedipal voice, the rhythms of the mother’s body, and the somatic experiences of pleasure (jouissance). White ink is fluid, non-linear, and multiple; it resists the black-and-white binaries of phallogocentric logic. By writing in white ink, women produce texts that are open-ended, filled with digressions, and resistant to final, absolute closures. This writing does not seek to master, define, or categorise the world, but to celebrate connection, process, and difference.Moreover, Cixous argues that this somatic excess breaks down the rigid syntax of male rationalism. Patriarchal language relies on a clear separation between the subject and the object, a logical progression of arguments, and a strict control of emotional and physical register. Écriture féminine disrupts this order by infusing prose with poetic rhythms, syntactic interruptions, and a voice that sings rather than merely declares. It is a writing that overflows the banks of conventional grammar, allowing the body’s desires to dictate the structure of the sentence. The maternal body becomes a reservoir of creative energy that enables women to write beyond the constraints of patriarchal reason, producing a discourse that is as nourishment-giving as it is revolutionary."There is always within her at least a little of that good mother's milk. She writes in white ink."Somatic Insurgency: Writing as a Space of Radical TransformationFor Cixous, the reclamation of writing is not merely an aesthetic choice or literary style but a profoundly political act. It is a form of somatic insurgency that seeks to transform the social, cultural, and political landscape. The historical exclusion of women from writing has been a key mechanism in the maintenance of patriarchal power, as it has allowed men to define the parameters of reality, history, and value. When women begin to write themselves, they disrupt these established definitions, introducing new perspectives and experiences that challenge the legitimacy of existing power structures. Cixous makes this clear when she describes the revolutionary potential of the feminine text:Writing is the precursory movement of revolution because it allows for the conceptualisation of alternative worlds and subjectivities. It is the space where the margins can speak back to the centre, where the repressed can find expression, and where the boundaries of the thinkable can be expanded. By putting themselves into the text, women perform an act of self-invention that escapes the ready-made roles allocated to them by patriarchal society. They refuse to be the passive objects of male representation and instead become the active subjects of their own narratives.This transformation requires a complete break with the conventions of patriarchal representation. Women cannot simply adopt the language of the father to tell their stories, as that language is already encoded with their subordination. Instead, they must engage in a process of linguistic subversion, using écriture féminine to destabilise the authority of the dominant discourse. This involves reclaiming words, inventing new forms, and celebrating the capacity of language to be playful, ambiguous, and polyphonic. By resisting the demands of linear logic and singular meaning, feminine writing exposes the contingency of patriarchal truth, showing that the dominant order is not natural or eternal, but a constructed system that can be dismantled and remade."...this being all the more serious and unpardonable in that writing is precisely the very possibility of change, the space that can serve as a springboard for subversive thought, the precursory movement of a transformation of social and cultural structures."The Afterlife of Somatic InscriptionCixous’s "The Laugh of the Medusa" has had an immense and enduring influence on the development of feminist literary theory, gender studies, and queer theory. Along with theorists like Luce Irigaray and Julia Kristeva, Cixous formed the core of what became known in the Anglophone academy as French Feminist Theory. Her concept of écriture féminine opened up new avenues for reading and writing, encouraging critics to pay close attention to the somatic, rhythmic, and poetic dimensions of texts, rather than focusing solely on thematic content or formal symmetry.In literary criticism, Cixous's ideas inspired the development of gynocriticism and feminine writing practices that seek to identify a distinct female literary tradition. Critics have applied her theories to the works of writers such as Virginia Woolf, Clarice Lispector, and Toni Morrison, arguing that these authors employ a fluid, somatic style that challenges traditional narrative structures. Furthermore, Cixous’s critique of psychoanalysis and her subversion of the castration myth laid the groundwork for subsequent queer and post-structuralist critiques of gender identity, including Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity, which similarly deconstructs the idea of a natural, stable body in favour of cultural inscriptions.However, Cixous’s somatic approach has also been a subject of critical debate. Some materialist and Marxist feminists have accused her of essentialism, arguing that by linking writing so closely to the female body and mother’s milk, she risks reducing women to their biological functions, thereby reinforcing the very nature/culture binaries she seeks to destroy. Critics have also questioned whether écriture féminine is accessible to all women, or if it remains a highly abstract, avant-garde practice limited to academic and elite circles.In response to these criticisms, it is crucial to recognise that Cixous’s concept of the body is not biological or essentialist, but phenomenological and historical. The body for Cixous is a site of social inscription, a historically situated medium through which power is exercised and resisted. Écriture féminine is not a biological default, but a conscious political practice, an invitation to write through the lived experience of marginalisation and somatic exclusion. By refusing to separate the mind from the body, and language from desire, Cixous’s essay continues to are an indispensable resource for anyone seeking to challenge the limits of patriarchal discourse and imagine new, liberating forms of textual expression. The Medusa’s laughter remains an open invitation to subvert, to play, and to write.
critical_works.ch65: Gilles Deleuze (1925–1995) and Félix Guattari (1930–1992)Original title: Kafka: Pour une littérature mineure1975 · French · France · Post-structuralism / Schizoanalysis · Critical MonographThe Cramped Space: Defining the Minoritarian PositionGilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari’s Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature, published in French in 1975 and translated into English by Dana Polan in 1986, is a revolutionary work of post-structuralist literary theory and political philosophy. The monograph represents a key development in the authors' joint project of "schizoanalysis," which they initiated in Anti-Oedipus (1972) to dismantle the bourgeois, individualist assumptions of Freudian psychoanalysis and orthodox Marxism. In Kafka, Deleuze and Guattari turn their attention to literary representation, proposing a new method of reading that rejects the traditional search for hidden symbols, archetypes, or private psychological complexes. Instead of asking what a text "means," they investigate how a text functions as a machine, how it connects with desire, power, and social assemblages.At the heart of this monograph is the definition of a "minor literature." Deleuze and Guattari immediately clarify that minor literature is not literature written in a minority language. Rather, it is the literature that a minority group constructs within a major, dominant language. They write:The primary exemplar of this condition is Franz Kafka, a Prague Jew who wrote in German. Kafka did not write in Czech, the language of the local population, nor did he write in Yiddish, the traditional language of Central European Jewish culture. Instead, he wrote in German, the official language of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which was the language of administration, commerce, and dominant culture. Writing in German placed Kafka in a double displacement: he was alienated from the Czech majority, yet excluded from the German-Austrian centre. This "cramped space" of the minority writer, operating within the territory of a major language that is not fully their own, is the defining condition of minor literature. Deleuze and Guattari argue that this marginal position, rather than being a limitation, provides the writer with a unique, revolutionary potential to subvert the dominant culture from within."A minor literature doesn't come from a minor language; it is rather that which a minority constructs within a major language."The Three Pillars of Minor InscriptionTo map the operations of minor literature, Deleuze and Guattari outline three distinct characteristics that differentiate it from the dominant, "major" literary tradition. These characteristics are not thematic labels, but structural and political operations that transform the very nature of language and expression.The first characteristic is the high coefficient of deterritorialisation that affects the language of a minor literature. When a minority writer uses a major language, they do not accept its canonical rules, its established metaphors, or its claims to universal truth. Instead, they stretch, strangle, and displace the dominant tongue, forcing it to vibrate with a foreign intensity. In Kafka’s case, this took the form of what the authors call a "paper German", a dry, bureaucratic, and sparse language that had been stripped of its rich, regional associations and historical depth. Rather than trying to enrich this language, Kafka intensified its poverty, using its very flatness to construct a new kind of expression. This process of deterritorialisation turns the major language into a site of nomadic wandering, rendering it foreign to its own native speakers and exposing the arbitrariness of its rules.The second characteristic of minor literature is that everything in it is political. In major literatures, the social milieu serves merely as a background or a passive frame for individual, private concerns. A traditional realist novel, for example, might focus on a domestic marriage dispute, treating the family as an isolated, private sphere separate from the state. In minor literature, by contrast, the cramped nature of the social space makes such isolation impossible. Because the minority writer exists at the margins, every individual concern is immediately connected to political immediacy. Deleuze and Guattari write:There is no room for private, apolitical concerns; a family dispute, a job interview, or a romantic encounter is instantly linked to the state bureaucracy, the judicial system, or the capitalist economy. The personal is more than political; it is directly connected to the machineries of power.The third characteristic is that everything in a minor literature takes on a collective value. In major literature, the author is celebrated as a sovereign, individual genius who speaks for themselves or creates unique characters with private interiorities. In minor literature, the scarcity of recognized authority and the pressure of marginalisation mean that there is no space for an individuated, master voice. Instead, the writer’s work functions as a collective machine of expression. Deleuze and Guattari state:The writer does not speak as an individual, but rather as a collective assemblage of enunciation. Their voice becomes the vehicle for the expression of a people-yet-to-come, a community in the process of defining its own identity and resistance."The second characteristic of minor literatures is that everything in them is political.""The third characteristic of minor literature is that in it everything takes on a collective value. Indeed, precisely because talent is not abundant in a minor literature, there are no possibilities for an individuated enunciation that would belong to this or that 'master' and could be separated from a collective enunciation."Evading the Father: Rhizomatic Lines of FlightA major target of Deleuze and Guattari’s critique in this monograph is the psychoanalytic habit of reading Kafka’s works through the lens of the Oedipus complex. Traditional critics have long argued that Kafka’s entire output, specifically The Trial, The Metamorphosis, and his Letter to His Father, is a grand projection of his personal psychological conflict with his dominant father, Hermann Kafka. Within this Oedipal framework, the bureaucratic monsters of The Trial and the unreachable authority of The Castle are interpreted as symbolic substitutes for the father, reducing Kafka’s complex political critiques to a private family drama.Deleuze and Guattari reject this reductionist reading, arguing that it serves to domesticate Kafka’s radicalism and neutralise his political insights. They assert that Kafka does not use the state to represent his father; rather, he uses the father to represent the bureaucratic and capitalist systems that oppress the individual. The father is not the origin of power, but merely its local, domestic agent. To focus on the father is to ignore the vast, impersonal networks of authority that structure modern life.To counter this Oedipal closure, Deleuze and Guattari introduce the metaphor of the rhizome. Unlike a tree, which has a single, deep root and grows hierarchically, a rhizome is a horizontal, underground network of stems that connects any point to any other point. It has no centre, no origin, and no fixed boundaries. A rhizome can be broken or ruptured at any point, but it will start up again along its old lines or on new lines. Deleuze and Guattari read Kafka’s texts as rhizomes: they are systems of multiple entries and exits that resist the singular, centralising logic of the Oedipal family.This rhizomatic structure is evident in Kafka’s animal stories, such as The Metamorphosis, Investigations of a Dog, and A Report to an Academy. In The Metamorphosis, Gregor Samsa’s transformation into a giant insect is not a passive symbol of psychological degradation or a cry of Oedipal defeat. Rather, it is a active line of flight, a physical attempt to escape the family household, the demands of his capitalist employer, and the constraints of human identity. By becoming-animal, Gregor deterritorialises his body and his voice, escaping the Oedipal triangle (Father-Mother-Son) in favour of a machinic connection with the material world. Similarly, the ape in A Report to an Academy does not seek human culture as a form of spiritual enrichment; he seeks a way out, an exit from his cage. The animal transformations in Kafka are not metaphors, but literal passages of desire, lines of flight that attempt to evade the dead-ends of family and state.The Machinic Assemblage: Bureaucracy and Desiring-MachinesFor Deleuze and Guattari, Kafka is not a prophet of despair or a chronicler of existential isolation. Instead, he is a highly political cartographer of modern power, an analyst of what they call the "bureaucratic machine." In The Trial and The Castle, Kafka maps the ways in which modern state and capitalist institutions operate not through centralised, rational planning, but through infinite, decentralized, and self-reproducing networks of desire and authority.In The Trial, the court is not a remote, transcendent authority located in a majestic courthouse. Instead, its offices are scattered throughout the attics of tenement buildings; its judges are corrupt, its clerks are listless, and its proceedings are open to constant, local negotiations. Josef K. is arrested not because he has violated a specific, identifiable law, but because he is caught within the machinic assemblage of the court. The law is not a set of clear prohibitions, but an infinite process of implication. Desire and power are not opposed in this system; rather, the subjects of the court are implicated in their own subjugation through their desire to navigate the bureaucracy.Kafka subverts this bureaucratic machine by exposing its internal contradictions and its dependency on local assemblages of desire. In The Castle, the surveyor K. attempts to contact the authorities not to submit to their power, but to find a space of connection within their systems. The castle, like the court, is a decentralised network of offices, messengers, and documents that constantly breaks down. Deleuze and Guattari argue that Kafka’s writing is a "desiring-machine" that plugs into these bureaucratic systems, accelerating their breakdowns and tracing lines of flight through their corridors. The writer does not represent the law; they map its limits, showing that even the most formidable institutions of power are nothing more than contingent, unstable assemblages that can be disrupted, deterritorialised, and re-engineered.The Afterlife of Minoritarian SubversionDeleuze and Guattari's Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature has had a profound impact on post-colonial theory, linguistics, translation studies, and political philosophy. By decoupling the concept of the "minor" from quantitative size or biological identity, the authors provided a powerful tool for analysing how marginalised groups use language to resist dominant cultures.In post-colonial studies, theorists like Homi Bhabha have drawn on the concept of minor literature to examine how colonised subjects employ the coloniser's language to subvert colonial authority. The idea of deterritorialising a major language has been central to the analysis of Anglophone and Francophone literatures from Africa, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where writers adapt English or French to local rhythms, idioms, and political struggles. Similarly, in translation studies, the concept has inspired "foreignising" translation practices that seek to preserve the foreignness of the source text within the target language, rather than domesticating it to suit the tastes of the dominant culture.Within political philosophy, the concept of the collective assemblage of enunciation has helped theorists think beyond the liberal humanist subject and the vanguard party, imagining new forms of collective action that are decentralized, horizontal, and rhizomatic. The monograph remains an indispensable guide for anyone seeking to understand the revolutionary potential of writing, showing that literature is not a silent mirror of reality, but a active machine of struggle, a vector of becoming that has the power to transform both language and the world.
critical_works.ch66: Wolfgang Iser (1926–2007)Original title: Der Akt des Lesens: Theorie ästhetischer Wirkung1976 · German · Germany (Constance School) · Reader-Response Criticism / Reception Aesthetics · Theoretical TreatiseThe Virtual Convergence: Artistic and Aesthetic PolesWolfgang Iser’s The Act of Reading: A Theory of Aesthetic Response, originally published in German in 1976 as Der Akt des Lesens: Theorie ästhetischer Wirkung and translated into English in 1978, represents a key statement of reader-response criticism and reception aesthetics (Rezeptionsästhetik). Operating as a leading figure of the Constance School alongside Hans Robert Jauss, Iser mounts a systematic challenge to the formalist and New Critical methodologies that had dominated mid-twentieth-century literary studies. While formalist critics treated the literary text as an autonomous, self-contained object whose meaning could be extracted through close linguistic analysis, and psychoanalytic or biographical critics focused on the author’s intentions, Iser shifts the analytical focus to the dynamic interaction between the text and the reader.Drawing on the phenomenological philosophy of Roman Ingarden and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Iser argues that a literary work cannot be identified solely with the printed text on the page, nor can it be reduced to the subjective projections of a reader’s imagination. Instead, the literary work exists as a virtual space created at the intersection of two distinct poles: the artistic and the aesthetic. Iser defines these poles and the virtual character of the work:The artistic pole represents the objective material created by the author, the linguistic structures, narrative strategies, and schematised aspects that form the skeletal frame of the text. The aesthetic pole represents the realization (Konkretisation) of these structures by the reader’s consciousness. Crucially, the work itself is virtual; it does not reside in either pole but is continually brought into existence through the active, dialectical engagement between the text's structures and the reader's creative activity. By reframing the work as a virtual event, Iser establishes the reader as an active collaborator in the production of literary meaning, transforming the act of reading from a passive consumption of information into a dynamic performance."The literary work has two poles, which we might call the artistic and the aesthetic: the artistic pole is the author's text and the aesthetic is the realization accomplished by the reader."The Implied Reader: Built-in Response-Inviting StructuresTo explain how the text guides and regulates this collaborative process without dictating a single, uniform interpretation, Iser formulates the concept of the "implied reader." Unlike actual readers, flesh-and-blood individuals who read texts in specific historical contexts with their own personal biases, psychological dispositions, and cultural frameworks, the implied reader is a textual construct. It designates a network of response-inviting structures embedded within the text itself that prepay the role the reader must assume to bring the work to fruition.The implied reader is not an idealized figure or a model of perfect understanding, but a structured role that the text offers to the actual reader. It represents the set of instructions and perspective-alignments that the actual reader must inhabit to navigate the narrative. The text contains various perspectives, such as those of the narrator, the characters, the plot, and the fictitious reader, and the implied reader is the standpoint that allows these perspectives to be synthesized into a coherent whole.Actual readers bring their own "repertoire" (the social, cultural, and literary norms of their historical moment) into contact with the text’s repertoire. When the actual reader adopts the role of the implied reader, a dialogic tension is established: the reader’s personal expectations and values are brought into dialogue with the text's structures. The text does not force the reader to submit to its logic; rather, it provides the conditions under which the reader can construct meaning. The concept of the implied reader thus bridges the gap between the objective structures of the text and the subjective activity of the actual reader, demonstrating how the text maintains a guiding authority even as it invites creative participation.The Unseen Joints: Gaps, Blanks, and LeerstellenA central pillar of Iser’s theory is the argument that no literary text can represent its fictional world completely or explicitly. By its very nature, a text is composed of schematised aspects and linguistic signs that contain points of indeterminacy, gaps, or "blanks" (Leerstellen). These blanks are not failures of clarity on the part of the author, nor are they mere absences of information. Rather, they are functional, structural components of the text that act as the primary catalyst for the reader's imaginative engagement. Iser writes:These blanks function as unseen joints because they mark the boundaries and transitions between different perspectives, schemata, and narrative segments. When a text shifts from one character's perspective to another, or from a narrator's commentary to a dramatic scene, it leaves a gap between these segments. The text does not formulate the logical connection between these elements; instead, it presents them as contiguous but separate. The reader must perform the cognitive work of bridging these gaps, linking the disparate segments together to construct a continuous narrative flow.When the reader fills in a blank, the blank "disappears," replaced by the reader's synthesis of the text's perspectives. This process of filling the blanks is what Iser calls "consistency-building." As the reader encounters indeterminacies, they project their own experiences, cultural norms, and logical assumptions to fill the gaps, making the text meaningful. However, the text’s structures also regulate this activity: the blanks limit the reader’s freedom, preventing arbitrary interpretation by directing the reader's imagination along specific paths. The blanks thus are the essential pivot of the communicative circuit between text and reader, ensuring that the reader remains actively involved in co-authoring the text's meaning."Blanks are the unseen joints of the text, and they as it were trigger the acts of ideation."The Wandering Viewpoint: Cognitive Synthesis and Gestalt FormationTo describe how the reader experiences and synthesizes these textual structures over time, Iser introduces the concept of the "wandering viewpoint" (Wanderblick). Because a literary work is a temporal medium, the reader cannot perceive the text all at once, as one might view a painting. Instead, the reader must travel through the text segment by segment, line by line. The reader's position is never fixed; it is a moving point of focus that travels along the narrative timeline. Iser defines the wandering viewpoint:As the reader’s viewpoint wanders through the text, it operates at the convergence of memory (retrospection, or what Husserl called retention) and expectation (protension). When the reader encounters a new sentence, they interpret it in light of what they have already read (memory), while anticipating what will follow (expectation). This dialectic movement is a continuous process of modification. A new event or revelation in the narrative might frustrate previous expectations, forcing the reader to look back and re-read earlier passages in a new light, modifying their memory of the text. Conversely, this reinterpretation increases the complexity of their expectations for the remainder of the work.Through this wandering viewpoint, the reader performs the cognitive synthesis necessary to form a "gestalt", a coherent, unified image of the text's meaning. The gestalt is not a static property of the text, but a dynamic, evolving construct that the reader continually revises as they progress. By tracking the movements of the wandering viewpoint, Iser provides a highly sophisticated account of the phenomenology of reading, showing how the construction of meaning is a temporal process of negotiation, correction, and cognitive adaptation."The wandering viewpoint is a means of describing the way in which the reader is present in the text. This presence is at a point where memory and expectation converge, and the resultant dialectic movement brings about a continual modification of memory and an increasing complexity of expectation."The Reception Aesthetics LegacyWolfgang Iser’s The Act of Reading has had a profound and lasting impact on literary theory, cognitive sciences, and cultural studies. By shifting the focus of analysis from the text-as-object to the reading process, Iser laid the theoretical foundations for the expansion of reader-response criticism in the late twentieth century.His work has been extensively applied in pedagogical theory, where educators have used the concepts of the implied reader and blanks to design active, reader-centred curricula that encourage students to engage critically with texts rather than passive memorisation of canonical interpretations. In the field of cognitive literary studies, contemporary researchers draw on Iser's phenomenological accounts of the wandering viewpoint and consistency-building, linking them to empirical studies of how the brain processes narrative, forms mental models of fictional worlds, and manages expectations.However, Iser's theory has also faced critical scrutiny. Critics from the Marxist and historical materialism traditions, such as Terry Eagleton, have argued that Iser’s model is overly formalist and apolitical. They contend that his "implied reader" is a highly refined, bourgeois academic subject whose reading practices are assumed to be universal, thereby ignoring the material, class-based, and institutional forces that govern how different social groups access and interpret literature. Similarly, American reader-response theorist Stanley Fish critiqued Iser from a radical pragmatist perspective, arguing that Iser’s division between the objective "textual structures" and the subjective "reader's realization" is unsustainable. Fish asserts that there is no objective text independent of the reader; rather, the text is entirely constructed by the "interpretive communities" to which the reader belongs, which pre-determine what can be read as a structure or a gap.In response to these critiques, it is important to emphasize that Iser does not present the reading process as a free-floating, apolitical encounter. The concepts of the repertoire and the implied reader are inherently historical; they represent the ways in which historical contexts, social norms, and literary codes are inscribed within the very fabric of the text and the consciousness of the reader. The Act of Reading does not collapse the text into subjective whim, nor does it lock it in formalist isolation. Instead, it maps the complex, regulated, and creative process by which human consciousness interacts with language to bring fictional worlds to life. The treatise remains an indispensable resource for understanding the communicative contract that underlies all literature, showing that the act of reading is nothing less than the virtual birth of the work itself.
critical_works.ch67: Luce Irigaray (1930–)Original title: Ce Sexe qui n'en est pas un1977 · French · France · French Feminist Theory / Psychoanalytic Critique · Feminist EssaysThe Specular Mirror: Dismantling the Phallogocentric MonopolyLuce Irigaray’s This Sex Which Is Not One, first published in French in 1977 as Ce Sexe qui n'en est pas un and translated into English by Catherine Porter in 1985, represents a fundamental disruption of Western psychoanalytic and philosophical traditions. At the heart of Irigaray’s project is a sustained, deconstructive critique of what she, following Jacques Derrida, terms phallogocentrism, the systematic collusion of phallocentrism and logocentrism that defines the singular masculine subject as the sole producer of meaning, truth, and value. Irigaray argues that Western culture operates under a specular logic, a system of representation that functions like a mirror. Within this specular economy, the female subject is never represented on her own terms; rather, she is constructed as the negative reflection, the dark reverse, or the passive boundary that consolidates and confirms the masculine subject’s identity.In her reading of Sigmund Freud and Jacques Lacan, Irigaray demonstrates how classical psychoanalysis conceptualises woman only in relation to man. Freud defines female sexuality through the lens of castration and lack, coding the female genitals as a blank space or a mutilated version of the male organ. For Freud, the little girl is merely a "little man" who must eventually accept her anatomical deficit and redirect her desires towards maternal reproduction. Lacan reinforces this phallic monism by asserting that the Symbolic Order, the system of language, law, and social relations, is structured by the Phallus as the primary transcendental signifier. Under this regime, woman is cast as the absolute signifier of castration, an empty vessel through which the masculine subject negotiates his own castration anxiety and desire. Irigaray rejects this definition of the feminine as a mere structural absence or negation:This resistance to definition is not a sign of cognitive or structural deficiency, but rather an indication that female subjectivity operates outside the binary logic of the phallocentric Symbolic Order. The masculine subject requires a singular, unified identity to maintain his position of dominance; he must be the "One" who defines the "Other." By exposing the specular nature of this relationship, Irigaray reveals that the patriarchal definition of woman is not a biological or ontological truth, but a cultural projection designed to preserve masculine authority. She invites women to step outside this mirror game, refusing to be the passive surface that reflects male narcissism, and instead to begin articulating their own autonomous forms of desire, language, and social existence."She is neither one nor two. Rigorously speaking, she cannot be identified either as one person, or as two. She resists all adequate definition."The Two Lips: Mapping a Plural and Fluid TextualityTo counter the singular, unitary logic of phallogocentrism, Irigaray proposes the powerful anatomical and philosophical metaphor of the "two lips" of the vulva. Unlike the male phallus, which presents itself as a singular, visible, and self-contained instrument of power, the female genitals are plural, hidden, and in constant self-affection. Irigaray uses this somatic reality to theorise a form of female sexuality and subjectivity that is inherently plural, autoerotic, and resistant to singular categorization. The two lips touch each other continuously, without the need for external mediation, establishing a relationship of intimacy that escapes the traditional subject-object division:This tactile plurality provides a model for parler-femme (speaking-woman), a style of writing and speaking that Irigaray champions as the linguistic expression of female difference. Parler-femme is characterised by its fluidity, its resistance to linear logic, and its refusal of absolute closures. If masculine language relies on clear definitions, stable syntax, and hierarchical structures, feminine speech is multiple, open-ended, and contradictory. It is a language that does not seek to master or categorise the world, but to express the shifting, non-unitary nature of female pleasure and experience.By linking textuality to the fluid mechanics of the female body, Irigaray challenges the philosophical privilege of the "solid." She argues that Western metaphysics has historically favoured solid, stable, and measurable forms (associated with the phallus and the ego) while repressing or marginalising the fluid, the formless, and the multiple (associated with female bodily currents and fluids). The mechanics of fluids, which Irigaray explores in detail, represents a critique of the scientific and philosophical demand for rigorous boundaries and static identities. Feminine writing, like a fluid, overflows and penetrates the rigid frameworks of patriarchal discourse, exposing the vulnerability of its assumptions and offering a more open, relational, and generative mode of textuality."Woman 'touches herself' all the time, and moreover no one can forbid her to do so, for her genitals are formed of two lips in continuous contact. Thus, within herself, she is already two—but not divisible into one(s)—that caress each other."Women on the Market: The Patriarchal Trade in CommoditiesIn the key essay "Women on the Market," Irigaray expands her critique from psychoanalysis to the realms of Marxist economics and structural anthropology. Engaging with Claude Lévi-Strauss’s theory of kinship structures and Karl Marx’s analysis of the commodity form, she argues that patriarchal society is built entirely upon the exchange of women between men. Within this economic and social system, women do not participate as subjects who trade or negotiate; rather, they are the commodities themselves, the passive objects of circulation whose value is determined solely by the men who possess and exchange them:Kinship structures, legal systems, and cultural alliances are established and maintained through this circulation of the female body. By being traded between fathers, husbands, and sons, women are the infrastructure that enables homosocial alliances, relationships of power, recognition, and debt between men. The female body is stripped of its singular use-value and converted into exchange-value, functioning as a signifier of male wealth, prestige, and social standing.Irigaray shows that within this patriarchal market, women are divided into three primary categories: the mother, the virgin, and the prostitute. The mother represents pure use-value, associated with reproduction and the maintenance of the domestic sphere; however, her value is strictly confined to the private realm and is subordinated to the name of the father. The virgin represents pure exchange-value, an untouched commodity whose circulation guarantees the transmission of patriarchal lineage and property. The prostitute represents a commodified form of direct utility, whose value is established by her availability for multiple transactions. In all three cases, the woman's value is external to her own subjectivity:This economic objectification leaves women alienated from their own bodies and desires. They are forced to occupy a split consciousness, existing on the one hand as physical entities and on the other as social signifiers whose value is defined by the patriarchal market. Irigaray’s critique exposes the homosocial foundations of Western culture, showing that the social contract is a heterosexual contract based on the exclusion of female agency and the exploitation of female labour and bodies."The society we know, our own culture, is based upon the exchange of women. Without the exchange of women, we are told, we would fall back into the anarchy of the natural world, the randomness of the animal kingdom.""The exchange value of two signs, two commodities, two women, is a representation of the needs/desires of consumer-exchanger subjects: in no way is it the 'property' of the signs/articles/women themselves."Mimicry and Deconstructive Irony: Overcoming the Symbolic PrisonTo escape the specular prison of phallogocentrism, Irigaray does not advocate for a simple withdrawal from language, which would only reinforce female silence and invisibility. Instead, she proposes the tactical practice of mimicry (or mimesis). Mimicry is a deliberate, playful, and subversive repetition of patriarchal discourse. By adopting the vocabulary, logic, and style of male philosophers and psychoanalysts, the female theorist can mimic their arguments with a subtle difference, exposing the gaps, contradictions, and repressed assumptions that underpin their claims to universal truth.Through mimicry, the female writer makes visible what was supposed to remain hidden: the masculine bias of supposedly objective concepts. For example, when Irigaray mimics Freud's lectures on femininity or Plato's cave allegory, she does more than reproduce their ideas; she exaggerates their rhetorical gestures, highlights their structural omissions, and introduces ironies that destabilise their authority. This tactic allows women to speak within the Symbolic Order while simultaneously undermining its power from within. It is a form of linguistic sabotage that opens up cracks in the patriarchal monolith, creating spaces where female difference can be heard.Furthermore, mimicry allows the female subject to negotiate her relationship with the maternal body. In patriarchal culture, the mother is typically silenced and swallowed by the name of the father; she is the matrix from which the subject emerges, but her own voice is erased. By mimicking the patriarchal erasure of the mother, the female writer can begin to deconstruct the primary maternal-filial bond, reclaiming the mother-daughter relationship as a site of mutual recognition and creative collaboration. This moves feminist critique beyond simple rebellion against the father and towards the construction of a positive genealogy of women, providing a foundation for female solidarity and autonomous cultural production.The Afterlife of Irigarayan DifferenceThe publication of This Sex Which Is Not One secured Luce Irigaray’s position as one of the pre-eminent figures of French Feminist Theory, alongside Hélène Cixous and Julia Kristeva. Her critique of psychoanalysis and her theorisation of sexual difference have had a profound and lasting impact on literary criticism, gender studies, queer theory, and continental philosophy. In literary studies, her concepts of the "two lips" and fluid textuality have inspired new ways of reading female writers, encouraging critics to pay close attention to the structural, syntactic, and somatic aspects of texts that resist patriarchal conventions.However, Irigaray’s work has also been the subject of significant critical debate. Materialist and Marxist feminists, such as Monique Wittig and Toril Moi, have criticized her for essentialism, arguing that her reliance on anatomical metaphors like the "two lips" risks reducing female identity to biological features and reinforcing the binary categories of sex. These critics suggest that by focusing so heavily on sexual difference, Irigaray neglects the historical, material, and institutional factors that shape women's lives. Similarly, some post-colonial critics have argued that her model of "woman" is based primarily on a white, Western, middle-class subject, ignoring the ways in which race and class intersect with gender oppression.In defence of Irigaray, supporters argue that her use of the body is not biological, but discursive and strategic. The "two lips" is not a literal description of female anatomy, but a tropological intervention designed to disrupt the phallic singular logic of Western philosophy. Furthermore, her later work has expanded to address international law, environmental ethics, and intercultural dialogue, demonstrating the versatility of her philosophy of difference. Ultimately, This Sex Which Is Not One remains a foundational text because it challenges us to think beyond the binary logic of identity and difference, providing a language with which we can imagine a world where the feminine is no longer a lack, but a site of limitlessness, multiplicity, and joy.
critical_works.ch68: Barbara Smith (1946–)Original title: Toward a Black Feminist Criticism1977 · English · United States · Black Feminist Theory / Intersectionality precursor · Critical EssayThe Unprecedented Intervention: Mapping the Intersection of OppressionsBarbara Smith’s "Toward a Black Feminist Criticism," first published in the radical feminist journal Conditions: Two in 1977, represents a foundational moment in modern literary theory and feminist thought. Before the formal coining of the term "intersectionality" by Kimberlé Crenshaw in the late 1980s, Smith’s essay outlines a pioneering critical framework that insists on the simultaneous analysis of race, gender, class, and sexuality in the study of Black women’s literature. Smith opens her essay by acknowledging the profound difficulty, even the danger, of attempting to carve out an autonomous intellectual space for Black women’s writing in an academy and a culture that systematically erases their presence:This declaration of vulnerability is more than personal; it is a diagnostic critique of the structural violence of the American literary canon and the critical institutions that police it. Smith argues that Black women writers inhabit a space of triple erasure, silenced by white male critics, Black male critics, and white feminist critics alike. To counter this erasure, Smith proposes a critical practice that refuses to isolate race from gender, or class from sexuality. She asserts that the creative production of Black women can only be understood if it is approached through a politics that recognises how these distinct systems of oppression interlock, shape, and reinforce one another.By centring the lived reality and historical experiences of Black women, Smith establishes that literature is never produced in a social vacuum. The texts written by Black women are deeply marked by their material struggles against racism, patriarchy, capitalism, and heteronormativity. Consequently, a criticism that attempts to analyse these works using only a singular lens, such as a feminist analysis that ignores race, or a racial analysis that ignores gender, is both incomplete and actively complicit in the distortion and devaluation of the literature. Smith’s intervention is therefore both an aesthetic and a political manifesto, demanding a complete overhaul of critical methodologies to accommodate the complex, multi-layered textuality of Black women’s writing."I do not know where to begin. Long before I tried to write this I realized that I was attempting something unprecedented, something dangerous merely by writing about Black women writers from a feminist perspective and about Black lesbian writers from any perspective at all"The Interlocking Matrix: Reconstructing the Literary HorizonAt the core of Smith’s critical methodology is the concept of "interlocking" factors of oppression, a term she also helped articulate as a founding member of the Combahee River Collective. In the essay, Smith demonstrates that this political framework is essential for reading the thematic and formal structures of Black women's literature:To ignore any single component of this matrix is to misread the text entirely. Smith illustrates this by showing how Black women writers construct narrative structures, character motivations, and thematic conflicts that reflect their unique position within the social hierarchy. For instance, the domestic spaces in Black women’s novels are never merely sites of gendered confinement, as they often are in white women’s literature; they are also spaces shaped by the legacies of racial violence, economic exploitation, and the struggle for communal survival.Smith argues that because Black women’s lives are structured by these interlocking oppressions, their writing naturally develops unique strategies of resistance, subversion, and solidarity. These strategies are often coded in language, imagery, and narrative forms that conventional, single-axis criticism fails to register. By applying an intersectional critical lens, Smith shows how writers like Zora Neale Hurston, Alice Walker, and Toni Morrison challenge the binary categories of Western literary analysis. They create characters who must navigate the double jeopardy of being Black and female in a white supremacist, patriarchal society, while also dealing with the class divisions that fragment their communities. Smith’s framework thus transforms the act of reading from a passive consumption of aesthetic forms into an active, political engagement with the material conditions of textual production."The politics of sex as well as the politics of race and class are crucially interlocking factors in the works of Black women writers."Naming the Blindness: Critiquing White Feminism and Black Male HegemonyA significant portion of "Toward a Black Feminist Criticism" is dedicated to a sharp, polemical critique of the existing literary and political establishments. Smith launches a dual critique, targeting both the white feminist movement and the Black male literary canon for their respective complicities in the erasure of Black women. She accuses the white feminist establishment of a profound, systemic racism that blinds it to any experience of womanhood that does not conform to the middle-class, white default:This blindness, Smith argues, manifests in the exclusion of Black women from feminist anthologies, course syllabi, and theoretical debates, reducing the feminist literary project to a parochial reflection of white privilege. White feminist critics often treat "gender" as a universal category, failing to see how their own racial and class positions protect them from the forms of violence and exploitation experienced by Black women.Simultaneously, Smith critiques the Black male literary establishment for its sexism and virulent homophobia. She argues that Black male critics and writers have historically constructed a nationalist literary canon that prioritises racial struggle at the expense of gender equality. In this male-dominated framework, Black women writers are either ignored or relegated to secondary roles, while Black lesbian writers are subjected to a massive, hostile silence. Smith exposes how Black male critics often dismiss the work of Black women as politically insignificant or divisive, using patriarchal standards of value to police the boundaries of Black literature.
