By challenging both the racism of white feminists and the sexism of Black nationalists, Smith deconstructs the false binaries of identity politics, showing that true liberation requires a critique that addresses all forms of domination simultaneously."It is galling that ostensible feminists and acknowledged lesbians have been so blinded to the implications of any womanhood that is not white womanhood and that they have yet to struggle with the deep racism in themselves that is at the source of this blindness"Breaking the Silence: A Lesbian Reading of SulaTo demonstrate the radical capability of her proposed framework, Smith provides a groundbreaking, "woman-identified" reading of Toni Morrison’s 1973 novel Sula. Smith focuses on the intense, lifelong bond between the protagonist, Sula Peace, and her childhood friend, Nel Wright. She argues that, regardless of whether the characters engage in literal sexual acts, their relationship can and should be understood through a lesbian critical lens:This reading was highly controversial at the time of its publication, as it challenged the pervasive heteronormative assumptions of both the Black community and the literary academy. Smith shows that Sula and Nel’s bond is the central emotional axis of the novel, a relationship of mutual recognition and self-actualisation that stands in sharp contrast to their unfulfilling relationships with men.Smith’s lesbian reading of Sula is not a simple attempt to label the characters, but a structural analysis of how female homosociality and desire function as forces of social disruption. In the novel, Sula’s refusal to conform to the traditional roles of wife and mother, combined with her deep intimacy with Nel, makes her a threat to the patriarchal order of the Bottom (their community). The community codes Sula as evil or "mad" precisely because she rejects the economy of heterosexual exchange and attempts to live autonomously. By reading this relationship as a lesbian text, Smith demonstrates how political and sexual taboos shape the reception of Black women's writing. She exposes the ways in which critics routinely pathologise or ignore intense female friendships in literature, showing that a Black feminist criticism must be willing to confront and dismantle the homophobia that silences lesbian expression."Consciously or not, Morrison's work poses both lesbian and feminist questions about Black women's autonomy and their impact upon each other's lives"The Afterlife of an Autonomous ManifestoThe legacy of "Toward a Black Feminist Criticism" is immense, serving as a foundational text that helped catalyze the development of Black women's studies and intersectional feminist theory. Along with her work in the Combahee River Collective and her co-founding of Kitchen Table: Women of colour Press in 1980, Smith’s essay laid the institutional and theoretical groundwork for a generation of scholars, including bell hooks, Patricia Hill Collins, Cheryl Wall, and Barbara Christian. The essay helped establish a distinct Black feminist literary canon, retrieving forgotten writers like Zora Neale Hurston from obscurity and validating the contemporary work of authors like Toni Cade Bambara, Gloria Naylor, and Audre Lorde.However, the essay also provoked significant debate and criticism. Some critics, including Toni Morrison herself, expressed reservations about Smith’s lesbian reading of Sula, arguing that it imposed an external, identity-based category onto a text that was primarily concerned with the complexities of female friendship and communal history. Other scholars questioned whether Smith’s emphasis on "woman-identified" experience risked establishing a new form of essentialism, or whether her focus on literature was too detached from the materialist, grassroots political organizing needed to dismantle capitalism.In response to these debates, it is essential to recognise that Smith’s criticism is always conceptualised as an extension of political activism. For Smith, literature and criticism are not mere academic exercises, but tools for consciousness-raising and coalition-building. Toward a Black Feminist Criticism remains a vital, living document because it refuses to separate the aesthetic from the political. By insisting that we must read the page through the prism of race, class, gender, and sexuality, Smith’s essay continues to challenge the limits of literary theory, offering a model of critical engagement that is as intellectually rigorous as it is politically transformative.
critical_works.ch69: Edward Said (1935–2003)Original title: Orientalism1978 · English · Palestine / United States · Postcolonial Theory (Foundational Text) · Theoretical Monograph / Discourse AnalysisThe Construction of the Hegemonic Other: The Positional Superiority of the WestEdward Said’s Orientalism, published in 1978, is a watershed moment in Western intellectual history, inaugurating the field of postcolonial theory and transforming the disciplines of comparative literature, cultural studies, and anthropology. The central thesis of the work is that "the Orient" is not a natural, inert, or objective geographical entity, but a complex cultural construct created by the West. Said argues that Western culture has historically constructed the Orient as its exotic, static, irrational, feminine, and inferior "Other." By producing this binary opposition between a rational, progressive, and superior West (the Occident) and a backward, stagnant, and inferior East (the Orient), Western imperial powers have been able to justify, maintain, and naturalise their colonial hegemony.Crucial to Said’s analysis is the concept of "flexible positional superiority." This term describes the rhetorical and political strategy whereby the Western observer always locates himself in a position of strength relative to the Oriental subject. The Westerner is the active, knowing subject who observes, maps, categorises, and judges, while the Oriental remains the passive, silent object of study. This positional superiority allows the West to speak for the Orient, defining its history, character, and future prospects. Said demonstrates that this relationship is not one of mutual exchange or objective curiosity, but an exercise in structural power. The construction of the Orient serves to reinforce the West’s self-image as the vanguard of civilisation, progress, and democratic values, creating a self-consolidating mirror that rationalises imperial domination as a benevolent, civilising mission.The Discursive Matrix: Foucaultian Power/Knowledge and Systematic RepresentationTo explain how this construction achieves such enduring authority, Said draws heavily upon the post-structuralist philosophy of Michel Foucault, specifically Foucault's concepts of discourse and the circular relationship between power and knowledge. Said insists that Orientalism is more than a collection of lies, fantasies, or crude prejudices that can be easily dismissed by objective facts. Rather, it is a vast, institutionalised, and highly systematic "discourse", an organized network of representation, language, and institutional authority that produces and regulates what can be thought, said, or written about the East:By treating Orientalism as a discursive formation, Said shows that it possesses a structural coherence that survives changes in political regimes or academic fashions. No writer, researcher, or administrator can engage with the Orient without navigating this pre-existing archive of texts, images, and concepts.However, Said also marks a crucial point of departure from Foucault's theory. While Foucault’s concept of discourse tends to be anonymous, decentralised, and deterministic, leaving little room for individual agency, Said insists on the "determining imprint" of individual authors. He argues that writers like Gustave Flaubert, Renan, or Arthur Balfour are more than passive mouthpieces of a discursive system; they actively shape, refine, and reinforce the discourse through their unique aesthetic choices and intellectual interventions. In this way, Said combines post-structuralist discourse analysis with a humanist commitment to individual responsibility. He demonstrates how the production of knowledge is always implicated in the exercise of power, showing that the supposedly objective, disinterested scholarship of Western academies is deeply entangled with the geopolitical interests of European empires."I have found it useful here to employ Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish, to identify Orientalism."The Three Dimensions of Orientalism: Academic, Imaginative, and Corporate ControlIn the introduction to Orientalism, Said outlines three distinct yet deeply interconnected dimensions of his subject, showing how it functions simultaneously as an academic discipline, a style of thought, and a political institution. The first dimension is the academic one, which comprises the long history of Western scholarship dedicated to the study of Eastern languages, cultures, histories, and religions:This academic tradition, which has its roots in medieval philology and theology, provides the factual authority and intellectual legitimacy that underpins the entire system of representation.The second dimension is the imaginative or ontological style of thought, which establishes a rigid division between the East and the West. This style of thought is found in literature, art, travel writing, and philosophy, and it relies on the assumption that there is an essential, unchanging difference between the Occident and the Orient. In this imaginative realm, the Orient is depicted as a landscape of sensuality, cruelty, despotism, and mystery, a space of childhood and developmental arrest that contrasts with the mature, law-governed world of the West.The third dimension is the corporate institution, which represents the direct intersection of knowledge and imperial administration:This corporate aspect became dominant during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as European empires established colonial bureaucracies, intelligence agencies, and administrative offices to manage their Eastern territories. Academics, writers, and politicians worked in concert to produce an archive of information that could be directly applied to the governance, pacification, and exploitation of colonized peoples."The most readily accepted designation for Orientalism is an academic one, and indeed the label still serves in a number of academic institutions. Anyone who teaches, writes about, or researches the Orient—and this applies whether the person is an anthropologist, sociologist, historian, or philologist—either in its specific or its general aspects, is an Orientalist, and what he or she does is Orientalism.""Orientalism can be discussed and analyzed as the corporate institution for dealing with the Orient—dealing with it by making statements about it, authorizing views of it, describing it, by teaching it, settling it, ruling over it: in short, Orientalism as a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient."Textual Imperialism: Balfour’s Paternalism and Flaubert’s DesiresTo illustrate how these dimensions operate in practice, Said provides detailed, critical readings of historical figures and literary texts, demonstrating the ways in which philology, literature, and political rhetoric participate in imperial domination. He examines the political rhetoric of Arthur James Balfour, who, in a famous 1910 speech to the House of Commons, defended the British occupation of Egypt by asserting that "England knows Egypt", meaning that Western scholars and administrators possessed a superior, objective understanding of Egyptian history and society that the Egyptians themselves lacked. This paternalistic knowledge, Balfour argued, justified British rule as a benefit to the subject population, who were deemed incapable of self-government.In the realm of literature, Said turns to the French novelist Gustave Flaubert, analysing his travels in Egypt and his encounter with the courtesan Kuchuk Hanem. Flaubert’s representation of Kuchuk Hanem becomes, for Said, a powerful microcosm of the Orientalist power dynamic. In his letters and travelogues, Flaubert constructs her as a silent, exotic, and highly sexualised figure, translating her presence into a symbol of "typically Oriental" sensuality:Kuchuk Hanem herself never speaks in Flaubert’s texts; she is denied her own voice, history, and agency. She exists only as a projection of Flaubert’s desires and as a signifier of the West’s capacity to possess, represent, and consume the East. Through these readings, Said demonstrates that literature, philology, and travel writing are not innocent aesthetic pursuits, but active instruments of empire that create the conceptual frameworks needed to justify physical occupation."He was foreign, comparatively wealthy, male, and these were historical facts of domination that allowed him not only to possess Kuchuk Hanem physically but to speak for her and tell his readers in what way she was 'typically Oriental.'"Postcolonial Paradigms and the Afterlife of Said's CritiqueThe publication of Orientalism provoked intense intellectual debate and revolutionized the humanities, laying the foundation for what is now known as postcolonial studies. Said’s work inspired scholars like Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Homi Bhabha, and Gauri Viswanathan to deconstruct the colonial subtexts of Western literature and history. His methodology of "contrapuntal reading", reading a text with a simultaneous awareness of both the metropolitan history and the colonial history it represses, became a standard critical practice.However, the book has also faced significant criticisms. Conservative scholars, most notably the historian Bernard Lewis, accused Said of bias, arguing that Orientalism was a polemical attack on Western scholarship that ignored the genuine achievements and linguistic mastery of European Orientalists. Lewis contended that Said’s thesis was anti-Western and that he had politicised a noble academic tradition. Marxist and materialist critics, such as Aijaz Ahmad, criticized Said for his reliance on post-structuralist theory, arguing that by focusing so heavily on textual representations, he neglected the material, economic, and institutional realities of capitalism and class struggle. Other critics have pointed out that Said constructs a homogeneous, monolithic view of "the West," ignoring the internal divisions, debates, and anti-imperialist traditions within European culture.Despite these debates, Orientalism remains an indispensable text for understanding the dynamics of cultural representation and geopolitical power. By exposing the ways in which knowledge is produced to serve imperial interests, Said’s work continues to challenge us to examine our own assumptions, to read the archives of history critically, and to work towards a world where the representation of the Other is no longer an exercise in domination.
critical_works.ch70: Sandra Gilbert (1936–2024) and Susan Gubar (1944–)Original title: The Madwoman in the Attic: The Woman Writer and the Nineteenth-Century Literary Imagination1979 · English · United States · Feminist Literary Criticism · Critical MonographThe Phallic Pen: Deconstructing the Anxiety of AuthorshipSandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar’s The Madwoman in the Attic, published by Yale University Press in 1979, represents a foundational monument in feminist literary criticism. The book opens with a radical, challenging interrogation of the historical relationship between literary authority and gender:By posing this provocative question, Gilbert and Gubar expose the deeply patriarchal assumptions that have historically governed the Western literary tradition. They argue that in nineteenth-century culture, the act of writing was conceptualised as a masculine, generative power, an extension of the father's authority to define, name, and inherit. Under this regime, the writer is viewed as a progenitor who "begets" his text, leaving female writers in a state of profound alienation.This exclusion leads to what Gilbert and Gubar term the "anxiety of authorship." They contrast this psychological struggle with Harold Bloom’s famous concept of the "anxiety of influence." While Bloom’s model depicts a patrilineal struggle in which a male poet fights for creative survival against his male precursors, the female writer faces a far more fundamental crisis. Lacking a legitimate female tradition, she does not worry about being secondary to a predecessor; rather, she doubts her very capacity to write. She must struggle against a culture that tells her that authorship is a male gift, and that a woman who writes is an unnatural, monstrous anomaly. To write at all, nineteenth-century women had to overcome the fear that the pen was a forbidden tool, navigating a psychic minefield of self-doubt, alienation, and social censure."Is a pen a metaphorical penis?"The Patriarchal Splitting: Angels in the House and Monsters in the ClosetTo understand how nineteenth-century female writers negotiated these constraints, Gilbert and Gubar analyse the recurring archetypes that dominate male-authored literature. They argue that women in the patriarchal imagination are systematically split between two extreme, unrealistic representations: the "angel in the house" and the "monster." The angel, derived from Coventry Patmore’s Victorian poem, is the idealised embodiment of purity, passivity, self-sacrifice, and domestic submissiveness. She exists only to comfort and validate the male subject, possessing no desires, voice, or agency of her own. Her opposite is the monster: the rebellious, assertive, and passionate woman who refuses to conform to domestic expectations. This figure is coded as destructive, mad, and demonic, a warning sign of the dangers of female autonomy.Gilbert and Gubar argue that these archetypes are not mere artistic conventions, but cultural prisons that stifle female creativity. For a woman writer to find her own voice, she must engage in a process of aesthetic exorcism, dismantling both representations:The angel must be killed because her submissiveness requires the silence of the woman writer; the monster must be killed because her pathologised rage leads to self-destruction. This dual struggle shapes the thematic structure of nineteenth-century female textuality. Women writers are forced to negotiate their relationship with these patriarchal doubles, often creating narratives that conform on the surface to the ideal of the domestic angel while secretly harboring the rebellious energy of the monster."And similarly, all women writers must kill the angel's necessary opposite and double, the 'monster' in the house, whose Medusa-face also kills female creativity."Thornfield's Secret: Bertha Mason and the Splitting of ConsciousnessThe primary metaphor of the book is Bertha Mason, the madwoman locked in the third-floor attic of Thornfield Hall in Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre. Rather than reading Bertha as a simple antagonist or a symbol of Gothic horror, Gilbert and Gubar interpret her as the literal projection of the heroine’s own repressed rage, desire, and split consciousness. Bertha is Jane Eyre’s "dark double," the physical embodiment of the anger and rebellion that Jane must suppress to maintain her position as a respectable governess:The authors show that Bertha’s eruptions into the narrative occur at precise moments when Jane’s autonomy is threatened by patriarchal figures. When Rochester attempts to turn Jane into a passive, kept woman, or when St John Rivers demands that she sacrifice her identity to his missionary zeal, it is Bertha who acts out the violent resistance that Jane cannot openly express.By burning down Thornfield Hall and blinding Rochester, Bertha performs a necessary act of destruction that allows Jane to eventually return to Rochester on equal terms. Through this analysis, Gilbert and Gubar demonstrate how the madwoman figure is a vital creative outlet for the woman writer. The attic becomes a space of repressed agency, where the female author projects her own rage against the patriarchal family, the marriage contract, and the legal structures that deny women autonomy. The madwoman is not an ornament; she is the creative double who speaks the unspeakable, exposing the violence hidden beneath the surface of Victorian domesticity."Bertha has functioned as Jane's dark double throughout the governess's stay at Thornfield. Specifically, every one of Bertha's appearances—or, more accurately, her manifestations—has been associated with an experience (or repression) of anger on Jane's part"Subversive Palimpsests: Strategies of Double-VoicingFaced with the necessity of conforming to patriarchal standards while desiring self-expression, nineteenth-century women writers developed what Gilbert and Gubar call "palimpsestic" literature. A palimpsest is a parchment that has been written upon, scraped clean, and then written upon again, leaving traces of the original script beneath the surface. Gilbert and Gubar argue that the works of writers like Jane Austen, Mary Shelley, the Brontë sisters, and Emily Dickinson operate in precisely this manner. On the surface, their novels and poems seem to conform to the conventions of Victorian morality, domestic romance, and female propriety; underneath, however, they contain a hidden, subversive subtext that critiques the very structures they seem to celebrate.In the case of Jane Austen, the authors show how her novels use irony, double-voicing, and structural reversals to critique the economic dependence of women on marriage, showing that her heroines' compliance with social rules is a survival strategy rather than a moral triumph. In Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, they read the monster as a metaphor for the female writer’s own sense of alienation, monstrous creation, and maternal abandonment. Emily Dickinson’s poetry is analysed as a series of coded texts that use fragmented metre, dashes, and intense imagery to express a radical, internal sovereignty that rejects the authority of a masculine God and a patriarchal society. Through these readings, Gilbert and Gubar reveal that the nineteenth-century female literary imagination is characterized by a profound, creative duplicity, a double-voiced discourse that allows women to speak to their male peers while simultaneously communicating a secret, liberating subtext to their female readers.A particularly vivid illustration of this double-voiced textuality is Gilbert and Gubar’s reading of Christina Rossetti’s poem "Goblin Market". On the surface, the poem is a Victorian moral fable warning children against the temptations of forbidden fruit and praising sisterly love. Underneath, however, the authors reveal a complex, subversive exploration of female desire, sexual exploitation, and the commodification of women in patriarchal society. The goblin men and their luscious, addictive fruits represent the deceptive allure of male artistic and sexual markets, which threaten to consume and destroy female creative genius (represented by Laura). Lizzie’s heroic sacrifice to save her sister is read as a model of female solidarity and mutual support, establishing an alternative, gynocentric community that rejects the commodity logic of the goblins. By retrieving the subversive, gendered anxieties hidden beneath Rossetti's domestic imagery, Gilbert and Gubar demonstrate how nineteenth-century women writers encoded their critique of patriarchal power structures in seemingly innocent moral tales, establishing a rich, underground language of resistance.The Legacy of the Attic and Its Critical AfterlifeUpon its publication, The Madwoman in the Attic was hailed as a landmark achievement, transforming the study of Victorian literature and establishing feminist criticism as a major academic discipline. It helped recover many neglected female writers and provided a powerful, psychological vocabulary with which to discuss female creativity and resistance. Its focus on doubling, repressed rage, and the politics of space has had an enduring influence on subsequent generations of critics and writers.However, the book has also been the subject of significant critical revision. Postcolonial and Black feminist critics, most notably Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak in her influential essay "Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism," have criticized Gilbert and Gubar for ignoring the imperial and racial dimensions of Bertha Mason's character. Spivak argues that the self-actualisation of the white, Western heroine (Jane) is achieved only through the literal and symbolic sacrifice of the colonial, Jamaican subject (Bertha), thereby exposing the colonial complicities of Western feminist criticism. Other critics have argued that the book's psychoanalytic framework remains too bound to the very patriarchal structures (such as Freudian doubling) it seeks to critique, and that it overemphasises the pathology of the female writer at the expense of her intellectual and historical agency.Despite these necessary critiques, The Madwoman in the Attic remains a classic text of feminist literary history. By exposing the structural barriers that have silenced women and showing how female writers used creative duplicity to write themselves into history, Gilbert and Gubar’s monograph continues to inspire critics to look beneath the surface of the text and listen for the voices that have been locked in the attic.
critical_works.ch71: Elaine Showalter (1941–)Original title: Towards a Feminist Poetics (published in Women Writing and Writing About Women, ed. Mary Jacobus)1979 · English · United States · Feminist Literary Criticism · Critical EssayThe Bifurcated Path: Defining the Feminist Critique and GynocriticsElaine Showalter’s "Towards a Feminist Poetics," originally published in Mary Jacobus’s edited collection Women Writing and Writing About Women (1979), is a watershed moment in the consolidation of feminist literary theory. Writing at a juncture when feminist criticism was frequently dismissed by the academic establishment as a political grievance search rather than a rigorous intellectual discipline, Showalter sets out to bring order, taxonomy, and theoretical autonomy to the field. She diagnoses the primary challenge of feminist criticism not as a lack of passion, but as a lack of a coherent, self-determined framework, noting that the discipline has suffered from a reliance on male-dominated critical paradigms. To resolve this theoretical confusion, Showalter proposes a fundamental division within feminist literary practice:By establishing this clear partition, Showalter seeks to steer the feminist critical project away from a purely reactive relationship with male writing. She argues that as long as feminist criticism remains confined to dissecting male-authored texts, it cannot develop an independent aesthetic theory. Through this conceptual mapping, she seeks to divide the critical territory into two distinct domains: the "feminist critique," which acts as a reader-centred, ideological intervention, and "gynocritics," which represents a writer-centred, constructive project of female literary history."Feminist criticism can be divided into two distinct varieties. The first type is concerned with woman as reader—with woman as the consumer of male-produced literature, and with the way in which the hypothesis of a female reader changes our apprehension of a given text, awakening us to the significance of its sexual codes. [...] The second type of feminist criticism is concerned with woman as writer—with woman as the producer of textual meaning, with the history, themes, genres and structures of literature by women."Woman as Reader: The Mechanics of the Feminist CritiqueThe first branch of Showalter's taxonomy, the "feminist critique," is reader-centred, consumer-oriented, and historically grounded. It examines how women engage with texts written within a patriarchal culture, focusing specifically on male-authored literature. The primary objective of the feminist critique is to expose the ideological assumptions that underpin the representation of gender in these works. It is a critical practice dedicated to decoding the "images of women" in literature, identifying prevailing stereotypes, exposing omissions and misconceptions, and uncovering the systemic exploitation of female characters.Showalter characterises this mode of criticism as highly political and polemical. In its execution, it functions as a form of ideological demystification, exposing how male writers construct a version of womanhood that serves to reinforce patriarchal authority. It reads against the grain of the literary canon, showing how works long celebrated for their universal humanism are, in fact, structured by gendered hierarchies and biases. However, Showalter warns that this method is subject to a serious structural limitation. Because it is dependent on male-authored texts for its subject matter, it remains bound to the very systems of authority it seeks to dismantle. The feminist critique is a reactive discourse; it is an analysis of oppression rather than an expression of liberation. It represents the "Old Testament" of feminist criticism, characterized by a necessary but ultimately limiting "angry or loving fixation on male literature." It identifies the sins and errors of patriarchal writing but cannot, by itself, lead the female reader into a land of creative autonomy.Woman as Writer: The Architectural Project of GynocriticsTo escape this dependency on the male canon, Showalter proposes the second branch of her taxonomy: "gynocritics." Coined from the French la gynocritique, this term describes a critical shift from the consumer to the producer of textual meaning. Gynocritics focuses on the woman as writer, seeking to analyse the history, styles, genres, structures, and themes of literature written by women. It is a constructive, rather than a deconstructive, project, aimed at mapping the contours of a distinct female literary tradition. Showalter outlines the expansive scope of this program:Under the gynocritical paradigm, the critic investigates the psychodynamics of female creativity, the evolution of female language, the trajectories of individual female careers, and the collective history of women’s writing. Gynocritics aims to recover lost or neglected female writers, rebuilding a fragmented literary heritage. It treats women’s writing not as a series of isolated, anomalous occurrences, but as a continuous, coherent subculture with its own evolutionary logic. If the feminist critique is the Old Testament of the discipline, gynocritics is its New Testament, offering a transition toward the "grace of imagination" and the affirmative creation of a female poetics. It offers an escape from the defensive posture of exposing male bias, allowing critics to ask productive questions about how women have historically navigated their lives and translated their experiences into art."In contrast to [an] angry or loving fixation on male literature, the program of gynocritics is to construct a female framework for the analysis of women's literature, to develop new models based on the study of female experience, rather than to adapt male models and theories."The Three Historical Phases: Feminine, Feminist, and FemaleA central component of Showalter’s project is her division of the history of women's writing into three sequential, developmental phases: the Feminine, the Feminist, and the Female. This developmental model, which she introduces in A Literature of Their Own (1977) and refines in this essay, trace the gradual emancipation of the female writer from the constraints of the dominant male tradition.The first period, the Feminine Phase (spanning roughly from 1840 to 1880), is defined by imitation and internalization. During this era, women writers operated under the heavy burden of dominant male traditions, values, and aesthetic standards. To gain publication and avoid a patronising reception, they often adopted male pseudonyms, such as George Eliot, George Sand, and the Brontë sisters writing as Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. Showalter argues that these writers internalized the patriarchal assumptions of their culture regarding female nature, writing in an effort to prove themselves the intellectual equals of men within the established rules of the game. Their work is characterized by a tension between their desire for creative expression and their adherence to Victorian standards of domesticity and feminine propriety.The second period, the Feminist Phase (lasting from 1880 to 1920), is characterized by protest and political advocacy. During this phase, which corresponds to the rise of the New Woman and the struggle for women's suffrage, female writers began to use literature as a weapon against patriarchal oppression. They rejected the passive roles of the Victorian angel, writing polemical, radical, and often utopian novels and plays that demanded social, legal, and creative equality. However, Showalter observes that this phase, too, remains structurally dependent on the male tradition. Because it is defined by protest against male values, it still takes the male establishment as its central point of reference. The feminist writer’s creative energy is focused on challenging the patriarch, leaving little room for the exploration of female subjectivity on its own terms.The third period, the Female Phase (beginning around 1920 and continuing into the contemporary era), is the phase of self-discovery and aesthetic autonomy. In this period, women writers reject both imitation and protest, recognizing that both are forms of dependency on male models. Instead, they turn inward to the specificities of female experience, using it as the primary source for an autonomous art. Showalter writes:This phase is marked by a search for a unique female style and language, seen in the modernist experiments of Dorothy Richardson and Virginia Woolf, and extending to contemporary writers who explore female biology, psychology, and personal history without the constant need to justify their work to a male audience."women reject both imitation and protest—two forms of dependency—and turn instead to female experience as the source of an autonomous art"The Rejection of Male Theory: Towards an Autonomous PoeticsA major target of Showalter’s critique is the academic tendency to analyse women's writing through the lens of male-centred critical theories. She argues that applying theories like Freudian psychoanalysis, Marxist sociology, structuralism, or post-structuralism to female texts is a form of intellectual capitulation. These frameworks are built on male experience and reinforce patriarchal structures of thought. When a feminist critic forces a female text into a psychoanalytic or Marxist model, she is merely subordinating the female voice to a male master narrative, repeating the erasure of female subjectivity that occurred in the original creation of those theories.Showalter asserts that a true feminist poetics cannot be imported from male institutions; it must be constructed from within the history of women's writing and the material conditions of female life. She does not advocate for a complete rejection of all existing methodologies, but she insists that they must be radicalised and subordinated to a specifically female framework. The critic must begin with the text and the life of the woman writer, drawing on disciplines like history, sociology, and anthropology to construct a localized, contextualized reading of the female subculture. By insisting on this methodological independence, Showalter aims to establish feminist criticism as a self-sustaining academic field that does not need to petition male-dominated departments for intellectual legitimacy.The Legacy of the Essay and Its Critical Afterlife"Towards a Feminist Poetics" exerted a profound influence on the development of Anglo-American feminist literary studies, providing the conceptual vocabulary that helped establish women's literature as a distinct field of academic inquiry. Showalter’s taxonomies of "feminist critique" and "gynocritics" became standard tools for scholars, and her historical divisions structured syllabus design and literary histories for decades. The essay's call for a self-contained female framework was instrumental in shifting the focus of feminist scholarship from exposing male bias to recovering the rich history of female writers.However, Showalter's gynocritical project soon drew sharp criticism from other quarters of the feminist movement. French feminist critics, such as Hélène Cixous, Luce Irigaray, and Julia Kristeva, challenged the Anglo-American focus on social realism and historical experience. Grounded in post-structuralism and Lacanian psychoanalysis, these critics argued that Showalter's concept of a female poetics was theoretically naive and essentialist, assuming a stable, pre-discursive female experience. They proposed instead the concept of écriture féminine (female writing), which defined the female voice not through historical authorship, but through a subversive relationship to language itself, rooted in the maternal body and the unconscious.Furthermore, Black feminist and postcolonial critics, such as Hazel Carby, bell hooks, and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, criticised gynocritics for its homogenizing assumptions. They argued that Showalter's "female experience" was implicitly that of white, middle-class, Western women, and that it systematically ignored the intersections of race, class, and empire. Spivak, in particular, demonstrated that the consolidation of the white female subject in Western literature often depended on the erasure or silencing of the third-world woman. Despite these critiques, "Towards a Feminist Poetics" remains a foundational text. By insisting that women's writing has a history, a structure, and an aesthetic value of its own, Showalter's essay laid the groundwork for all subsequent efforts to read women into the literary canon.
critical_works.ch72: Jean-François Lyotard (1924–1998)Original title: La Condition postmoderne: Rapport sur le savoir1979 · French · France · Postmodernism / Post-structuralism · Philosophical / Sociological ReportThe Crisis of Legitimation: Incredulity Toward MetanarrativesJean-François Lyotard’s The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge, commissioned by the Conseil des Universités of the government of Quebec and published in 1979, is arguably the most famous and enduring tract on the nature of postmodernity. What began as a sociological report on the state of knowledge in highly developed societies quickly evolved into a sweeping philosophical diagnosis of a historical epoch. Lyotard opens the work with a formulation that has since become the defining catchphrase of postmodern theory:By "metanarratives" (or grand narratives), Lyotard refers to the overarching, totalising frameworks of thought that have historically been used to legitimise social institutions, scientific endeavors, and political projects. The modern age, he argues, was characterised by a reliance on these grand stories to justify its pursuits. The Enlightenment, for instance, was structured around the metanarrative of progressive human emancipation through scientific reason; German idealism, particularly the Hegelian system, was legitimised by the grand narrative of the dialectical realization of absolute knowledge; while Marxism relied on the metanarrative of a classless society achieved through proletarian revolution.In the postmodern epoch, Lyotard asserts, these grand narratives have lost their legitimising power, or what he terms their "narrative function." They have been eroded by the horrors of twentieth-century history, the rise of technoscience, and the fragmentation of social life. Postmodernity is characterised by a scepticism toward any system of thought that claims to offer a universal, absolute key to human history or truth. With the collapse of these overarching frameworks, knowledge can no longer find its justification in a grand destiny; instead, it must look for localized, pragmatic, and highly contingent forms of legitimacy."Simplifying to the extreme, I define postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives."The Mercantile Transformation: Computerisation and the Commodification of KnowledgeA central thesis of Lyotard's report is that the nature of knowledge undergoes a radical mutation as societies enter the post-industrial age and the computerised era. Knowledge is no longer pursued as an end in itself, such as the romantic ideal of self-cultivation (Bildung) or the pursuit of universal truth. Instead, it is systematically exteriorised from the knower, translated into informational quantities, and treated as a mercantile commodity. Lyotard anticipates the digital age with remarkable clarity, writing:This commodification of knowledge shifts the question of its legitimacy away from truth or justice toward "performativity" (performativité). Under the rule of performativity, the value of knowledge is determined solely by its capacity to optimize the input/output ratio of a system. Universities and research institutes are no longer tasked with producing wise citizens or discovering truth; instead, they are restructured to produce operational skills and marketable data.The question is no longer "Is it true?" but "Is it saleable?" and "What is its utility?" Lyotard warns that this mercantilisation turns knowledge into a major stake in global power struggles. As nation-states and multinational corporations compete for control over information networks, knowledge becomes a force of production, an informational currency that determines geopolitical dominance. In this technocratic environment, the state loses its role as the grand educator and custodian of national culture, becoming instead a manager of systemic efficiency and informational flow."Knowledge is and will be produced in order to be sold, it is and will be consumed in order to be valorized in a new production: in both cases, the goal is exchange. It ceases to be an end in itself, it loses its 'use-value'."Language Games: The Fragmentation of DiscourseTo explain how knowledge operates in the absence of metanarratives, Lyotard draws on Ludwig Wittgenstein’s concept of "language games" (jeux de langage). He argues that discourse is not a single, unified system, but is rather composed of a multiplicity of distinct games, each governed by its own internal rules. A language game is defined by the specific moves that are permitted within it; for example, the rules of scientific description (which demand empirical verification) are entirely different from the rules of ethical prescription (which demand moral evaluation) or narrative history.Lyotard asserts that there is no universal "metalanguage" capable of translating or unifying all these diverse games. Each game is autonomous and self-contained; its rules cannot be subordinated to a single, totalising system without committing what he calls a différend, an act of injustice where the rules of one game are violently imposed on another. The modern attempt to construct a grand narrative was an effort to create such a metalanguage, forcing the heterogeneous variety of human discourse into a single, authoritarian story.In the postmodern condition, however, we must accept the radical plurality of language games. Lyotard describes the social bond not as a grand consensus, but as a complex, shifting web of linguistic interactions. The individual is situated at the intersection of many different games, navigating between them without the guidance of a universal code. Society, therefore, is not an organic whole or a functional machine, but a fragmented landscape of localized, competing language games.Paralogy: The Postmodern Model of DissentIf modern knowledge was legitimised by consensus, how is postmodern knowledge to be legitimised? Lyotard rejects the model of consensus proposed by thinkers like Jürgen Habermas, who argue that communication should aim for a universal, rational agreement. For Lyotard, such a consensus is both impossible in a fragmented society and is also inherently terroristic, as it requires the suppression of dissent and the silencing of non-conforming language games.Instead, Lyotard proposes "paralogy" (paralogie) as the postmodern alternative for the legitimation of knowledge, particularly in the sciences. Paralogy is the practice of producing dissent, creating imaginative leaps, and inventing new moves or rules within language games. It is not about confirming what is already known or agreeing on common ground; rather, it is about destabilising established frameworks and generating new ways of thinking. Lyotard writes:Postmodern science, in this view, does not progress by consolidating consensus, but by generating paradoxes and revealing the limits of precise control. Paralogy is the work of the inventor, the artist, and the dissenter who refuses to play by the established rules of performativity. By focusing on paralogy, Lyotard seeks to define a model of open-ended, democratic debate that does not seek to reach a final, totalising agreement, but instead aims to sustain the play of differences and encourage the generation of new ideas."Postmodern science—by concerning itself with such things as undecidables, the limits of precise control, conflicts characterized by incomplete information, 'fracta,' catastrophes, and pragmatic paradoxes—is theorizing its own evolution as discontinuous, catastrophic, nonrectifiable, and paradoxical. [...] And it suggests a model of legitimation that [...] has as its basis difference understood as paralogy."The Postmodern Sublime: Witnessing the UnpresentableIn the famous appendix to the report, "Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism?", Lyotard connects his sociological analysis of knowledge to aesthetic theory, turning to Immanuel Kant’s concept of the "sublime." For Kant, the sublime is an aesthetic experience that occurs when the imagination is confronted by something so vast or powerful (like the ocean or a mountain range) that it fails to represent it visually, even though the mind can conceive of it as an intellectual concept. The sublime is thus a tension between the presentable and the conceivable, a painful but exhilarating awareness of the limits of our representation.Lyotard adapts this Kantian framework to define the task of the postmodern artist and writer. While modern art sought to represent the unrepresentable by giving it a beautiful, harmonious form (thereby offering comfort to the viewer), postmodern art refuses such consolations. The postmodern sublime occurs when the artwork bears witness to the fact that there is an "unpresentable", something that can be conceived but cannot be shown. It is an art of radical experimentation that rejects realistic representation, stable forms, and comforting narratives. Lyotard concludes his essay with a famous, rallying cry:To "wage a war on totality" is to reject the totalising systems of political power, scientific performativity, and aesthetic realism that seek to reduce the complexity of the world to a single, manageable representation. Postmodern aesthetics must act as a disruptive force, exposing the fissures in our systems of thought and celebrating the radical differences that refuse to be synthesized."Let us wage a war on totality; let us be witnesses to the unpresentable; let us activate the differences and save the honor of the name."The Legacy of the Report and Its Critical AfterlifeThe Postmodern Condition had an immediate, explosive impact on international intellectual life, transforming the term "postmodernism" from a specialized architectural concept into a major paradigm for cultural, philosophical, and political analysis. Lyotard’s diagnostic vocabulary, particularly "metanarratives," "performativity," and "paralogy", became standard tools for analysing late capitalist culture, media theory, and the digital humanities. His prediction that knowledge would become an informational commodity has been vindicated by the rise of the internet, database economies, and the corporate restructuring of higher education.However, the report also provoked intense debate and hostility. The most prominent challenge came from Jürgen Habermas, who defended the Enlightenment as an "unfinished project." Habermas argued that Lyotard’s rejection of universal reason and consensus led to a dangerous political quietism or neo-conservatism, as it deprived social movements of any shared, rational standards with which to critique injustice. Without a commitment to communicative reason, Habermas warned, postmodernism degenerates into a relativistic field of competing interests where power, rather than truth, decides the outcome.Other critics, particularly Marxist theorists like Fredric Jameson and Terry Eagleton, argued that Lyotard’s focus on language games and local narratives ignored the very real, totalising force of global capitalism. They suggested that the fragmentation Lyotard described was not a liberation from metanarratives, but was itself the cultural logic of late capitalism, which commodifies difference and profits from the disintegration of collective social identities. Despite these challenges, Lyotard's report remains a vital document. By exposing the ideological limits of our grand stories and championing the creative potential of dissent, The Postmodern Condition continues to are an indispensable guide to the shifting landscapes of contemporary knowledge.
critical_works.ch73: Stanley Fish (1938–)Original title: Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities1980 · English · United States · Reader-Response Criticism / Pragmatism · Critical EssaysThe Situational Anecdote: Deconstructing Textual ObjectivityStanley Fish’s Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities, published by Harvard University Press in 1980, represents a landmark intervention in the development of reader-response criticism and American pragmatism. The book, which collects essays written throughout the 1970s, begins with an anecdote that is both its title and its central conceptual metaphor. On the first day of a college semester, a student asks a professor a seemingly straightforward question: "Is there a text in this class?" The professor, operating under the assumption that the student is asking a pragmatic question about course requirements, replies: "Yes, it is the Norton Anthology of Literature." The student, however, clarifies her inquiry: "No, I mean in this class do we believe in poems and things, or is it just us?"For Fish, this brief exchange exposes the profound limitations of the formalist belief in textual objectivity. The professor's initial misunderstanding does not arise because the student's words are ambiguous or because the professor is careless. Rather, it occurs because the same sentence can carry entirely different meanings depending on the situational context and the institutional expectations in force. In the context of a student-teacher relationship at the start of a term, the words naturally evoke the question of a physical textbook. In the context of a classroom debate about literary theory, the same words evoke a philosophical inquiry into the ontological status of the text. Fish uses this anecdote to argue that meaning is never an inherent property of words on a page waiting to be discovered, nor is it a subjective fantasy; it is always a function of the institutional situation in which utterances are produced and received.The Reader-Response Pragmatism: Rejecting the Formalist and Subjectivist IllusionsIn Is There a Text in This Class?, Fish wages a sustained war on two dominant, opposing camps in literary theory: the New Critical objectivists who champion the "text itself," and the romantic subjectivists who champion the absolute freedom of the reader. He argues that both camps are caught in the same philosophical trap, assuming that the text and the reader are independent, self-contained entities that somehow come into contact during the act of reading.Fish rejects the New Critical illusion of textual objectivity, which he calls the "formalist myth." Formalists argue that the text is a stable, self-sufficient structure of meaning that exists independently of any reader. Fish counters that a text cannot be said to exist prior to interpretation. The very act of identifying a marks on a page as a "word," a "sentence," or a "poem" is itself an interpretive act. Without an interpreting mind, the text is merely black marks on paper.At the same time, Fish rejects the romantic or subjectivist view that the reader is an autonomous agent who can arbitrarily impose any meaning they desire on a text. If readers were completely free, literary criticism would degenerate into a chaotic, solipsistic free-for-all where no interpretation could be validated or shared. Fish resolves this apparent paradox by proposing that the reader and the text are not separate entities, but are instead mutually constituted by the same institutional situation. Meaning is not found in the text, nor is it created by the reader; rather, it is produced by the interpretive activities that the reader performs within a specific situation.Interpretive Communities: The Social Constitution of Textual PropertiesTo explain how interpretations can be shared and validated without relying on the myth of textual objectivity, Fish introduces his most famous and controversial concept: the "interpretive community." He argues that readers do not approach texts as isolated individuals, but as members of social groups who share a common set of reading strategies, institutional training, and interpretive assumptions. It is these shared strategies, rather than the text itself, that write the text and determine its meaning. Fish writes:Under this view, an interpretive community is more than a group of people who agree on the meaning of a text; it is the very source of the text's properties. For example, when a group of literary scholars reads a poem, they do not discover its poetic structure; rather, they employ "strategies" (such as looking for irony, paradox, or complex metre) that construct the poem as an object of study. Fish demonstrates this in his famous classroom experiment where he writes a list of names of linguistic theorists on a blackboard and tells his students it is a religious poem. The students immediately deploy their shared strategies of literary analysis, finding intricate patterns of Christian symbolism, themes of mortality, and complex wordplay in the list. The experiment proves that the poetic structure was not in the text but was produced by the interpretive strategies the students set in motion."Interpretive communities are made up of those who share interpretive strategies not for reading (in the conventional sense) but for writing texts, for constituting their properties and assigning their intentions. In other words, these strategies exist prior to the act of reading and therefore determine the shape of what is read rather than, as is usually assumed, the other way round."The Fallacy of Normal Language: All Language is Already InstitutionalA key target of Fish’s critique is the formalist distinction between "ordinary" (or "normal") language and "literary" language. Formalists and structuralists often argue that ordinary language is literal and context-free, whereas literary language is metaphorical, ambiguous, and requires special interpretation. Fish argues that this distinction is a complete fallacy. There is no such thing as "literal" or "ordinary" language that exists outside of a context. All language, no matter how simple, is always already situated and pre-interpreted.To illustrate this, Fish analyses simple, everyday utterances, showing that their "literal" meaning is just as dependent on institutional context as the most complex poem. A sign that reads "Private Property" or a sentence like "The cat is on the mat" is only clear and unambiguous because we are already operating within a shared system of legal and spatial assumptions. If we were to alter the context, the literal meaning would change immediately.Therefore, the difference between reading a scientific manual and reading a Shakespearean sonnet is not a difference between ordinary and literary language; it is a difference between the interpretive communities and reading strategies we choose to apply. We do not first decode a literal meaning and then add interpretation; rather, we perceive meaning immediately because we are always already inhabiting a situation that gives the words their shape.Rebutting Relativism: The Constraints of the Communal ContextBecause Fish argues that "all objects are made and not found, and [...] they are made by the interpretive strategies we set in motion," he has faced persistent accusations of solipsism and radical relativism. Critics charge that if meaning is entirely a product of interpretive strategies, then a reader can make a text mean anything they want, and there is no way to choose between competing interpretations.Fish rejects this charge of relativism, arguing that it is based on a misunderstanding of how the human mind operates. An individual reader cannot interpret a text arbitrarily because the reader is never an isolated, autonomous subject. The reader is always already a member of an interpretive community; their thoughts, categories of perception, and reading strategies are not their own private property, but are the shared property of the community that trained them. Fish explains in his Preface:A reader is always constrained by the institutional situations they inhabit. They cannot choose to see a text as a random jumble of letters, because their training as a reader makes it impossible for them to escape the rules of language and interpretation. Disagreements between readers are not evidence of a lawless relativism, but are conflicts between different interpretive communities, each of which is internally stable, logical, and authoritative."There isn't a text in this or any other class if one means by text what E. D. Hirsch and others mean by it—an entity that remains constant across interpretations... but there is a text in this and every class if one means by text the structure of meanings that is obvious and inescapable from the perspective of whatever interpretive assumptions happen to be in force."The Legacy of the Work and Its Critical AfterlifeIs There a Text in This Class? remains one of the most influential works of American literary theory, playing a crucial role in shifting the focus of academic scholarship from text-based criticism to reader-response theory, institutional critique, and new historicism. Fish’s pragmatic insistence that meaning is tied to institutional practice anticipated the "practical turn" in cultural studies and legal theory, where his concepts have been widely applied to analyse constitutional interpretation and contract law.However, the book also provoked significant critical opposition. Many critics, particularly those aligned with Marxism, postcolonialism, and feminism, argued that Fish’s concept of interpretive communities was politically conservative and insular. They pointed out that by defining the community as the sole source of authority, Fish leaves no room for external critique or systemic change. If the rules of the community determine what is true, then there is no way to challenge the dominant power structures within that community.Furthermore, post-structuralist critics argued that Fish’s model assumes a stable, harmonious consensus within communities that ignores the internal conflicts, power dynamics, and exclusions that characterise all institutional life. Despite these critiques, Fish’s monograph continues to challenge scholars to confront the social and institutional conditions of their own work, reminding us that the texts we read are always, to some extent, the texts we have been trained to write.
critical_works.ch74: Stephen Greenblatt (1943–)Original title: Renaissance Self-Fashioning: From More to Shakespeare1980 · English · United States · New Historicism / Cultural Poetics · Historical Literary Criticism / MonographThe Poetics of Culture: Redefining Literary HistoryStephen Greenblatt’s Renaissance Self-Fashioning: From More to Shakespeare, published in 1980 by the University of Chicago Press, is the foundational text of New Historicism, a school of critical practice that Greenblatt himself prefers to call "cultural poetics". The monograph represents a decisive break from both the formalist confinement of New Criticism, which isolates the literary work as an autonomous, self-contained aesthetic object, and the teleological narrative of traditional literary history, which treats literature as a passive reflection of a stable, pre-existing historical background. Instead, Greenblatt proposes a methodology that conceives of literature as an active participant in a complex, reciprocal network of cultural transactions. In his view, there is no separation between the text and the world; literary works are produced by, and simultaneously help to produce, the political, social, and religious discourses of their historical moment.Central to Greenblatt’s cultural poetics is the rejection of the idea that a literary text possesses a single, transhistorical meaning that can be extracted by the detached critic. Rather, he asserts that literature is embedded in the "social energy" of its era, a force that circulates through various cultural practices, from legal codes and church liturgies to theatrical performances and domestic rituals. To capture this circulation, Greenblatt employs the characteristic New Historicist technique of the historical anecdote. By opening chapters with seemingly marginal, non-literary documents, such as a Protestant merchant's diary, a trial record, or a report on colonial encounters, he establishes a dialogic relationship between the marginal historical event and the canonical literary text. The goal is not to use history to explain literature, but to read both as co-equal texts that participate in the same cultural grammar. This method acknowledges the critic's own historical situatedness, with Greenblatt admitting that "the questions I ask of my material and indeed the very nature of this material are shaped by the questions I ask of myself" (p. 5). Thus, cultural poetics functions as a self-reflexive mode of inquiry, aware of its own inability to fully reconstruct the past while remaining committed to tracing the complex ways in which texts negotiate power.The Mechanics of Identity: External Authority and the Hostile OtherAt the heart of the monograph is the concept of "self-fashioning", which Greenblatt defines as the performative, conscious construction of identity and subjectivity in sixteenth-century England. In the medieval period, identity was largely perceived as an inherited, divinely ordained status, tied to one's place in a cosmic and social hierarchy. The Renaissance, however, witnesses a marked shift toward what Greenblatt terms "an increased self-consciousness about the fashioning of a human identity as a manipulable, artful process" (p. 1). This process is characterised by the belief that a distinctive personality or a characteristic address to the world can be actively shaped, designed, and managed. However, Greenblatt is quick to complicate any naive humanist notion of absolute individual autonomy. Self-fashioning is not a celebration of free will or unconstrained self-expression; rather, it is a highly restricted process that is always shaped by, and dependent on, external structures of authority.Greenblatt outlines several crucial rules that govern the practice of self-fashioning in the sixteenth century. First, it requires a submission to a set of external authorities, such as the family, the state, the monarch, the church, or a political patron. These institutions provide the linguistic and cultural codes through which an individual can conceptualise and express their identity. Second, and perhaps most importantly, self-fashioning is relational and oppositional; it requires the creation and systematic exclusion of a threatening, alien "Other". An individual fashions their identity by defining what they are not, projecting all that is forbidden, chaotic, or sinful onto an external figure, be it the heretic, the Turk, the savage, the peasant, or the witch. The alien Other is both a passive scapegoat and an active threat that must be continually conquered, suppressed, or destroyed for the self to preserve its coherence. The fashioned identity is therefore always marked by anxiety and division, built upon the repressed presence of the very forces it seeks to exclude. Greenblatt notes that "fashioning may suggest the achievement of a less tangible shape: a distinctive personality, a characteristic address to the world, a consistent mode of perceiving and behaving" (p. 2), but this shape is only achieved through a continuous struggle against an internalised or externalised enemy.Subversion and Containment: The Paradox of Royal AuthorityOne of the most controversial and influential arguments in Renaissance Self-Fashioning is Greenblatt's thesis regarding the structural relationship between subversion and containment. Drawing heavily on the post-structuralist political philosophy of Michel Foucault, Greenblatt challenges the traditional liberal assumption that literature is a natural site of resistance to authority. He argues that while Tudor literature frequently expresses subversive ideas, critiques of the monarchy, or challenges to religious orthodoxy, this subversion is rarely autonomous. Instead, Greenblatt contends that power, specifically the absolute authority of the Tudor state, actively produces the very subversion it needs to consolidate its own control. By permitting or even generating localised expressions of rebellion, authority makes those rebellions visible, categorises them as monstrous or alien, and then systematically contains them, thereby demonstrating the absolute necessity of state power for the maintenance of social order.This Foucauldian dynamic, often encapsulated in the famous formulation from Greenblatt's later essay on Shakespeare's history plays ("there is subversion, no end of subversion, only not for us"), is demonstrated throughout the monograph’s analysis of major Renaissance figures. In his chapters on William Tyndale, Sir Thomas More, and Sir Thomas Wyatt, Greenblatt traces how these writers attempted to fashion autonomous identities in resistance to the crown or the established church, only to find their language, their writings, and ultimately their bodies recaptured by the absolute power of the monarch. For instance, Tyndale’s Protestant self-fashioning, built upon the literal translation of the Bible, is shown to be deeply dependent on the very Catholic authority it seeks to overthrow, eventually leading to his martyrdom. Similarly, Thomas More's public performance of holy detachment is shown to be a highly artful, theatrical construction that is ultimately contained by Henry VIII’s absolute demand for political conformity. In the case of Edmund Spenser’s The Faerie Queene, Greenblatt argues that the epic poem's moral allegory works to contain the chaotic forces of the Irish wildness and Catholic rebellion, showing that the fashioning of the Christian knight is inseparable from the violent colonial policies of the Elizabethan state. Subversion is not the opposite of power; it is the very currency through which power negotiates its own preservation.The Improvisation of Power: Iago and the Narrative Unfashioning of OthelloThe final chapter of the monograph, "The Improvisation of Power", contains Greenblatt's most celebrated literary analysis: a reading of Shakespeare’s Othello that locates the tragedy within the cultural history of Western colonialism and narrative manipulation. Greenblatt focuses on the character of Iago, whom he reads not as a conventional stage villain or a figure of "motiveless malignity", but as the supreme embodiment of what he terms "improvisational power". Greenblatt defines improvisation as "the ability both to capitalize on the unforeseen and to transform given materials into one's own scenario" (p. 227). This ability, he argues, is a characteristically Western mode of cultural strategy, a highly developed "mobile sensibility" that allows an individual to enter into the culture, beliefs, and narratives of another person, to appear to empathise with them, and then to redirect those narratives to their own destructive ends.To explain Iago’s improvisational technique, Greenblatt engages with the modern sociological work of Daniel Lerner, who defined "empathy" as a positive, modernising capacity to project oneself into the position of another. Greenblatt rejects this benign view, asserting that "what Professor Lerner calls 'empathy,' Shakespeare calls 'Iago'" (p. 225). Iago does not hate Othello out of pure malice; rather, he possesses an extraordinary, cold capacity to inhabit Othello’s psychic structure, locate its latent anxieties, and turn them against him. Othello is peculiarly vulnerable to this manipulation because of the nature of his own self-fashioning. As a Moor and a mercenary who has risen to high office in Venice, Othello has fashioned himself in relation to Christian, patrician Venetian ideals that are alien to his origins. His identity is entirely narrative; he has "fashioned himself as a story", winning Desdemona by telling tales of his exotic travels and military exploits. Iago recognises that "an identity that has been fashioned as a story can be unfashioned, refashioned, inscribed anew in a different narrative" (p. 238).Iago exploits Othello’s deep-seated sexual anxiety, which is itself a product of the Christian marriage codes of the Renaissance. Greenblatt explains that Catholic theology of the era viewed excessive passion within marriage as a form of adultery; therefore, Othello is haunted by a latent guilt regarding his intense desire for Desdemona. Iago enters this narrative gap, playing the role of the loyal friend while subtly editing Othello's story, transforming Othello's passionate love into a monstrous vision of Desdemona’s infidelity. Because Othello has fully internalised the Venetian cultural codes that brand him as an outsider and view female desire as inherently corruptible, he quickly adopts Iago's narrative. The tragedy concludes not with a simple act of murder, but with Othello executing himself as the ultimate alien, the "circumcised dog" who has threatened the Venetian order. Othello’s self-fashioning is thus shown to be a trap; by adopting the language of his masters, he has provided the very instruments of his own destruction.A Critical Afterlife: The Legacy of Cultural PoeticsRenaissance Self-Fashioning exerted an immediate and transformative impact on the field of Renaissance studies and literary theory more broadly, effectively inaugurating the New Historicist movement in the United States and shaping critical debates for over two decades. By insisting that literature be read as a site of political struggle and cultural negotiation, Greenblatt revitalised historical criticism, making it a dynamic alternative to the ahistorical methods of deconstruction that dominated the academy in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The monograph opened up new pathways for reading canonical texts alongside non-canonical documents, building a rich, interdisciplinary dialogue between literary studies, anthropology, history, and sociology. Its influence extended far beyond Shakespearean studies, inspiring similar historicist approaches in medieval, nineteenth-century, and modern literary fields.However, Greenblatt's work also drew sharp criticism from multiple theoretical directions. Marxist critics, such as Walter Cohen and Terry Eagleton, attacked the book's reliance on the containment thesis, arguing that by presenting power as an all-powerful, self-generating system that effortlessly absorbs all opposition, Greenblatt had constructed a politically defeatist model of history that denied the possibility of genuine revolutionary change. They argued that New Historicism was a symptomatic product of the conservative Reagan-Thatcher era, reflecting a disillusioned leftism that had abandoned hope in political resistance. Similarly, feminist and postcolonial scholars pointed out that while Greenblatt analysed the exclusion of the Other, his primary focus remained on elite, male subjects, monarchs, courtiers, and writers, thereby replicating the very exclusions he sought to critique. Despite these challenges, Renaissance Self-Fashioning remains an indispensable reference point in literary theory, a work that permanently dismantled the illusion of the autonomous author and the pure text, replacing them with a complex, challenging vision of the self as a product of historical negotiation.
critical_works.ch75: Fredric Jameson (1934–2024)Original title: The Political Unconscious: Narrative as a Socially Symbolic Act1981 · English · United States · Marxist Literary Theory / Cultural Studies · Theoretical TreatiseThe Transhistorical Imperative: History as the Inescapable HorizonFredric Jameson’s The Political Unconscious: Narrative as a Socially Symbolic Act, published in 1981 by Cornell University Press, represents one of the most ambitious and influential works of Marxist literary theory in the twentieth century. The monograph opens with a famous, uncompromising command that is its central methodological principle: "Always historicize!" (p. 9). For Jameson, this is both a recommendation to check the historical context of a text and "the one absolute and we may even say transhistorical imperative of all dialectical thought" (p. 9). History, in the Marxist-Hegelian sense that Jameson adopts, is not a static list of dates, a collection of past events, or a mere background against which cultural texts can be read. Rather, history is the ultimate, inescapable horizon of all human experience, cultural production, and intellectual interpretation. It is the raw material and the structuring limit of all that we can think, write, or construct.Jameson argues that we can never escape history because history is the very ground of our existence. However, he does not view history as a simple, transparent narrative that is easily accessible to the critic. Instead, drawing on the French Marxist theorist Louis Althusser, Jameson conceives of history as an absent cause. History cannot be directly perceived; it is only accessible to us through its textualisation, that is, through the narratives, documents, and cultural representations we construct to make sense of it. Yet, the reality of history remains absolute and material, making itself felt through the limits it imposes on our desires and our actions. In a memorable formulation, Jameson declares that "History is what hurts, it is what refuses desire and sets inexorable limits to individual as well as collective praxis" (p. 102). History is that which resists our attempts to imagine a world free of contradiction; it is the ultimate necessity that humbles our utopian fantasies and forces us to confront the material realities of class struggle and economic organisation. Therefore, the task of the Marxist critic is to reconstruct the relationship between the literary work and this absent cause, exposing the historical necessity that structures the text's formal and thematic choices.The Aesthetic Resolution of Contradiction: Defining the Political UnconsciousTo explain how history shapes literature without resorting to a crude reflectionist model (where the text is merely a passive mirror of its economic base), Jameson introduces the central concept of the "political unconscious". He argues that the human mind, operating within the ideological constraints of class society, seeks to repress the painful contradictions of history. Just as the individual unconscious in Freudian psychoanalysis represses traumatic memories and desires, only for them to return in disguised forms such as dreams and neuroses, so the collective political consciousness of a society represses the real, irresolvable socio-historical conflicts of its era. These repressed conflicts return in the form of narrative.Under this view, a literary text is not a passive document of historical facts, but an active, "socially symbolic act". It is a complex aesthetic structure that seeks to resolve, at the level of imagination, form, and language, the real contradictions that cannot be resolved in historical reality. For example, a nineteenth-century novelist might be confronted with the devastating social division between the industrial working class and the bourgeoisie, a conflict that, in the real world, can only be resolved through revolutionary struggle. Unable to resolve this crisis, the novelist constructs a narrative that attempts to harmonise these opposing forces symbolically, perhaps through a romantic marriage between a wealthy factory owner and a sympathetic working-class woman, or through a moral conversion that defuses class hostility. The task of the critic is not to accept this symbolic resolution at face value, but to perform a symptomatic reading of the text, exposing the gaps, silences, and formal tensions that reveal the repressed historical contradictions the narrative is attempting to manage. The text's very form, its plot structure, its narrative perspective, and its generic choices, is a response to a historical situation, a symbolic strategy designed to negotiate the anxieties of class conflict.The Three Interpretive Horizons: From Textual Resolution to Modes of ProductionIn the monograph's magisterial first chapter, "On Interpretation: Literature as a Socially Symbolic Act", Jameson outlines a systematic, three-tiered interpretive framework that allows the critic to trace the operations of the political unconscious across different levels of social reality. He terms these levels the "interpretive horizons".The first horizon focuses on the individual literary work, conceived as a localised, symbolic resolution to a concrete historical contradiction. At this level, the critic reads the text as a discrete aesthetic act, analysing how the individual author uses form and theme to manage a specific historical conflict. The text is treated as a unique utterance, and the critic's goal is to lay bare the subtext, the repressed historical reality, that the text is trying to rewrite.The second horizon expands the analysis to the level of society. Here, the individual text is no longer read in isolation, but as an utterance in the collective, ongoing dialogue of class discourses. The focus shifts from the individual author to the broader social groups that contest power within a given society. At this level, Jameson introduces the concept of the "ideologeme", which he defines as the basic unit of class struggle, a narrative paradigm or conceptual structure that is a weapon in the ideological warfare between classes.
