Katherine Hayles (1943–)Original title: How We Became Posthuman: Virtual Bodies in Cybernetics, Literature, and Informatics1999 · English · United States · Posthumanism / Cybernetics / Media Theory / Science Fiction Criticism · Theoretical Monograph / Literary CriticismThe Dematerialisation of Information: Shannon, Wiener, and the Macy ConferencesN. Katherine Hayles’s How We Became Posthuman: Virtual Bodies in Cybernetics, Literature, and Informatics, published in 1999, is a foundational text in critical posthumanism and media studies. Hayles’s central theoretical project is to trace the historical and cultural processes through which information came to be conceptualised as a disembodied entity, separate from the physical substrate that carries it. In modern informatics and cybernetics, information is often treated as if it has no body, floating freely across different media and platforms. Hayles argues that this abstraction is not a self-evident scientific truth, but a historically contingent construction that has profound ethical and political consequences. The belief that information is separate from matter legitimises a new form of technological disembodiment, encouraging the fantasy that human consciousness can be uploaded into a computer and achieve a digital immortality. To counter this fantasy, Hayles insists on the recovery of embodiment, showing that information is always materialised in physical bodies and systems.To reconstruct how information was denuded of its body, Hayles examines the Macy Conferences on Cybernetics, held between 1946 and 1953, where scientists from diverse disciplines gathered to establish a unified theory of communication and control. A key debate at these conferences centred on the definition of information. Claude Shannon and Norbert Wiener championed a mathematical definition of information that was independent of meaning and context. In Shannon’s formulation, information is a measure of statistical probability, representing the surprise value of a message rather than its semantic content. This probability-based model required the exclusion of the receiver's subjective response and the physical conditions of transmission. Although British researcher Donald MacKay proposed an alternative model, arguing that information should be defined in relation to its effect on the receiver, thereby incorporating meaning and embodiment, the conferences ultimately adopted Shannon’s disembodied definition. By prioritising code over context, the founders of cybernetics established a framework where information could be manipulated as a pure, mathematical pattern, inaugurating the cultural perception that Hayles terms virtuality:This definition of information as a disembodied pattern allowed cybernetics to cross the boundary between human and machine. If both humans and machines are essentially information-processing systems, then their differences can be minimised, and their functions can be integrated. However, this integration came at a high cost. By treating the physical body as a secondary, accidental container for a primary informational pattern, early cybernetics prepared the ground for the erasure of embodiment. The body was reduced to a passive medium, a fashion accessory or a temporary vehicle for the self, rather than the essential ground of human experience and consciousness."Virtuality is the cultural perception that material objects are interpenetrated by information patterns." (p. 13)The Virtual Body: Cybernetic Waves and the Construction of the PosthumanHayles organises the history of cybernetics into three distinct historical waves, showing how each wave reformulated the relation between information and materiality. The first wave, spanning from 1945 to 1953, was dominated by the concept of homeostasis, the capacity of a system to maintain stability through feedback loops. Norbert Wiener’s early work compared the homeostatic mechanisms of animals to those of automated weapons and telecommunication networks. In this first wave, the human was still understood as an autonomous individual, but one who was increasingly integrated into feedback loops with machines. The focus remained on control, stability, and the preservation of boundaries.The second wave of cybernetics, extending from 1960 to 1980, shifted the focus from homeostasis to reflexivity and autopoiesis. Pioneered by Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, autopoiesis (self-creation) describes a system that recursively generates and maintains its own organisational boundaries. Unlike homeostatic systems, which react to external inputs to maintain balance, autopoietic systems are closed networks that interpret their environment only through their internal dynamics. This shift de-centred the traditional scientific observer, showing that the observer is always part of the system being observed. Maturana and Varela's work highlighted the recursive, self-referential nature of life, showing that the boundaries of the self are not fixed, but are dynamically produced through structural coupling with the environment. However, by defining life as a recursive pattern of organisation rather than a specific material substance, autopoiesis inadvertently contributed to the posthuman view that the pattern is more important than the physical body.The third wave of cybernetics, beginning in the mid-1980s, is characterised by the concept of virtuality and the emergence of artificial life (ALife). In this wave, researchers use computer simulations to model biological processes, attempting to evolve virtual organisms that exhibit lifelike behaviour. The goal of ALife is to demonstrate that the logical pattern of life can be extracted from carbon-based chemistry and recreated in silicon. Hayles critiques this project, showing that it relies on a Platonic gesture: it treats the material world as a corrupt copy of a pure, digital origin. By claiming that biological life is merely one instantiation of a universal informational process, ALife researchers suggest that the virtual body is more real than the physical body. This virtuality marks the completion of the posthuman shift, where the material world is subordinated to the patterns of code, and the biological body is treated as an obsolete technology.The Erasure of Embodiment: The Turing Test and the Liberal Humanist SubjectThe conceptual culmination of the posthuman is the erasure of embodiment, a move that Hayles critiques by analysing the cultural significance of the Turing Test. Formulated by Alan Turing in 1950, the test asks whether a human interrogator, communicating solely through typed text, can distinguish between a human and a computer. Hayles argues that the Turing Test is a highly symbolic performance of disembodiment. For the test to work, the physical bodies of the participants must be hidden in separate rooms, and their genders, races, and physical attributes must be translated into digital text. The Turing Test asserts that intelligence is a property of symbol manipulation, independent of physical instantiation:By defining the human as an informational pattern that can be copied without loss into a machine, the Turing Test perpetuates the traditional anxieties and desires of the liberal humanist subject. The liberal subject has historically been defined by autonomy, rational self-mastery, and the possession of a body that is treated as property. In the posthuman era, this liberal dream of total control is translated into the fantasy of escape from the limitations of the physical body.However, Hayles argues that this posthuman nightmare of disembodiment is not the only possible path. She distinguishes between a nightmare version of the posthuman, which seeks to escape finitude, and a dream version, which embraces the possibilities of technology while remaining grounded in the physical world:This dream version of the posthuman rejects the Cartesian division between mind and body, subject and object. It understands that human consciousness is not an autonomous programmer dictating terms to a passive body, but is an emergent property that arises from our bodily enaction in the physical world. Rather than using technology to master nature or escape biological limits, the embodied posthuman uses technology to cultivate a deeper awareness of our integration into the biosphere, acknowledging our dependence on non-human systems and resources."The Turing test is designed to show that a machine can think if it can pass as human in a game of imitation. Crucially, the test succeeds by erasing the body, suggesting that intelligence is a formal property of symbol manipulation rather than an enaction in the human life world." (p. 2)"If my nightmare is a culture inhabited by posthumans who regard their bodies as fashion accessories rather than the ground of being, my dream is a version of the posthuman that embraces the possibilities of information technologies without being seduced by fantasies of unlimited power and disembodied immortality, that recognises and celebrates finitude as a condition of human being, and that understands human life is embedded in a material world of great complexity, one on which we depend for our continued survival." (p. 5)The Literary Feedback Loop: Science Fiction as Theoretical PracticeIn the second half of her monograph, Hayles demonstrates that literature, particularly science fiction, is not a simple reflection of scientific developments, but is an active site of theoretical enunciation where the boundaries of the human are negotiated. Science fiction operates as a feedback loop with science, testing the cultural and psychological implications of new technologies before they are fully realised.Hayles analyses Bernard Wolfe’s 1952 novel Limbo, showing how it critiques the first-wave cybernetic obsession with control. In Limbo, a society devastated by war adopts voluntary amputation, replacing biological limbs with cybernetic prostheses to eliminate the physical impulses that lead to violence. The novel exposes the self-destructive logic of this posthuman project: the attempt to master the body by destroying it leads to a new form of totalitarian control. The prostheses, designed to liberate the citizens, become instruments of state surveillance and physical subjugation, showing that the erasure of the body is inseparable from the erasure of political freedom.She also examines the work of Philip K. Dick, particularly Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968), as a key critique of the second wave’s autopoietic boundaries. Dick’s novels are haunted by the difficulty of distinguishing between humans and androids, showing how the collapse of the boundary between organic and inorganic life destabilises the liberal subject's sense of reality. The androids in Dick's work are not simple machines; they are complex information-processing systems that mimic human emotion and memory, exposing the artificiality of human identity itself. Through close readings of Dick, Greg Egan, and Neal Stephenson, Hayles shows that science fiction is a crucial space for ethical reflection, offering narratives that challenge the technophilic drive toward disembodiment and helping us imagine what kind of posthumans we will be:By reading science fiction alongside the history of science, Hayles deconstructs the linear narrative of technological progress, showing that the posthuman is not a sudden departure from the human, but a recognition of the hybridity and integration that have always characterised our existence. The task of the critic is to resist the fantasies of disembodiment that dominate contemporary cyberculture, promoting instead a critical posthumanism that values the physical body as the indispensable ground of human being and ethical responsibility."We should value the late evolutionary add-ons of consciousness and reason not because they are foundational, but because they allow the human to emerge out of the posthumans we have always already been." (p. 279)
critical_works.ch92: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick (1950–2009)Original title: Touching Feeling: Affect, Pedagogy, Performativity2003 · English · United States · Affect Theory / Queer Theory / Postcritique · Theoretical EssaysThe Textures of Affect: Shame, Performativity, and Speech ActsEve Kosofsky Sedgwick’s Touching Feeling: Affect, Pedagogy, Performativity, published in 2003, is a seminal text that helped launch the "affective turn" in literary and cultural studies. Sedgwick’s central critical intervention is to challenge the cognitive, language-centred bias of late twentieth-century critical theory. While post-structuralism and deconstruction often treated the world as a system of signs and texts, reducing human experience to linguistic codes, Sedgwick redirects attention to the tactile, emotional, and visceral dimensions of existence. By focusing on affect, specifically the textures of feeling and the relationship between touch and meaning, she seeks to develop tools and techniques for nondualistic thought, moving beyond the rigid binaries of mind/body, surface/depth, and language/matter. For Sedgwick, affect is not a pre-verbal, irrational force that opposes reason; rather, it is a highly organised, relational system that operates in tandem with cognition and language to shape how we inhabit the world.To theoretically ground this exploration, Sedgwick draws on the affect theory of Silvan Tomkins, who argued that the affect system is autonomous from biological drives. Unlike drives, which are quantitative and have specific biological objects (such as hunger demanding food), affects are qualitative and highly flexible, capable of attaching to any object or idea. Sedgwick concentrates on shame, which Tomkins identified as a particularly powerful and complex affect. Shame occurs when an interest or excitement that has been flowing toward an object is suddenly interrupted. Unlike guilt, which is concerned with violating a law or committing a bad act, shame is ontological, touching the very definition of the self. Shame is an experience of exposure, where the subject feels their boundary compromised in the gaze of another. However, shame is also relational; it can only occur where there is a pre-existing desire for connection. Sedgwick writes:This double character of shame makes it a crucial site for performativity and identity-formation. Shame isolates the subject, making them feel painfully unique, yet it is also contagious, easily spreading to observers and creating a shared, tacit understanding. In the essay "Shame, Theatricality, and Queer Performativity," Sedgwick analyses how queer identities are frequently constructed through and against shame. Rather than treating shame as a purely negative experience to be repressed or overcome, she argues that queer performativity is the creative transformation of shame into a site of artistic and political enunciation. When queer writers (like Henry James) or activists cite shame, they do not simply submit to it; they theatricalise it, using it to disrupt heteronormative speech acts and build new, non-normative forms of social attachment. Performativity, in this affect-oriented model, is not a simple linguistic declaration, but a bodily performance that is deeply inflected by the textures of shame, interest, and excitement."shame is both peculiarly contagious and peculiarly individuating..." (p. 36)The Hermeneutics of Suspicion: Paranoia as a Critical DefaultThe most famous and debated essay in the collection is "Paranoid Reading and Reparative Reading, or, You're So Paranoid, You Probably Think This Essay Is About You." In this text, Sedgwick diagnoses a striking methodological uniformity within the academic humanities: the absolute dominance of the "hermeneutics of suspicion." Drawing on Paul Ricoeur, she argues that literary critics have default-established paranoia as the only legitimate critical practice. Paranoid reading is characterised by a persistent suspicion of the text's surface meaning, seeking always to dig beneath the words to expose hidden operations of power, ideology, racism, patriarchy, or class domination. Paranoia has become so institutionalised that a critic who does not practice suspicion is often viewed as naive, complicit, or intellectually lazy.Sedgwick deconstructs the structural characteristics of paranoia, showing that it operates as a psychological defence mechanism designed to prevent surprise. Paranoia is anticipatory, constantly looking to the horizon to predict and ward off potential trauma:Because the paranoid reader believes that the worst has already happened or is about to happen, they must maintain a rigid, hyper-vigilant posture. This anticipatory logic means that paranoia is also recursive and self-confirming. A paranoid reading can never be surprised by new information; it always finds exactly what it set out to find, namely, the ubiquitous operations of systemic oppression. Paranoia is exposure-oriented, believing that the act of exposing a hidden crime is itself a form of political efficacy.However, Sedgwick points out the limits of this critical default. First, the political efficacy of exposure is highly questionable; in a world where states and corporations often operate their oppressions openly, the act of demystifying what is already visible achieves very little. Second, paranoia is ascetic and closed to pleasure. It demands that the critic maintain a cold, detached distance from the text, treating the literary object as an adversary to be decoded rather than a potential source of nourishment. Paranoia is a defensive love that demands nothing from its object, because it refuses to risk the vulnerability of attachment:By exposing paranoia as a contingent, affect-driven critical practice rather than the only valid methodology, Sedgwick opens the space for alternative ways of reading. She does not advocate for the abandonment of political critique; rather, she argues that paranoia is a partial, defensive strategy that has exhausted its critical utility by becoming a rote academic habit."That paranoia is anticipatory is clear from every account and theory of the phenomenon..." (p. 130)"Of all forms of love, paranoia is the most ascetic, the love that demands least from its object." (p. 132)Melanie Klein’s Positions: Paranoid-Schizoid vs. Depressive HermeneuticsTo explain the psychological dynamics of these reading practices, Sedgwick draws on Melanie Klein's psychoanalytic theory of object relations, specifically the distinction between the "paranoid-schizoid position" and the "depressive position." In Kleinian theory, these positions are not developmental stages that are left behind; they are persistent mental orientations that the subject vacillates between throughout life.The paranoid-schizoid position is characterised by splitting, projection, and aggression. Faced with the anxiety of existence, the infant splits the maternal breast into a "good breast" (which feeds and comforts) and a "bad breast" (which frustrates and threatens). The infant projects its own aggressive impulses onto the bad object, viewing the world as a battleground of pure, opposed forces. This position corresponds directly to the binary logic of paranoid reading, which divides the cultural landscape into pure resistance and pure complicity, self and other, coloniser and colonised. The paranoid critic, operating in the paranoid-schizoid position, seeks to destroy the bad object (the text's ideological complicity) to protect the good self, remaining trapped in a cycle of suspicion and defensive aggression.The depressive position, by contrast, is characterised by integration, ambivalence, and reparation. In the depressive position, the infant recognises that the good breast and the bad breast are actually parts of the same, complex maternal object. The infant realises that its own aggressive impulses have damaged the loved object, leading to a deep sense of guilt and anxiety. To resolve this anxiety, the subject engages in reparation, the active process of repairing, restoring, and piecing together the damaged object. The depressive position is marked by a tolerance for ambiguity and a willingness to accept that the loved object is imperfect and split. This position corresponds to reparative reading. Instead of seeking to destroy or demystify the text, the reparative reader accepts the text's complicities and limitations, focusing instead on assembling its fragments to gather resources for survival and hope.The Reparative Turn: Gathering Resources for Queer SurvivalThe resolution of Sedgwick's theoretical project is the formulation of a "reparative reading" practice. To read from a reparative position is to surrender the defensive comfort of paranoia to open oneself to the vulnerability of surprise. While paranoia is driven by the fear of being hurt or fooled, reparation is driven by the desire for pleasure, nourishment, and local healing. The reparative reader treats the text not as an adversary to be cross-examined, but as a potential ally that can offer solace and ethical guidance.Reparative reading is a strategy of cultural survival, particularly for marginalised and queer subjects who have historically been excluded from hegemonic systems of power. While a paranoid reading of a homophobic culture can easily map the ubiquity of heteronormative oppression, it cannot offer the resources needed to live a life that is livable. The reparative reader, by contrast, searches the archives of the dominant culture to find local, fragmented spaces of hope and pleasure. They piece together these fragments to build a sustaining environment for themselves and their community. Reparative reading is thus a creative, constructive act; it does not assume that the text is pure or perfect, but it chooses to value its capacity to sustain life.Ultimately, Sedgwick's work is a radical invitation to reform the ethical orientation of literary studies. By shifting the critical focus from suspicion to reparation, she transforms the act of reading from an aggressive exercise in demystification into a hopeful dialogue of care and assembly. Touching Feeling remains a landmark text, showing that the study of literature is both a technology of critique and is a practice of ethical responsibility, offering stories, images, and textures that can guide us toward a more sustainable and hopeful future.
critical_works.ch93: Achille Mbembe (1957–)Original title: Nécropolitique2003 (essay), 2019 (English expanded monograph) · French · Cameroon / France / South Africa · Postcolonial Theory / Political Philosophy / Critical Theory · Philosophical Essay / Theoretical MonographBeyond Biopolitics: Sovereign Power and the Right to KillAchille Mbembe’s Necropolitics, initially published as an essay in the journal Public Culture in 2003 and later expanded into a book-length French monograph in 2016 (translated into English by Steven Corcoran in 2019), represents a major paradigm shift in contemporary critical theory, political philosophy, and postcolonial studies. Mbembe’s central intellectual intervention is to challenge and extend Michel Foucault’s concept of biopolitics. Foucault famously characterised biopower as the transition from the classical sovereign power to "take life or let live" to a modern power aimed at "making live and letting die." For Foucault, biopolitics is the mechanism by which the state regulates, manages, and optimises the biological life of the population. Mbembe argues that this Foucaultian model, while useful, is inadequate for explaining the extreme forms of subjugation and systemic violence that characterise the modern global order. In colonial contexts, under apartheid regimes, and in contemporary occupied territories, sovereign power does more than manage life; it systematically organises, produces, and inflicts death.To name this sovereign management of mortality, Mbembe coins the terms necropolitics and necropower. In the original 2003 essay translation by Libby Meintjes, Mbembe asserts that "the ultimate expression of sovereignty resides, to a large degree, in the power and the capacity to dictate who may live and who must die" (p. 11). Steven Corcoran’s 2019 translation of the expanded monograph similarly defines this ultimate expression as "the power and capacity to dictate who is able to live and who must die" (p. 66). Sovereignty, in Mbembe's formulation, is not defined by the maintenance of juridical order, the promotion of reason, or the preservation of individual autonomy, as classical liberal political theorists suggest. Instead, sovereignty is the capacity of the state or non-state actors to define who is human and who is not, who is disposable and who is protected, and ultimately, who is designated for life and who is marked for death. By focusing on the structural power to kill, Mbembe exposes the hidden, violent foundations of modern political systems, arguing that the sovereign state of exception is not an aberration but the organising principle of late-modern politics.The Plantation and the Colony: Historical Laboratories of NecropowerMbembe traces the genealogy of necropolitics back to the historical sites of the transatlantic slave plantation and the European colony, which he describes as the primary spaces where the absolute negation of human life was first institutionalised. Long before the concentration camps of twentieth-century Europe, the colony and the plantation operated as legal and spatial laboratories for the exercise of unrestricted sovereign violence. In these zones, the sovereign suspends the normal rule of law under the guise of maintaining order or civilising the native population. The colony is defined by a perpetual state of exception, where the normal juridical protections of the state are inapplicable, and the division between war and peace is completely erased. In this lawless space, the coloniser exercises a form of power that is unconstrained by constitutional limits, operating in a zone where violence is normal and the native subject is reduced to a status below that of the human.The slave plantation represents a particularly intense manifestation of necropower, where the slave is kept in a state of civil death. Stripped of all political rights, ownership of their own body, and connection to their ancestors or descendants, the slave is reduced to a form of animate property. Mbembe argues that the slave is kept alive only to the extent that their physical labour can be exploited by the master. This suspension between life and death constitutes a unique form of existence: the slave is the living dead, a biological body that has been denuded of all human subjectivity and political agency. Crucially, Mbembe shows that this systematic reduction of human beings to disposable material relies on the concept of race. Race is the foundational technology of necropolitics; it is the taxonomic category that allows the sovereign to divide the human species into groups, establishing a biological hierarchy that legitimises the destruction of one group for the security or prosperity of another. The colonial laboratory thus creates a precedent where sovereign power is exercised not to cultivate life, but to manage the distribution of death.Late-Modern Warfare and the Architecture of Death-WorldsIn the latter sections of his study, Mbembe examines how necropolitics has evolved in contemporary settings, shifting from the traditional territorial conquests of early imperialism to the diffuse, highly technological warfare of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. Modern warfare is no longer characterised by conflicts between equal sovereign states governed by international treaties and clear territorial boundaries. Instead, contemporary conflicts are asymmetric, involving a complex assemblage of state armies, private mercenary corporations, rebel militaries, and local warlords. In these contexts, territory is more than occupied; it is fragmented, compartmentalised, and subjected to what Mbembe calls vertical sovereignty. Using the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories as a primary example, Mbembe describes how sovereign power operates through a three-dimensional control of space, controlling the ground with checkpoints, bypass roads, and concrete walls; the underground by restricting access to water and archaeological sites; and the air through drone surveillance, helicopter gunships, and electromagnetic control.This vertical architecture of control creates what Mbembe defines as death-worlds. These are "new and unique forms of social existence in which vast populations are subjected to conditions of life conferring upon them the status of living dead" (2003, p. 40). In a death-world, the sovereign does not necessarily conduct a single, mass campaign of execution. Instead, the state systematically destroys the infrastructural conditions necessary for the maintenance of life. By cutting off access to clean water, electricity, medical supplies, and freedom of movement, and by subjecting the population to perpetual surveillance and unpredictable military incursions, the sovereign power renders daily survival an agonizing struggle. The population is kept in a state of permanent precarity, suspended in a liminal zone where physical survival is decoupled from political existence. Mbembe’s concept of the death-world shows how modern military technology and spatial planning are deployed to wage a war of attrition against the basic biological conditions of human life, transforming entire territories into open-air prisons where death is slow, bureaucratic, and omnipresent.The Suicide Bomber and the Instrumentality of DeathOne of the most controversial and theoretically dense sections of Mbembe’s work is his analysis of the suicide bomber, a figure that represents the absolute collision of necropolitics and subjective resistance. In the face of overwhelming sovereign force, where the occupied subject is stripped of conventional military weapons and political recourse, the body itself becomes the ultimate site of struggle. Mbembe argues that the suicide bomber turns their own body into a weapon, transforming their impending death into a tactical instrument of destruction. By choosing to die to kill the occupier, the suicide bomber challenges the sovereign's monopoly on the power of death. The sovereign’s ultimate threat, the threat of execution, loses its coercive power when the subject has already embraced death as a necessary sacrifice.This tactical embrace of death represents a radical inversion of the relation between sovereignty and the subject. In this moment, the subject exercises a grim, paradoxical form of self-determination. By seizing control over the timing and manner of their own demise, the bomber attempts to reclaim a form of agency that has been systematically denied to them in life. Mbembe writes that the suicide bomber's action collapses the distinction between active resistance and passive victimhood, showing that in the extreme conditions of the death-world, the only remaining form of sovereignty for the oppressed may be the sovereign control over their own destruction. However, Mbembe does not romanticise this act; he presents it as a tragic manifestation of how necropolitics corrupts the possibility of human freedom, forcing the subject to adopt the very logic of death that the sovereign has used to subjugate them. The suicide bomber demonstrates the terrifying limit of necropower, where the struggle for liberation is waged not in the name of life, but through the mutual annihilation of both the self and the enemy.A Critique of Enmity: Democracy and the Pharmakon of SovereigntyIn the expanded 2019 book edition, Mbembe deepens his critique of liberal democracies, arguing that the violent practices of necropolitics are not external to democratic institutions but are their historical and structural shadow. Mbembe conceptualises democracy as a pharmakon, a Greek term meaning both a medicine and a poison. While democracy presents itself as a cure for violence, offering peace, equality, and human rights to its citizens, it historically functions as a poison by externalising its violence to the colonial periphery and maintaining internal hierarchies based on race and class. The freedom enjoyed by the citizens of Western democracies has always been subsidised by the subjugation and exploitation of non-citizens in the global South. When democracies feel threatened by economic instability or geopolitical shifts, the poison of the pharmakon resurfaces in the form of the politics of enmity.This politics of enmity is characterised by the systematic creation of the "enemy" as a figure of existential threat. The state uses the fear of the racialised other, the migrant, the refugee, the terrorist, to justify the expansion of surveillance, the militarisation of borders, and the suspension of civil liberties. The boundary between the citizen and the enemy becomes the defining line of contemporary politics, legitimising the creation of detention centres, offshore processing centres, and militarised border zones where human rights are suspended. Mbembe warns that this obsession with security and exclusion leads to a contraction of democracy, transforming it into a security state that governs through the management of fear. To counter this destructive trajectory, Mbembe calls for the conceptualisation of an "earthly community", a political project that moves beyond the segregation of nations and races to recognise our shared, ecological vulnerability on a finite planet. The future of humanity, he argues, depends on our ability to dismantle the necropowers that divide us, reclaiming the Earth as a common home where the power to kill is replaced by a collective responsibility to sustain and nourish life.
critical_works.ch94: Franco Moretti (1950–)Original title: Graphs, Maps, Trees: Abstract Models for a Literary History2005 · English · Italy / United States · Digital Humanities / Quantitative Literary Sociology / Distant Reading · Theoretical Monograph / Literary CriticismDistant Reading: The Quantitative Challenge to the CanonFranco Moretti’s Graphs, Maps, Trees: Abstract Models for a Literary History, published by Verso in 2005, represents one of the most radical methodological interventions in literary studies of the twenty-first century. Moretti’s central project is to challenge the hegemony of "close reading," a method that has dominated literary criticism since the mid-twentieth century through movements such as New Criticism and deconstruction. Close reading, Moretti argues, relies on a massive selection bias. By focusing on the minute textual analysis of a tiny, highly selective canon of "great works," traditional literary history ignores the vast majority of literary production. Moretti points out that the standard canon of nineteenth-century British novels consists of at least two hundred works, which sounds extensive but actually represents less than one per cent of the novels published during that era. Close reading is structurally incapable of addressing the remaining ninety-nine per cent of the literary field, which remains an unread, historical archive.To address this massive scale, Moretti proposes the concept of distant reading. Rather than examining a few texts in detail, distant reading aggregates large corpora of literary data to identify macro-patterns, trends, and systemic structures that are invisible to the individual reader. Distant reading is more than a quantitative shortcut; it is a conceptual shift that redefines the object of literary study from the individual text to the collective system. To construct a systematic methodology for this approach, Moretti imports three abstract models from disciplines outside the humanities: quantitative history (graphs), geography (maps), and evolutionary biology (trees). By applying these models, Moretti seeks to reconstruct literary history as a materialist science of forms, demonstrating that the development of literature is governed by cyclical market rhythms, geographic constraints, and evolutionary morphological laws:This methodological shift aims to bridge the historical divide between formalist aesthetics and sociological history, showing that literary forms are not autonomous products of individual genius, but are systematic structures shaped by material conditions and historical forces."Literature, the old territory; but within it, a shift from the close reading of individual texts to the construction of abstract models. The models are drawn from three disciplines—quantitative history, geography and evolution." (p. 1)Graphs: Markets, Cycles, and the Rhythms of GenreIn the first chapter of the monograph, Moretti introduces the model of the graph, drawing on quantitative history and the longue durée methods of the French Annales School. By plotting the number of novels published per year in various national markets, including Britain, France, Spain, Italy, India, and Japan, Moretti reveals that the growth of the novel is not a linear, continuous progression, but a series of cyclical waves. These waves are characterised by sudden expansions, periods of stability, and subsequent contractions. Crucially, Moretti observes that different literary genres emerge, peak, and disappear in cycles that last approximately twenty-five to thirty years. This duration corresponds to the length of a human generation, suggesting that the lifecycle of genres is tied to the generational replacement of the reading public, who seek new formal structures to express their historical experience.The graph allows Moretti to analyse the book market as a competitive ecosystem where different genres struggle for survival. When a new genre emerges, such as the epistolary novel, the Gothic romance, or the historical novel, it undergoes a rapid expansion, saturating the market and replacing older forms. After a period of dominance, the form becomes conventionalised and loses its hold on readers, leading to a decline and the eventual emergence of a new genre. Moretti demonstrates that these cyclical waves are remarkably consistent across different national literatures, even when the historical dates of emergence differ. The graph thus exposes the limitations of traditional literary histories that present the novel as a unified, continuous form. Instead, the novel is a constellation of distinct, competing genres that rise and fall in response to systemic market pressures. By focusing on these macro-historical rhythms, Moretti de-emphasises the exceptional writer in favour of the collective system, showing that even the most celebrated authors are embedded in larger, structural cycles of literary production.Maps: Spatial Narratology and the Geometry of NarrativeThe second chapter transitions from chronology to cartography, importing the model of the map from geography. Moretti argues that space is not a neutral container for narrative action, but an active, structuring force that shapes the plot. By cartographically mapping the geographic settings of specific literary works, such as Mary Mitford’s Our Village (1824–1832) or John Galt’s The Entail (1823), Moretti demonstrates that narrative space possesses its own internal geometry, which exerts a pressure on the characters' movements and the development of the plot. Maps allow the critic to visualize the spatial relationships within a text, transforming geographic data into an abstract pattern that reveals the underlying logic of the narrative.For example, when mapping the spatial dynamics of Mary Mitford’s village sketches, Moretti reveals a concentric pattern. The narrator’s walks originate in the village centre and move outwards in circular paths, returning to the centre at the end of each narrative. This circular geometry reflects a conservative ideological desire to construct a stable, self-contained community, insulating the village from the destabilising forces of modern industrial capitalism. In contrast, Moretti maps the domestic novel, showing that it relies on a linear, fragmented geometry of conflict between different social classes and locales, such as the tension between the country estate and the metropolis. By translating the spatial descriptions of literature into abstract maps, Moretti shows that plot structures are directly dependent on the geography they inhabit. The map becomes an analytical tool that exposes how ideology is spatialised in the narrative, demonstrating that the structural organization of a text is inseparable from the material geography of its historical context.Trees: Cladistics and the Evolutionary Morphology of FormIn the third chapter, Moretti adopts the model of the tree, importing evolutionary theory and cladistics from biological science. Drawing on Charles Darwin’s concept of the phylogenetic tree, Moretti conceptualises literary history as a process of branching divergence. Rather than a linear chain of influence where one writer directly inspires the next, literary forms develop through a series of morphological splits, where a single ancestral form diverges into multiple experimental variations. Moretti uses this model to trace the history of British detective fiction from Edgar Allan Poe to Arthur Conan Doyle, mapping the presence or absence of specific formal devices, such as the inclusion of clues, the presence of a sidekick, or the use of red herrings, on a branching cladogram.This evolutionary tree reveals that the development of detective fiction was not a straightforward progression toward the Sherlock Holmes formula. Instead, nineteenth-century writers experimented with numerous variations of the mystery story, most of which failed to find a reading audience and became extinct. The success of Arthur Conan Doyle’s formula was the result of a process of natural selection: Doyle’s specific combination of devices, particularly the integration of decipherable clues that allowed the reader to participate in the deduction, was selected by the reading public as the most satisfying morphological form. Moretti’s evolutionary model argues that form and history are two dimensions of the same process. History provides the changing environmental pressures (such as the rise of the modern metropolis and the police force), while morphology provides the formal variations that adapt to these pressures. By using the evolutionary tree, Moretti provides a systematic way to study the divergence and selection of literary forms, showing that genres develop through a materialist process of morphological adaptation:The evolutionary tree thus allows the scholar to map the morphospace of literature, identifying both the realised forms that survived and the unrealised forms that disappeared, providing a comprehensive view of the systemic development of genres."And indeed, in contrast to literary studies—where theories of form are usually blind to history, and historical work blind to form—for evolutionary thought morphology and history are truly the two dimensions of the same tree: where the vertical axis charts..." (p. 90)Materialist Formalism: The Scientific Reconstruction of Literary HistoryThe ultimate ambition of Moretti’s Graphs, Maps, Trees is to establish a materialist formalism that combines the structural analysis of forms with the sociological analysis of history. By using quantitative, geographic, and evolutionary models, Moretti seeks to rescue literary studies from what he perceives as a lack of methodological rigour and an obsession with subjective interpretation. Distant reading does not mean abandoning the study of form; rather, it means studying form at a scale that can account for the collective literary system. The abstract models presented in the monograph are not mere metaphors; they are analytical tools that force the critic to look at literature in a new way, revealing structures that would remain invisible to the close reader.Moretti’s work has generated significant debate within the academy. Sceptics argue that distant reading reduces the aesthetic complexity of literature to cold data, ignoring the singular texture of prose, the play of language, and the subjective experience of reading. Marxist critics, while sympathetic to Moretti’s materialist focus, argue that his reliance on biological and quantitative models risks naturalising historical processes, treating social conflicts as if they were governed by immutable evolutionary laws. Despite these critiques, Moretti’s monograph has been a primary catalyst for the growth of the digital humanities, prompting scholars to use computational tools to analyse corpora of thousands of novels. Graphs, Maps, Trees demonstrates that by stepping back from the individual text, we can gain a clearer view of the larger literary field, transforming our understanding of how genres develop, how narratives occupy space, and how the literary market operates.
critical_works.ch95: Sianne Ngai (1971–)Original title: Ugly Feelings2005 · English · United States · Affect Theory / Aesthetic Theory / Feminist Criticism / Marxist Literary Theory · Theoretical Essays / Cultural CritiqueThe Politics of Dysphoria: Minor Affects and Obstructed AgencySianne Ngai’s Ugly Feelings, published by Harvard University Press in 2005, represents a major contribution to the "affective turn" in literary and cultural studies. Ngai’s central theoretical project is to investigate a range of "minor" and politically ambiguous negative affects, including envy, irritation, anxiety, paranoia, and stuplimity, that have historically been marginalised in aesthetic theory in favour of grand, cathartic passions like anger, terror, grief, or love. While traditional aesthetics, from Aristotle to the present, prioritises emotions that lead to decisive action or moral resolution, Ngai focuses on feelings that are amoral, non-cathartic, and characterised by blocked or suspended agency. These dysphoric feelings do not offer the satisfying release of classical tragedy or the heroic resistance of political melodrama. Instead, they register the subjective experience of powerlessness, complicity, and structural constraint that defines the individual subject under late-modern global capitalism:By analysing these minor affects, Ngai provides a sophisticated vocabulary for diagnosing the political blockages of the contemporary era. Unlike anger, which clearly identifies an object of opposition and motivates direct action, ugly feelings are characterised by an inability to find a clear outlet or to resolve themselves through practice. They represent a state of being "puppeteered" by larger, systemic forces, such as bureaucratic organisation, imperial administration, or market commodification, that exceed the subject's capacity to act or resist. Ngai argues that these feelings are both personal psychological failures and are indexical diagnoses of the social conditions that produce them. They function as political allegories of the late-modern condition, where the individual subject is caught in a network of global relations that they can neither control nor escape."Envy, irritation, paranoia—in contrast to powerful and dynamic negative emotions like anger, these non-cathartic states of feeling are associated with situations in which action is blocked or suspended" (p. 3)The Non-Cathartic Aesthetic: Blocked Action and the Bartlebyan TextAt the heart of Ngai's study is the concept of a non-cathartic aesthetic, which she defines as a mode of artistic production that deliberately refuses to provide the reader or viewer with emotional resolution. Traditional narrative structures rely on catharsis, the purification or release of pent-up emotion, to restore a sense of balance and ideological coherence. By contrast, a non-cathartic aesthetic produces and foregrounds a failure of emotional release, keeping the audience suspended in a state of unresolved discomfort. This aesthetic choice is not a form of political defeatism, but is itself a form of politics. Refusing to offer a false sense of resolution forces the reader to confront the material contradictions of their historical situation:Ngai identifies Herman Melville's short story "Bartleby, the Scrivener" (1853) as a primary example of this non-cathartic aesthetic. Bartleby’s famous formula, "I would prefer not to," represents a radical suspension of both active compliance and active rebellion. Bartleby does not refuse his work with the dynamic energy of anger; instead, he adopts a passive, immobile stance that stymies his employer and the reader alike. The text offers no catharsis, no moral lesson, and no psychological explanation for Bartleby’s behaviour. By staying in this state of suspended action, Melville’s story indexes the quiet, bureaucratic violence of Wall Street, showing that the only form of agency available to the alienated clerk is the passive refusal to participate in the circuit of productive labour.This passive stance, which Melville positions within the grey offices of a legal copyist, acts as a solvent on the social relations of the workplace. Bartleby's refusal is not an assertion of a sovereign, heroic will, but rather a stubborn, silent inertia that exposes the legal and economic machinery of the office. By refusing to copy, he halts the reproduction of legal documents, yet by refusing to leave, he prevents the attorney from simply replacing him. The lawyer is forced into a state of cognitive and emotional paralysis, reflecting the structural helplessness of the liberal humanist subject when confronted with the limits of its own contractual logic. Ngai uses this reading to argue that the non-cathartic aesthetic does not seek to inspire the reader to revolution, but rather to outline the contours of our shared captivity within the system, using the scrivener's inertia to disrupt the smooth flows of administrative capitalism."The noncathartic feelings in this book could be said to give rise to a noncathartic aesthetic: art that produces and foregrounds a failure of emotional release (another form of suspended ‘action’) and does so as a kind of politics" (p. 9)Tone and the Commodified Text: Affect as Global AtmosphereIn the first chapter of the monograph, Ngai introduces the concept of tone, which she defines as a literary text’s global, objectified affect. Unlike individual emotions experienced by characters or readers, tone is the ambient atmosphere of the text itself, the "unfelt but perceived feeling" that determines how the work is received as an aesthetic totality. Tone is the formal quality that allows critics to describe a work as paranoid, melancholic, or cynical. Crucially, Ngai argues that tone is the site where the text's relation to the capitalist market is most clearly materialised. In a consumer society, the literary work is always a commodity, and its tone is the aesthetic surface that registers this commodification.To demonstrate how tone operates as a site of social struggle, Ngai analyses Herman Melville’s novel The Confidence-Man (1857). The novel is characterised by a highly unstable, slippery tone that oscillates between sincerity and irony, trust and suspicion. This tonal instability reflects the anxiety of a emerging market economy where social relations are increasingly mediated by financial contracts and paper money. The text’s tone becomes a form of "objectified emotion" that mimics the deceptive, fluctuating values of the marketplace, forcing the reader into a position of perpetual paranoia. By analysing tone as a global formal category, Ngai demonstrates that affect is both a subjective psychological state and is an objective, material structure that is built into the form of the artwork, reflecting the social and economic forces of its production context.Stuplimity and Envy: The Rhythms of Late-Capitalist AestheticsNgai coins the term stuplimity to describe a unique aesthetic category that combines shock and boredom. Unlike the traditional sublime, which involves an encounter with an infinite, terrifying nature that ultimately elevates the human spirit, stuplimity is an encounter with a massive, repetitive accumulation of man-made information and commodities. It is characterised by a series of small, repetitive shocks that lead not to spiritual transcendence, but to fatigue and mental exhaustion. Ngai traces this aesthetic in the work of avant-garde writers like Gertrude Stein and Samuel Beckett, whose texts use obsessive repetition and grammatical exhaustion to stultify the reader.Gertrude Stein’s massive novel The Making of Americans (1925), for instance, uses a highly repetitive, restricted vocabulary to present the history of a family. The constant repetition of slightly varied phrases does not build toward a grand narrative climax; instead, it generates a cumulative, exhausting weight that fatigues the reader. Similarly, Samuel Beckett's How It Is (1961) presents a narrator crawling through mud in the dark, repeating fragments of phrases in a stultifying, mechanical rhythm. The reader is subjected to a double bind: the shock of the characters' degraded existence is combined with the crushing boredom of the text's repetitive syntax. In both cases, stuplimity functions as a morphological register of the mechanical, repetitive nature of modern industrial and administrative labour, converting the sensory overload of late-capitalist society into a formal aesthetic of exhaustion.In her chapter on envy, Ngai reclaims this historically despised emotion as a politically diagnostic affect. In classical psychoanalysis and moral philosophy, envy is treated as a petty, destructive sin, often associated with women and marginalised groups who covet the possessions or power of others. Ngai challenges this pathologisation, arguing that envy is a response to structural inequality. Envy arises when the subject recognises a systemic disparity in power or resources but is blocked from taking action to redress it. By reframing envy as a form of "unhappy self-assertion," Ngai shows that it indexes a real, historical grievance. The feeling of envy is a symptom of a social system that promises equality but structurally denies it, making the affect a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying the sites of social and gendered conflict.Diagnostic Criticism: Dysphoric Affects as Cognitive MapsThe ultimate ambition of Sianne Ngai’s Ugly Feelings is to establish a method of diagnostic criticism that uses dysphoric affects to construct cognitive maps of the contemporary social order. In a globalised capitalist system where power is diffuse, bureaucratic, and highly mediated, it is increasingly difficult for the individual subject to locate the sources of their oppression or to imagine alternative political futures. Traditional forms of ideology critique, which seek to expose the hidden lies of the state, are often insufficient in an era where everyone is already cynical and aware of systemic corruption.In this context, minor affects like anxiety, irritation, and paranoia are valuable cognitive maps. They are visceral registerings of a system that is too complex to be comprehended by the individual mind. Paranoia, for example, is more than a delusion; it is a desperate attempt to trace the systemic connections of global power, to map the invisible networks of capital and state surveillance. By studying these ugly feelings, the critic can locate the points where the social system exerts its greatest pressure on the individual subject. Diagnostic criticism does not seek to cure these feelings, nor does it offer a comforting path to political redemption. Instead, it insists on remaining in the discomfort of non-resolution, using the very failure of catharsis to expose the limits of the current historical moment and to preserve the memory of a blocked desire for freedom.
critical_works.ch96: Rita Felski (1956–)Original title: Uses of Literature2008 · English · United Kingdom / United States · Postcritique / Affect Theory / Neo-Phenomenology · Theoretical Monograph / Literary Criticism ManifestoBeyond Suspicion: The Postcritical Turn in Literary StudiesRita Felski’s Uses of Literature, published by Wiley-Blackwell in 2008, is a foundational text in the emergence of "postcritique," a theoretical movement that seeks to redefine the methods and goals of academic literary criticism. Felski’s central critical intervention is to challenge the absolute dominance of suspicious reading in the humanities. Drawing on Paul Ricoeur’s concept of the "hermeneutics of suspicion," Felski argues that modern literary studies have become institutionalised around a habit of vigilant exposure. Critics are trained to treat the literary text as a symptom of hidden political or ideological pathologies, reading against the grain to expose the work's complicity with capitalism, imperialism, patriarchy, or heteronormativity. While acknowledging the historical achievements of this suspicious method, Felski warns that it has become a rote, professionalised ritual that alienates students and disconnects the academy from the diverse reasons why people actually read.To counter this institutionalised suspicion, Felski advocates for a postcritical approach that treats the literary text not as a patient to be diagnosed, but as an active partner in a dialogue. Literature, she insists, is not a passive reflection of social structures; it is an active force that does something in the world, shaping readers' subjectivities, building communities, and generating knowledge. Rather than treating aesthetic pleasure and emotional attachment as naive forms of false consciousness, Felski argues that these experiences are the indispensable ground of reading. She proposes a "neo-phenomenological" framework that values the immediate, lived experience of reading, attempting to bridge the gap between academic criticism and common readerly practice:By validating the positive dimensions of reading, Felski seeks to construct an accessible, democratic literary theory that combines suspicious vigilance with an openness to beauty, pleasure, and emotional connection."there is no reason why our readings cannot blend analysis and attachment, criticism and love" (p. 22)Recognition: The Interfused Subject and the Mirror of OthernessIn the first chapter of the monograph, Felski explores the concept of recognition, which she describes as the primary mode through which readers relate to literature. In traditional academic theory, recognition is often dismissed as a naive, egotistical desire to find one’s own reflection in the text, a form of identity politics that ignores the formal alterity of the artwork. Felski challenges this dismissal, arguing that recognition is a complex, active cognitive process. When a reader recognises themselves in a character or a situation, they are more than confirming what they already know. Instead, they are engaging in a dialectical process where the familiar is juxtaposed with the unfamiliar, and the self is mediated by the other:Recognition is thus a social phenomenology. It allows the reader to perceive their own private experiences as part of a larger, collective structure, translating personal suffering or desire into a shared political reality. Crucially, Felski notes that recognition is also about the encounter with difference. By reading about characters whose lives are radically different from their own, readers can recognise a common humanity or a shared vulnerability, cutting across rigid lines of race, class, and gender.Felski's concept of recognition also challenges the classic structuralist view that the reader is merely a passive effect of the text's linguistic codes. By treating recognition as a dynamic, interactive dialogue, she restores a sense of agency to the reader, showing that our personal histories, social environments, and emotional needs are active participants in the construction of meaning. Recognition is not a simple mirror; it is an optical instrument that helps us see aspects of our lives that were previously invisible, providing a form of self-knowledge that is inseparable from our relation to the other."self and society are always interfused; there is no clear place where one ends and the other begins. Subjectivity is always caught up with intersubjectivity, personal experience awash with social and political meanings" (p. 16)Enchantment: Aesthetic Immersion and the Rapture of ReadingThe second chapter of the monograph addresses enchantment, a mode of engagement that is particularly suspect in the eyes of suspicious critics. Enchantment describes the experience of being completely absorbed or spellbound by a literary work, a state of rapturous self-forgetting where the ordinary world recedes and the reader is pulled into the sensory and temporal flow of the narrative. Suspicious critics historically pathologise this immersion, viewing it as a passive capitulation to bourgeois ideology, a form of escapism that disables critical thought. Felski counters this critique by defending enchantment as a vital, active mode of aesthetic experience. Enchantment is not a loss of consciousness, but an intensification of it:Felski describes enchantment as a neo-phenomenological event that disrupts our ordinary experience of time and space. When we are enchanted by a text, our attention is concentrated, and we experience a sense of wonder and presence that is rare in the distracted rhythms of late-capitalist society. Enchantment has a therapeutic and restorative value; it offers an escape from the instrumental, means-end logic of modern life, allowing the reader to experience a state of pure, non-instrumental attention.This rapturous absorption is particularly important in an era dominated by cognitive overload and constant digital distractions. Enchantment offers a form of deep attention that is increasingly rare, serving as a sanctuary from the relentless demands of productivity and self-optimisation. When we are enchanted, we are not passive consumers; rather, we are actively engaged in the imaginative co-creation of the narrative world, showing that aesthetic pleasure is a vital source of subjective renewal and cognitive flexibility. Far from being a politically regressive state, enchantment is the very condition that allows literature to move us, preparing the ground for deeper cognitive and ethical transformations."a state of intense involvement, a sense of being so entirely caught up in an aesthetic object that nothing else seems to matter" (p. 54)Knowledge and Shock: Cognitive Maps and the Disruption of the Common-SenseFelski’s third and fourth chapters examine knowledge and shock as two distinct, yet complementary, uses of literature. Felski defends the cognitive value of literature, arguing that fiction is a crucial source of social and historical knowledge. Unlike the abstract, generalising knowledge of sociology or economics, literary knowledge is specific, concrete, and phenomenological. Literature does more than state facts; it renders the texture of a distinctive life-world, showing what it feels like to inhabit a particular social position, historical moment, or psychological state. This knowledge is not detached or objective; it is gained through emotional attachment and imaginative identification, providing a deep intersubjectivity that allows us to understand the social world from the inside out.Shock represents the opposite side of this cognitive coin. If knowledge builds a stable picture of a life-world, shock disrupts it. Felski analyses shock both as an avant-garde formal technique designed to startle the bourgeois public and as an experience that invades our consciousness, wreaking havoc on our common-sense assumptions and moral complacency. Shock forces the reader to confront the radically alien, the offensive, or the traumatic, disrupting our comfortable ways of ordering the world.This disruptive power of shock is not limited to avant-garde stylistic experimentations or transgressive themes. Shock can also arise when a reader is confronted by a perspective that directly challenges their own deeply held political or ethical beliefs. For Felski, shock is a valuable counter-balance to recognition: while recognition builds bridges and establishes commonalities, shock highlights the radical incommensurability of different life-worlds, forcing us to acknowledge the limits of our own empathy and understanding. In this sense, shock is a crucial tool for democratic pluralism, preventing the reader from simply assimilating the other into the self, and showing that the power of literature lies as much in its capacity to disturb us as in its capacity to comfort us.Towards a Neo-Phenomenology: Blending Attachment and AnalysisThe ultimate goal of Rita Felski’s Uses of Literature is to establish a neo-phenomenology of reading that can reconcile academic rigour with the ordinary pleasures of textual engagement. Postcritique does not mean a return to a naive, pre-theoretical impressionism, nor does it advocate for the abandonment of political analysis. Rather, it calls for a critical practice that is more honest about its own attachments and motivations. Felski argues that the critic’s role is not to stand above the text in a position of suspicious superiority, but to acknowledge their own involvement in the circuit of reading, tracing the complex attachments and associations that connect the reader, the text, and the social world.Drawing on Bruno Latour’s actor-network theory, Felski suggests that we treat the literary work as an active mediator, a non-human actor that is capable of establishing new connections and transforming its environment. Literature is not a passive container for social forces, but an active participant in the assembly of the social. By blending attachment and analysis, criticism and love, postcritique opens up new avenues for humanities research, encouraging critics to explore the diverse ways literature functions in the real world. Uses of Literature is a delinquent manifesto for a new era of literary studies, prompting us to suspect our own habits of suspicion and to listen more closely to the voices of the texts we read.
critical_works.ch97: Mark Fisher (1968–2017)Original title: Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative?2009 · English · United Kingdom · Capitalist Realism / Hauntology / Marxist Cultural Critique · Political Essay / Cultural MonographThe Horizon of the Possible: Ideological Saturation and the End of AlternativesMark Fisher’s Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative?, published by Zero Books in 2009, is a central text in contemporary cultural criticism and Marxist theory. Fisher’s foundational intellectual intervention is to define and analyse "capitalist realism", the widespread, unconscious belief that capitalism is both the only viable political and economic system and that it is now impossible even to imagine a coherent alternative to it. Fisher builds on Fredric Jameson’s famous observation, which he adopts as the opening premise of his study:This ideological condition is not characterised by a loud, propaganda-driven celebration of free-market virtues. Rather, capitalist realism operates as a quiet, atmospheric horizon that structures our thoughts and actions. It presents the market economy as a natural fact, like the weather, rendering all anti-capitalist aspirations naive, utopian, or historically discredited. Under capitalist realism, the systemic inequalities and ecological crises produced by capitalism are accepted as inevitable features of reality, rather than historically contingent arrangements that can be contested and transformed.Fisher describes this condition as an invisible barrier that limits our thinking, a quiet background noise that whispers that nothing can ever change. It is not that people actively adore capitalism; on the contrary, they may despise it, but they behave as if there is no alternative. This cynicism is the very mechanism that keeps the system running. Rather than relying on positive identification, capitalist realism thrives on our reflexive impotence, the widespread conviction that we cannot influence the structures that govern our lives, turning us into passive spectators of our own exploitation. Fisher argues that this saturation of the cultural imagination has led to a profound sense of political paralysis, where the desire for social change is replaced by a cynical resignation."It is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism." (p. 1)Subsumption and Commodification: The Marketisation of CritiqueA key mechanism of capitalist realism is its capacity to subsume and co-opt all forms of culture, including those that are explicitly critical of the capitalist system. Fisher observes that under late capitalism, anti-capitalist critique is no longer an external threat to the market; instead, it is an active commodity that is packaged and sold back to consumers. The system easily absorbs its own opposition, translating revolutionary impulses into consumer choices. Whether it is a radical political tract or an anti-corporate film, these cultural products are assigned a monetary value and integrated into the circuit of capital. The role of capitalist ideology is to conceal the fact that the operations of capital do not depend on any sort of subjective, assumed belief. It is not necessary for people to believe in capitalism; it is only necessary that they participate in its transactions.Fisher analyses how this commodification of dissent is reflected in popular culture, citing films like Children of Men (2006) or the music of Nirvana. Kurt Cobain’s career represents a tragic illustration of this dynamic: a musician whose raw, anti-commercial angst was instantly transformed into a highly profitable fashion trend, leaving him caught in the very market machinery he sought to resist. Cobain's suicide was a devastating punctuation mark that exposed the unbearable tension between subjective rebellion and market incorporation. In the capitalist realist framework, even his death was subsumed, becoming another cultural myth to be sold and consumed by a generation of fans. This complete enclosure demonstrates that capitalism does not require our belief, but only our behaviour; we can mock it, hate it, or critique it, as long as we continue to perform in its marketplace. Capitalist realism creates a closed loop where the critique of the market is itself marketised. This reflexive absorption of dissent reinforces the perception that there is no escape from the capitalist horizon, transforming collective struggles into individual lifestyle statements and cementing the belief that no alternative is possible.The Privatisation of Stress: Mental Health under NeoliberalismOne of the most significant and widely cited arguments in Fisher’s monograph is his critique of how capitalist realism depoliticises mental health, a process he terms the privatisation of stress. Under neoliberalism, psychological distresses, such as depression, anxiety, and attention deficit disorders, are treated as individual, chemical problems that originate inside the brain of the singular subject. The state and the medical establishment pathologise these conditions, offering pharmacological solutions that seek to adjust the individual to the demands of the market:Fisher challenges this biologisation of distress, arguing that the epidemic of mental illness in late-modern societies is a direct, systemic consequence of social causation. The constant precarity of the neoliberal labour market, the erosion of social safety nets, and the relentless pressure to self-optimise produce a state of perpetual anxiety and exhaustion. By treating these systemic effects as individual medical issues, capitalist realism prevents the conceptualisation of a collective political response. Stress is privatised, leaving the individual to feel personally responsible for their own suffering. Fisher calls for the repoliticisation of mental health, arguing that the rise of depression and anxiety should be understood as a collective grievance, a structural failure of the capitalist order that demands a political, rather than merely chemical, solution."The current ruling ontology denies any possibility of a social causation of mental illness. The chemico-biologization of mental illness is of course strictly commensurate with its depoliticization." (p. 21)Audit Culture and Target Proliferation: The Proliferation of BureaucracyIn his analysis of public services and education, Fisher exposes the hypocrisy of neoliberalism’s claim to have liberated society from the constraints of state bureaucracy. Rather than disappearing under the influence of market forces, bureaucracy has merely changed its form and expanded. Neoliberal capitalism has inaugurated an era of audit culture and target proliferation, where workers are subjected to a relentless regime of self-monitoring, performance indicators, and bureaucratic reporting. This "business ontology" forces public institutions, such as universities, hospitals, and schools, to operate as if they were commercial corporations, replacing the actual goal of public service with the mechanical pursuit of arbitrary statistical targets.This target culture does more than measure performance; it actively creates a simulated reality where the document is more important than the actual work. Fisher calls this market Stalinism, a system where the bureaucratic representation of achievement is prioritised over the actual achievement itself. In education, this leads to a state where teachers teach to the test and students study only to pass, destroying the intrinsic value of learning. The audit becomes a self-serving mechanism that justifies its own existence, forcing workers to participate in a collective performance of productivity that drains their time and energy, and prevents them from forming solidarity with one another. Fisher argues that this target-driven bureaucracy is a key tool of capitalist realism: it occupies workers' time and energy, preventing them from imagining different ways of organising public life, and forcing them to internalise the market's values of efficiency and quantification as the only rational criteria of worth.Puncturing the Grey Curtain: Reflexive Impotence and Collective ActionFisher introduces the concept of reflexive impotence to describe the psychological state that characterises the contemporary subject under capitalist realism. Reflexive impotence describes the condition where subjects are fully aware of systemic corruption, environmental destruction, and economic inequality, but feel completely powerless to change them. Unlike the traditional subject of ideology who is ignorant of the truth, the subject of capitalist realism is cynical and highly informed; they know that the system is broken, but they behave as if nothing can be done. This passive resignation is the ultimate strength of capitalist realism: it governs not through our belief, but through our paralysis.Fisher uses Gothic metaphors to describe this parasitic nature of capital, writing that capital is an abstract vampire that feeds on human subjectivity:To puncture this grey curtain of reaction, Fisher insists that we must expose the internal contradictions and inconsistencies of capitalist realism. Capitalist realism presents itself as a pragmatic, realistic system, yet it is demonstrably untenable in three areas: the environmental crisis, the mental health epidemic, and the proliferation of target-driven bureaucracy. By showing these systemic failures, critical theory can show that capitalism’s ostensible realism is an ideological construction. Fisher calls for the creation of new forms of political organisation and collective action that can move beyond individualised resistance. Puncturing the illusion of capitalist realism is the necessary first step toward reclaiming the future, showing that from a situation where nothing can happen, suddenly anything is possible again."Capital is an abstract parasite, an insatiable vampire and zombie maker; but the living flesh it converts into dead labor is ours, and the zombies it makes are us." (p. 15)
critical_works.ch98: Cary Wolfe (1959–)Original title: What is Posthumanism?2009 · English · United States · Critical Posthumanism / Animal Studies / Systems Theory · Theoretical Essays / Philosophical MonographCritical Posthumanism vs. Transhumanism: The Rejection of Disembodied FantasiesCary Wolfe’s What is Posthumanism?, published by the University of Minnesota Press in 2009, is a foundational text in contemporary critical theory, animal studies, and environmental philosophy. Wolfe’s central intellectual project is to define a rigorous "critical posthumanism" that stands in direct opposition to popular forms of "transhumanism." While transhumanism is a technophilic movement that seeks to transcend biological limitations through cybernetic enhancement, artificial intelligence, and genetic engineering, Wolfe argues that transhumanism is actually an extreme extension of liberal humanism. Transhumanism perpetuates the Cartesian fantasy of disembodiment, encouraging the dream that human consciousness can be uploaded into a digital substrate and escape the constraints of physical matter. Critical posthumanism, by contrast, rejects these fantasies of disembodiment and autonomy, insisting on the recovery of our material, biological, and ecological immersion:For Wolfe, posthumanism is not about a chronological future where the human species has been replaced by machines. Instead, it is a critical method that seeks to deconstruct the philosophical foundations of humanism, exposing how the concept of "the human" has historically been constructed through the exclusion of the non-human. Critical posthumanism does not abandon the human, but rather seeks to locate human subjectivity within a complex, hybrid network of biological, technological, and environmental relations:By decentring the autonomous, rational subject of humanist philosophy, Wolfe opens up new possibilities for conceptualising ethics, justice, and politics in a multispecies world."Posthumanism in my sense isn't posthuman at all—in the sense of being 'after' our embodiment has been transcended—but is only posthumanist, in the sense that it opposes the fantasies of disembodiment and autonomy, inherited from humanism itself" (p. xv)"it is humanism, not the human in all its embodied and prosthetic complexity, that is left behind in posthumanist thought" (p. xvi)The Question of the Animal: Decentring Carno-PhallogocentrismA central focus of the first half of Wolfe’s monograph is the "question of the animal," which he describes as the primary site where the limits of humanist ethics are exposed. Wolfe argues that traditional liberal theories of animal rights, such as the utilitarianism of Peter Singer or the deontological ethics of Tom Regan, remain trapped within humanist frameworks. These theories seek to extend ethical protections to animals only to the extent that those animals exhibit "human-like" qualities, such as reason, language, or sentience. By making humanity the measure of ethical worth, these frameworks reinforce the very speciesist hierarchy they seek to challenge.To construct a genuinely posthumanist critique of speciesism, Wolfe draws on Jacques Derrida’s concept of carno-phallogocentrism. This term describes the sacrificial structure of Western philosophy and law, which legitimises the systematic exploitation and killing of non-human animals to secure the sovereignty of the rational human subject.
