He does not excuse the cannibal; he insists that the word "barbarian" must also be tested against European conduct.This insistence on self-examination is what separates "Of Cannibals" from simple travel literature. The New World is a mirror. Looking into it, the European sees his own face, distorted by the violence of his religious wars and the corruption of his laws. The cannibal is not the opposite of the civilized man; he is the standard against which the civilized man's failures become visible.The Poetry of the CannibalOne of the most remarkable sections of the essay is Montaigne's discussion of Tupinambá culture, specifically their poetry and their conception of the soul. He records two of their songs. One is a war song, in which a captive taunts his captors, telling them that by eating him they will also eat their own ancestors who served as his food in past battles. The other is a love song, addressed to an adder:"Adder, stay; stay, adder, that my sister may take from the pattern of thy painted skin the fashion and work of a rich ribbon I may present to my love; so may thy beauty and thy disposition be preferred to all other serpents."Montaigne observes that these songs do not sound like the utterances of beasts. He finds in the love song an "anacreontic" quality, a lyric grace that reminds him of classical poetry. The comparison with Greek and Roman models is deliberate: it gives the passage a standard of recognisable literary humanity while also exposing the limits of the European observer's categories.This cultural recognition is crucial. The Tupinambá are not simply a blank slate upon which nature has written its laws; they have their own art, their own history, their own ways of negotiating the world through language. Their poetry is evidence of a human consciousness that is complex and self-aware, even if it does not use the written word.The Open EndingThe essay ends, as it began, with the three Brazilians in Rouen. Montaigne records their observations about the child-king and the beggars, and then concludes with a line of famous irony:"All this is not too bad; but what of it? They wear no breeches."This final sentence (Tout cela ne va pas trop mal: mais quoi? ils ne portent point de hauts de chausses) is a masterpiece of rhetorical understatement. The reader has just been presented with a profound critique of European society, its political illegitimacy, its economic cruelty, its capacity for religious violence, and the essay collapses this critique into a trivial detail of dress.The irony is double. It mocks the European spectator who is willing to ignore the intelligence of the Brazilian critique because of a difference in costume, but it also mocks the essayist's own attempt to bridge the gap between the two worlds. The difference remains. The Tupinambá, with their nakedness and their natural laws, cannot be fully integrated into the European world of breeches and parliaments. The boundary between them is real, and the essayist's job is not to dissolve it, but to show where it lies and what it reveals about those who stand on either side.
essays.ch7: Michel de MontaigneOriginal title: "De l'expérience" (Essay III.13)Date: 1588 (first publication, Essais, Book III)Original language: FrenchCountry/tradition: FrancePeriod/movement: French Renaissance; humanism; late-career skepticismGenre: Philosophical essay; personal reflectionThere is no desire more natural than the desire for knowledge. We try every means that can lead us to it; when reason fails us, we employ experience. This is how Michel de Montaigne begins the final and longest essay of his Essais, "Of Experience" (De l'expérience, Essay III.13). The essay does not open with a statement of triumph but with a boundary line: the point where reason, the grand tool of the philosophical tradition, stops working. When reason is exhausted by the complexity of the world, we are left with experience, which is irregular, inconsistent, personal, and stubbornly resistant to being organized into general laws.This boundary line is the pressure point of the essay. Montaigne is writing at the end of his life, suffering from kidney stones, watching France collapse into civil war, and looking back on the twenty-year project of writing his book. "Of Experience" is his final reckoning with the possibility of self-knowledge and the problem of how to live a human life in a body that is decaying and in a world that refuses to behave predictably. By placing experience above theory, Montaigne rejects the classical search for universal rules of conduct in favor of a detailed, daily study of his own habits, physical sensations, and mental fluctuations.The Multiplication of LawsMontaigne begins with a critique of the legal system of his day, which he sees as a symptom of a broader intellectual pathology: the belief that we can control the world by multiplying rules. He observes that France has more laws than all the rest of the world put together, yet this abundance has not produced justice. Instead, it has produced an endless cycle of interpretation and disputation:"Why is it that our common language, so easy for all other uses, becomes obscure and unintelligible in a contract or a will, and that he who writes so clearly in all other matters finds no way of expressing himself in these that does not fall into doubt and contradiction? It is because the creators of these instruments, in trying to foresee every possible dispute, multiply the clauses and terms to such an extent that they lose themselves in the details."This legal critique is also a critique of scholastic philosophy. Just as the lawyers try to anticipate every case by adding sub-clauses, so the theologians and philosophers try to explain the world by adding distinctions, glosses, and commentaries. The result is a library of books about books, in which the original subject has been lost under layers of interpretation: "There is more work in interpreting interpretations than in interpreting the things themselves, and more books on books than on any other subject. We do nothing but write glosses on one another."Against this proliferation of texts, Montaigne proposes a return to the thing itself: the individual experience, unmediated by authority. He argues that the study of one's own life is a more reliable guide to conduct than all the volumes of moral philosophy: "If I were a good scholar, I would find enough in my own experience to make me wise. Whoever remembers the heat of his past anger, and how far this fever carried him, will see the deformity of this passion better than in Aristotle."The Authority of the BodyThe shift from textual authority to bodily experience is the most radical move in the essay. Montaigne was suffering from nephrolithiasis, kidney stones, a condition that was then untreatable and extremely painful. Instead of treating this illness as a distraction from his intellectual work, he treats it as a primary source of knowledge. The physical details of his suffering, the passage of the stone, the color of his urine, the nature of his pain, are recorded with clinical precision and philosophical interest.The stone, Montaigne argues, teaches him things that philosophy cannot:"It is a struggle between the stone and the body, and the stone has the upper hand. But it is also a lesson in patience and endurance. I find that I can bear the pain better than I had feared when I was healthy. The imagination paints the illness as much worse than it is when it actually arrives."This physical realism is not self-pity. It is an attempt to reclaim the body as a site of philosophical inquiry. The classical tradition, from Plato onward, had tended to treat the body as a prison or a obstacle to the soul's search for truth. Montaigne insists on their unity: the soul must inhabit the body, conform to its rhythms, and accept its limitations. To seek to escape the body through intellectual abstraction is to mistake our nature: "They want to get out of themselves and escape from the man. That is folly; instead of transforming themselves into angels, they transform themselves into beasts; instead of raising themselves, they lower themselves."The detailed account of his physical habits, his preference for soft beds, his dislike of gloves, his habit of eating so fast that he occasionally bites his tongue, his reactions to different kinds of wine, is not trivia. It is the necessary content of a philosophy that seeks to understand the human condition from the inside. If we do not know how we eat, sleep, and defecate, we do not know ourselves in any meaningful sense.The Art of LivingThe conclusion of "Of Experience," and therefore the conclusion of the Essais as a whole, is a meditation on what Montaigne calls the "great and glorious masterpiece" of human life: to live appropriately (vivre à propos).This is not a call for heroic achievement or philosophical detachment. It is a defense of the ordinary, the small-scale, and the immediate:"To compose our character is our duty, not to compose books, and to win, not battles and provinces, but order and tranquillity in our conduct. Our great and glorious masterpiece is to live appropriately. All other things, ruling, hoarding, building, are at best but accessories and administrative details."To live appropriately means to accept the mixed, imperfect nature of our existence. It means enjoying pleasure when it is present, without anxiety about its loss or guilt about its indulgence, and bearing pain when it arrives, without despair. It means refusing the false choice between the active life and the contemplative life, between the public role and the private self.Montaigne notes with approval the behavior of Julius Caesar, who, in the middle of his military campaigns, was able to enjoy the pleasures of the table and the company of women: "He was able to step down from his high position to enjoy ordinary human activities. That is a sign of a truly great mind, to be able to bend and adjust itself to different conditions."Against the rigid codes of his contemporaries, who were dying for theological abstractions or political ambitions, Montaigne proposes a morality of flexibility and attentiveness. The good life is not a monument to be constructed according to a plan; it is a sequence of moments to be inhabited with as much clarity and good humor as we can manage.The Final InscriptionThe essay ends with a return to the physical reality of the aging body. Montaigne is old, his teeth are failing, his energy is decreasing, but his appetite for experience remains undiminished. He concludes with a tribute to the earth and to the senses:"We are great fools. 'He has spent his life in idleness,' we say; 'I have done nothing today.' What, have you not lived? That is not only the fundamental but the most illustrious of your occupations."This passage is the final rejection of the work ethic of the coming modernity and the theological asceticism of his own day. To live is enough. The value of life is not measured by its products, its fame, or its consistency, but by the quality of the attention we pay to it. The Essais began as an attempt to record a self; they end as an invitation to the reader to inhabit their own life with the same curiosity, skepticism, and patience that Montaigne brought to his.
essays.ch8: Francis BaconOriginal title: "Of Studies" (first published in the 1625 enlarged Essayes)Date: 1625 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: English Renaissance; early modern empiricismGenre: Aphoristic essay; educational theory"Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability." With this opening triad, Francis Bacon establishes the tone for "Of Studies," included in his enlarged 1625 collection. The sentence has the speed of a bullet. It contains no qualifying clauses, no personal anecdotes, and no classical references. It is a direct, functional categorization of the purposes of reading, designed to be memorized, quoted, and applied.This opening triad is the pressure point of the essay. Bacon is introducing a new kind of prose to the English language: the aphoristic essay, which rejects the conversational, digressive method of Montaigne in favor of a condensed, balanced, and highly structured style. The essay is not an exploration of the self, but a manual for the active citizen. It investigates how a gentleman should acquire and use knowledge to advance his career and serve the state. By framing studies in terms of their practical utility, Bacon marks the transition from the contemplative humanism of the Renaissance to the utilitarian empiricism of the early modern scientific revolution.The Aphoristic Method and the Three EditionsTo understand "Of Studies," one must distinguish the essay from Bacon's collection history. Bacon's Essayes appeared in 1597, was enlarged in 1612, and reached a fifty-eight-essay edition in 1625; “Of Studies” belongs to that final enlarged edition.The 1597 version is remarkably brief. It consists of a series of blunt, parallel assertions that read like a list of maxims from a notebook. There are no transitions; one thought is placed next to another with the expectation that the reader will supply the connections. This is the "aphoristic" style that Bacon defended in his philosophical work, The Advancement of Learning. He argued that aphorisms are superior to systematic treatises because they represent knowledge in its raw state, unfinished and open to further inquiry:"Aphorisms, representing a knowledge broken, do invite men to enquire farther; whereas Methods, carrying the show of a total, do secure men, as if they were at furthest."By 1625, however, Bacon's style had changed. The final version of "Of Studies" is longer, more balanced, and uses more connective tissue. He added examples, refined the parallelisms, and introduced transitions that make the prose flow more smoothly. Yet the underlying structure remains aphoristic. The sentences are built around sharp contrasts and balanced clauses, using a rhetorical device known as tricolon (groups of three) to create a sense of completeness and authority.The result is a style that feels both authoritative and open. The reader is presented with a series of structured observations that seem like universal laws of the mind, yet the compression of the language forces the reader to slow down and think about what is being left out.The Division of Labor in ReadingThe core of the essay is a series of distinctions about how books should be read and how different minds respond to study. Bacon is famous for his division of books into categories based on their value:"Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention."This is a pragmatic approach to reading. Bacon does not treat all books as sacred vessels of truth. He recognizes that time is limited and that most books are not worth a thorough reading. The reader must be a consumer, selecting the appropriate method for each text: "tasting" the superficial ones, "swallowing" the informational ones, and "chewing" the few that contain real substance.This division of labor extends to the use of assistants. Bacon suggests that for less important subjects, a man can rely on summaries and extracts made by others: "Some books also may be read by deputy, and extracts made of them by others; but that would be only in the less important arguments, and the meaner sort of books; else distilled books are like common distilled waters, flashy things."This utilitarian view of reading was controversial in a culture that still treated study as a form of moral cultivation. For Bacon, reading is an instrument for the training of the mind, and the mind is an instrument for action in the world. He has no patience for the scholar who spends his life in his study without applying what he has learned: "To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament, is affectation; to make judgment wholly by their rules, is the humor of a scholar."The Remedial MindThe second half of the essay develops a theory of mental exercise that is explicitly medical in its terminology. Bacon treats the mind as a muscle that can be strengthened and corrected through specific studies:"Histories make men wise; poets witty; the mathematics subtile; natural philosophy deep; moral grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend. Abeunt studia in mores [Studies pass into manners]. Nay, there is no stond [impediment] or impediment in the wit but may be wrought out by fit studies; like as diseases of the body may have appropriate exercises."This is the concept of studies as intellectual medicine. If a man's mind is prone to wander, Bacon recommends the study of mathematics, because in mathematical proofs, if the mind wanders even for a moment, the entire demonstration must begin again. If his mind is not good at making distinctions, he should study the schoolmen (the scholastic philosophers), who are "splitters of hairs" (cymini sectores). If he is not quick at finding arguments, he should study the law cases.This view of education is functional and corrective. The goal is not to fill the mind with facts, but to develop specific cognitive capacities. Bacon's list of studies and their effects is organized as a series of balances: reading makes a full man, conference a ready man, and writing an exact man. The symmetry of these formulations is part of their power; they make the training of the mind look like a rational, predictable process that can be managed with the same precision as the training of the body.Bacon vs. Montaigne: Two Paths for the EssayThe comparison between Bacon's essays and Montaigne's is one of the classic debates of early modern literary history. It represents two different understandings of what the essay can do.For Montaigne, the essay is an attempt to catch the self in the act of thinking. The prose is informal, digressive, personal, and skeptical of all systems. Montaigne writes to find out who he is, and his essays are full of contradictions, changes of mind, and physical details that have no obvious public utility.For Bacon, the essay is a collection of civil and moral counsels. The prose is formal, structured, objective, and aimed at action. Bacon writes to instruct the public servant, the courtier, the man of affairs. He does not write about his own habits or his own physical suffering; he writes about "Truth," "Revenge," "Simulation and Dissimulation." His essays are designed to be useful in the chamber and the court, not in the library of retirement.This difference in purpose produces a difference in style. Montaigne's sentences are long, flowing, and follow the movements of a mind thinking in real time. Bacon's sentences are short, balanced, and present the results of thought after the thinking has been completed. One is a process; the other is a product.The Legacy of Utility"Of Studies" remains the most famous introduction to Bacon's intellectual project because it summarizes his attitude toward knowledge as a whole. In his major philosophical works, he argued that the goal of science is the "relief of man's estate", the practical improvement of human life through the understanding of natural laws.In "Of Studies," he applies this principle to the individual mind. Studies are not an end in themselves; they are a means to an end, and that end is action in the world. The essay's value comes from its refusal to romanticize the scholarly life. By treating study as a discipline to be managed rather than a retreat to be enjoyed, Bacon established a model of intellectual life that would shape English education and public policy for centuries. The aphorisms of "Of Studies" are the early modern ancestors of the administrative memo: clear, concise, balanced, and designed to get things done.
essays.ch9: Francis BaconOriginal title: "Of Truth" (first published in the expanded edition of Essays, 1625)Date: 1625 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: English Renaissance; early modern empiricismGenre: Philosophical essay; moral inquiry"What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer." With this invocation of the Roman procurator of Judea, Francis Bacon begins "Of Truth," the essay he chose to place at the very front of his final, definitive collection in 1625. Pontius Pilate's question is not asked in a spirit of philosophical inquiry; it is a dismissive, impatient gesture, the reaction of a politician who has no time for absolute standards in a world of administrative compromise. By refusing to wait for Christ's response, Pilate acts as the prototype for a particular kind of human mind: the skeptic who believes that truth is either undiscoverable or politically inconvenient, and who prefers the ease of doubt to the labor of inquiry.This opening scene is the pressure point of the essay. Bacon is writing in the last year of his life, after his fall from political power, he had been impeached for corruption, stripped of the Lord Chancellorship, and banished from the court, and his return to his study was a return to the questions that had occupied his youth. "Of Truth" is his attempt to reconcile the absolute claims of philosophy and theology with the compromised, practical reality of civil life. By analyzing why human beings are so consistently drawn to lies, Bacon does not simply write a moral sermon; he investigates the cognitive, social, and political utility of falsehood, and argues that the search for truth is the primary duty of both the individual soul and the state.The Appeal of the LieBacon's first question is psychological: why do men love lies? He observes that the preference for falsehood is not simply a matter of difficulty, the fact that finding the truth requires hard work, but a natural inclination of the mind itself:"But it is not only the difficulty and labor which men take in finding out of truth, nor yet that when it is found it imposeth upon men's thoughts, that doth bring lies in favor; but a natural though corrupt love of the lie itself."This "love of the lie itself" is a key Baconian insight. He argues that the mind finds the unvarnished truth cold and demanding. A lie, by contrast, adds color, variety, and comfort to life. He uses the image of candlelight to explain this preference: "Truth may perhaps come to the price of a pearl, that showeth best by day; but it will not rise to the price of a diamond or carbuncle, that showeth best in varied lights. A mixture of a lie doth ever add pleasure."If you remove from men's minds all their vanity, their false hopes, their incorrect estimations of their own worth, and their suspicious imaginations, Bacon suggests, you would leave them "poor shrunken things," full of melancholy and boredom. The lie is a necessary social lubricant; it shields us from the harshness of our own insignificance and the indifference of the world. This is a remarkably modern observation, prefiguring the work of later psychologists and sociologists who study the role of "positive illusions" and social performance in maintaining mental stability and social cohesion.The Three Domains of TruthTo analyze truth systematically, Bacon divides it into three distinct domains: theological truth, philosophical truth, and civil or practical truth.Theological truth is the highest. Bacon describes the creation of the world as a sequence of light: first the light of the senses, then the light of reason, and finally the Sabbath work of the Holy Spirit, which is the illumination of the human mind:"The first creature of God, in the works of the days, was the light of the sense; the last was the light of reason; and his Sabbath work ever since is the illumination of his Spirit."Philosophical truth is the search for this light through the study of nature and the mind. Bacon compares the mind that has arrived at this truth to a spectator standing on a high cliff above a stormy sea: "It is a heaven upon earth, to have a man's mind move in charity, rest in providence, and turn upon the poles of truth." The image is borrowed from the Roman poet Lucretius, but Bacon modifies it: the spectator's pleasure should not come from watching the suffering of those below, but from the security of his own understanding, which allows him to look down with pity and a desire to help.Civil truth, which Bacon calls "truth of civil business," is the application of truth to daily affairs. Here, the tone of the essay shifts from the poetic to the pragmatic. Bacon admits that in the business of the world, complete honesty is not always possible: "It will be acknowledged even by those that practice it not, that clear and round dealing is the honor of man's nature; and that mixture of falsehood is like alloy in gold and silver, which may make the metal work the better, but it embaseth it."This comparison with metallurgy is classic Bacon. The alloy makes the metal harder and more useful for daily transactions, but it lowers its purity. The man who lies in business or politics may achieve his immediate goals more easily, but he has debased his character. Bacon has no patience for the systematic liar; he quotes Montaigne's observation that to tell a lie is to be brave toward God and a coward toward men: "For a lie faces God, and shrinks from man."The Political Consequences of FalsehoodThe transition from individual morality to political utility is the essay's most significant move. Bacon was a statesman who had served under two monarchs, and he had seen how easily a court could be corrupted by flattery, dissimulation, and rumors. In "Of Truth," he argues that the health of a state depends on the integrity of its communications.When a government or a court becomes a place where lies are valued over truth, the state loses its capacity to act rationally. The leaders are fed false information by flatterers; the citizens lose trust in the institutions; the laws become instruments of faction rather than justice. The "jesting Pilate" who refuses to wait for an answer is not just a bad philosopher; he is a dangerous ruler, because his skepticism leads to administrative cynicism and the collapse of public trust.Bacon's defense of truth is therefore not merely an ethical position; it is a political necessity. The search for truth in the natural sciences, the project he called the Instauratio Magna, is inseparable from the search for truth in civil life. Both require the removal of what he called the "Idols of the Mind": the prejudices, linguistic confusions, and philosophical dogmas that obstruct our view of the world.The Aphoristic Structure of TruthFormally, "Of Truth" is one of Bacon's most accomplished essays. It is built around a series of balanced contrasts: truth vs. lies, light vs. darkness, pearls vs. diamonds, gold vs. alloy. These binary oppositions structure the argument, giving the prose a classical symmetry that mirrors the order Bacon believed existed in the universe.Yet the essay is not a rigid treatise. It moves easily from biblical allusion (Pilate, the Creation, the Fall) to classical poetry (Lucretius) to contemporary social observation. The transitions are quick, the language is dense, and the metaphors are drawn from the physical world, commerce, gems, metals, light. This mixture of the high-philosophical and the low-material is the signature of Bacon's prose. It is designed to demonstrate that truth is not an abstract concept to be kept in a temple, but a practical reality that must be tested on the street and in the market.The Restless SearchThe essay concludes with a warning that is both moral and historical. Bacon observes that the ultimate consequence of civil falsehood is the collapse of society itself:"Surely the wickedness of falsehood and breach of faith cannot be so highly expressed, as in that it shall be the last peal to call the judgments of God upon the generations of men; it being foretold, that when Christ cometh, he shall not find faith upon the earth."This final reference to the apocalypse places the problem of truth in its largest possible frame. The loss of truth is not a minor moral failure; it is the dissolving agent that destroys the human community. When trust is gone, when faith cannot be found, the social contract dissolves and the world returns to chaos.By ending on this cosmic note, Bacon answers the jesting Pilate who opened the essay. The procurator's question was an attempt to dismiss truth as irrelevant to the business of empire. Bacon's response is that without truth, there is no empire, no science, and no community. The search for truth is the work that keeps the world from falling apart.
essays.ch10: Francis BaconOriginal title: "Of Revenge" (first published in the expanded edition of Essays, 1625)Date: 1625 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: English Renaissance; early modern jurisprudenceGenre: Philosophical essay; moral and political counsel"Revenge is a kind of wild justice; which the more man's nature runs to, the more ought law to weed it out." With this striking metaphor, Francis Bacon introduces "Of Revenge," one of the most politically acute essays in his 1625 collection. The description of revenge as "wild justice" is both an acknowledgment of its appeal and a declaration of its illegitimacy. It is "justice" because it seeks to correct a wrong, to restore an equilibrium that has been disrupted by an injury. It is "wild" because it operates outside the law, in the untamed territory of personal passion, where the judge is also the victim and the executioner.This metaphor is the pressure point of the essay. Bacon is writing during a period in English history when the private duel was a major social problem among the aristocracy, and when the memory of the blood feuds of the Middle Ages was still fresh. "Of Revenge" is his attempt to show that private vengeance is not a noble act of honor, but a regression to a pre-civilized state that undermines the authority of the state. By analyzing the psychology of revenge, Bacon argues that the person who seeks vengeance is trapped in the past, and that the only rational response to an injury is either legal redress or philosophical forgiveness.The Temporal Trap of VengeanceBacon's first argument against revenge is psychological and temporal: it traps the mind in a past that cannot be changed. The person who broods over an injury is keeping their own wounds green when they could otherwise heal:"This is certain, that a man that studieth revenge, keeps his own wounds green, which otherwise would heal, and do well. Public revenges are for the most part fortunate; as that for the death of Caesar; for the death of Pertinax; for the death of Henry the Third of France; and many more. But in private revenges it is not so. Nay rather, vindictive persons live the life of witches; who, as they are mischievous, so end they infortunate."The contrast between public revenge and private revenge is crucial. Public revenge, the execution of regicides, the punishment of traitors, the collective retribution of a state against its enemies, is "fortunate" because it restores order and reinforces the authority of the law. It is an act of justice that looks to the future, establishing a precedent that deters further crimes.Private revenge, by contrast, is a personal obsession that looks backward. The vindictive person is like a witch: isolated, driven by malice, and destined for a bad end. By spending their energy on past wrongs, they neglect the present and the future: "A man that hath no virtue in himself, ever envieth virtue in others. For men's minds will either feed upon their own good, or upon others' evil; who wanteth the one, will prey upon the other."To seek private revenge is to allow the person who injured you to control your mind. You are no longer living your own life; you are living in reaction to their act, reproducing their violence in yourself and extending the damage of the original injury.The Offence and the LawBacon is careful to distinguish among the kinds of injuries that provoke revenge. He notes that most offences are committed not out of pure malice, but out of self-interest, vanity, or weakness:"Why should I be angry with a man, for loving himself better than me? And if any man should do wrong, merely out of ill-nature, why, yet it is but like the thorn or briar, which prick and scratch, because they can do no other."This is a remarkably cool, Stoic observation. To be angry with a selfish person is as irrational as being angry with a thorn bush for having thorns. Self-love is the default condition of human nature, and we should expect people to act in their own interest, even when it harms us. If a person acts out of pure malice, their behavior is a natural defect, a deformity of the character that should be pitied rather than met with fury.When an injury is committed, the rational response is to seek legal redress. The law is a neutral arbiter, free from the personal passion that distorts private vengeance. The law punishes the crime without anger, restoring order without initiating a new cycle of violence.However, Bacon admits there is one exception: the case where the law cannot help:"The most tolerable sort of revenge, is for those wrongs which there is no law to remedy; but then let a man take heed, the revenge be such as there is no law to punish; else a man's enemy is still beforehand, and it is two for one."This is the pragmatist speaking. If a man has been injured in a way that the law does not recognize, a slight to his reputation, a betrayal by a friend, and he chooses to take revenge, he must do so in a way that does not break the law himself. If he breaks the law to avenge a private wrong, he has handed his enemy a second victory: the enemy has harmed him once, and now the state will harm him a second time. The transaction is economically unfavorable: "it is two for one."The Performance of RevengeEven when revenge is tolerable, Bacon argues that its execution should be transparent. The avenger must make sure the victim knows why they are being punished:"Some when they take revenge, are desirous the party should know whence it cometh. This is the more generous. For the delight seemeth to be, not so much in doing the hurt as in making the party repent. But base and crafty cowards are like the arrow that flieth in the dark."The desire to have the victim know the source of the revenge is "generous" (noble) because it aims at reformation. The goal is not simply to inflict pain, but to force the offender to recognize their guilt, to make them repent their action. This is a form of moral correction, albeit a violent one.The person who takes revenge secretly, by contrast, is a coward. They are not interested in justice or reformation; they are interested only in the safe indulgence of their malice. They are like an arrow in the dark, striking without warning and without taking responsibility for the blow. This secret revenge does not restore order; it simply adds suspicion and fear to the social environment.The Aphoristic Order of Civil PeaceFormally, "Of Revenge" is a model of Bacon's compressed, analytical style. The essay moves from a broad definition (wild justice) to a psychological analysis of the avenger, to a classification of injuries, to a distinction between public and private revenge, and finally to a moral conclusion. The language is spare, the sentences are balanced, and the metaphors are drawn from the natural world (weeds, thorns, green wounds, wild plants).This organic imagery is important. By describing revenge as a "wild" plant and the law as the gardener who must "weed it out," Bacon suggests that civilization is a process of cultivation. Human nature left to itself will produce the weeds of vengeance and malice; the law is the artificial instrument that keeps these natural inclinations in check, maintaining the garden of civil peace.This view of human nature is pessimistic but realistic. Bacon does not expect men to be saints; he expects them to be selfish, weak, and vindictive. But he believes that through the rational application of law and the cultivation of the intellect, we can construct a civil society in which these destructive impulses are managed.The Value of ForgivenessThe essay concludes with an appeal to a higher standard of conduct, citing the examples of historical figures who chose forgiveness over vengeance:"Cosmus, Duke of Florence, had a desperate saying against perfidious or neglecting friends, as if those wrongs were unpardonable: You shall read (saith he) that we are commanded to forgive our enemies; but you never read, that we are commanded to forgive our friends. But yet the spirit of Job was in a better tune: Shall we (saith he) take good at God's hands, and not be content to take evil also? And so of friends in a proportion."By contrasting the cynical realism of Cosimo de' Medici with the patience of Job, Bacon shows the limits of political pragmatism. Cosimo's view is that betrayal by a friend is an absolute wrong that must be punished. Job's view is that we must accept the bad with the good, recognizing that all human relationships are imperfect.Bacon sides with Job. To demand perfection from our friends is as irrational as demanding that the world produce no storms. The capacity to overlook injuries, to let them go without seeking retribution, is a sign of a superior mind: "It is the glory of a man, to pass by an offence." By rising above the desire for revenge, a man demonstrates his independence from his enemy and his commitment to the future. The wild justice of revenge is, in the end, a dead end; the cultivated garden of the law and the quiet mind of forgiveness are the only ways forward.
essays.ch11: Francis BaconOriginal title: "Of Marriage and Single Life" (first published in Essays, 1612; revised in 1625)Date: 1612 / 1625 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: English Renaissance; early modern sociologyGenre: Philosophical essay; civil and moral counsel"He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune; for they are impediments to great enterprises, either of virtue or mischief." With this cold, unsentimental sentence, Francis Bacon begins his meditation "Of Marriage and Single Life." The phrase "hostages to fortune" is one of Bacon's most durable coinages. It treats the family not as a sanctuary of affection or a moral duty, but as a liability, a set of vulnerabilities that a man exposes to the unpredictable movements of fate. If you have hostages, you are not free to act; your decisions are constrained by the need to protect those who depend on you.This opening assertion is the pressure point of the essay. Bacon is analyzing the institution of marriage from a perspective that is almost entirely sociological and utilitarian. He is not interested in the theological sacrament of marriage or the romantic ideal of love. He is investigating a practical question: how do marriage and celibacy affect a man's capacity to serve the state, conduct business, and achieve greatness? By framing the choice between marriage and single life in terms of public utility, Bacon offers a clear-eyed analysis of how domestic arrangements shape the public sphere.The Public Value of the Unmarried ManBacon's first observation is that the most significant contributions to society, the "great enterprises" of virtue, science, and public works, have historically been the work of unmarried or childless men:"Unmarried men are best friends, best masters, best servants; but not always best subjects; for they are light to run away; and almost all fugitives are of that condition. A single life is proper for churchmen; for charity will hardly water the ground where it must first fill a pool."The imagery here is precise. The unmarried man's resources are undivided. His charity is like water that can irrigate the general ground of society because it does not have to be collected in the private "pool" of his own family's needs. He is free to take risks, to devote himself entirely to his office, and to dedicate his fortune to public institutions.This freedom, however, has a political cost. The single man is "light to run away." Lacking the domestic anchors of property and family, he is less invested in the stability of the state. He can easily flee when trouble arrives. The married man, by contrast, is bound to the soil and the community by his dependents; he is a more reliable subject because he has more to lose.Bacon's analysis of the unmarried man is therefore double-edged. He is a superior instrument for specific, high-risk tasks, the celibate priest, the soldier of fortune, the explorer, but a less stable citizen for the daily business of a settled commonwealth.The Domestic Discipline of MarriageIf the single life offers freedom, the married life offers discipline. Bacon argues that marriage is a school of moral character, training men in the habits of responsibility, patience, and care:"Wives are young men's mistresses; companions for middle age; and old men's nurses. So as a man may have a quarrel to marry when he will. But yet he was reputed one of the wise men, that made answer to the question, when a man should marry? A young man not yet, an elder man not at all."The description of a wife's role at different stages of life, mistress, companion, nurse, is a classic example of Bacon's developmental psychology. Marriage is not a static state; its character changes as the partners age. For the young man, it is a site of passion; for the middle-aged man, a partnership of equals; for the old man, a system of care.By committing to these roles, a man is forced to look beyond his own immediate desires. He must learn to manage a household, provide for children, and negotiate the daily compromises of domestic life. This discipline, Bacon suggests, makes married men more humane and less prone to the harsh, self-absorbed eccentricity that often characterizes the lifelong bachelor:"Chaste women are often proud and froward, as presuming upon the merit of their chastity. It is one of the best bonds, both of chastity and obedience, in the wife, if she think her husband wise; which she will never do, if she find him jealous."The psychology of the relationship is analyzed in terms of power and respect. A wife's obedience is not something to be enforced by jealousy or restriction, but a natural consequence of her respect for her husband's wisdom. If the husband is jealous, he reveals his own insecurity, and in doing so, he destroys the foundation of his authority.The Economic and Social LedgerThroughout the essay, Bacon balances the advantages of marriage against its costs, producing a ledger of social utility.On the negative side, marriage limit's a man's mobility and resources. It makes him more cautious, more conservative, and less willing to challenge authority: "He that hath wife and children... they are impediments to great enterprises." The married man must think of his dependents before he speaks truth to power or takes a financial risk.On the positive side, marriage is the primary agent of social reproduction. It domesticates the wilder impulses of the young, turning them into stable, tax-paying citizens who are invested in the future of the community. It provides a natural welfare system for the sick and the old, reducing the burden on the state. It promotes the virtues of sobriety, industry, and order: "But the most ordinary cause of a single life is liberty, especially in certain self-pleasing and humorous minds, which are so sensible of every restraint, as they will go near to think their girdles and garters to be bonds and shackles."The bachelor who refuses to marry because he values his absolute freedom is, in Bacon's view, a figure of fun. His desire to avoid all restraint is a form of childishness, a refusal to grow up. The married man's "bonds and shackles" are the necessary weight that gives his life gravity and direction.The Aphoristic Balance of LifeFormally, "Of Marriage and Single Life" is structured as a series of counter-weighted clauses. Bacon rarely makes an assertion on one side of the question without immediately balancing it with an assertion on the other. Unmarried men make the best friends, but they are not always the best subjects. Single life is good for churchmen, but it makes soldiers cruel. Wives are mistresses to the young, but they are nurses to the old.This syntax of comparison is not just a stylistic preference; it is the formal expression of Bacon's method. He is not trying to persuade the reader to marry or to remain single. He is presenting the evidence, organized as a balanced sheet, so that the reader can make a rational decision based on his own circumstances and his own capacity for responsibility.The language is dry, dense, and free from the emotional color that usually attaches to discussions of family life. Bacon writes about marriage with the same cool detachment that he would bring to a report on the trade of the realm or the state of the fortifications. This detachment is what makes the essay still readable: it refuses to lie to us about the cost of our attachments, and it treats the domestic life not as a separate sphere of sentiment, but as an integral part of the political economy of the state.The Wisdom of the LimitThe essay ends, characteristically, with a classical anecdote that undercuts the possibility of a simple rule. He quotes the philosopher Thales, who, when asked by his mother when he would marry, answered "Not yet" when he was young, and "Not at all" when he was old.This anecdote is the final qualified conclusion. It suggests that from a purely rational, philosophical perspective, there is never a perfect time to marry. When you are young and full of energy, you have better things to do; when you are old and need care, it is too late to start a partnership.Yet Bacon does not expect his readers to be philosophers like Thales. Most men will marry, and they will do so for reasons of custom, convenience, or passion. His job is not to change this fact, but to show them what they are doing when they do it: that they are giving hostages to fortune, accepting a necessary discipline, and participating in the collective work of building a stable human community.
essays.ch12: Francis BaconOriginal title: "Of Gardens" (first published in the expanded edition of Essays, 1625)Date: 1625 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: English Renaissance; early modern landscape designGenre: Philosophical essay; aesthetic and practical design manual"God Almighty first planted a garden. And indeed it is the purest of human pleasures. It is the greatest refreshment to the spirits of man; without which buildings and palaces are but gross handyworks." With this theological and aesthetic declaration, Francis Bacon begins "Of Gardens," one of the most expansive and sensory essays in his 1625 collection. The opening sentence moves from the divine act of creation in Genesis to the immediate experience of human pleasure. Bacon is establishing a hierarchy of achievement: a king or a nobleman may build a magnificent palace, but if he neglects the garden, his architecture is merely "gross handywork," a brute imposition of stone upon the earth that lacks the life, scent, and movement of a cultivated landscape.This hierarchy is the pressure point of the essay. Bacon is writing at the end of his life, having spent years developing his own estate at Gorhambury, and the essay is both a practical design manual and a philosophical reflection on the relationship between art and nature. "Of Gardens" is his attempt to show how a rational man should organize the natural world to produce a space that is both beautiful and useful. By analyzing the scents, colors, and layouts of the ideal garden, Bacon does not simply write a guide for rich landowners; he models the early modern scientific project of understanding, classifying, and managing the natural world for human benefit.The Calendar of Scent and ColorBacon's first requirement for the ideal garden is that it must be green and alive throughout the year. He has no patience for gardens that look beautiful in June and barren in November. He proposes a calendar of planting that ensures a constant succession of growth:"I do hold it, in the royal ordering of gardens, there ought to be gardens for all the months in the year; in which severally things of beauty may be then in season."The list that follows is a masterpiece of botanical classification. Bacon moves systematically through the months, naming the plants that survive and bloom in each: sweet marjoram and rosemary in January; primroses and violets in March; roses and lavender in June; medlars and services in October. This calendar is not just a list of names; it is a sensory inventory, organized to show how a designer can manage time itself, ensuring that the garden never loses its capacity to refresh the spirits.Bacon is particularly attentive to scent. He distinguishes between flowers that smell sweet only when you hold them to your nose and those that "perfume the air" as you walk past them:"And because the breath of flowers is far sweeter in the air (where it comes and goes like the warbling of music) than in the hand, therefore nothing is more fit for that delight, than to know what be the flowers and plants that do best perfume the air."His favorite scent-producing plant is not the rose, which he notes is sweet only when close at hand, but the sweet-brier, the wild strawberry leaves when dying, the wall-flower, and above all, the musk-rose and the double violet. He recommends planting whole alleys of these fragrant herbs, so that when a visitor walks down them, their footsteps will crush the leaves and release the scent into the air: "you pay for your pleasure with a gentle bruising of the earth."The Architecture of the Triple GardenFrom the botanical inventory, the essay moves to the spatial layout of the garden. Bacon proposes a highly structured, symmetrical design for a "royal garden" of thirty acres. This space is divided into three distinct parts: a green at the entrance, a main garden in the middle, and a wilderness or "heath" at the end.The green (four acres) is a simple lawns of closely cut grass, designed to provide a quiet, open space that prepares the visitor's mind for the complexity of the main garden. It is bordered by covered alleys of trees, providing shade and shelter from the wind.The main garden (twelve acres) is the site of formal artifice. It is laid out in a grid of alleys, hedges, and flower beds, but Bacon warns against the over-elaborate designs that were then fashionable in continental Europe. He particularly dislikes "knots" of colored earth and figures cut into hedges:"As for the making of knots or figures with divers colored earths, that they may lie under the windows of the house on that side which the garden stands, they be but toys; you may see as good sights many times in tarts. Images cut out in juniper or other garden stuff, they be for children."This rejection of the "toyish" and the "tart-like" is a key Baconian principle. Art should assist nature, not caricature it. He prefers open, spacious alleys that allow the eye to range, and simple, elegant structures like mounds and summer-houses that provide views of the surrounding country.The third part of the garden, the heath or wilderness (six acres), is the most innovative part of the design. It is a space where nature is allowed to look wild, though it is actually carefully managed:"I wish it to be framed, as much as may be, to a natural wildness. Trees I would have none in it, but sweet-brier and honeysuckle, and some wild vine amongst; and the ground set with violets, strawberries, and primroses. For these are sweet, and prosper in the shade. And these to be in the wild ways, not in single lines."This "natural wildness" prefigures the English landscape garden movement of the eighteenth century, which would reject the formal symmetry of French and Italian gardens in favor of winding paths, irregular lakes, and simulated wilderness. For Bacon, the heath is a necessary balance to the formal artifice of the main garden. It reminds the visitor of the raw material from which the garden was constructed, and provides a different kind of refreshment: the illusion of escape from the social world into the forest.The Management of WaterA major section of the essay is dedicated to the design of fountains and pools. Bacon treats water as the life-blood of the garden, but he warns against the dangers of stagnation:"For fountains, they are a great beauty and refreshment; but pools mar all, and make the garden unwholesome, and full of flies and frogs."Water, Bacon argues, must be kept in constant motion. He distinguishes between two kinds of fountains: the "spurt" of water that rises and falls in a basin, and the "fair receipt" of water that flows steadily through a decorated pool. Both must be kept clean, the basins washed regularly to prevent the growth of algae, and the water sourced from clean springs rather than muddy ponds.This attention to sanitation and movement is consistent with Bacon's scientific work. In his natural philosophy, he wrote extensively about the role of moisture and heat in the decay and preservation of organic matter. The clean, moving water of the garden is not just an aesthetic pleasure; it is a sanitary necessity, maintaining the health of the plants and the visitor alike.The Metaphor of the StateThe ordered garden is, throughout Bacon's work, a recurring metaphor for the well-governed state. Just as the gardener must weed out the wild plants of revenge, select the appropriate trees for different soils, manage the flow of water, and balance formal artifice with natural wildness, so the statesman must manage the different classes, laws, and resources of the commonwealth.The royal garden of thirty acres is a small model of the realm. It is divided into zones of different function and character; it requires constant maintenance, clean water, and a careful balance of structure and liberty. The king who plants a garden is demonstrating his capacity to govern: if he can bring order, beauty, and health to a piece of wild land, he shows that he has the patience and the intelligence to bring the same qualities to his kingdom.Formally, the essay is structured as a walkthrough. Bacon guides the reader through the space, moving from the entrance green to the alleys of the main garden, up the central mound, past the fountains, and into the wilderness at the far end. The language is rich in sensory detail, the scent of strawberry leaves, the color of musk-roses, the sound of moving water, making the reading experience itself a kind of refreshment to the spirits.The Return to the GroundThe essay concludes with a characteristic return to the practical limits of the project. Bacon admits that his design is expensive and requires a large estate, but he insists that even a small garden, if planned with the same attention to scent, color, and seasons, can provide the same quality of pleasure:"This which I have demised is a model of a princely garden, partly by maps and partly by writing, not a model of a private man's garden. But yet, if a man will look into the details, he will find that the principles of scent, order, and wildness can be applied to any plot of ground, however small."By ending on this note of accessibility, Bacon rescues his design from being merely a fantasy of royal luxury. The garden is not a status symbol; it is a site of human activity, a place where the mind can find relief from the business of the court and the city. In the final estimation, the essay asserts that the cultivation of the earth is a form of self-cultivation. The man who plants a garden is participating in the divine work of creation, bringing order to the wildness of nature and finding, in the gentle bruising of the earth, the purest of human pleasures.
essays.ch13: Richard SteeleOriginal title: The Tatler, No. 181 (June 6, 1710)Date: 1710 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; early eighteenth-century periodical pressGenre: Periodical essay; personal reflection; memoirIn the early summer of 1710, readers of The Tatler opened issue number 181 to find their familiar guide, the elderly astrologer Isaac Bickerstaff, in an unusually somber mood. He had spent the evening in his room, he told them, watching the shadows lengthen and thinking about the friends he had lost. The meditation that followed was not a satirical look at London manners or a political report from the St. James's Coffee-house. It was a memory of a childhood event: the death of his father when he was not quite five years old, and the sight of his mother's intense, silent grief.This memory is the pressure point of the essay. The periodical turns to the private, emotional life of the family, specifically childhood grief and the persistence of memory, rather than to public policy or abstract philosophy. Its intimate register makes domestic feeling available for critical attention without making the episode a general history of its readers' emotions.The Astrologer's GriefThe use of Isaac Bickerstaff as a persona is crucial to how the essay works. Bickerstaff was a fictional character invented by Jonathan Swift and adopted by Steele to serve as the editor and chief voice of The Tatler. In most issues, Bickerstaff is a comic figure: an eccentric, well-meaning old bachelor who uses his astrological charts to comment on the fashions, scandals, and political debates of the day.In issue 181, however, the comic mask slips, or rather, it is used to give the sentimentality a frame:"The first sense of sorrow I ever knew was upon the death of my father, at which time I was not quite five years of age; but was rather amazed at what all the house meant, than possessed with a real understanding of my loss."The child's perspective is recorded with extraordinary psychological realism. The young boy does not understand what death means; he is simply confused by the disruption of the household, the closed shutters, the weeping servants, and his mother's behavior. Steele describes how the child, seeing his mother weeping over the coffin, went to her and beat her with his battle-door (a toy racket), crying out that she should not hurt his father, whom he believed was merely sleeping inside the box.This detail of the battle-door is remarkable. It is a specific, material memory that has no place in the classical theory of the passions, but has everything to do with how a real child experiences a family crisis. The child's anger at his mother is a reaction to his own confusion and fear: he wants the domestic order restored, and he strikes out at the person who seems to be disrupting it by her weeping.The Mother's SorrowThe center of the memory is the figure of the mother, whose grief is described not as a dramatic performance, but as a silent, physical transformation:"My mother, who was a very beautiful woman, of an extraordinary spirit, was so drowned in tears and grief, that she was inconsolable. I remember, when she was in the height of her distress, she would often take me in her arms, and, looking at me with an eye that was at once full of tenderness and sorrow, weep over me, and tell me I was the very image of my father."This image of the mother's face, marked by the double print of love for her child and grief for her husband, is the emotional anchor of the essay. Steele is describing a state of emotional inheritance: the child becomes the vessel of the dead father's memory, and the mother's look is the medium through which this memory is transferred.The domestic scene gives the essay an ethical scale without requiring it to become a general theory of family life. In this reading, grief at home becomes a test of attention to another person's vulnerability: the child cannot comprehend the loss, but the scene makes the force of his mother's suffering legible. That movement from confused observation to fellow-feeling is a formal possibility of the essay, not evidence for a universal history of eighteenth-century emotion.The Periodical and the Public SphereThe periodical setting matters because a public persona can carry an intimate memory into a shared reading space. The Tatler joins observation, commentary, and changing registers of address; No. 181 uses that flexibility to move from the persona's public voice toward private recollection. The chapter treats this as a formal contrast, not as a complete account of Queen Anne London or the periodical's reforming programme.The periodical essay was the primary instrument of this reform. By publishing three times a week, The Tatler entered the daily life of its readers, lying on the coffee-house tables and the tea-tables of the suburbs. It spoke in a voice that was conversational, accessible, and polite, bridging the gap between the scholarly world of the universities and the commercial world of the city.In "Recollections of Childhood," Steele uses this accessibility to make a case for the value of grief. He argues that the memory of sorrow is not a weakness to be overcome, but a possession that enriches the character:"There is a sort of pleasing melancholy that arises from the contemplation of past griefs, which is far more desirable than the most noisy mirth. The memory of a friend we have lost is like the evening light, which, though it is not so bright as the noon, is sweeter and more quiet."The passage makes melancholy into an occasion for reflection rather than simply a feeling to be expelled. Its value lies in the essay's conversion of remembered loss into a measured address to readers. Any relation to later poetry or fiction is a possible comparative context, not a direct line of influence asserted here.The Style of SentimentFormally, the essay is structured as a transition from the public to the private. It begins with Bickerstaff in his study, looking out at the street and observing the busy world of London, before turning inward to his papers and his memory. The language is simple, direct, and free from the Latinate vocabulary and balanced syntax of Bacon's prose.This simplicity is deliberate. Steele is trying to write in a style that sounds like a gentleman speaking to his friends in a parlor. The sentences are loose, conversational, and follow the movements of memory rather than a formal proof. He does not use classical quotations to prove his points; he uses them to evoke a mood, citing the Roman poet Virgil not as an authority on politics, but as a poet who understood the tears of things (lacrimae rerum).The conversational style makes the piece feel exploratory rather than systematic. Its shifts between persona, scene, recollection, and general reflection illustrate one available mode of the familiar essay; the chapter does not claim a direct, comprehensive line of influence from Steele to later writers.The Persistence of MemoryThe essay concludes with Bickerstaff returning to his present situation. He is an old man, his childhood is long past, and the mother he remembered is dead. But the memory remains, as fresh and as demanding as it was in 1710:"I am now an old man, and have seen many changes in the world; but that image of my mother's face, as she looked at me when she told me I was my father's picture, is still before my eyes. It is the one thing that has not changed."By ending on this note of persistence, Steele answers the cynical world of the coffee-houses. The gossip, the political disputes, and the commercial calculations of London are temporary; they will pass with the season. The private memory of love and loss, however, remains. It is the quiet center around which a human life is constructed, and the essay is the medium that allows us to share this center with others, transforming private grief into a collective possession.
essays.ch14: Richard SteeleOriginal title: The Spectator, No. 2 (March 2, 1711)Date: 1711 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; early eighteenth-century periodical pressGenre: Periodical essay; character sketch; social satireOn the second day of March in 1711, readers of the newly launched daily sheet The Spectator were introduced to a small group of gentlemen who met regularly in a London tavern. The Spectator Club is a narrative frame that gathers figures associated with country gentry, commerce, the military, law, the church, and town fashion.The pressure point of the essay is the tension among these different social interests, specifically the emerging conflict between the landed aristocracy and the rising mercantile class. The Tory country squire, represented by Sir Roger de Coverley, and the Whig merchant, represented by Sir Andrew Freeport, belonged to worlds that were politically, economically, and culturally at war. By placing these figures in the same club, sitting around the same table, and engaging in polite conversation, Steele and his partner Joseph Addison did not simply reflect English society; they proposed a model for its reconciliation. The club is a neutral space where the divisions of the seventeenth century are defused through the new code of politeness and commerce.The Squire and the Merchant: A Conflict of ValueThe most significant figures in the club are Sir Roger de Coverley and Sir Andrew Freeport, because they embody the two main forms of wealth and power in early eighteenth-century England.Sir Roger is introduced first. He is a gentleman of Worcestershire, a baronet whose estate has been in his family for generations. He is beloved by his tenants, eccentric in his habits, and deeply conservative:"He is a gentleman that is very singular in his behavior, but his singularities proceed from his good sense, and are contradictions to the manners of the world, only as he thinks the world is in the wrong. However, this humor creates him no enemies, for he does nothing with sourness or obstinacy; and his being unconfined to the modes of the world, makes him only the readier and more capable to please and oblige when he is in it."Sir Roger represents the old order: the paternalistic country estate, where social relationships are governed by custom, loyalty, and the authority of the Church of England. Yet he is also a figure of mild fun. His "singularities", his habit of shouting at the parson during church, his long-past disappointment in love with a beautiful widow, his obsession with his family history, show that his world is sliding into eccentricity, becoming a museum of outdated manners rather than a dynamic political force.Sir Andrew Freeport, by contrast, represents the future. He is a London merchant of great eminence, industrious, wealthy, and pragmatic:"He is a person of indefatigable industry, strong reason, and great experience. His notions of trade are noble and generous, and (as every rich man has usually some sly way of jesting, which would make no great figure were he not a rich man) he calls the sea the British Common. He is acquainted with commerce in all its parts, and will tell you that it is a stupid and barbarous way to extend dominion by arms; for true power is to be got by arts and industry."Sir Andrew's view of the world is commercial and global. True power, he argues, is not won by military conquest or inherited land, but by the "arts and industry" of trade. The sea is not a barrier; it is the "British Common," a highway for the exchange of goods and the accumulation of wealth. His language is full of maxims about frugality, diligence, and the national benefit of commerce.By placing Sir Roger and Sir Andrew in the same club, Steele forces them to talk to each other. Their disputes are not settled by swords or factional pamphlets; they are conducted in the polite vocabulary of the tavern table. The essay suggests that the merchant's industry and the squire's generosity are not incompatible; both are necessary for the prosperity of the nation. The club is the laboratory where this national synthesis is tested.The Supporting Characters of the MicrocosmAround the main conflict between the squire and the merchant, Steele arranges four other characters who represent other key aspects of English life.There is the Templar, a student of law at the Inner Temple who is more interested in the theater than in his textbooks. He represents the cultural life of the town: he knows the latest plays, reads the classical critics, and is a judge of wit: "He is a great observer of what occurs in the town, and has a very good taste in all the arts."There is Captain Sentry, a military man of courage and integrity who has retired from the army because his modesty prevented him from seeking promotion through court flattery: "He is one of those that deserve well, but are not liked; because they cannot show themselves in a light that is not natural to them." Sentry represents the older, heroic model of service, which is now out of place in a court governed by intrigue and patronages.There is Will Honeycomb, an aging gallant who has spent his life in the fashionable world of the West End. He knows the history of every woman of fashion, understands the grammar of dress and gesture, and is a master of the small-talk of the town: "He is very ready at all the common-places of talk, and can tell you when the fashion of the periwig was first introduced, and what lady of quality was the first that wore a patch." Will represents the social surfaces, the light, often ridiculous manners that the paper seeks to reform through gentle irony.Finally, there is the Clergyman, a man of learning and piety who rarely visits the club because of his health, but whose presence provides a moral and philosophical anchor when he does attend: "He is a person of great learning and virtue, and has a very good understanding of human nature, but his life has been spent in the discharge of his duty."The Character Sketch as Rhetorical DeviceFormally, "The Spectator Club" is a masterpiece of the "character" genre, a literary form that goes back to the Greek philosopher Theophrastus and was popular in seventeenth-century England. In the older tradition, characters were abstract types: the "Envious Man," the "Superstitious Man," the "Squire." Steele's innovation is to make these types look like individual human beings.He achieves this through the use of specific, quirky details: Sir Roger's disappointment in love; Sir Andrew's habit of calling the sea the British Common; Will Honeycomb's memory of seventeenth-century periwigs. These details are not necessary for the typological category, but they are essential for the illusion of reality. The characters read as if they were people Steele had actually met in the taverns of London, and this realism is what allowed readers to identify with them.This identification was crucial for the paper's educational project. By reading about the members of the club, the citizen of London could see his own reflection and the reflections of his neighbors. He was invited to laugh at Sir Roger's eccentricities and Sir Andrew's dry calculations, but also to respect their virtues. The characters are designed to be exemplary: they show how men of different backgrounds, opinions, and interests can live together in harmony, provided they submit to the rules of polite conversation.The Neutral ObserverThe club is framed by the narrator of the paper: the Spectator himself, who introduces the members but remains silent throughout their meetings. The Spectator is a man who has traveled widely, read everything, and knows the world, but who refuses to speak in public: "I have passed my life in the character of a spectator, and have ever since I can remember looked on the actions of others with an eye that was at once full of curiosity and indifference."This silence is the Spectator's primary asset. Because he does not speak, he does not take sides; he is a neutral observer, a camera that records the behavior of the club without participating in its disputes. He is the ultimate figure of the polite public sphere: the man who listens, compares, and writes, providing the medium through which the different factions of the nation can communicate.The club is, in the end, an image of the ideal society The Spectator was trying to build. It is a society that is diverse, commercial, polite, and self-regulating. The tavern table is the new senate; the daily sheet is the new forum. By reading about the club three times a week, the readers of London were trained to think of themselves as members of a larger, more civilized community, where the divisions of the past could be resolved through the shared pleasures of conversation and trade.
essays.ch15: Joseph AddisonOriginal title: The Spectator, No. 159 (September 1, 1711)Date: 1711 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; early eighteenth-century periodical press; OrientalismGenre: Allegorical essay; dream vision; philosophical taleOn the fifth day of the moon, which according to the custom of his forefathers he always kept holy, a man named Mirzah ascended the high hills of Bagdat to spend the day in meditation and prayer. Looking down from the summit, he fell into a profound contemplation of the vanity of human life, comparing the valley below him to a vast scene of misery and change. While he was thus musing, he heard the sweet sound of a flute, played by a shepherd who sat on a nearby rock. The music was unlike any he had ever heard; it was so full of sadness and beauty that it drew him toward the player, who revealed himself to be a genius, a supernatural being, sent to show him a vision of the human condition.This vision of the bridge and the tide is the pressure point of "The Vision of Mirzah" in The Spectator (No. 159, September 1, 1711). Rather than use the familiar conversational tone of Bickerstaff or the club portraits, it adopts an imagined Eastern setting and allegory to address mortality, time, and the afterlife. The setting is a literary construction, not evidence about the cultures it evokes.The Architecture of the BridgeThe center of the vision is a vast valley through which flows a great tide of water, representing the passage of time. Across this tide stands a magnificent bridge, representing the lifespan of human life:"The bridge, thou seest, said he, is Human Life; consider it attentively. Upon a more leisurely survey of it, I found that it consisted of threescore and ten entire arches, with several broken arches, which, added to those that were entire, made up the number about a hundred."The bridge is not a stable structure. It is surrounded by a thick mist at both ends, representing the darkness of our origins before birth and the darkness of our destination after death. Millions of people are walking across the bridge, but their progress is irregular and dangerous. The bridge is full of hidden trapdoors, through which the travelers fall into the tide below:"I saw multitudes of people passing over it, and a black cloud hanging on each end of it. As I looked more attentively, I saw several of the passengers dropping through the bridge into the great tide that flowed underneath it; and upon farther examination, perceived there were innumerable trap-doors that lay concealed in the bridge, which the passengers no sooner trod upon, but they fell through them into the tide, and immediately disappeared."The psychology of this allegory is remarkable. The trapdoors are not placed only at the end of the bridge, near the threescore and ten arches that represent old age. They are scattered thickest at the very entrance, so that a large number of travelers fall through almost as soon as they set foot on the structure, an image of the high infant mortality rates of the early modern world.Furthermore, the travelers are so busy chasing bubbles, fighting with one another, or looking at the scenery that they do not notice the traps at their feet. They are distracted by their passions, their ambitions, and their trivial concerns, moving forward in a state of blind confidence until they step on a hidden door and vanish.The Instruments of DistractionThe genius directs Mirzah's attention to the specific ways in which the passengers waste their time on the bridge. He points out the figures of men running to and fro with swords, others with bags of money, and others with crowns and titles:"I saw several others that was busied in the pursuit of bubbles that glittered in their eyes and danced before them; but often when they thought themselves within the reach of them, their footing failed and they fell through the bridge. There were also several persons that were bent upon catching the shadows of others, and some that were trying to push their companions off the bridge, to make room for themselves."These "bubbles" and "shadows" represent the false values of the world: wealth, reputation, fashion, and power. The pursuit of these distractions makes the travelers more vulnerable to the hazards of the bridge: by looking up at the glittering bubbles or across at their neighbors' shadows, they neglect the ground beneath them.The act of pushing others off the bridge is a image of the political and commercial competition of Addison's London. In the coffee-houses and the exchange, men were constantly plotting to ruin their rivals, to clear a space for their own advancement. Addison's allegory suggests that this competition is not only cruel but irrational: all the competitors, the winners and the losers alike, are moving toward the same mist at the end of the bridge, and the person who pushes his neighbor off today will step on his own trapdoor tomorrow.This critique of ambition is consistent with Addison's moral philosophy. Throughout The Spectator, he warned against the dangers of envy, pride, and the obsession with status. The Vision of Mirzah is a visual demonstration of the vanity of these passions when viewed from the perspective of eternity.The Consolatory IslandsIf the first half of the vision is a dark account of human mortality and distraction, the second half provides a consolation. Mirzah, overwhelmed by the sight of so many people falling into the tide, asks the genius if human life is merely a journey of misery:"Alas, said I, man was made in vain! How is he given away to misery and mortality! tortured in life, and swallowed up in death! The genius being moved with compassion towards me, bid me quit so melancholy a prospect."The genius directs his eyes beyond the mist that hangs over the far end of the tide. The mist clears to reveal a vast ocean, stretching to infinity, and within it a multitude of green islands, floating in the light. These are the "islands of the blessed," the destination of those who fall through the bridge:"I saw the valley opening, and the ocean spreading itself from one end of it to the other, with a vast number of islands that were covered with fruits and flowers, and inhabited by thousands of happy people. I could see them walking in the meadows, resting under the shade of trees, and listening to the music of birds that sang in the branches."The islands are organized in a hierarchy, each designed for a different capacity of soul. The people who inhabit them are free from the care, ambition, and physical suffering of the bridge.
