They are reunited with the friends they lost, living in a state of eternal youth and quiet.This description of the afterlife is notable for its lack of orthodox Christian imagery. There are no angels with harps, no judgment seats, no flames of hell. The consolation is presented in the vocabulary of classical pastoral and Eastern romance: green fields, singing birds, sweet scents, and quiet retirement. By using these images, Addison provides a consolation that is universal, appealing to the imagination of his readers without engaging their theological prejudices.The Style of the Oriental TaleFormally, "The Vision of Mirzah" is built around a sequence of visual transformations: the hills of Bagdat, the valley of misery, the tide of time, the bridge of life, the hidden trapdoors, the misty boundary, and finally the ocean of eternity and the green islands.The language is rhythmic, clear, and elevated, using the parallelisms and repetition of the King James Bible to create a sense of solemnity and wonder. The transitions are slow and deliberate: "I looked," "I saw," "I perceived." This structure mimics the process of revelation, drawing the reader along with Mirzah as he learns to see the hidden structure of the world.This elevated style was a key part of Addison's rhetorical strategy. He believed that the essay should not only instruct the mind but delight the imagination:"The imagination is the most fruitful source of pleasure, and the writer who knows how to address it through beautiful images and noble allegories will always go farther than the one who relies on dry arguments."In "The Vision of Mirzah," Addison demonstrates this principle. The allegory of the bridge and the trapdoors is more memorable and more convincing than a dozen sermons on mortality. It provides a visual image that remains in the mind, helping the reader to find, in the middle of their daily distractions, a quiet perspective on their own mortality.The Return to the HillsThe essay ends with the sudden disappearance of the vision. Mirzah turns to ask the genius a question about the islands of the blessed, but the genius is gone, the tide has vanished, the bridge has disappeared, and he is left alone on the high hills of Bagdat, looking down at the quiet valley and the sheep grazing on the slopes.This return to the physical world is the final qualified conclusion. The vision is over; the mystery of death remains unsolved in any scientific sense. But Mirzah returns to his daily life with a mind that is "refreshed and quieted." He has seen the islands beyond the mist, and that sight is enough to help him bear the journey across the bridge. The essay suggests that while we cannot see the future, we can live with hope, trusting that the tide which swallows us up is not the end of the journey, but the passage to a wider ocean.
essays.ch16: Joseph AddisonOriginal title: The Spectator, Nos. 411–421 (June 21 – July 3, 1712)Date: 1712 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; early eighteenth-century aestheticsGenre: Periodical essay; philosophical essay; aesthetic theory"Our sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our senses. It fills the mind with the largest variety of ideas, converses with its objects at the greatest distance, and continues the longest in action without being tired or satiated with its proper enjoyments." With this claim about the primacy of vision, Joseph Addison begins his famous series of essays "On the Pleasures of the Imagination," published in The Spectator across eleven consecutive issues in the summer of 1712. The opening sentence moves from the physical mechanism of the eye to the internal landscape of the mind. Addison is not interested in the optics of Isaac Newton or the theological arguments about light as a divine substance; he is interested in the psychology of perception.This focus on the mind's internal reaction is the pressure point of the essays. “On the Pleasures of the Imagination” studies how a spectator responds to a landscape, poem, or building rather than simply cataloguing formal rules. By dividing pleasures into “primary” and “secondary” categories, Addison makes perceptual response a central object of analysis. The resemblance to later aesthetic questions is a critical comparison, not a claim of single-handed intellectual origin.Primary and Secondary PleasuresThe core of Addison's theory is the distinction between two kinds of imaginative pleasure.Primary pleasures are those that arise directly from the sight of outward objects:"I divide the pleasures of the imagination into two kinds: those which we receive from such objects as are immediately before our eyes; and those which we receive from the ideas of visible objects, when they are called up into our memories, or formed into agreeable images by painting, statuary, or description. The first I call the primary pleasures of the imagination, which entirely proceed from the sight of outward objects; the second are secondary."Primary pleasures are triggered by three qualities in the natural or artificial world: greatness (the sublime), novelty (the uncommon), and beauty.Greatness refers to the vast, the irregular, and the infinite. Addison describes the effect of looking at a wide, uncultivated desert, a high mountain range, or the open sea. These sights, he argues, stretch the mind beyond its ordinary limits: "The mind of man naturally hates everything that looks like a restraint upon it, and is apt to fancy itself under a sort of confinement, when the sight is pent up in a narrow compass." The pleasure of the great is the pleasure of freedom, the feeling of the mind expanding to fill the space it contemplates.Novelty is the pleasure of surprise and curiosity. The mind is constantly restless for new information, and when it encounters something uncommon or unexpected, it receives a pulse of energy: "It is this that recommends variety, where the mind, when it has run through one set of objects, immediately finds itself in another, and is kept in a constant state of attention."Beauty is the pleasure of proportion, harmony, and color. Addison notes that while we are drawn to the beauty of our own species for biological reasons, we also find a disinterested pleasure in the colors and forms of nature: the green of a meadow, the shape of a flower, the symmetry of an animal. This pleasure is quiet, soothing, and immediate, working on the spirits without the need for rational calculation.Secondary pleasures, by contrast, are those that arise from representation: memory, painting, sculpture, and literature. Here, the pleasure comes not from the object itself, but from the mind's recognition of the likeness between the representation and the original: "It is this that gives us a secret satisfaction when we compare the copy with the original, and see the skill of the artist in bringing them together."The Art of the LandscapeOne of the most influential sections of the essays is Addison's application of these principles to landscape design and architecture. He argues that the traditional formal gardens of Europe, with their clipped hedges, straight alleys, and symmetrical beds, are less pleasing than the irregular designs of nature:"There is something more bold and masterly in the rough careless strokes of nature, than in the nice touches of art. A forest or a meadow is a more delightful object than the finest garden that was ever laid out by rule."This preference for the uncultivated over the formal was a direct challenge to the French style of gardening, represented by Versailles, which sought to impose human geometry upon the earth. Addison suggests that the ideal garden should resemble a natural landscape: it should have winding paths, irregular groups of trees, and views of the surrounding country, so that the spectator feels the freedom of the great and the surprise of the novel.This aesthetic, which would become known as the English landscape garden, was not merely a change in horticulture. It was a political and philosophical statement. The French garden represented the absolute authority of the monarch, who could force the earth to conform to his will. The English garden represented the liberty of the citizen, who lived in harmony with natural laws. The "rough careless strokes of nature" are the visual signs of a free society.The Power of DescriptionIn the second half of the series, Addison turns to the secondary pleasures of the imagination as they are experienced through literature. He argues that the writer has a unique power to excite the imagination because he is not limited by the physical reality of the objects he describes:"The description of a forest, a mountain, or a sea, may be more beautiful and more moving than the objects themselves. For the writer can select the finest details, leave out what is disagreeable, and highlight what is striking."The writer can also represent things that do not exist in the physical world: monsters, spirits, fairies, and gods. Addison calls this "the fairy way of writing," a genre that depends entirely on the strength of the writer's imagination and his capacity to make the impossible look plausible. He cites Shakespeare and Spenser as masters of this style, arguing that their creations are pleasing because they satisfy the mind's natural desire for novelty and the marvelous.This defense of the imaginary was a significant move in a culture that was increasingly suspicious of fiction. The rise of the new science and the empirical philosophy of John Locke had made many writers defensive about the value of poetry, which looked to some like a form of lie. Addison's response is that the imagination has its own truth, which is the truth of human response. If a description of a fairy or a ghost makes the heart beat faster or fills the mind with wonder, it has performed its work, and that work is a valuable contribution to human pleasure.The Social and Moral Value of TasteThroughout the essays, Addison argues that the cultivation of taste, the capacity to receive pleasure from the imagination, has important social and moral benefits.On the individual level, taste is a source of innocent pleasure that is available to anyone, regardless of their wealth or social standing. The man of taste can enjoy a landscape or a work of art without needing to own it: "He can look on the world as a great estate, and find a secret satisfaction in its beauty, while the owner is perhaps worried about the rent."On the social level, taste is a civilizing agent. It refines the manners, tempers the passions, and provides a neutral ground for conversation. The man who is sensitive to the beauty of a garden or the harmony of a poem is less likely to be obsessed with the vulgar competitions of politics and wealth. Taste is a form of moral hygiene, keeping the mind clean and quiet in the middle of the noise of the city.This view of taste was central to The Spectator's larger project. Addison and Steele were trying to create a new class of reader: the polite gentleman who could discuss literature, philosophy, and art with the same ease that he discussed business and politics. "On the Pleasures of the Imagination" provided this reader with a vocabulary and a framework for understanding his own aesthetic responses, transforming what had been a specialized branch of philosophy into a common possession of the educated public.The Limits of the SightThe series concludes with a reflection on the limits of the human mind. Addison notes that while the imagination is a powerful instrument, it is still dependent on the physical sense of sight, which is itself limited. We cannot see the smallest particles of matter or the infinite expanse of the universe; our minds are pent up in a narrow compass of space and time.Yet this limitation is not a cause for despair. It is a reminder of our position in the order of creation. The very fact that we can imagine things we cannot see, that the mind can long for the infinite while looking at the finite, is evidence of our connection to a higher reality. The pleasures of the imagination are, in the end, a preview of a larger freedom. By training the eye to see the beauty of the earth, we prepare the mind for the contemplation of the infinite.
essays.ch17: Jonathan SwiftOriginal title: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country, and for Making Them Beneficial to the PublickDate: 1729 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: Ireland / United KingdomPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; Irish national resistance; Augustan satireGenre: Satirical essay; political pamphlet"A young healthy child well nursed is at a year old a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food, whether stewed, roasted, baked, or boiled; and I make no doubt that it will equally serve in a fricassee or a ragout." With this quiet, monstrous assertion, the narrator of A Modest Proposal introduces his solution to the poverty and overpopulation of eighteenth-century Ireland. The sentence is notable for its culinary precision. It does not speak in the vocabulary of anger or moral indignation; it uses the neutral, descriptive language of the kitchen and the market, listing the different ways a child can be prepared for the table with the same interest that one would apply to a recipe for veal or mutton.This culinary detail is the pressure point of the essay. Jonathan Swift is writing during a period of famine and economic collapse in Ireland, caused largely by British trade restrictions, high rents imposed by absentee landlords, and the indifference of the Dublin parliament. A Modest Proposal is his final, desperate response to this crisis, written after dozens of serious, practical pamphlets on trade and agriculture had been ignored by the authorities. By adopting the persona of a "projector", an early modern political economist or social planner, Swift pushes the logic of British economic policy to its literal, cannibalistic extreme, showing that if you treat human beings as raw material for the market, there is no rational argument against eating their children.The Persona of the ProjectorTo understand how the satire works, one must separate Swift from his narrator. The speaker of A Modest Proposal is not a monster; he is a well-meaning, public-spirited citizen who wants to be useful to his country. He is a man of reason, a student of the new science of "political arithmetic", the early modern ancestor of economics and statistics, who believes that all social problems can be solved through calculation and measurement.The projector's tone is characterized by its absolute calm, its concern for the public good, and its lack of self-interest. He begins by describing the shocking sight of Dublin streets crowded with female beggars and their starving children:"It is a melancholy object to those who walk through this great town, or travel in the country, when they see the streets, the roads, and cabin doors crowded with beggars of the female sex, followed by three, four, or six children, all in rags, and importuning every passenger for an alms."The projector's distress is real, but it is not moral; it is economic. He sees these children as a waste of national resources, a burden on the taxpayer, and a threat to public order. His goal is to find a way to make them "beneficial to the public."When he reveals his proposal, he does so with the pride of a mathematician who has solved a difficult problem. He presents his calculations: there are roughly 120,000 children born to poor parents in Ireland each year; they cannot be employed in agriculture or manufacture, since there is no work to be had; they cannot be exported as slaves; and they cannot survive by stealing until they are at least six years old. The only solution is to turn them into an agricultural product, to be bred, fattened, and sold to the rich at one year old.The humor is black and relentless. The projector suggests that a child of twelve kilograms will make four dishes of excellent meat, and recommends reserving twenty thousand for breeding, of which only a fourth part should be males, "which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine."The Satire of British PolicyUnderneath the projector's calculations is a furious attack on the British administration in Ireland and the Anglo-Irish landlords who executed its policies.The landlords, Swift suggests, have already consumed the parents, so they have a natural right to the children:"I grant this food will be somewhat dear, and therefore very proper for landlords, who, as they have already devoured most of the parents, seem to have the best title to the children."The word "devoured" is not a metaphor. The absentee landlords, who lived in London and spent their Irish rents on English luxuries, had reduced the Irish peasantry to a state of near-starvation. By charging high rents and refusing to invest in the land, they had eaten the substance of the country, leaving the tenants with nothing but their bodies. The proposal to buy the children is simply the logical next step: if you have taken the land and the food, you might as well take the flesh.Swift also attacks the British trade restrictions that prevented Ireland from developing its own manufactures. The Navigation Acts had forbidden the export of Irish wool and glass to foreign markets, and limited trade with the colonies, ensuring that Ireland remained an economic colony of England. The projector refers to this policy when he notes that the children's flesh cannot be exported, because it will not keep: "this food would not bear exportation, the flesh being of too tender a consistence to admit a long continuance in salt." Ireland must consume its own products, even when that product is its own youth.The Hidden ProposalsThe most tragic part of the essay is the list of real, practical proposals that Swift hides within the projector's text. Near the end, the projector lists several alternative solutions that he claims are impractical and should not be discussed:"Therefore let no man talk to me of other expedients: of taxing our absentees at five shillings a pound: of using neither clothes nor household furniture except what is of our own growth and manufacture: of utterly rejecting the materials and instruments that promote foreign luxury: of curing the expensiveness of pride, vanity, idleness, and gaming in our women: of introducing a vein of parsimony, prudence, and temperance: of learning to love our country..."These "other expedients" are the very policies Swift had spent twenty years defending in his serious pamphlets. He had argued for a tax on absentee landlords; for a boycott of English goods in favor of Irish manufacture; for an end to luxury imports; and for a spirit of national pride and industry.By having the projector dismiss these proposals as "vain, idle, visionary thoughts," Swift reveals his own despair. He had tried reason, he had tried economics, he had tried patriotism, and he had failed. The only thing left was to show them that if they refused these moderate policies, they were choosing cannibalism. The list of real proposals, placed in the mouth of a narrator who finds them too difficult, is a monument to Swift's political frustration: he had to pretend to be a monster to get his countrymen to look at their own faces.The Rhetoric of Scientific IndifferenceFormally, A Modest Proposal is a parody of the scientific pamphlet of the early modern period. Swift parodies the style of the Royal Society, with its insistence on objective observation, measurement, and the suppression of emotion.The projector uses a variety of rhetorical devices to maintain this illusion of objectivity. He uses passive verbs to hide his own agency; he cites authorities (including a "very knowing American" who assured him of the quality of human flesh); he anticipates objections and answers them with calculations; and he concludes with a declaration of his own disinterestedness:"I profess in the sincerity of my heart, that I have not the least personal interest in endeavoring to promote this necessary work, having no other motive than the public good of my country, by advancing our trade, providing for infants, relieving the poor, and giving some pleasure to the rich. I have no children by which I can propose to get a single penny; the youngest being nine years old, and my wife past child-bearing."This final sentence is the masterstroke of the persona. It proves the projector's credentials as a scientist: he cannot benefit from his own scheme, so his testimony must be pure.The power of the satire comes from this tension between the monstrous content of the proposal and the polite, reasonable style in which it is delivered. If the narrator were angry or cruel, the reader could reject him. Because he is polite, rational, and concerned for the public good, the reader is forced to follow him to the end, realizing that the real monsters are not the cannibal projectors, but the statesmen, landlords, and citizens who allow the starvation of a nation to be treated as an administrative detail.The Monument of AngerThe essay ends with the projector holding his ground. He has presented his calculations, answered the objections, and declared his lack of interest. The proposal stands, unresolved, a challenge to anyone who thinks they can solve the problem of poverty without addressing the question of justice.A Modest Proposal remains the classic example of literary irony because it refuses to blink. Swift does not step out of character at the end to explain his meaning or to reassure the reader that he is only joking. The joke is too serious for that. By leaving the proposal on the table, Swift forces the reader to make a choice: either accept the cannibalism, or change the policies that make it look like a rational option. The essay is a monument to a particular kind of anger: the cold, clear-eyed kind that does not tear down the house, but simply opens the windows so that those inside can hear the screaming on the street.
essays.ch18: Samuel JohnsonOriginal title: The Rambler, No. 117 (April 30, 1751)Date: 1751 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; mid-eighteenth-century periodical literatureGenre: Periodical essay; character sketch; satire on the literary life"It has been the custom of all ages to identify the highest degrees of wisdom and virtue with the highest parts of the earth, and to believe that the mind of man, as it rises above the smoke and noise of the valley, becomes more clear, active, and noble." With this pseudo-philosophical assertion, the narrator of "The Garret" begins his letter to the editor of The Rambler in the spring of 1751. Writing under the Greek pseudonym Hypertatus, "he who lives above", the speaker is a gentleman who has spent several years living in the top room of a London lodging house, and who writes to defend the garret not as a symbol of poverty, but as the ideal home for a philosopher, writer, or astronomer.This opening assertion is the pressure point of the essay. In the mid-eighteenth century, the "garret" was the standard trope for the poverty, desperation, and failure of Grub Street writers, the men and women who churned out pamphlets, translations, and reviews for booksellers while living in the cheapest, coldest, and dampest rooms of the city. By having his narrator defend this space as a site of intellectual privilege, Samuel Johnson does not simply write a light satire on the literary life; he investigates the relationship between material conditions and mental work, mocking the classical idea that the mind can achieve independence from the body and the environment by a simple act of elevation.The Geography of Grub StreetThe paper does not present itself as a documentary account of Johnson's career or of London lodging. Its speaker adopts the borrowed name Hypertatus and turns the garret into a subject for mock scholarship. The joke depends on the distance between the grand explanations he offers and the ordinary room those explanations are meant to dignify.That distance matters because the paper repeatedly makes a literary convention literal. Classical mountains, elevated dwellings, rarefied air, and the language of intellectual ascent are gathered into a single comic theory. The garret is therefore less a biographical fact than a device for testing how easily prestige can be manufactured by rhetoric.Hypertatus, however, has transformed this setting into a philosophical temple. He lists the historical precedents for his elevation, citing the philosophers, astronomers, and poets who sought out high places for their work:"I have found by experience that the mind of man is modified by the place of his dwelling, and that elevation of site has a natural tendency to produce elevation of thought. The philosophers of antiquity did not study in cellars or valleys, but sought out the highest hills, that they might be closer to the stars and free from the distraction of the crowd."The humor is in the literalness of the connection. Hypertatus argues that the thin air of the garret is superior for the production of light, airy thoughts, whereas the heavy air of cellars produces only dull, material ideas: "It is certain that the density of the air in low places has a depressing effect on the animal spirits; the writer who sits in a basement will always write in a heavy, pedantic style."The Satire of Philosophical ElevationThe critique of this "elevation of thought" is directed first at the theory itself. Hypertatus treats figurative associations between height and intelligence as if they were physical laws, and the paper lets the reader watch that mistake become more elaborate with every paragraph.Johnson was deeply skeptical of any philosophy that claimed to make the mind independent of the body. Throughout his essays, he insisted on the physical limits of human life: we are subject to hunger, cold, disease, and the passage of time, and our moral decisions are always constrained by these realities. The sage who pretends to be indifferent to his environment is a fraud or a fool.Hypertatus's description of his life in the garret reveals these limits, even as he tries to hide them under philosophical terms:"In this room, which is the highest in the house, I sit above the noise and distraction of the street. The cries of the fishmongers, the rattling of the coaches, and the disputes of the coal-carters do not reach me here. I am like the god of Epicurus, who looks down on the world without being disturbed by its changes."The paper's material counterweight is not a narrated hardship but the body and the atmosphere. Hypertatus claims that air, motion, altitude, and even the earth's rotation alter intellectual powers. His proposed barometrical science turns the language of mental elevation into an absurdly measurable system, exposing the desire to give vanity the authority of experiment.The paper's final joke extends the same logic to literary judgement. Hypertatus claims that the height of an author's dwelling can be inferred from the quality of the writing, then signs the letter before the theory can become a genuine system. The philosopher who has raised himself above ordinary measures ends by making his own pretension the measure of the joke.The Class Structure of the Lodging HouseThe lodging house in "The Garret" supplies a vertical diagram for the argument, but the paper does not require that diagram to stand as a social survey. Hypertatus turns floors and stories into intellectual categories:"The house in which I live is divided into different zones, according to the wealth and status of the tenants. The ground floor is occupied by a merchant, who is always busy and noisy; the first floor by a gentleman of fashion, who sleeps all day and stays out all night; the second floor by a family of quiet, industrious tradespeople; and the garret by myself."Hypertatus's attempt to invert this hierarchy is a comic defence of elevation. He makes the upper room the seat of intellectual honour and turns ordinary spatial difference into a theory of mental capacity. The manoeuvre is persuasive only while the reader accepts the terms he has invented.The irony lies in the speaker's confidence, not in a separately narrated story of poverty. His claim that a change of elevation can produce wit is continually enlarged until the explanation defeats itself. The garret remains a room; the theory makes it a cosmology.The Prose of Weight and BalanceFormally, "The Garret" is a model of Johnson's prose style, which is often called "Johnsonian" because of its distinctive weight, balance, and Latinate vocabulary. Unlike the conversational style of Steele or the light grace of Addison, Johnson's sentences are built around parallel structures, balanced clauses, and abstract nouns.This style is often criticized as heavy or pedantic, but in "The Garret," it performs a specific comic function. The weight of the language contrasts with the triviality and delusion of the narrator's claims: the balanced, Latinate clauses are used to defend the thin air of the roof and the history of high-dwelling writers. The style gives the narrator's illusions a fake gravity, making his eventual collapse into the physical reality of his room more comic.Yet the weight of the prose also carries a real moral gravity. Even in his lightest satires, Johnson is always looking for the universal truth of the human condition. The narrator's delusion is not unique to writers; it is a version of the vanity that runs through all human life, the desire to escape the limits of our nature by some artificial elevation of our role or our circumstances.The Descent to the StreetThe essay ends with Hypertatus's signature, not with a narrated descent or conversion. The letter stops at the point where its mock science has reached its most extravagant form. That open stop preserves the joke's central pressure: the theory never has to meet a final refutation because its excess has already exposed it.Johnson's Rambler paper leaves the reader with a double impression. We laugh at Hypertatus's theories of thin air, planetary motion, and literary altitude, but we also recognise the serious human wish beneath them: to make circumstances answer to an account of one's own importance. The paper's form keeps that wish comic without reducing it to a single biographical case.
essays.ch19: Samuel JohnsonOriginal title: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia, Chapter VIDate: 1759 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: EnglandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; mid-eighteenth-century philosophical taleGenre: Philosophical essay; allegorical tale; early science fictionAmong the artists drawn to the Happy Valley is a man eminent in the mechanical arts, whose engines serve both use and recreation. Rasselas visits him because he is interested in knowledge and hopes that what he learns may help him in the open world. The artist's project of flight becomes a test of that hope: it turns an abstract desire for escape into a practical experiment with bodies, air, and gravity.This encounter is the pressure point of the episode known here as "On the Art of Flying," originally Chapter VI of Samuel Johnson's philosophical fable Rasselas (1759), and frequently anthologised as a standalone selection. The chapter moves from mechanical speculation to a conversation between the artist and Rasselas about the feasibility and consequences of flight. By focusing on the artist's confidence and eventual failure, Johnson investigates the limits of human ambition while also imagining how a new power might alter the security of cities and states.The Irony of the LeapThe climax of the essay is the inventor's attempt to fly, which is recorded with dry, physical realism:"The artist was, for a year, busy in his work; and, at the end of the year, came to Rasselas with wings on his shoulders. He went to the top of a promontory, and leaped into the air. He did not rise, but fell immediately into the lake below; where his wings, which were made of wood and feathers, kept him from sinking until the Prince's servants came and pulled him out."The transition from the grand ambition of the year-long preparation to the immediate fall into the lake is a study in understatement. The artist does not soar like Icarus or die like a tragic hero. He falls, and the wings that fail in the air sustain him in the water until Rasselas draws him to land.This comic resolution belongs to Johnson's larger inquiry into human projects. Throughout Rasselas, characters seek happiness, wisdom, and power through competing schemes. The fall into the lake gives that inquiry a physical form: desire and ingenuity do not guarantee mastery over the conditions in which action takes place. The return to the ground is comic, but it also exposes the limits of confidence detached from experience.The Warning of the Sky-WarWhat raises "On the Art of Flying" above simple comedy is the inventor's conversation with Rasselas before the attempt. Rasselas is enthusiastic about the project, imagining the pleasure of looking down on the world from above and traveling without the obstacles of mountains, rivers, and borders. The inventor, however, is anxious about the potential misuse of his invention:"If men were to fly, they would soon use their wings for war. A city could not be defended against an army that could descend from the clouds; the palace of the king, the cottage of the peasant, the storehouses of the merchant would all be open to destruction from above. I will not reveal the secret of my invention to the world, lest I should be the author of its ruin."This warning is a thought experiment within a 1759 philosophical tale. Later readers can recognise in it a speculation about how flight might change the security of cities and states, but the chapter need not be treated as a literal prediction of modern warfare. Its immediate subject is the moral risk of giving ambitious people a new power before deciding how that power should be governed.The warning is grounded in the tale's suspicion that ingenuity does not automatically produce virtue. The artist can imagine a technical solution without resolving the political and moral consequences of distributing it. Johnson therefore keeps invention and judgement in tension rather than presenting progress as a simple route to improvement.The Happy Valley and the Prison of EaseThe setting of the essay is also crucial to its meaning. The Happy Valley is a paradise of ease and luxury, surrounded by high mountains that prevent the inhabitants from leaving. The Prince Rasselas is bored by this perfection; he wants to see the world, to experience the variety of human life, and to find his own "choice of life."The inventor's attempt to fly responds to this confinement. The sky appears to offer a route beyond the mountains, and flight becomes a way of imagining escape from a paradise that has become a prison. The project is therefore connected to Rasselas's desire to enter the wider world, even though the artist's motives are also shaped by curiosity and confidence in his own powers.This context complicates the inventor's failure. His fall is not only a personal embarrassment; it is a setback for the hope that technology can dissolve every boundary. The valley remains a place from which Rasselas still wants to escape. The episode suggests that freedom cannot be secured by physical movement alone, because the restless mind carries its dissatisfaction with it.The Style of the Moral FableFormally, "On the Art of Flying" is a philosophical-tale episode, using a simple, stylised narrative to investigate a moral question. The language is balanced and economical, with little of the local detail that would belong to a realistic travel narrative. Rasselas is named, but the artist remains an unnamed figure, and the Happy Valley functions as a generalised symbolic landscape.This abstraction is deliberate. Johnson is not trying to write a technical description of a flying machine or a realistic account of Abissinia. He creates a fable of human ambition in which the wings stand for an attempt to rise above ordinary limits. The mechanical details matter because they keep that allegory attached to the resistance of material conditions.The symmetry of the dialogue is also a key feature of the style. The conversation between Rasselas and the inventor is organized as a series of balances: the prince's hope vs. the inventor's fear; the utility of travel vs. the danger of war; the beauty of the design vs. the weakness of the arm. This structure allows Johnson to present both sides of the question of progress without resolving them too quickly, showing that the desire for advancement and the fear of its consequences are both permanent parts of our intellectual condition.The Return to the GroundThe episode ends with the artist being drawn from the lake, half dead with terror and vexation. His wings have no use in the air but sustain him in the water. Johnson stops at that physical reversal rather than narrating a return to the workshop or a new programme of practical machines.The reversal supplies the episode's qualified conclusion. The artist who imagined himself rising above the world is returned to the material conditions he had hoped to overcome. This is comic rather than tragic, but the comedy does not erase the seriousness of the experiment. It makes ambition answerable to the body and to the limits of the medium through which it acts.The essay suggests that the true work of the intellect is not the pursuit of the impossible, but the management of the possible. We must accept the ground, accept the gravity that pulls us down, and find our happiness in the daily, useful work of the valley rather than in the dangerous, wet leaps from the cliff. The art of flying is a dream; the art of living in a world of gravity is the real task.
essays.ch20: Jean-Jacques RousseauOriginal title: Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes (Second Discourse)Date: 1755 CEOriginal language: FrenchCountry/tradition: France / SwitzerlandPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; political philosophy; pre-RomanticismGenre: Philosophical essay; political treatise"The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the real founder of civil society." With this declaration, Jean-Jacques Rousseau begins the second part of his Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Men (1755). The sentence has the force of a historical myth. It does not describe a legal contract or a gradual economic development; it describes a sudden, arbitrary act of usurpation that was accepted through the simplicity of others.This act of enclosure is the pressure point of the essay. Rousseau is writing in response to a essay competition set by the Academy of Dijon, which asked: "What is the origin of inequality among men, and is it authorized by natural law?" Rousseau's response was a radical challenge to the political theory of his day. Unlike Thomas Hobbes, who argued that the state of nature was a war of all against all and that the state was necessary to preserve life, and John Locke, who argued that private property was a natural right based on labor, Rousseau argues that private property is the source of all our crimes, wars, and miseries, and that civil society is a trick played by the rich on the poor to secure their stolen wealth.The Physicality of Natural ManTo understand how inequality arose, Rousseau begins by stripping away all the additions of civilization to reconstruct the "natural man." He describes a figure that is physically robust, solitary, and free from the anxieties of the modern mind:"I see him satisfying his hunger under an oak, quenching his thirst at the first brook, finding his bed at the foot of the same tree on which he has dined, and with that, all his wants are supplied."Natural man has no language, no home, no family, and no concept of the future. He lives entirely in the present, his mind governed by two natural instincts: the desire for self-preservation (amour de soi) and a natural repugnance at the sight of another sentient being's suffering (pitié or pity).This natural pity is the moral anchor of the essay. Rousseau argues that pity is not a social virtue learned from religion or philosophy, but a biological capacity that precedes all reason. It is what keeps the strong from exploiting the weak in the state of nature: "Pity is what, in the state of nature, takes the place of laws, morals, and virtue, with the advantage that no one is tempted to disobey its sweet voice."Civilization, in Rousseau's account, works by suppressing this natural pity. By training us to think in terms of calculation, competition, and property, civil society isolates us from one another. The philosopher, looking out his window at a riot on the street, can close his eyes and argue himself into indifference: "He has only to say to himself, 'Perish if you will; I am secure.'"The Leap into Property and Division of LaborThe transition from this natural state to civil society is not a linear progress, but a series of accidents and technological changes. The key developments are the invention of metallurgy and agriculture:"To the poet, it is gold and silver, but to the philosopher, it is iron and corn, which have civilized mankind and ruined the human race."The division of labor created by iron and corn led inevitably to the concept of property. The blacksmith needed the farmer's grain, and the farmer needed the blacksmith's tools; they began to exchange their products, and in doing so, they had to calculate the value of their labor and their land. This calculation led to the first claims of ownership: once a man had cultivated a piece of land, he felt he had a right to its harvest, and that right was soon extended to the land itself.Property created a new kind of inequality: not the physical inequality of strength or age, which Rousseau calls "natural or physical inequality," but the social inequality of wealth, power, and prestige, which he calls "moral or political inequality."This social inequality produced a state of war, but unlike Hobbes, Rousseau places this war at the end of the historical development, not at the beginning. It was not the natural man who fought for survival; it was the civilized man, corrupted by property and vanity (amour-propre), who fought for dominance. The rich, having accumulated land and goods, found themselves in a position of constant danger: they had no legal title to their wealth, which had been taken by force, and they were surrounded by a majority of poor people who had nothing to lose by taking it back.The Usurpation of the Social ContractThe solution to this crisis was the invention of the social contract, which Rousseau describes as the most clever trick in human history:"The rich man, pressed by necessity, conceived at last the most exquisite project that ever entered the human mind: to employ in his favor the very forces of those who attacked him, to make allies of his adversaries, and to give them institutions that would protect his property."The rich man addressed the poor, proposing that they should join together to establish a power that would protect everyone from violence, maintain justice, and secure each person in his possessions. The poor, simple and tired of conflict, accepted the proposal: "They ran headlong into their chains, believing they were securing their liberty."This contract was a fraud. It took a state of violent usurpation and turned it into a legal right. It secured the wealth of the rich and the poverty of the poor, establishing the state as an instrument for the protection of property rather than the preservation of liberty. The laws of civil society, Rousseau suggests, are merely the chains that keep the poor in place while the rich enjoy the harvest.The Psychology of the Modern SlaveThe final section of the Discourse is a psychological study of the civilized man, whom Rousseau compares to a slave who has learned to love his chains.He contrasts the natural man, who lives within himself, with the citizen, who lives entirely in the opinions of others:"The savage lives within himself; the sociable man, always outside himself, knows how to live only in the opinion of others, and it is, so to speak, from their judgment alone that he draws the experience of his own existence."This "sociable man" is a figure of constant anxiety. He must perform a role, maintain a reputation, accumulate luxuries he does not need, and flatter those he despises, simply to feel that he exists. He has traded his physical health and his freedom for the "chimera" of social status.This psychological analysis was highly influential. It prefigured the Marxist concept of alienation, the sociological study of consumer culture, and the Romantic rebellion against the conventions of the court and the salon. Rousseau's critique of civilization is not merely an economic or political argument; it is a diagnosis of a mental illness that has infected the modern world, making us strangers to our own feelings.The Rhetorical Strategy of the TreatiseFormally, the Discourse on Inequality is structured as a speculative history. Rousseau admits that we cannot know the state of nature in any scientific sense; it is a state that "no longer exists, which perhaps never existed, and probably never will exist, but of which it is nevertheless necessary to have correct notions."He uses a variety of rhetorical strategies to make this speculative history persuasive. He uses dramatic set-pieces (the act of enclosure, the speech of the rich man); he draws analogies from the natural world and the travel literature of his day; and he writes in a style that is urgent, passionate, and directly addresses the reader's moral conscience.This emotional intensity is what distinguishes Rousseau from his Enlightenment contemporaries. Where Voltaire and Montesquieu wrote with the cool irony of the salon, Rousseau wrote with the fury of the outsider. He does not seek to reform the institutions of his day; he seeks to expose their fundamental illegitimacy. The Discourse is not an administrative proposal; it is a declaration of war against the social order.The Open WoundThe essay ends with a vision of the contemporary world, in which the inequality of wealth and power has reached its extreme: a world where a child commands an old man, a fool leads wise men, and a handful of rich people are bloated with superfluities while the starving multitude lacks the necessities of life.Rousseau concludes that this state of affairs is not only a moral failure, but a violation of natural law:"It is manifestly contrary to the law of nature, however defined, that a child should command an old man, that an imbecile should lead a wise man, and that a handful of people should gorge themselves with superfluities, while the starving multitude lacks common necessities."This final sentence leaves the wound open. Rousseau does not offer a solution in the Discourse; he does not tell us how to return to the state of nature (which he admits is impossible) or how to build a just state (which he would attempt later in The Social Contract). He simply presents the diagnosis, leaving the reader with the realization that the civilization they inhabit is built on a fraud. The first man who enclosed a piece of land is still there, and the chains he forged are still around our necks.
essays.ch21: Benjamin FranklinOriginal title: Father Abraham's Speech, published as the preface to Poor Richard's Almanack (1758)Date: 1758 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: United States (Colonial America)Period/movement: The Enlightenment; American pragmatism; early capitalismGenre: Periodical essay; advice literature; compilation of maxims"I stopped my horse lately where a great number of people were collected at a vendue of merchant goods. The hour of sale not being come, they were conversing on the badness of the times, and one of the company called to a plain clean old man, with white locks, 'Father Abraham, what think you of the times? Won't these heavy taxes quite ruin the country? How shall we ever be able to pay them? What would you advise us to?'" With this framing scene, Benjamin Franklin begins "The Way to Wealth," the preface to the twenty-fifth and final edition of his Poor Richard's Almanack in 1758. The setting is a "vendue", a public auction, where a crowd of colonials has gathered to buy imported luxuries, while complaining about the taxes imposed by the British crown and the general difficulty of making a living.This framing scene is the pressure point of the essay. Franklin is writing at the transition from colonial dependency to independent commercial power. "The Way to Wealth" does not address the question of taxes or political representation through constitutional theory or legal arguments. It addresses it through the character of Father Abraham, who responds to the crowd by quoting the proverbs about industry, frugality, and self-reliance that had appeared in the Almanack over the past quarter-century. By compiling these maxims into a single speech, Franklin does not simply write a manual for financial success; he defines the moral and psychological basis of the American middle-class character, showing that true independence is not won on the battlefield or in the assembly, but in the ledger and the workshop.The Irony of the AuctionTo read the essay well, you must watch the ending. After Father Abraham finishes his long sermon on thrift and industry, the auction begins:"The old gentleman ended his harangue, and the people heard it, and approved the doctrine, and immediately practiced the contrary, just as if it had been a common sermon; for the vendue began, and they began to buy extravagantly, notwithstanding all his cautions."This double irony is the key to Franklin's humor. The crowd listens to the sermon, agrees with every word, praises the speaker's wisdom, and then immediately turns to buy the very luxury goods he had warned them against. They behave toward the economic sermon exactly as they behave toward Sunday sermons: they accept the theory and reject the practice.Franklin's narrator, Poor Richard (Saunders), is the only one who actually changes his behavior: "I resolved to be the better for the echo of it; and though I had at first determined to buy stuff for a new coat, I went away resolved to wear my old one a little longer."This resolution is a small, quiet act of independence. By refusing to buy the new coat, Richard escapes the debt, dependency, and vanity that the auction represents. The new coat is not just a piece of cloth; it is a "bondage" to the merchant and the tax-collector. The old coat is a symbol of self-determination.The Theology of the LedgerThe proverbs compiled in Father Abraham's speech are famous for their compression, rhythm, and home-spun wisdom:"God helps them that help themselves. Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labor wears; while the used key is always bright. But dost thou love life, then do not squander time, for that's the stuff life is made of."This view of time and labor was a secularization of the Puritan ethic that had shaped New England. For the seventeenth-century Puritans, industry and thrift were signs of religious election, duties performed for the glory of God. For Franklin, they are practical tools for the achievement of personal independence and civic virtue.Franklin has no patience for the romantic view of poverty or the aristocratic contempt for work. He treats labor as a source of dignity and power: "He that hath a trade hath an estate, and he that hath a calling hath an office of profit and honor."Frugality is the necessary companion to this industry. Franklin warns that a man who works hard but spends extravagantly is like a vessel with a leak: "A small leak will sink a great ship." He is particularly sharp on the purchase of imported luxuries, which he sees as a form of self-taxation that is far more expensive than any tax imposed by the government: "You call them goods, but if you do not take care, they will prove evils to some of you."Debt is the ultimate consequence of this extravagance. Franklin describes the debtor as a slave who has surrendered his liberty to his creditor: "When you run in debt, you give to another power over your liberty. If you cannot pay at the time, you will be ashamed to see your creditor; you will be in fear when you speak to him; you will make poor pitiful sneaking excuses."This psychological description of the debtor's shame is one of the most realistic passages in the essay. The loss of financial independence leads to a loss of moral character; the debtor is forced to lie, to flatter, and to hide, becoming a "sneaking" figure who has lost the right to speak truth in the public sphere.The Rise of the Bourgeois Character"The Way to Wealth" was one of the most widely reprinted texts in the Atlantic world. It was translated into dozens of languages, published as a broadsheet to be hung on the walls of workshops, and distributed as a pamphlet for the education of the working class. It was the founding document of what the German sociologist Max Weber called the "Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism."Weber argued that Franklin's maxims represent the capitalist spirit in its purest form: the conviction that the accumulation of wealth is a moral duty, and that time, credit, and labor are commodities to be managed with rational calculation.Yet Franklin's pragmatism is not simply about greed. He does not recommend wealth for its own sake, or for the luxury it can buy, luxury is, after all, the very thing he warns against. He recommends wealth because it is the only secure foundation for personal and political liberty. In a world where the poor are dependent on the rich, and the colonies are dependent on the mother country, the only way to be free is to be self-sufficient. Frugality is a political strategy: the man who does not need the merchant's goods cannot be controlled by the merchant's king.This connection between private character and public politics was central to the American Revolution. The boycotts of British goods (the Non-Importation Agreements) that preceded the war were based on the principles of "The Way to Wealth": the colonists had to learn to wear homespun, drink domestic tea, and manage their own resources, before they could challenge the British army.The Prose of the MarketFormally, the essay is structured as a double frame. We have the narrator, Poor Richard, who introduces the speech; we have Father Abraham, who delivers the speech; and we have the proverbs themselves, which are quoted from the past editions of the Almanack. This structure allows Franklin to create a distance between himself and the moralizing voice of the sermon.Poor Richard is a comic persona: he is poor, he is vanity-driven, and he is delighted to hear his own proverbs quoted by the wise old man: "The frequent mention of me by name by the old gentleman, did not a little please my vanity, though I was conscious that not a tenth part of the wisdom was my own."This irony prevents the essay from becoming a dry, self-righteous lecture. Franklin is mocking his own ambition as a moral teacher, showing that the proverbs are common property, and that the teacher is subject to the same vanity and weakness as the crowd.The style of the proverbs is characterized by its use of concrete, physical metaphors: keys, rust, ships, leaks, purses, coats. This is the language of the market and the workshop, designed to make the abstract virtues of industry and frugality look like material objects that can be handled and measured.The Open LedgerThe essay ends, as we saw, with the crowd buying extravagantly at the auction and Poor Richard walking away with his old coat. The sermon is over, the ledger remains open, and the conflict between our reason and our desires is unresolved."The Way to Wealth" remains a classic because it refuses to pretend that moral advice is easy to follow. Franklin knows that the crowd will always go to the auction, that vanity will always want the new coat, and that debt will always be a trap. The value of the essay is in its clear presentation of the choice: we can either practice the frugality that leads to independence, or run headlong into the dependency of the vendue. The plain old man with the white locks has spoken, the auctioneer has raised his hammer, and the crowd is already bidding.
essays.ch22: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)Original title: Traité sur la tolérance, specifically Chapter XXIII, "Prière à Dieu" (Prayer to God)Date: 1763 CEOriginal language: FrenchCountry/tradition: FrancePeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; anti-clerical campaignsGenre: Philosophical essay; political tract; philosophical prayer"No longer then to men, but to thee, God of all beings, of all worlds, and of all ages, do I address myself: if it is permitted to feeble creatures, lost in the immensity of the universe, to dare to ask anything of thee..." With this invocation, Voltaire begins the twenty-third chapter of his Treatise on Tolerance (1763). This chapter, known as the "Prayer to God" (Prière à Dieu), is the emotional and rhetorical peak of the treatise, and has frequently been anthologized as a standalone essay "On Tolerance." The address is not a conventional prayer; it is a rhetorical performance that bypasses the ecclesiastical hierarchies and theological vocabularies of his day to appeal to a distant, benevolent creator on behalf of a suffering humanity.This prayer is the pressure point of the essay. Voltaire is writing in the immediate aftermath of the judicial murder of Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant in Toulouse who had been falsely accused of murdering his son to prevent him from converting to Catholicism. Calas was tortured, broken on the wheel, and strangled by the authorities, in a trial that was driven by religious fanaticism and anti-protestant prejudice. Voltaire spent three years campaigning to clear Calas's name, writing letters, pamphlets, and this treatise to expose the cruelty of the Toulouse judges. By placing a prayer at the heart of his political campaign, Voltaire does not seek to defend the Protestant faith or to promote a new theology; he uses the language of religion to show that religious intolerance is not only a moral crime, but a ridiculous vanity when viewed from the scale of the universe.The Scale of the Universe and the Vanity of DogmaThe primary strategy of the "Prayer to God" is the reduction of human differences through the use of cosmic scale. Voltaire places the human spectator in the context of the new Copernican astronomy, looking at a vast, infinite universe in which the earth is merely a point:"Look down with pity on the errors which belong to our nature. Let not these errors prove our ruin. Thou hast not given us hearts to hate one another, nor hands to strangle one another; make us help one another to bear the burden of a painful and transitory life."Against this immensity, the theological disputes that divide Christians, the differences in liturgy, the weight of vestments, the translation of scripture, look like the arguments of insects. Voltaire is particularly sharp on the pride of those who believe they have exclusive access to the divine will:"May the trifling differences between the clothes that cover our frail bodies, between our inadequate languages, our ridiculous customs, our imperfect laws, our foolish opinions, between all our conditions so disproportionate in our eyes and so equal in thine, may all these little variations which distinguish the atoms called 'men' not be the signals for hatred and persecution."This description of human beings as "atoms" is a key Enlightenment move. By reducing humanity to physical particles, Voltaire strips away the claims of status, rank, and theological authority. The king's robes and the peasant's rags, the Catholic's Latin and the Protestant's vernacular, are merely "trifling differences" in the eyes of the creator. To kill a man because of these variations is as absurd as one grain of sand persecuting another because of its shade of color.This deistic view of God is central to Voltaire's campaign. The God of the "Prayer" is not the active, jealous deity of the Old Testament or the dogmatic judge of the Counter-Reformation. He is the architect of a rational universe, who has given men reason to govern their conduct and pity to temper their passions. The responsibility for justice and tolerance lies with us, not with a divine intervention: "Thou hast not given us hearts to hate one another, nor hands to strangle one another."The Calas Affair and the Historical ContextTo understand the fury behind the prayer, one must look at the details of the Calas trial, which Voltaire analyzes in the earlier chapters of the Treatise. The prosecution had relied on the testimony of superstitious neighbors, the rumors of the mob, and a medieval legal system that allowed torture to be used to extract confessions. Calas's execution was not an isolated event; it belonged to a history of religious violence in France that included the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) and the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), which had forced hundreds of thousands of French Protestants into exile.Voltaire's treatise is a systematic demolition of the arguments used to justify this persecution. He shows that the classical world, the Greeks and the Romans, was generally tolerant of religious differences, provided they did not threaten the stability of the state. He argues that the early Christians were persecuted not because of their beliefs, but because they refused to participate in the civic rituals of the empire. The introduction of systematic intolerance was, in his view, the work of the medieval church, which used the threat of heresy to maintain its wealth and political power.The "Prayer to God" is the rhetorical resolution of this historical analysis. By turning from the details of legal corruption to a direct address to the creator, Voltaire forces his readers to look at the Calas trial from the perspective of eternity. The judges of Toulouse are no longer merely corrupt administrators; they are violators of the natural law of the universe.The Irony of the DeistFormally, the "Prayer" is a model of Voltaire's ironic style, which is often called persiflage, a mixture of politeness, wit, and moral outrage. He adopts the form of the liturgy, using the pronouns of address (Tu or Thou) and the parallel structures of the psalms, but fills them with deistic and anti-clerical content.The prayer is structured as a series of petitions: "May all men remember...", "May they look with horror...", "May the trifling differences...". The language is elevated, but the metaphors are drawn from the material world: atoms, clothes, coins, burdens. This mixture of the high-religious and the low-material is designed to expose the absurdity of religious pride:"May those who light candles at noon to worship thee bear with those who are content with the light of thy sun; may those who cover their robes with black wool to say that we must love thee not despise those who say the same thing in white linen."The contrast between the "candles at noon" and the "light of thy sun" is a classic Voltairean image. The candle is the symbol of human artifice, theological dogma, and institutional religion; the sun is the symbol of natural reason, the deistic creator, and the common ground of humanity. To persecute someone because they prefer the sun to the candle is the ultimate form of intellectual blindness.This irony is not merely a literary device; it is a political weapon. By making the persecutors look ridiculous, Voltaire strips them of their authority. The judge who breaks a man on the wheel because of his faith is no longer a figure of terror; he is an object of laughter, a foolish atom who has mistaken his own candle for the sun.The Legacy of the TreatiseVoltaire's campaign for Jean Calas was successful. In 1765, two years after the publication of the Treatise, the King's Council in Paris unanimously declared Calas innocent, cleared his family's name, and ordered the judges of Toulouse to pay damages. The trial became the first major victory for the new public opinion of the Enlightenment, demonstrating that the authority of the state and the church could be challenged by a writer with a printing press.The Treatise on Tolerance became the foundational text of the modern secular movement, establishing the principle that the state has no right to police the conscience of its citizens. The "Prayer to God" remains the most famous section because it summarizes this principle in a form that is emotionally compelling: it translates the dry arguments of political philosophy into the language of the heart.The Silent HeavensThe essay ends with the prayer remaining in the air. The God of Voltaire does not speak; the heavens remain silent, and the "atoms" are left on their grain of sand to work out their own survival.This silence is the final qualified conclusion. The prayer is not a petition for a miracle; it is a challenge to those who read it. If God will not intervene to stop the executioner, we must do so ourselves. The "light of the sun" is already there; the responsibility to see it belongs to us. The deist's prayer is, in the end, an invitation to action: it clears away the candles of dogma so that we can see one another's faces in the common light of day.
essays.ch23: Oliver GoldsmithOriginal title: "On National Prejudices", published in The British Magazine (August 1760); later anthologized in Essays (1765)Date: 1760 / 1765 CEOriginal language: EnglishCountry/tradition: Ireland / United KingdomPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; mid-eighteenth-century periodical essayGenre: Periodical essay; social satire; moral reflection"As I am one of that sauntering tribe of mortals, who spend the greatest part of their time in taverns, coffee-houses, and other places of public resort, I have thereby an opportunity of observing an infinite variety of characters..." With this conversational opening, Oliver Goldsmith introduces his essay "On National Prejudices," published in The British Magazine in 1760. The setting is a London tavern, where the narrator, a self-described member of the "sauntering tribe," finds himself in the company of half a dozen gentlemen who are discussing the political situation of Europe. The conversation soon turns to national character, and one of the company, with a look of great solemnity, declares that the English are the only brave, generous, and free people on the earth, while the French are a nation of cowards, the Dutch are avaricious pack-horses, and the Germans are blockheads.This tavern scene is the pressure point of the essay. Goldsmith is writing in 1760, during the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), but the surviving essay does not establish a direct connection to a particular campaign or press controversy. Its immediate subject is the psychology of national self-flattery. By examining the ease with which a speaker turns inherited national reputation into personal merit, Goldsmith argues that narrow patriotism can become a form of collective vanity, and proposes instead the ideal of the "citizen of the world" who treats other nations with greater fairness and curiosity.The Tavern Patriots and the Taxonomy of PrejudiceThe core of the essay is the narrator's objection to the tavern patriot's declarations. When asked for his opinion, the narrator suggests that the other European nations also have their virtues: that the French are polite and lively, the Dutch are industrious and clean, and the Germans are patient and brave. This moderate response is met with silent disapproval by the company:"This declaration of mine was met with a general look of disgust by the whole company; one of them, with a sneer, told me he believed I had more of the French than the English in my blood; and another remarked that he was sorry to find a gentleman of my appearance so lacking in love for his country."The psychology of this reaction is recorded with great accuracy. To the nationalist, any attempt to be fair to the enemy is treated as a form of treason; the world must be divided into absolute categories of good and evil, and the critic who refuses this division is accused of a lack of patriotism.Goldsmith's narrator analyzes this prejudice not as an individual defect alone, but as a social habit. He argues that national prejudice is a lazy shortcut for the intellect: it allows a man to feel superior to others without the trouble of acquiring virtue or knowledge himself. The tavern patriot can feel himself the master of Europe simply by repeating the clichés of his class:"He who has no character of his own is always the readier to value himself upon the character of his country. He believes that he inherits the courage of his ancestors and the wealth of his merchants, without having contributed a single penny or a single act of bravery to either."This critique of inherited merit places the essay in an Enlightenment register, but its force comes from the particular satire rather than from a general theory of the period. Goldsmith is arguing that virtue is an individual achievement, not a collective property. The citizen who boasts of his nation's greatness while living an idle, useless life is like a beggar who boasts of his father's estate.The "Citizen of the World" and the Cosmopolitan IdealAgainst the narrow patriotism of the tavern, Goldsmith proposes the ideal of the cosmopolitan:"Is it not much more generous, and more consistent with the character of a rational being, to look upon ourselves as citizens of the world? to consider the whole human race as one great family, and the different nations as different rooms in the same house?"This image of the world as a "house" with different rooms is one of the most beautiful metaphors in eighteenth-century literature. It suggests that national differences are domestic variations rather than natural divisions. The French, the Dutch, and the Germans are not our enemies; they are our housemates, whose rooms have been decorated in different styles due to the accidents of history and climate.The essay's cosmopolitan vocabulary belongs to a wider eighteenth-century debate about national character and human fellowship. This chapter does not treat that debate as a uniform Enlightenment consensus, or claim that Goldsmith speaks for every writer associated with a republic of letters. Its narrower point is that Goldsmith turns an abstract ideal into a test of everyday conversation: can a person admire a country without converting that admiration into contempt for everyone else?Goldsmith's essay is an attempt to translate this intellectual cosmopolitanism into a daily practice of civil life. The "citizen of the world" is not a philosopher who refuses all local attachments; he is a gentleman who remains open to the variety of human life, who enjoys the company of foreigners, and who refuses to let the accidents of birth limit his sympathy.The Critique of PatriotismGoldsmith is careful to distinguish between a rational love of one's country and the vulgar patriotism of the tavern:"I would not be understood to mean that we should have no affection for the country of our birth. A rational love of our country is a natural and necessary virtue; it is what leads us to obey the laws, to support the institutions, and to defend the state when it is genuinely threatened. But this love should be quiet, modest, and consistent with the respect we owe to the rest of mankind."The target of the essay is the "vulgar" patriotism that is built on the hatred of others. Goldsmith presents this as a distortion of ordinary affection for home. The essay's own evidence is conversational and satirical, not a documented study of state propaganda, so its political implication should be stated carefully: language that turns national difference into contempt makes violence easier to imagine and defend.Goldsmith's critique gains historical pressure from its 1760 setting, but the chapter does not infer a complete media history from the tavern scene. The essay gives us a small public exchange in which national stereotypes circulate as common sense. Its intervention is to interrupt that circulation, asking the reader to replace inherited assertion with observation, comparison, and self-scrutiny.The Conversational Grace of the EssayFormally, "On National Prejudices" can be read in relation to the familiar-essay tradition associated with Steele and Addison, without requiring a direct line of influence for every feature. Goldsmith's language is conversational and comparatively plain, and its ease is part of the satire's method.Goldsmith writes in the voice of the "saunterer", the relaxed, observant traveler who has no urgent business and no factional loyalties. This persona is crucial to the essay's work. Because the narrator is not an administrator or a politician, he has no interest in defending the policies of the state or the prejudices of the mob. He is free to observe, to listen, and to comment with the quiet irony of the spectator.The transitions are quick and natural, moving from the tavern conversation to a historical reflection on Rome and Greece, to a philosophical analysis of the passions, and back to the tavern. The metaphors are drawn from the domestic sphere, houses, rooms, clothes, families, making the cosmopolitan ideal look like a natural extension of family life.The essay's final turnThe essay does not end with a narrated departure from the tavern. It ends by giving preference to the older figure of the "citizen of the world" over narrower national appellations. That ending keeps the argument modest. Goldsmith does not offer a programme for abolishing local attachment; he asks the reader to refuse the claim that love of country requires contempt for other countries.The form of the conclusion is therefore less theatrical than the scene that precedes it. The narrator's final movement is conceptual: he turns from the company’s confident taxonomy of nations to a principle of enlarged fellowship. The essay leaves the reader with a choice of judgement rather than a documented change in the tavern patriots themselves. Its lasting pressure lies in that shift from inherited identity to examined sympathy.
essays.ch24: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecoeur (Michel-Guillaume Saint-Jean de Crèvecoeur)Original title: Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, "What Is an American?"Date: 1782 CEOriginal language: English (originally drafted in English, later translated and expanded in French by the author)Country/tradition: France / United StatesPeriod/movement: The Enlightenment; early American republic; agrarianismGenre: Epistolary essay; travel literature; social geography"What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations." With this question and genealogical observation, the narrator of Letters from an American Farmer, writing under the persona of "Farmer James," begins his famous inquiry in Letter III: "What Is an American?" The focus is the "strange mixture of blood" that was then forming on the eastern seaboard of North America. The narrator is not interested in the political theory of the British constitution or the theological heritage of the Puritans; he is interested in the biological and social geography of the New World.This focus on the "new man" is the pressure point of the essay. Crèvecoeur is writing during the American Revolutionary War, and the book was published in London in 1782, before the conflict had formally ended. The biographical circumstances behind the narrator's displacement should not be treated as identical with Farmer James's story: this chapter does not assert a specific family division, a flight as a suspected loyalist, or a completed personal loss of the farm without a separate biographical witness. "What Is an American?" is instead read here as a constructed attempt to explain to a European audience what made the British colonies in North America different from the old societies of Europe. Its language helped furnish a later vocabulary of American exceptionalism, but calling it the first such myth would overstate the evidence.The Rebirth of the PoorThe core of Crèvecoeur's argument is that America is a site of physical and moral resurrection for the poor of Europe. He contrasts the condition of the European peasant, who has no land, no political rights, and no hope of advancement, with the condition of the American farmer:"In Europe they were as so many useless plants, wanting vegetative mould, and refreshing showers; they withered, and were mowed down by want, hunger, and war; but now, by the power of transplantation, like all other plants they have taken root and flourished! They receive ample dust, and have become men."The analogy with botany is typical of Crèvecoeur. He treats human beings as plants whose character is determined entirely by the "soil" in which they are placed. The European soil, crowded with landlords, kings, and priests, has exhausted its nutrients; the peasant is mowed down like grass. The American soil, open, cheap, and free from feudal obligations, allows the immigrant to "transplant" himself, taking root and developing into a fully realized human being.This resurrection is achieved through labor. In America, the immigrant works for himself, not for a landlord or a bishop. The laws are simple, taxes are low, and the fruit of his labor belongs to his family: "We have no princes, for whom we toil, starve, and bleed: we are the most perfect society now existing in the world. Here man is free; as he ought to be; nor is this pleasing equality so transitory as many others."Within Letter III, this is presented as a distinctive form of equality. It is not the equality of the Spartan barracks or the Platonic republic; it is the idealised equality of the family farm, where the independent cultivator appears free from the obligations that governed the European peasant.The Melting Pot and the New RaceThe second key concept in the essay is the "melting" of different European nationalities into a single American identity:"He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. He becomes an American by being received in the broad lap of our great Alma Mater. Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world."This description of the "melting" of nationalities prefigured the concept of the melting pot, which would become the dominant metaphor for American immigration in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Crèvecoeur is arguing that the immigrant must leave behind his "ancient prejudices", the religious wars, national rivalries, and class divisions of Europe, to participate in the new society.In the letter's rhetoric, this melting is a transformation rather than a simple loss of identity.
