Almost immediately, soldiers force him into military service. He is beaten, nearly executed, and sent through a war in which villages are destroyed and civilians slaughtered. Pangloss's lesson survives because every disaster can be renamed as part of a universal good.Voltaire's satire moves with brutal speed. Before one catastrophe can be mourned, another arrives. The pace does not suggest that suffering is trivial. It shows how easily a neat philosophical system can continue speaking while actual people are crushed beneath it.A philosophical tale in disguiseCandide, or Optimism appeared anonymously in 1759, with a title page pretending that it had been translated from the German of Dr Ralph. Voltaire used the short philosophical tale to test ideas through exaggerated action. Instead of writing a formal argument against optimism, he sends an innocent believer through war, earthquake, religious persecution, slavery, disease, and greed.The target is often associated with the idea that an all-good and all-powerful providence must have created the best possible world. Voltaire does not provide a careful account of Leibniz's philosophy. Pangloss is a comic simplification: a teacher who can convert any evidence into proof of what he already believes.The historical world behind the comedy was violent. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 killed many thousands and became a major European argument about providence and evil. The Seven Years' War began soon afterwards. Voltaire places recognisable forms of organised suffering inside a tale that moves as quickly as gossip.Disaster without pauseCandide wanders through the ruins of war and reaches Lisbon with Pangloss. The earthquake destroys much of the city. Religious authorities respond by holding an auto-da-fe, believing that punishment of supposed heretics may prevent further earthquakes. Pangloss is hanged and Candide is flogged.Cunegonde, believed dead, reappears. She has survived murder, rape, and enslavement, and is being shared by two powerful men. Candide kills them and escapes with her and an old woman. The old woman then tells a history of suffering even more extreme, dismantling the belief that any single character possesses a unique claim to misery.In South America, Candide loses Cunegonde again. He travels with the resourceful Cacambo and reaches Eldorado, where gold has no special value, religious conflict is absent, and useful learning flourishes. Candide nevertheless chooses to leave. He wants Cunegonde, but he also imagines returning rich enough to command status elsewhere.The decision is understandable and foolish. Eldorado cannot reform someone who still measures happiness through possession and recognition. Most of the treasure is soon lost through accident, theft, and fraud.The world as a machine for excusesCharacters repeatedly return after apparent death. Pangloss survives hanging. Cunegonde's brother survives Candide's sword. Their reappearances make the plot openly absurd, but they also deny Candide the comfort of believing any disaster has completed his education.Pangloss remains loyal to his system even when life has made him miserable. His explanations grow funnier and more desperate because admitting error would require him to rethink his identity. Martin, a pessimistic scholar who later travels with Candide, offers the opposite certainty: the world is dominated by evil.Candide moves between these voices. Pangloss explains too much; Martin expects too little. Neither position tells him how to act in a specific moment. Voltaire's short chapters repeatedly expose people who use general principles to avoid responsibility for particular suffering.The satire extends beyond philosophers. Priests violate their teachings. Governments kill under legal forms. Merchants cheat. Aristocrats cling to rank after losing everything else. In Suriname, Candide meets an enslaved man whose hand and leg have been cut off through the plantation system. The encounter gives European luxury a mutilated human body.The women in the tale repeatedly expose another part of that system. Cunegonde, the old woman, and Paquette survive rape, sale, forced dependence, and disease. They tell their histories in direct language because the world around them treats such violence as ordinary. Voltaire gives them room to speak, but his speed also creates discomfort: suffering can become another item in the comic competition over who has endured the most. The tale makes that competition absurd while showing why people cling to it. Misery is one of the few possessions no one can easily take from them.The old woman's story is especially important. Born into privilege, she passes through piracy, war, slavery, plague, and starvation. Her survival defeats any belief that social rank offers lasting protection. It also challenges Candide's habit of treating his own losses as uniquely terrible. Experience should enlarge sympathy, yet characters often use it to defend their own despair.Cunegonde found againCandide eventually reaches Constantinople and recovers Cunegonde. She is no longer the radiant figure he remembers from the castle. Hardship has changed her, and Candide no longer desires her in the same way. He marries her because he promised to do so and because her brother still claims that a man of Candide's birth is unworthy of the family.The marriage therefore fulfils the romance while emptying it of fantasy. Cunegonde becomes difficult and unhappy. Pangloss continues arguing. Martin continues doubting. The group possesses enough experience to discuss the world's misery indefinitely.A small farmer offers another model. He works his land with his children and avoids political speculation. His life is limited, active, and relatively secure. Candide concludes that the household must cultivate its garden.The final garden is not Eldorado and not a return to innocence. Work does not explain earthquakes, undo slavery, or make the world just. It reduces idleness, dependence, and empty argument. Voltaire offers a practice rather than a complete philosophy.After optimismCandide compresses an enormous range of eighteenth-century violence into a remarkably short book. Its speed is part of its ethics. Pangloss never receives enough quiet time to make disaster sound noble. Another damaged body interrupts him.Yet the comedy has its own danger. Repetition can turn suffering into a mechanism of surprise, especially when women recount sexual violence or entire populations appear briefly as evidence. Voltaire's satire depends on exaggeration while asking readers not to become as indifferent as the systems it attacks.Candide begins by accepting a world already explained for him. He ends without a grand explanation. The garden is smaller than the castle, the battlefield, or Eldorado, but it is a place where action can be judged by what it produces.The closing lesson is deliberately modest. Human beings may not solve the structure of providence. They can refuse to make suffering sound necessary, and they can begin the work in front of them.
novels.ch9: Date: 1759-1767 | Original language: English | Country/tradition: Eighteenth-century British and Irish experimental fiction | Genre: Mock autobiography; digressive and typographic novelA life story that cannot get startedTristram Shandy wants to tell the story of his life. He begins before his birth, at the moment of his conception, but his parents are interrupted by a question about whether the clock has been wound. He then moves backwards to explain his family, sideways into theories, and forward only by accident.By the third volume, Tristram has finally been born. His nose is crushed by forceps. His father plans to give him the grand name Trismegistus, but a servant forgets it and the child becomes Tristram, a name the father detests. Later, a falling window sash causes another bodily disaster.These accidents sound like the plot of a broad comedy. Laurence Sterne makes them part of a larger joke about explanation. Walter Shandy, Tristram's father, has a theory for everything: names shape destiny, noses affect character, education can be systematised. Life keeps answering his theories with chance, misunderstanding, and badly designed windows.Nine volumes of interruptionSterne published The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767. The title promises a conventional autobiography. The book instead spends far more time on Tristram's father Walter, his Uncle Toby, Corporal Trim, Dr Slop, Parson Yorick, and the problem of writing the book itself.The narrator knows that he is falling behind. It takes him longer to describe a year than to live one. Each explanation creates the need for another explanation. A character cannot enter a room until Tristram has described the argument that brought him there, the ancestor whose habits shaped the argument, and the reader's likely impatience with the delay.Sterne calls digressions the sunshine of reading. In most narratives, a digression leaves the main road and later returns. Here the side road is the journey. The story advances because it wanders.This wandering draws on theories of the association of ideas, especially those connected with John Locke. One thought calls up another through habit, sound, memory, or private obsession. Conversation fails because each person follows a different chain. Walter hears one meaning, Toby another, and the reader may see both.The page joins the comedyThe experiment is not limited to sentences. Sterne makes the printed page perform. A black page mourns Yorick. A marbled page claims to be the varied emblem of the whole work. A blank page invites the reader to imagine Widow Wadman's beauty. Curving lines diagram the movement of earlier volumes. Chapters may be extremely short, misplaced, or apparently missing.These devices remind us that a book is a physical object arranged by an author. They also turn the reader into a participant. Tristram addresses us, predicts our response, scolds us for reading badly, and withholds information until we have formed the wrong expectation.The narrator therefore controls the book while performing his lack of control. He can stop the story and draw a line, but he cannot make his life obey chronological order. The freedom of narration answers the accidents of experience.The body keeps defeating every attempt at tidy intellectual order. Conception is interrupted by habit. Birth becomes a medical accident. A name is lost in transmission. A window turns domestic architecture into injury. Walter responds with theories because theory promises that misfortune can be understood after the fact. Sterne's comedy comes from the gap between the elegance of an explanation and the stubborn physical event it cannot reverse.This bodily comedy can be crude, but it is more than childish. Eighteenth-century debates about medicine, education, heredity, names, and the association of ideas enter the Shandy household as practical disasters. Learned systems do not remain in books. They shape decisions made for a child who cannot consent to them.Walter's systems and Toby's woundWalter Shandy loves systems because they promise mastery. When something goes wrong, he often responds by producing a theory large enough to contain it. His learning is comic, inventive, and useless at the moment of need.Uncle Toby is different. He received a groin wound during the siege of Namur and spends years trying to explain exactly how it happened. Words and maps prove insufficient, so he and Corporal Trim rebuild fortifications on a bowling green and reenact military campaigns in miniature.The hobby-horse begins as an attempt to communicate pain. It becomes a private world of forts, trenches, sieges, and shared labour. Toby's obsession is ridiculous, but it is also gentle. He cannot bear cruelty, even towards a fly. His military games contain little hatred because his imagination separates the craft of fortification from the desire to harm.Trim's loyalty deepens this part of the novel. Their conversations move between comedy and feeling without announcing the change. Sterne can mock obsession while protecting the human need that produced it.The courtship of Widow WadmanLate in the book, Widow Wadman decides to discover whether Toby's wound has made marriage impossible. Toby believes she wants to understand military geography. Their courtship becomes another failure of shared meaning.She asks where he was wounded. Toby sends for a map of Namur so that he can point to the location. Her concern is anatomical; his answer is geographical. Trim tries to help, but explanation only multiplies embarrassment.This long-delayed courtship reveals the novel's tenderness and its limits. Toby's innocence protects him from suspicion but leaves him unable to understand desire. Widow Wadman is intelligent and practical, though the joke often places readers on the men's side of her question.The story does not build towards a decisive marriage or completed autobiography. It ends during another family conversation, with a tale about a bull dismissed as a cock-and-bull story. The phrase names nonsense, evasion, and the entire book's refusal to deliver what its title promised.What digression can holdTristram Shandy is often called modern or postmodern before its time because it exposes narration, rearranges chronology, and plays with typography. Those labels identify real features, but they can make the novel sound like a cold technical exercise.Its experiments grow from a humane problem: no life can be told without losing most of what gives it texture. Chronology is clear but false to the way memory works. A straight line cannot show how a name recalls a theory, a wound produces a hobby, or a gesture opens an old grief.Digression allows Sterne to preserve small things that an efficient plot would discard: Trim's posture before a speech, Walter's collapse when a theory fails, Toby's kindness, the reader's interruption, the shape of silence on a page.Tristram never completes his life because completion would betray his method. A person is not a sequence of public events but a crowded movement of associations, accidents, bodies, words, and other people. The novel's disorder becomes its form of fidelity.The apparent chaos is therefore carefully made. Sterne must know where a chronological account would go in order to avoid it so inventively. Behind every interruption lies a strong sense of timing: a delayed answer, a chapter arriving too late, or a solemn expectation punctured by the wrong word. The novel does not abandon form. It makes delay, recurrence, and interruption into form.
novels.ch10: Original Title: Les Liaisons dangereusesDate: 1782 | Original language: French | Country/tradition: French ancien regime fiction | Genre: Epistolary and psychological novelA private letter begins a public disasterA young woman has just left a convent. Cecile de Volanges knows little of society, less of desire, and almost nothing of the marriage being arranged for her. In another Parisian house, the Marquise de Merteuil sees Cecile's innocence as an opportunity. Cecile is to marry Gercourt, a former lover who has offended Merteuil. Merteuil decides that the most satisfying revenge will be to send him a bride who is innocent only in reputation.She asks the Vicomte de Valmont, her former lover and present rival, to carry out the corruption. Valmont refuses, not from conscience but vanity. He is pursuing a more difficult conquest: Madame de Tourvel, a married woman known for religious principle and marital fidelity. To seduce Cecile would be easy. To make Tourvel surrender would confirm his mastery.This is the cold machinery that begins Dangerous Liaisons. Yet Laclos does not tell the story from above. The novel consists of 175 letters written by its characters. We read plots before their victims recognise them, declarations that may be sincere for a moment, and reports designed to flatter the person receiving them. Every writer arranges reality. Every reader within the novel risks believing the wrong arrangement.The storyCecile falls in love with the young music teacher Chevalier Danceny. Their feelings are timid and confused, but Merteuil encourages them while pretending to guide Cecile. Valmont becomes the carrier of their letters. This gives him access to Cecile's confidence and bedroom. One night he enters her room and forces her into sexual submission. His own account presents calculated coercion as a successful campaign. The difference between his language and Cecile's powerlessness is essential: the novel shows how an aggressor can use elegant words to disguise violence.Merteuil becomes Cecile's tutor in deception. She teaches the girl how to conceal meetings, manipulate appearances, and separate public innocence from private behaviour. Cecile's education is the inverse of moral growth. Society has left her ignorant, and the libertines fill that ignorance with methods that serve them.Valmont meanwhile establishes himself near Tourvel at the country house of his aunt, Madame de Rosemonde. Tourvel knows his reputation and tries to resist him. He performs generosity, sends carefully shaped letters, spies upon her feelings, and converts every refusal into another stage of pursuit. His campaign is disturbing because genuine emotion begins to enter it. He may come to love Tourvel, but he cannot experience love without treating it as a contest witnessed by Merteuil.When Tourvel finally yields, Valmont has achieved the victory he claimed to want. Merteuil refuses to reward him by renewing their former relationship. She insists that he prove his independence by abandoning Tourvel. He does so through a brutally repetitive letter whose excuses reduce human pain to a formula. Tourvel, psychologically and physically broken, retreats to a convent.The alliance between the two plotters now becomes open war. Merteuil has taken Danceny as a lover. Valmont reveals this to Cecile and tries to turn Danceny against Merteuil. Merteuil, in return, tells Danceny enough to provoke a duel. Danceny mortally wounds Valmont. Before dying, Valmont gives him the letters that expose Merteuil's conduct.The final letters gather the consequences. Tourvel dies after hearing of Valmont's death. Cecile withdraws to a convent rather than proceed towards marriage. Merteuil's correspondence circulates through society, destroying the reputation she spent years constructing. She loses a lawsuit and much of her fortune, contracts smallpox, and is left disfigured. She then disappears, reportedly taking her remaining valuables with her. The cleverest manager of appearances ends as an object of public scrutiny.Letters that do thingsIn many novels, a letter carries information. Here a letter can seduce, threaten, test, instruct, betray, or manufacture an alibi. The same event looks different depending upon who describes it and to whom. Valmont boasts to Merteuil, pleads with Tourvel, and behaves respectfully before Madame de Rosemonde. These are not simply lies placed beside a hidden true self. His identity is the collection of performances, and each performance seeks power over a reader.The form also makes us uncomfortable participants. Because we know the schemes, we may admire their timing or verbal precision even while condemning their purpose. Laclos uses our pleasure in intelligence against us. The novel asks whether aesthetic brilliance can be separated from the suffering it produces.Letters also travel beyond the writer's control. A message intended for one pair of eyes may be copied, intercepted, returned, or preserved for later revenge. Secrecy therefore depends upon material objects moving through bedrooms, servants' hands, country houses, and Parisian society. The libertines imagine that they command this circulation, but their own archive finally defeats them. They have documented themselves too thoroughly.For modern readers, the vocabulary of seduction requires particular caution. Valmont narrates resistance as an obstacle whose eventual defeat proves his skill. That description belongs to his self-excusing code, not to a neutral account of events. Cecile's youth, ignorance, isolation, and fear leave her unable to negotiate freely. Recognising the coercion sharpens rather than simplifies the book: sophisticated society supplies Valmont with a graceful language in which violence can appear as romance.Merteuil's self-creation is particularly complex. As a woman in aristocratic society, she has less sexual freedom than Valmont and faces greater punishment if exposed. She explains that she learned to control her face, observe others, and conceal her knowledge because openness would make her vulnerable. Her discipline is a response to inequality. Yet the novel does not turn that response into innocence. She uses the arts of survival to dominate younger and less powerful women.Why it remains greatPublished in 1782, seven years before the French Revolution, Dangerous Liaisons depicts an aristocratic world rich in polish and poor in responsibility. Its characters understand manners perfectly but treat other people as material. The coming Revolution is not predicted in the plot, yet the social order appears incapable of moral self-correction.The ending does not offer easy justice. Valmont dies with a final gesture that may be remorse, revenge, or both. Merteuil is punished through public shame and the destruction of her beauty, penalties shaped by the same society the novel criticises. Tourvel dies; Cecile loses her future; Danceny survives with knowledge that cannot repair what happened.Nor does exposure guarantee reform. Society eagerly reads Merteuil's letters because scandal is entertaining. The public that condemns her has previously admired the surfaces that allowed her to operate. Laclos leaves us uncertain whether the community has learned anything or merely found a new spectacle.Laclos's achievement is to make narrative form inseparable from moral inquiry. We never stand outside the network of influence. We open one letter after another, learning how language can create intimacy while secretly arranging harm. By the last page, private writing has become public evidence, but truth arrives only after nearly everyone who needed it has been destroyed.
novels.ch11: Date: Mid-eighteenth-century manuscript circulation; first printed edition 1791 | Original language: Chinese | Country/tradition: Qing Chinese fiction | Genre: Family saga; philosophical, domestic, and encyclopaedic novelA boy born with a piece of jadeJia Baoyu enters the world with a piece of jade in his mouth. Before his human birth, the novel has already told us of a supernatural Stone that longs to experience mortal life. The Stone is carried into the world, where splendour, love, grief, and loss will prove inseparable. This immense novel therefore begins with a warning: everything solid may also be a dream, and every possession may already contain the possibility of disappearance.For a new reader, the Jia family can feel overwhelming. There are two main branches of a great aristocratic clan, many relatives with similar names, servants, maids, officials, monks, nuns, visitors, and dependants. The best way to begin is not to memorise everyone. Follow Baoyu and the young women around him, especially Lin Daiyu and Xue Baochai. Let the household become familiar as a house does in life, room by room and voice by voice.The storyBaoyu grows up protected by wealth but alienated from the future planned for him. His father expects seriousness, classical study, official examinations, and service to the state. Baoyu dislikes the ambitions of conventional men and prefers the company of girls, whose intelligence and emotional truth he values. This preference is more than romantic. It places him at odds with the patriarchal order he is meant to inherit.Lin Daiyu, his orphaned cousin, comes to live with the Jia family. She is brilliant, sensitive, proud, frequently ill, and acutely conscious that she depends upon other people's favour. Baoyu and Daiyu recognise one another almost at once. Their intimacy grows through teasing, jealousy, shared reading, quarrels, reconciliations, and an understanding deeper than either can safely declare.Xue Baochai offers a contrast. She is composed, tactful, learned, and better suited to the family's idea of an excellent bride. If Daiyu represents exposed feeling, Baochai has mastered the social art of containing it. The novel does not reduce them to a simple contest between passion and coldness. Both women are intelligent; both inhabit a structure in which marriage decisions belong largely to others.After an imperial daughter of the family visits home, the magnificent Grand View Garden becomes the residence of Baoyu and his female cousins. For a time it seems to preserve youth from the adult world. The residents form poetry clubs, exchange gifts, stage performances, celebrate festivals, and create intense private meanings around flowers, handkerchiefs, fans, medicines, and lines of verse. The narrative's attention to meals, clothes, rooms, servants, and ceremonies is not decorative excess. It shows how a civilisation is lived through details.But the garden is never protected. Deaths, illnesses, humiliations, and forced marriages accumulate. Servants can be dismissed on suspicion. Young women are praised as family treasures while being exchanged for family advantage. Money is wasted, accounts are mismanaged, and the clan's political security weakens. The household that appears inexhaustible is consuming its own foundations.In the familiar 120-chapter version, Baoyu's health declines as his jade disappears. The family decides that marriage may restore him. They know he loves Daiyu, but they prefer Baochai. A deception is arranged: Baoyu is allowed to believe that the veiled bride is Daiyu. While he marries Baochai, Daiyu dies, burning the poems and tokens that carry the history of their attachment.The family suffers official confiscation and disgrace, though part of its position is later restored. Baoyu eventually sits the civil examinations and succeeds, apparently fulfilling his worldly duty. Then he disappears. His father later sees a shaven-headed figure in a red cloak who bows and vanishes into the snow with a monk and a Daoist. The Stone's mortal experience has reached its end. Baochai remains behind, pregnant, within the damaged family line.An ending with an unsettled authorshipThis conclusion requires an important qualification. Cao Xueqin's novel circulated in manuscript versions of about eighty chapters before his death. The first printed edition, prepared by Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E in 1791, contained 120 chapters. Scholars have long debated who wrote or assembled the final forty and how much lost material by Cao may survive in them.This is not a minor technical puzzle. The early chapters contain prophecies and songs pointing towards disaster, yet the printed ending sometimes seems to soften the family's ruin. Readers should therefore hold two truths together: the 120-chapter ending has shaped the novel's worldwide reception, and it cannot be treated as an unquestionably complete expression of Cao's design.The household as a worldDream of the Red Chamber enlarges the novel by taking domestic existence with absolute seriousness. A conversation between a mistress and a maid can reveal class power. A poetry competition can disclose rivalry, loneliness, and the limits placed upon women's talent. A missing object can connect supernatural destiny with household disorder.The book is also unusually alive to emotional misunderstanding. Baoyu and Daiyu love each other, yet their very closeness makes them vulnerable to testing and suspicion. Daiyu's sharpness often protects a frightened dependence. Baochai's calm may conceal costs that the household prefers not to notice. No single label is enough for them.Translation shapes an English reader's experience. The title appears as Dream of the Red Chamber, A Dream of Red Mansions, and The Story of the Stone. Names and poems differ across versions, and the verse presents special difficulties. A good modern translation should therefore be chosen deliberately rather than treated as a transparent window.Even the word "red" carries associations that English readers can miss. Within the novel's culture it belongs both to sensuality and to youth, prosperity, celebration, and the enclosed apartments of privileged women. A translated title therefore directs attention differently: one version stresses the dream of an aristocratic interior, another the supernatural Stone that records its journey. Neither title alone contains the whole book.The large servant population is equally important. Rank operates within rank: a senior maid may possess authority unavailable to a poor relation, yet remain vulnerable to dismissal. The household's intimate knowledge is distributed among people whom formal history would scarcely name. By following their quarrels and loyalties, the novel reveals that a great family is maintained by labour as well as lineage.Why it remains greatFew novels contain so much life without losing the feeling that life is passing. The Jia clan's decline is economic and political, but it is also a history of vanished rooms, dead friends, scattered servants, and poems whose occasions can never return. The grand scale is built from intimate losses.The supernatural frame does not dismiss ordinary feeling as unreal. It makes feeling more precious because it is temporary. Baoyu's withdrawal may be spiritual release, personal failure, or both. He escapes the system that has destroyed much of what he loves, but Baochai and the surviving women must remain within its consequences.The novel becomes a memorial to a world and especially to its women. It records their wit, artistry, cruelty, generosity, and sorrow with a fullness that official family history would not preserve. The Stone returns from splendour bearing a story. What seemed to be a dream has become literature, and literature becomes the form in which the lost household continues to live.
novels.ch12: Date: 1813 | Original language: English | Country/tradition: English Regency fiction | Genre: Novel of manners; courtship novel; social comedyThe man who refuses to danceAt a crowded assembly in the small town of Meryton, Fitzwilliam Darcy stands apart. He is wealthy, handsome, and unwilling to please. When someone suggests that he dance with Elizabeth Bennet, she overhears his judgement that she is tolerable but not attractive enough to tempt him. Elizabeth laughs at the insult and repeats it among her friends.That moment appears to tell us who they are. Darcy is proud; Elizabeth is quick, intelligent, and unafraid. Yet Pride and Prejudice is built upon the danger of a convincing first interpretation. Darcy's behaviour is genuinely rude. Elizabeth's response is genuinely lively. The error begins when each treats a partial truth as a complete person.The storyThe Bennets have five daughters and no son. Their home, Longbourn, is entailed upon the nearest male heir, Mr Collins, which means that Mrs Bennet and her unmarried daughters face an insecure future after Mr Bennet's death. Mrs Bennet's noisy pursuit of husbands is comic, but the danger beneath it is real.The arrival of the cheerful, wealthy Charles Bingley offers hope. He and the gentle Jane Bennet quickly fall in love. His friend Darcy is drawn to Elizabeth despite resisting her lower connections and his own first judgement. Elizabeth, meanwhile, is ready to dislike him.Mr Collins arrives at Longbourn, pompous with borrowed importance and devoted to his aristocratic patron Lady Catherine de Bourgh. He proposes to Elizabeth. She refuses, even though marriage would keep Longbourn within her reach. Her friend Charlotte Lucas accepts him instead. Charlotte is twenty-seven, has little fortune, and does not expect romantic happiness. Her decision exposes the narrow field in which women must make practical choices.Elizabeth then meets George Wickham, an attractive militia officer with easy manners. Wickham claims that Darcy denied him the living intended by Darcy's father. His story fits Elizabeth's prejudice, so she accepts it with little examination.Bingley suddenly leaves Netherfield, and Jane receives no proposal. Elizabeth rightly suspects that Darcy helped separate them. Visiting Charlotte near Lady Catherine's estate, she meets Darcy again. He proposes marriage, but his declaration stresses the inferiority he has struggled to overcome. Elizabeth refuses him. She accuses him of ruining Jane's happiness and mistreating Wickham.Darcy responds with a letter. He admits separating Bingley and Jane, believing Jane indifferent and the Bennet family imprudent. He then reveals that Wickham rejected a church living for money, spent the money, and later attempted to elope with Darcy's fifteen-year-old sister for her fortune. Elizabeth must confront an uncomfortable fact: she has been sharp about other people's vanity and blind to her own.Months later she visits Darcy's estate, Pemberley, with her aunt and uncle Gardiner. Expecting Darcy to be absent, she hears his housekeeper describe a generous master and brother. Darcy unexpectedly arrives and behaves with civility. Pemberley matters because Elizabeth sees his character embodied in responsibilities, relationships, and a place he does not need to advertise.The change is interrupted by disaster. Elizabeth's youngest sister Lydia has run away with Wickham without marriage. The scandal could damage every Bennet sister. Darcy quietly finds the couple, pays Wickham's debts, purchases his military commission, and arranges the marriage. He acts partly from love for Elizabeth and partly because he failed to expose Wickham earlier.Bingley returns and proposes to Jane. Lady Catherine then visits Elizabeth, demanding a promise that she will never marry Darcy. Elizabeth refuses. When Darcy learns of this refusal, he understands that her feelings may have changed. He proposes again, without superiority, and she accepts. The novel ends with Jane and Bingley married, Elizabeth at Pemberley, and the Gardiners welcomed as beloved relations.How Austen lets us misjudgeAusten's narration often stays close to Elizabeth's mind. We see what she notices and enjoy the speed of her conclusions. Yet the narrator does not formally announce that Elizabeth is always right. This flexible closeness, often called free indirect discourse, allows a character's language and the narrator's language to mingle.The result is a special kind of surprise. Darcy does not become a different man after the letter; the evidence is rearranged. Elizabeth's intelligence remains real, but intelligence without self-questioning can become another form of vanity. Darcy's correction is equally necessary. He learns that rank and good intention do not excuse contemptuous behaviour.The title belongs to both of them. Darcy's pride is obvious, but Elizabeth takes pride in her discernment. Her prejudice is obvious, but Darcy's assumptions about class and family are prejudgements too. Their love becomes possible only when each accepts an unwelcome account of the self.Marriage, money, and comedyThe novel's marriages form a scale of possibilities. Mr and Mrs Bennet show the lasting damage of marrying beauty without respect. Charlotte and Collins create a workable arrangement without intimacy. Lydia and Wickham unite appetite, vanity, and financial irresponsibility. Jane and Bingley possess affection but need greater firmness. Elizabeth and Darcy approach equality because both change.Austen's comedy never removes money from love. Property determines who can wait, who must accept, and whose mistakes become permanent. Elizabeth can refuse Collins because her father supports her, but that freedom has limits. Charlotte's choice should not be dismissed as stupidity when it is an intelligent response to material insecurity.The Bennet parents deepen this economic problem. Mrs Bennet understands the urgency but responds without tact or foresight. Mr Bennet sees absurdity clearly but mistakes detached amusement for responsible judgement. His wit has made him a favourite with many readers, yet the Lydia crisis exposes the cost of his withdrawal. He has laughed at disorder instead of governing a household whose daughters will bear its consequences.Class in the novel is more flexible than Lady Catherine wishes and more substantial than romance sometimes admits. The Gardiners earn their money in trade, but their intelligence and generosity exceed the manners of several aristocratic characters. Darcy's welcome of them marks real growth. Elizabeth does not enter Pemberley by denying her relations; Darcy becomes worthy of her by learning to value them.Why it remains greatPride and Prejudice makes moral education pleasurable. Its great scenes are conversations, letters, dances, visits, proposals, and embarrassing family performances. Nothing looks historically momentous, yet reputations and futures are being made in every room.Elizabeth remains lovable because correction does not extinguish her wit. Darcy becomes worthy not because wealth turns romantic, but because he learns to act without demanding applause. Their final happiness feels earned through knowledge rather than granted through attraction alone.The novel's enduring freshness lies in its precision. It knows that people often understand a stranger too quickly and themselves too slowly. It also knows that laughter can be part of wisdom, provided we learn when the joke includes us.
novels.ch13: Date: 1818; revised 1831 | Original language: English | Country/tradition: British Romantic fiction | Genre: Gothic novel; philosophical novel; early science fictionThe creator runs awayVictor Frankenstein works alone until a body assembled from the dead opens a dull yellow eye. This is the moment towards which his studies have driven him. He has imagined the gratitude of a new species and the glory of defeating mortality. When life appears, however, he sees only horror. He leaves the room.That flight is the moral centre of Frankenstein. The novel is often reduced to a warning against scientific ambition, but Mary Shelley's question is larger. What does a maker owe to the life he has made? Victor's first response is not care, explanation, or responsibility. It is abandonment.Stories inside storiesThe novel begins far from Victor's laboratory. Robert Walton is leading an expedition towards the North Pole and writing letters to his sister in England. He longs for discovery and for a friend who can understand him. His ship encounters Victor on the Arctic ice, exhausted by pursuit. Victor tells Walton his history as a warning.Victor grows up in Geneva within an affectionate family and studies natural philosophy at Ingolstadt. Fascinated by the boundary between life and death, he discovers a method of animation. He gathers materials, enlarges the human scale to make his work easier, and isolates himself from everyone who loves him. Success arrives, and he cannot bear it.The abandoned Creature disappears. Victor falls ill and is nursed by his friend Henry Clerval. When Victor returns home, his young brother William has been murdered. The family's servant Justine is accused after a miniature is found upon her. Victor suspects his creation but remains silent. Justine is convicted and executed.In the Alps, the Creature confronts Victor and asks to be heard. His narrative occupies the centre of the novel. Alone and without language, he learned sensation painfully. Fire warmed and burned him. Human beings fled or attacked. Hiding beside the cottage of the impoverished De Lacey family, he watched their kindness and suffering, learned to speak, and educated himself through books.He hoped that the blind father might receive him without prejudice. The conversation begins peacefully, but the returning family reacts with violence and terror. The Creature's hope collapses. He later meets William and imagines that a child may be free of adult prejudice. William rejects and insults him; learning that the boy is a Frankenstein, the Creature kills him and places the miniature upon Justine.He asks Victor to create a female being like himself. If given a companion, he promises to leave humanity forever. Victor reluctantly agrees and travels to a remote island in the Orkneys. But while constructing the second being, he imagines that she may refuse the bargain, reproduce, or become more destructive than her intended mate. He tears the unfinished body apart while the Creature watches.The Creature promises to be with Victor on his wedding night. He kills Clerval and ensures that Victor is accused before being released. Victor assumes that he himself is the threatened victim. On the wedding night, the Creature murders Elizabeth. Victor's father soon dies from grief.Victor devotes what remains of his life to revenge, pursuing the Creature northwards. He dies aboard Walton's ship. The Creature then appears over his body. He mourns his creator, acknowledges the horror of his crimes, and describes a misery that revenge never relieved. He declares that he will build a funeral pyre and die. Walton watches him disappear into the darkness on the ice. The novel does not confirm the promised death.Who is the monster?The Creature is never given a personal name. Popular culture often calls him Frankenstein, transferring the creator's name to the creation. The mistake is revealing. Victor and the Creature become doubles: isolated, eloquent, self-dramatising, and driven by injuries they use to justify new injuries.The Creature is not born murderous. He begins with a desire for contact and develops language through observing affection. Yet suffering does not absolve him. He chooses to kill the innocent in order to wound the guilty. Shelley allows us to understand his formation without asking us to approve his revenge.Victor's responsibility is equally complex. He cannot control every action of an independent being, but he creates life in secrecy, abandons it, conceals crucial knowledge, and repeatedly values his own anguish above the safety of others. Even his destruction of the female creature is performed without speaking to her, as though her future will could be known in advance.Knowledge and companionshipWalton mirrors Victor at an earlier stage. He risks other people's lives for a magnificent discovery and complains of intellectual loneliness. Victor's story gives him the chance Victor rarely takes: to hear a warning and change course. When the crew demands a return home, Walton finally agrees. His decision does not look heroic, but it may be the novel's clearest act of responsible leadership.The nested form keeps every testimony open to question. Walton records Victor, Victor reports the Creature, and the Creature interprets the family he secretly watches. Each speaker wants sympathy. Readers must judge while recognising that judgement itself can become monstrous when it refuses to listen.Books help create the Creature's consciousness. Through works of history, poetry, and moral reflection, he acquires ideals of virtue, family, and heroic identity. Education enlarges him but also gives names to what he lacks. He can imagine belonging more fully than he can attain it. Shelley therefore refuses the comforting idea that knowledge automatically improves circumstances; education without a community may intensify pain.The female creature raises another unresolved question. Victor describes the dangers she might pose, but every possibility comes from his imagination. She never awakens and never speaks. His fear of her independence, sexuality, and reproductive power becomes a death sentence delivered before life. The episode repeats his habit of making solitary decisions whose consequences fall upon others.The 1818 and 1831 editions also differ. Mary Shelley revised language, biography, and emphasis, with the later version giving fate a stronger role in Victor's history. Readers should know which text they hold; the novel's argument about choice and responsibility can feel different across editions.Why it remains greatWritten by a young Mary Shelley after the famous ghost-story challenge of 1816 and first published anonymously in 1818, Frankenstein joins Gothic terror to philosophical inquiry. It asks about scientific power, but also about parenting, education, social rejection, disability, race, gender, and the human need to be recognised.Its deepest terror is relational. Catastrophe begins when Victor looks at a living being and decides that appearance cancels obligation. Every later demand for sympathy returns us to that refusal.The Creature vanishes beyond the ship, carrying both guilt and grief. Victor is dead, his family destroyed, and Walton turns towards home. No invention can undo the past. Yet Walton's retreat suggests that a story may still prevent repetition. Listening becomes the modest alternative to Victor's lonely dream of mastery.
novels.ch14: Original Title: Le Rouge et le NoirDate: 1830 | Original language: French | Country/tradition: French Restoration fiction | Genre: Psychological, historical, and realist novel; BildungsromanA young man reading above a sawmillJulien Sorel's father and brothers work with timber in the provincial town of Verrieres. Julien hides with a book. He is slight, educated, and despised by a family that values physical strength. His secret hero is Napoleon, whose rise once made talent seem more powerful than birth. But Napoleon's age is over. In Restoration France, advancement appears to require obedience to the monarchy and the Church.Julien learns the Latin Bible so perfectly that local notables consider him suitable for a religious career. Faith, ambition, resentment, imagination, and fear become difficult to separate. He does not simply deceive society. He tries to become the person that each opportunity demands, then discovers that performance has entered his desires.The storyMonsieur de Renal, the mayor of Verrieres, hires Julien as tutor to his children, partly to display status before a rival. Madame de Renal initially fears the severe cleric she imagines is coming. Instead she meets a shy young man. Julien's gentleness with the children surprises the household.He begins to treat seducing Madame de Renal as a duty owed to his own pride. In the garden at night, taking her hand feels like a military campaign. But the affair becomes more than calculation. Madame de Renal experiences a love that overturns her moral and social world; Julien discovers happiness while repeatedly translating it back into the language of conquest.Anonymous warnings and local suspicion make the relationship dangerous. Julien leaves for the seminary at Besancon. There his intelligence and inwardness isolate him. The institution rewards conformity and strategic humility more readily than thought. The perceptive Abbe Pirard recognises Julien's ability and eventually recommends him to the Marquis de La Mole in Paris.As the Marquis's secretary, Julien enters aristocratic society. He performs difficult work well and learns its codes, yet remains divided between contempt for the nobles and hunger for their recognition. The Marquis's daughter Mathilde is bored by the polished young men around her. Julien's lower birth, intensity, and imagined danger attract her.Their affair is a struggle of pride. Mathilde wants an exceptional destiny and dreams of heroic ancestors. Julien alternates between passion and strategy, sometimes using jealousy according to advice supplied by a worldly prince. When Mathilde becomes pregnant, she insists upon marriage. The Marquis is furious but begins to arrange Julien's elevation, providing money, rank, and a military commission. Julien appears to have crossed the class barrier.Then the Marquis seeks information from Verrieres. Under pressure from her confessor, Madame de Renal writes that Julien is a calculating adventurer who seduces influential women to advance himself. Much of the accusation resembles Julien's own worst understanding of his conduct. The Marquis cancels the marriage plan.Julien travels back to Verrieres, enters the church during Mass, and shoots Madame de Renal. She is wounded but survives. He makes little serious effort to escape. In prison, the ambitious future that organised his life falls away. Madame de Renal visits him, forgives him, and admits that the condemning letter was dictated by clerical influence. Their love becomes simpler when it can no longer produce social advancement.Mathilde works passionately to save him, seeking influence and planning appeals. Julien, however, rejects the performance of repentance that might help. At his trial he addresses the class meaning of the case: he is a peasant who acquired education and attempted to enter a higher world. The jury condemns him to death.Julien is guillotined. Mathilde takes his severed head and buries it in a ceremonial echo of an ancestral legend she has admired. Madame de Renal, faithful to a promise not to take her own life, dies three days later while embracing her children.Ambition after NapoleonThe historical setting is not background decoration. Julien belongs to a generation taught to admire Napoleonic achievement but forced to live under a restored hierarchy of nobles, priests, and inherited position. Military glory, often associated with the red of the title, seems closed to him; the black clothing of the Church offers a route upward. Yet the title resists any single explanation. Its colours can also suggest passion and calculation, blood and death, or the hazards of a game.Julien's hypocrisy is real, but society requires it. The seminary distrusts intelligence. Aristocrats enjoy bold individuality until it threatens marriage and inheritance. Provincial officials speak of honour while competing through money and display. Julien is condemned for pretending, but nearly everyone around him is acting a role.What distinguishes him is the violence of his inward division. He monitors his own conduct as if commanding a soldier. A touch, silence, or declaration becomes a tactical move. This habit makes spontaneity almost impossible. He may feel love most clearly when he believes he has failed in ambition.The narrator both enters and interrupts this inward drama. At one moment Julien's smallest decision feels heroic because we experience its terror from within; at another, an ironic turn exposes the disproportion between his Napoleonic fantasy and a provincial drawing room. This double vision is central to Stendhal's realism. Social facts do not cancel imagination, and imagination does not erase social facts.The novel also draws upon contemporary legal reportage and the public fascination with criminal cases. Julien's trial gathers private passion, attempted murder, political suspicion, and class resentment into one civic performance. The verdict concerns the shooting, but Julien understands that the educated carpenter's son is himself on trial as a social offence.Women who see different JuliensMadame de Renal and Mathilde are more than stages in Julien's ascent. Madame de Renal sees his vulnerability before she understands his pride. Her love develops without a literary plan and terrifies her conscience. Mathilde, surrounded by privilege, desires a life grand enough to resemble historical romance. She sees Julien as material for exceptional drama.Both perceptions contain truth and fantasy. Julien is tender with Madame de Renal but also begins by treating her as a conquest. He is genuinely unusual, as Mathilde senses, but her theatrical imagination turns his death into an occasion for legend. The ending contrasts Mathilde's ceremony with Madame de Renal's quiet death among her children.Why it remains greatPublished in November 1830, though its first edition bears 1831 on the title page, The Red and the Black stands between Romantic intensity and modern realism. It offers duels of feeling, attempted murder, prison love, and execution, yet it also studies salaries, appointments, elections, gossip, clerical networks, and the minute humiliations of class.Stendhal's irony moves rapidly between sympathy and exposure. We inhabit Julien's calculations closely enough to feel their necessity, then suddenly see their absurdity. He is neither a pure victim of society nor a simple villain. His talents are real, the barriers are real, and the destructive choices are his.Only in prison does Julien stop trying to become visible to the powerful. That freedom arrives too late and after an act of terrible violence. The novel's tragedy lies there: a man spends his life seeking the conditions in which he might be himself, and recognises himself only when society has decided to kill him.
novels.ch15: Original Title: Evgenii OneginDate: Composed 1823-1831; complete edition 1833 | Original language: Russian | Country/tradition: Russian Romanticism and the emerging Russian novel | Genre: Novel in verseA letter sent too earlyTatyana Larina writes through the night to a man she scarcely knows. She has grown up in the country reading European novels, and Eugene Onegin seems to have stepped out of them: handsome, distant, experienced, and unhappy. Her letter is an act of emotional courage, but it is also an act of imaginative authorship. Before she understands Onegin, she gives him a role in the story she hopes to live.Onegin answers with restraint. He does not exploit her confession, yet he does not love her. Marriage, he says, would make them both miserable. His refusal sounds responsible, but its cool authority also reveals a man who believes he has exhausted experience before life has truly tested him.Years later, their positions reverse. Onegin will write desperately to Tatyana, and she will decide what love can and cannot require. Between the two letters lie a duel, a death, travel, reading, and the slow education of desire.A novel made from verseAlexander Pushkin composed Eugene Onegin between 1823 and 1831, publishing chapters separately before the first complete edition of 1833. He called it a novel in verse. Its principal unit, now known as the Onegin stanza, consists of fourteen lines of iambic tetrameter arranged through a demanding sequence of rhymes.That form gives the narrative unusual mobility. A stanza can begin with a character, turn towards social comedy, interrupt itself with the narrator's memory, and close upon a polished surprise. The book can behave like a novel while retaining poetry's concentration of sound and pattern. Translation must choose what to preserve: exact meaning, easy speech, metre, or rhyme. No English version can reproduce every pressure at once.The narrator is not invisible. He knows Onegin, remembers his own youth, comments upon fashion and literature, and occasionally withholds material. His personality surrounds the plot with friendship, irony, regret, and the sense that lives continue beyond the portions art selects.This narrator also makes time felt. He can pause an event to remember a theatre, a winter, or an earlier version of himself. Such departures resemble the digressive freedom of Tristram Shandy, but Pushkin contains them within strict stanzaic form. Freedom of thought and formal discipline coexist, much as Tatyana's final choice joins continuing love to deliberate restraint.The storyOnegin begins as a fashionable young man in St Petersburg. He knows how to dress, dine, flirt, attend the theatre, and appear cultivated. Pleasure has become routine. When an uncle dies, Onegin inherits a country estate and leaves the capital, hoping that change may cure his boredom.In the country he introduces a modest reform for his peasants but soon becomes tired of his neighbours. His one close companion is Vladimir Lensky, a young poet recently returned from Germany. Lensky is earnest where Onegin is sceptical. He is engaged to Olga Larina, a cheerful girl whose elder sister Tatyana is quiet, solitary, and imaginative.Tatyana falls in love with Onegin and sends her letter. After rejecting her, Onegin continues visiting the Larins through his friendship with Lensky. At Tatyana's name-day celebration, he finds himself trapped among provincial guests and blames Lensky for bringing him. To punish his friend, he repeatedly dances and flirts with Olga.Lensky interprets the performance as betrayal and challenges Onegin to a duel. Both men have opportunities to stop. Onegin recognises the absurdity but fears the judgement of society and the duel's officious organiser. Lensky spends his final night writing poetry and imagining possible futures. In the morning, Onegin shoots and kills him.The duel reveals how social performance governs men who imagine themselves independent. Onegin could apologise, refuse to fire, or accept ridicule, but he submits to an unwritten code. His supposed indifference proves weak before the opinion of an absent audience. Lensky dies because pride and convention turn a trivial act of revenge into irreversible violence.Olga grieves briefly, then marries a soldier and leaves. Onegin abandons his estate and travels. Tatyana, still drawn to him, enters his empty house. She reads his books and studies the marks he has made beside particular passages. This is her second education in Onegin. Instead of receiving the heroic figure created by her novels, she encounters a man assembled from fashionable attitudes, borrowed poses, genuine intelligence, and weary self-consciousness.Tatyana's family eventually takes her to Moscow, where she enters society and marries a distinguished general. When Onegin later returns to Petersburg, he meets her again. The awkward country girl has become a woman of composure and social authority. He now falls violently in love.He writes letters, waits, suffers, and finally enters her room uninvited. Tatyana does not deny the past. She remembers his earlier coldness and suspects that her present rank helps produce his passion. She admits that she still loves him. Yet she has married and will remain faithful to her husband. She leaves Onegin standing there, and the narrator ends the novel without repairing his loss.Tatyana learns to read a personTatyana's development is not a movement from foolish emotion to cold respectability. She remains capable of love. What changes is her understanding of the relation between feeling, imagination, and conduct.Her first letter assumes that emotional truth should determine the future. Onegin's library teaches her that identity is less pure. People imitate books, social types, and desired versions of themselves. Her later life in society might look like another performance, but she now performs knowingly. The social self does not cancel the private one; neither is allowed absolute rule.Onegin changes too late. His boredom once protected him from commitment. The duel exposes that detachment as submission to convention: he kills a friend because he lacks the courage to appear ridiculous. When he finally desires without reserve, Tatyana refuses to let his emotional awakening destroy another person's claim upon her.The first of the unnecessary menLater Russian criticism associated Onegin with the "superfluous man": an educated, privileged figure whose abilities find no responsible purpose. He can perceive the emptiness of society but cannot create a better relation to it. This type will recur across nineteenth-century Russian fiction.Yet Pushkin does not turn Onegin into a diagnosis. The narrator likes him, criticises him, and recognises parts of himself in him. Lensky's idealism is also treated with affection and irony. Even Tatyana, the novel's moral centre, is shaped by reading and role-playing. No one stands outside culture.The ending therefore refuses the easy symmetry of romance. Tatyana loved when Onegin could not; Onegin loves when Tatyana will not act. Their feelings are real, but reality does not promise that genuine feeling arrives at the proper hour. Pushkin leaves Onegin inside that belated knowledge, while the perfectly controlled stanza closes around an unfinished life.
novels.ch16: Original Title: Le Pere GoriotDate: Serialised 1834-1835; book edition 1835 | Original language: French | Country/tradition: French Restoration realism | Genre: Social and realist novel; education-of-ambition narrativeA boarding house that smells of defeatThe Maison Vauquer stands in a shabby Paris neighbourhood, and its rooms form a social ladder. Better-paying residents live on the lower floors. Poverty climbs towards the attic. The furniture, wallpaper, food, and odours seem to have absorbed years of disappointment.Among the residents are Eugene de Rastignac, a provincial law student with aristocratic connections but little money; Vautrin, a powerful middle-aged man with suspicious knowledge of society; and Pere Goriot, once a prosperous maker of vermicelli. Goriot has moved steadily into cheaper rooms, selling his possessions until other boarders treat him as a ridiculous old pauper.The reason for his ruin is love. He has given nearly everything to his two daughters, who are ashamed to be seen visiting him except when they need more.Paris as a systemBalzac published Le Pere Goriot in the Revue de Paris from December 1834 to February 1835, followed by a book edition in 1835. It became a central work in the vast sequence later organised as La Comedie humaine. Balzac's innovation was not merely to write many novels about society. Characters could reappear across them, older, richer, defeated, or transformed. The fictional world acquired a history beyond any single plot.The novel's dense description makes rooms legible. A carpet reveals income; a carriage opens doors; an address can announce success or disgrace. This is realism as social interpretation. Material objects do not simply make the setting convincing. They show how money enters intimacy.Balzac's recurring-character method deepens this effect. A person who occupies the centre of one novel may cross another as a familiar name, a rumour, or a powerful official. Rastignac's challenge to Paris is therefore both an ending and a beginning. Later works reveal what becomes of his ambition, making knowledge of society cumulative rather than confined to one hero's education.The education of RastignacRastignac arrives with ambition but without a method. His distant cousin Madame de Beauseant introduces him to high society and teaches him that appearances, lovers, marriage, and wealth operate according to rules rarely stated aloud. Through her salons he encounters Goriot's daughters: Anastasie de Restaud, married to a count, and Delphine de Nucingen, married to a wealthy banker.Goriot adored both girls after their mother's death. He supplied enormous dowries and continued paying their debts. Their husbands restrict their access to money, yet the daughters also exploit their father. They want his resources without the social embarrassment of his presence. Goriot interprets every demand as proof that he remains necessary to them.Rastignac begins courting Delphine. His motives are mixed. He desires her, pities her unhappy marriage, and understands that association with her can advance him. Goriot encourages the relationship because it may bring his daughter closer. He spends his remaining money preparing an apartment for the young pair.Vautrin offers a harsher route. He sees that Rastignac lacks the fortune required for rapid advancement. Victorine Taillefer, another boarder, would become a wealthy heiress if her estranged brother died. Vautrin proposes to arrange the brother's death in a duel, leaving Rastignac free to marry Victorine. The plan exposes the violence beneath respectable inheritance.Rastignac refuses to consent, but the machinery is already moving. Victorine's brother is killed. Before Vautrin can complete his design, the police identify him as Jacques Collin, an escaped convict known as Trompe-la-Mort. Mademoiselle Michonneau betrays him for money, and he is arrested. His wig falls away, revealing a marked and formidable criminal body beneath the genial boarder's appearance.A father consumed by fatherhoodMeanwhile, Anastasie and Delphine bring Goriot new crises. Anastasie has sold family jewels to pay the debts of her lover. Delphine struggles against her banker husband. Their quarrels in Goriot's room make his helplessness unbearable. He has spent the capital that once allowed him to solve their problems. After another emotional shock, he suffers a stroke.Rastignac and the medical student Bianchon nurse him. Goriot calls for his daughters, excuses them, accuses them, and imagines their arrival. Both remain occupied with their own social and marital emergencies. Delphine prepares for a ball; Anastasie comes too late to offer meaningful comfort. Goriot dies having recognised, then partly denied, the emptiness of the devotion he purchased.The daughters send empty carriages bearing their coats of arms to the funeral but do not attend. Rastignac and a poorly paid attendant accompany the coffin. After the burial at Pere-Lachaise, Rastignac looks down upon Paris. He challenges the city and goes to dine with Delphine. Goriot's death becomes the final lesson before Rastignac enters the struggle more consciously.Three teachers of ambitionMadame de Beauseant, Vautrin, and Goriot offer different accounts of society. Madame de Beauseant teaches elegant self-command while privately suffering abandonment. Vautrin insists that law and morality disguise competition, so success belongs to anyone ruthless enough to act directly. Goriot believes love can exist outside calculation, yet his own giving becomes a destructive economy.Rastignac does not simply choose one teacher. He absorbs something from each. His care for Goriot is genuine, but he also uses Goriot's relationship with Delphine. He rejects murder, yet accepts a social world sustained by less visible forms of sacrifice.Goriot's love is moving because it is absolute and frightening because it recognises no limit. He has trained his daughters to experience him as an inexhaustible resource. His self-erasure does not teach gratitude; it removes the resistance through which affection might become mutual.His daughters are nevertheless more than emblems of ingratitude. Their marriages place them under husbands who control wealth and reputation, while lovers create further financial demands. They reproduce cruelty, but they also inhabit a system in which women often exercise power indirectly through beauty, secrecy, and family money. Balzac condemns their abandonment without pretending that their choices occur in freedom.The city after the graveBalzac joins melodrama to economic analysis. Secret identities, criminal schemes, adulterous affairs, and a deathbed operate beside exact accounts of rent, dowries, debts, and inheritances. The extremes belong together because money turns private feeling into public consequence.The ending does not show Rastignac suddenly corrupted. It shows him crossing a threshold. At the grave he sees the city as a field of combat, yet his first movement is towards Delphine, whose absence helped kill her father. Ambition survives the knowledge of its cost.Pere Goriot makes Paris feel larger than any individual and intimate enough to enter every room. The city promises transformation, but someone pays for each ascent. Goriot descends floor by floor while his daughters rise in society; Rastignac begins climbing as the old man's coffin enters the ground.
novels.ch17: Original Title: Mertvye dushiDate: 1842 | Original language: Russian | Country/tradition: Russian satire and early realism | Genre: Prose "poem"; picaresque; grotesque social satireA buyer asks for people who no longer existPavel Ivanovich Chichikov arrives in an unnamed provincial town with an ordinary carriage, an attentive servant, and a talent for pleasing everyone. He learns the ranks and interests of local officials, praises the town, attends dinners, and makes himself agreeably unremarkable.Then he begins visiting landowners with a strange proposal. He wants to buy their dead serfs.Under the Russian census system of the period, landowners continued paying taxes on male serfs who had died since the previous count. These people remained alive in official records. Chichikov offers to assume the burden by purchasing their names. The sellers may save money, but no one can understand why a sensible man wants legal ownership of the dead.The journey through ownershipGogol published Part One of Dead Souls in 1842 and called it a poem, though it is written in prose. The designation points towards its mock-epic ambition. Chichikov's journey resembles a hero's progress across a nation, but his quest concerns fraudulent paperwork, and the people he meets are enlarged into comic grotesques.His first seller, Manilov, is gently sentimental and incapable of effective action. His pleasant phrases float free of thought, much as his estate lacks practical order. He gives Chichikov the dead souls without payment, delighted by the appearance of friendship.Korobochka is a cautious widow who fears making a bad bargain. She accepts the sale but worries that dead souls might have a market price she has failed to discover. Her suspicion is limited but persistent, and it will later help undo Chichikov.Nozdryov is a liar, gambler, bully, and compulsive maker of disorder. He tries to force Chichikov into games and dubious exchanges. When Chichikov refuses, the visit nearly ends in violence. Nozdryov sells nothing but gains knowledge he cannot keep quiet.Sobakevich is heavy, blunt, and commercially alert. His house and furniture seem built in his own bodily image. He bargains hard and praises the skills of dead serfs as though they might still perform labour. Plyushkin, the final great figure in the sequence, has allowed miserliness to consume a once functioning estate. Food rots, objects accumulate, peasants flee, and wealth becomes indistinguishable from waste. He possesses many dead names and sells them eagerly.Each encounter changes the rhythm, yet all reveal the same moral confusion: human beings have become entries in accounts. Chichikov's scheme is scandalous because it exploits the system, but the system already treats people as transferable property.The word "souls" was an administrative term for male serfs counted for taxation, but Gogol activates its religious meaning. The joke is inseparable from serfdom. Chichikov never meets the dead labourers whose names support his plan; they survive as lists, prices, claimed skills, and taxable absences. Officials notice the unusual transaction while accepting human ownership as ordinary.Rumour discovers infinityBack in town, Chichikov submits the purchases for legal registration. Officials assume he is a wealthy landowner acquiring hundreds of serfs and celebrate him. At a ball he pays marked attention to the governor's young daughter, provoking speculation about marriage.The fraud begins to crack through accident rather than investigation. Nozdryov publicly declares that Chichikov has been buying dead souls. Korobochka arrives in town to ask whether she sold too cheaply. Officials and their wives attempt to explain the mystery, producing rumours more fantastic than the truth. Chichikov becomes a kidnapper, counterfeiter, government inspector, fugitive, or disguised Napoleon.The prosecutor is so overwhelmed that he dies, immediately becoming another body whose social meaning depends upon interpretation. Chichikov falls ill, discovers that invitations have stopped, and learns enough of the rumours to flee.Only near the end does the narrator provide his history. Chichikov was taught to obey superiors and save money. He has worked patiently, endured reversals, and repeatedly crossed legal boundaries in pursuit of security and respectability. His plan is to mortgage the purchased names as if they were living property, obtain capital, and establish himself as a genuine landowner.Part One closes with his carriage speeding across the landscape while the narrator turns towards Russia itself. The movement becomes lyrical and visionary, but its destination remains unknown.Bodies, houses, and habitsGogol's descriptions do more than caricature. A character's body seems to continue into furniture, food, clothing, speech, and land. Sobakevich's objects are solid and bear-like. Plyushkin's estate has taken the shape of hoarding. Manilov's unfinished plans materialise his vague mind.This method makes personality comic and environmental. The landowners are not isolated sinners placed inside neutral estates. Their habits organise entire worlds, affecting peasants, servants, buildings, and production. Chichikov adapts his language to each world because he has no strong substance of his own beyond appetite and calculation.The narrator is equally unstable. He mocks provincial vanity, apologises for choosing an unheroic subject, wanders into reflection, and suddenly addresses Russia with prophetic intensity. Satire keeps opening into yearning. The book wants to expose national degradation and imagine renewal, but it cannot easily connect the two.Language repeatedly escapes practical purpose. Nozdryov's lies grow without strategic control. Officials generate impossible rumours because uncertainty is intolerable. The narrator's comparisons may expand until the object being described almost disappears. Speech produces rival realities, just as census documents preserve dead men more effectively than memory does.The ending Gogol could not completeGogol planned a larger design in which Chichikov might pass through punishment and moral regeneration. He continued working on a second part, destroyed manuscripts, rewrote, and shortly before his death burned another substantial version. Surviving Part Two chapters are fragmentary and textually uncertain.The incompletion matters. Part One can be read as a powerful whole, but its final road opens towards a transformation that the finished book never supplies. Chichikov escapes immediate exposure and continues moving. Russia is compared to a rushing vehicle while the question of direction remains unanswered.Surviving fragments of Part Two show Chichikov meeting figures who might have participated in a corrective design, but they cannot be treated as a completed ending. Gogol's destruction and rewriting belong to the history of the text, not to its fictional resolution. Editions that include the fragments must mark their uncertain sequence and unfinished state.The dead souls are therefore more than a pun with a fixed moral. They are deceased serfs alive on paper, living owners emptied by appetite, officials animated by rumour, and perhaps characters awaiting a spiritual life the projected epic never reaches. Gogol creates a nation of records, objects, mouths, roads, and voices, then leaves it in motion between comic exposure and impossible redemption.
novels.ch18: Original Title: Jane Eyre: An AutobiographyDate: 1847 | Original language: English | Country/tradition: Victorian English fiction | Genre: Fictional autobiography; Bildungsroman; Gothic romanceA child refuses the story told about herJane Eyre is locked in the red-room for resisting her cousin John Reed. The room belonged to her dead uncle, who had brought the orphan into his family. Its cold grandeur turns punishment into terror. Jane sees herself in the mirror as a strange little figure and fears that her uncle's spirit may return to judge the household that has broken its promise to protect her.The scene establishes the struggle of the whole novel. Other people repeatedly define Jane as dependent, plain, poor, rebellious, or ungrateful. Her survival depends upon answering them without allowing anger to become her only identity. Because Jane later narrates her own life, the book itself becomes her final act of authority: she decides what her experience means.Gateshead and LowoodCharlotte Bronte published Jane Eyre: An Autobiography in October 1847 under the name Currer Bell. The disguise protected the author's gender, but the fictional autobiography announces an intimate first-person voice. Adult Jane recounts the formation of the child who became her.At Gateshead, Mrs Reed and her children treat Jane as an inferior intruder. Before sending her away, Mrs Reed tells the clergyman Mr Brocklehurst that Jane is deceitful. Jane's direct accusation of her aunt gives her a first taste of self-liberation, though it does not remove her vulnerability.Lowood School combines charity with deprivation. Brocklehurst preaches humility while the girls suffer cold, hunger, poor clothing, and disease. Jane's friend Helen Burns offers a Christian patience that differs from Brocklehurst's punitive religion. Helen endures injustice without hatred, but Jane cannot fully accept her willingness to submit.A typhus outbreak exposes the school's neglect and leads to reform. Helen dies of consumption in Jane's arms. Jane remains at Lowood for eight years, first as pupil and then teacher. When the beloved superintendent Miss Temple leaves, Jane recognises that security has become confinement and advertises for work.Thornfield and its locked roomJane becomes governess to Adele Varens at Thornfield Hall. A governess occupies an uncertain social position: educated and respectable, yet employed and neither servant nor family. This in-between status sharpens Jane's awareness of rank.She meets Edward Rochester after his horse slips on an icy road. He is the master of Thornfield, older, wealthy, commanding, and emotionally restless. Their conversations are contests in which Jane's directness interrupts his authority. She falls in love but refuses to imagine that feeling erases inequality.The house produces Gothic signs. Jane hears strange laughter. Rochester's bed curtains are set on fire, and Jane saves him. A visitor, Richard Mason, is attacked during the night. Rochester explains each crisis incompletely while asking Jane for trust.He also stages an elaborate deception around Blanche Ingram, encouraging the belief that he will marry her. Jane prepares to leave. Rochester finally proposes to Jane, and she accepts after insisting that spiritual equality matters more than beauty, wealth, or rank.The wedding is stopped by the revelation that Rochester is already married. His wife, Bertha Mason, lives confined in the attic under the care of Grace Poole. Rochester describes a disastrous marriage arranged in Jamaica and asks Jane to live with him abroad as his partner outside law.Jane loves him and recognises the loneliness of his life, but she refuses. Her conscience is meaningful precisely because no external authority can easily enforce it. She leaves Thornfield with little money and nearly dies on the moors.Independence before returnThe Rivers siblings, Diana, Mary, and St John, shelter Jane. She becomes a village schoolteacher and discovers that they are her cousins. An uncle has left her a substantial inheritance. Jane divides it equally among the four cousins, converting money into kinship rather than domination.St John Rivers is disciplined, intelligent, and emotionally severe. He plans missionary work in India and asks Jane to marry him. He values her courage and usefulness but does not love her. His proposal offers purpose at the price of inward extinction. Jane agrees that she might work beside him but refuses to become his wife.At the point when his pressure nearly succeeds, Jane seems to hear Rochester calling her name across a great distance. She returns to Thornfield and finds it burned. Bertha set the fire and died after jumping from the roof.
