A victorious general returns home after a ten year war at the head of his army. His estranged wife meets him at the palace gates. She does not offer a warm embrace; instead, she orders her handmaidens to roll out a path of crimson-dyed cloths stretching from his chariot to the palace doors. The general hesitates. He knows that treading on these precious fabrics, wasting the wealth of his own estate, is an act of pride (hubris) that risks angering the gods. Yet his wife coaxes him down through a sequence of sharp verbal maneuvers. As his bare feet touch the deep red fabric, he walks into his palace and his grave.This confrontation is the visual and symbolic focus of the play. The red cloths are not just decoration. They are a physical map of the blood already spilled and the blood about to flow. They recall the sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia, whom Agamemnon killed ten years earlier to buy favourable winds for the Greek fleet. They also predict the murder of Agamemnon in his bath. Aeschylus turns this walk into a physical expression of the tragic cycle of blood-vengeance. The red path is a road of no return. It demonstrates how ancient drama uses a simple theatrical prop to carry the weight of inheritance, guilt, and the return of past crimes.By stepping onto the red fabrics, Agamemnon seals his own fate. The act is a public demonstration of his pride. He tries to justify his walk by claiming he does it under protest, yet he yields to Clytemnestra’s demands. This surrender reveals his inner weakness. He has conquered Troy, but he cannot conquer his wife's rhetoric. The physical touch of the dyed wool under his feet connects the distant slaughter in Troy with the domestic slaughter waiting for him inside. It is a transition from public triumph to private execution.The Sovereign Queen and the Language of PowerClytemnestra is one of the most formidable creations in ancient theatre. From her first appearance, the watchman describes her as possessing a "man’s mind" (androboulon kear). This description would have unsettled an all-male Athenian audience. In a society that kept women out of public political life, Clytemnestra dominates the scene. She organises the city's defence, manages the palace, and dictates terms to the elders of Argos. Her intelligence shows in her command of language. She maps the movement of light across mountains and seas like an invading army when she describes the beacon system she set up to flash the news of Troy’s fall across the Aegean Sea.Clytemnestra’s rhetoric is her primary weapon. During the red path scene, she plays upon Agamemnon's vanity and exhaustion. She turns his reluctance into compliance by arguing that Priam, the defeated king of Troy, would have walked on such fabrics without hesitation, and she challenges Agamemnon to match the stature of his defeated rival. Once Agamemnon enters the palace, Clytemnestra’s language shifts from deceptive praise to ritualistic justification. As she stands over the corpses of her husband and Cassandra, she describes the murder not as a crime, but as a long delayed act of justice (dike). She trapped Agamemnon in a net of robes while he was in the bath and struck him down like an animal at the altar. For Clytemnestra, this is the final payment for the slaughter of Iphigenia. She presents herself not as a murderer, but as the instrument of the ancestral curse that haunts the House of Atreus.The Voice of the Watchman and the Chorus of ArgosAeschylus frames this domestic tragedy within a broader civic and historical context. The play begins not with kings or queens, but with a humble watchman stationed on the palace roof. He has spent a year waiting for a signal fire. His opening speech creates a mood of exhaustion and dread. He knows that the house is not ruled as well as it used to be. He must keep silent, which suggests a political instability that goes beyond the royal family. When the beacon light finally appears, his joy is checked by a dark premonition. This prepares the audience for a tragedy where victory and catastrophe are bound together.The Chorus of Argive elders is central to the drama. They sing nearly half the lines. Their long odes are historical and moral investigations. They recount the departure of the Greek fleet, the omen of eagles devouring a pregnant hare, and the agonizing decision Agamemnon faced at Aulis. The Chorus dwells on the details of Iphigenia’s sacrifice. They recount her cries of "Father" and the robes she held about her as she was lifted over the altar, keeping the memory of her death as a physical presence on the stage. As the play progresses, their songs reflect the growing anger of the citizens of Argos, who resent the high cost of a war fought for a single unfaithful woman. The Chorus represents the civic consciousness of Argos. Their warnings show how a dynastic feud threatens the stability of the entire state.The elders are not helpless observers; they represent the voice of the community. They question the queen’s news and doubt the beacon report until the herald arrives to confirm it. Their skepticism highlights the division between the ruler and the ruled. Even as they mourn Agamemnon, they refuse to accept Aegisthus’s rule, showing that the palace coup has not fully subdued the city. Their voice remains a threat to the tyrants.The Silence of Apollo: Cassandra and the Temporal TrapIf the carpet scene is the play's visual center, Cassandra’s scene is its prophetic climax. Brought back from Troy as a captive concubine, Cassandra sits in Agamemnon’s chariot. She refuses to speak or acknowledge Clytemnestra's commands. Her prolonged silence creates a powerful theatrical tension. Once Clytemnestra leaves, Cassandra breaks her silence in wild, ecstatic cries to Apollo, the god who cursed her with the gift of prophecy joined to the doom of never being believed.Cassandra’s scene collapses the linear time of the play. She does not merely predict the future; she witnesses the past. She looks at the palace walls and sees the ghosts of Thyestes' children, whose hands are filled with their own flesh, the feast of slaughter that initiated the family curse. She then describes the murder occurring inside the palace in real-time. She warns the Chorus of the net of death and the cow striking down the bull in the stall. Cassandra’s presence expands the scope of the tragedy. Her vision links the mythological past of the House of Atreus to the immediate horror of Agamemnon’s death. Her voluntary entry through the palace doors, knowing she is walking to her slaughter, is the ultimate example of tragic necessity.The Net of Death: Tragic Closure and the Cycle of DikeThe final section of the play exposes the instability of the justice that Clytemnestra claims to have achieved. When she emerges from the palace, standing over the dead bodies, she is accompanied by Aegisthus, her lover and Agamemnon’s cousin. Aegisthus boasts of the murder as a righteous act of revenge for his father Thyestes, whom Agamemnon's father, Atreus, fed the flesh of his own children. By showing Aegisthus’s cowardice, since he stayed behind during the Trojan War while Clytemnestra committed the deed, Aeschylus undermines the moral authority of the queen’s cause. The justice she claimed to establish is revealed to be another link in the chain of retributive violence.The play ends with an uneasy peace rather than a resolution. The Chorus confronts the new rulers, warning them that Orestes, Agamemnon's exiled son, will return to avenge his father. Clytemnestra attempts to soothe Aegisthus, promising that they will rule the house and set things right, but their tyranny is built upon a foundation of blood and resentment. Aeschylus leaves the conflict unresolved and prepares the audience for the subsequent plays of the trilogy. He shows that the cycle of blood-feud cannot cure itself. True justice cannot be achieved through individual acts of vengeance. It requires a transformation of the law itself, a shift that will only occur when the scene moves from the blood-stained palace of Argos to the democratic courts of Athens.
plays.ch3: Original Title: MedeiaDate: 431 BCE (first performance) | Original language: Classical Greek | Country/tradition: Classical Athens | Period/movement: Golden Age of Athenian Tragedy / Late Classical Realism | Genre: TragedyThe Fury of the Outsider: Tragedy as a Domestic ThrillerModern readers do well to treat Euripides’s Medea not as a remote myth of gods and sorcery, but as a claustrophobic domestic thriller. The play opens with a situation that remains recognisable today: a marriage has collapsed, a husband has abandoned his family for a younger bride of higher social standing, and a wife is left stranded in a foreign city with her young children. But Euripides turns this familiar tale of domestic betrayal into a campaign of terror. The abandoned wife does not simply mourn. She plans a cold revenge that strikes at the root of her husband's domestic and political ambitions. She challenges the audience to confront the destructive capacity of a human mind pushed to the absolute limit.What makes the play so gripping is that the protagonist is an outsider. Medea is a Colchian princess who fled her homeland, murdered her brother, and used her magical arts to secure Jason's fame. Yet in Corinth she is a stateless refugee, a foreign woman in a Greek city-state that values citizens and views immigrants with suspicion. Her husband, Jason, rationalises his betrayal as a pragmatic career move to secure their children's financial future. This collision between cold political opportunism and raw, passionate outrage drives the dramatic action. Euripides tests the audience's sympathy at every turn, forcing them to navigate the narrow boundary between understanding Medea’s rage and recoiling from her violence.The Rhetoric of Exile: The Female Citizen and the ForeignerMedea’s first appearance on the stage is a demonstration of rhetorical skill. Emerging from the palace doors, she does not launch into a wild barbarian lament. Instead, she delivers a measured, analytical speech to the Chorus of Corinthian women. She appeals to their shared experience, detailing the systemic oppression of women in Greek society. She argues that women must buy their husbands at great expense, accept them as masters of their bodies, and face the dangers of childbirth while men fight in wars. She declares that she would rather stand three times in the front line of battle than bear one child. In this way, she subverts the classical Greek heroic code, placing the pain and risk of childbirth on par with the courage of male hoplites.This speech establishes a bond between Medea and the Corinthian women. They promise to keep silent as she plots her revenge. But Medea’s plight is complicated by her status as a foreigner. In 431 BCE, when the play was performed, Athens was under Pericles’s citizenship law of 451 BCE, which decreed that a child could only be a citizen if both parents were Athenian. To the audience, Jason's marriage to Creon’s daughter would have been recognized as a standard legal move to secure legitimate heirs, while Medea's children by a foreign mother would remain marginalized. Medea’s exile is not just a personal displacement; it is a civic erasure. She uses her intellect, the very cleverness (sophia) that the Corinthian rulers fear, to manipulate King Creon into giving her one day’s delay, demonstrating how a marginalised outsider can exploit the fears of the ruling class.Jason's arguments reveal the self-serving logic of the Greek imperialist mindset. When he confronts Medea, he insists that he has done her a favour by bringing her to Greece from a barbarian land. He claims that in Greece she enjoys the protection of law rather than the rule of force, and that she has become famous for her wisdom. This defense is hollow. Jason views Medea as a tool that has outlived its usefulness. His patronising tone only fuels Medea's anger, showing how the dominant culture uses legalistic arguments to justify the exploitation of foreign subjects.The Battle of the Mind: Passion, Reason, and the InfanticideMedea’s monologue in the fifth episode is the psychological focus of the play. She sends her children to the palace with a poisoned robe and crown that will destroy Jason's new bride, and then she hesitates. As she looks upon her sons, her maternal love battles her desire for revenge. This speech is the earliest representation in Western literature of an internal psychological conflict, illustrating the division of the self. Euripides contrasts thumos, the seat of passion, anger, and honour, with bouleumata, the rational plans and deliberations of the mind.Medea knows the horror of what she is about to do. She confesses that she knows the evil she intends to do, but declares that her thumos is stronger than her rational thoughts. This is not a moment of madness; it is a conscious, rational choice. Medea recognises that in a society that has stripped her of her home, her husband, and her honour, the only way to inflict absolute ruin on Jason is to destroy his lineage. To leave the children alive would expose them to the mockery and vengeance of her enemies. She kills her sons. This act murders her own maternal happiness, but it also achieves a complete victory over Jason. Euripides traces this psychological calculation with chilling clarity, refusing to allow the reader the comfort of viewing Medea as a simple monster.The Dragon Chariot: Subverting the Machinery of the GodsThe ending of Medea is one of the most controversial in theatrical history. Jason rushes to the palace to save his children, only to find the doors barred. Suddenly, Medea appears above the stage in a winged chariot drawn by dragons, sent by her grandfather Helios, the Sun God. She holds the corpses of her sons and refuses to allow Jason to bury them or even touch their skin. This staging is a radical subversion of the Deus ex Machina, the theatrical device where a god appears on a crane (mechane) at the end of a tragedy to resolve the plot and restore order.Here, the machine is occupied not by a god, but by a child-murderer. Euripides grants Medea a divine escape, which denies the audience the satisfaction of a moral resolution. There is no punishment for the killer, no comfort for the grieving father, and no restoration of civic order. The gods do not intervene to protect the innocent; instead, they provide the means for Medea’s flight to Athens. The play ends with the moral order in ruins. Jason is left a broken, unheroic figure, while Medea rises above the human world, transformed by her grief and her vengeance into a terrifying force of nature.The Afterlife of the SorceressThe influence of Medea on subsequent drama lies in its challenge to the conventions of tragic characterisation. Seneca’s Latin adaptation, Medea, emphasized the occult aspects of her character, turning her into a gothic witch whose magic dominates the action. This version influenced the dark, sorcerous heroines of Renaissance and Jacobean theatre. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, the play has undergone a significant critical revival, particularly through feminist and postcolonial adaptations. Writers have recast Medea as a symbol of colonial resistance, a woman of colour fighting against a white imperialist order, or a mother struggling against the crushing pressures of patriarchal society.Whether read as a study in psychological division, a critique of gender inequality, or an exploration of the violence born of exile, Medea remains a disturbing work. It refuses to offer easy answers or moral comfort, showing how easily the systems of law, marriage, and empire can drive the outsider to commit the unspeakable.
plays.ch4: Original Title: LysistrateDate: 411 BCE (first performance) | Original language: Classical Greek | Country/tradition: Classical Athens | Period/movement: Old Attic Comedy | Genre: ComedyThe Political Power of Abstinence: Old Comedy's Absurd PremiseFor anyone looking to understand the political range of ancient Athenian theatre, Aristophanes's Lysistrata offers a sharp contrast to the dark tragedies of Aeschylus and Sophocles. Written in 411 BCE, the play presents a premise that is both hilarious and sharp: the women of Greece, tired of the endless slaughter of the Peloponnesian War, unite under the leadership of an Athenian woman named Lysistrata. They declare a total sex strike until their husbands agree to a peace treaty. What begins as a bawdy farce about marital frustration becomes a serious critique of war and imperial politics. By using the physical realities of the human body as political leverage, Aristophanes delivers a powerful plea for peace during one of the darkest periods of Athenian history.To appreciate the urgency of this comedy, one must understand its historical context. Performed shortly after the catastrophic failure of the Athenian Sicilian Expedition, where Athens lost its entire fleet and thousands of lives, the city faced financial ruin, political instability, and the constant threat of Spartan invasion. In the midst of this despair, Aristophanes does not offer a somber lament. Instead, he uses the licence of Old Comedy, with its obscenity, political satire, and carnivalesque fantasy, to imagine a resolution. The strike is not just a domestic joke; it is a seizure of political power. The women do not merely withhold sex. They occupy the Acropolis, the religious heart of the city and the storage place of the public treasury, which shuts down the financial machinery of the war.The Battle of the Acropolis: Seizing the TreasuryThe spatial dynamics of the performance are central to the play's meaning. The skene building is the gateway to the Acropolis, which the women barricade from within. This setting allows Aristophanes to stage a physical battle of the sexes through the double chorus. The Chorus of Men, old and decrepit, arrive bearing heavy logs and smoking torches, intending to burn down the gates and smoke the women out. They are met by the Chorus of Women, carrying heavy water pitchers, who drench the men and extinguish their fires. The physical confrontation ends with the men shivering and soaked. It is a visual metaphor for the play's inversion of power: the old men's dry, destructive fire is completely neutralised by the women's wet, life-giving water.By occupying the Acropolis, the women hit the state where it hurts most: its treasury. The money stored in the Parthenon, largely collected from tribute-paying allies, was the funding for the Athenian navy. By locking up these funds, the women prevent the Magistrate and the senate from building new warships or paying the mercenaries. When the Magistrate arrives with archers to force open the gates, he is met not with submissive pleas, but with an organised wall of women who drive his forces away. Aristophanes turns the sacred citadel of Athens into a domestic fortress. This suggests that the survival of the city requires a complete disruption of its military and financial administration.Spinning the State: The Wool Metaphor and the AgonThe formal debate (agon) between Lysistrata and the Magistrate is the intellectual core of the play. When the Magistrate demands to know why women have locked up the treasury, Lysistrata explains that women have long managed domestic household budgets (oikonomia) and are therefore qualified to manage the public finances of the state. She rejects the Magistrate's claim that war is a man's business, declaring instead that war shall be the business of women. This statement directly subverts Hector's famous command in Homer's Iliad, where he tells Andromache to return to her loom because war is a man's job. She suggests that the domestic labour of women gives them a direct stake in the preservation of the state.To explain how women would fix the corrupted politics of Athens, Lysistrata uses the metaphor of spinning wool. She compares the state to a tangled fleece that has been neglected and dirtied:"First we must wash it in a bath,clean out all the dung and burrs,then card it to tease out the knots,and spin it all together into a great ballfrom which we can weave a new, warm cloak for the people."(translated by Alan H. Sommerstein, p. 166, lines 574–586)This wool metaphor is a powerful political claim. Lysistrata argues that the current politicians have tangled the state through factionalism and corruption. The process of cleaning and spinning represents a corrective policy: cleaning out the corrupt demagogues, integrating the marginalised allies and residents into a unified body, and weaving a new civic garment that protects everyone. Through a domestic, female task, Aristophanes describes the art of statecraft and challenges the male monopoly on political wisdom.The Anatomy of Seduction: Myrrhine, Cinesias, and the Spartan TreatyThe comic energy of the play's second half is driven by the physical reality of the sex strike. Aristophanes stages this frustration through the encounter between Myrrhine and her husband, Cinesias. Cinesias arrives at the Acropolis in extreme physical torment, carrying their crying child in an attempt to guilt his wife into returning home. Myrrhine descends, pretending to comply, but she teases him in a series of delays. She brings out a cot, then a mattress, a pillow, a blanket, and oil, repeatedly promising to submit before she runs back into the citadel and locks the door. The scene reduces the heroic pretensions of the male citizens to a state of absolute, ridiculous vulnerability.The physical distress of the Athenians is mirrored by that of the Spartans, who send a herald to negotiate a treaty. Both sides are represented by actors wearing prominent, oversized phallic costumes, which makes their biological frustration a visible, inescapable part of the performance. When Lysistrata returns to negotiate the peace, she introduces a silent, naked female figure representing Reconciliation (Diallage). The Spartan and Athenian delegates use the body of Reconciliation as a physical map. They negotiate the partition of territories and fit their political demands to the woman's limbs. While this scene relies on objectifying comic tropes, it has a serious diplomatic purpose. Lysistrata lectures both sides on their shared history, their mutual debts, and their common danger from foreign empires. She advocates for a Panhellenic unity that transcends the rivalries of individual city-states.The Afterlife of the Disbander of ArmiesThe subsequent history of Lysistrata reveals a shift in how the play is understood. In classical antiquity, it was viewed primarily as a carnivalesque fantasy, an example of the world-upside-down motif typical of comic festivals rather than a literal political blueprint. The idea of women staging a political strike was considered so absurd that it could only exist in the realm of comedy. However, in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the play was rediscovered as a foundational text of feminist and anti-war literature. Modern directors have stripped away the ancient performance contexts to present the play as a serious critique of militarism and a celebration of female agency.Aristophanes shifts the focus of statecraft from the assembly to the household, and from the battlefield to the body. In doing so, he creates an enduring work that asks who truly pays the cost of war and who has the right to demand peace.
plays.ch5: Original Title: MrcchakatikaDate: c. 3rd–5th century CE | Original language: Sanskrit and Prakrit dialects | Country/tradition: Ancient India (Ujjayini) | Period/movement: Classical Sanskrit Literature (Gupta Dynasty) | Genre: Sanskrit Drama (Prakarana)The Gold and the Clay: World Drama in the Streets of UjjayiniFor readers accustomed to the remote kings and mythological gods of classical Sanskrit drama, The Little Clay Cart (Mrcchakatika) offers a refreshing plunge into the bustling, earthy reality of ancient Indian city life. The play’s central metaphor is a simple domestic scene. A young boy, Rohasena, the son of the impoverished merchant Charudatta, is weeping because he has been given a simple toy cart made of baked clay, while the neighbour's child plays with one made of solid gold. His maid attempts to soothe him, but it is Vasantasena, a wealthy and cultured courtesan who loves Charudatta, who steps in. She strips off her golden jewels, heaps them into the clay cart, and tells the boy that he may now buy his golden toy.This simple act of generosity is the event that sets the entire drama in motion. The clay cart is the raw, unadorned reality of poverty, mortality, and the earth itself, while the golden cart is the artificiality, wealth, and corruption of the royal court. By filling the clay cart with gold, Vasantasena does not merely quiet a crying child. She bridges the social chasm that divides the noble but bankrupt merchant class from the wealthy but marginalised world of the courtesans. The play, attributed to the legendary King Sudraka, uses this domestic symbol to frame a vast, ten-act narrative that combines romance, burglary, political revolution, and a dramatic legal trial. It shows how classical drama can find its greatest insights in the dirty streets of a cosmopolitan city.The Prakarana Form: Subverting the Sanskrit Court TraditionTo understand the formal originality of Mrcchakatika, one must contrast it with the dominant genre of Sanskrit drama: the Nataka. Heroic plays, such as Kalidasa’s Shakuntala, typically draw their plots from sacred epics like the Mahabharata, featuring kings, sages, and gods speaking in elevated, poetic Sanskrit. Sudraka, however, writes in the Prakarana tradition, which is a social comedy of manners with an invented plot set in the contemporary world. Instead of sages and deities, the stage is populated by a crowd of gamblers, shampooers, thieves, cart-drivers, court executioners, and political rebels.This social diversity shows in the play's unique linguistic structure. Sudraka employs a complex system of code-switching between classical Sanskrit and various Prakrit dialects. While the high-status male characters, the merchant Charudatta, his Brahman friend Maitreya, and the intellectual thief Sharvilaka, speak in refined Sanskrit verse, the women, including Vasantasena, and the lower-class characters speak in different forms of Prakrit. The villainous Samsthanaka speaks Magadhi Prakrit, a dialect associated with easterners and court hangers-on, which immediately signals his lack of culture and refinement to the audience. This linguistic division does not merely reflect Gupta-era social structures. It is a source of comic characterisation and social critique, and it allows the lower-class characters to comment satirically on the pretensions of the ruling elite.The Web of Rogues: Sharvilaka and the Art of TheftThe play's subplots show a remarkable sympathy for the criminal and marginalised classes of Ujjayini. The most famous example is the burglary scene in Act III. Sharvilaka, a well-educated Brahman who has turned to theft to secure the funds to buy his lover Madanika's freedom, approaches Charudatta’s house. Before breaking in, he delivers a soliloquy that parodies the scientific and religious manuals of ancient India, treating burglary as a sacred, systematic art. He debates whether to make a breach in the wall in the shape of a lotus, a crescent moon, or a sun, and invokes Skanda, the god of thieves, as his patron.This scene is more than a comic interlude. It exposes the hypocrisy of a society where wealth is hoarded while virtue goes unrewarded. When Sharvilaka successfully steals Vasantasena's jewels, Charudatta is devastated, not by the loss of the property, but by the threat to his honour as a custodian. His wife, Dhuta, secretly surrenders her own pearl necklace to replace the stolen jewels, demonstrating a quiet, noble generosity that matches Charudatta's own. Sudraka portrays these characters, the burglar, the courtesan, the impoverished merchant, and the self-sacrificing wife, as bound together by a shared code of honour. This code contrasts with the lawless greed of the king's brother-in-law, Samsthanaka. Sudraka shows that true nobility (sajjana) has nothing to do with caste or wealth.The Trial and the Gallows: Public Justice and Private VirtueThe climax of the play occurs in the court trial of Act IX, a scene that provides one of the most detailed accounts of ancient Indian jurisprudence in world literature. Charudatta is accused of murdering Vasantasena for her gold. A judge who is committed to justice but hamstrung by Samsthanaka’s political influence presides over the trial. Sudraka exposes the vulnerability of the legal system to manipulation and false evidence. When Vasantasena’s gold jewels, which she had hidden in the clay cart, are found in Maitreya’s pocket during a scuffle, the circumstantial evidence is overwhelming.Charudatta’s response to the accusation is a dignified silence. He refuses to defend himself, partly because he believes Vasantasena is dead, and partly because he is protecting the rebel Aryaka, whom he helped escape in his carriage in Act VII. This silence highlights the conflict between public legal justice and private moral duty. The court condemns Charudatta to death. He is led to the execution ground by two outcaste executioners, who delay the sentence in the hope that a miracle will occur. This delay allows Vasantasena to arrive at the last second, expose Samsthanaka’s crime, and save Charudatta. She was revived by a Buddhist monk, her former shampooer, after Samsthanaka strangled her and left her for dead.The Alchemy of the Toy: The Play's AfterlifeThe resolution of the play is not merely a romantic reunion; it is a political transformation. As Charudatta is saved, news arrives that Aryaka has slain the tyrant Palaka and established a new, just administration. The new king immediately elevates Vasantasena’s social status, releasing her from the legal restrictions of her class and allowing her to marry Charudatta as a legitimate wife. The outcaste executioners are rewarded, and the Buddhist monk is appointed head of all monasteries. This double resolution of romance and politics suggests that private virtue and public justice are bound together: a corrupt state produces a corrupt court, while a just ruler restores moral order to the household.The Little Clay Cart was one of the first Sanskrit plays translated into Western languages, attracting wide acclaim in Europe and America during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Western critics praised its realistic characterisation, its rapid narrative pacing, and its freedom from the rigid mythological conventions that dominated later Indian drama. By centering the action on a child’s toy cart, Sudraka created a work that continues to speak to modern readers. He shows how the raw clay of human life can be transformed through generosity, love, and political courage.
plays.ch6: Original Title: AbhijnanasakuntalamDate: c. 4th–5th century CE | Original language: Sanskrit and Prakrit dialects | Country/tradition: Ancient India (Gupta Empire) | Period/movement: Classical Sanskrit Literature (Gupta Dynasty) | Genre: Sanskrit Drama (Nataka)The Curse of Forgetfulness: The Forest and the CourtMany readers find classical Sanskrit literature remote, knowing it only for its elaborate courtly conventions and mythological genealogies. Yet Kalidasa's The Recognition of Shakuntala (Abhijnanashakuntala) opens with a narrative device that is universally compelling: the tragic loss of memory. A king meets a beautiful maiden in a forest sanctuary. They marry in secret, and he leaves her with his royal signet ring as a pledge of his return. But when she arrives at his court, pregnant and seeking her place, she discovers that a sage's curse has wiped all memory of her from the king's mind. The ring that could prove her identity has slipped from her finger during her journey, leaving her helpless against his accusations of deceit.This epistemic tragedy, the struggle to prove who one is in the face of an absolute blank in another's memory, drives the emotional movement of the play. Kalidasa does not treat this conflict as a simple domestic misunderstanding. Instead, he uses it to explore the tension between two different worlds. On one side is the forest hermitage of Sage Kanva, a sanctuary of plants and animals where human life exists in harmony with nature. On the other side is the royal court of Hastinapura, a space of law, duty (dharma), and political administration. The play traces the painful journey of the protagonist as she is cast out of both spaces, only to find a higher, spiritual reconciliation in a celestial realm. This shows how ancient drama can transform a simple romance into a profound meditation on memory, nature, and the moral responsibilities of power.The Nataka Genre and Rasa Theory: The Aesthetic of EmotionTo understand the artistic success of Shakuntala, one must examine it through the lens of classical Indian dramaturgy. The play is the supreme example of the Nataka genre, a heroic drama in seven acts that draws its plot from epic mythology, in this case the Mahabharata. It features noble characters, elevated poetry, and a focus on the emotional experience of the audience. Unlike Western drama, which often prioritises conflict, action, and character development, classical Sanskrit theatre is structured around Rasa theory, which aims to evoke a specific, refined aesthetic flavour or state of mind in the spectator.Kalidasa designs the play to evoke Sringara Rasa, the romantic or erotic aesthetic, which is divided into two phases: love-in-union (sambhoga) and love-in-separation (vipralambha). The first three acts develop the union of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, painting their forest encounters with a delicate, sensory poetry that captures the first flush of desire. Acts IV through VI transition into the agonising phase of separation, where Shakuntala is rejected and Dushyanta, once his memory is restored, is consumed by grief and regret. The final act, set in a celestial hermitage, achieves a synthesis of these emotions. It transforms the raw passion of their initial meeting into a mature, spiritual love that has been purified by suffering. This structure indicates that true love cannot be resolved in the court or the forest alone. It requires a cosmic trial to harmonise individual desire (kama) with universal duty.The Forest as Sanctuary: Ecological Sympathy in the HermitageThe most celebrated section of the play is Act IV, which details Shakuntala's departure from the forest hermitage to join her husband at court. In this act, Kalidasa treats the natural world not merely as a decorative background, but as an active, feeling character. The plants, vines, and animals of the hermitage are described as Shakuntala’s siblings. When she prepares to leave, Sage Kanva calls upon the trees to bless her journey, noting that she refused to drink water until they were watered and loved them more than her own ornaments.The response of the forest is immediate and tender. The trees offer bridal gifts of silk and jewellery, the deer tear at her garments to prevent her from leaving, and the peacocks stop their dances in grief. This depiction of ecological sympathy is more than a poetic exaggeration. It reflects the philosophical belief in the interconnectedness of all living things. By showing Shakuntala’s deep pain at leaving her forest home, a pain matched by Kanva’s own grief as an adoptive father, Kalidasa establishes the hermitage as a lost paradise of innocence. This makes her subsequent rejection at the cold, legalistic court of Hastinapura all the more devastating.The Structural Magic of the Curse: Vindicating the KingKalidasa’s most significant artistic achievement lies in how he altered his source material. In the original story in the Mahabharata, King Dushyanta is a pragmatic, calculating ruler who remembers Shakuntala perfectly when she arrives at his court. He rejects her solely to protect his royal reputation and avoid public scandal, only accepting her when a voice from heaven (akashavani) validates her claim. While this behaviour is acceptable for a legendary monarch in an epic, it makes him an unsympathetic protagonist in a drama, violating the theatrical requirement that the king be a noble, virtuous hero (dhirodatta).To solve this moral problem, Kalidasa introduced the curse of the volatile Sage Durvasa. By making the king's rejection of Shakuntala the result of an external curse rather than a personal choice, Kalidasa vindicates Dushyanta’s character. The king's harsh words in Act V are not the result of cruelty or cowardice, but of an involuntary, tragic blindness. This change shifts the dramatic conflict from a moral failing to an epistemic tragedy. The audience watches the pregnant Shakuntala plead with a husband who genuinely does not know her, which creates a powerful tragic irony. The recovery of the ring in Act VI, which breaks the curse and restores the king's memory, initiates a period of profound penance and grief that prepares the king for his eventual reunion with his wife and son.The Universal Ring: The Play's AfterlifeThe subsequent history of Shakuntala is an important moment in the development of world literature. Translated into English by Sir William Jones in 1789, the play was the first Sanskrit work to reach a Western audience, triggering a wave of enthusiasm among European Romantics. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was so moved by the play that he composed a celebrated poem in its honour:"Wouldst thou the young year's blossoms and the fruits of its decline,And all by which the soul is charmed, enraptured, feasted, fed,Wouldst thou the earth and heaven itself in one sole name combine?I name thee, O Shakuntala, and all at once is said."Goethe even adapted the structural device of the Sanskrit play's prologue, where the director and actress discuss the performance, for his own masterpiece, Faust.Beyond its historical reception, the play remains a touchstone for the study of dramatic form. It shows how the Indian theatrical tradition developed a highly sophisticated aesthetic system independent of Aristotle's Poetics. By balancing the private passion of the forest with the public duties of the court, and resolving them in a celestial sanctuary, The Recognition of Shakuntala demonstrates that the search for identity is a cosmic journey. It requires both the physical token of the ring and the spiritual purification of memory.
plays.ch7: Original Title: Atsumori (敦盛)Date: c. 1400 | Original language: Classical Japanese | Country/tradition: Muromachi Japan | Period/movement: Noh theatre (Mugen Noh) | Genre: Noh drama / warrior play (shura-mono)The Flute on the Shore: The Ghostly Requiem of Enemy and FriendTo the modern reader, Atsumori presents an extraordinary subversion of the traditional ghost story. Rather than a tale of restless vengeance, Zeami Motokiyo’s fifteenth-century masterpiece offers a profound dramatic ritual of guilt, memory, and mutual salvation. The play frames a universal human conflict, the traumatic aftermath of war, not through the lens of triumphalism, but through the shared sorrow of the victor and the vanquished. A veteran warrior, tormented by the memory of executing a sixteen-year-old boy on a wind-swept beach, renounces his military standing and returns to the scene of his crime. There, he encounters the ghost of his young victim. Yet, instead of a sword-clashing climax of revenge, the drama dissolves the boundaries between enemy and friend, showing how the act of mourning can bind two lives in an eternal spiritual partnership.Composed during the Muromachi period (1336–1573) and first performed in Kyoto by the Kanze troupe, the play was developed for an audience of aristocratic samurai and the shogunal court. Zeami adapted the narrative from the late thirteenth-century military epic Heike monogatari (The Tale of the Heike), specifically the famous episode detailing the Battle of Ichi-no-tani in 1184. In the epic, the rugged warrior Kumagai Naozane defeats the young courtier Taira no Atsumori, only to discover that the boy is the same age as his own son. Forced by military necessity to decapitate him, Kumagai is so devastated by the youth's beauty and the discovery of a flute in his sash that he abandons the warrior path. Zeami’s dramatic choice was to locate the action years after this historical event. He transforms the epic battle into a mugen (dream or vision) Noh drama, where the past is recollected, re-enacted, and ultimately transcended through Buddhist prayer. Using the translation by Royall Tyler, we can analyse how the play uses performance, poetry, and music to dismantle the enmity of war and lead both characters toward enlightenment.Suma Shore: The Setting of Mourning and ImpermanenceThe physical stage of the Noh theatre, with its polished cypress floor, open pillars, and painted pine tree, becomes the melancholic setting of the Suma shore. In Japanese literary tradition, Suma is not merely a geographic location; it is a poetic space associated with exile, loneliness, and the transience of worldly success. It is the shore where Prince Genji suffered his banishment in The Tale of Genji, and it is the site of the catastrophic defeat of the Taira clan. By setting the play on this shore, Zeami creates an atmosphere where the natural world mirrors the internal grief of the characters. The sound of the wind in the pines and the crashing of the waves are auditory representations of the restless spirits that haunt the place.The play opens with the entrance of Renshō, the monastic identity assumed by Kumagai Naozane after his renunciation of the warrior life. As the waki (the supporting actor), Renshō represents the waking world, entering the stage to initiate the spiritual journey. In his opening chant, Renshō establishes the metaphysical framework of the drama:"The world is all a dream, and he who wakes,casting it from him, may yet know the real."This declaration introduces the Buddhist concept of mujō (impermanence), which suggests that the fierce battles of the Genpei War and the glory of the warrior class are nothing more than fleeting illusions. Renshō’s travel song (michiyuki) details his journey from the capital to Suma, a physical pilgrimage that corresponds to his internal quest for absolution. By returning to Suma, Renshō seeks to confront the source of his trauma, intending to offer prayers (nenbutsu) to release Atsumori’s soul from the cycle of suffering. The shore is a liminal space where the living and the dead, the guilty and the slain, can meet to resolve their shared destiny.The Duplicity of the Mask: Grass-Cutter and AristocratAs Renshō arrives at the Suma shore, the silence is broken by the sound of a flute, introducing the central musical motif of the play. This sound heralds the entrance of the maeshite (the first-act protagonist in disguise) and his companions, who appear as humble grass-cutters. This choice of disguise is highly significant. In the social hierarchy of medieval Japan, grass-cutters represent the lowest stratum of rural labourers, yet they enter playing a refined bamboo flute, an instrument associated with the highest levels of Heian court culture. This juxtaposition creates a sense of surprise for Renshō, who speaks to them in wonder:Renshō: I have a question for you mowers. How is it that men of your class, who gain their bread by the sweat of their brow, should play so sweet a melody upon the flute?Grass-cutter: You speak of us as men of low estate, yet music is no respecter of persons. The wind that blows through the reeds does not ask whether they grow in a palace garden or on a barren shore.Renshō: Indeed, your words speak of a wisdom that does not belong to your station. Who are you, then, that cut grass on this lonely shore?Grass-cutter: We are but dwellers in the shadow of Suma, but the memories of the past are not hidden from us.This dialogue (mondō) highlights the democratic potential of art and spiritual practice within the Buddhist worldview. The maeshite argues that even the most impoverished labourers can participate in the beauty of the cosmos, citing the wind in the reeds as a natural flute that plays for all alike.The dramatic irony of the scene is intense: Renshō is conversing with the ghost of the very youth he slew, yet he sees only a rustic mower. The mask worn by the shite actor during this act represents a humble, weathered face, concealing the aristocratic beauty of the historical Atsumori. This concealment mirrors the spiritual ignorance of the characters, who must look past external forms to recognise their deeper connection. When the other grass-cutters depart, the first mower remains behind. He asks Renshō to repeat a ten-fold prayer (nenbutsu) for the dead. As Renshō chants "Namu Amida Butsu," the mower reveals his connection to the deceased courtier. He states that he is "one of Atsumori's kin" before he vanishes into the twilight. This exit (nakairi) is the transition from the earthly disguise of the first act to the supernatural revelation of the second.The Narrative Anchor: The Ai-Kyōgen InterludeFollowing the disappearance of the grass-cutter, the play features an ai-kyōgen interlude, during which a local villager enters to speak with Renshō. In Noh performance, this interlude has a clear structural purpose. While the main acts are written in highly stylised, poetic classical Japanese and performed with slow, ritualistic movements, the kyōgen actor speaks in the vernacular prose of the Muromachi period, providing a clear, realistic summary of the historical events. The villager recounts the details of the Battle of Ichi-no-tani, describing how the Taira clan was driven to the water’s edge and forced to flee on their ships.The narrative focuses on Atsumori's tragic mistake. As the ships withdrew, the young warrior realised he had left behind his beloved flute, Saeda ("Little Branch"), which had been gifted to his grandfather by the Emperor. Returning to the shore to retrieve it, he was cut off from the retreating fleet. Kumagai Naozane spotted him riding his horse through the surf and challenged him to turn back and fight. The villager describes the ensuing combat, emphasizing the contrast between Kumagai's seasoned, battle-hardened strength and Atsumori's delicate, aristocratic grace. When Kumagai unmasked the youth, he was struck by the resemblance to his own son, who had been wounded that same day. He wished to spare the boy, but the arrival of other Minamoto horsemen forced his hand.This prose retelling anchors the poetic, dream-like atmosphere of the drama in concrete historical reality. It ensures that the audience is fully aware of the physical violence and emotional agony that underpin the ghostly encounters. Because they hear the story from the perspective of an objective local witness, the audience can appreciate the depth of Renshō’s guilt and the tragic nature of Atsumori's death, preparing them for the stylized, emotional confrontation that follows in the second act.The Choreography of the Battle and the Lotus ThroneThe second act opens with the entrance of the nochishite (the second-act protagonist), who now appears in his true form as the ghost of Atsumori. He wears a splendid courtier-warrior mask and the magnificent robes of a Taira general, complete with a sword at his waist. Summoned by Renshō’s persistent prayers, the ghost enters to the dramatic, percussive music of the Noh orchestra, which creates an immediate contrast with the quiet, flute-led atmosphere of the first act. Atsumori’s ghost does not seek revenge; rather, he seeks to tell his story, to make Renshō—and the audience—witness the tragic beauty of his short life and the horror of his end.The core of this act is the kuse, a long narrative chant accompanied by a highly stylised dance (chū-no-mai). The chorus (jiutai) sings the narrative while the shite actor mimes the actions, translating the words into elegant physical gestures. The chant describes the cultural life of the Taira clan, who, despite their military power, had adopted the refined, artistic customs of the imperial court. The chorus evokes the final banquet held by the Taira in their temporary palace at Suma:"The Taira lords sat in council,drinking the night away, while the windwhistled through the grass.Atsumori took his flute, Saeda,and played a song of parting,a melody so sweet that even the wild geesestopped to listen in the dark."As the chorus describes this scene, the shite performs the dance with slow, controlled movements, holding his fan to represent the flute. This performance shows the central irony of the Taira warriors: they were soldiers who carried flutes into battle, artists who were forced to become killers.The dance rises in tempo as the narrative shifts to the battle itself. Atsumori mimes the chaotic retreat, the riding of his horse into the waves, and the sudden confrontation with Kumagai. The choreography does not aim for realistic violence; instead, it uses Noh movement to express the internal struggle of the characters. The raise of a hand, the stamping of a foot, and the sweep of a sleeve represent the clash of swords and the desperation of the dying youth. Through this performance, the historical trauma is re-enacted as a living memory that must be processed and resolved on the stage.The climax of the play is the kiri, the final rapid section, which dramatises the resolution of the conflict. In a sudden flash of his past identity, Atsumori’s ghost sees Renshō and recognises him as his murderer:"Now karma brings us face to face again.'You are my foe!' Atsumori shouts,and clears his sword to strike."The ghost draws his sword and advances toward the waki, who remains seated at the front-right pillar of the stage. This physical movement represents the peak of dramatic tension, as the ghost seeks to enact the vengeance that has kept him trapped in the warrior's hell.However, the resolution of this conflict is achieved not through violence, but through a spiritual transformation. Renshō does not raise a weapon; instead, he responds by chanting the nenbutsu, offering his prayers to Amida Buddha for the salvation of his enemy. The power of this prayer disarms the ghost:"But Kumagai with kindness has repaidold enmity, calling the Nameto give the spirit peace.The sword is lowered, the hand is stayed."Atsumori’s ghost realises that the man who killed him is the only person who is actively working to save him. The enemy who cut down his physical life has become the priest who will give him eternal spiritual life.The play concludes with a powerful vision of reconciliation. The chorus sings the final lines as the ghost of Atsumori backs away toward the exit bridge (hashigakari), his form fading into the distance. They shall at last be reborn together upon one lotus throne in paradise (ichiren-takashō). This image is the supreme symbol of Buddhist reconciliation. It suggests that in the ultimate reality of the Western Paradise, the distinction between victor and victim is dissolved. Through this resolution, Zeami’s Atsumori transcends the specific historical trauma of the Genpei War, offering its audience a universal model for the healing of political and personal division. The play demonstrates that peace is achieved not by defeating the enemy, but by recognising our shared humanity.
plays.ch8: Original Title: EverymanDate: c. 1510 | Original language: Middle English | Country/tradition: Late Medieval England | Period/movement: Late Medieval Morality Drama | Genre: Morality PlayThe Unexpected Audit: The Morality Play as Existential TrialModern readers do well to approach Everyman not as a relic of medieval Catholic dogma, but as the archetype of the existential audit. The play is a psychological thriller in which the protagonist is suddenly handed an eviction notice from life itself. A successful, complacent individual is stopped on the street by an unbribable collector and told that he must immediately pack his bags for a long, perilous journey from which there is no return. He must bring a ledger detailing every action, word, and thought he has ever had, to be audited by a supreme judge. The play is a dramatic simulation of the ultimate isolation chamber: the process of dying. It strips its central character of every external prop, wealth, family, friends, and even his own physical and mental faculties, until he stands entirely alone on the brink of the grave.Written in the late fifteenth century and printed in London in the early sixteenth century (between 1510 and 1530 by John Skot and Richard Pynson), Everyman is a classic of the morality play genre. Unlike the earlier mystery cycles, which staged the grand sweep of biblical history from Creation to Doomsday, or miracle plays, which dramatised the lives of the saints, the morality play focuses on the moral journey of the individual human soul. The characters are allegorical personifications of abstract concepts, social relations, and physical attributes. The play is an adaptation of the Dutch play Elckerlijc, written by Peter van Diest and first printed in 1506. In the pre-Reformation context of Tudor England, the play acted as a sermon on the necessity of the Catholic sacramental system. Using A. C. Cawley's edition of the text, we can analyse how the play converts theological doctrine into compelling dramatic action, presenting the dissolution of the self as a universal human experience.The Architecture of Abandonment: The Failure of the WorldThe dramatic momentum of the first half of Everyman is driven by a series of confrontations that systematically dismantle the protagonist's worldly attachments. The action begins with God's monologue, in which the Creator laments that humanity is drowned in sin and blind to spiritual reality. God summons Death, his mighty messenger, to deliver the decree of judgment to Everyman. When Death encounters the protagonist, Everyman is walking in carefree ease, his mind occupied with worldly pleasures and financial transactions. This sudden intrusion creates the central conflict between human time, which is perceived as infinite, and cosmic time, which is absolute and unpredictable. Everyman’s immediate reaction is to attempt to buy his way out of the summons, offering Death a thousand pounds to defer the matter. This futile attempt at bribery is a satire on the commercial values of the rising Tudor merchant class; Everyman assumes that the transaction-based logic of the marketplace applies to the absolute economy of mortality.When Death refuses the bribe but allows Everyman to seek companions for his journey, the play enters its phase of systematic abandonment. Everyman first turns to Fellowship, who stands for social intimacy, friendship, and the camaraderie of the tavern. Fellowship’s initial declarations of loyalty are extravagant. He promises to accompany Everyman through any danger, even to hell itself. However, the moment Fellowship learns that the destination is the grave and the purpose is the final audit before God, he recoils:"If we should take that journey,I should have no pleasure in that land.Nay, Everyman, I will not go that way!I will not look upon that book of accounts,For all the gold in the world."(translated by A. C. Cawley, lines 249-253)Fellowship’s departure is swift and brutal, exposing the superficiality of social bonds when confronted by the reality of death. Everyman next turns to Kindred and Cousin, who stand for the bonds of family and blood. Like Fellowship, they make grand promises of support, only to retract them with comical haste. Cousin excuses himself by claiming a sudden cramp in his toe, while Kindred offers to send his maid instead.The most devastating rejection comes from Goods, the personification of Everyman's accumulated wealth and material possessions. Goods is discovered lying in a dark corner of the stage, surrounded by chests, bags, and sacks of gold. This staging is a physical metaphor for the spiritual paralysis of a life dedicated to the accumulation of property. Everyman appeals to Goods to ease his sorrow, but Goods reveals that his presence is actually the cause of Everyman’s damnation:"Nay, Everyman, I say no.As for a while I was lent to thee,But now I must be gone.My love is contrary to the love of the Creator;If thou hadst loved me moderately,Thou mightest have been saved."(translated by A. C. Cawley, lines 472-477)Goods explains that wealth is merely a loan from God, not a possession. By worshipping the gift rather than the giver, Everyman has sealed his ruin. Goods’s mocking departure leaves Everyman in a state of absolute spiritual bankruptcy. This shows that the things we own during life are the very things that own and destroy us at the moment of death.The Bind of Sin and the Sacramental RescueHaving been stripped of Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, and Goods, Everyman is forced to look inward. He remembers Good Deeds, the personification of his charitable actions and moral virtues. However, when he approaches her, he finds her lying cold in the ground, bound hand and foot by his sins. Good Deeds is so weak she cannot even stand, let alone walk with him on his pilgrimage. This staging is a clear representation of the Catholic doctrine of sin: bad actions do not merely accumulate in a ledger; they actively cripple the soul's capacity for virtue. Everyman's neglect of his spiritual life has left his Good Deeds paralysed and useless.The turning point occurs with the introduction of Knowledge, the sister of Good Deeds. Knowledge represents the intellectual understanding of Christian doctrine and the teachings of the Church. She is the guide who promises to stand by Everyman in his hour of need. Knowledge does not save Everyman directly; instead, she leads him to the house of Confession. Confession is a holy man living in a sanctuary, who gives Everyman the scourge of penance. The physical act of scourging on the stage is a crucial dramatic gesture. It represents the mortification of the flesh, the active punishment of the body that has led the soul into sin. As Everyman kneels, prays, and scourges himself, he participates in a ritual of purification. Good Deeds is suddenly freed from her bonds and rises to her feet.This dramatic sequence is an defence of the pre-Reformation Catholic sacramental system. The play insists that good works alone are insufficient for salvation; they must be activated and purified through the sacraments of the Church. Without the institutional priesthood and the rite of confession, Everyman’s good deeds would remain buried in the clay. Once Good Deeds is restored, she joins Knowledge in preparing Everyman for the final stage of his journey. They instruct him to put on the garment of contrition and to summon his internal, personal attributes: Strength, Beauty, Discretion, and his Five Wits.The Dissolution of the Self: The Edge of the GraveThe final movement of the play represents the ultimate stage of the existential trial: the dissolution of the physical and mental self. Unlike Fellowship and Goods, who represent external relationships, Strength, Beauty, Discretion, and Five Wits are internal to the human subject. They are the components of human identity. As Everyman approaches the grave, he believes that these loyal companions will go down into the earth with him. They make solemn vows of fidelity, with Strength declaring that he will stand by him till he sees him go into the grave.However, when Everyman reaches the edge of the pit and prepares to step in, the physical reality of decay asserts itself. One by one, these internal faculties abandon him, tracing the progressive collapse of the body during the process of dying. Beauty is the first to flee, horrified by the sight of the open grave. Strength follows immediately after, refusing to spend his power in the dust. Discretion, witnessing the departure of Strength, also takes his leave, arguing that when strength fails, discretion must depart as well. Finally, Five Wits deserts the protagonist, leaving him blind, deaf, and insensible to the world.This sequence of abandonment is the most poetically and dramatically intense part of the play. It stages the systematic dismantling of the ego. The protagonist is stripped of his looks, his power, his judgment, and his senses, leaving only the bare core of the spirit. Even Knowledge must stop at the edge of the grave. She can watch him descend, she can explain the mystery of his transition, but she cannot cross the threshold into the afterlife. Only Good Deeds, the sole entity that was once too weak to stand, descends into the dark earth with him:"All earthly things is but vanity.Beauty, Strength, and Discretion do forsake me;Five Wits and Knowledge run from me;Only my Good Deeds will go with me."(translated by A. C. Cawley, lines 867-870)The descent of Everyman and Good Deeds into the grave is followed by the appearance of an Angel, who receives Everyman's soul and announces that his account is clear. The play ends with a sermon by a Doctor (a theologian), who reminds the audience that after death, no physician, no lawyer, and no amount of gold can help them. Only their good deeds, purified by the sacraments, will stand between them and eternal damnation.The Afterlife of the Mortal SummonsDespite its deeply medieval Catholic theology, Everyman remains popular in modern theatre. This popularity shows that its existential theme is universal. During the Reformation, the play was suppressed in England because of its explicit praise of the priesthood and its emphasis on sacramental penance. It remained unperformed for nearly four centuries until it was rediscovered in 1901 by the theatre director William Poel. Poel staged the play in the master's court of the Charterhouse in London, using simple staging and a restrained, ritualistic style. The production was an unexpected success, establishing Everyman as a masterpiece of world drama rather than a historical curiosity.In 1911, the Austrian playwright Hugo von Hofmannsthal adapted the play as Jedermann (Everyman), translating the medieval English text into German rhyming couplets and expanding the narrative to focus on the capitalist greed and redemption of a wealthy merchant. Staged by Max Reinhardt in front of the Salzburg Cathedral, Jedermann became the founding production of the Salzburg Festival, where it has been performed annually ever since. In the twenty-first century, the play’s structure has been reinterpreted by contemporary dramatists. In 2017, Branden Jacobs-Jenkins adapted the play as Everybody, in which the roles are assigned to the actors by a lottery at the beginning of each performance, reflecting the unpredictable nature of Death’s summons. By translating the medieval figures of Fellowship and Goods into modern concepts like "Friendship" and "Stuff," Jacobs-Jenkins demonstrates that the core conflict of Everyman, the sudden, terrifying demand to account for the value of one's life, remains as urgent to modern audiences as it was to the churchgoers of Tudor England.
plays.ch9: Original Title: The Spanish Tragedy, or Hieronimo is Mad AgainDate: c. 1587 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan Drama / Early Modern Revenge Tragedy | Genre: Revenge TragedyThe Ancestor of Hamlet: The Theatre of Bloody RetributionModern readers do well to treat The Spanish Tragedy not as a crude predecessor to Shakespeare’s masterpieces, but as the foundational archetype of the revenge thriller. Long before Hamlet paced the ramparts of Elsinore or planned to catch the conscience of a king, Thomas Kyd’s Elizabethan play established the grammar of theatrical vengeance. The play is a parent's worst nightmare: a father, who is the chief judge of the realm, wakes in the middle of the night to the screams of his child, only to find his son's bloody corpse hanging from a tree in his own garden. When the legal system fails him, blocked by political corruption and the Machiavellian schemes of the royal family, the father is forced to turn himself from a minister of justice into an executioner. He stages a play that is ostensibly a harmless courtly entertainment, but which conceals a lethal reality, transforming the theatre itself into a slaughterhouse.Composed around 1587 and first printed in 1592, The Spanish Tragedy was a massive bestseller of the Elizabethan stage. It was performed dozens of times in the 1590s by companies such as Strange’s Men and the Admiral’s Men, drawing large crowds at venues like the Rose Theatre. Kyd, the son of a London scrivener, lacked the university education of contemporaries like Christopher Marlowe or Robert Greene, yet he possessed an extraordinary sense of theatrical design and rhetorical pacing. He fused the formal structures of Roman Senecan tragedy, specifically its ghosts, underworld imagery, and rhetoric of extreme grief, with the fast paced, violent plotting of popular English drama. Using Philip Edwards’s edition of the text, we can analyse how Kyd uses metatheatrical frames, symbolic settings, and the breakdown of language to explore the moral corruption of private revenge and the failure of earthly justice.Metatheatre and the Underworld Frame: Spectators to SlaughterThe most innovative structural feature of The Spanish Tragedy is its metatheatrical design, which establishes three distinct levels of reality and spectatorship on the stage. Before the action of the Spanish and Portuguese courts begins, the play introduces a supernatural frame. The Ghost of Don Andrea, a Spanish nobleman slain in the wars with Portugal, enters with the personification of Revenge. Having traversed the classical underworld, which Kyd describes in vivid terms that map a subterranean geography of judgment, Andrea returns to the mortal world. Revenge promises him that he will witness the destruction of his killer, Prince Balthazar. The two supernatural figures do not exit. Instead, they sit down on the edge of the stage, serving as a permanent audience within the theatre.This frame changes the way the main plot is received by the audience. The political intrigues, the love affairs, and the violent deaths of the Spanish court are framed not as open-ended events, but as a pre-ordained performance staged for the satisfaction of a ghost. The characters on stage believe they act with free will, choosing their lovers and plotting their crimes. Yet the audience is constantly reminded that their actions are merely scenes in a cosmic script of retribution. When the main action slows down, the Ghost of Andrea complains that his enemies are prospering, only for Revenge to urge patience, reminding him that the tragedy moves inexorably toward its bloody climax. This structural device forces the theatre audience to share the position of the ghost, viewing the characters as doomed puppets whose lives are already forfeit to the gods of the underworld.The Garden Bower: The Topography of Love and MurderThe turning point of the dramatic action occurs in Hieronimo’s garden, a setting that Kyd uses as a symbolic space. In Elizabethan literature, the garden or arbor is typically a place of courtly love, pastoral innocence, and social retreat. It is a space protected from the corrupting influence of the court, where characters can speak their minds and express their desires. Kyd establishes this expectation in Act II, Scene 2, as Horatio and Bel-imperia meet in the arbor to declare their love. Their dialogue is written in highly stylised verse, where their voices alternate in symmetrical patterns that mimic the formal design of a Renaissance garden:Horatio: My love is pure, and lives in thy look.Bel-imperia: My look is yours, and in your heart is writ.Horatio: Then let us join our hands to seal this vow.Bel-imperia: And let our hearts be joined in holy bond.This pastoral innocence is violently shattered in Act II, Scene 4. As the lovers meet again by night in the bower, they are ambushed by Lorenzo, Balthazar, and their servants. The attackers hang Horatio's body from a tree in the arbor and stab him repeatedly. This act of violence desecrates the garden space, turning a site of fertility and love into a gallows and a slaughterhouse.When Hieronimo enters in his nightshirt, summoned by Bel-imperia's screams, he finds his son's corpse hanging from the tree. The physical image of the father gazing up at his suspended child is the central emblem of the play’s grief. The garden is no longer a private retreat; it has become a monument to trauma. Hieronimo dips a handkerchief in Horatio’s blood, vowing never to bury his son or part with the bloody cloth until he is avenged. The arbor itself is a character in the tragedy of Hieronimo’s wife, Isabella, who is driven mad by the sight of the barren trees. In Act IV, Scene 2, she returns to the garden with a knife, cursing the earth for allowing the murder to happen:"Down with these branches and these loathsome boughsThat shadowed my Horatio’s death!...Earth, curse no more thy womb, but clear thy fruit,For here Horatio’s blood was shed!"By cutting down the trees before stabbing herself, Isabella seeks to destroy the natural world that witnessed her son's murder. Kyd uses this topography to show how trauma infects the physical environment, transforming the beauty of nature into an intolerable reminder of loss.Rhetoric, Madness, and the 1602 AdditionsHieronimo responds to his son's murder by descending into a grief-induced madness, a psychological state that Kyd explores through formal rhetoric. In the sixteenth century, madness on the stage was often represented through wild, disjointed speech, but Kyd initially maintains a high degree of rhetorical symmetry in Hieronimo's laments. The famous soliloquy in Act III, Scene 2, begins with a series of balanced, antithetical lines:"O eyes, no eyes, but fountains fraught with tears;O life, no life, but lively form of death;O world, no world, but mass of public wrongs,Confus'd and fill'd with murder and misdeeds!"This use of anaphora and symploce suggests that Hieronimo is attempting to impose a formal, legal order on his grief. As the Knight Marshal, the chief judge of Spain, he is trained to resolve conflict through the structured language of the law. However, as his appeals to the King are repeatedly blocked by Lorenzo, the symmetry of his speech begins to break down. This shows the collapse of his faith in earthly justice.The representation of Hieronimo’s madness was significantly altered by the publication of the 1602 quarto, which included five major additions to the text. These passages, commonly attributed by modern scholars to William Shakespeare rather than Ben Jonson, focus on the psychological depth of Hieronimo’s grief. In the painter's scene, Hieronimo commissions a painter to paint a picture of his house, his family, and the murder of his son. He asks the painter to capture the exact sound of his cries and the physical sensation of his despair. This scene shifts the focus of the madness from a rhetorical posture to a desperate attempt to represent the unrepresentable. The additions suggest that Hieronimo’s mind has been shattered by the specific, intolerable reality of his son's absence. By showing Hieronimo digging at the dirt with his dagger or mistaking an old man for his own reflection, Kyd and his later reviser represent madness as the only logical response to a world where justice is dead.The Severed Tongue and the Play-Within-a-PlayThe climax of the tragedy is the performance of Hieronimo’s play-within-a-play, The Tragedy of Soliman and Perseda, before the Spanish King and the Portuguese Viceroy. This play-within-a-play lets Hieronimo execute his revenge under the guise of courtly theatricality. He assigns the roles of the play to Lorenzo and Balthazar, while he and Bel-imperia play the remaining parts. He insists that the play be performed in multiple languages, Latin, Greek, Italian, and French, a detail that creates a sense of confusion and ritualistic distance. During the performance, Hieronimo and Bel-imperia use real weapons instead of stage props. They stab Lorenzo and Balthazar to death in front of their unsuspecting fathers.The theatrical power of this scene comes from the division between the courtly audience, who applaud the realistic acting, and the theatre audience, who know that the deaths are real. The boundary between illusion and reality collapses. When the play ends and Hieronimo reveals the corpse of his son Horatio, he stops the performance to deliver his final explanation. He has used the theatre to bypass the corrupt legal system, turning the stage into a court of absolute retribution.Yet the most radical moment of the play occurs after the slaughter is revealed. When the King and the Duke of Castile demand that Hieronimo speak and name his accomplices, Hieronimo refuses to comply. In a shocking act of self-mutilation, he bites out his own tongue:"What, lesser than a heliotrope?Didst thou think I would have spoke?No! My tongue shall never betray my heart;And thus I bite it out to seal my silence."This act rejects the rhetoric Hieronimo uses throughout the play. Having used language to deceive his enemies and stage his revenge, Hieronimo realises that words are no longer sufficient to contain his trauma. His self-mutilation is a physical rejection of the courtly world that denied him justice. By biting out his tongue, Hieronimo enters a state of absolute silence, which suggests that the ultimate reality of grief lies beyond the reach of theatrical representation. When he calls for a knife to mend his pen and instead stabs Castile and himself, he confirms that in Kyd's tragic world, the only final statement is the act of death itself. The Spanish Tragedy ends by silencing its chief orator, leaving the stage littered with corpses. The play leaves the task of final judgment to the supernatural audience of Andrea and Revenge, who return to lead the characters to their respective heavens and hells.
plays.ch10: Original Title: The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor FaustusDate: c. 1592 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan Drama / Renaissance Humanism | Genre: TragedyThe Humanist Bargain: The Tragedy of Intellectual OverreachingModern readers easily recognise the dilemma in Doctor Faustus: the temptation to barter one's spiritual integrity for immediate, absolute power. Christopher Marlowe’s play is the classic exploration of this bargain. It takes a universal human fantasy—the desire to escape the physical and temporal limits of our existence—and subjects it to the rigorous theology of Tudor England. Faustus is a brilliant scholar who has reached the summit of human learning, only to find the view from the peak disappointing. His tragedy begins not with a desire to do evil, but with a restless boredom. He has mastered logic, medicine, law, and theology, yet he remains "still but Faustus, and a man." In his Wittenberg study, surrounded by the monuments of human civilisation, he searches for a discipline that can offer him more than mere understanding; he demands agency, dominion, and a kind of godhead on earth.This quest for absolute autonomy is the defining feature of the Renaissance humanist project, but Marlowe frames it as a dangerous transgression. The opening chorus, performed by a singular figure who acts as a moral commentator, establishes Faustus’s low origins. Born of "parents base of stock" in Germany, Faustus rises through merit and intellect, gaining the title of doctor in divinity. However, the Chorus warns that Faustus’s intellectual growth is like the flight of Icarus:"Waxen wings did mount above his reach,And melting heavens conspir'd his overthrow.For, falling to a devilish exercise,And glutted now with learning's golden gifts,He surfeits upon cursed necromancy."When Faustus enters his study, he systematically reviews and rejects the traditional university curriculum. He dismisses Aristotelian logic because its only end is "to dispute well"; he rejects Galenic medicine because, despite his ability to cure plagues, he cannot bring the dead back to life; he discards Justinian's law as a paltry legacy fit only for a mercenary mind; and he misreads the Holy Scriptures. By combining the biblical passages "The wages of sin is death" and "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves," Faustus constructs a fatalistic syllogism: we must sin, and therefore we must die an everlasting death. He choices to abandon divinity in favour of magic, which promises to make him "a mighty god." By focusing solely on the certainty of damnation and ignoring the Protestant doctrine of grace, Faustus rationalises his descent into the occult as an act of logical necessity.The Divided Self: Morality Conventions and Humanist PsychologyDoctor Faustus stands at the historical threshold between the medieval theatrical tradition and the early modern professional theatre. Structurally, the play is heavily indebted to the late medieval English morality play, a genre where allegorical characters fight for the soul of a representative figure, such as in Everyman. Marlowe retains many of these formal devices, including the Good and Evil Angels, who appear at key moments of hesitation to offer conflicting counsel, and the pageant of the Seven Deadly Sins, summoned by Lucifer to entertain Faustus and distract him from thoughts of repentance. Even the comic characters, such as the clown Robin and the horse-courser, function as low-comedy reflections of the protagonist's spiritual degradation. They show how Faustus’s high-minded desire for cosmic power is mirrored by the base appetites of the vulgar.However, Marlowe transforms these medieval conventions by relocating the conflict from a universal cosmic stage to the internal, psychological space of the individual. The Good and Evil Angels are not merely objective celestial messengers; they represent the fractured chambers of Faustus’s own conscience. When they speak, they voice the internal arguments that torment Faustus in his moments of isolation. The Good Angel appeals to Faustus’s memory of divine order and the promise of heaven, while the Evil Angel appeals to his pride, his lust for sensory pleasure, and his fear of damnation. This internal conflict, known as psychomachia, is expressed through Marlowe’s innovative use of the tragic soliloquy. Unlike the flat, rhetorical speeches of earlier English drama, Faustus’s soliloquies capture the erratic movement of a mind in torment. He vacillates between arrogance and terror, intellectual confidence and spiritual despair.This psychological depth is further enhanced by Mephistophilis, who serves as a complex dramatic foil to Faustus. Unlike the typical comic devils of the medieval stage, who were designed to terrify and amuse the audience with firecrackers and grotesque masks, Mephistophilis has a quiet, melancholy grandeur. He is a servant of Lucifer, but he is also a tragic figure who knows the reality of what he has lost. When Faustus asks how Mephistophilis can be out of hell, the devil responds with an agonising definition of eternal loss:"Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it.Think'st thou that I, who saw the face of God,And tasted the eternal joys of heaven,Am not tormented with ten thousand hellsIn being depriv'd of everlasting bliss?"The tragedy of the scene lies in the intellectual inversion of the speakers.
