Mephistophilis, the immortal spirit, warns Faustus of the reality of damnation, while Faustus, the mortal man, arrogantly tells the devil to "scorn those joys, and write them trivial." Faustus’s intellectual pride blinds him to the warnings of the very demon he has summoned, showing how the humanist quest for self-determination can degenerate into a wilful refusal of reality.The Geography of Damnation: Hell as a State of ConsciousnessOne of Marlowe’s most radical theological innovations in Doctor Faustus is the dematerialisation of hell. In the late sixteenth century, the popular imagination still conceived of hell as a physical location, a subterranean pit of fire, brimstone, and physical torture. Marlowe, however, presents a modern, subjective, and psychological view of damnation. When Faustus asks Mephistophilis where hell is located, the devil replies:"Hell hath no limits, nor is circumscrib'dIn one self place; for where we are is hell,And where hell is, must we ever be.And, to conclude, when all the world dissolves,And every creature shall be purified,All places shall be hell that is not heaven."Under this definition, hell is not a geographical space but an existential state: the condition of being permanently separated from the presence of God. This conceptualisation shifts the focus of the tragedy from external punishment to internal torment. Faustus’s damnation does not begin when he is dragged off the stage at the end of the play. It begins the moment he signs the pact, as he gradually alienates himself from his fellow humans and his Creator.This internalised hell shows in the triviality of Faustus’s achievements. Having sold his soul for twenty-four years of absolute power, Faustus spends his time performing cheap theatrical tricks. He travels to Rome on a dragon, only to make himself invisible and box the ears of the Pope; he visits the court of the Emperor Charles V, where he conjures the horns of Actaeon onto the head of a sceptical knight; and he swindles a local horse-courser with a horse that turns into a bundle of straw. In the context of the play's moral structure, these comic scenes demonstrate the vanity of Faustus's bargain. The grand, cosmic ambitions that Faustus articulates in the opening scene, to join the hills that bind the African shore, to search the ocean for pearls, and to read the secrets of foreign kings, curdle into cheap conjuring and petty court entertainment. The power of the devil is sterile and performative, unable to create anything of genuine value or to satisfy the restless intellect of the scholar. Faustus’s geographical wanderings across the map of Europe are a flight from himself, a desperate attempt to escape the growing realisation that the hell he feared is already expanding within his own mind.The Desolate Epilogue: Despair and the Rhetoric of the Final HourThe emotional climax of the play is Faustus’s final hour on earth, represented by a soliloquy that is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements of English dramatic poetry. Marlowe structures the scene with a terrifying temporal precision. The stage direction indicates the passage of time: "The clock strikes eleven," then "half-past," and finally "twelve." This mechanical progression contrasts with Faustus's desperate desire to stop the movement of the cosmos. He begins by crying out:"Stand still, you ever-moving spheres of heaven,That time may cease and midnight never come!Fair Nature's eye, rise, rise again, and makeNew day an everlasting hour;Or let this hour be but a year, a month, a week, a natural day,That Faustus may repent and save his soul!"The rhetoric shifts from the grand command of "Stand still" to the pathetic begging for "but a year, a month." Faustus appeals to the cosmological order he once sought to master, but the universe remains indifferent to his cries, continuing its steady, mechanical march toward his destruction.The tragic tension of the final scene is rooted in the Protestant theology of repentance and despair (wanhope). Throughout the play, Faustus is reminded that repentance is always possible. Even in the fifth act, the Old Man arrives to assure Faustus that "mercy is suggested to thy soul" and that Christ's blood can wash away his sins. Yet Faustus is unable to repent. His inability is not due to a lack of divine grace, but to his own psychological paralysis. He has lived so long in the belief that he is uniquely damned that he cannot imagine himself as an object of divine mercy. When he looks to the heavens in his final hour, he sees the blood of Christ streaming in the firmament, but he cannot reach it:"See, see where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!One drop would save my soul, half a drop: ah, my Christ!Ah, rend not my heart for naming of my Christ!Yet will I call on him: O, spare me, Lucifer!"The swift transition from "ah, my Christ!" to "O, spare me, Lucifer!" shows the absolute fracture of Faustus's will. He is caught in a spiritual struggle, desiring salvation but terrified of the devil’s immediate physical violence. His despair is the ultimate expression of his pride. He believes his sins are so great that not even the blood of Christ can wash them away, thereby claiming an exceptional status in damnation that mirrors his exceptional status in learning. In his final moments, Faustus pleads to be transformed into an animal, whose soul dissolves into the earth at death, or to be reduced to water drops that cannot be identified. He seeks to escape his human identity, the very self-fashioning he had sought to celebrate. The tragedy closes with his final, desperate cry: "I'll burn my books!—Ah, Mephistophilis!" (5.2.190), a poignant admission that his search for knowledge was the engine of his destruction.The Textual Double and the Faustian LegacyThe performance history and textual transmission of Doctor Faustus are as complex as the play's theological concerns. The play was first performed around 1592 by the Lord Admiral's Men. The lead role was played by Edward Alleyn, whose physical stature and powerful delivery were custom-built for Marlowe's mighty blank verse. The complexity of the play is further compounded by its division into two distinct printed versions: the A-text of 1604 and the B-text of 1616. The A-text is shorter, containing 1,517 lines, and is generally preferred by modern critics who value its focus on Faustus's internal psychological torment. The B-text, printed twelve years later, is significantly longer at 2,121 lines. It contains substantial additions, including expanded anti-Catholic satire in the Rome scenes, more elaborate comic subplots involving the characters Robin, Dick, and Benvolio, and a much more active and visible presence of the devils, who mock Faustus and witness his final descent into hell. Scholars believe that the B-text represents the collaborative revisions paid for by the theatre manager Philip Henslowe in 1602. The choice between the A and B texts shapes the overall meaning of the tragedy. The A-text presents a humanist tragedy of individual despair, while the B-text offers a more spectacular Jacobean play that emphasises the external machinery of damnation.Despite these textual divisions, the figure of Faustus has remained a cornerstone of Western literature. Marlowe’s play established the Faustian myth in the English-speaking world, providing the template for subsequent explorations of the theme, most notably Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Faust (1808). While Goethe’s protagonist is saved through his restless strive and the intervention of divine love, Marlowe’s Faustus remains locked in the darker Calvinist universe of his own making. Mann’s novel Doctor Faustus (1947) used the myth to explore Germany's descent into fascism, framing the nation's collapse as a pact with the devil. In an age of nuclear weapons, genetic engineering, and artificial intelligence, Marlowe’s portrait of a brilliant mind destroyed by its own refusal to accept limits remains a prophetic warning. The play warns us that the pursuit of absolute power over the natural world, when divorced from moral responsibility and human limits, leads inevitably to the disintegration of the self.
plays.ch11: Original Title: The Troublesome Reign and Lamentable Death of Edward the SecondDate: c. 1592 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan Drama / History Play | Genre: History Play / Chronicle HistoryThe Crown and the Companion: The Tragedy of Personal SovereigntyModern audiences recognise Edward II as a sharp study of political crisis. The play explores the explosive point where a ruler's personal desires collide with the security of the state. One might compare Edward’s plight to the abdication crisis of King Edward VIII in 1936, who chose his relationship with Wallis Simpson over the British throne, or to any leader whose attachments invite charges of corruption. Christopher Marlowe’s drama is not a patriotic celebration of English history; it is a clinical, brutal analysis of political vulnerability. The play asks a fundamental question: does a king have the right to a private life, or does the crown demand the absolute surrender of the self? Edward’s tragedy is that he insists on treating his kingdom as his personal property and his royal authority as a shield for his private attachments. For Edward, the crown is not a sacred duty, but a source of personal pleasure and a treasury to be spent on his beloved companion, Piers Gaveston.This confusion of the personal and the political is established in the very first scene. The drama opens not with a royal council or a battlefield, but with Piers Gaveston reading a letter from the newly crowned king. The letter invites him to share the wealth of England: "My father is deceased, come Gaveston, / And share the kingdom with thy dearest friend." When Edward enters, he immediately clashes with the established nobility, Lancaster, Warwick, and the Mortimers, who object to Gaveston’s recall from exile. Edward’s response is petulant defiance. He declares that he would rather see his kingdom divided or flooded than be separated from his favourite:"Thy worth, sweet friend, is far above my gifts,Therefore, to equal it, receive my heart;If for these dignities thou be envied,I'll give thee more, for but to honour thee,Is Edward pleas'd with kingly regiment."By defining his "regiment" (his sovereign rule) purely as a means to honour Gaveston, Edward abdicates the responsibilities of his office. He turns the state into a currency for the purchase of personal affection, setting himself on a collision course with a nobility that views the king's private passions as a threat to their privileges and the stability of the realm.The Anatomy of the Favourite: Class, Foreignness, and Aristocratic PrideThe conflict between Edward and his barons is often read as a struggle between absolute monarchy and aristocratic oligarchy, but Marlowe grounds this political debate in the realities of class resentment and cultural xenophobia. Piers Gaveston is not merely a passive object of the king's devotion; he is an active, insolent social climber who delights in mocking the martial traditions of the English nobility. In his opening monologue, Gaveston reveals his plan to captivate the king through Italianate pageantry, music, and sensual entertainment, importing continental customs to corrupt the English court. He describes how he will draw the king with "wanton poets, pleasant wits, / Musicians, that with touching of a string / May draw the pliant king which way they please." To the barons, Gaveston is a double threat: he is a foreigner who threatens the cultural purity of the court, and he is a low-born upstart who threatens the feudal hierarchy.The barons' objections to Gaveston are framed in language that betrays a deep anxiety over social mobility. Mortimer Junior is particularly outraged by Gaveston's insolent display of wealth, describing how the favourite walks through the streets of London in lavish garb and foreign silks, looking down upon the native nobility:"He wears a lord's revenue on his back,And Midas-like he walks darling the wind,With base outlandish hangers at his heels,Who, at his nod, do take the wall of him,And jet it in the court, under our noses."The image of Gaveston wearing "a lord's revenue on his back" is a direct attack on the economic basis of aristocratic power. The barons view Edward's favouritism as a form of economic theft. The lands and titles that should be used to reward the loyal service of the nobility are instead lavished on an upstart who mocks them. This class conflict is repeated later with the rise of Baldock and the Spencers, who similarly climb to power through the king's favour. Marlowe shows that the barons’ rebellion is driven not by a patriotic desire to reform the commonwealth, but by a conservative, aristocratic pride that cannot tolerate the subversion of the traditional social order.The Machiavellian Ascent: Mortimer Junior and the Realpolitik of UsurpationIn sharp contrast to Edward's political passivity, Mortimer Junior represents the rapid, ruthless rise of the Machiavellian politician. Mortimer begins the play as a hot-headed baron, defending his family's honour and the feudal rights of the nobility. However, as the conflict with the king intensifies, Mortimer’s character undergoes a dark transformation. He becomes a cold, calculating politician who recognises that authority is not a divine right, but a product of force and cunning. Following the defeat of the barons at Boroughbridge, Mortimer is imprisoned in the Tower, but he quickly escapes to France, where he aligns himself with the neglected Queen Isabella. Together, they raise an army and return to England, not to restore order to the state, but to seize control of it.Mortimer’s usurpation of the throne shows a complete disregard for traditional moral and legal boundaries. Having deposed Edward II, Mortimer rules England as Lord Protector, keeping the young King Edward III under his control. He recognises that his power is illegitimate and can only be maintained through violence and terror. This realpolitik shows in his decision to execute the deposed king. To shield himself from the legal consequences of regicide, Mortimer employs a double-meaning Latin letter sent to the king's jailers:"Edwardum occidere nolite timere bonum est.Fear not to kill the king, 'tis good he die.But read it thus, and that's another sense:To kill the king fear not, 'tis good to fear.Unpointed as it is, thus shall it go,That being dead, if it should be betray'd,Our letters shall equivocate the deed."This linguistic manipulation shows how Mortimer uses language as a weapon of statecraft, exploiting ambiguity to avoid responsibility for the crime. His rise represents the displacement of traditional feudal loyalty by a modern, cynical politics of survival. Yet Mortimer’s triumph is short-lived. His fall is as rapid as his rise, showing the mechanical operation of Fortune's wheel. When the young Edward III asserts his authority and condemns Mortimer to death, the usurper accepts his fate with a Stoic indifference:"Base Fortune, now I see, that in thy wheelThere is a point, to which when men aspire,They tumble headlong down: that point I touch'd,And, seeing there was no place to mount up higher,Why should I grieve at my declining fall?"Mortimer views his life and death not as a moral drama of sin, but as a mechanical consequence of political ambition. He has played the game of power to its absolute limit, touched the highest point of the wheel, and accepts his fall as an inevitable law of political mutability.The Shattered Body Politic: The Filth and Terror of Berkeley CastleThe final act of Edward II contains some of the most harrowing scenes in early modern English drama, focusing on the systematic physical and psychological degradation of the captured king. Marlowe exploits the legal-theological theory of "the King's Two Bodies"—the concept that the monarch consists of a natural, mortal body subject to disease, and a symbolic, immortal body politic that represents the state. Throughout his imprisonment at Kenilworth and Berkeley castles, Edward is subjected to a process of physical degradation designed to strip him of his symbolic royal identity. He is forced to stand in a channel of sewage, sleep-deprived, and shaved with puddle water. This physical defilement is the literal pollution of the crown itself.This process of degradation culminates in the forced abdication scene at Kenilworth Castle, where Edward is pressured to surrender the crown to his son. The scene shows the king’s reluctance to separate his natural self from his symbolic identity. He clings to the crown as if it were a physical extension of his body:"But what are kings, when regiment is gone,But perfect shadows in a sunshine day?My nobility is ruin'd, muck and trash,And I must keep my court in Berkeley Castle."Edward recognises that without the "regiment" of sovereign power, the king is reduced to a shadow. The crown, once a symbol of divine authority, is a burden that has destroyed the man who wore it.The climax of this physical degradation is Edward's murder, performed by the professional assassin Lightborn. The name "Lightborn" is a literal translation of "Lucifer," which indicates the diabolical nature of his office. Lightborn has a chilling professionalism; he takes pride in his craft, boasting of the various ways he can execute a man without leaving a trace of violence on the body. The murder of the king in the dark dungeon of Berkeley Castle, using a hot spit, is a scene of grotesque, unnatural violence that mirrors and punishes the king's transgressive desires. By executing the king through his body natural, Mortimer and Lightborn attempt to destroy the symbolic authority of the crown. However, Marlowe shows that the murder backfires. The graphic horror of the king's death provokes a powerful wave of sympathy from the audience and the young King Edward III. This transforms the weak, selfish monarch into a tragic martyr and starts the rapid downfall of his killers.Deconstructing the History Play: The Legacy of Marlovian CynicismThe historical significance of Edward II in the development of English drama lies in its deconstruction of the chronicle history play. When Marlowe wrote the play around 1591, the dominant mode of historical drama on the London stage was patriotic and providential. These dramas typically presented English history as a moral narrative guided by divine providence, where rebellion was a sin that brought down divine retribution. Marlowe, however, strips the history play of its providential framework. In Edward II, there are no battles of national destiny, no heroic speeches before the walls of foreign cities, and no sense that God is guiding the affairs of England. The stage is dominated by factional infighting, personal jealousy, and Machiavellian intrigue.This cynical vision of history had a direct influence on William Shakespeare. His Richard II (c. 1595) is heavily indebted to Marlowe's play, adopting a similar structure that focuses on a weak king deposed by a pragmatic usurper. However, a comparison of the two plays reveals Shakespeare's more conservative design. While Richard II’s deposition is accompanied by debates on the sacredness of royal authority, Marlowe’s play treats Edward's deposition as a raw exercise of force. Furthermore, Shakespeare completely strips his source material of the homosexual content that is central to Marlowe's tragedy, replacing the intimate, erotic bond between Edward and Gaveston with a focus on Richard's poetic vanity and political incompetence.In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, Edward II has experienced a major theatrical renaissance, reclaimed as a pioneering text of queer history. Bertolt Brecht’s adaptation, The Life of Edward II of England (1924), emphasised the play's class dynamics and political cynicism. In 1991, the British director Derek Jarman adapted the play into a landmark film that juxtaposed Marlowe’s Elizabethan text with contemporary gay rights protests. By staging the play’s historical violence through a contemporary lens, Jarman demonstrated the enduring power of Marlowe’s drama to expose the dark, coercive mechanisms of political authority.
plays.ch12: Original Title: Every Man in His HumourDate: 1598 (first performance) | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan Comedy / Humours Comedy | Genre: Humours Comedy / City ComedyThe Theatre of the Obsessed: The Comedy of Human EccentricityModern audiences easily recognise the portraits of human eccentricity in Every Man in His Humour. We see their descendants daily in television sitcoms that feature characters trapped in repetitive, predictable loops of behaviour, whether it is the pathologically neat flatmate, the boastful colleague who collapses at the first sign of real conflict, or the anxious parent who interprets every youthful hobby as a descent into moral ruin. Long before modern psychology categorised these traits, Ben Jonson saw that human beings have a natural tendency to let a single, obsessive preoccupation dominate their entire character. Jonson calls this obsession a "humour." In his drama, a humour is not a temporary mood, but a consuming psychological bias that runs "all one way," blinding the individual to common sense and social reality. The play is a comic anatomy of these obsessions, inviting the audience to laugh at the rigidity of the characters while suggesting that the fluid environment of the modern city requires flexibility rather than rigid, mechanical behaviour.The dramatic interest of the play is not driven by an elaborate, romantic plot, but by the systematic collision of these eccentric personalities. Jonson rejects the sprawling, fantastical narratives of his Elizabethan contemporaries, choosing instead to present a tightly structured comedy of manners. The opening scenes introduce us to a gallery of characters defined by their specific behavioural biases. Old Kno'well is the anxious father who intercepts a letter meant for his son and immediately assumes the youth is being corrupted by the decadent culture of London. Kitely is the wealthy merchant whose life is tormented by a pathological, groundless jealousy, fearing that every young gallant who enters his shop is plotting to seduce his wife. Master Stephen is the country gull who believes that adopting a fashionable, melancholic posture is the key to aristocratic sophistication. By bringing these characters together in the bustling streets and taverns of London, Jonson creates a series of comic friction points that expose the absurdity of their pretensions.The London Metamorphosis: Neoclassical Realism and the Italianate ShiftThe artistic significance of Every Man in His Humour is deeply connected to its complex textual history and Jonson's dramatic theory. The play was first performed in September 1598 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Curtain Theatre in Shoreditch, with William Shakespeare himself listed in the cast, likely playing the conservative father Kno'well. When the play was first published in the 1601 Quarto, it followed the fashionable convention of setting comedies in Italy. The action was set in Florence, and the characters bore Italian names: Old Kno'well was Lorenzo Senior, his son was Lorenzo Junior, Wellbred was Prospero, and Kitely was Thorello. This Italian setting allowed the play to operate as a conventional, somewhat distant romantic comedy, shielding the English audience from direct satirical attack.However, when Jonson prepared the play for his landmark 1616 Folio edition of his Works, he undertook a radical revision that transformed the nature of the drama. He relocated the setting from Florence to contemporary London, changed the character names to English equivalents, and added a critical Prologue that serves as a manifesto for neoclassical realism. In the Prologue, Jonson attacks the popular historical and romantic dramas of his day, including Shakespeare’s chronicle plays, mocking their disregard for the classical unities and their reliance on cheap stage effects:"To make a child, now swaddled, to proceedMan, and then groom, then man, then age and breed,With three rusty swords,And help of some few foot-and-half-foot words,Fight over York and Lancaster's long jars..."In place of these sprawling histories, Jonson promises to present "deeds, and language, such as men do use." The relocation of the play to London was vital for this realistic aesthetic. By mapping the action onto a precise, recognisable local geography, moving from the suburban fields of Hoxton to the Windmill Tavern in Coleman Street, the Old Jewry, and Moorfields, Jonson turned the play from a generic comedy into a vivid, immediate social anatomy of late Elizabethan London. The audience was no longer looking at the follies of distant Italians, but at the mirror image of their own neighbours.Natural vs. Fashionable Pathologies: The Comedy of AffectationJonson’s satirical method rests on a distinction between two types of humours: "natural" humours, which are genuine, involuntary psychological distortions, and "artificial" or "fashionable" humours, which are affectations adopted by insecure individuals to project a false social identity. Jonson argues that a true humour occurs when "some one peculiar quality / Doth so possess a man, that it doth draw / All his affects, his spirits, and his powers, / In their confluctions, all to run one way." This is the case with Kitely’s jealousy or Old Kno'well’s parental anxiety. These characters do not choose their obsessions; they are tormented by them. Kitely recognises the irrationality of his suspicion, yet he cannot stop himself from searching for signs of infidelity in every word and gesture of his wife. His jealousy is a genuine pathology that destroys his domestic peace.In contrast, the gulls in the play, Master Stephen, Master Matthew, and Captain Bobadill, suffer from artificial humours. They adopt fashionable eccentricities in a desperate attempt to appear sophisticated and aristocratic in the competitive environment of the city. Stephen, the country gull, believes that a gentleman must be characterised by a sullen, rustic melancholy, declaring: "I am mightily given to melancholy... I will be more melancholy and gentlemanlike than I have been, I'll promise you." Matthew, the city gull, pretends to be a poet of deep sensitivity, but his verses are shown to be plagiarised fragments stolen from the works of Christopher Marlowe and other popular writers.The most complex of these artificial humours is embodied in Captain Bobadill. He presents himself as a valiant, experienced soldier who lives by a strict code of honour and possesses an absolute mastery of foreign fencing terms. He delivers magnificent, mathematical calculations of how he and a small band of select gentlemen could defeat an entire army:"I would select nineteen more, to myself, throughout the land; gentlemen they should be, of good spirit, strong and able constitution; I would choose them by an instinct, charactered in their faces... and we would teach these nineteen the special rules, as your punto, your reverso, your stoccata, your imbroccata, your passada, your montanto... and we would slay more than forty thousand of our enemies!"This verbal display is shown to be a complete fabrication. When confronted by the blunt, angry Downright, Bobadill refuses to draw his sword and allows himself to be beaten, claiming he was bound by a legal warrant. Jonson uses Bobadill to expose the empty, performative nature of military bravado in the city. Bobadill’s humour is a mask designed to hide his actual poverty, cowardice, and social marginalisation. By contrasting these artificial affectations with the natural anxieties of Kitely and Old Kno'well, Jonson satirises a commercial culture where identity is treated as a commodity to be bought and performed.The Trickster as Artist and the Restoration of BalanceThe complex plot of Every Man in His Humour is driven not by chance, but by the active, creative intelligence of Brainworm, the clever servant of the Kno'well household. Brainworm is the direct descendant of the clever slave of Plautine and Terentian Roman comedy, but Jonson updates him to serve as a surrogate playwright within the drama. Brainworm’s primary function is to orchestrate the exposure of the other characters' humours. He does this by adopting a series of physical disguises, first appearing as Fitzsword, a disabled veteran begging for charity, then as a city sergeant, and finally as a magistrate's clerk.These disguises allow Brainworm to move freely through the different social spheres of London, manipulating the characters by exploiting their specific psychological vulnerabilities. Brainworm’s success shows Jonson's belief that the "humourous" man is inherently predictable and therefore easily manipulated. Because Old Kno'well is blinded by his parental anxiety, and Kitely is blinded by his jealousy, they cannot see through Brainworm’s transparent deceptions.The resolution of the play occurs in the home of Justice Clement, an eccentric, merry magistrate whose character represents Jonson's ideal of comic authority. Jonson characterises Clement as a man of eccentric wit and common sense, who understands that the social disorders of London cannot be cured by legal coercion alone. Clement's court functions as a therapeutic space where the characters are forced to strip away their affectations and confront their true selves.Clement’s method of justice is performative and corrective. When Bobadill and Matthew arrive to sue Downright for assault, Clement mocks their cowardice and orders Matthew's plagiarised verses to be burned in a mock-funeral pyre, declaring that such bad poetry is a crime against nature and art. He forces Kitely and his wife to confront the absurdity of their mutual suspicion, exposing the false messages that Wellbred used to inflame their jealousy. When Brainworm's disguises are finally unmasked, Clement is so delighted by the servant's ingenuity that he dresses in Brainworm's armour, toasts his wit, and invites him to join the festive celebration.The play ends not with imprisonment or exile, but with a feast of reconciliation. Clement orders all the characters to purge their humours and celebrate the night with laughter and good cheer, declaring:"Come, I conjure the rest to put off all discontent...Let us preserve our relation; and as we havebegun in mirth, so let us end in friendship."This festive ending indicates that Jonson's satire, while sharp, is ultimately corrective and therapeutic rather than destructive. The humourous characters are not expelled from society; they are integrated back into the community once their obsessions have been exposed and deflated by laughter. Through this festive purge, Jonson demonstrates the social utility of comedy, framing the theatre as a vital institution for the correction of manners in the modern metropolis.
plays.ch13: Original Title: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of DenmarkDate: c. 1600–1601 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan/Jacobean Tragedy | Genre: Revenge Tragedy / Tragedy of ConsciousnessThe Architecture of Suspicion: Hamlet and the Early Modern CrisisModern readers find Hamlet a familiar nightmare: the experience of living within a surveillance state where every conversation is monitored, every friend is a potential informant, and the language of public life is severed from private truth. Before it is a classical tragedy, the play is a dark thriller set in a court thick with suspicion. Shakespeare introduces Elsinore not through the pageantry of royalty, but through the shivering anxiety of soldiers on a dark, freezing platform who do not know whom to trust. The opening question, "Who's there?" is not a mere exchange of watchmen. It is the central question of the entire drama, establishing an atmosphere of uncertainty and political dread. Hamlet, returning from the university at Wittenberg to find his father dead, his mother married to his uncle Claudius, and his rightful crown usurped, is thrust into a world where outward appearances are designed to deceive.This atmosphere of spying turns Elsinore into a theatrical prison. Claudius and Polonius deploy Ophelia as a decoy while they hide behind tapestries to observe Hamlet's behaviour; Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, Hamlet's schoolfellows, are hired to parse his psyche and report his secrets to the crown; even Polonius sends a servant to France to spread rumours about his own son Laertes to verify his conduct. In this environment of relentless observation, Hamlet adopts his "antic disposition" as a defensive shield. His madness is not a psychological collapse, but a performance designed to carve out a space of privacy in a world where privacy has been outlawed. By acting mad, Hamlet exploits the licence of the fool, speaking lethal truths under the guise of nonsense, turning the court's gaze back upon itself. The play shifts the traditional medieval narrative of physical revenge into a Renaissance crisis of interiority. It shows a protagonist who must navigate the gulf between what he calls the "actions that a man might play" and that "which passeth show."First performed around 1600–1601 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Globe, with Richard Burbage in the title role, the play met with immediate success. It was published in a corrupt, abbreviated Quarto in 1603 (Q1), a larger Quarto in 1604–1605 (Q2), and later in the First Folio of 1623 (F1). The discrepancies between these texts suggest a work that was revised in the theatre, reflecting performance demands. Shakespeare structures the drama as an investigation into the limits of human knowledge, showing how the obligation to act is paralysed by the difficulty of knowing the truth in a world governed by theatre.Purgatory and Wittenberg: The Theological Fault Lines of ElsinoreThe intellectual crisis of the play is anchored in a theological contradiction that had a sharp, immediate resonance for a late Elizabethan audience. Hamlet is a student at Wittenberg, the university famous as the birthplace of the Protestant Reformation, where Martin Luther championed the doctrine of justification by faith and dismissed the existence of Purgatory as a Catholic superstition. Yet the Ghost that appears on the battlements of Elsinore describes a state of torment that is explicitly Purgatorial:"I am thy father's spirit,Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night,And for the day confin'd to fast in fires,Till the foul crimes done in my days of natureAre burnt and purg'd away."This confrontation between the Protestant intellectual training of Hamlet and the Catholic demands of his father's spirit establishes the play's epistemic deadlock. Protestant theology taught that ghosts were not the spirits of the dead but demons sent by the Devil to tempt living souls into despair and damnation. Hamlet cannot simply execute the Ghost's command of vengeance. He must first determine whether the apparition is a "spirit of health or goblin damn'd."The need for absolute proof becomes Hamlet's primary justification for delay. His hesitation is not a sign of psychological weakness, but a rational response to an irrational command. The Ghost demands that Hamlet bypass the legal and moral structures of society to perform an act of extrajudicial murder. In a world where the divine right of kings protects the ruler, Hamlet is asked to assassinate the sitting monarch on the authority of a night-time vision. The intellectual tools Hamlet acquired at Wittenberg—scepticism, logical analysis, and humanistic inquiry—are useless in resolving this supernatural dilemma. He is caught between a traditional code of honour that demands immediate blood-revenge and a modern consciousness that recoils from the moral consequences of murder. The tragedy lies in the fact that Hamlet is forced to act in a world where moral clarity is impossible.The Mirror of Metatheatre: Staging the MousetrapTo resolve his doubts, Hamlet turns to the theatre, recognising that in a world of political performance, only a theatrical illusion can expose the truth. The arrival of the travelling players in Act II allows Shakespeare to engage in a metadramatic meditation on the nature of acting. Hamlet's advice to the players in Act III, urging them to "hold, as 'twere, the mirror up to nature," is not merely an aesthetic statement, but a political strategy. By staging The Murder of Gonzago—renamed The Mousetrap—before Claudius, Hamlet seeks to capture the conscience of the king.The play-within-the-play is an exercise in structural doubling. The performance mirrors the exact method of the murder described by the Ghost: the pouring of poison into the ear of a sleeping king. As the court watches the players, Hamlet watches Claudius, and the theatre audience watches Hamlet watching Claudius. This layering of spectatorship collapses the distance between the stage and the world. It suggests that Elsinore itself is a theatrical performance where everyone is acting a part. When Claudius rises at the moment of the poisoning, calling for "light," the theatrical illusion succeeds. The king's sudden departure is a confession of guilt written on the body, proving the reliability of the Ghost and giving Hamlet the licence to act.However, the metadramatic structure also exposes Hamlet's own entrapment in theatricality. He complains that the player, weeping for the mythical Hecuba, can perform passion more convincingly than he can live it:"What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba,That he should weep for her? What would he do,Had he the motive and the cue for passionThat I have? He would drown the stage with tearsAnd cleave the general ear with horrid speech..."Hamlet is trapped in the role of the revenger, a conventional theatrical type that he is too complex to inhabit comfortably. Even when he confronts his mother in her chamber, the scene is structured as an interrogation where he sets up "a glass / Where you may see the inmost part of you." In his fury, he stabs Polonius through the tapestry, killing the court's chief director of surveillance. This sudden violence is a tragic mistake. It shows that when Hamlet attempts to act without calculation, he becomes the very thing he despises: an arbitrary killer who destroys the innocent and perpetuates the cycle of blood-revenge.The Rhetoric of Infection and the Stoic HorizonShakespeare reflects the moral corruption of Elsinore through a network of linguistic patterns that centres on disease, rot, and poison. The physical murder of the late king, accomplished by pouring poison into his ears, is the central metaphor for the political corruption of Denmark. Under Claudius's rule, the entire state is infected; the ear of the nation is poisoned by lies and official propaganda. Marcellus's famous observation that "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark" is validated by the language of the characters, which is thick with references to ulcers, cankers, and hidden abscesses.This theme of division is reinforced by Shakespeare's use of the rhetorical figure hendiadys—the joining of two nouns by a conjunction to express a single, complex idea. Instead of using an adjective to modify a noun, characters use doublets: "post and haste," "law and heraldry," or "the expectancy and rose of the fair state." Hendiadys creates a sense of stylistic imbalance, suggesting that the language of the court is diseased, split, and unable to achieve unity. It highlights the gap between words and the things they represent, mirroring the hypocrisy of Claudius, who speaks of "discretion" while hiding his fratricide.Hamlet's own language is a weapon of resistance against this linguistic corruption. He uses puns and double meanings to disrupt the smooth rhetoric of the court. When Claudius addresses him as "my cousin Hamlet, and my son," Hamlet retorts in an aside, "A little more than kin, and less than kind." By exploiting the slippage of language, Hamlet refuses to be incorporated into Claudius's political order. However, this linguistic brilliance also isolates him, turning his mind into a self-consuming labyrinth where words become substitutes for action. As he tells Polonius, the content of his reading is nothing but "Words, words, words."The final act of the play introduces a dramatic shift in Hamlet's character, marked by a transition from anxious self-scrutiny to a quietist, stoic acceptance of mortality. This transition is staged in the graveyard of Act V, a scene that strips away the social and political distinctions of Elsinore to reveal the democratic reality of the grave. Holding the skull of Yorick, Hamlet realises that all human ambition, intelligence, and beauty must resolve into common dust. The physical decay of the body is now accepted as an inevitable law of nature.This shift from intellect to acceptance prepares Hamlet for the final catastrophe. He tells Horatio of the sudden actions that saved his life, concluding that "There's a divinity that shapes our ends, / Rough-hew them how we will." When Horatio warns him that he will lose the fencing match against Laertes, Hamlet rejects the warning in a passage that is the ethical summit of the play:"Not a whit, we defy augury: there is a specialprovidence in the fall of a sparrow. If it be now,'tis not to come; if it be not to come, it will benow; if it be not now, yet it will come. Thereadiness is all."The phrase "the readiness is all" replaces the anxious question "To be, or not to be." Hamlet abandons his demand for certainty, realising that human action cannot be planned with perfect foresight in an unpredictable universe. He submits himself to the flow of events, allowing the plot of Claudius and Laertes to carry him to his revenge.The final duel is a scene of chaotic violence that matches this stoic vision. The poisoned cup and the poisoned foil, designed by Claudius and Laertes to ensure Hamlet's death, are turned against their creators through a series of accidents. Gertrude drinks from the poisoned cup, Laertes is wounded by his own toxic weapon, and Claudius is finally killed by the very poison he imported to Denmark. Hamlet's act of revenge is not a calculated political coup, but a spontaneous reaction to the unfolding horror. As he dies, he commands Horatio to survive to "report my cause aright," recognising that the survival of his story is the only form of immortality available in a fallen world.
plays.ch14: Original Title: Twelfth Night, or What You WillDate: c. 1601–1602 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Elizabethan England | Period/movement: Elizabethan Romantic Comedy | Genre: Romantic Comedy / Festive ComedyThe Mirror of Misrule: Gender, Desire, and the Illyrian DreamModern readers do well to treat Twelfth Night not as a simple romantic comedy, but as an exploration of identity and reinvention. The play captures the experience of the shipwreck, where a person is cast onto a strange shore, the obligations of past life are erased, and one is free to construct a new self. Shakespeare begins the drama with Viola, a young woman shipwrecked in the mysterious land of Illyria, who believes her twin brother Sebastian has drowned. Finding herself alone in a foreign country, she resolves to conceal her gender, disguise herself as a young man named Cesario, and enter the service of the local ruler, Duke Orsino. This disguise is a catalyst that exposes the fluid, performative nature of human desire. In the court of Illyria, identity is a mirror that reflects whatever the characters wish to see, dissolving the boundaries between male and female, master and servant, sanity and madness.The setting of the play, Illyria, is a space of psychological holiday. The title refers to the Christian feast of Epiphany, which in early modern England was celebrated with a spirit of misrule, a carnival where social structures were temporarily inverted and the normal rules of decorum were suspended. First performed on February 2, 1602 (Candlemas) by the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Middle Temple Hall, London, the play was designed to appeal to an audience of lawyers and students who were familiar with the licence of academic revelry. When it was published in the First Folio of 1623, it was recognised as a major achievement of Shakespeare's romantic comedies. Yet, beneath the festive music and the laughter, the play contains a persistent undercurrent of sadness. The characters are driven by excess: Orsino is in love with love, Olivia is in love with grief, and Sir Toby Belch is in love with drink. Viola's arrival disrupts these self-indulgent performances, introducing a note of genuine feeling into a court that has turned emotion into a theatrical style.Shipwrecks and Siblings: The Optics of the DoubleThe central complication of Twelfth Night rests on the visual symmetry of the twins, Viola and Sebastian. This doubling creates a series of comic errors that are resolved only when the two are brought face-to-face in the final scene. For the characters in the play, this encounter is a moment of ontological shock. Orsino describes it as "A natural perspective, that is and is not!"—a reference to the early modern optical toy that presented different images depending on the angle from which it was viewed. The twins suggest that identity is not a unique, indivisible essence, but a double that can be divided and shared. Olivia, who has fallen in love with Cesario, finds her desire fulfilled by marrying Sebastian, while Orsino, who has grown close to Cesario, transfers his affections to Viola once her female attire is restored.This resolution shows the arbitrary nature of romantic desire. Olivia falls in love not with a specific biological male, but with a performance of courtly wooing delivered by a cross-dressed woman. Her love is directed at an image, a voice, and a style of speech. When Sebastian replaces Viola in her bed, Olivia remains satisfied, showing that the object of her desire is interchangeable. The play suggests that desire is fundamentally metadramatic; it is stimulated by the theatricality of the beloved rather than their stable reality. The erotic tension of the play is most acute in the scenes between Orsino and Cesario. Orsino, while believing Viola to be a young man, is drawn to "his" feminine qualities, the rubious lip and the voice that is shrill and sound. The exchange in Act II highlights the homoerotic intimacy that develops under the cover of disguise:"My father had a daughter loved a man,As it might be, perhaps, were I a woman,I should your lordship....A blank, my lord. She pined in thought,And with a green and yellow melancholyShe sat like patience on a monument,Smiling at grief."Here, Viola speaks of herself in the third person, performing her grief while remaining invisible to the man she loves. The scene shows how the theatrical convention of the boy actor playing a woman who disguises herself as a young man allows Shakespeare to layer multiple levels of identity, exposing gender as a costume that can be put on and cast off.The Purged Court: Malvolio and the Puritan ShadowWhile the aristocratic characters navigate the complications of romance, the domestic household of Olivia becomes the battleground for a political and cultural conflict. The steward Malvolio is the emerging threat of Puritanism, a religious movement that viewed the theatre, festive holidays, and traditional sports as sinful distractions from a godly life. Malvolio is a man of absolute sobriety, obsessed with order, hierarchy, and self-love. His name, which translates to "ill-will," stands in opposition to the festive spirit of Twelfth Night. When he attempts to suppress the late-night drinking and singing of Sir Toby Belch, Sir Andrew Aguecheek, and Feste, Sir Toby delivers a rebuke that outlines the conflict between the old festive England and the new Puritan austerity: "Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?"To punish Malvolio for his presumption, Maria, Olivia's waiting-woman, devises a plot that exploits his secret ambition. She writes a letter in Olivia's hand that flatters Malvolio's belief in his own superiority, convincing him that the countess is in love with him. The letter instructs him to adopt a series of bizarre behaviours, wearing yellow stockings, being cross-gartered, and smiling constantly. Malvolio's subsequent appearance before Olivia is a masterclass in comic humiliation. His mechanical compliance with the letter's instructions makes him appear mad to the court, leading to his imprisonment in a dark room.The dark room scene introduces a disturbing element into the comedy. Feste, disguised as "Sir Topas the Curate," torments the bound steward, attempting to force him to confess to a madness he does not possess. Malvolio's persistent assertion of his sanity, "I am as well in my wits, fool, as thou art," shifts the tone of the play from light-hearted mockery to psychological cruelty. When he is finally released in Act V and realises the extent of the conspiracy against him, he refuses to join in the general reconciliation. His exit line, "I'll be reveng'd on the whole pack of you!" remains a discordant note that hangs over the final marriages. Malvolio's punishment is a conservative reassertion of class boundaries; he is punished not merely for his Puritanism, but for his attempt to transcend his social station and marry into the aristocracy. His exclusion from the comic resolution suggests that the festive community of Illyria can exist only by ejecting those who refuse to play.The Anatomy of Melancholy: Feste's Music and the Passing of TimeWhat distinguishes Twelfth Night from Shakespeare's earlier comedies is its pervasive sense of melancholy. The play is saturated with a consciousness of decay, aging, and the transience of youth. Feste the fool embodies this elegiac tone. Feste is not a buffoon, but a professional observer who stands outside the main action of the play, commenting on the foolishness of his superiors. He is the only character who moves freely between the household of Olivia and the court of Orsino, showing that the melancholia of the lover is identical to the melancholia of the mourner. Feste's wit is sharp and philosophical; he proves to Olivia that she is a fool to mourn her brother's soul if she believes it to be in heaven, and he mocks Orsino's emotional instability, comparing his mind to an opal that changes colour in the light.Feste's songs are the emotional anchor of the play. They do not interrupt the dramatic action, but articulate the themes of mortality and decay that the other characters try to ignore. In Act II, he sings "O Mistress Mine," warning that "Youth's a stuff will not endure." In Act II, Scene 4, he sings "Come Away, Death," a song of unrequited love that Orsino calls "silly sooth," but which describes the cold reality of the grave. Feste's music reminds the audience that the carnival of Illyria is temporary; the holiday will end, the actors will leave the stage, and the cold winter of reality will return.Shakespeare ends the play with Feste's solitary song of rain and decay, "When that I was and a little tiny boy," which traces the stages of a human life from childhood to old age, punctuated by the refrain, "For the rain it raineth every day." The song shifts the perspective of the audience from the fantasy world of Illyria to the everyday world of early modern London, where knaves are ruled by foolish wits, and beds are hard to find. He suggests that comedy is not an escape from reality, but a fragile sanctuary built against the relentless passage of time. The dream of Illyria is beautiful precisely because it cannot last.
plays.ch15: Original Title: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of VeniceDate: c. 1603–1604 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Jacobean England | Period/movement: Jacobean Tragedy | Genre: Domestic Tragedy / Tragedy of JealousyThe Poisoned Chamber: Othello and the Tragedy of IntimacyFor modern readers, Othello is the most painful of Shakespeare's tragedies because it scales down the theatre of statecraft to the suffocating confines of the bedroom. While Hamlet and King Lear deal with the collapse of kingdoms, Othello is a domestic horror story. It is a play about the destruction of trust from the inside out, tracing the process by which an intimate sanctuary is transformed into a torture chamber. Shakespeare structures the drama around a simple premise: how easily a noble, loving mind can be poisoned by malicious suggestion. The protagonist, Othello, is a celebrated general, a man of action who has survived shipwrecks, deserts, and the chaos of battle. Yet his military expertise is useless in the domestic sphere. The qualities that make him a formidable commander—his simplicity, his absolute trust in his subordinates, and his lack of courtly sophistication—are the vulnerabilities that his ancient, Iago, exploits to destroy him.The play opens in the dark, narrow streets of Venice, where Iago and Roderigo awaken the senator Brabantio with obscene, racialised announcements of his daughter Desdemona's marriage. This juxtaposition of the public and the private establishes the central tension of the drama. Othello is an outsider, a Moor hired by the Venetian republic to lead its armies but never fully integrated into its social fabric. The threat of a Turkish invasion of Cyprus forces the state to tolerate Othello's marriage to Desdemona, but the social anxiety surrounding their union remains acute. First performed on November 1, 1604, by the King's Men at the court of King James I in Whitehall Palace, the play confronted Jacobean audiences with the fragile position of the non-European subject in a cosmopolitan society. Published in Quarto form in 1622 and later in the First Folio of 1623, it is a masterpiece of dramatic compression. It shows how the public defence of Christian civilisation is ultimately destroyed by the private infection of jealousy.The Rhetoric of Infection: Iago and the Chemistry of InsinuationThe tragic movement of the play is driven by the linguistic sorcery of Iago. Iago is Shakespeare's most terrifying villain because his motives are fluid, evasive, and secondary to his delight in destruction. Samuel Taylor Coleridge famously described Iago's soliloquies as the "motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity." Iago claims to hate Othello because he was passed over for promotion in favour of Cassio, because he suspects Othello of sleeping with his wife Emilia, and because he suspects Cassio of doing the same. These shifting justifications suggest a mind searching for rational explanations for a deeper impulse of envy. Iago is a dramatic artist of malice, using his understanding of human weakness to rewrite the lives of those around him.Iago's method of manipulation is not based on direct lies, but on the rhetoric of insinuation. He acts as a mirror that reflects Othello's own latent anxieties, using silence, hesitation, and echo to make Othello do the work of self-destruction. The garden scene in Act III is the structural hinge of the play, tracing the process by which Iago infects Othello's mind. When Cassio departs from Desdemona, Iago begins his assault with a seemingly casual murmur:"Ha! I like not that....Nothing, my lord; or if—I know not what....Cassio, my lord? No, sure, I cannot think it,That he would steal away so guilty-like,Seeing you coming."By refusing to speak clearly, Iago forces Othello to demand information. He turns Othello into the investigator of his own wife's supposed infidelity. Iago plays the part of the honest, reluctant witness. He uses phrases like "I think Cassio's an honest man" and warns Othello against jealousy to implant the very monster he pretends to ward off. Othello's mind, caught in this linguistic web, begins to collapse under the weight of unconfirmed suspicion. His language, which began the play with a majestic dignity, degenerates into fragmented prose, animalistic cries, and physical collapse. Iago's poison is rhetorical. He pours his words into Othello's ear just as Claudius poured physical poison into the ear of Hamlet's father, destroying Othello's sanity.The Spotted Handkerchief: The Materiality of SuspicionThe dramatic power of Othello lies in the way Shakespeare attaches this psychological crisis to a trivial domestic object: a strawberry-spotted handkerchief. Thomas Rymer, writing in the late seventeenth century, ridiculed the play as a "tragedy of a handkerchief," arguing that the plot was too minor to justify the tragic suffering of its characters. Yet Shakespeare recognises that in a world of domestic suspicion, the mind requires physical props to sustain its illusions. The handkerchief, Othello's first gift to Desdemona, is a symbolic object. As Othello explains, it was woven by an Egyptian sybil, dyed in the consecrated snow of maidens' hearts, and contains a magic that ensures the fidelity of the owner.The handkerchief functions as a token for Desdemona's body and her chastity. The white linen spotted with red strawberries matches the blood-stained sheets of the wedding bed, signifying the physical consummation of the marriage. When Desdemona accidentally drops it, Emilia retrieves it and gives it to Iago, who recognises its value as "ocular proof." By placing this intimate token in Cassio's chamber and arranging for Othello to see Cassio give it to the courtesan Bianca, Iago translates a subjective suspicion into a visible, material fact. For Othello, the sight of the handkerchief in Cassio's possession is the final confirmation of his ruin. The handkerchief becomes a distorting lens that transforms Desdemona's innocent gestures of charity into evidence of monstrous lust. By focusing the entire tragedy on this small piece of fabric, Shakespeare shows how easily human reason can be unseated by the manipulation of signs. He demonstrates that "trifles light as air / Are to the jealous confirmations strong / As proofs of holy writ."The Barbarian Within: Race and the Venetian MirrorThe ultimate tragedy of Othello is his internalisation of the very racist prejudices that Venice harbours against him. Throughout the play, Othello is subjected to a barrage of xenophobic imagery that represents him as an animal and a barbarian. Iago refers to him as an "old black ram" and a "Barbary horse," while Brabantio believes Othello must have used spells bought of mountebanks to seduce his daughter. Othello initially resists these stereotypes, presenting himself as a Christian defender of Venice whose royal lineage and military services outweigh the disadvantage of his skin colour. He speaks with a calm authority that commands the respect of the Venetian senate.However, as Iago's poison takes effect, Othello's confidence crumbles. He begins to see himself through the eyes of his Venetian hosts, doubting his own capacity to inspire love in Desdemona because of his race and age: "Haply, for I am black, / And have not those soft parts of conversation / That chamberers have." His jealousy is a social condition; it is the anxiety of a man who knows that his position in Venetian society depends on his performance of a nobility that his peers suspect he does not truly possess.In the final scene, this division within Othello's identity is dramatised with clarity. Having strangled Desdemona in her bed, he learns from Emilia that Iago has deceived him. In his final speech, Othello attempts to reclaim his public narrative and his military identity before the Venetian officials:"And say besides, that in Aleppo once,Where a malignant and a turban'd TurkBeat a Venetian and traduc'd the state,I took by the throat the circumcised dog,And smote him thus."As he speaks the word "thus," Othello stabs himself with his hidden dagger. This suicide is a divided action. Othello plays the part of the Christian defender of Venice executing the malignant Turk, but the Turk he executes is himself. He has become the barbarian he was hired to fight, the destroyer of Venice's most precious jewel. Through this suicide, Othello attempts to expiate his crime, but his death on the bed of Desdemona remains a monument to the destructive power of a society that could use his sword but could never accept his love.
plays.ch16: Original Title: The Tragedy of King LearDate: c. 1605–1606 | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Jacobean England | Period/movement: Jacobean Tragedy | Genre: Tragedy / Cosmic TragedyThe Naked Kingdom: King Lear and the Dismantling of the SelfModern readers find King Lear a devastating tragedy because it dramatises the universal human terror of loss: the fear of growing old, losing one's authority, and being cast out into the cold by the children one has raised. Shakespeare begins the drama not with a cosmic catastrophe, but with a family dispute that escalates into civil war. The protagonist, Lear, is an absolute monarch who confuses the official deference paid to his crown with genuine personal love. In his desire to abdicate the responsibilities of rule while retaining the "name, and all th' addition to a king," he stages a public "love test," demanding that his three daughters compete for their shares of the kingdom by declaring who loves him most. When his youngest and favourite daughter, Cordelia, refuses to participate in this theatrical flattery, Lear's pride is wounded. He disowns her, banishes his loyal councillor Kent, and divides his realm between his elder daughters, Goneril and Regan. This act of arrogance starts a systematic dismantling of Lear's identity, stripping him of his knights, his shelter, his sanity, and eventually his life.First performed on December 26, 1606, by the King's Men before King James I at Whitehall Palace, the play served as a warning to a newly crowned Scottish king who was attempting to unite England and Scotland into a single kingdom. The historical audience, observing the division of the legendary British kingdom on stage, would have recognised the immediate political dangers of disunity. The play survived in two early printed versions, the First Quarto of 1608 (Q1) and the First Folio of 1623 (F1), whose differences show Shakespeare revising the text to intensify its bleakness. Shakespeare shifts the action from the legendary, redemptive chronicle of early British history into a raw, indifferent cosmos. He creates a work that transcends its immediate Jacobean context to become a study of human vulnerability in a world stripped of divine and social protection.The Rhetoric of Nothing: The Love Test and the Collapse of LanguageThe tragedy of the play is initiated by a failure of language, specifically the clash between the inflated rhetoric of the court and the silence of genuine feeling. When Cordelia is asked what she can say to win a third of the kingdom more opulent than her sisters', she replies with a single word: "Nothing." Lear's shocked response, "Nothing will come of nothing: speak again," establishes the central philosophical motif of the play. For Lear, "nothing" is a void, a lack of value that must be rejected. Yet, the dramatic movement of the play reverses this judgment, showing that the elder sisters' declarations of love are the true "nothing"—empty verbal performances designed to deceive—while Cordelia's silence contains the substance of true loyalty.As Lear is banished from his daughters' houses and driven onto the storm-swept heath, the word "nothing" echoes through the dialogue and marks the collapse of his social and physical identity. The Fool, who acts as Lear's externalised conscience, repeatedly mocks the king for having voluntarily reduced himself to a cipher: "Now thou art an O without a figure: I am better than thou art now; I am a fool, thou art nothing." By dividing his land, Lear has dismantled the hierarchy that gave his words the force of law. His curses against Goneril and Regan are impotent, and his commands during the storm are ignored by a nature that does not recognise his sovereignty. Language itself begins to break down, dissolving into the fragmented prose of Lear's madness, the nursery rhymes of the Fool, and the mock-demonic jargon of Edgar disguised as Poor Tom. Through this linguistic collapse, Shakespeare suggests that the social contract is a fragile fiction. When the language of authority is severed from moral truth, the human community descends into chaos.The Mirror Plot: Gloucester and the Double TragedyShakespeare amplifies the tragedy of Lear by pairing it with a closely mirrored subplot involving the Earl of Gloucester and his two sons, Edgar and Edmund. This double-plot structure, adapted from Sir Philip Sidney's Arcadia, prevents the play from being read as a unique, isolated case of a single mad king. Instead, the duplication of Lear's suffering in Gloucester's fate suggests that the collapse of filial duty is a systemic, universal condition. Gloucester, like Lear, is a father who misjudges his children, believing the lies of his illegitimate son, Edmund, and outlawing his loyal, legitimate son, Edgar.The parallels between the two plots are precise. Both fathers banish the child who loves them; both trust the child who plots their destruction; and both are physically ejected from their homes. However, while Lear's suffering is primarily psychological, culminating in madness, Gloucester's suffering is physical, culminating in the horrific onstage gouging of his eyes by Cornwall and Regan in Act III. This violence is the physical expression of the spiritual blindness that Gloucester confessed earlier in the play: "I stumbled when I saw."The subplot also introduces Edmund, who represents the modern, Machiavellian individualist who rejects the traditional, feudal concept of a moral "Nature" governed by divine law. Edmund's goddess is the raw force of nature that favours the strong and the cunning:"Thou, nature, art my goddess; to thy lawMy services are bound. Wherefore should IStand in the plague of custom, and permitThe curiosity of nations to deprive me,For that I am some twelve or fourteen moonshinesLag of a brother?"Edmund's naturalism is predatory; he views his father's credulity and his brother's honesty as weaknesses to be exploited. His rise to power, which involves the betrayal of his own father to torture, mirrors the cruel pragmatism of Goneril and Regan. Shakespeare contrasts this modern, opportunistic philosophy with Lear's traditional assumptions, showing the collapse of an entire social order, leaving a world where "humanity must perforce prey on itself, / Like monsters of the deep."The Theatre of the Storm: Poor Tom and the Unaccommodated ManThe climax of the play's action occurs on the storm-swept heath in Act III, where Lear's internal psychological tempest is projected onto the cosmic scale of the elements. In the middle of the storm, Lear is confronted with Edgar disguised as "Poor Tom"—a naked, shivering beggar who eats frogs and speaks of being chased by devils. This encounter is the intellectual hinge of the play. Lear, who has spent his life surrounded by the luxury of the court, is forced to look upon the reality of human poverty. He realised that the beggar is the true representative of humanity when stripped of the artificial protections of civilisation:"Is man no more than this? Consider him well. Thou ow'st the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep no wool, the cat no perfume. Ha! Here's three on 's are sophisticated. Thou art the thing itself; unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art. Off, off, you lendings! Come, unbutton here."In his madness, Lear attempts to tear off his own clothes to align himself with Poor Tom, recognising that clothing is a social "lending" designed to hide the biological vulnerability of the body. This scene is a radical critique of Jacobean social inequality. Lear realises that during his reign, he neglected the suffering of his poorest subjects, admitting that he took "too little care of this."The heath is a levelling space where the social distinctions between king, noble, fool, and beggar are dissolved. Lear's madness is an epistemic liberation; it allows him to see through the hypocrisy of the law and the state. In Act IV, he tells the blind Gloucester that "a dog's obey'd in office" and exposes the corruption of judges who punish the poor while pardoning the wealthy. As he loses his mind, Lear gains the moral wisdom he lacked when he sat on the throne. He shows that in a corrupt world, only the madman and the fool can speak the truth.The Existential Horizon: The Bleakness of Dover and the Dead DaughterThe final act of King Lear delivers a devastating ending, rejecting the traditional, redemptive conclusion of the chronicles in favour of a confrontation with death. In 1681, Nahum Tate adapted the play to fit the neoclassical taste for poetic justice, providing a happy ending where Edgar and Cordelia survive to marry. This version held the stage for over a hundred and fifty years, because audiences and critics—including Samuel Johnson—found Shakespeare's original ending too painful to bear. Indeed, the sight of Lear entering the stage carrying the dead Cordelia in his arms represents a collapse of all providential comfort:"Howl, howl, howl, howl! O, you are men of stones:Had I your tongues and eyes, I’d use them soThat heaven’s vault should crack. She’s gone for ever!I know when a one is dead, and when she lives;She’s dead as earth."Lear's despair is absolute. His fourfold repetition of "howl" is an animalistic rejection of human language, a cry of physical grief that matches the bleakness of the universe.The play ends without any of the traditional consolations of tragedy. There is no promise of a renewed state, no clear assertion of a divine order, and no reward for virtue. Cordelia is hanged on the orders of Edmund, who tries to recall the execution warrant too late. Kent, having served his master in disguise throughout the play, prepares for his own death, stating that he has "a journey, short, to go." Edgar and Albany are left to rule a ruined kingdom, but their final words are marked by exhaustion: "The weight of this sad time we must obey; / Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say." Whether read as a forerunner to the Theatre of the Absurd or a pagan warning against political division, King Lear remains a tragedy of the human condition, showing us that when all our social roles, titles, and illusions are stripped away, we are left only with the capacity to suffer and the obligation to love.
plays.ch17: Original Title: Volpone; or, The FoxDate: 1606 (first performance) | Original language: Early Modern English | Country/tradition: Jacobean England | Period/movement: Jacobean Satire / City Comedy | Genre: Comedy / Satiric Comedy / Beast FableThe Altar of the Golden CalfThe desire to get rich without working, to trick others, and to watch the greedy destroy themselves in their own traps is a common human impulse. In Volpone; or, The Fox, Ben Jonson takes this moral vulnerability and transforms it into a dark comedy that exposes the predatory undercurrents of the early seventeenth century. Written in early 1606 and premiered by the King’s Men at the Globe Theatre, the play is a sharp critique of a society pivoting from feudal obligations to the speculative frenzy of mercantile capitalism. Jonson sets his drama in Venice, the European capital of commerce, luxury, and moral decadence, using this exotic locale to hold up a distorting mirror to the citizens of London.The play opens with an act of mock-religious devotion. Volpone, a wealthy Venetian magnifico, stands before his hidden hoard of gold and commands his parasite, Mosca, to withdraw the curtain:"Good morning to the day; and, next, my gold!Open the shrine, that I may see my saint."This opening soliloquy is a piece of blasphemous rhetoric. Volpone does not merely appreciate wealth; he deifies it. His language conflates Christian mysticism with pagan alchemy, elevating gold to the status of the "world’s soul" and the source of all light, outshining the sun itself. Yet Jonson shows that Volpone’s obsession is not that of a simple miser. Volpone is an aesthete of deception:"Yet I gloryMore in the cunning purchase of my wealth,Than in the glad possession, since I gainNo common way; I use no trade, no venture;"Volpone’s pleasure derives from the intellectual superiority of the con artist. He rejects the traditional paths of the merchant, the investor, or the landowner, choosing instead to exploit the greed of others. The play’s dramatic engine is thus set in motion: Volpone feigns a mortal illness, and his victims, believing he has no heirs, flock to his chamber with expensive gifts, hoping to be named sole beneficiary of his estate. Jonson presents a world where the pursuit of wealth has hollowed out human society, replacing religious piety and domestic affection with the transactional logic of the marketplace.The Anatomy of the CarnivoraTo structure his critique, Jonson revitalises the classical beast fable, assigning animal identities to his characters that dictate their dramatic behaviour. The title character, Volpone, is the Fox (volpone in Italian), which stands for traditional cunning and predatory intelligence. His companion and instrument is Mosca, the Fly (mosca), an opportunistic insect that feeds on the carcasses of the rich. The legacy hunters who circle Volpone's supposedly dying body are depicted as carrion birds, eagerly waiting for the corpse to rot.There is Voltore, the Vulture (voltore), an advocate whose legal eloquence is entirely at the service of the highest bidder; Corbaccio, the Raven (corbaccio), an old man so decrepit that he is practically on the edge of the grave himself, yet who is consumed by the desire to outlive Volpone; and Corvino, the Crow (corvino), a pathologically jealous merchant who is willing to sacrifice his wife’s chastity to secure the inheritance. Jonson uses these animal associations to strip his characters of psychological interiority, presenting them instead as creatures driven by basic urges of consumption.The interactions between Volpone and these legacy hunters are structured as a series of repetitive, highly ritualised performances. Volpone lies beneath the bedsheets, groaning and mimicking the symptoms of death, while Mosca acts as the stage manager, whispering lies to each visitor. When Corbaccio enters, Mosca convinces him that Volpone’s end is imminent. The irony is heavy: Corbaccio is himself physically decaying, yet he leans over the bed to peer at Volpone’s closed eyes, muttering about the symptoms of mortality with senile satisfaction.Mosca manipulates Corbaccio into disinheriting his own son, Bonario, to make Volpone his heir, promising that this display of generosity will induce Volpone to reciprocate in his own will. Similarly, when Corvino arrives, Mosca suggests that the physicians have ordered a young, healthy woman to lie beside Volpone as a therapeutic heat source. Corvino’s immediate reaction of jealousy is overridden by his desire for gold, and he agrees to bring his wife, Celia, to Volpone’s bed. Jonson shows that in this avian world, the values of family, honour, and chastity are merely commodities to be bartered for speculative gain.The Theatricality of DeceptionAt its core, Volpone is a play about the power and danger of theatre. Volpone and Mosca do not merely lie; they create elaborate scripts, costuming, and scenarios, transforming Volpone's bedchamber into a private stage where they direct the performances of their victims. Volpone is an actor who delights in the physical transformation of his roles, whether he is playing the bedridden invalid or the disguised Scoto Mantuano, a travelling mountebank selling a miraculous elixir beneath Celia's window.The mountebank scene is a bravura display of Jonsonian language. Disguised as Scoto, Volpone stands on a temporary stage in the street and delivers a long, bombastic speech that parodies the promotional rhetoric of Jacobean quack doctors. He uses a mixture of mock-scientific jargon, classical allusions, and slang to dazzle the crowd, presenting his medicine as a cure-all for physical decay. This performance is not merely a plot device to allow Volpone to see Celia; it is a thematic microcosm of the play’s wider world. Just as Scoto sells worthless grease as a divine elixir, so do Volpone and Mosca sell false hopes of inheritance to the legacy hunters.The danger of this theatricality becomes apparent when the scene shifts to the Scrutineo, the Venetian courtroom. When Bonario rescues Celia from Volpone's attempted rape, exposing the plot, Mosca and Voltore must defend their master by transforming the court into a theatre of justice. Voltore uses his oratorical skill to present a completely inverted version of reality, painting the innocent Celia and Bonario as adulterous lovers who conspired to frame Volpone. To secure the verdict, Volpone is carried into the courtroom on a stretcher, presenting a spectacle of physical ruin that mimics the evidence of his innocence. The judges are completely deceived by this theatrical display and the testimonies of the legacy hunters. Jonson shows that when language and performance are divorced from moral truth, the institutions of justice are easily subverted.The Domestic Sacrifice and the English MirrorThe moral darkness of the play culminates in the confrontation between Volpone and Celia in Act III. Celia represents the rare presence of genuine moral value in the play, but in Jonson's Venice, virtue is vulnerable. Her husband, Corvino, forces her into Volpone's bedchamber, dismissing her pleas for her honour with furious abuse. Corvino's transformation from a jealous husband who keeps his wife locked behind iron bars to a pander who demands her submission to another man is one of the savage ironies in Jacobean drama.When Volpone is left alone with Celia, he leaps from his bed, shedding his sick persona to reveal his true vigour. He attempts to seduce her not with brute force initially, but with a luxurious song:"Come, my Celia, let us prove,While we can, the sports of love;Time will not be ours for ever,He, at length, our good will sever;"This song, with its elegant lyricism, contrasts with the prose of the legacy hunters. Yet Volpone's aesthetic refinement is merely a mask for sexual violence. When Celia rejects his offers, pleading with him to spare her, Volpone's poetic seduction collapses. He declares that if she will not yield, he will take her by force. This moment of near-rape is interrupted by Bonario, who leaps from his hiding place to rescue her. Bonario represents the standard heroic virtue of romantic comedy, yet Jonson refuses to allow this rescue to lead to a clean moral triumph. Jonson warns that in a corrupt society, passive virtue and naive innocence are insufficient defences against organised deception.While the Venetian plot presents a dark vision of moral corruption, Jonson balances it with the English travel subplot involving Sir Politic Would-Be and his wife. Sir Politic is a foolish English knight who believes he is a master of espionage, seeing hidden state conspiracies in the movement of cabbages. Sir Politic's folly is a harmless version of Volpone's cunning. While Volpone designs real conspiracies, Sir Politic invents imaginary ones.
