Horn ruled the poem had redeeming social importance, establishing precedent for First Amendment protection of literary speech. Prosecution focused on frank sexuality ("who let themselves be fucked in the ass by saintly motorcyclists") and drug references; defence called critics Mark Schorer, Kenneth Rexroth, and Walter Van Tilburg Clark. The trial publicised Beat writing globally and linked Howl to civil liberties as much as to aesthetics.Formally, Howl rejects New Critical irony for public utterance, incantatory, repetitive, addressed to live audience. Ginsberg's Jewish queer identity inflects the poem's outsider saints; "negro streets" and solidarity with the marginalised anticipate later political commitments even where language now reads dated. Compared to Eliot's fragmented allusion, Ginsberg's references (Moloch, Rockland, Marx, Rimbaud) serve immediate vocal drive rather than scholarly density.In three parts and a footnote, Ginsberg conducts us from best minds destroyed by madness through Moloch's cement sphinx and robot apartments, through I'm with you in Rockland, to holy everything and everyman's an angel. Howl remains the definitive Beat prophesy: the claim that post-war America's machinery devours its visionaries, that institutional madness inherits maternal pain, and that holiness must be shouted into filth and suburb alike. The poem does more than describe a San Francisco coterie; by Whitmanesque anaphora and courtroom survival, it enacts the right to ecstatic, obscene, sacred speech, and inherits Whitman's America as both starry dynamo and Moloch's bomb.Word count (body): 1,029
poems.ch83: Gwendolyn Brooks (1917–2000)Original title: "We Real Cool"Written 1959; first published 1960 (The Bean Eaters, Harpers) · English (African American vernacular) · Chicago Black Arts; mid-century American lyric; Bronzeville community portraiture · Eight-line dramatic monologue in couplets with terminal enjambment; syncopated pool-hall vignette from The Bean EatersSeven at the Golden Shovel: Pool Players, Place, and Dramatic SceneGwendolyn Brooks's "We Real Cool"—written in 1959 after the poet passed the Golden Shovel pool hall at the corner of 31st and Cottage Grove on Chicago's South Side, and first published in The Bean Eaters (Harpers, 1960)—compresses an entire marginal subculture into eight lines and twenty-eight words. Brooks, first African American to win the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry (1950, for Annie Allen), spent decades rendering Bronzeville's kitchens, parlours, and streets; here she overhears seven pool players who speak as collective "we." The poem's subtitle functions as stage direction: The Pool Players. Seven at the Golden Shovel. Golden Shovel names a real establishment Brooks observed; the epithet also puns darkly, gold sought by digging, shovel as grave tool, leisure site shadowed by mortality. George E. Kent's A Life of Gwendolyn Brooks and Brooks's own reportage in Report from Part One record composition: she wondered what the boys inside thought of her, recognised their performed defiance, and crafted lines to be read "light, with a lilt." For UGC NET English candidates tracing African American poetry from Harlem Renaissance through Black Arts, "We Real Cool" exemplifies how miniaturist form, vernacular voice, and enjambment convert street observation into tragic prophecy.The opening asserts identity through grammar that breaks standard English:"We real cool" drops the copula (are), adopting Black English economical syntax; cool names both temperature of attitude and post-war youth rebellion. Period after "cool" and enjambment of solitary "We" at line end, Brooks's crucial formal decision, delay completion: the pronoun hangs, waits, syncopates. Each subsequent line ends similarly with "We," forcing breath pause before the next verb phrase begins. Brooks noted that young readers often misread the poem as celebration; the terminal "We" actually thins the voice, as if players speak between shots, between heartbeats.We real cool. WeLeft school. We(Brooks, "We Real Cool", ll. 1–2; The Bean Eaters, 1960)Lurk Late, Strike Straight: Syncopation, Couplets, and the Grammar of DefianceStanzas two through four catalogue rebellious activities in monosyllabic punch:Lurk late, nocturnal existence outside legitimate schedules; strike straight, pool-table competence extended to life's aim; sing sin and thin gin, vice as art and dilution as economy. Internal rhyme (late/straight, sin/gin) and alliteration bind couplets musically; syncopation arises from line-final "We" that never begins a completed sentence at the same line. The poem must be read with lilt, Brooks insists, not ponderous moralism. Form mirrors jazz phrasing: statement, rest, statement, rest. Seven players, seven "We" endings before the final line breaks the pattern, numerical symmetry suggests ritual, gang charter, countdown.Brooks places the poem within The Bean Eaters, a collection naming elderly couples as well as street youth; "We Real Cool" thus contrasts beans-and-franks endurance with adolescent bravado. Critics including Henry Louis Gates Jr. read the dropped copula as signifying tradition, speech that signifies on standard English by selective rule-breaking. The pool hall becomes classroom abandoned: left school, education exchanged for street education. Brooks later reflected that she had known such boys, "seven of them", and that their bravado masked fear; the poem's discipline lies in refusing either sermon or sociological footnote while still arriving at die soon. In mid-century Chicago, segregated housing, school attrition, and limited labour markets structured the cool performance the poem records; Brooks's formal restraint keeps that history implicit, audible only in what the boys claim for themselves and in what the ending withholds.Lurk late. WeStrike straight. WeSing sin. WeThin gin. We(Brooks, "We Real Cool", ll. 3–6; The Bean Eaters, 1960)Jazz June and Die Soon: Prophecy, Season, and the Broken RefrainThe closing couplet abandons terminal "We" for catastrophic forecast:Jazz June, summer festivity, musical verb, sexual suggestion, collides with monosyllabic "Die soon." The last line contains no "We"; collective voice fractures into blunt fate. Brooks reported that listeners who chanted the poem celebratively missed the funeral embedded in Golden Shovel's name and in this ending. June's jazz cannot sustain seven lives outside school, law, and morning; lurk late becomes prelude to early death. The poem's brevity enacts lives foreshortened: twenty-eight words, eight lines, no stanzaic expansion, no elegiac consolation.Interpretive debates turn on sympathy versus critique. Brooks neither ridicules nor wholly endorses the players; she renders their cool as survival performance within segregated Chicago where opportunities narrow. Feminist and Black Arts critics later reclaimed Brooks, especially after her 1967 Fisk University conference turn toward more explicit militancy, as architect of voice for the unheard. "We Real Cool" predates that shift yet already trusts vernacular speakers with poem's centre stage.Jazz June. WeDie soon.(Brooks, "We Real Cool", ll. 7–8; The Bean Eaters, 1960)Enjambment, Performance, and the Poetics of MiniatureBrooks's form lesson, ending each line with "We", teaches how layout shapes meaning. Printed poem resembles pool table rectangle; couplets suggest paired players or mirrored shots. Reading aloud, audience participates in syncopation: "We real cool. [pause] We left school." The pause is where cool lives, in hesitation before next risk. Compared to Ginsberg's expansive Howl or Plath's theatrical tercets, Brooks's miniature proves that scale does not limit scope.Influence extends through spoken-word pedagogy and anthologies; the poem is among America's most taught lyrics, sometimes reduced to slogan. Brooks resisted simplification: light reading carries heavy prophecy. Sound devices, monosyllables, internal rhyme, anaphoric "We", create memorable chant; semantic darkness waits in final two words. Teachers who assign the poem often debate whether to emphasise formal enjambment or social context; Brooks insisted both matter, that without the lilt, die soon arrives as punchline rather than elegy, and without attention to left school, cool reads as endorsement rather than diagnosis. The Golden Shovel thus functions as metonym: leisure economy on a corner where gold is scarce and the shovel waits.In eight coupleted lines and seven terminal "We"s, Brooks conducts us from real cool and left school through lurk late and strike straight, through sing sin and thin gin, to jazz June and die soon. "We Real Cool" remains the definitive Bronzeville pool-hall lyric: the claim that defiance spoken in dropped copulas and syncopated pronouns cannot outrun structural violence, that Golden Shovel gilds a grave, and that the poem's lilt must not deafen readers to its closing funeral. The poem does more than describe seven pool players; by enjambing "We" at every line's edge until the voice breaks on die soon, it enacts the gap between performed cool and foreshortened life, and leaves the shovel digging.Word count (body): 1,072
poems.ch84: Sylvia Plath (1932–1963)Original title: "Lady Lazarus"Written 23 October 1962; first published 1965 (Ariel, Faber) · English (American idiom, Holocaust and circus diction) · Confessional poetry; Cold War American lyric; post-Holocaust metaphor in women's writing · Dramatic monologue in tercets with irregular rhyme; suicide-survivor performance poem from the Ariel manuscriptsI Have Done It Again: Lazarus, the Ariel Voice, and Three AttemptsSylvia Plath's "Lady Lazarus"—composed 23 October 1962 at Court Green, Devon, in the burst of poems written after separation from Ted Hughes, and published posthumously in Ariel (Faber, 1965, edited by Hughes)—transforms the biblical resurrection of Lazarus into a woman's repeated suicide and theatrical comeback. Plath wrote the poem on the same day as "Tulips" and near "Daddy" and "Ariel" in the famous October sequence; the Ariel manuscripts (Smith College, British Library) show her tightening tercets and sharpening performative diction. Lady Lazarus speaks as ringmaster of her own deaths:Done it again, suicide as habit, decennial rhythm. One year in every ten I manage it: the first attempt at ten, second at twenty, successful third anticipated at thirty. Plath's biographers (Anne Stevenson, Linda Wagner-Martin, Heather Clark) correlate the poem with her 1953 overdose, 1962 crisis, and prophetic staging of death at thirty. Jacqueline Rose's The Haunting of Sylvia Plath and Christina Britzolakis's Sylvia Plath and the Theatre of Mourning analyse Holocaust metaphor and gendered spectacle. For UGC NET English candidates tracing confessional poetry, feminist criticism, and the ethics of atrocity imagery, "Lady Lazarus" demands scrutiny of how tercet form, circus diction, and Nazi allusion produce a voice at once victim and avenger.I have done it again.One year in every tenI manage it——(Plath, "Lady Lazarus", ll. 1–3; Ariel, 1965)Herr Doktor, Herr Enemy: Medical Power, Audience, and the Peeling ShowThe speaker casts resurrection as grotesque entertainment for paying spectators:Peanut-crunching crowd shoves to see unwrap hand and foot, the big strip tease. Medical examination becomes burlesque; Herr Doktor and Herr Enemy (later lines) fuse clinician and persecutor. The peeling napkin scene extends the metaphor:Sour breath of doctors vanishes; Lady Lazarus outlasts institutional salvage. Circus and concentration-camp imagery interweave: lamp-shade skin, paperweight skull, fine linen wrap, objects that recall Nazi atrocity while describing one woman's body on display. Critics debate whether Plath's Holocaust metaphors trivialise genocide or expose how post-war consciousness processes trauma through inadmissible analogy; the poem's power partly derives from that unease.The peanut-crunching crowdShoves in to seeThem unwrap me hand and foot——The big strip tease.Gentlemen, ladiesThese are my handsMy knees.(Plath, "Lady Lazarus", ll. 26–32; Ariel, 1965)The nose, the eye pits, the full set of teeth?Your sour breathWill vanish in a day.(Plath, "Lady Lazarus", ll. 13–15; Ariel, 1965)Ash, Phoenix, and Out of the Ash I Rise: Tercets, Fire, and Resurrection IronyPlath's tercets, three-line stanzas associated with Dante and terza rima, pace the monologue with clipped momentum:Out of the ash I rise with my red hair / And I eat men like air, the closing lines invert Lazarus's biblical emergence: phoenix rather than obedient restored corpse, red hair as flame and witch sign, eating men like air as impalpable revenge. Earlier stanzas prepare the fire:Dying is an art, done exceptionally well, confessional boast that refuses pathos. Each death is opus; each return is curtain call. Ash imagery links Holocaust cremation, cigarette ash, and phoenix myth into single residue. The tercet form contains explosion: short lines prevent melodramatic sprawl while rhyme (Kamikaze/man's day, shroud/crowd) knits music to horror.Out of the ashI rise with my red hairAnd I eat men like air.(Plath, "Lady Lazarus", ll. 82–84; Ariel, 1965)DyingIs an art, like everything else.I do it exceptionally well.(Plath, "Lady Lazarus", ll. 43–45; Ariel, 1965)Holocaust Metaphor, Daddy, and the Cold War Confessional Stage"Lady Lazarus" belongs to the October 1962 cluster with "Daddy," which names Auschwitz and fascist father explicitly. Here Nazi imagery operates by allusion, Herr God, Herr Lucifer, lampshade, million celluloid viewers, without familial narrative frame. Plath's Jewish heritage (maternal Austrian grandparents; father Otto Plath's German birth) inflects metaphor some read as identification, others as appropriation. Cold War bomb culture and televised atrocity ("It is a theatrical / Comeback in broad day / To the same place, the same face, the same brute / Amused shout") situate private suicide within mass-media spectacle.Performance vocabulary dominates: opus, valentine, charge a dollar, big strip tease, call it miracle. Lady Lazarus monetises her suffering; audience complicity implicates reader. When she warns "Beware / Out of the ash / I rise," threat replaces martyrdom, survivor as predator. Confessional mode here exceeds autobiography into mythic aggression; Plath's Ariel voice, named for Shakespeare's airy spirit and for the horse she rode, claims elemental power.Ariel Manuscripts, Posthumous Fame, and Feminist ReadingHughes's ordering of Ariel placed "Lady Lazarus" among opening poems, establishing its centrality. Feminist critics from Adrienne Rich onward reclaimed Plath's rage as a direct response to patriarchal and literary domination. This school of thought views the speaker's defiance as a rebellion against the stifling domestic expectations of the mid-twentieth century. Later scholarship, such as Heather Clark's Red Comet, contextualises October 1962 within domestic crisis, literary ambition, and psychiatric history without reducing the poem to a mere transcript of suffering. The poem's influence spans pop culture (references in music, film) and the poetics of extremity, inspiring generations of writers who explore personal and collective trauma.Formally, irregular rhyme in tercets sustains chant; anaphora and refrain ("I do it so it feels like hell / I do it so it feels real") build incantatory pressure. Compared to Brooks's miniature "We Real Cool," Plath's monologue expands theatrical space; compared to Celan's "Todesfuge," both deploy Holocaust imagery but from different positions of witness and language.In tercets numbering three deaths and one prophesied end, Plath conducts us from I have done it again through peanut-crunching crowd and Herr Doktor, through dying is an art and lampshade skin, to out of the ash I rise and I eat men like air. "Lady Lazarus" remains the definitive confessional performance of suicide-survival: the claim that resurrection is strip tease for paying voyeurs, that medical and Nazi masters merge in Herr Doktor, and that the woman who rises from ash consumes rather than forgives. The poem does more than document Plath's crises; by peeling the napkin of skin and staging comeback in broad day, it enacts art's dangerous power to turn private annihilation into public myth, and leaves us among the peanut-crunching crowd, billed for the next miracle.Word count (body): 1,023
poems.ch85: Philip Larkin (1922–1985)Original title: "Church Going"Written 1954; first published 16 July 1955 · English · The Movement; post-war English realism; Hull librarian poetics · Meditative lyric in seven nine-line stanzas (predominantly iambic pentameter with ABABCADCD rhyme scheme); secular pilgrimage through an empty parish churchBicycle Clips and Bicycle-Helmet: The Movement Voice and Anti-Romantic PilgrimagePhilip Larkin's "Church Going"—written in 1954 at Hull, where Larkin was university librarian, first published in The Spectator (16 July 1955) and collected in The Less Deceived (Marvell Press, 1955)—transforms a casual bicycle stop at an empty church into the Movement's most sustained meditation on belief, ritual, and what survives when religion declines. The poem belongs to the post-war English reaction against High Modernist difficulty: Larkin, Kingsley Amis, Donald Davie, and their contemporaries favoured accessible diction, empirical observation, and sceptical intelligence over Symbolist obscurity. James Booth's Philip Larkin: Life, Art and Love and Andrew Motion's biography situate the poem within Larkin's agnostic temperament and his fascination with English parish architecture as cultural residue. For UGC NET English candidates tracing twentieth-century poetry from T. S. Eliot and W. H. Auden through The Movement to Seamus Heaney, "Church Going" exemplifies how post-war lyric converts Gray's churchyard elegy and Matthew Arnold's "Dover Beach" into conversational meditation without forfeiting solemnity.The opening stanza establishes self-deprecating secular pilgrimage through bicycle clips and awkward decorum:Once sure that nothing is going on, no service, no congregation, the speaker steps inside and lets the door thud shut with accidental profanity. Another church: the indefinite article registers serial habit; this is one among many parish buildings toured by a non-believer who cannot quite stay away. Matting, seats, stone, little books, brownish cut flowers, brass and stuff at the holy end, small neat organ, the catalogue inventories rather than spiritualises, converting sacred space into observable detail. Tense, musty, unignorable silence is brewed God knows how long: the colloquial oath punctures piety while acknowledging atmosphere's power. Hatless, the speaker removes cycle-clips in awkward reverence, substituting bicycle gear for worshipper's hat in a gesture that is simultaneously comic and sincere. The nine-line stanza's ABABCADCD rhyme scheme and iambic pentameter ground elevated meditation in pedestrian habit.Once I am sure there's nothing going onI step inside, letting the door thud shut.Another church: matting, seats, and stone,And little books; sprawlings of flowers, cutFor Sunday, brownish now; some brass and stuffUp at the holy end; the small neat organ;And a tense, musty, unignorable silence,Brewed God knows how long. Hatless, I take offMy cycle-clips in awkward reverence,(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza I; The Less Deceived, 1955)Matting, Seats, and Stone: Empty Church as Detailed InventoryStanza II extends inventory into botanical and liturgical specificity while the speaker questions his own compulsion:Running a hand around the font, mounting the lectern, perusing hectoring large-scale verses, pronouncing "Here endeth" too loudly, the speaker performs liturgical gestures without belief, and the echoes snigger briefly at the performance. Signing the visitor's book and donating an Irish sixpence converts pilgrimage into tourist transaction; reflecting that the place was not worth stopping for introduces self-mockery that the poem will progressively undermine. Stanza III names the compulsion directly:Yet stop he does, often, always ending at a loss, wondering what to look for and what anyone could hope to get from churches. The conversational tone, "really, I wonder", refuses mystification while admitting recurrent need. Larkin's speaker is neither hostile nor devout; he occupies the vast English middle ground of cultural Christianity without doctrinal commitment. The Movement's empirical method insists on what can be seen, touched, and heard: roof almost new, cleaned or restored, someone would know.Move forward, run my hand around the font.From where I stand, the roof looks almost new—Cleaned, or restored? Someone would know: I don't.Mounting the lectern, I peruse a fewHectoring large-scale verses, and pronounce"Here endeth" much more loudly than I'd meant.The echoes snigger briefly. Back at the doorI sign the book, donate an Irish sixpence,Reflect the place was not worth stopping for.(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza II; The Less Deceived, 1955)Yet stop I did: in fact I often do,And always end much at a loss like this,Wondering what to look for; and, really, I wonderWhat anyone could ever hope to get from it.(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza III, ll. 1–4; The Less Deceived, 1955)A Serious House on Serious Earth: Ritual, Birth, and MarriageStanza IV pivots from inventory to argument, proposing that churches persist because they hosted life's serious occasions:A serious house on serious earth: the double "serious" elevates diction without invoking supernatural guarantee. Blent air where compulsions meet, are recognised, and robed as destinies, marriage, birth, death clothed in liturgical garment, supplies the church's enduring function. That much never can be obsolete, since someone will forever surprise a hunger in himself to be more serious and gravitate to ground heard proper for growing wise among the dead. Larkin's argument is anthropological rather than theological: churches matter because human beings need occasions of gravity, and consecrated ground marks where generations have confronted mortality. The stanza inherits Gray's country churchyard meditation and Arnold's sea of faith receding, yet refuses both Romantic melancholy and Victorian doubt by locating value in social practice rather than metaphysical certainty.The poem's central claim, that churches survive because they robe compulsions as destinies, resonates across Larkin's oeuvre from "An Arundel Tomb" (marriage's stone fidelity) to "The Whitsun Weddings" (ritual departure). For UGC NET candidates comparing ecclesiastical poems, "Church Going" differs from Herbert's temple lyrics and Donne's holy sonnets by treating the building as cultural infrastructure rather than divine address. Marriage, birth, death, and thoughts of these constitute the irreducible trilogy that no secular institution has fully replaced; the church's shell persists because these events still demand a gravity that supermarket atria and civic registrars cannot supply.A serious house on serious earth it is,In whose blent air all our compulsions meet,Are recognised, and robed as destinies.And that much never can be obsolete,Since someone will forever be surprisingA hunger in himself to be more serious,And gravitating with it to this ground,Which, he once heard, was proper to grow wise in,If only that so many dead lie round.(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza IV; The Less Deceived, 1955)What Shall We Turn Them Into?: Secular Inheritance and the Power of PlaceStanza V poses the poem's central historical question, what happens when churches fall completely out of use:When churches fall completely out of use, what shall we turn them into, museums with parchment, plate, and pyx in locked cases, or ruins rent-free to rain and sheep? Shall we avoid them as unlucky places, or will dubious women bring children to touch particular stones, pick simples for cancer, see walking dead on advised nights? Larkin imagines superstition persisting after doctrine evaporates: the hunger for serious ground outlasts the theology that consecrated it. The stanza's speculative grammar, "if we shall keep," "will dubious women come", projects a future England where parish churches become heritage sites, ruins, or folk-magic venues. Post-war Britain was already witnessing declining church attendance; Larkin's question is sociological prophecy dressed as casual wondering.Stanza VI proposes a more probable fate, power of place surviving ownership:Power of some sort will continue in games and riddles; superstition like belief must die; what remains is grass, weedy pavement, brambles, buttress, sky, a shape less recognisable each week, a purpose more obscure. Who will be last to seek this place for what it was, one of the crew that tap and jot and know what rood-lofts were? Larkin the librarian imagines final antiquaries documenting architectural vocabulary after living faith departs. The poem thus links personal bicycle pilgrimage to civilisational archive: the speaker is precursor to that last knowledgeable visitor.When churches fall completely out of useWhat we shall turn them into, if we shall keepA few cathedrals chronically on show,Their parchment, plate, and pyx in locked cases,And let the rest rent-free to rain and sheep.Shall we avoid them as unlucky places?Or, after dark, will dubious women comeTo make their children touch a particular stone;Pick simples for a cancer; or on someAdvised night see walking a dead one?(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza V; The Less Deceived, 1955)Power of some sort or other will go onIn games, in riddles, seemingly at random;But superstition, like belief, must die,And what remains when disbelief has gone?Grass, weedy pavement, brambles, buttress, sky,A shape less recognizable each week,A purpose more obscure. I wonder whoWill be the last, the very last, to seekThis place for what it was; one of the crewThat tap and jot and know what rood-lofts were?(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza VI; The Less Deceived, 1955)Death and Destiny: The Unrobing, Unbribable PriestThe final stanza delivers the poem's most solemn projection, a future worshiper and the church's ultimate destiny:Some ruin-bibber randy for antique, Christmas-addict craving gown-and-bands, or will he be the speaker's representative, bored and uninformed, knowing ghostly silt dispersed yet tending this cross of ground through suburb scrub because it held unspilt so long what since is found only in separation: marriage, birth, death, and thoughts of these. Though the accoutred frowsty barn's worth is unknown, standing in silence pleases, the final admission that scepticism has not extinguished appetite for consecrated pause. Critics from Barbara Everett to Terry Eagleton debate whether Larkin's conclusion affirms human seriousness or merely documents its nostalgia; the poem's form enacts the tension through colloquial opening modulating into elevated repetition of stanza IV's central lines."Church Going" influenced Heaney's sacred sites, Douglas Dunn's parish poems, and contemporary British poets who treat churches as secular heritage. Compared to Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, Larkin interiorises pilgrimage, the speaker enters the building rather than contemplating externals, and replaces mute inglorious Miltons with bicycle clips and Irish sixpences. Compared to Arnold's "Dover Beach," Larkin locates residual seriousness in architecture and rite rather than in love's remaining shore.In seven nine-line stanzas, Larkin conducts us from cycle-clips and awkward reverence through matting, seats, and stone, through hectoring verses and Irish sixpences, through a serious house on serious earth where compulsions meet robed as destinies, through churches fallen out of use and dubious women touching stones, through power that continues in games and riddles, to the bored representative tending cross of ground where marriage, birth, and death remain found only in separation. "Church Going" remains the definitive expression of post-war English religious scepticism that cannot abandon sacred architecture: the claim that someone will forever surprise a hunger to be more serious and gravitate to ground proper for growing wise among the dead, that churches robe compulsions as destinies even when belief has departed, and that an accoutred frowsty barn pleases the agnostic who stands in silence because so many dead lie round. The poem does more than describe an empty parish church; by moving from comic cycle-clips to solemn meditation on what survives when superstition and belief have died, it enacts the very hunger for seriousness it diagnoses, a Movement landmark that proves realism can ascend without ceasing to be conversational.Word count (body): 2,062Some ruin-bibber, randy for antique,Or Christmas-addict, counting on a whiffOf gown-and-bands and organ-pipes and myrrh?Or will he be my representative,Bored, uninformed, knowing the ghostly siltDispersed, yet tending to this cross of groundThrough suburb scrub because it held unspiltSo long and equably what since is foundOnly in separation—marriage, and birth,And death, and thoughts of these—for which was builtThis special shell? For, though I've no ideaWhat this accoutred frowsty barn is worth,It pleases me to stand in silence here;A serious house on serious earth it is,In whose blent air all our compulsions meet,Are recognised, and robed as destinies.And that much never can be obsolete,Since someone will forever be surprisingA hunger in himself to be more serious,And gravitating with it to this ground,Which, he once heard, was proper to grow wise in,If only that so many dead lie round.(Larkin, "Church Going", stanza VII; The Less Deceived, 1955)
poems.ch86: Robert Lowell (1917–1977)Original title: "For the Union Dead"Written 1960; first published 1964 · English · Confessional poetry; New England historical lyric; Boston Brahmin decline · Meditative public elegy in unrhymed quatrains with irregular line lengths; juxtaposition of childhood memory, Civil War memorial, and Civil Rights-era urban decayThe Old Aquarium and the Pit: Childhood Memory versus Modern BostonRobert Lowell's "For the Union Dead"—composed in 1960, read at the Boston Arts Festival on the Common, and collected in the volume For the Union Dead (Farrar, Straus, 1964)—replaces the patriotic certainties of Ralph Waldo Emerson's "Concord Hymn" with a meditation on memorial erosion, racial injustice, and commercial greed in mid-century Boston. The poem revises Lowell's earlier "Colonel Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th" (1943), deepening the childhood aquarium memory and sharpening the Civil Rights-era urgency. Ian Hamilton's Robert Lowell: A Biography and Steven Gould Axelrod's Robert Lowell: Life and Art contextualise the poem within Lowell's conversion from formal Lord Weary's Castle Catholicism to the looser, confessional mode of Life Studies (1959). For UGC NET English candidates tracing American poetry from Whitman and Dickinson through Modernism to Lowell, Bishop, and Plath, "For the Union Dead" exemplifies how New England historical consciousness absorbs personal memory into public elegy without surrendering political critique.The opening quatrains establish childhood wonder at the South Boston Aquarium before its demolition:The old South Boston Aquarium stands in a Sahara of snow, desert imagery applied to New England winter, converting urban decay into geological barrenness. Broken windows boarded, bronze weathervane cod losing half its scales, airy tanks dry: the catalogue registers abandonment before memory restores animation. Once the child's nose crawled like a snail on glass and hand tingled to burst bubbles drifting from noses of cowed, compliant fish, sensory immersion that the present tense of recollection revives within ruin. The fish's compliance anticipates the poem's closing image of servile modernity; childhood wonder already contained submission within its aesthetic pleasure. Hand drawing back from present desolation, the speaker sighs still for the lost kingdom:The dark downward and vegetating kingdom of fish and reptile sustains Edenic memory against Boston's new barbed fence. One morning last March the adult speaker presses against galvanised enclosure while yellow dinosaur steamshovels grunt, cropping mush and grass to gouge an underworld garage, the parking structure that will bury the Shaw monument's foundations. The aquarium's dried tanks and the Common's excavated earth form parallel voids: natural wonder replaced by civic earthworks.The old South Boston Aquarium standsin a Sahara of snow now. Its broken windows are boarded.The bronze weathervane cod has lost half its scales.The airy tanks are dry.Once my nose crawled like a snail on the glass;my hand tingledto burst the bubblesdrifting from the noses of the cowed, compliant fish.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 1–8; For the Union Dead, 1964)My hand draws back. I often sigh stillfor the dark downward and vegetating kingdomof the fish and reptile. One morning last March,I pressed against the new barbed and galvanizedfence on the Boston Common. Behind their cage,yellow dinosaur steamshovels were gruntingas they cropped up tons of mush and grassto gouge their underworld garage.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 9–16; For the Union Dead, 1964)Colonel Shaw and Saint-Gaudens: Bronze Relief and Civil War SacrificeLowell pivots from excavation to August Saint-Gaudens's bronze relief of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th Regiment:Parking spaces luxuriate like civic sandpiles, commercial convenience sprawling where memory should concentrate. Orange Puritan-pumpkin girders brace the tingling Statehouse, shaking over excavations as it faces Colonel Shaw and his bell-cheeked Negro infantry on Saint-Gaudens's shaking Civil War relief, propped by plank splint against the garage's earthquake. The monument literally trembles from construction vibration: heroic bronze meets municipal indifference. Two months after marching through Boston, half the regiment was dead at Fort Wagner (1863); at the 1897 dedication, William James could almost hear the bronze Negroes breathe, philosopher's testimony to the relief's uncanny vitality. Lowell treats Shaw's sacrifice as simultaneously immortalised and imperilled, suspended between Saint-Gaudens's art and the steamshovel's gouge.Parking spaces luxuriate like civicsandpiles in the heart of Boston.A girdle of orange, Puritan-pumpkin colored girdersbraces the tingling Statehouse,shaking over the excavations, as it faces Colonel Shawand his bell-cheeked Negro infantryon St. Gaudens' shaking Civil War relief,propped by a plank splint against the garage's earthquake.Two months after marching through Boston,half the regiment was dead;at the dedication,William James could almost hear the bronze Negroes breathe.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 17–28; For the Union Dead, 1964)The Ditch Is Nearer: Public History and Commercial DecayThe poem's central historical passage contrasts Shaw's moral clarity with modern Boston's commercial and atomic desecration:Their monument sticks like a fishbone in the city's throat: discomfort that cannot be swallowed or expelled. Colonel Shaw is lean as a compass-needle, with angry wrenlike vigilance and greyhound's gentle tautness; he seems to wince at pleasure and suffocate for privacy, aristocratic conscience personified. He is out of bounds now, rejoicing in man's lovely, peculiar power to choose life and die; when he leads his black soldiers to death, he cannot bend his back, Lowell's Shaw embodies rigid moral choice that contemporary Boston has abandoned. Shaw's father wanted no monument except the ditch where his son's body was thrown and lost with his "niggers"—Lowell retains the historical slur to expose the racism that accompanied Union sacrifice. The ditch is nearer: mass grave supersedes bronze memorial as authentic site of honour.Lowell widens the lens to New England's abstract memorials and atomic commerce:On a thousand small town New England greens, old white churches hold sparse sincere rebellion while frayed flags quilt Grand Army graveyards, regional piety persisting as decorative remnant. Abstract Union Soldier statues grow slimmer and younger, wasp-waisted, dozing over muskets, generic memorials ageing into fashionable anachronism. No statues for the last war; on Boylston Street a commercial photograph shows Hiroshima boiling over a Mosler Safe, the "Rock of Ages" that survived the blast, atomic horror enlisted to sell bank vaults. Space is nearer: the cosmos of destruction closer than sacred ground. Television brings drained faces of Negro school-children rising like balloons: Lowell wrote during Boston's school-desegregation crisis, and the Civil Rights movement charges Civil War memory with unfulfilled promise.Their monument sticks like a fishbonein the city's throat.Its Colonel is as leanas a compass-needle.He has an angry wrenlike vigilance,a greyhound's gentle tautness;he seems to wince at pleasure,and suffocate for privacy.He is out of bounds now. He rejoices in man's lovely,peculiar power to choose life and die—when he leads his black soldiers to death,he cannot bend his back.Shaw's father wanted no monumentexcept the ditch,where his son's body was thrownand lost with his "niggers."The ditch is nearer.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 29–44; For the Union Dead, 1964)On a thousand small town New England greens,the old white churches hold their airof sparse, sincere rebellion; frayed flagsquilt the graveyards of the Grand Army of the Republic.The stone statues of the abstract Union Soldiergrow slimmer and younger each year—wasp-waisted, they doze over musketsand muse through their sideburns . . .There are no statues for the last war here;on Boylston Street, a commercial photographshows Hiroshima boilingover a Mosler Safe, the "Rock of Ages"that survived the blast. Space is nearer.When I crouch to my television set,the drained faces of Negro school-children rise like balloons.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 45–60; For the Union Dead, 1964)A Savage Servility: Civil Rights Era and Memorial ErosionLowell returns to Shaw suspended between historical honour and contemporary paralysis:Colonel Shaw is riding on his bubble, waiting for the blessèd break, the moment of racial justice that the 54th Regiment's sacrifice promised yet Boston in 1960 has not delivered. The bubble imagery converts monument into fragile, floating insubstantiality: Shaw waits eternally while steamshovels gouge his ground and television broadcasts school-children's drained faces. Where the 1943 version treated Shaw as static bronze, the 1964 revision animates him as impatient witness, out of bounds, unable to bend his back, still clenching sword and flag while the city buries his regiment beneath parking concrete.Critics from Helen Vendler to James E. B. Breslin read "For the Union Dead" as Lowell's definitive public poem, balancing Life Studies intimacy with civic responsibility. The unrhymed quatrains, descended from Lowell's revision of formal metre yet retaining visual stanzaic order, create episodic collage akin to television channel-switching between aquarium, monument, Hiroshima advertisement, and parking-garage excavation. Comparative study links the poem to Yeats's "Easter, 1916" (monument and historical sacrifice), Virgil's Aeneid (empire's cost), and Elizabeth Bishop's restrained historical lyrics, yet Lowell's Boston particularity and television-mediated Civil Rights imagery remain distinctive.Colonel Shawis riding on his bubble,he waitsfor the blessèd break.(Lowell, "For the Union Dead", ll. 61–64; For the Union Dead, 1964)Giant Finned Cars: The Poem's Closing Fish and American GreedThe poem's conclusion returns to fish imagery with transformed menace:The Aquarium is gone; everywhere giant finned cars nose forward like fish, a savage servility slides by on grease. Where childhood fish were cowed and compliant behind glass, modern cars are giant, predatory, and servile simultaneously: American consumer culture as obedient violence, chrome fins substituting for moral backbone. Grease replaces water as the medium of movement; the natural wonder of the aquarium yields to petroleum-propelled conformity. Lowell's closing oxymoron, savage servility, condenses the poem's political argument: post-war America preserves the forms of freedom while submitting to commercial and racial structures that betray the Union dead's sacrifice. The fish arc completes itself: compliant aquarium fish become finned automobiles, and the monument stuck like a fishbone in the city's throat finds its grotesque mirror in chrome creatures nosing forward on grease.For UGC NET candidates, key interpretive threads include: (1) the aquarium-to-automobile fish arc as American innocence corrupted into consumer predation; (2) Shaw as eternal waiter on his bubble versus the ditch as nearer truth; (3) the parking garage burying the 54th Regiment as literal metaphor for historical amnesia; (4) television school-children connecting 1863 to 1960s desegregation; (5) Saint-Gaudens's bronze as fishbone in civic throat, memorial that cannot be digested or removed; (6) Hiroshima over Mosler Safe as commerce profiting from annihilation.In unrhymed quatrains, Lowell conducts us from the boarded South Boston Aquarium and cowed compliant fish through dinosaur steamshovels gouging the Common's underworld garage, through Colonel Shaw and his bell-cheeked Negro infantry on Saint-Gaudens's shaking relief, through a monument stuck like a fishbone and a Colonel lean as a compass-needle, through Shaw's father wanting only the ditch and Hiroshima boiling over a Mosler Safe, through Negro school-children rising like balloons and Colonel Shaw riding on his bubble, to giant finned cars nosing forward like fish while savage servility slides by on grease. "For the Union Dead" remains the definitive expression of Civil Rights-era New England conscience confronting its own monuments: the claim that the ditch is nearer than bronze, that Shaw waits out of bounds for a blessèd break that has not come, and that the aquarium's wonder has been replaced by chrome servility on grease. The poem does more than commemorate Colonel Shaw; by collapsing childhood memory, Civil War relief, atomic commerce, and televised desegregation into a single Boston site, it enacts the very historical layering it mourns, a confessional public elegy that proves personal recollection can bear the weight of national betrayal without releasing us from complicity in the parking garage's excavation.Word count (body): 2,002The Aquarium is gone. poems.ch87: Elizabeth Bishop (1911–1979)Original title: "One Art"Written 1975–1976; first published 1976 · English · Post-war American lyric; Brazilian-influenced cosmopolitan poetics · Villanelle (nineteen lines, five tercets and one quatrain, two rhymes, two refrains); meditation on loss escalating from trivial objects to the belovedThe Villanelle's Rigour: Form as Emotional ContainmentElizabeth Bishop's "One Art"—drafted across multiple versions between 1975 and 1976, published in Geography III (Farrar, Straus, 1976) and written during Bishop's final years when she was confronting the death of Alice Methfessel's predecessor Lota de Macedo Soares and her own mortality, perfects the villanelle as an instrument for managing grief through procedural mastery. The nineteen-line French form, five tercets followed by a quatrain, employing only two rhymes (-aster / -ent) and two refrains ("The art of losing isn't hard to master" and "disaster")—imposes obsessive repetition that Bishop exploits to simulate the mind's attempt to convince itself that loss is acceptable. Brett C. Millier's Elizabeth Bishop: Life and the Memory of It and Lorrie Goldensohn's Elizabeth Bishop: The Biography of a Poetry document the poem's extensive drafting history, revealing how Bishop revised toward greater emotional concealment behind ever more casual diction. For UGC NET English candidates tracing fixed forms from Villon and Dylan Thomas's "Do not go gentle" to Sylvia Plath's formal experiments, "One Art" exemplifies how strict prosody can intensify rather than restrain feeling by forcing the speaker's composure to crack along predetermined fault lines.The opening tercet establishes the poem's instructional tone and first refrain:The art of losing isn't hard to master: the flat declarative opens a curriculum in deprivation, presenting loss as acquirable skill rather than catastrophe. So many things seem filled with the intent to be lost that their loss is no disaster, the first appearance of the second refrain word "disaster," rhyming with "master" and establishing the poem's limited sonic field. Bishop's choice of villanelle is strategic: the form's refrains compel the speaker to repeat the same sentences with minor variation, mimicking the psychological process of rehearsing acceptance until belief arrives. Yet the very need for rehearsal betrays the grief it denies.The art of losing isn't hard to master;so many things seem filled with the intentto be lost that their loss is no disaster.(Bishop, "One Art", ll. 1–3; Geography III, 1976)From Lost Door Keys to Lost Cities: The Escalating CatalogueStanzas two through four escalate from domestic triviality to geographical and temporal enormity:Lose something every day: the imperative converts grief into homework. Accept the fluster of lost door keys, the hour badly spent, minor dislocations that train the will for greater severances. Then practice losing farther, losing faster: places, names, where it was you meant to travel, geographical and mnemonic losses that map Bishop's peripatetic life from Nova Scotia through New York, Key West, Brazil, and Cambridge. None of these will bring disaster: the refrain's negation grows less convincing as catalogue accumulates. Mother's watch, family heirloom, precedes three loved houses, of which the last or next-to-last went: Bishop lost her childhood home in Great Village, her Key West house, and her Brazilian home in Ouro Preto after Lota's death. Each tercet ends with the refrain "The art of losing isn't hard to master," but the inserted losses grow heavier, testing the form's composure.Stanza five introduces cities and continents:Two cities, lovely ones, likely alluding to Rio de Janeiro and Ouro Preto, yield to vaster realms: two rivers, a continent. I miss them, but it wasn't a disaster: the first admission of emotional register ("I miss them") arrives precisely where the speaker denies disaster, creating characteristic Bishopian understatement that intensifies through qualification. The hyperbolic "realms I owned" treats geographical belonging as proprietorship, then surrenders it, Bishop's cosmopolitan existence becomes curriculum in losing farther, losing faster.Lose something every day. Accept the flusterof lost door keys, the hour badly spent.The art of losing isn't hard to master.Then practice losing farther, losing faster:places, and names, and where it was you meantto travel. None of these will bring disaster.I lost my mother's watch. And look! my last, ornext-to-last, of three loved houses went.The art of losing isn't hard to master.(Bishop, "One Art", ll. 4–12; Geography III, 1976)I lost two cities, lovely ones. And, vaster,some realms I owned, two rivers, a continent.I miss them, but it wasn't a disaster.(Bishop, "One Art", ll. 13–15; Geography III, 1976)Drafting History: How Bishop Hid Raw Emotion Behind FormBishop's manuscripts, held at Vassar College and examined by Millier and Goldensohn, reveal a poem that moved from explicit personal grief toward strategic impersonality. Early drafts named the beloved directly and employed more conventional elegiac diction; Bishop revised toward the pedagogical "you" address and the casual catalogue structure that conceals autobiography behind universal lesson. The villanelle's refrains function as emotional dam: each repetition of "The art of losing isn't hard to master" attempts to hold back the "disaster" that the form simultaneously requires. Drafting records show Bishop experimenting with the order of losses, debating whether to include the mother's watch, and refining the penultimate stanza's parenthetical breakdown, "(Write it!)", that marks the poem's formal and emotional crisis.Stanza five continues the escalation toward personal catastrophe:Even losing you, the shift from abstract lesson to particular beloved ruptures the poem's pedagogical frame. The joking voice, a gesture I love: specific intimate detail that autobiography cannot fully contain yet refuses to conceal. I shan't have lied: the speaker's integrity depends on maintaining the thesis that loss is masterable. It's evident the art of losing's not too hard to master—"evident" replacing the earlier refrain's confident declaration, weakening the claim. Though it may look like (Write it!) like disaster: the parenthetical command "(Write it!)" breaks the villanelle's smooth surface, as if the form itself must be forced to admit the word the speaker has deferred through eighteen lines. The slant rhyme of "master" / "disaster" in the final couplet violates the poem's strict rhyme scheme (-aster / -ent), enacting formal breakdown at the moment of emotional surrender.—Even losing you (the joking voice, a gestureI love) I shan't have lied. It's evidentthe art of losing's not too hard to masterthough it may look like (Write it!) like disaster.(Bishop, "One Art", ll. 16–19; Geography III, 1976)Write It: The Refrain's Breakdown and the Lost YouThe villanelle's architecture demands that both refrains appear in the final quatrain, and Bishop deploys them with calculated asymmetry:Reading the complete poem reveals how refrains function as psychological tic: "The art of losing isn't hard to master" appears at the end of tercets one through four and twice in the final quatrain (lines 6, 9, 12, 18), while "disaster" closes tercets one through three and the final quatrain (lines 3, 6, 9, 12, 19). The asymmetry, "disaster" withheld from tercets four and five until the final line, creates structural pressure that the "(Write it!)" parenthesis releases. Critics from Helen Vendler to Thomas Travisano note that Bishop's villanelle answers Dylan Thomas's defiant "Do not go gentle" with acquiescent mastery: where Thomas rages against loss, Bishop proposes to school herself in its acceptance.The art of losing isn't hard to master;so many things seem filled with the intentto be lost that their loss is no disaster.Lose something every day. Accept the flusterof lost door keys, the hour badly spent.The art of losing isn't hard to master.Then practice losing farther, losing faster:places, and names, and where it was you meantto travel. None of these will bring disaster.I lost my mother's watch. And look! my last, ornext-to-last, of three loved houses went.The art of losing isn't hard to master.I lost two cities, lovely ones. And, vaster,some realms I owned, two rivers, a continent.I miss them, but it wasn't a disaster.—Even losing you (the joking voice, a gestureI love) I shan't have lied. It's evidentthe art of losing's not too hard to masterthough it may look like (Write it!) like disaster.(Bishop, "One Art", complete text; Geography III, 1976)(it's evident) the art of losing's not too hard to master: Disastrous ConclusionThe poem's final lines achieve their power through accumulated qualification. "It's evident" appeals to obvious truth yet follows an em-dash admission of losing you. "Not too hard" replaces "isn't hard," introducing the first hedging adverb, the art is not too difficult, the speaker suggests, but difficulty has not been eliminated. "Though it may look like (Write it!) like disaster", the doubled "like" stammers toward the word the villanelle has been circling, and the parenthetical imperative suggests the form itself resists naming catastrophe. Bishop's drafting history confirms she considered alternatives ("catastrophe," "a disaster") before settling on the stammered final phrase that enacts reluctance.Comparative study situates "One Art" within Bishop's broader poetics of restraint: like "The Fish" (triumph held in check until the final release) and "In the Waiting Room" (child's terror managed through catalogue), the villanelle disciplines emotion through formal requirement. Unlike Sylvia Plath's confessional explosiveness or Robert Lowell's autobiographical directness, Bishop hides raw feeling behind procedure, geography, and grammar, yet the hiding fails at the poem's close, and that failure is the poem's triumph.For UGC NET candidates, essential interpretive coordinates include: (1) villanelle structure, nineteen lines, ABA rhyme, refrains at lines 1, 6, 12, 18 and 3, 9, 15, 19; (2) escalating catalogue from door keys to cities to "you"; (3) drafting history demonstrating revision toward concealment; (4) the "(Write it!)" parenthesis as formal and emotional rupture; (5) relationship to Bishop's Brazilian exile and Lota de Macedo Soares's death; (6) contrast with Villon's formal ballades and Thomas's villanelle.Bishop's influence extends through contemporary formal poetry, Marilyn Hacker, Seamus Heaney's villanelles, and countless workshop exercises treating "One Art" as the form's gold standard. Debates persist whether the poem's "you" is necessarily Lota or a composite beloved; whether the instructional tone mocks self-help rhetoric or sincerely proposes coping strategy; whether mastering loss is possible or the poem's thesis is itself the lie the final line almost confesses.The villanelle's origin in French pastoral poetry (Jean Passerat's sixteenth-century template) and its revival by W. E. Henley, Edwin Arlington Robinson, and William Empson precede Bishop's mastery. Yet "One Art" distinguishes itself by refusing the form's traditional subjects, courtly love, pastoral retreat, metaphysical devotion, and substituting modern displacement, serial exile, and the death of a beloved woman. The poem's pedagogical "you" may address reader, self, or lost lover simultaneously; Bishop's pronoun ambiguity sustains universal application while autobiography presses against the seams.Technical brilliance resides in Bishop's management of the two rhymes across nineteen lines: -aster (master, disaster, vaster, last or, hard to master) and -ent (intent, spent, meant, went, continent, evident). The limited rhyme pool forces semantic clustering, intent to be lost, hour badly spent, where you meant to travel, houses went, continent, evident, so that sound pattern reinforces thematic accumulation. The final slant rhyme of "master" / "disaster" in the quatrain's closing couplet formally enacts the poem's argument that mastery and disaster are nearly but not quite identical.In five tercets and a concluding quatrain, Bishop conducts us from the art of losing isn't hard to master through lost door keys and hours badly spent, through practice losing farther and mother's watch and three loved houses, through two cities and two rivers and a continent, to even losing you with the joking voice and gesture loved, to the evident art of losing's not too hard to master though it may look like (Write it!) like disaster. "One Art" remains the definitive expression of grief disciplined by formal mastery: the claim that so many things seem filled with the intent to be lost, that none of these will bring disaster until the lost you arrives, and that the villanelle's refrains can contain bereavement only until the form commands the speaker to write what every stanza has denied. The poem does more than describe coping with loss; by escalating from door keys to continents to the beloved while repeating that mastery is easy, it enacts the very self-deception it nearly confesses, a nineteen-line curriculum in which the final parenthetical imperative proves that the art of losing is, finally, the art of admitting one has not mastered it at all.Word count (body): 2,039
poems.ch88: Derek Walcott (1930–2017)Original title: "A Far Cry from Africa"Written c. 1960; first published 1962 · English (Caribbean inflection) · West Indian / Caribbean postcolonial lyric; St Lucian Anglophone poetry; decolonisation-era political verse · Lyric poem in irregular rhyme and shifting stanzas; meditation on colonial violence, racial inheritance, and the poet's divided allegiance during the Mau Mau UprisingA Far Cry: Kenya, the Veldt, and the Title's Double MeaningDerek Walcott's "A Far Cry from Africa"—composed during the closing years of the Mau Mau Emergency in Kenya and first published in In a Green Night: Poems 1948–1960 (Jonathan Cape, 1962)—is one of the defining lyrics of postcolonial moral crisis. Walcott, born in Castries, St Lucia, in 1930 to parents of African and European descent, writes from the Caribbean rather than the African continent, yet the poem's occasion is the Kikuyu-led insurgency against British colonial rule in Kenya (1952–1960), reported in international press as savagery on every side. The title performs its first ambiguity immediately: a far cry may denote a distant call or lament reaching the poet across oceans, but the idiomatic phrase a far cry from also signals radical difference, this Africa of massacre is a far cry from any romanticised ancestral homeland. Bruce King's Derek Walcott: A Caribbean Life and Edward Baugh's critical studies situate the poem within Walcott's early negotiation of empire, language, and race. For UGC NET English candidates mapping postcolonial poetry from Yeats and Eliot through Walcott, Heaney, and Ezekiel, "A Far Cry from Africa" exemplifies how a West Indian writer confronts African political violence without the consolation of uncomplicated solidarity, and how English metre becomes both inheritance and betrayal.The opening stanza converts landscape into wounded animal body:Africa wears a tawny pelt ruffled by wind; the image fuses continent and fauna into a single organism under stress. Kikuyu fighters batten upon bloodstreams like flies upon carrion, and corpses lie scattered through what should be paradise. The worm, promoted to colonel of carrion, commands that compassion be withheld from the separated dead, military rank applied to decomposition, as though war's bureaucracy extends into putrefaction. Walcott's diction refuses a single villain: the veldt bleeds, the dead are separated from one another and from the living, and even the command not to waste pity arrives in quoted speech that sounds like official doctrine.A wind is ruffling the tawny peltOf Africa. Kikuyu, quick as flies,Batten upon the bloodstreams of the veldt.Corpses are scattered through a paradise.Only the worm, colonel of carrion, cries:"Waste no compassion on these separated dead!"(Walcott, "A Far Cry from Africa", stanza I; In a Green Night, 1962)Mau Mau Violence and the Colonial Arithmetic of BlameThe poem's second movement widens the historical lens, measuring centuries of colonial injury against the immediacy of revolt:Generals who watched civil war with detached amusement, whether in Europe or in colonial campaigns, now crouch in marble as they crouched in life, their monuments reproducing the posture of indifference. Walcott insists that the present catastrophe in Kenya cannot be isolated from the longer theatre of imperial violence. The Mau Mau Uprising, which British authorities represented as atavistic terror, enters the poem as one eruption within a geology of conquest. Kikuyu violence is not denied; it is contextualised within a system that trained populations in dispossession and then feigned innocence when dispossessed peoples struck back.Walcott's description of colonised labourers, "thirty thousand beasts who labour in the earth / Without salt, without soap", invokes the dehumanising rhetoric by which empire classified African bodies as beasts of burden. The poem reverses the accusation: those who named others beasts now confront a revolt they cannot metabolise into civilised narrative. When Walcott writes of "savages, expendable as Jews," he yokes colonial racism to the twentieth century's other genocidal logic, refusing the British Empire's claim to moral superiority. The simile shocks deliberately: expendability is the shared grammar of empire and extermination.Statues of generals who previouslyWith their own blood and others' blood hadWatched civil war with detached amusement,Are crouched in marble as they crouch in life.(Walcott, "A Far Cry from Africa", stanza II; In a Green Night, 1962)Caliban, Prospero, and the English Tongue the Poet LovesThe poem's psychological centre is the split colonial subject who inherits blood from more than one civilisation and language from the conqueror. Walcott never names Caliban or Prospero, yet Shakespeare's The Tempest haunts the lyric's structure: the poet is educated in Prospero's language, enchanted by English cadence, yet classified by the tradition he masters as kin to Caliban, poisoned, bestial, ungrateful if he rebels, traitorous if he assimilates. Walcott's later essays, especially "The Muse of History," and dramas including Pantomime and A Branch of the Blue Nile, elaborate this Tempest matrix; "A Far Cry from Africa" compresses it into the cry of a man who cannot claim pure African identity from St Lucia and cannot disown the English tongue that gives him his art.The stanza of division states the crisis with anatomical precision:Poisoned with the blood of both, African and European, the speaker is divided to the vein, a phrase that converts nationality into circulatory system. He has cursed the drunken officer of British rule, aligning moral rage with the colonised, yet he cannot renounce the English tongue he loves without renouncing poetry itself. Betray them both, or give back what they give: the syntax offers no ethical exit, only reciprocal injury. The closing questions, how can I face such slaughter and be cool? How can I turn from Africa and live?, reject stoic detachment and suicidal abandonment alike. To be cool is to become another detached general; to turn from Africa is to amputate a portion of the self that the poem has already established as vascularly necessary.I who am poisoned with the blood of both,Where shall I turn, divided to the vein?I who have cursedThe drunken officer of British rule, how chooseBetween this Africa and the English tongue I love?Betray them both, or give back what they give?How can I face such slaughter and be cool?How can I turn from Africa and live?(Walcott, "A Far Cry from Africa", closing stanzas; In a Green Night, 1962)Kikuyu, Carrion, and the Impossible Neutrality of WitnessBetween historical survey and personal crisis, Walcott stages the particular horror of the Mau Mau period as landscape metamorphosis. Ibises and zebras become casualties in a paradise turned abattoir; the natural world participates in moral judgment without offering redemption. The Kikuyu, named as a people rather than reduced solely to metaphor, appear "quick as flies" upon bloodstreams, a simile that risks dehumanisation even as the poem indicts those who dehumanised them. Critical readers have long debated whether Walcott's fly imagery reproduces colonial stereotype or implicates every side in carrion logic; the worm's command to waste no compassion suggests the latter reading, extending moral numbness across spectators, combatants, and poets who would aestheticise suffering.Walcott's irregular rhyme scheme and stanza lengths enact formal restlessness: the poem cannot settle into heroic couplets or sonnet resolution because its subject refuses closure. Lines of extraordinary beauty, "Corpses are scattered through a paradise", sit beside bureaucratic brutality and journalistic cliché, mimicking the mind's inability to synthesise Africa's news into a single tone. The poet who writes in English about African slaughter for a readership in London or Port of Spain occupies the same divided position the lyric confesses: every descriptive choice is also a political allegiance questioned before it is offered.Slaughter, Coolness, and the Postcolonial Poet's Unfinished Choice"A Far Cry from Africa" concludes not with resolution but with interrogatives that have shaped postcolonial literary studies for decades. Walcott does not choose between Africa and the English tongue; he dramatises the impossibility of choice without self-mutilation. The poem's enduring power lies in its refusal of propagandist simplicity: it does not excuse British counter-insurgency, does not sanctify every act of Mau Mau resistance, and does not permit the Caribbean observer a posture of innocent solidarity. Instead, it grants the speaker the right to love the language of Shakespeare, Milton, and Marvell while cursing the drunken officer, a love that Caliban, in Walcott's lifelong reading of The Tempest, is supposed to feel as Stockholm syndrome but here appears as genuine, treacherous, indispensable devotion.Influence radiates forward into Walcott's own Omeros, which rewrites Homeric epic from a Caribbean village, and backward toward Fanon's analyses of colonial psychosis, though Walcott's tone is more lyrically ambivalent than manifesto. Compared to politically declarative verse of the 1960s, "A Far Cry from Africa" preserves complexity at the cost of comfort: us leaves the poem still asking how one faces slaughter without coolness, how one turns toward Africa without hypocrisy, how one writes in English without complicity.In irregular stanzas that move from tawny pelt and Kikuyu bloodstreams through generals crouched in marble to the poet poisoned with the blood of both, Walcott conducts us from continental violence to personal division and the English tongue he loves. "A Far Cry from Africa" remains the definitive early expression of Caribbean witness to African anti-colonial war: the claim that corpses scatter through paradise, that compassion itself may be colonised by carrion officers, and that the postcolonial writer's veins divide before his conscience can choose. The poem does more than describe Mau Mau headlines from a safe distance; by closing on how can I face such slaughter and be cool and how can I turn from Africa and live, it enacts the irresolvable double bind of language, race, and loyalty that Walcott's career will spend decades mapping, without ever pretending that mapping is the same as escape.Word count (body): 1,568
poems.ch89: Derek Walcott (1930–2017)Original title: OmerosWritten 1989–1990; first published 1990 · English (Caribbean inflection; Homeric and Dantean allusion) · West Indian epic; St Lucian Anglophone poetry; postcolonial revision of classical and medieval forms · Epic poem in seven books and sixty-four chapters; modified terza rima in hexameter lines; narrative of fishermen, tourists, and ancestral wounds on St LuciaSeven Books and the Sea's Hexameter: Form as Caribbean HomerDerek Walcott's Omeros—composed 1989–1990 and published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux in 1990, the year before Walcott receives the Nobel Prize in Literature, reimagines Homer's Iliad and Odyssey on the island of St Lucia, replacing bronze-age warriors with fishermen, market women, and retired colonials while retaining the epic's scope, wound, and return. Where Homer's dactylic hexameter rides the Aegean, Walcott's long lines, adapted from Dante's terza rima but loosened into supple, often six-beat English hexameters, mimic the Caribbean sea's heave and recession, line breaking across rhyme in waves rather than in neat Italian tercets. Jahan Ramazani's The Hybrid Muse and Robert D. Hamner's studies of Walcott's epic phase analyse how formal inheritance becomes creolisation: terza rima is not copied but salt-watered. For UGC NET English candidates tracing epic continuity from Homer and Virgil through Dante to Walcott, Omeros demonstrates how postcolonial literature absorbs European form while renaming every god, wound, and wanderer in local tongue.The opening chapter establishes method, ordinary labour elevated to mythic fabrication:One sunrise, the world is cut down to size: epic begins not with armadas but with scavenged tin, palm leaves, and sand for the first church on the island. Walcott's humility of materials, rolled tin, ocean's benedictions, signals that Caribbean epic will honour the makeshift, the recycled, the sacred built from refuse. The first church is also the first frame of the poem's theatre: history on St Lucia is architecture assembled from what empire and ocean discard.This is how, one sunrise, we cut down to sizethe fabric of this world: a frame of rolled tinscavenged from the ocean's benedictions,a covering of palm leaves, a floor of sandfor the first church on this island, and that was it.(Walcott, Omeros, Book I, ch. 1; 1990 text)Achille, Hector, and Helen: Fishermen in Homeric ArmourThe human triangle at Omeros's centre maps the Trojan War onto Gros Islet and Castries. Achille and Hector are fishermen and canoe-men who compete for Helen, a beautiful house servant associated with a yellow dress and with the tourism economy's commodified desire. Their rivalry is at once domestic, two men in love with the same woman, and civilisational: Walcott imports Homeric names without requiring us to forget St Lucian poverty, rum shops, and outboard motors. When the men race their canoes or clash over Helen's attention, the poem asks whether ancient myth explains Caribbean life or whether Caribbean life reclaims myth from colonial schoolrooms, where Walcott himself first encountered Homer in English translation imposed as cultural superiority.Helen is never merely Helen of Troy. She carries the island's beauty as both blessing and curse, the yellow dress radiates in sunlight, yet her desirability triggers violence between men who should be kin. Walcott refuses to blame Helen simplistically; instead, he shows how patriarchal possession and touristic looking reproduce the epic's wars of property. Achille's name preserves Homer's Achilles while sounding local; Hector's doom acquires Caribbean specificity when pride and labour collide on a sea that feeds and kills. Through these characters, Omeros argues that the Trojan War was always also a fishermen's quarrel enlarged by poetry into cosmos.Philoctete's Wound and the Colonial Trauma That Will Not CloseIf Achille and Hector supply Iliadic combat, Philoctete embodies the unhealed injury that colonialism inflicts on body and community. His shin wound, reeking and ulcerous, echoes Homer's archer abandoned on Lemnos, but Walcott's Philoctete is a St Lucian fisherman whose sore will not close because history will not close. Slave ships, plantation labour, and the Middle Passage live in the wound's smell; local villagers can tolerate Philoctete's suffering until it becomes inconvenient, much as empire tolerates postcolonial pain as picturesque poverty. Ma Kilman, obeah woman and herbal healer, ultimately discovers the African-rooted flower that begins Philoctete's cure, a narrative of diasporic return in which healing knowledge survives transplantation and suppression.The wound's symbolism extends to Walcott's poetics: Caribbean literature cannot achieve epic wholeness while pretending amnesia about slavery. Philoctete's cry is the sound the poem must hear before it can sing triumphantly. Critics including Paul Breslin and Edouard Glissant's theorisation of Caribbean memory read Philoctete as collective trauma personified; Walcott's treatment is gentler than allegory yet more concrete than slogan. Achille's visionary voyage to ancestral Africa, where he encounters his namesake Afolabe and reclaims a pre-slavery name severed by the Middle Passage, parallels Philoctete's physical healing: both men recover what empire stole, one through dream-journey, one through Ma Kilman's herbal ritual. When the wound finally receives treatment, the epic does not end in sterile victory but in the possibility of continuance, fishing resumes, love reconfigures, the sea remains.Omeros, Seven Seas, and the Figure of Homer on St LuciaThe title itself performs Walcott's central conceit: Omeros is Homer transliterated into Caribbean sound, omeros, the name locals give the blind bard figure who walks with Walcott on beaches and cliff paths. Seven Seas, another bardic persona, and the narrator's encounters with the eponymous Omeros collapse the distance between ancient Greece and contemporary St Lucia. Homer is not imported statue; he is island elder, sea-voice, and mirror in which Walcott confronts his vocation. The poet who spent childhood reciting European classics in an English-medium school now claims Homer as neighbour, not master. Dante's Virgil guided the pilgrim; Walcott's Omeros guides the Caribbean writer through history's inferno of slavery and tourism without promising paradiso at the end, only clearer sight.Plunkett, the Anglo-Irish retired officer who compiles local history, represents the colonial archive's persistence: he names villages for his wife Maud, records battles, and tries to possess St Lucia through documentation. Walcott allows Plunkett intelligence and loneliness while exposing the imperial habit of renaming what one does not own. The epic juxtaposes Plunkett's ledgers with Achille's muscle and Ma Kilman's herbs, asking which record-keeping counts as truth. Omeros/H omer moves between these worlds, blind yet seeing deeper than sighted historians, because epic memory is auditory and tidal rather than bureaucratic.Terza Rima, Tourism, and the Healing of Historical AmnesiaWalcott's modified terza rima, interlocking rhymes stretched across long hexameter lines, creates a continuous surf-sound that binds seven books into one prolonged breath. Rhyme does not decorate; it remembers. Each returning sound is an echo of Africa, Europe, and the Americas meeting in Creole speech rhythms. Where Dante's tercets march with theological certainty toward beatific vision, Walcott's interlocking lines pause at coves, markets, and battlefields, allowing digression, anecdote, and environmental catalogue to share epic dignity. The hexameter's length accommodates compound adjectives and patois phrases without forcing them into iambic regularity; the line breaks where the breath of a St Lucian fisherman might break when hauling nets. The poem also confronts late-twentieth-century tourism: cruise ships, hotels, and the global gaze that reduces islanders to background for vacationers' self-discovery. Walcott, who elsewhere diagnoses "the smell of salt fish and money," here examines how economic dependency re-colonises independence, turning Helen's beauty into brochure photograph and fishermen's labour into folkloric display for strangers.Yet Omeros is ultimately a poem of healing rather than despair. Ma Kilman's descent to retrieve ancestral medicine, Philoctete's gradual recovery, Achille's vision of ancestral Africa during a fishing voyage, and the sea's perpetual offer of renewal counterbalance massacre, enslavement, and environmental theft. Walcott does not erase British and French imperial history on St Lucia; he walks us through forts, cannons, and renamed headlands until history becomes embodied rather than abstract. The epic form itself is therapeutic: to narrate at length is to refuse the amnesia global capitalism prefers.Compared to Joyce's Ulysses, which confines Homeric parallel to a single Dublin day, Omeros spreads its network across centuries and continents while remaining rooted in village speech. Compared to Walcott's earlier "A Far Cry from Africa," which ends in paralysing division, Omeros advances toward reconciliation without cheap grace, the English tongue remains, but it now speaks with sea-swift and market woman, obeah and outboard motor.In seven books and sixty-four chapters of modified terza rima, Walcott conducts us from scavenged tin and palm-leaf churches through Achille and Hector's rivalry for Helen, through Philoctete's stinking wound and Ma Kilman's healing herbs, through Plunkett's colonial ledgers and walks with the blind Omeros, to a sea that continues sounding after every empire's departure. Omeros remains the definitive Caribbean epic of the late twentieth century: the claim that Homer lives on St Lucia under local name, that the Middle Passage persists in Philoctete's shin until diasporic medicine answers it, and that terza rima hexameter can carry salt wind as surely as Dante carried Florentine bell towers. The poem does more than allude to classical epic; by renaming its heroes fishermen and its muse the sea, it enacts the recovery of history from tourism and textbook, turning colonial trauma into song that refuses to forget, and refuses, finally, to die quietly in the wound.Word count (body): 1,470
poems.ch90: Nissim Ezekiel (1924–2004)Original title: "Night of the Scorpion"Written c. 1963–1964; first published 1965 · English (Indian English inflection) · Indian English poetry; Bombay Jewish literary circle; post-Independence secular humanism · Narrative poem in free verse; domestic vignette of rural crisis contrasting peasant ritual with rationalist scepticismMonsoon, Rice Sack, and the Night the Scorpion CameNissim Ezekiel's "Night of the Scorpion"—written in the early 1960s and first published in The Exact Name (1965), the collection that consolidates Ezekiel's reputation as foundational architect of Indian English verse, recreates a single night in a rural Indian village when a scorpion's sting threatens a mother and summons the community's competing systems of belief. Ezekiel, born in Bombay in 1924 into a Bene Israel Jewish family, writes as insider and observer: he knows village India through extended family networks and post-Independence cultural journalism, yet his education and cosmopolitan scepticism align him partly with the rationalist father figure. R. Parthasarathy's anthology Ten Twentieth-Century Indian Poets and Bruce King's Modern Indian Poetry in English position Ezekiel as the poet who legitimises Indian English as literary medium rather than colonial mimicry. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Indian English poetry from Tagore and Sarojini Naidu through Ezekiel, Kamala Das, and Ramanujan, "Night of the Scorpion" exemplifies narrative clarity, ironic restraint, and the fusion of folk ritual with modern psychological realism.The poem opens with the child's mnemonic certainty:I remember: the adult speaker recovers a childhood scene with photographic sequence. Ten hours of steady rain precede the scorpion's refuge beneath a sack of rice, domestic storage becomes accidental shelter for the predator. Ezekiel's lineation, characteristically short and measured, controls emotion through parataxis: one fact follows another without hysterical amplification. The scorpion is not demonised in advance; it acts according to rain and refuge, part of the village ecology that includes mud, monsoon, and human vulnerability.I remember the night my motherwas stung by a scorpion. The rainhad driven him beneath a sack of rice.(Ezekiel, "Night of the Scorpion", opening lines; The Exact Name, 1965)Villagers, Candles, and the Chanting of Peasant BeliefWhen news of the sting spreads, neighbours arrive as a collective chorus. Their torches and lanterns multiply shadows; their voices weave a theology of cause and consolation:Peasants come like swarms of flies, an image that recalls Walcott's controversial simile in "A Far Cry from Africa" but here serves different purpose: communal urgency, not imperial contempt. They buzz the name of God a hundred times to paralyse the Evil One, converting prayer into incantation with measurable repetition. Candles and lanterns throw giant scorpion shadows on mud-baked walls, externalising the threat while the actual scorpion remains unfound.
