The clicked tongues and proverbial logic, every movement the scorpion makes moves poison in Mother's blood, express a sympathetic magic in which cosmic justice and biological suffering intertwine.The villagers' speeches, reported in indirect discourse, articulate a folk eschatology:Previous birth's sins may burn away tonight; present suffering may decrease next birth's misfortunes; evil's sum may balance against good and diminish through Mother's pain. Ezekiel records these beliefs without authorial mockery: the chants possess dignity as communal attempt to render arbitrary pain meaningful within karmic arithmetic. The unreal world phrase hints at the speaker's later philosophical distance, yet the poem grants villagers eloquence and sincerity. Their presence is not mere superstition but social solidarity, the mother is not left alone with her agony.The peasants came like swarms of fliesand buzzed the name of God a hundred timesto paralyse the Evil One.With candles and with lanternsthrowing giant scorpion shadowson the mud-baked wallsthey searched for him: he was not found.They clicked their tongues.With every movement that the scorpion made his poison moved in Mother's blood, they said.(Ezekiel, "Night of the Scorpion", mid-poem; The Exact Name, 1965)May the sins of your previous birthbe burned away tonight, they said.May your suffering decreasethe misfortunes of your next birth, they said.May the sum of all evilbalanced in this unreal worldagainst the sum of goodbecome diminished by your pain, they said.(Ezekiel, "Night of the Scorpion", villagers' chants; The Exact Name, 1965)Father, Rationalist, and the Empire of RemediesAgainst the villagers' metaphysical chanting, the father embodies post-Enlightenment scepticism and desperate pragmatism. He is sceptic, healer, and patriarch simultaneously:Sceptic and rationalist, the father nonetheless tries every curse and blessing, powder, mixture, herb and hybrid, Ezekiel's polysyndeton lists remedies with comic exhaustiveness. Paraffin on the bitten toe, set alight: the rationalist's extremity borders on folk ordeal, and the child watches the flame feeding on my mother with horrified literalness. Holy man's incantation runs parallel to father's experiment; neither pure science nor pure religion wins exclusive authority. After twenty hours, the poison loses its sting: duration, not any single remedy, resolves crisis, a narrative anticlimax that refuses heroic medicine.The father's brief prayer, mentioned earlier in the poem, "my father, / sceptic, rationalist, / trying every curse and blessing", captures India's twentieth-century intellectual condition: Nehruvian rationalism living beside inherited ritual because catastrophe leaves no option of purity. Ezekiel, educated at Wilson College and abroad, writes from this divided inheritance without forcing the father to become villain or sole hero. His love expresses itself as frantic tinkering; his scepticism does not prevent him from burning his wife's toe when terror demands action.My father, sceptic, rationalist,trying every curse and blessing,powder, mixture, herb and hybrid.He even poured a little paraffinupon the bitten toe and put a match to it.I watched the flame feeding on my mother.I watched the holy man perform his ritesto tame the poison with an incantation.After twenty hoursit lost its sting.(Ezekiel, "Night of the Scorpion", father's remedies; The Exact Name, 1965)Mother, Silence, and the Sacrifice That Redefines the PoemThroughout the crisis, the mother speaks little; pain occupies her body while others theorise about it. Ezekiel withholds her screams, focusing instead on the circus of responses around her stillness, a formal choice that centres female endurance rather than male interpretation. When speech finally arrives, it overturns every preceding argument:My mother only said, only, as if all night of chanting and paraffin distilled into one quiet sentence. Thank God the scorpion picked on me and spared my children: reversal of expected complaint. She does not curse the insect, villagers, father, or fate; she translates personal agony into maternal gratitude that the wound fell on her body rather than on her offspring. The line redefines sacrifice without Sanskrit glossary or theological footnote: it is village mother's ethics, Christianised idiom absorbed into Indian English, Jewish poet's transcription of Hindu-peasant cosmos in which parental substitution is holy logic.The closing triplet's understatement is the poem's emotional detonation. After flies, candles, incantations, and flame, the mother's words expose how peasant belief and rationalist remedy alike circled around the truth that love accepts pain on behalf of the vulnerable. Ezekiel's irony is gentle but decisive: the sceptical father's pyrotechnics and the villagers' karmic algebra cannot match the moral clarity of a woman who thanks God for being stung.My mother only saidThank God the scorpion picked on meAnd spared my children.(Ezekiel, "Night of the Scorpion", closing lines; The Exact Name, 1965)Indian English, Irony, and the Domestic Epic of Post-Independence India"Night of the Scorpion" established conventions later Indian English poets adapt and resist: domestic setting, childhood narrator, colloquial speech rendered in formal verse, ironic gap between speaker's adult literacy and village orality. Ezekiel's English is deliberately unpoetic in diction, sack of rice, mud-baked walls, clicked tongues, yet meticulously paced in line breaks that slow reading to ritual tempo. The poem's free verse refuses regular stanza because village crisis does not organise itself into sonnet or ghazal; it arrives in bursts of neighbours, rain, and flame.Critics note Ezekiel's affinities with William Carlos Williams's documentary clarity and with T. S. Eliot's ironic juxtaposition, yet the poem's soul is Indian rather than imported. It belongs to post-Independence negotiation between tradition and modernity without reducing either term to caricature. Villagers are not fools; father is not enlightened saviour; mother is not silent saint only, she possesses agency in her final speech that reorients the entire narrative.Compared to Kamala Das's confessional ferocity or Ramanujan's family micro-myths, Ezekiel remains observational, almost ethnographic, yet the withheld emotion in "I watched the flame feeding on my mother" betrays the child's trauma beneath adult composure. The poem thus anticipates later postcolonial critique of rationalism's limits while honouring the father's love expressed in wrong remedies.In free verse that moves from monsoon rain and rice-sack refuge through swarming villagers and karmic chants, through a sceptic father's paraffin flame and holy man's incantation, to a mother's twenty hours of pain and her final thanks that the scorpion spared her children, Ezekiel conducts us from ecological accident to communal theology to domestic heroism. "Night of the Scorpion" remains the definitive introduction to Indian English narrative poetry for international readers: the claim that village belief and modern scepticism speak simultaneously during catastrophe, that twenty hours of suffering may end without a single victorious remedy, and that a mother's quiet sentence can outweigh every incantation the night contained. The poem does more than document rural superstition; by closing on maternal sacrifice rather than rationalist triumph, it enacts the discovery that India's modernity must make room for a love that thanks God for wounds, because wounds, in that ethics, are proof the children still breathe.Word count (body): 1,570
poems.ch91: Kamala Das (1934–2009)Original title: "An Introduction"Written c. 1964–1965; first published 1965 · English (Indian English inflection; Malayalam substrate) · Indian English poetry; Kerala confessional lyric; post-Independence feminist voice · Lyric poem in free verse; autobiographical manifesto rejecting patriarchal gender roles and colonial linguistic policingMalabar, Brown Skin, and the Defiant First-PersonKamala Das's "An Introduction"—written in the mid-1960s and first published in Summer in Calcutta (1965), the collection that announces her as India's most scandalously honest woman poet, opens not with metaphor but with declaration: a speaker who names her nation, complexion, and birthplace before any critic can name her on her behalf. Das, born Kamala Surayya (née Madhavikutty) in 1934 in the Malabar region of Kerala into a literary Nair family, writes as daughter of the poet Balamaniamma and as wife in a conservative Hindu society that expects feminine reticence. Bruce King's Modern Indian Poetry in English, R. Parthasarathy's Ten Twentieth-Century Indian Poets, and Devindra Kohli's studies of Das position "An Introduction" as foundational text of Indian English confessional feminism: the poem that refuses to apologise for writing in the coloniser's language while exposing the colonisation of women's bodies by domestic ideology. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Indian English poetry from Toru Dutt and Sarojini Naidu through Kamala Das, Nissim Ezekiel, and A. K. Ramanujan, "An Introduction" exemplifies how free verse becomes political instrument, how the autobiographical I challenges both patriarchal India and nationalist linguistic purism, and how a brown woman from Malabar rewrites Whitman's democratic catalogue into postcolonial female desire.The poem's opening lines establish identity as geography and pigment before ideology:I am Indian, very brown, born in Malabar: the speaker refuses euphemism about colour in a literary culture still shaped by Anglo-Indian gentility. She speaks three languages, Malayalam, English, and perhaps Hindi or another Indian tongue, writes in two, dreams in one, suggesting that the unconscious remains rooted in a single mother tongue while public articulation must navigate bilingual or trilingual fracture. The lineation breaks Malabar across the margin, isolating regional specificity against the abstract noun Indian: Kerala's coast is not interchangeable with Delhi's metropolitan nationalism. Das writes before the term intersectionality enters academic discourse, yet her opening performs it: gender, region, language, and pigment arrive as inseparable coordinates of selfhood.I am Indian, very brown, born inMalabar,I speak three languages, write inTwo, dream in one.(Das, "An Introduction", opening lines; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)Politics, Gender Roles, and the Catalogue of Patriarchal CommandHaving established who she is, the speaker turns to what society demands she become, and what she refuses. Das's middle sections catalogue the instructions issued to Indian girls and wives with bitter, conversational clarity:Don't write in English, they said, the language is not yours: the nationalist and conservative chorus treats English as foreign property, as though Malayalam alone could contain a woman's erotic and psychological truth in a nation still negotiating colonial aftermath. Why not leave me alone, critics, friends, visiting cousins, every one of you, Das names the domestic surveillance network that polices female speech as aggressively as any state censor. The language I speak becomes mine, its distortions, its queernesses all mine, mine alone: a manifesto that anticipates postcolonial linguistic theory (Ashcroft, Griffiths, Tiffin) in plain vernacular. English is not borrowed; it is inhabited, bent, owned through use. Queernesses here denotes strangeness, deviation from standard idiom, the very marks of a colonised subject's creative appropriation.The gender instructions follow with equal ferocity:Dress in sarees, be girl, be wife: patriarchy reduces womanhood to costume and function. Be embroiderer, be cook, be quarreller with servants, domestic competence and class performance packaged as feminine virtue. Fit in. Oh, belong, cried the multitude: the pressure toward social conformity sounds almost religious, a chorus demanding erasure of difference. Don't sit on walls or peep through lace-draped windows: girls who observe, who occupy liminal spaces, threaten the architecture of propriety. Be Amy, or Kamala, or better still, Madhavikutty, a name that blends the home and alien: Das exposes how Indian women carry split nomenclature, Christian or Western pet names alongside regional identities, none of which grant autonomy.Earlier in the poem, the speaker confesses political illiteracy while naming power, a paradox that deflates masculine intellectual pretension:I don't know politics but I know the names of those in power: Das ironises the public sphere as a roster of male celebrities whose dates and disasters women memorise without being permitted to judge. Wars, revolutions, assassinations, allergy of old meetings, car accidents, the list collapses epochal violence and trivial mishap, suggesting that official history and gossip share the same tonal flatness in a woman's oral archive. I am not a critic of my times, oh no: the exclamation performs false modesty while the poem itself constitutes devastating critique.Don't write in English, they said, the language is not yours.Why not leaveMe alone, critics, friends, visiting cousins,Every one of you? Why not let me speak inAny language I like? The language I speakBecomes mine, its distortions, its queernessesAll mine, mine alone.(Das, "An Introduction", language passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)Dress in sarees, be girlBe wife, they said. Be embroiderer, be cook,Be a quarreller with servants. Fit in. Oh,Belong, cried the multitude. Don't sitOn walls or peep in through our lace-draped windows.Be Amy, or Kamala, or betterStill, Madhavikutty, a name that blends the home and alien.(Das, "An Introduction", gender roles passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)I don't know politics but I know the namesOf those in power, and can repeat them likeDates of history, Dates of birth of kings,Wars, revolutions, assassinations,Allergy of old meetings, car accidents, butI am not a critic of my times, oh no!(Das, "An Introduction", politics passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)Confession, Desire, and the Body the Poem Refuses to Hide"An Introduction" is confessional in the lineage of Sappho, Whitman, and Plath, yet Das's confession is specifically South Asian: it names arranged marriage, marital rape's emotional architecture, adulterous longing, and alcohol without converting suffering into redemptive narrative. The speaker describes girlhood shrinking into adolescence, the body policed before it understands its own heat:When I asked for love, not knowing what else to ask for: desire enters the poem as naive petition, not yet armed with feminist vocabulary. He drew a youth of sixteen into the bedroom and closed the door: the husband figure, Das's marriage to Madhava Das at fifteen is biographical substrate, claims conjugal right without tenderness. He did not beat me but my sad woman-body felt so beaten: physical absence of violence does not equal absence of injury; the body registers coercion as defeat. Das's phrase sad woman-body personifies flesh as grieving entity separate from the speaking mind, anticipating later feminist phenomenology that treats the female body as site of contested sovereignty.The poem's erotic candour escalates in passages where the speaker admits restlessness, fantasy, and the hunger for a lover's mouth, material that scandalised 1960s Indian readers and secured Das's reputation as taboo-breaker. She drinks lonely drinks at midnight; she seeks strangers in cheap hotels; she names the body's betrayal of domestic vows. Yet confession here is not mere titillation: each admission answers the earlier command to fit in and belong. If society demands the mask of saree and servitude, the poem rips the mask and displays the face beneath, hungry, angry, bored, alive.Das also addresses the male poet's monopoly on sexual lyric:The lines assert that female utterance participates in a collective inheritance while remaining personally stamped. Das refuses the solitude of genius; she claims kinship with every woman told to be silent, transforming private shame into public syntax.When I asked for love, not knowing what else to askFor, he drew a youth of sixteen into theBedroom and closed the door. He did not beat meBut my sad woman-body felt so beaten.(Das, "An Introduction", marriage passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)I have words to say, and a voice to say them,But the words and the voice are not mine alone.(Das, "An Introduction", voice passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)English, Malayalam, and the Postcolonial Right to Queer the TongueDas's linguistic manifesto within "An Introduction" remains among the most quoted passages in Indian English criticism because it resolves the false choice between authenticity and English:Half English, half Indian, funny perhaps, but honest: Das anticipates the humour and hybridity later theorists celebrate in Hinglish and Mallu English, yet she stakes moral claim on honesty rather than entertainment. It is as human as I am human: language and speaker share one flawed, hybrid, legitimate being. The question don't you see? addresses us directly, implicating anyone who would deny Indian English the status of literary medium, a denial Ezekiel and Ramanujan likewise combat, each by different temper.Das's free verse refuses regular stanza because her consciousness refuses compartmentalisation. Lines break where breath breaks, in the middle of prepositions, across place names, after the word oh, enacting the same restlessness the content describes. The poem is not song; it is argument delivered as intimate speech, closer to kitchen confession than podium oratory. Compared to Ezekiel's ironic narrative control or Ramanujan's mythic compression, Das spills; compared to Plath's crystalline rage, Das wanders, repeats, addresses cousins and critics mid-line. The form is the freedom she claims.Critics note biographical fallout: Das's family and Kerala society recoiled from her candour; later conversion to Islam and adoption of the name Kamala Surayya complicated feminist canonisation. Yet "An Introduction" predates those later chapters and is the adolescent and young wife's declaration, written when Indian English poetry needed a female I who would not ask permission.The language I speakBecomes mine, its distortions, its queernessesAll mine, mine alone. It is half English, halfIndian, funny perhaps, but it is honest,It is as human as I am human, don'tYou see?(Das, "An Introduction", ownership passage; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)Feminist Legacy, UGC NET Context, and the Poem That Introduces a SelfFor examination readers, "An Introduction" offers manageable thematic clusters: (1) postcolonial language ownership; (2) patriarchal gender scripting; (3) confessional body politics; (4) free-verse conversational form; (5) autobiography as resistance. The poem pairs productively with Ezekiel's "Night of the Scorpion" (village India, different gaze), Ramanujan's family elegies, and international confessional poets from Sappho through Plath. Das's claim I am Indian, very brown also converses with Walcott's racial division and Rich's gendered recovery of voice, positioning Indian English within global postcolonial and feminist lyric.Das's closing movement returns to the speaking subject who will not be fixed:It is I who drink, laugh, make love, feel shame, lie dying: the anaphora hammers agency, no passive construction, no male mediator. I am sinner, I am saint: religious moralism collapses into paradoxical coexistence. I am the beloved and the betrayed: erotic subject and victim simultaneously, refusing the simplification that would cast her as only fallen or only wronged.In free verse that moves from Malabar brownness and trilingual consciousness through patriarchal commands to dress, belong, and stay silent, through the claim that English becomes hers by distortion and queerness, through confessions of loveless marriage and restless desire, to the closing catalogue of sin, sainthood, betrayal, and voice, Das conducts us from introduction as biography to introduction as manifesto. "An Introduction" remains the definitive opening salvo of Indian English feminist confessional poetry: the claim that a brown woman may write in English without treason, that the body may speak what the saree conceals, and that the language of the coloniser becomes postcolonial property the moment a Malabar woman bends it to her loneliness, laughter, and rage. The poem does more than introduce Kamala Das; by refusing every instruction to fit in, it introduces the possibility that Indian women's experience is itself a literary tradition, half English, half Indian, wholly human, and not asking leave to exist.Word count (body): 2,046It is I who drink lonelyDrinks at twelve, midnight, in hotels of strange towns,It is I who laugh, it is I who make loveAnd then, feel shame, it is I who lie dyingWith a rattle in my throat. I am sinner,I am saint. I am the beloved and theBetrayed.(Das, "An Introduction", closing self-definition; Summer in Calcutta, 1965)
poems.ch92: A. K. Ramanujan (1929–1993)Original title: "Obituary"Written c. 1968–1970; first published 1971 · English (Indian English inflection; Tamil cultural substrate) · Indian English poetry; Tamil Brahmin diaspora; Chicago School comparative literature · Lyric poem in unrhymed three-line stanzas; ironic family elegy that undercuts Hindu funeral solemnity with documentary detachmentFather's Death, Thirteen Days, and the Tone That Refuses MourningA. K. Ramanujan's "Obituary"—composed in the late 1960s and first published in Relations (1971), the collection that maps family memory across continents, records a father's death not as spiritual transcendence but as administrative residue: ashes, debts, subscriptions, and children scattered like unsettled accounts. Ramanujan, born in Mysore in 1929 into a Tamil Brahmin family, emigrated to the United States in 1962 to teach at the University of Chicago, becoming simultaneously folklorist, translator of Tamil and Kannada classics, and poet of microscopic domestic ironies. Vinay Dharwadker's editions, Guillermo Rodríguez's When Mirrors Are Windows, and Bruce King's surveys position Ramanujan as the poet who imports structuralist precision into Indian English elegy: every object in the parental house becomes semantic unit in a kinship grammar. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Indian English poetry from Ezekiel's urban ironies through Ramanujan's ethnographic miniatures and Kamala Das's confessions, "Obituary" exemplifies how three-line stanzas can contain epic family history, how ironic detachment performs grief otherwise, and how Hindu funeral rites appear through the lens of a son who counts what ritual leaves behind.The poem opens with death converted to travel itinerary:Father, when he passed on: the euphemism passed on immediately collides with the material list that follows, dust on a table of papers, debts and daughters, bedwetting grandson named by the toss of a coin. Ramanujan's parataxis refuses hierarchical ordering: daughters occupy the same syntactic plane as debts; a grandson's incontinence sits beside testamentary neglect. A man named an afterthought in his will: the father's carelessness extends into posthumous legal document, exposing how patriarchal authority distributes recognition arbitrarily. The stanza's flat declaration is the poem's tonal contract: no keening, no Sanskritised lament, only inventory.The celestial journey is likewise diminished:Forty years a journalist: profession defines the dead man more than soul-status. He will know who they are when he arrives at the railway station at Sourashtra on a thirteen day trip to heaven: Hindu mourning calendars and ancestral geography enter as railway timetable, Sourashtra as platform, heaven as thirteen-day package tour. Ramanujan's comedy is ethnographic, not cruel; he records how modern Indian families metabolise eschatology through bureaucratic metaphor. The journalist father who spent life recording others' events now becomes headline himself, journey narrated in the obituary genre he once supplied.ObituaryFather, when he passed on,left dust on a table of papers,left debts and daughters,a bedwetting grandsonnamed by the tossof a coin and a mannamed an afterthought in hiswill.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", opening stanzas; Relations, 1971)Father, forty years a journalist,will know who they arewhen he arriveson the day of his deathat the railway stationat Sourashtraon a thirteen daytrip to heaven(Ramanujan, "Obituary", heaven passage; Relations, 1971)Dust, Paper, and the Legacy Reduced to ObjectsThroughout "Obituary," inheritance materialises as clutter and obligation rather than wisdom or land. Ramanujan's method, what critics call his anthropological eye, treats each domestic detail as cultural signifier stripped of sentimental varnish:Dust on a table of papers: the father's intellectual labour decays into particulate matter on unread documents; journalism, letters, and bureaucratic residue share one grey coating. Debts and daughters: daughters are not metaphorically debts, yet the line's rhythm yokes financial obligation to female dependents as parallel burdens the living must settle. Ramanujan writes from the son who inherits emotional and fiscal arrears simultaneously, the diaspora son who cannot perform daily filial duty yet cannot escape its arithmetic.The poem specifies bodily aftermath with equal dryness:These details are filed in a hotel room in Madras: the speaker processes death from touristic distance, hotel room, made bed, turning fan, domestic comfort divorced from the house where father died. In the heart's small cupboards there is nothing worth keeping: emotional inheritance empties; the son finds no heirloom feeling, only facts. Ramanujan's metaphors stay small, cupboards, not cathedrals, consistent with his aesthetic of scaled-down revelation.Hindu cremation rites appear, but refracted through irony:They turned his body into dust and heat and gave it to the skies and earth to avoid the shame of disposal: sacred dispersal rephrased as municipal problem-solving, cremation as dignified alternative to garbage. Ramanujan does not blaspheme; he translates ritual into the language a sceptical son uses when jet lag and geography prevent full participation. The ashes will return to the poem as tangible object, not mystical symbol.left dust on a table of papers,left debts and daughters,(Ramanujan, "Obituary", legacy list; Relations, 1971)These details are filedin a hotel room in Madras.The bed is made, the fanturns. In the heart'ssmall cupboardsthere is nothing worthkeeping.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", Madras passage; Relations, 1971)They turned hisbody into dust and heatand gave it to the skiesand earthto avoid the shameof disposal(Ramanujan, "Obituary", cremation passage; Relations, 1971)Sons, Daughters, and the Arithmetic of Dispersal"Obituary" maps filial scattering across continents and temperaments, refusing the elegiac convention of united mourning household:Sons who never learned to read or write squat on the highway among beggars: literacy, class mobility, and paternal example collapse into roadside poverty, the journalist father's progeny include those literacy failed. The eldest son gone for years returns for funeral rites: diaspora biography enters obliquely; the speaker's return mirrors Ramanujan's own transcontinental shuttling, yet the poem distributes guilt and estrangement across the family system rather than confessing autobiographically in first person throughout.The daughters' fates receive similarly compressed reportage:Daughters, married, cry in their bathrooms: private grief exiled to tiled rooms behind husbands' houses, no public keening permitted married women. The line's brevity is devastating; Ramanujan grants daughters one sentence of tears, then moves on, mimicking how patriarchal narrative allocates space to female sorrow.Age and diminished stature haunt the father's portrait:At sixty, a mere son, he was a younger brother to his own children: maturity does not bring authority; the father remains childlike in family hierarchy, perhaps dominated by his own mother or elder siblings, a reversal that explains emotional immaturity passed downstream. Ramanujan's psychoanalytic hint arrives without jargon: the dead man was never fully adult, so his obituary cannot pretend he was patriarchal colossus.His sonswho never learned to read or writeare squatting on the highwayamong the beggars.The eldest son,who was gone for years, returnsfor the funeral rites.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", sons passage; Relations, 1971)Daughters, married,cry in their bathrooms.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", daughters line; Relations, 1971)At sixty, a mere son,he was a younger brotherto his own children.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", age passage; Relations, 1971)Irony, Stanza Form, and the Hindu Rites Undercut"Obituary" employs unrhymed tercets, three-line stanzas without regular metre, creating visual and rhythmic units that feel like clipped newspaper paragraphs or filed index cards. The tercet honours terza rima's associative gravity while abandoning Dante's theological architecture; each triplet is self-sufficient fact, separable from the next, like family stories told without connective moral. Enjambment across stanza breaks mimics how grief interrupts and resumes inappropriately, funeral rites proceed while the mind tallies debts.Ramanujan's irony differs from Ezekiel's urban satire and Das's confessional heat: it is quiet, ethnographic, almost affectionate in its precision. He names the shame of disposal, the toss of a coin naming a grandson, the afterthought in the will, details that could sound accusatory yet land as observation because the speaker includes himself among inheritors of dust. Hindu funeral rites, thirteen-day journey, cremation, ashes in holy pot, persist as cultural backdrop, but the poem's consciousness belongs to a modern son who files details in hotel rooms and measures heaven in railway days.Comparative readers link "Obituary" to Gray's "Elegy" for its communal portrait of the dead's social web, yet Ramanujan refuses Gray's moralising closure. Yeats's family poems provide another axis, but Ramanujan's father is not Anglo-Irish aristocrat or mythic symbol, he is journalist with debts, dust, and daughters. The poem converses with Kamala Das's patriarchal portraits and Ezekiel's family vignettes, completing a triad of Indian English domestic realism.For translation scholars, Ramanujan's career bridges classical Tamil poetics and American academic folklore studies; "Obituary" imports neither Tamil metre nor mythic plot, yet its itemisation of kinship roles reflects the structural anthropology he practises elsewhere, each relative a node, each ritual a performance whose script outlives sincerity.Ashes, Holy Pot, and the Closing Books of the DeadThe poem's late movement gathers ashes and subscriptions into final inventory:A grandson born after his death is given his name. His name is an empty cupboard: nominal immortality, naming the newborn after grandfather, collides with domestic image of bare storage. Inheritance is hollow furniture, not living memory.In the holy pot of his ashes there are no answers: cremation's theological promise, that remains concentrate spirit, dissolves under the son's scrutiny. The pot is holy; its contents offer no wisdom, no forgiveness, no instruction. Ramanujan ends elegy where philosophy cannot proceed, only facts remain.The journalistic father's profession reverberates: he spent life recording others' deaths and scandals; his own death becomes son's obituary poem, continuing the circuit of documentation without redemption. Dust and paper, two motifs from the opening, frame a life that reduced to particulate and print. The daughters cry in bathrooms; the beggar sons squat on highways; the diaspora eldest performs rites; the bedwetting grandson receives a name by coin toss. No single image dominates; cumulative flatness is the elegy's emotional strategy, grief expressed as the inability to inflate the dead into hero.In unrhymed three-line stanzas that move from father's passing and dust on papers through the thirteen-day railway journey to heaven, through sons on highways and daughters crying in bathrooms, through cremation's dust and heat offered to skies and earth, through ashes in a holy pot that hold no answers, Ramanujan conducts us from obituary as genre to obituary as anti-elegy. "Obituary" remains the definitive Indian English poem of filial detachment that is also filial attention: the claim that a journalist father's legacy is debts and daughters rather than wisdom, that Hindu rites proceed while the heart's cupboards stay empty, and that naming a grandson after the dead does not fill the cupboard his name becomes. The poem does not mourn less because it mourns dryly; by refusing solemn diction, it honours the particular shame of modern sons who inherit dust, paper, and railway timetables to heaven, then write poems that file what ritual could not resolve.Word count (body): 1,814A grandsonborn after his deathis given his name.His name is an empty cupboard.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", naming passage; Relations, 1971)In the holy potof his ashesthere are no answers.(Ramanujan, "Obituary", ashes passage; Relations, 1971)
poems.ch93: Seamus Heaney (1939–2013)Original title: "Digging"Written 1964–1965; first published 1966 · English (Hiberno-English inflection; Ulster speech rhythms) · Irish poetry; Northern Irish rural realism; post-Yeats lyric excavation · Lyric poem in free verse with irregular stanzas; vocational manifesto equating pen with spadeThe Squat Pen, Snug as a Gun, and the Opening FrameSeamus Heaney's "Digging"—composed in 1964–1965, first published in The New Statesman and then as the opening poem of Death of a Naturalist (Faber, 1966), the debut collection that announces the most influential Irish poet since Yeats, establishes its entire career metaphor in the first two lines: the writer's hand holds a pen that rests like weapon, like tool, like inheritance. Heaney, born in 1939 at Mossbawn, County Derry, into a Catholic farming family, writes from the tension between peat-cutting labour and literary education, between father's spade and son's scholarship. Neil Corcoran's The Poetry of Seamus Heaney, Helen Vendler's Seamus Heaney, and the Nobel citation of 1995 position "Digging" as signature statement: poetry as excavation of personal and tribal memory. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Irish poetry from Yeats and Kavanagh through Heaney, Mahon, and Longley, "Digging" exemplifies how tactile rural imagery enters modern free verse, how the poet negotiates guilt of departure from manual class, and how a single extended metaphor, digging, organises an entire aesthetic programme.The opening places pen between finger and thumb with startling simile:Between my finger and my thumb: the hand position echoes gun grip or tool handle, preparing us for labour's physical grammar. The squat pen rests; snug as a gun: snug suggests comfortable fit, domestic warmth, yet gun introduces violence and political resonance in a Northern Ireland edging toward Troubles violence. Critics debate whether the simile signals aggression of art or merely tight fit; either reading keeps writing embodied, dangerous, purposeful. Heaney's pen is not quill in study; it is implement held like father's spade or partisan's pistol.The speaker looks down from window to father digging:Under my window: the poet occupies elevated interior space, literacy, leisure, separation, while father works visible earth below. Clean rasping sound when the spade sinks into gravelly ground: onomatopoeia renders digging audible before visual; gravelly ground specifies Mossbawn soil, resistant, mineral. My father, digging. I look down: the verb look down carries double force, physical gaze from window and potential social condescension the poem will work to erase by honouring labour.Between my finger and my thumbThe squat pen rests; snug as a gun.(Heaney, "Digging", opening lines; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)Under my window, a clean rasping soundWhen the spade sinks into gravelly ground:My father, digging. I look down(Heaney, "Digging", father scene; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)Father's Spade, Potato Drill, and the Music of Manual SkillHeaney's father becomes first exemplar of digging artistry, ten minutes' work condensed into sensory catalogue:Straining rump among flowerbeds: unglamorous body part, honest exertion, Heaney refuses pastoral prettification. Comes up twenty years away: time collapses; present digging unearths memory simultaneously, establishing the poem's method, present action triggers ancestral scene. Stooping in rhythm through potato drills where he was digging: rhythm converts labour into tacit metre, predecessor of the poet's cadence.The father's expertise receives praise in vernacular idiom:By God, the old man could handle a spade: oath anchors admiration in rural speech; handle implies mastery, bodily intelligence. Just like his old man: skill passes patrilineally; the poem's digging is genealogical vocation before it is metaphor.The potato drills evoke 1940s wartime subsistence and Ulster small-farming economy, flowerbeds above, edible tubers below, the father's body moving between decorative and nutritive earth. Heaney's precise nouns, gravel, drills, flowerbeds, ground abstraction; this is not generic peasant but Derry-specific husbandry remembered from childhood window.Till his straining rump among the flowerbedsBends low, comes up twenty years awayStooping in rhythm through potato drillsWhere he was digging.(Heaney, "Digging", father's movement; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)By God, the old man could handle a spade.Just like his old man.(Heaney, "Digging", father's skill; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)Grandfather on Toner's Bog, Turf-Cutting, and the Deep PastThe memory excavates further generation, intensifying labour's physicality and competitive pride:My grandfather cut more turf in a day than any other man on Toner's bog: boast becomes elegy; competitive superlative measures worth through output. He and his neighbours drained the bog and carried sods to build a wall: communal land reclamation, bog as shared resource transformed by collective muscle. Toner's bog names local topography; Heaney's poetry gains authority from ordnance-survey fidelity.The grandfather stanza's sensory climax is among Heaney's most anthologised passages:Cold smell of potato mould: olfactory memory triggers involuntary return, Proustian peat. Squelch and slap of soggy peat: alliteration reproduces wet resistance under blade. Curt cuts of an edge through living roots: violence to living matter acknowledged; excavation wounds what it penetrates. Awaken in my head: memory erupts into present consciousness, disrupting window scene. But I've no spade to follow men like them: vocational crisis stated plainly, the educated son cannot inherit manual tool, only guilt and admiration.The line living roots awaken in my head fuses botanical and neurological imagery: grandfather's cuts disturb roots; roots disturb poet's brain; writing will become substitute digging into strata of language and tribe. Heaney's later bog poems (North, "Bog Queen") extend this archaeology into Iron Age sacrifice; "Digging" plants the seed.My grandfather cut more turf in a dayThan any other man on Toner's bog.He and his neighbours drained the bogAnd carried the sods to build a wall.(Heaney, "Digging", grandfather passage; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)The cold smell of potato mould, the squelch and slapOf soggy peat, the curt cuts of an edgeThrough living roots awaken in my head.But I've no spade to follow men like them.(Heaney, "Digging", sensory memory; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)Pen as Shovel, Vocational Guilt, and the Closing CovenantThe poem's resolution does not abandon spade for pen as triumphalist modernity narrative; it acknowledges rupture then forges continuity through metaphor:I've no spade to follow men like them: class mobility's cost, literary vocation as betrayal of patrilineal craft. Between my finger and my thumb the squat pen rests: opening image returns, but gun simile absent in final frame, pen now purely tool, not weapon. I'll dig with it: future tense covenant; digging redefined as literary excavation rather than turf or potato retrieval. The monosyllable dig closes the poem on active verb, not noun, process, not object.Heaney's free verse stanzas vary in length, mimicking irregular thrusts of spade into resistant ground. Enjambment carries motion across line breaks as father's stooping carries rhythm through drills. The poem's structure descends literally and mnemonically: window → flowerbeds → potato drills → Toner's bog → head → pen. Each level deeper in earth or memory until writing reverses direction, bringing buried material to surface as text.Critics connect "Digging" to Kavanagh's parish poetry and Yeats's tower meditations, yet Heaney's tactile materialism differs from Yeatsian symbolism. Patrick Kavanagh's Monaghan clay and Heaney's Derry gravel share anti-pastoral honesty; both reject Celtic Twilight mist for sweat. Heaney adds post-war Northern Ireland's sectarian undertow, the gun simile's shadow, without explicit politics, a restraint Troubles-era readers nonetheless felt.For UGC NET English, thematic clusters include: (1) labour versus literacy; (2) patrilineal inheritance; (3) memory and sense impression; (4) metaphor of excavation; (5) Irish rural realism in free verse. Pair with Wordsworth's Prelude ground-breaking, Larkin's social realism, and Heaney's own later "Requiem for the Croppies" for historical deepening.I've no spade to follow men like them.Between my finger and my thumbThe squat pen rests.I'll dig with it.(Heaney, "Digging", closing lines; Death of a Naturalist, 1966)Irish English, Class, and the Poem That Digs ForwardHeaney's diction preserves Ulster speech rhythms, By God, old man, Toner's bog, without phonetic dialect spelling that might exoticise. The poem's humility toward father and grandfather avoids sentimental idealisation of peasant life: flowerbeds and drills include straining rump, cold mould, curt cuts through roots. Labour is honoured because it is hard, not because it is picturesque.The pen-as-gun opening troubled early critics who saw glorification of violence; Heaney later contextualised it as acoustic and tactile snugness plus Northern Ireland's ambient threat. The closing I'll dig with it answers unease by channelling energy into craft, poetry as disciplined extraction, not random shooting.Influence radiates across Heaney's oeuvre: bog bodies, border watchtowers, and ancestral spades recur; "Digging" is manifesto and origin myth. For international postcolonial poetry, the pattern of son who writes while father digs parallels Ramanujan's hotel-room filial distance and Walcott's divided allegiance, different continents, shared vocational guilt.In free verse that moves from the squat pen snug as a gun through the clean rasp of father's spade in gravelly ground, through rhythm in potato drills and grandfather's turf-cutting on Toner's bog, through cold smells and curt cuts through living roots awakening in the head, to the closing covenant that the pen will dig because no spade remains to follow men like them, Heaney conducts us from literary self-consciousness to manual genealogy and back to writing as excavation. "Digging" remains the definitive opening poem of late twentieth-century Irish lyric: the claim that roots live in the head as violently as under bog, that a poet's window view of father's labour is both blessing and wound, and that digging with a pen is not betrayal of the spade but its continuation at another depth. The poem does more than compare writing to farming; by returning to between my finger and my thumb without the gun, it enacts the discovery that the snug fit of vocation, however squat, however humble, is enough to break living ground.Word count (body): 1,592
poems.ch94: Adrienne Rich (1929–2012)Original title: "Diving into the Wreck"Written 1971–1972; first published 1973 · English (American literary standard; feminist revisionist diction) · American poetry; second-wave feminism; anti-war political lyric · Extended allegorical lyric in free verse; deep-sea dive as feminist recovery of submerged historyBook of Myths, Preparation, and the Dive as AllegoryAdrienne Rich's "Diving into the Wreck"—composed during the early 1970s and published as the title poem of Diving into the Wreck (W. W. Norton, 1973), the collection that marks Rich's decisive turn from formalist elegance to feminist activism, deploys scuba descent as allegory for a woman entering patriarchal history's wreckage to recover stories erased from canonical myth. Rich, born in Baltimore in 1929, educated at Radcliffe, began as poet of meticulous craft (A Change of World, 1951, selected by W. H. Auden for the Yale Younger Poets prize) before Vietnam-era politics and lesbian feminist consciousness transformed her project. Sandra M. Gilbert and Susan Gubar's No Man's Land, Jane Roberta Cooper's criticism, and Rich's own essay "When We Dead Awaken" position the poem as manifesto of feminist archaeology. For UGC NET English candidates tracing American poetry from Plath and Lowell through Rich, Audre Lorde, and Heaney, "Diving into the Wreck" exemplifies how extended metaphor organises political lyric, how free verse enacts gendered discovery, and how the phrase I am she: I am he dissolves binary myth-making.The poem opens with communal invitation that narrows to solitary quest:We leave this page of words and begin the other journey: reading yields to embodied expedition; language's page gives way to oceanic text. I put on the body-armor of black rubber: diving suit as combat gear, feminised body armoured for hostile environment. The absurd flippers, the grave and awkward mask: self-conscious comedy undercuts heroism, equipment is clumsy, almost vaudevillian, before depths swallow humour. Rich insists that feminist exploration requires protection because wreck site is not neutral museum but active damage zone.The speaker carries instruments of documentation and myth:I came to explore the wreck: purpose stated without ornate mystery. The words are purposes. The words are maps: meta-poetic declaration, language navigates rather than decorates. Damage that was done and treasures that prevail: dual mission acknowledges catastrophe and survival simultaneously; wreck holds both violence and valuables patriarchal history mislabels or buries.The book of myths arrives as central image:The wreck and not the story of the wreck: Rich distinguishes material reality from male-authored narrative about it, feminist epistemology in one line. The thing itself and not the myth: direct knowing opposes mythography that excludes women's experience. Drowned face always staring toward the sun: human casualty submerged yet oriented toward light, death that still gestures toward consciousness. Evidence of damage worn by salt and sway into threadbare beauty: destruction aged into aesthetic object, complicating pity and admiration. Ribs of disaster curving their assertion among tentative haunters: ship's skeleton persists; ghostly observers hover without claiming wreck, perhaps earlier travellers who never descended.We leave this page of wordsand beginthe other journeyI put onthe body-armor of black rubberthe absurdflippersthe grave and awkward mask.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", preparation passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)I came to explore the wreck.The words are purposes.The words are maps.I came to see the damage that was doneand the treasures that prevail.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", purpose passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)I stroke the beam of my lampslowly along the flankof something more permanentthan fish or weedthe thing I came for:the wreck and not the story of the wreckthe thing itself and not the myththe drowned face always staringtoward the sunthe evidence of damageworn by salt and sway into this threadbare beautythe ribs of the disastercurving their assertionamong the tentative haunters.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", wreck passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)Ladder, Camera, and the Descent Through Patriarchal DepthsRich's dive proceeds through ritualised stages, preparation, ladder descent, water entry, each mapped onto feminist consciousness entering institutions men built:There is a ladder. The ladder is always there: fixture so familiar it appears innocent, Rich names how patriarchal structures seem neutral until used by those excluded. Hanging innocently close to the side of the schooner: ship of state, ship of culture, schooner as gendered maritime tradition. We know what it is for, we who have used it: collective memory of women who climbed before, ladder as inheritance of dangerous access.The camera signifies documentary ethics:My camera's lens deliberately focused on evidence not lying beside the wreck: photography as forensic truth-telling; evidence not the myth's decorative lie. Rich insists feminist recovery is empirical as well as imaginative, see the ribs, the drowned face, the damage.Water entry dissolves ordinary identity:Air colour sequence charts depth and dissociation, blue to bluer to green to black. I am blacking out and yet my mask is powerful: surrender and agency coexist; technology enables survival in hostile medium. It pumps my blood with power: artificial respiration as metaphor for feminist anger fueling exploration, anger as life support, not pathology.There is a ladder.The ladder is always therehanging innocentlyclose to the side of the schooner.We know what it is for,we who have used it.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", ladder passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)my camera. My camera's lensis deliberately focusedon the evidencenot lying beside the wreck.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", camera passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)First the air is blue and thenit is bluer and then green and thenblack I am blacking out and yetmy mask is powerfulit pumps my blood with power(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", descent passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)Androgynous Diver, Mermaid, and "I Am She: I Am He"The poem's centre collapses gender binaries that myth and wreck alike enforce:I am she: I am he: the diver occupies both pronouns, not sequential disguise but simultaneous identification with female victim and male explorer. Whose drowned face sleeps with open eyes: death that watches, unclosed lids refusing oblivion. Whose breasts still bear the stress: female body marked by catastrophe's pressure. Silver, copper, vermeil cargo lies obscene before its proper admiring face: treasure displayed for patriarchal gaze that labels it obscene when exposed without male framing, wealth and sexuality commodified by wreck's original economy.Earlier Rich imagines mermaid and bullfighter fused:Mermaid whose dark hair streams black, the merman just as he was: aquatic androgyny merges folkloric feminine seduction with masculine form, mythic beings reconvened at wreck site where official history failed them.The book of myths whose pages omit our names returns in closing cadence:Carrying knife, camera, book of myths in which our names do not appear: tools triangulate survival, cutting, recording, rewriting. Our names do not appear: collective exclusion named; wreck exploration aims to inscribe names patriarchal mythography omitted. Shift from I to we in poem's late movement expands solitary dive into movement consciousness.I am she: I am hewhose drowned face sleeps with open eyeswhose breasts still bear the stresswhose silver, copper, vermeil cargo liesobscene, before its proper admiring face(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", androgyny passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)And I am here, the mermaid whose dark hairstreams black, the merman—just ashe was.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", mermaid passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)the one who find our wayback to this scenecarrying a knife, a cameraa book of mythsin whichour names do not appear.(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", closing passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)Feminist Recovery, Vietnam-Era Politics, and Free-Verse Architecture"Diving into the Wreck" emerged alongside Rich's lesbian feminist awakening and anti-war activism; the wreck allegorises multiple catastrophes, marriage as institution, imperial war, literary canon, without reducing poem to single referent. 1973 publication situates it after Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (1963) and The Will to Change (1971); the dive is mature statement, not inaugural gesture.Rich's free verse employs short lines, heavy enjambment, and white space that mimics water pressure and cautious movement. Repetition (the words are purposes, the ladder is always there) creates incantatory certainty within exploratory uncertainty. Compared to Plath's Ariel intensity or Lowell's confessional turbulence, Rich's dive is deliberate, procedural, feminist patience as method.For UGC NET English, link to Homer's maritime epic (Odysseus's katabasis), Donne's conceits, Walcott's Omeros wreckage and recovery, and Heaney's excavation metaphors in "Digging." Rich's wreck is cultural rather than peat-bog historical, yet both poets dig for what surface history buried.Critical debate centres on androgyny: some read I am she: I am he as universal humanism; others insist Rich critiques male explorer while temporarily wearing his equipment to reach wreck. The poem supports latter reading: diver needs mask and armour because wreck is male-built; androgyny is tactic, not erasure of feminist stake.The knife carries ambiguity, tool for cutting entanglement or weapon? Camera promises evidence. Book of myths, once excluding our names, may be rewritten after dive. Rich does not promise easy rescue; wreck remains wreck; diver returns with documentation, not treasure salvaged for market.Surface, Circle, and the Poem That Maps the DamageRich's closing stanzas emphasise circular return, having reached wreck, divers must surface with knowledge:We circle silently about the wreck: ritual circumambulation, respect without conqueror's claim. Great mother of waters: ocean as feminine origin, womb and grave, patriarchal wreck rests inside matriarchal depth. Creep over ribs: humble movement, not triumphal stride.The poem refuses closure that salvages ship intact; feminist recovery means witnessing damage, retrieving evidence, naming exclusion. Rich's later career, The Dream of a Common Language, An Atlas of the Difficult World, extends dive into lesbian erotics, disability, and global injustice; "Diving into the Wreck" remains the allegorical template.In free verse that moves from body-armour and awkward mask through the ladder always hanging innocently, through blue air darkening to black water, through the wreck itself rather than the story of the wreck, through the drowned face and ribs of disaster, through the declaration I am she: I am he, to the return carrying knife, camera, and book of myths in which our names do not appear, Rich conducts us from preparation to depth to collective witness. "Diving into the Wreck" remains the definitive feminist poem of the 1970s: the claim that myth excludes our names until divers write new pages, that damage and treasure coexist in patriarchal wreckage, and that androgynous courage is the mask required to see what surface stories never tell. The poem does more than allegorise scuba diving; by insisting on the thing itself and not the myth, it enacts the discovery that feminist poetry must descend, armed, absurd in flippers, powerful in mask, and circle the ribs until evidence becomes map for those who follow.Word count (body): 1,858We circle silentlyabout the wreckwe dive into the great mother of watersand creep over the ribs(Rich, "Diving into the Wreck", circling passage; Diving into the Wreck, 1973)
poems.ch95: Mahmoud Darwish (1941–2008)Original title: "Sajil ana Arabi" (سجل أنا عربي)Written 1964; first published 1964 · Arabic (Modern Standard Arabic; Palestinian colloquial substrate in rhythm) · Palestinian resistance poetry; Arab modernist lyric; anti-colonial bureaucratic confrontation · Public lyric / resistance poem with refrains; bureaucratic dialogue asserting Arab identity against occupationSajil, Record!, and the Bureaucratic Theatre of IdentityMahmoud Darwish's "Identity Card"—composed in 1964 and published in Leaves of the Olive Tree (أوراق الزيتون), the debut collection that made the twenty-two-year-old poet voice of Palestinian defiance, transforms the humiliating checkpoint encounter into declarative epic. Darwish, born in al-Birwa, Galilee, in 1941, experienced internally displaced childhood after his village's destruction in 1948; the poem's speaker confronts an Israeli soldier's demand for identification papers with a catalogue of Arab being that escalates from personal facts to collective threat. Anton Shammas's critical studies, Fady Joudah's translations, and the Oxford anthology Mahmoud Darwish: Selected Poems position "Sajil ana Arabi" as founding text of modern Palestinian resistance verse. For UGC NET English candidates tracing world poetry in translation from Tagore and Neruda through Darwish, Heaney, and Walcott, "Identity Card" exemplifies how refrain structure builds political lyric, how bureaucratic language becomes poetic weapon, and how Arab identity assertion converses with postcolonial identity poems from Kamala Das's "An Introduction" to Rich's wreck-diving recovery of erased names.The poem's refrain commands the clerk-soldier to inscribe what he hears:سجل! / Record!: imperative addressed to power's recording apparatus, register this, file this, cannot erase this. أنا عربي / I am an Arab: declaration before explanation; identity precedes bureaucratic validation. ورقم بطاقتي خمسون ألف / identity card number is fifty thousand: absurd specificity mocks the system's numbering of human beings, fifty thousand reduces person to seriality while speaker reclaims number as proud signature.The Arabic original's rhythmic insistence, short declarative lines, repeated Sajil!, creates incantatory momentum translatable only approximately in English. Bilingual citation honours that Palestinian resistance poetry's force resides in Arabic sonic architecture: the poem was chanted in demonstrations, set to music by Marcel Khalife, circulated orally before print canonisation. English translations vary (Denys Johnson-Davies, Abdullah al-Udhari, Fady Joudah); this guide cites parallel Arabic and English to foreground original authority.سجل!أنا عربيورقم بطاقتي خمسون ألفRecord!I am an ArabAnd my identity card number is fifty thousand(Darwish, "Sajil ana Arabi" / "Identity Card", opening refrain; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964; trans. collective tradition)Forgotten Village, Address, and the Geography of DispossessionHaving demanded recording, the speaker supplies address that maps colonial displacement:عنواني في قرية مندثرة / my address is in a forgotten village: mendathra—effaced, erased, buried, names the Nakba geography of destroyed Palestinian villages; address exists in memory and resistance, not in postal registry occupation recognises. The forgotten village is al-Birwa's class, places Israel renamed or erased from maps while survivors carry coordinates in blood.Occupation of personal data continues:Administrative name and family name both innocent child: bureaucracy infantilises or fossilises Arab identity in registers that refuse adult political agency; innocence also claims moral ground against occupation's violence. Darwish's speaker performs compliance, here is my name, here is my number, while each fact indicts the system requesting it.Work and class enter the identity catalogue:Work with brothers and children in my field: agricultural labour anchors identity to land, field is my field despite occupation's deeds. Darwish echoes Mu'allaqat boast traditions and Whitmanian democratic lists, yet list here is legal testimony: every line another entry soldier must record.سجل!أنا عربيوعنواني في قرية مندثرةRecord!I am an ArabAnd my address is in a forgotten village(Darwish, "Identity Card", village refrain; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)اسمي الولائي اسم طفل بريءاسم عائلتي اسم طفل بريءMy administrative name is the name of an innocent childMy family name is the name of an innocent child(Darwish, "Identity Card", naming passage; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)أنا أعمل في…أعمل مع إخوتي في حقليومع أبنائي في حقليI work in…I work with my brothers in my fieldAnd with my children in my field(Darwish, "Identity Card", labour passage; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)Father, Grandfathers, and the Lineage Paper Cannot ConfiscateThe poem widens from individual to generational Arab being:My father was a labourer: working-class dignity; father's sweat precedes son's poetry. Grandfather and great-grandfather follow in many translations as farmers on their land, genealogy of cultivation contradicting occupier narrative of empty land awaiting civilisation.The car and workers' backs image economic violence:Car he did not own broke backs of other workers: class solidarity within Arab society acknowledged without romanticisation, father's labour included complicity in peer exploitation, yet poem's focus targets occupation's structural theft. Darwish refuses pristine victimhood; labourer father exists inside capitalism's injuries before occupation compounds them.Family scale becomes political arithmetic:Eight children, ninth after a year: fertility as defiance, population growth counters ethnic cleansing logic; personal family fact transforms into demographic resistance. Soldier recording identity must also record Palestinian persistence in reproduction.سجل!أنا عربيورقم بطاقتي خمسون ألفأبي كان عاملاًRecord!I am an ArabAnd my identity card number is fifty thousandMy father was a labourer(Darwish, "Identity Card", father refrain; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)سيارته التي لا يملكهاكسرت ظهور عمال آخرينHis car, which he did not own,broke the backs of other workers(Darwish, "Identity Card", car passage; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)لنا ثمانية أولادالتاسع سيكون بعد عامWe have eight childrenThe ninth will come after a year(Darwish, "Identity Card", children passage; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)Stolen Orchards, Hunger, and the Refrain That Becomes WarningThe poem's late movement escalates from assertion to confrontation:You have stolen my ancestors' orchards: second-person accusation breaks bureaucratic politeness—you is soldier, state, settler project. Left us only a little: ellipsis reproduces diminishing territory; repetition of qalil (little) measures Nakba's spatial theft.Rocks remain:Refrain accumulates like dossier thickening, each repetition adds facts occupation cannot assimilate.The closing movement delivers famous warning:I do not hate people nor encroach: ethical preamble refuses antisemitic misreading, hatred targets usurpation, not ethnicity. If I am made hungry, usurper's flesh will be my food: cannibal metaphor transforms passive victim into existential threat, hunger politicised by occupation becomes violence of survival. Beware of my hunger and my anger: dual closing imperatives; hunger and anger (جوعي / غضبي) rhyme in Arabic, sealing sonic warning.Darwish was arrested after poem's circulation; "Identity Card" became anthem of Palestinian consciousness, proving poetry's power to threaten state security apparatus. Marcel Khalife's musical setting amplified public performance; refrain Sajil! became crowd chant.سجل!أنا عربيأنت سرقت أرض أجداديوحرثتها أنت وأولادكوتركت لنا القليل… القليلRecord!I am an ArabYou have stolen my ancestors' orchardsAnd the land you and your children workedYou left us only a little… a little(Darwish, "Identity Card", orchards refrain; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)سجل!أنا عربيورقم بطاقتي خمسون ألفولكني أعمل في…وعندي ثمانية أولادوالتاسع سيكون بعد عامRecord!I am an ArabAnd my identity card number is fifty thousandBut I work in…And I have eight childrenAnd the ninth will come after a year(Darwish, "Identity Card", cumulative refrain; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)لا تغضبفلستُ أحب الحربغير أني إذا جعتسآكل لحم مغتصبياحذر…احذر…من جوعيومن غضبي!I do not hate peopleNor do I encroach upon othersBut if I am made hungryThe usurper's flesh will be my foodBeware…Beware…Of my hungerAnd my anger!(Darwish, "Identity Card", closing warning; Leaves of the Olive Tree, 1964)Resistance Lyric, Translation, and the Arab Poet's Bureaucratic Epic"Identity Card" employs repetitive bureaucratic form ironically: the poem is identity document exceeding card's space, overflowing registry with Arab history soldier thought to compress into number. Confrontational address inverts power dynamic, speaker commands Record! while soldier supposedly controls access. Structure resembles ghazal refrain and modernist catalogue (Whitman, Ginsberg) while remaining legible as popular resistance song.For UGC NET English, compare Kamala Das's claim to English language, Walcott's divided allegiance, Rich's book of myths excluding names, Darwish fights for name's inscription in occupier's file. Postcolonial poetry courses pair "Identity Card" with Heaney's digging into tribal ground and Ramanujan's family inventories, different geographies, shared excavation of what power erases.Translation ethics matter: Arabic Sajil carries legal-administrative weight (register, record, inscribe); English Record! must stay imperative. Usurper (مغتصب) preserves property crime semantics central to Palestinian land discourse. Readers without Arabic should know poem's rhythm depends on refrain returning like checkpoint interrogation loop, each cycle adds evidence until warning erupts.Darwish's later career, Journal of an Ordinary Grief, Memory for Forgetfulness, State of Siege, deepens lyrical complexity; "Identity Card" remains early, declarative, accessible, teaching poem that introduces Palestinian poetry to world anthologies. Its directness does not lack artistry; refrain architecture and escalating lists are formal mastery disguised as spontaneous speech.Critics note masculine speaker voice; gendered resistance poetry by Fadwa Tuqan and later Darwish evolve nuances "Identity Card" summarises in collective male labourer figure. Historicise accordingly while honouring 1964's urgency.In refrains that command Record! / سجل! while declaring أنا عربي / I am an Arab, in addresses of forgotten villages and identity numbers fifty thousand, in fathers who laboured and fields worked with brothers and children, in stolen orchards and eight children with a ninth coming, to the closing beware of my hunger and my anger, Darwish conducts us from bureaucratic humiliation to collective indictment. "Identity Card" remains the definitive Palestinian resistance poem of the 1960s: the claim that Arab identity cannot be reduced to occupation's paper, that every personal detail builds toward land theft's accusation, and that hunger plus anger transform the filed subject into warning the recorder must heed. The poem does more than describe a checkpoint; by repeating سجل! until usurper's flesh becomes food for hunger, it enacts the discovery that identity asserted under erasure is itself revolution, and that the poet's voice, like the identity card, forces the state to write what it wishes to forget.Word count (body): 1,712
poems.ch96: Sylvia Plath (1932–1963)Original title: "Tulips"Written 1961; first published 1962; collected in Ariel (1965) · English (American idiom, hospital and floral diction) · Confessional poetry; feminist modernism; post-war American lyric · Lyric poem in nine septets (seven-line stanzas); hospital-room meditation on peace, erasure, and the disruptive force of lifeWhite Walls, Red Tulips, and the Hospital's Gift of NothingSylvia Plath's "Tulips"—written in 1961 during her recovery from an appendectomy at St Botolph's Hospital in Boston, first published in The New Yorker in 1962, and collected posthumously in Ariel (Faber, 1965)—inverts the usual floral lyric's celebration of bloom and desire. Where roses and daffodils conventionally symbolise vitality, Plath's tulips arrive as an unwanted intrusion upon a white room cultivated for emptiness. The speaker, propped in surgical stillness, seeks not resurrection but subtraction: a temporary vacation from name, history, family, and the explosive selfhood that other Ariel poems will theatricalise. Christina Britzolakis's Sylvia Plath and the Theatre of Mourning and Jacqueline Rose's The Haunting of Sylvia Plath situate "Tulips" within Plath's 1961–1962 hospital sequence, where medical space becomes metaphysical laboratory. For UGC NET English candidates tracing confessional poetry, feminist readings of the body, and the Ariel manuscripts' contrast between erasure and performance, "Tulips" offers the essential counter-voice to "Lady Lazarus": where Lady Lazarus returns from death to eat men like air, the tulips speaker longs to stay emptied out, watched only by white walls and indifferent nurses.The poem's opening septet establishes chromatic and seasonal opposition:Too excitable, the tulips offend before they enter the room, their redness philosophically incompatible with winter's enclosure. White everything: walls, bed, hands, snowed-in quiet. The speaker learns peacefulness as a discipline, lying by herself while light lies parallel on surfaces. I am nobody rehearses Odysseus's trick in Polyphemus's cave, but here anonymity is sought rather than tactical: she has surrendered name, day-clothes, history, and body to institutional custodians. The anesthetist receives history; surgeons receive body, a division of self into administrable parcels that anticipates the poem's later desire to be utterly empty.The tulips are too excitable, it is winter here.Look how white everything is, how quiet, how snowed-in.I am learning peacefulness, lying by myself quietlyAs the light lies on these white walls, this bed, these hands.I am nobody; I have nothing to do with explosions.I have given my name and my day-clothes up to the nursesAnd my history to the anesthetist and my body to surgeons.(Plath, "Tulips", opening septet; Ariel, 1965)Septets, the Eye Between Lids, and Nursing as Indifferent WaterPlath's nine septets, seven-line stanzas without regular rhyme, pace the meditation with measured breath, each stanza a ward-shift of perception. The form is less performative than the tercets of "Lady Lazarus" or "Daddy"; "Tulips" whispers where those poems declaim. The second septet converts the speaker into watched object:Head propped like an eye between white lids that will not shut: the hospital enforces wakefulness while promising rest. Stupid pupil must take everything in, passive retina obliged to record. Nurses pass like gulls in white caps, interchangeable, countless. The simile domesticates the seascape Plath knew from Massachusetts and Devon coasts, yet here gulls are not ominous but merely procedural. My body is a pebble to them, they tend it as water / Tends to the pebbles it must run over, smoothing them gently: erosive care, not intimate nursing. Bright needles bring numbness and sleep, the only gifts the institution reliably delivers.They have propped my head between the pillow and the sheet-cuffLike an eye between two white lids that will not shut.Stupid pupil, it has to take everything in.The nurses pass and pass, they are no trouble,They pass the way gulls pass inland in their white caps,Doing things with their hands, one just the same as another,So it is impossible to tell how many there are.(Plath, "Tulips", second septet; Ariel, 1965)Baggage, Nuns, and the Communion Tablet of Perfect PeaceThe poem's third movement deepens the fantasy of self-dissolution through domestic and religious metaphors. Patent leather overnight case like a black pillbox, husband and child smiling from family photo, their smiles catch onto my skin, little smiling hooks. Baggage is explicitly rejected:Lost myself and sick of baggage: recovery redefined as divestment. The family photo's smiles hook into skin, love as attachment the speaker cannot bear while pursuing purity. The cargo-boat metaphor extends the nautical imagery: a thirty-year-old cargo boat / stubbornly hanging on to my name and address, associations swabbed clear on the green plastic-pillowed trolley. Watched teaset, bureaus of linen, books sink out of sight; water goes over my head. I am a nun now, I have never been so pure: hospital asceticism borrowed from Catholic imagery Plath deploys elsewhere with ambivalence.The fourth septet states the anti-floral thesis with Keatsian echo reversed, where Keats's "Ode to a Nightingale" desires easeful death, Plath desires easeful vacancy:Hands turned up and utterly empty: cruciform passivity without redemption narrative. Peacefulness so big it dazes, scale overwhelms rather than comforts. Dead shutting mouths on it like a Communion tablet: Eucharistic language inverted; peace is wafer-dry, dissolving identity rather than conferring grace. The speaker imagines death's mouthful as the hospital's white silence, a chilling alignment that distinguishes "Tulips" from "Lady Lazarus," where death is stage and comeback.Now I have lost myself I am sick of baggage——My patent leather overnight case like a black pillbox,My husband and child smiling out of the family photo;Their smiles catch onto my skin, little smiling hooks.(Plath, "Tulips", third septet; Ariel, 1965)I didn't want any flowers, I only wantedTo lie with my hands turned up and be utterly empty.How free it is, you have no idea how free——The peacefulness is so big it dazes you,And it asks nothing, a name tag, a few trinkets.It is what the dead close on, finally; I imagine themShutting their mouths on it, like a Communion tablet.(Plath, "Tulips", fourth septet; Ariel, 1965)Tulips That Breathe, Eat Oxygen, and Correspond with WoundsWhen tulips arrive, presumably a gift from visitors, the poem's colour field shifts from white monochrome to violent red. Too red in the first place, they hurt me. Even through gift paper I could hear them breathe / Lightly, through their white swaddlings, like an awful baby: the central metaphor of the ledger, tulips as breathing animal, demanding and infantile. Their redness talks to my wound, it corresponds: chromatic dialogue between surgical incision and floral insistence. A dozen red lead sinkers round my neck: tulips as drowning weight, bouquet as execution.Nobody watched me before, now I am watched: tulips restore the violating gaze the hospital had suspended. Flat, ridiculous, cut-paper shadow between sun and tulips, self reduced to silhouette. I have wanted to efface myself; vivid tulips eat my oxygen: life as consumption of the air the speaker needs for nothingness. Before they came the air was calm enough, / Coming and going, breath by breath, without any fuss. Then the tulips filled it up like a loud noise: floral gift as acoustic assault. River snags round sunken rust-red engine: mechanical corpse in water, tulips as industrial wreckage.Nobody watched me before, now I am watched.The tulips turn to me, and the window behind meWhere once a day the light slowly widens and slowly thins,And I see myself, flat, ridiculous, a cut-paper shadowBetween the eye of the sun and the eyes of the tulips,And I have no face, I have wanted to efface myself.The vivid tulips eat my oxygen.(Plath, "Tulips", sixth septet; Ariel, 1965)Dangerous Animals, African Cats, and the Contrast with Lady LazarusThe final septets intensify menace: tulips should be behind bars like dangerous animals; / They are opening like the mouth of some great African cat. Heart opens and closes / Its bowl of red blooms out of sheer love of me, organ and flower fused in unwanted reciprocity. Warm salt water like the sea, from a country far away as health: taste of amniotic or oceanic return, health receding to foreign territory.Against "Lady Lazarus"—composed 23 October 1962, reportedly the same creative burst as other Ariel triumphs—"Tulips" refuses theatrical resurrection. Lady Lazarus performs death and comeback, addresses peanut-crunching crowds, eats men like air. The tulips speaker flees audience, hooks, and red insistence. Both poems anatomise the female body under medical and social scrutiny; both deploy red as life-force that wounds. Yet "Tulips" chooses passivity where "Lady Lazarus" chooses apotheosis of rage. Read together, they map Plath's bifurcated genius in the Ariel year: one voice that would disappear into white peace, another that would rise from ash and devour. Critics including Susan Van Dyne and Lynda K. Bundtzen note that hospital poems precede the October eruption; "Tulips" documents the exhaustion from which Lady Lazarus's performance will erupt as counter-statement.In nine septets that move from white snowed-in walls and surrendered name through nun-like purity and Communion-tablet peace to red tulips that breathe, correspond with wounds, eat oxygen, and open like African cats, Plath conducts us from desired erasure to forced re-entry into colour and watchfulness. "Tulips" remains the indispensable Ariel poem of negative desire: the claim that flowers can hurt, that peacefulness dazes like death's mouthful, and that the hospital's white gift of being nobody is preferable to the family's smiling hooks. The poem does more than describe post-operative recovery; by closing on salt water far away as health and a heart that blooms red without consent, it enacts the war between passivity and the world's excitable insistence on life, a war "Lady Lazarus" will answer from the opposite trench, rising to devour the air the tulips consume.Word count (body): 1,597
poems.ch97: Norman MacCaig (1910–1996)Original title: "An Ordinary Day"Written c. 1969; first published in A Man in My Position (1969) · English (Scottish inflection; Highland and island observation) · Scottish modernism; Edinburgh Renaissance; nature lyric with metaphysical wit · Lyric poem in free verse; meditation on consciousness, perception, and the mystery of the commonplaceMind and Feet: Which Walks Whom on an Ordinary DayNorman MacCaig's "An Ordinary Day"—composed around 1969 and published in A Man in My Position (Hogarth Press, 1969), the collection that consolidates MacCaig's mature voice after decades of friendship with Hugh MacDiarmid and affiliation with the Edinburgh literary world, takes as its subject not event but the quality of attention that transforms a coastal walk into metaphysical encounter. MacCaig, born in Edinburgh in 1910, divided his life between the capital and Assynt in Sutherland, where the poem's cormorants, ducks, and tidal rocks locate themselves. Maurice Lindsay's Modern Scottish Poetry and Roderick Watson's The Literature of Scotland position MacCaig as the poet of precise looking: his lines favour clarity over Celtic mist, wit over nationalist slogan. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Scottish modernism from MacDiarmid through MacCaig, Edwin Morgan, and Iain Crichton Smith, "An Ordinary Day" exemplifies how free verse conducts philosophical inquiry without abandoning accessible diction, and how the ordinary becomes extraordinary through the reflexive act of observing observation itself.The opening stanza establishes the poem's central epistemological joke:I took my mind a walk / Or my mind took me a walk: agency dissolves between perceiver and perceived, walker and walked. Whichever was the truth of it suspends judgment with conversational shrug, MacCaig's signature refusal of metaphysical certainty dressed as plain speech. Light glittered on the water / Or the water glittered in the light: chiasmus repeats the ambiguity at grammatical level. Is consciousness active or passive?
